15.tq: Match each element to its concept.
n: Inclusive growth requires education. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Education improves capabilities. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Inclusive growth requires health. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Health improves human capital. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Inclusive growth requires access to credit. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Access to credit enables productive activity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]
Inclusive growth provides shared economic benefits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 101-102]

16.s: The Human Development Report primarily compares countries with reference to
o: Environment, defence expenditure and literacy alone
16.x: The report compares countries on education, health and per-capita income as the principal dimensions of human development.
16.tq: Identify the three broad dimensions rather than a related development indicator.
xs: The Human Development Report compares countries on **education, health and per-capita income** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
These match the three HDI dimensions: **long and healthy life**, **education** and **decent standard of living**.
Exports, fiscal deficit, defence spending or tax revenue are not HDI dimensions.
xa: The HDR is published by **UNDP**; the first appeared in **1990**.
Income is measured as **GNI per capita (PPP $)**, using its **logarithm**.
HDI does not capture **inequality, poverty, human security, empowerment or environment**.

16.s: Which one of the following illustrates the role of policy choices in determining human development outcomes?
o: HDI is determined exclusively by GNI per capita
Malaysia has higher GNI per capita than Chile, but Chile has a higher HDI
Chile has higher GNI per capita and lower HDI than Malaysia
Both countries have identical life expectancy and schooling outcomes
16.x: Malaysia has higher GNI per capita, but Chile has a much higher HDI because of better life expectancy and schooling outcomes.
16.tq: Compare the income ranking with the HDI ranking instead of assuming that income alone determines development.
xs: **Malaysia has higher GNI per capita than Chile, but Chile has a higher HDI** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Chile has about **7 years** more life expectancy and **3 more years** of expected schooling, lifting its HDI.
Same income, different HDI shows the role of **national policy choices** (APPSC-G1 2024); HDI is not determined by GNI alone.
xa: Core idea: **GNI cannot replace HDI** — income is a **means, not the end**.
HDI = **geometric mean** of health, education and income indices, so a weak dimension is not offset by a strong one.
Life expectancy goalposts are **20–85 years**; expected schooling **0–18 years**.

16.s: Which of the following statements is correct regarding income and HDI?
o: GNI is a means of development, whereas HDI captures broader human development outcomes
GNI can completely replace HDI because income is the end of development
HDI ignores all non-income dimensions of development
Countries with higher GNI per capita must always have higher HDI
16.x: Income is a means rather than the end of development, and HDI incorporates health and education along with income.
16.tq: Reject absolute claims and select the option that preserves the distinction between income and human outcomes.
xs: **GNI is a means of development, whereas HDI captures broader human development outcomes** — so option **(1)** is correct.
GNI **cannot replace** HDI, because income is not the end of development.
HDI explicitly includes the non-income dimensions **health** and **education**; higher GNI need not mean higher HDI (Malaysia vs **Chile**).
xa: HDI uses **GNI**, not GDP, per capita — a change brought in by the **2010** revision.
Income enters as a **logarithm**, reflecting **diminishing returns** to income.
Chile has about **7 years** more life expectancy than Malaysia despite lower GNI per capita.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the capability approach:
1. Development is viewed as the expansion of real freedoms.
2. Martha Nussbaum extended the approach by presenting a list of central human capabilities.
3. The approach treats income as the final objective of development.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because income is a means to development, not its ultimate end.
16.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the means-and-end distinction in human development.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the capability approach sees development as **expanding real freedoms** (Amartya Sen, **Development as Freedom**).
Statement 2 is correct: **Martha Nussbaum** extended it with a list of **central human capabilities**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **income is a means, not the end** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: **Mahbub ul Haq** conceived the HDI with **Amartya Sen**; **Inge Kaul** was also on the team.
Nussbaum's work is titled **Women and Human Development**.
The ultimate criteria of development are **people and their capabilities**.

16.s: Which one of the following is NOT a component indicator of the Human Development Index?
o: GNI per capita in PPP dollars
16.x: Environmental quality is not included in the HDI. The index uses life expectancy, schooling indicators and GNI per capita.
16.tq: Find the excluded environmental indicator among the three HDI dimensions.
xs: **Environmental quality** is not an HDI indicator — so option **(3)** is correct.
HDI indicators are **life expectancy at birth**, **expected** and **mean years of schooling**, and **GNI per capita (PPP $)**.
HDI ignores **environment** — hence the **Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI)** introduced in **2020**.
xa: PHDI adjusts HDI for **CO2 emissions and material footprint**.
HDI also leaves out **inequality, poverty, human security, empowerment and participation**.
Income uses the **logarithm** of GNI per capita, goalposts **$100–$75,000**.

16.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding HDI goalposts:

List-I (Indicator)
a. Life expectancy
b. Expected years of schooling
c. Mean years of schooling
d. GNI per capita

List-II (Minimum–Maximum)
i. 0–18 years
ii. 100–75,000 PPP dollars
iii. 20–85 years
iv. 0–15 years

Select the correct answer using the code below.
16.x: The goalposts are 20–85 years for life expectancy, 0–18 for expected schooling, 0–15 for mean schooling and 100–75,000 PPP dollars for GNI per capita.
16.tq: Start with the distinctive GNI range and then eliminate codes using the schooling ranges.
xs: Correct goalposts: life expectancy **20–85 years**, expected schooling **0–18**, mean schooling **0–15**, GNI per capita **$100–$75,000** — so option **(1) a–iii, b–i, c–iv, d–ii** is correct.
Dimension index = **(actual − min)/(max − min)**.
xa: ⚠ Expected schooling max is **18**; mean schooling max is **15** — a common trap.
GNI per capita is in **2011 PPP $** and enters as a **logarithm**.
Education index = **arithmetic mean** of the two schooling sub-indices.

16.s: The education index in the HDI is obtained by taking the:
o: Geometric mean of life expectancy and income indices
Simple ratio of expected years to mean years of schooling
Arithmetic mean of the expected-years and mean-years schooling sub-indices
Weighted mean of GNI and schooling indices
16.x: The education index is the arithmetic mean of the indices for expected years of schooling and mean years of schooling.
16.tq: Identify the specific aggregation method used within the education dimension.
xs: The education index is the **arithmetic mean** of the **expected-years** and **mean-years** schooling sub-indices — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **geometric mean** is used for the overall HDI, not the education index.
No ratio of expected to mean years, and no GNI weighting, is involved.
xa: ⚠ Education index = **arithmetic** mean; HDI = **geometric** mean.
Goalposts: expected schooling **0–18**, mean schooling **0–15**.
Both schooling indicators came in with the **2010** revision, along with **GNI**.

16.s: Why is the logarithm of GNI per capita used in calculating the income index of the HDI?
o: To convert GNI into life expectancy
To give income a zero weight
To reflect diminishing returns to income
16.x: The logarithm captures diminishing returns: an additional unit of income contributes less to human development at higher income levels.
16.tq: Link the mathematical transformation with its economic rationale rather than treating it as a unit conversion.
xs: The **logarithm** of GNI per capita is used to reflect **diminishing returns** to income — so option **(4)** is correct.
Each extra dollar matters less for human development at higher incomes — **diminishing importance of income**.
Purchasing-power differences are handled by **PPP dollars**, not by the logarithm.
xa: Income goalposts: **$100** minimum, **$75,000** maximum (**2011 PPP $**).
HDI uses **GNI**, not GDP, per capita since the **2010** revision.
Indicator for **decent standard of living** = GNI per capita (PPP $).

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the HDI:
1. It is the geometric mean of the three dimension indices.
2. The geometric-mean method was introduced in 2010.
3. Under this method, a strong dimension can fully offset a weak dimension.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the geometric mean prevents a strong dimension from fully offsetting a weak one.
16.tq: Test the effect of geometric aggregation by rejecting the reversed implication about offsetting weaknesses.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: HDI is the **geometric mean** of the three normalised dimension indices.
Statement 2 is correct: the geometric-mean method came in **2010**.
Statement 3 is wrong: with a geometric mean a **weak dimension is not offset** by a strong one — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: ⚠ Education index uses the **arithmetic** mean of its two sub-indices.
Worked example: **Georgia 0.769 = High** human development.
The **2010** revision also brought in **GNI** and the two schooling indicators.

16.s: If the actual value of an HDI indicator is 50, with a minimum goalpost of 20 and a maximum goalpost of 80, the dimension index will be:
16.x: The dimension index is calculated as (actual value − minimum value)/(maximum value − minimum value), which is (50−20)/(80−20) = 0.50.
16.tq: Apply the normalized-index formula rather than recalling the formula mechanically.
xs: Dimension index = **(actual − min)/(max − min)** = (50 − 20)/(80 − 20) = **0.50** — so option **(2)** is correct.
0.40, 0.60 and 0.75 come from using the wrong numerator or denominator.
xa: Real life-expectancy goalposts are **20** and **85** years.
Education index = **arithmetic mean** of the two schooling indices; HDI = **geometric mean** of the three dimensions.
Worked example: **Georgia 0.769 = High** category.

16.s: Which one of the following is NOT captured by the HDI, although it is related to human development?
16.x: HDI does not capture human security. It also does not directly capture inequality, poverty, empowerment, participation or the environment.
16.tq: Separate the core index indicators from wider human-development concerns.
xs: **Human security** is not captured by the HDI — so option **(4)** is correct.
**GNI per capita**, **life expectancy** and **expected years of schooling** are all HDI indicators.
HDI also omits **inequality, poverty, empowerment, participation and environment**.
xa: HDI is criticised for ignoring **inequality, sustainability and gender** — hence **IHDI, GDI, GII and MPI**.
**MPI** (**2010**) measures **overlapping deprivations**.
**PHDI** (**2020**) adjusts HDI for **CO2 emissions and material footprint**.

16.s: Which statement about the Human Poverty Index is correct?
o: HPI-1 applied to developing countries and HPI-2 to developed countries
HPI was introduced in 1995 and measures only income poverty
HPI measures only gender disparities in HDI
16.x: HPI-1 was designed for developing countries and HPI-2 for developed countries. The HPI was later replaced by MPI in 2010.
16.tq: Distinguish the two HPI variants by country group and avoid reversing the replacement sequence.
xs: **HPI-1** applied to **developing** countries and **HPI-2** to **developed** countries — so option **(1)** is correct.
HPI was introduced in **1997** (not 1995) and measured deprivation in HDI dimensions, not only income.
It was **replaced by the MPI in 2010** — not the other way round.
xa: The **MPI** measures **overlapping deprivations**.
**1995** is the year of the **GDI** (ratio of female to male HDI).
**Capability Poverty Measure** (**1996**) measured lack of basic capabilities.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index:
1. IHDI was introduced in 2010.
2. It discounts HDI for inequality.
3. IHDI is lower than HDI whenever inequality exists.
4. The difference between HDI and IHDI represents the loss due to inequality.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: All four statements are correct. IHDI adjusts potential human development for inequality and the gap from HDI indicates the loss due to inequality.
16.tq: Check each defining property of the index, including the interpretation of the HDI–IHDI gap.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **IHDI** was introduced in **2010**.
Statement 2 correct: it is HDI **discounted for inequality**.
Statements 3 and 4 correct: **IHDI < HDI** whenever inequality exists, and the gap is the **loss** — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
xa: With no inequality, **HDI = IHDI**.
HDI = **"potential"** human development; IHDI = **"actual"** human development.
**GII** and **MPI** also came in **2010**.

16.s: The Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI adjusts HDI for:
16.x: PHDI, introduced in 2020, adjusts HDI for planetary pressures represented by carbon dioxide emissions and material footprint.
16.tq: Match the environmental adjustment with the index carrying the planetary-pressures label.
xs: The **Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI)** adjusts HDI for **CO2 emissions and material footprint** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was introduced in **2020**.
Gender inequality belongs to the **GII**, which covers reproductive health, empowerment and labour market.
xa: HDI by itself does not cover **environment** or sustainability.
**IHDI** discounts HDI for inequality; **GDI** is the female-to-male HDI ratio.
**MPI** (**2010**) measures overlapping deprivations.

16.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: GII — reproductive health, empowerment and labour market
PHDI — adjustment for CO2 emissions and material footprint
IHDI — ratio of female HDI to male HDI
16.x: The ratio of female to male HDI is the GDI. IHDI is HDI discounted for inequality.
16.tq: Find the swapped definition by distinguishing the closely related gender and inequality indices.
xs: **IHDI — ratio of female HDI to male HDI** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **ratio of female to male HDI** is the **GDI**; IHDI is HDI **discounted for inequality**.
GII (reproductive health, empowerment, labour market), PHDI (CO2, material footprint) and MPI (overlapping deprivations) are correctly matched.
xa: **IHDI < HDI** whenever inequality exists; the gap is the loss.
**PHDI** was introduced in **2020**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's position in HDR 2025:
1. Sri Lanka ranked higher than India.
2. Maldives ranked higher than India.
3. India was the lowest-ranked among the five original BRICS countries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: All three statements are correct. Sri Lanka and Maldives ranked above India, and Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa all ranked above India among the original BRICS members.
16.tq: Combine neighbour comparison with the BRICS comparison instead of treating them separately.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 correct: **Sri Lanka** and **Maldives** performed better than India in **HDR 2025**.
Statement 3 correct: India is **lowest among the five original BRICS** (Brazil, Russia, China, South Africa above) — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: India's HDI value **0.685** puts it in the **Medium** category.
Comparative: India **149th** by nominal GDP per capita and **119th** by PPP in **2026**.

16.s: India's HDI value of 0.685 in HDR 2025 places it in which category?
16.x: An HDI value from 0.550 to 0.699 falls in the medium human development category. India's 0.685 is just below the high-category threshold of 0.700.
16.tq: Apply the category threshold to the given numerical value.
xs: India's **0.685** falls in **Medium human development** (**0.550–0.699**) — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
It is just below the **0.700** threshold for **High**.
xa: ⚠ Older notes loosely say "Medium/High" — the correct answer is **Medium**.
Sub-national dataset gives a national average of **0.732** — use **0.685** for UNDP questions.
**Bihar** is the lowest state at **0.650**.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly gives the HDI category thresholds?
o: Very high: 0.900 and above; High: 0.800–0.899; Medium: 0.600–0.799; Low: below 0.600
Very high: 0.750 and above; High: 0.650–0.749; Medium: 0.500–0.649; Low: below 0.500
Very high: 0.850 and above; High: 0.700–0.849; Medium: 0.500–0.699; Low: below 0.500
Very high: 0.800 and above; High: 0.700–0.799; Medium: 0.550–0.699; Low: below 0.550
16.x: The categories are very high at 0.800 and above, high at 0.700–0.799, medium at 0.550–0.699, and low below 0.550.
16.tq: Compare all four thresholds carefully, especially the boundary values.
xs: Thresholds: **Very high 0.800 and above; High 0.700–0.799; Medium 0.550–0.699; Low below 0.550** — so option **(4)** is correct.
India's **0.685** is therefore **Medium**.
xa: Worked example: **Georgia 0.769 = High**.
**Goa** and **Kerala** are above **0.86** in the state series.
**Assam 0.699** (24th of 29), **West Bengal 0.719**.

16.s: According to the Human Development Report 2023–24, based on HDI values for 2022, India was ranked:
16.x: India was ranked 134th among 193 countries in the HDR 2023–24, based on HDI values for 2022.
16.tq: Distinguish the report edition, reference year and total number of countries before selecting the rank.
xs: In **HDR 2023-24** (HDI values for **2022**), India ranked **134th out of 193 countries** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC 2024 key).
**124th**, **130th** and **139th** are distractors; the key figure is **134th**.
xa: India's HDI value **0.685** = **Medium** category.
In **HDR 2025**, **Sri Lanka** and **Maldives** were above India.
India is lowest among the five original **BRICS**.

16.s: The ‘Kerala Model’ in the context of State human development refers to Kerala’s position as
o: The State with the highest income inequality alone
The State with the lowest HDI in India
The first State to publish a Human Development Report
A consistently top-performing State in human development
16.x: Kerala consistently tops Indian States in human development and is commonly associated with the Kerala Model.
16.tq: Distinguish a broad development model from the separate state-report milestone.
xs: **Kerala** consistently **tops** Indian states in human development — the **"Kerala Model"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The first state HDR was **Madhya Pradesh** (**1995**), not Kerala; the lowest states are **Bihar, UP, MP**.
xa: **Goa and Kerala** are above **0.86**; Kerala is **2nd** in the state series.
Kerala is moving to **extreme-poverty-free** status.
**Bihar** is lowest at **0.650**.

16.s: Which group of States is identified as occupying the lowest end of the State human-development ranking?
o: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh
West Bengal, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu
16.x: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh are identified among the lowest-ranking States in human development.
16.tq: Recall the low-performing group rather than the consistently high-performing States.
xs: **Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh** are at the lowest end of state HDI — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Bihar** is lowest at **0.650** vs India's **0.685** (**2023**).
**Kerala** and **Goa** are at the top, above **0.86**.
xa: **Assam 0.699** (24th of 29); **West Bengal 0.719**.
Sub-national national average: **0.732** (2023).
⚠ **0.685** = UNDP India value; **0.732** = sub-national average.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the National Human Development Report with its year?
16.x: The first NHDR was published in 2001 and the second, titled India Human Development Report, was published in 2011.
16.tq: Match successive editions with their years and reject the state-report date.
xs: The **first NHDR** came in **2001** and the **second** in **2011** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The second was the **India Human Development Report** (Planning Commission/**IAMR**).
**1995** is the first **state** HDR (Madhya Pradesh); **1990** is the first global HDR.
xa: The first NHDR was published by the **Planning Commission**.
District-level HDIs are prepared by **NITI Aayog** and state planning bodies.

16.s: The first State Human Development Report in India was prepared by:
16.x: Madhya Pradesh had the distinction of producing the first State Human Development Report in 1995.
16.tq: Distinguish the first state-level report from the first national report.
xs: **Madhya Pradesh** prepared India's **first State HDR** in **1995** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**2001** is the first **NHDR**; **2011** the second NHDR; **1990** the first global HDR by UNDP.
xa: **Kerala** consistently tops state HDI ("Kerala Model").
**Bihar** is lowest at **0.650**.
⚠ **1995** is also the year the **GDI** was introduced in the HDR.

16.s: Which district had the lowest multidimensional-poverty headcount ratio among the Andhra Pradesh districts listed?
16.x: West Godavari had the lowest listed headcount ratio at 2.42 per cent and an MPI of 0.010.
16.tq: Identify the minimum value before comparing the district options.
xs: **West Godavari** has the lowest MPI headcount at **2.42%** (MPI **0.010**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
The others are higher: **Guntur 4.36%**, **Krishna 4.38%**, **Chittoor 5.66%** (2024-25).
xa: AP overall headcount **6.06%** vs India **14.96%**.
AP ranks **9th** among States.

16.s: Which of the following correctly describes Andhra Pradesh's multidimensional poverty position as reported for 2024-25?
o: MPI 0.16 and headcount ratio 14.96%, above the national average
MPI 0.103 and headcount ratio 10.30%, equal to the national ratio
MPI 0.025 and headcount ratio 6.06%, below half the national headcount ratio of 14.96%
MPI 0.002 and headcount ratio 0.60%, below Kerala's MPI value
16.x: Andhra Pradesh's MPI was reported at 0.025 and its headcount ratio at 6.06%, which was under half the national headcount ratio of 14.96%. The improvement was credited to DBT and welfare delivery.
16.tq: Match the State with both its MPI value and headcount ratio; distractors mix figures belonging to other States or measures.
xs: AP: **MPI 0.025** and **headcount ratio 6.06%**, **below half** the national **14.96%** — so option **(3)** is correct.
India's MPI is **0.066**; AP's improvement is credited to **DBT** and welfare delivery.
xa: Rural headcount: AP **7.71%** vs India **19.28%**; urban AP **2.20%** vs India **5.27%**.
Intensity: AP **41.12%** vs India **44.39%**.
Data source: **NITI MPI 2023**, **NFHS-5**.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the income-poverty percentages for Andhra Pradesh and India in 2011–12?
16.x: In 2011–12, income poverty was 9.20% in Andhra Pradesh and 21.92% for India.
16.tq: Match each percentage with the correct State or national figure and avoid reversing the comparison.
xs: Income poverty in **2011-12** (Planning Commission): **AP 9.20%**, **India 21.92%** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**6.06%** and **14.96%** are the MPI headcount ratios of AP and India, not income poverty.
xa: AP income poverty: rural **10.96%**, urban **5.81%**.
The government now leans on **MPI** over income poverty lines.
RBI Rangarajan-line update: rural poverty lowest in **Himachal (0.4%)**, highest in **Chhattisgarh (25.1%)**.

16.s: Which of the following correctly matches an instrument of inclusive growth with its principal contribution?
o: Self-Help Groups — women's credit and livelihood support
Financial inclusion — exclusion of small borrowers from formal finance
DBT — replacement of welfare transfers by export subsidies
16.x: Self-Help Groups support women's credit and livelihoods. MSMEs are associated with labour-intensive jobs, while financial inclusion and DBT broaden access and delivery.
16.tq: Match each instrument with its stated inclusive-growth function and reject reversed effects.
xs: **Self-Help Groups** provide **women's credit and livelihood** support — so option **(1)** is correct.
**MSMEs** create **labour-intensive jobs** (not reduce them); financial inclusion widens access, and **DBT** delivers welfare.
xa: Three pillars of inclusive growth: **Market economics, Empowerment and Pragmatism**.
**Eleventh Plan (2007-12)** theme: "**Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth**".

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding inclusive growth in India:
1. Its three pillars are Market Economics, Empowerment and Pragmatism.
2. The Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12) carried the theme 'Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Both are correct. The three pillars (APPSC 2025 key) are Market Economics, Empowerment and Pragmatism - not 'Antyodaya, Empowerment, Poverty and Unemployment'. The Eleventh Plan, the first to make inclusive growth its objective, was titled 'Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth'. Hence neither '1 only' nor '2 only' nor 'Neither'.
16.tq: Pillars: Market, Empowerment, Pragmatism; 11th Plan theme.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the three pillars of inclusive growth are **Market economics, Empowerment and Pragmatism** (APPSC 2025).
Statement 2 correct: the **Eleventh Plan (2007-12)** theme was "**Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth**" — so option **(3) Both 1 and 2** is correct.
xa: Instruments: **SHGs** (women's credit), **MSMEs** (labour-intensive jobs), financial inclusion, **DBT**.
RBI FI-Index rose to **67.0** in 2025 from **53.9** in 2021.
Gini fell from **36.8** to **32.1**.

16.s: Which of the following best describes human capital formation?
o: Transfer of all public resources from agriculture to services
Investment in education, health, skills, migration and information that raises people's productive capacity
Accumulation of foreign exchange reserves through international trade
Investment in physical infrastructure alone to increase industrial output
16.x: Human capital formation includes investment in education, health, skills acquired through on-the-job training, migration and information, all of which enhance people's productive capacity.
16.tq: Identify the option that combines the complete components of the concept rather than a narrow definition.
xs: Human capital formation is **investment in education, health, skills, migration and information** that raises people's **productive capacity** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Physical infrastructure or forex reserves are not human capital.
xa: Skills include **on-the-job training**.
Returns: **higher productivity and earnings**, faster growth, **lower poverty**.
Poverty **35.1%** (no formal education) vs **14.9%** (post-secondary).

16.s: According to the updated Rangarajan poverty estimates based on HCES 2022-23, which of the following is correctly matched?
16.x: Rural poverty was lowest in Himachal Pradesh at 0.4% and highest in Chhattisgarh at 25.1%; urban poverty was lowest in Tamil Nadu at 1.9%.
16.tq: Check both the location and direction of each poverty comparison to catch reversed labels.
xs: **Lowest urban poverty — Tamil Nadu, 1.9%** is correctly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
Rural poverty was lowest in **Himachal (0.4%)**, not Chhattisgarh, and highest in **Chhattisgarh (25.1%)**, not Himachal — so options (1) and (2) swap the states.
**Tamil Nadu 1.9%** is the lowest, not the highest, urban figure.
xa: These come from the **RBI's update of the Rangarajan line** on **HCES 2022-23** (Oct 2025).
The government now leans on **MPI** over income poverty lines.
Planning Commission **2011-12**: AP income poverty **9.20%** vs India **21.92%**.

16.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the emerging policy preference regarding poverty measurement?
o: The Government has abandoned all multidimensional measures in favour of nominal GDP.
The Government now leans on MPI over income poverty lines.
The Government treats HDI as a complete substitute for all poverty measures.
The Government uses only the urban poverty ratio for policy decisions.
16.x: The policy discussion indicates that the Government now leans on the Multidimensional Poverty Index rather than relying only on income poverty lines.
16.tq: Choose the precise policy-direction statement and reject absolute claims such as only or all.
xs: **The Government now leans on MPI over income poverty lines** — so option **(2)** is correct.
MPI captures **overlapping deprivations**, which income lines miss; HDI is not a substitute for poverty measures.
xa: AP's MPI **halved** — from **0.053** to **0.025**.
AP headcount ratio **6.06%** is under half India's **14.96%**.
RBI's Rangarajan update: rural poverty highest in **Chhattisgarh (25.1%)**.

16.s: Which State is noted as moving to extreme-poverty-free status?
16.x: Kerala is moving to extreme-poverty-free status, a current development in poverty debates.
16.tq: Kerala: first in elderly welfare, now extreme-poverty-free.
xs: **Kerala** is moving to **extreme-poverty-free** status — so option **(4)** is correct.
Kerala also **consistently tops** state HDI (the **"Kerala Model"**).
xa: **Goa and Kerala** are above **0.86** in the state HDI series.
**Himachal** has the lowest rural poverty (**0.4%**); **Tamil Nadu** the lowest urban (**1.9%**).
**Bihar** is lowest on HDI at **0.650**.

16.s:
Assertion (A): The human development approach is broader than a primarily economic measure.
Reason (R): It focuses on people, opportunities and choices.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true: the human development approach is broader than an economic measure because it looks at people, their opportunities and their choices, not just output. R explains A.
16.tq: Ask whether the focus explains the breadth.
n: The human development approach focuses on people, opportunities, and choices. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
GDP or per-capita income is primarily an economic measure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
Human development is a broader, people-centred approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

16.s:
Assertion (A): Amartya Sen’s capability approach forms the intellectual foundation of human development.
Reason (R): The human development approach focuses on capabilities and well-being.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true: Sen's capability approach is the foundation of human development, and the approach focuses on capabilities and well-being. That the approach shares Sen's focus does not show it was built on his work, so R does not explain A.
16.tq: Ask whether a shared focus proves the origin.
n: Amartya Sen provided the intellectual foundation through the capability approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
Human development focuses on capabilities and well-being. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: MPI measures multidimensional poverty.
Statement B: MPI is published by UNDP alone.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
16.x: A is true and B is false: the MPI measures multidimensional poverty, but it is produced by OPHI and UNDP together, not UNDP alone.
16.tq: Watch for 'alone'.
n: The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measures multidimensional poverty. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The MPI is associated with OPHI and UNDP. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mahbub-ul-Haq developed the human development approach.
II. Amartya Sen’s capability approach provided its intellectual foundation.
III. The first Human Development Report was published in 1990.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: All three are correct: Mahbub-ul-Haq built the human development approach on Amartya Sen's capability approach, and the first Human Development Report came out in 1990.
16.tq: Recall the origins of the HDR.
n: Mahbub-ul-Haq developed the human development approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
Amartya Sen provided the intellectual foundation through the capability approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The first Human Development Report was published in 1990. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

(a) Mahbub-ul-Haq
(b) Amartya Sen
(c) UNDP
(d) OPHI + UNDP

16.tq: Match each name to its contribution.
n: Mahbub-ul-Haq developed the human development approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
Amartya Sen provided the intellectual foundation through the capability approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

(a) GDP
(b) Human development
(c) HDI
(d) MPI

List-II
(i) Measures human development
(ii) Measures multidimensional poverty
(iii) Primarily economic measure

n: GDP or per-capita income is primarily an economic measure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
Human development is a broader, people-centred approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The Human Development Index (HDI) measures human development. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measures multidimensional poverty. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) First Human Development Report
(b) First inclusion of MPI in HDR
(c) Human Development Report publisher
(d) MPI purpose

List-II
(i) 2010
(ii) UNDP

16.x: The first HDR came out in 1990, the MPI was first included in the 2010 HDR, the UNDP publishes the HDR, and the MPI measures multidimensional poverty. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
16.tq: Discriminate 1990 from 2010.
n: The first Human Development Report was published in 1990. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) publishes the Human Development Report. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measures multidimensional poverty. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The MPI was first included in the Human Development Report in 2010. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. HDI measures human development.
II. MPI measures multidimensional poverty.
III. Both HDI and MPI are described with health, education and living-standard dimensions.
IV. HDI is a primarily economic measure.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: I, II and III are correct: the HDI measures human development, the MPI multidimensional poverty, and both use health, education and living standards. IV is false because GDP is the mainly economic measure.
16.tq: Discriminate HDI from GDP.
n: GDP or per-capita income is primarily an economic measure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The Human Development Index (HDI) measures human development. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measures multidimensional poverty. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The HDI considers health, education, and standard of living. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]
The MPI considers health, education, and living standards. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 100-101]

17.s: The Human Poverty Index introduced in the Human Development Report 1997 primarily measured deprivation in
o: longevity, knowledge and a decent standard of living
gender parity, inflation and literacy alone
17.x: The HPI measured deprivation in longevity, knowledge and a decent standard of living. It was developed to complement the HDI.
17.tq: Direct concept recall using the three component areas.
xs: The **Human Poverty Index** measured deprivation in **longevity, knowledge and a decent standard of living** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was introduced in **HDR 1997** and developed by the UN to **complement the HDI**.
xa: HPI was **replaced by the MPI** in **HDR 2010**.
HPI **indicates the standard of living** (APPSC-GS 2018 key).
⚠ Sequence: **1995 GDI/GEM – 1996 CPM – 1997 HPI – 2010 MPI/GII/IHDI**.

17.s: Which pair of indices was introduced as an earlier companion to the Human Poverty Index in the Human Development Report 1995?
17.x: The Gender-related Development Index and Gender Empowerment Measure were both introduced in the HDR 1995 as earlier companion indices.
17.tq: Pair the indices with their common introduction period.
xs: The **Gender-related Development Index (GDI)** and **Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM)** came in **HDR 1995** as earlier companions of the HPI — so option **(1)** is correct.
**GII, MPI and IHDI** all came in **2010**; the **CPM** in **1996**.
xa: **GII** was introduced to address the **GDI's shortcomings**.
A **GDI of 1 = gender parity**; countries go into **5 groups** by distance from parity.

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT an indicator of the Capability Poverty Measure?
o: Births unattended by trained health personnel
Children under five who are underweight
17.x: Male labour-force participation is not a CPM indicator. The CPM uses child underweight, unattended births and female illiteracy.
17.tq: Find the indicator outside the three-item CPM set.
xs: **Male labour-force participation** is not a CPM indicator — so option **(2)** is correct.
CPM's three indicators are **underweight children under 5**, **births unattended by trained health personnel** and **female illiteracy**.
Female and male labour force participation belongs to the **GII's labour-market** dimension.
xa: CPM was introduced in **HDR 1996**.
**BPSC 2025 key**: child malnutrition + female illiteracy both included.
HPI (**1997**) measured deprivation in longevity, knowledge and standard of living.

17.s: When inequality exists, the relationship between HDI and IHDI is correctly expressed as
o: IHDI is always higher than HDI
IHDI is equal to HDI in every country
HDI is calculated by subtracting IHDI from zero
17.x: When inequality exists, the IHDI is lower than the HDI because it discounts achievement for unequal distribution.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about the Gender Inequality Index (GII):

Statement 3 is wrong: a value of 1 meaning parity describes the GDI (ratio of female to male HDI), not the GII. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses statement 2, and the other two include statement 3.
17.tq: GDI 1 = parity; GII higher = worse.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the **GII** came in **HDR 2010** to address the **GDI's shortcomings**.
Statement 2 correct: **higher GII = greater inequality**.
Statement 3 wrong: a value of **1 = gender parity** describes the **GDI** — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: GII dimensions: **reproductive health, empowerment, labour market**.
GII is built on the **IHDI framework**.
GDI groups countries into **5 groups** by distance from parity.

17.s: The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index is associated with which institutions?

MPI = **headcount ratio × intensity** of poverty.
xa: National MPI has **3 equally weighted dimensions** and **12** indicators.

Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen

xa: MPI = **headcount ratio × intensity**.

17.s: Which of the following is the correct classification of the indicators under the Global MPI?
o: Health—nutrition and child mortality; Education—years of schooling and school attendance; Living standards—six indicators including cooking fuel and sanitation

17.x: The Global MPI covers nutrition and child mortality under health; years of schooling and school attendance under education; and cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing and assets under living standards.

xs: Health = **nutrition, child mortality**; Education = **years of schooling, school attendance**; Living standards = six indicators incl. **cooking fuel and sanitation** — so option **(1)** is correct.

17.s: Under the Alkire-Foster method used for the Multidimensional Poverty Index, the MPI value is obtained as:
o: Headcount ratio multiplied by the intensity of poverty
Headcount ratio plus the intensity of poverty
Geometric mean of three normalised dimension indices
Share of population living below one dollar a day
17.x: MPI = headcount ratio (H) x intensity (A), which is why values are small (e.g. India 0.066). Adding the two is wrong; the geometric mean of dimension indices is how the HDI is computed; and the MPI is not a $1-a-day income measure (the UPPSC 2025 trap).
17.tq: MPI = H x A.
xs: Under **Alkire-Foster**, MPI = **headcount ratio multiplied by the intensity of poverty** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **geometric mean** of three dimension indices is the HDI's formula; MPI is not a $1-a-day measure.
xa: This product explains small values like **0.069** (exam traps 0.690, 0.096).
National MPI 2023: headcount **14.96%** × intensity **44.39%** → MPI **0.066**.
MPI-poor = deprived in at least **one-third** of weighted indicators.

**0.061** is the **Global MPI 2025** value.

**414 million** moved out of poverty from 2005-06.

18.x: The report functioned as a ready reckoner for foreign investors by comparing business regulations across economies.

xs: The Doing Business report served as a ready reckoner for **foreign investors** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC 2019 key).
It compared business regulation for investment decisions — not for employees, tourists or farmers.
xa: Published by the **World Bank**; succeeded by **B-READY**.
What counts: **Single Window System**; not per-capita income, inflation, literacy.

18.s: The successor to the World Bank's Doing Business report is
18.x: B-READY is the successor to the discontinued Doing Business report.

The other names are not the successor named in the notes.

India is in the **3rd report**, expected around **Sep 2026**.
Allied index: **IMD World Competitiveness** rank **43 (2021) → 41 (2025)**.

18.s: Which one of the following was counted in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business assessment?
18.x: A Single Window System for business clearances counts towards Ease of Doing Business. Per capita income, inflation and literacy are macro or social indicators that the assessment does not count (APPSC 2019).

xs: A **Single Window System** counts in Ease of Doing Business — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC 2019).
**Per-capita income, inflation and literacy** do NOT count.
xa: Report purpose: a ready reckoner for **foreign investors**.
India lagged in **paying taxes**; **enforcing contracts 163/190**.

18.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's performance in the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) 2026:
1. India ranked 176th out of 177 countries overall.
2. India ranked 175th in the Air Quality sub-index.
3. India ranked 130th in Climate Mitigation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: All three statements are correct: India ranked 176th of 177 overall, 175th in Air Quality and 130th in Climate Mitigation in the EPI 2026.
18.tq: Check the overall rank and each sub-rank separately before selecting the complete combination.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **EPI 2026** — India **176th** of **177**.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: **Air Quality 175th**, **Climate Mitigation 130th** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: EPI 2026 has **47 indicators**.
MoEFCC **rejected the EPI methodology in 2022**.
Counter-evidence: **23rd in CCPI 2026**; **50% non-fossil** capacity in 2025.

18.s: Which of the following is a criticism concerning the use of perception surveys and absolute-emission metrics in international indices?
o: They exclude all environmental indicators from the assessment.
They systematically favour populous developing countries.
They may disadvantage populous developing countries.
They measure only the formal employment sector of an economy.
18.x: Perception surveys and absolute-emission metrics may disadvantage populous developing countries, particularly because absolute emissions can be high due to population size.
18.tq: Apply the stated criticism to identify the consequence of the measurement approach rather than recalling a rank.
xs: **Perception surveys + absolute-emission metrics disadvantage populous developing countries** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) says the opposite — they do not favour such countries.
xa: India's EPI objection: favours **absolute emissions over per-capita**.
GoI's GHI objection: undernourishment rests on an opinion poll of about **3,000** respondents.

o: The Global Financial Stability Report is published by the IMF.

18.s:
The Global Hunger Index is based on which four indicators?
1. Undernourishment
2. Child stunting
3. Child wasting
4. Child mortality
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: The four Global Hunger Index indicators are undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting and child mortality.
18.tq: Recall the complete four-part composition instead of relying on an incomplete older list.
xs: The four GHI indicators are **undernourishment**, **child stunting**, **child wasting** and **child mortality** — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
This fits India's objection that **three of the four** indicators concern **children only**; the fourth is **undernourishment**.
xa: India also objects that the **undernourishment** figure comes from a **small opinion-poll-type sample**.
The same objections apply to **FAO SOFI** indicators.
**Absorption/utilisation** (the body's ability to use food) is the dimension child stunting/wasting reflect.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the functions of the environment:

List-I (Function)
a. Supplies resources
b. Assimilates waste
c. Sustains life
d. Aesthetic services

List-II (Meaning)
i. Scenery and amenity
ii. Absorbs and neutralises wastes
iii. Genetic and biodiversity
iv. Renewable and non-renewable resources

Select the correct answer using the code below.
19.x: The environment supplies renewable and non-renewable resources, assimilates wastes, sustains genetic and biological diversity, and provides scenery and amenity.
19.tq: Start with the distinctive meanings of aesthetic services and waste assimilation, then complete the code.
xs: The environment **supplies resources** (renewable and non-renewable), **assimilates waste** (absorbs and neutralises), **sustains life** (genetic and biodiversity) and gives **aesthetic services** (scenery and amenity) — so option **(2) a–iv, b–ii, c–iii, d–i** is correct.
**Supplies resources** covers renewable (**trees, fish**) and non-renewable (**fossil fuels**) resources.
xa: The **first function** is the **supply/production of raw materials** (APPSC-GS 2023 key).
Renewable examples: **trees, fish**; non-renewable: **fossil fuels**.
Crisis arises when **extraction > regeneration** and **waste > absorptive capacity**.

19.s: The first function of the environment is the:
o: Assimilation of all pollutants without limits
Supply or production of raw materials
19.x: The first function of the environment is the supply or production of raw materials.
19.tq: Test the ordered classification directly by identifying the first function.
xs: The first function of the environment is the **supply or production of raw materials** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2023 key).
Assimilating waste is a function only **within absorptive capacity**, not "without limits".
xa: Other functions: **assimilates waste**, **sustains life**, **aesthetic services**.
Resources may be **renewable** (trees, fish) or **non-renewable** (fossil fuels).
The world is at the **threshold of an environmental crisis**.

19.s: The absorptive capacity of the environment refers to its ability to:
o: Convert all non-renewable resources into renewable resources
Prevent all human extraction of resources
Absorb degradation and process and neutralise pollutants without harm
19.x: Absorptive capacity is the ability of the environment to absorb degradation, or the maximum pollutant load an ecosystem can process and neutralise without harm.
19.tq: Use the operational definition and distinguish pollutant-processing capacity from resource production.
xs: **Absorptive capacity** is the ability to **absorb degradation** — the **maximum pollutants an ecosystem can process and neutralise without harm** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2024 key).
It does not mean producing resources or stopping extraction.
xa: Crisis: **waste > absorptive capacity** and **extraction > regeneration**.
**Resource depletion** = use **faster than regeneration**.
The environment's waste function: **absorbs and neutralises wastes**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Green Revolution:
1. HYV monoculture and chemical fertilisers contributed to a decline in soil fertility.
2. Irrigation requirements of HYV crops contributed to depletion of the water table.
3. Fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides polluted land, water and air and reduced biodiversity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: All three statements correctly describe the environmental consequences associated with HYV-based Green Revolution agriculture.
19.tq: Test the complete chain of effects rather than relying on a single familiar consequence.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **HYV monoculture + chemical fertilisers** cut **soil fertility**.
Statement 2 correct: HYV irrigation needs caused **water-table depletion**.
Statement 3 correct: **fertilisers, pesticides, herbicides** polluted land, water and air and **reduced biodiversity** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: **Urea** is about **56%** of fertiliser use; overuse degrades soil and water.
Low-carbon alternative: **green urea** (green hydrogen + captured CO2).
**Chemical-intensive farming** is a human-driven cause of degradation.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about human pressure on global land and water resources:
1. About one-third of global land has been transformed by humans.
2. More than 60% of the world's rivers have been dammed or diverted.
3. About 60% of the Earth's land is degraded.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct (about one-third of land transformed). Statement 2 is correct (60%+ of rivers dammed or diverted). Statement 3 is wrong: about 40%, not 60%, of the Earth's land is degraded; 60% is the rivers figure. So B; A omits statement 2, C and D include the wrong statement 3.
19.tq: One-third land transformed, 60%+ rivers dammed, 40% land degraded - do not swap 60 and 40.
xs: Statement 1 correct: about **one-third** of global land is **transformed** by humans.
Statement 2 correct: **60%+** of rivers are **dammed or diverted**.
Statement 3 wrong: about **40%**, not 60%, of Earth's land is **degraded** — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: India: **97.85 Mha = 29.77%** degraded (**2018-19**, ISRO-SAC Atlas).
India restored **21.76 Mha** in **2011-2020**.

19.s: Which combination is identified as the main reason for India’s low Environmental Performance Index score?
o: Urban particulate pollution and coal-based power
Rural noise pollution and tidal energy
19.x: Urban particulate pollution and coal-based power are identified as the main reasons for India’s low Environmental Performance Index score.
19.tq: Apply the ‘main reasons’ wording and avoid substituting unrelated environmental indicators.
xs: **Urban particulate pollution + coal-based power** are the main reasons for India's low **EPI** score — so option **(2)** is correct.
Forest tourism, rural noise, agricultural exports or solar power are not named as reasons.
xa: Other sector causes: **urea** overuse (**56%** of fertiliser use) degrades soil and water.
Human-driven causes include **industrial emissions** and **road and urban expansion**.
India's two threats: **poverty-induced degradation** and **pollution from affluence**.

19.s: Which of the following is NOT a human-driven cause of environmental degradation?
o: Expansion of roads and urban areas
19.x: Wildlife conservation is a conservation practice, not a human-driven cause of environmental degradation. Groundwater over-extraction, industrial emissions and urban expansion are causes.
19.tq: Find the conservation measure hidden among the listed degradation causes.
xs: **Wildlife conservation** is a conservation practice, not a cause of degradation — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2024 options).
**Road and urban expansion**, **industrial emissions** and **groundwater over-extraction** are human-driven causes.
xa: ⚠ Odd ones out: **sustainable agriculture, renewable energy production, wildlife conservation**.
Other causes: **deforestation** (APPSC-GS 2024 key), chemical-intensive farming, **dams**, **overfishing**.

19.s: Which pair correctly represents the two environmental threats faced by India?
o: Poverty-induced degradation and pollution from affluence and rapid industrial growth
Rural literacy and excessive renewable energy production
Only natural disasters and seasonal rainfall variation
19.x: India faces poverty-induced degradation as well as pollution associated with affluence and rapid industrial growth.
19.tq: Distinguish the dual-source formulation from single-cause and unrelated alternatives.
xs: India faces **poverty-induced degradation** and **pollution from affluence and rapid industrial growth** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Both coexist: degradation from **poverty** and pollution from **affluence and rapid industrial growth**.
xa: The **poor** (slums, flood-prone areas) bear most of the cost.
World Bank (**2013**): degradation costs about **5.7% of GDP**.
Main reasons for India's low EPI: **urban particulate pollution + coal-based power**.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding resource depletion:

List-I (Resource)
a. Groundwater
b. Topsoil
c. Biodiversity habitats
d. Sustainable forest managed for timber while retaining biodiversity

List-II (Associated condition)
i. Expansion of agriculture
ii. Deep bore tubewells for irrigation
iii. Brick production
iv. Not an instance of resource depletion

Select the correct answer using the code below.
19.x: Deep bore tubewells are associated with groundwater depletion, brick production with topsoil loss, and agricultural expansion with habitat loss. A sustainably managed forest retaining biodiversity is not an instance of resource depletion.
19.tq: Start from the sure resource–cause pairs and eliminate codes containing a mismatched pair.
xs: **Groundwater — deep bore tubewells**, **topsoil — brick production**, **biodiversity habitats — expansion of agriculture**, sustainable forest — **not depletion** — so option **(1) a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 match).
⚠ A forest managed sustainably for timber while keeping biodiversity is **not** depletion.
xa: **Resource depletion** = use **faster than regeneration** (APPSC-GS 2024 key).
Four-pair question key: **A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4**.

19.s: Resource depletion occurs when:
o: The rate of resource use is equal to its regeneration in every season
A forest is managed sustainably while biodiversity is retained
Resources are used faster than they can regenerate
The rate of resource use is slower than its regeneration
19.x: Resource depletion occurs when resources are used faster than their rate of regeneration. Sustainable forest management with retained biodiversity does not represent depletion.
19.tq: Translate the scenario into the rate comparison between extraction and regeneration.
xs: **Resource depletion** = resources **used faster than they can regenerate** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2024 key).
A forest managed sustainably with biodiversity retained is **not** depletion; use equal to or below regeneration is sustainable.
xa: Groundwater depletion: **deep bore tubewells**; topsoil: **brick production**.
Crisis: **extraction > regeneration** + **waste > absorptive capacity**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about land restoration in India during 2011-2020:
1. About 21.76 million hectares were restored.
2. Andhra Pradesh restored the largest area, while Telangana was among the top five States.
3. The restored area is about 84% of the target of 26 million hectares by 2030.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct: 21.76 Mha were restored in 2011-2020. Statement 2 is wrong: Telangana was first (4.18 Mha) and Andhra Pradesh was among the top five. Statement 3 is correct: 21.76 Mha is about 84% of the 26 Mha by 2030 target. So C; A omits 3, B and D include the wrong statement 2.
19.tq: Telangana first, AP top five; 21.76 of 26 Mha = 84%.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **21.76 Mha** restored in **2011-2020**.
Statement 2 wrong: **Telangana** was first (**4.18 Mha**); **AP** was among the top five.
Statement 3 correct: it is **84%** of the **26 Mha by 2030** target — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Restoration stored **461.14** Mt carbon and beat the original **Bonn** pledge.
Target linked to **UNCCD COP17**.

19.s: The trade-off view regarding growth and environmental protection is represented by the argument that:
o: Environmental protection is always costless in the short term
Economic growth and environmental protection can never conflict under any circumstances
Environmental rules may slow growth and countries should grow first and clean up later
19.x: The trade-off view argues that environmental rules can slow growth and reflects the ‘grow first, clean up later’ approach associated with Environmental Kuznets Curve logic.
19.tq: Recognise the characteristic slogan of the trade-off position.
xs: The **trade-off view**: environmental rules **slow growth** — "**grow first, clean up later**" (EKC logic) — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **necessity view** instead says degradation raises **health costs** and lowers **labour efficiency**.
xa: Protection is an **investment for long-term prosperity**.
The **poor** bear most of the cost.
World Bank (**2013**): cost ≈ **5.7% of GDP**.

19.s: Which groups are stated to bear most of the costs of environmental degradation?
o: Only large corporations and high-income households
People living in slums and flood-prone areas
19.x: The poor, particularly people living in slums and flood-prone areas, bear most of the costs of environmental degradation.
19.tq: Identify the distributional dimension rather than the aggregate economic argument.
xs: The **poor** — in **slums and flood-prone areas** — bear most of the cost — so option **(4)** is correct.
Costs are not borne only by corporations, forest residents or organised workers.
xa: India's twin threats include **poverty-induced degradation**.
Necessity view: degradation raises **health costs** and lowers **labour efficiency**.
Cost ≈ **5.7% of GDP** (World Bank **2013**).

19.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Environmental Impact Assessment in India:
1. It was first used in 1978 for river valley projects.
2. The EIA Notification was issued in 1994 and revised in 2006.
3. Environmental clearance is compulsory for 39 project categories.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: EIA was first used in 1978 for river valley projects; the notification dates are 1994 and 2006, and clearance is compulsory for 39 project categories.
19.tq: Check the dates and the numerical category count together.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **EIA** first used in **1978** for **river valley projects**.
Statement 2 correct: **EIA Notification 1994**, revised **2006**.
Statement 3 correct: clearance compulsory for **39** project categories — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: **Green Credit Rules 2023** come under the **EP Act 1986**.
**Sovereign Green Bonds** are a green financing tool.

19.s: The Green Credit Rules, 2023 were framed under which legislation?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
19.x: The Green Credit Rules, 2023 were framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
19.tq: Use the ‘under the Act’ relationship and avoid confusing neighbouring environmental statutes.
xs: The **Green Credit Rules 2023** were framed under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The Forest Rights Act, Water Act and Biological Diversity Act are not its parent law.
xa: **EIA Notification**: **1994**, revised **2006**; **39** project categories need clearance.
**Sovereign Green Bonds** = green financing tool.
EIA was first used in **1978**.

19.s: According to the World Bank assessment published in 2013, India's annual cost of environmental degradation was approximately what proportion of its GDP?
19.x: B. The World Bank's 2013 assessment put India's annual cost of environmental degradation at about 5.7% of GDP (Rs 3.75 lakh crore, for 2009), through higher healthcare spending and lower labour productivity.
19.tq: Use the precise institution-year-figure combination rather than a nearby percentage.
xs: **World Bank (2013)**: degradation costs India ≈ **5.7% of GDP** a year (Rs **3.75** lakh crore, **2009**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Mechanism: **higher healthcare spending + lower labour productivity**.
xa: The World Bank also developed the **Green Index**.
The **poor** bear most of the cost.
ISRO-SAC: **29.77%** of India's area degraded.

19.s: Which one of the following best explains the mechanism through which environmental degradation imposes an economic cost on India?
o: Higher healthcare spending and lower labour productivity
Higher exports and lower public expenditure
Lower healthcare spending and higher labour productivity
Lower agricultural output and higher foreign exchange reserves
19.x: Environmental degradation raises healthcare expenditure and reduces labour productivity, creating a combined economic cost.
19.tq: Identify the cause-effect chain rather than selecting unrelated economic indicators.
xs: Degradation costs the economy through **higher healthcare spending and lower labour productivity** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses both effects.
xa: World Bank (**2013**): ≈ **5.7% of GDP**.
Necessity view: degradation raises **health costs** and lowers **labour efficiency**.
Protection = **investment for long-term prosperity**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about the Expert Group on Green National Accounts:
1. It was chaired by Sir Partha Dasgupta.
2. It was set up in 2011.
3. It submitted its report in 2013.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: The Expert Group was chaired by Sir Partha Dasgupta, set up in 2011 and reported in 2013.
19.tq: Link the chairperson with the two chronological milestones.
xs: Statement 1 correct: chaired by **Sir Partha Dasgupta**.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: set up **2011**, report **2013** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: ⚠ **NEW** = **Paul Samuelson**; **MEW** = **Nordhaus and Tobin**.
The **World Bank** developed the **Green Index**.
**MoSPI** compiles accounts on **SEEA**.

19.s: Which Indian State was the first to adopt green GDP in the form of Gross Environment Product (GEP)?
19.x: Uttarakhand was the first Indian State to adopt green GDP in the form of Gross Environment Product.
19.tq: Test the state-level first-mover fact against plausible state alternatives.
xs: **Uttarakhand** was the first state to adopt green GDP, as its **Gross Environment Product (GEP)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**GEP** is Uttarakhand's **state-level green GDP**.
xa: **Green GDP** = conventional GDP net of **natural-resource depletion** and degradation costs.
Other FIRSTs: **EIA** first used **1978**; **Telangana** first in land restoration (**4.18** Mha).
**Sir Partha Dasgupta** chaired the Expert Group on Green National Accounts.

19.s: Which of the following pairs relating to older welfare-adjusted measures is correctly matched?
o: NEW — Paul Samuelson; MEW — Nordhaus and Tobin
NEW — Nordhaus and Tobin; MEW — Paul Samuelson
NEW — Simon Kuznets; MEW — Sir Partha Dasgupta
NEW — World Bank; MEW — United Nations Statistical Commission
19.x: NEW is associated with Paul Samuelson, while MEW is associated with Nordhaus and Tobin.
19.tq: Start with the author–measure association and reject swapped names.
xs: **NEW — Paul Samuelson**; **MEW — Nordhaus and Tobin** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps them; **Partha Dasgupta** chaired the Expert Group on Green National Accounts.
xa: Both are **older welfare-adjusted measures**.
The **World Bank** developed the **Green Index**.
Expert Group: set up **2011**, report **2013**.

19.s: Green GDP is best described as:
o: Conventional GDP adjusted for resource depletion and environmental degradation
GDP excluding the contribution of the services sector
GDP adjusted only for changes in the price level
GDP calculated only from renewable-energy industries
19.x: Green GDP adjusts conventional GDP for environmental consequences, particularly resource depletion and environmental degradation.
19.tq: Distinguish environmental adjustment from sectoral or price adjustment.
xs: **Green GDP** = **conventional GDP adjusted for resource depletion and environmental degradation** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not a price-level adjustment or a services/renewables-only measure.
xa: **Uttarakhand**'s state version is the **Gross Environment Product (GEP)**.
Criticism: **GDP ignores depletion**, so growth can hide loss of natural capital.
**Partha Dasgupta** Expert Group on Green National Accounts (**2011**).

19.s: The concept of a green economy primarily focuses on
o: fostering green industries and creating green jobs
maximising GDP growth irrespective of resource use
expanding fossil-fuel subsidies to reduce poverty
19.x: A green economy fosters green industries and green jobs that preserve or restore environmental quality while decoupling development from resource use and pollution (APPSC-GS 2025 key). Growth at any cost and fossil-fuel subsidies run against it, and it does not ban industry.
19.tq: Green economy = green industries + green jobs + decoupling.
xs: A green economy focuses on **fostering green industries and creating green jobs** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
It **decouples** development from resource use, so growth at any cost or fossil-fuel subsidies run against it; it does not ban industry.
xa: **Green jobs** preserve or restore environmental quality.
It reduces **environmental risks and ecological scarcities**.

19.s: Which organisation compiles India’s environment accounts in accordance with the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)?
o: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
19.x: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation compiles environment accounts based on SEEA and has released ecosystem and natural-asset accounts since 2018.
19.tq: Ask ‘which body performs this function?’ to avoid swapping ministries and institutions.
xs: **MoSPI (Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation)** compiles environment accounts on **SEEA** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It has released ecosystem and natural-asset accounts **since 2018**.
xa: SEEA Central Framework adopted by the UN Statistical Commission in **2012**.
MoSPI also publishes **EnviStats India** (annual), based on **FDES 2013**.

19.s: The 'Green Index' used in green accounting was developed by
19.x: The Green Index was developed by the World Bank. MoSPI compiles India's SEEA-based accounts and EnviStats India; UNEP and OECD are not named as its developers.
19.tq: Green Index -> World Bank.
xs: The **Green Index** was developed by the **World Bank** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**MoSPI** compiles SEEA accounts and **EnviStats India**, not the Green Index.
xa: World Bank (**2013**) also estimated degradation cost at **5.7% of GDP**.
**NEW** = Samuelson; **MEW** = Nordhaus and Tobin.

19.s: Under the AP Common Zoning Regulations 2026, which of the following groups is identified as development-restricted?
o: Forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas and CRZ
Agricultural fields, industrial zones, towns and highways
Only coastal settlements and irrigation canals
19.x: Forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas and Coastal Regulation Zone areas are development-restricted under the regulations.
19.tq: Find the complete restricted-category list and reject options that omit or replace categories.
xs: **Forests, hills, water bodies, eco-sensitive areas and CRZ** are development-restricted — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) lists only part of the group.
xa: The regulations set **nine** land-use categories.
AP has **638** green building projects.

19.s: Why can conventional GDP growth conceal environmental degradation?
o: GDP directly deducts the depletion of natural capital from output
GDP excludes all healthcare and productivity-related expenditure
GDP ignores depletion of natural resources, allowing growth to hide the loss of natural capital
GDP measures only biodiversity and ecosystem services
19.x: Conventional GDP does not account for the depletion of natural resources; consequently, recorded growth can coexist with a loss of natural capital.
19.tq: Apply the distinction between aggregate output and natural-capital accounting.
xs: **GDP ignores depletion of natural resources**, so growth can **hide the loss of natural capital** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) is false — conventional GDP does not deduct depletion; that is what **Green GDP** does.
xa: **Green GDP** = GDP net of natural-resource depletion and degradation costs.
**Uttarakhand** adopted green GDP as **GEP**.
MoSPI's **SEEA** accounts track natural assets **since 2018**.

20.s: The decision to develop the Sustainable Development Goals was taken at which event?
20.x: The 2012 Rio+20 Conference, formally the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, took the decision to develop the SDGs.
20.tq: Distinguish the closely related Rio, Rio+10 and Rio+20 milestones.
xs: The decision to develop the SDGs was taken at **Rio+20** (UN Conference on Sustainable Development), **2012** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rio 1992** (UNCED) gave the **Rio Declaration**; **Johannesburg 2002** was the **WSSD**.
xa: **Agenda 2030** was adopted on **25 Sep 2015** in **New York**.
Roots of Agenda 2030: **MDGs** (8 goals, **2000-2015**) + the **Rio+20** outcome.
The SDGs end in **2030**.

20.s: The Brundtland Commission was chaired by:
20.x: The World Commission on Environment and Development was chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, who was the Prime Minister of Norway.
20.tq: Use the person-title and country association to identify the chairperson.
xs: The Brundtland Commission was chaired by **Gro Harlem Brundtland**, **Norway's Prime Minister** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Its formal name is the **World Commission on Environment and Development**.
xa: Its report **"Our Common Future"** (**1987**) first **defined** sustainable development.
APPSC 2025 key: popularised by the **Brundtland Commission Report 1987**, not the Rio Declaration **1992**.
Core goal: meet present needs **without reducing the options of future generations**.

20.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with a 2015 Agenda 2030 milestone?
o: Adopted on 5 June 1992 at Rio de Janeiro
Adopted on 25 September 2015 at New York
20.x: Agenda 2030 was adopted on 25 September 2015 in New York. The other dates and places do not correspond to its adoption.
20.tq: Combine the exact date and venue to defeat swapped conference details.
xs: **Agenda 2030** was adopted on **25 September 2015** in **New York** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Johannesburg** hosted the **WSSD** (**2002**); **Rio** hosted UNCED (**1992**).
xa: Decision to develop SDGs: **Rio+20**, **2012**.
The SDGs carry **169 targets** (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
Principles: **universal**, interconnected, **"leave no one behind"**.

20.s: Which commission is credited with the first formal definition of sustainable development?
o: United Nations Commission on Human Settlements
World Trade Organization Commission on Development
World Commission on Environment and Development
International Union for Conservation of Nature Commission on Climate
20.x: The World Commission on Environment and Development, popularly called the Brundtland Commission, is credited with first defining sustainable development in Our Common Future.
20.tq: Identify the institution associated with the landmark definition.
xs: The **World Commission on Environment and Development** (Brundtland Commission) first defined sustainable development — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its report was **"Our Common Future"** (**1987**).
**IUCN** (with UNEP, WWF) issued the **World Conservation Strategy** (**1980**), an early use of the term, not the definition.
xa: Chair: **Gro Harlem Brundtland**, Norway's PM.
APPSC 2025 key: first defined by the **Brundtland Report**, not Paris, Montreal or Kyoto.

20.s: The report 'Limits to Growth' was associated with:
o: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
20.x: Limits to Growth was associated with the Club of Rome and appeared in 1972.
20.tq: Match the landmark report with its originating group.
xs: **"Limits to Growth"** (**1972**) was by the **Club of Rome** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Brundtland Commission** produced **"Our Common Future"** (**1987**).
xa: Its theme: Earth's **finite carrying capacity**.
**Carrying capacity** = maximum population an environment can support **indefinitely without degradation**.
**World Conservation Strategy** (**1980**) by IUCN, UNEP, WWF.

20.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of sustainability?
20.x: The three pillars are economic growth, social inclusion or equity, and environmental protection. Military strength is not a pillar of sustainability.
20.tq: Identify the outsider against the standard three-pillar framework.
xs: **Military strength** is not a pillar of sustainability — so option **(3)** is correct.
The three pillars are **economic growth**, **social inclusion and equity**, and **environmental protection**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the odd-one-out is anything outside these three, e.g. **military strength**.
Approach: **balance all three**; do not maximise any one.
Overlaps: **socio-economic, socio-environmental, eco-environmental**.

20.s: Sustainable development requires the three pillars of sustainability to be:
o: Balanced without maximising any one pillar in isolation
Ranked with economic growth above all other considerations
20.x: Sustainable development seeks a balance among economic growth, social inclusion and environmental protection rather than maximising one pillar alone.
20.tq: Apply the balancing principle to a policy situation instead of selecting a single-pillar approach.
xs: The three pillars must be **balanced**, without **maximising any one** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Putting growth above all, or environment alone, breaks the balance.
xa: Overlaps: **socio-economic; socio-environmental; eco-environmental**.
Odd ones out of the core goal: **growth at any cost**, **profit maximisation**.
Agenda 2030 is **universal** — not only for developing countries.

20.s: The basic goal of sustainable development is to:
o: Maximise present profits regardless of future effects
Exploit all available resources before they become scarce
Meet present needs while preserving choices for future generations
Suspend economic development until environmental degradation ends
20.x: The core goal is to meet present needs without reducing the options available to future generations, within the Earth’s carrying capacity.
20.tq: Reject extreme present-only and growth-denial options and apply the intergenerational principle.
xs: The core goal: **meet present needs** while **not reducing the options of future generations** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is **intergenerational equity** within Earth's **carrying capacity**.
⚠ Odd ones out: **growth at any cost**, **exploiting resources for present gains**, **profit maximisation**.
xa: First defined in the **Brundtland Report** (**1987**).
**Intergenerational equity** was also a **Rio 1992** principle.

20.s: Carrying capacity refers to:
o: The total quantity of minerals in the Earth’s crust
The maximum population an environment can support indefinitely without degradation
The annual rate of economic growth of a country
The maximum number of industries a city can legally establish
20.x: Carrying capacity is the maximum population that an environment can support indefinitely without degradation.
20.tq: Distinguish an ecological population concept from resource stocks and economic measures.
xs: **Carrying capacity** = the **maximum population an environment can support indefinitely without degradation** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not a mineral stock, a growth rate or a legal limit on industries.
xa: Earth's **finite carrying capacity** concerned **"Limits to Growth"**, **"Our Common Future"** and **UNCED 1992**.
**Earth Overshoot Day** marks when yearly demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate.
Sustainable development = intergenerational equity **within carrying capacity**.

20.s: Earth Overshoot Day is the date on which:
o: The global temperature first exceeds a fixed legal limit
Humanity’s annual demand on nature exceeds the Earth’s regeneration capacity for that year
The Earth completes one full cycle around the Sun
All countries formally adopt their annual environmental budgets
20.x: Earth Overshoot Day marks the point when humanity’s demand on nature in a year exceeds what the Earth can regenerate during that year.
20.tq: Identify the precise demand-versus-regeneration relationship in the definition.
xs: **Earth Overshoot Day** is when **humanity's yearly demand on nature exceeds what Earth can regenerate** that year — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is computed **yearly** by the **Global Footprint Network**.
xa: It is computed by the **Global Footprint Network**, yearly.
**Plastic Overshoot Day** is an analogue.
Related idea: **carrying capacity**.

20.s: Which of the following principles was NOT endorsed at the 1992 Rio process?
20.x: The precautionary principle, polluter pays principle and common but differentiated responsibilities were endorsed at Rio 1992. Unrestricted resource exploitation is contrary to sustainable development.
20.tq: Find the policy principle that contradicts the Rio sustainability framework.
xs: **Unrestricted resource exploitation** was not a Rio principle — so option **(4)** is correct.
Rio **1992** principles: **intergenerational equity**, **precautionary principle**, **polluter pays**, **CBDR**.
