27.tq: Select the correct numerator and denominator in a demographic formula.
xs: Dependency ratio = **(0–14 years + 65 years and above) ÷ (15–64 years)** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) is the inverse; **0-14** = young-age ratio and **65+** = old-age ratio.
xa: A **lower** ratio signals a **dividend** (UPSC).
Dependency falls because **fertility fell**.
**Youth** (National Youth Policy **2014**) = **15-29**.

27.s: A lower dependency ratio generally indicates:
o: higher fertility and higher child dependency
population decline caused only by migration
a larger dependent population relative to workers
27.x: A lower dependency ratio means fewer dependants relative to the working-age population and is a favourable condition for a demographic dividend.
27.tq: Apply the meaning of a ratio to its economic implication.
xs: A lower dependency ratio signals a **potential demographic dividend** — option **(3)** is correct (UPSC).
A **larger** dependent population relative to workers means a **higher** ratio — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Without health, education, skills and jobs → **"demographic nightmare"**.

27.s: The decline in India's dependency ratio is primarily associated with:
o: an increase in the child population
27.x: The dependency ratio is falling primarily because fertility has declined, reducing the proportion of children.
27.tq: Identify the demographic cause behind a ratio trend.
xs: Dependency is falling because **fertility fell** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **child population** is shrinking (0-19 share **41%** → **25%**), not rising.
xa: TFR **below replacement** for the **fifth year running**.
Lower dependency ratio signals a **dividend**.

27.s:
Which of the following is essential for India to convert its demographic potential into a demographic dividend?
1. Better health and education
2. Skill development
3. Adequate employment opportunities
4. Deliberate reduction in female labour-force participation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
27.x: Better health, education, skills and adequate jobs are necessary to realise the dividend. Reducing female labour-force participation would undermine it.
27.tq: Find the one reversed policy condition among otherwise correct statements.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** — option **(2)** is correct.
Preconditions (ES **2018-19**): better **health, education, skills and adequate jobs**.
Item 4 is wrong: **female LFPR** actually rose from **23.3%** to **41.7%** — reducing it is no precondition.
xa: Without these → **"demographic nightmare"**.
Unemployment rate fell **5.6%** → **3.2%**.
**Youth** = **15-29** (National Youth Policy **2014**).

27.s: If the working-age population is not provided with adequate health, education, skills and jobs, the demographic dividend may turn into a:
27.x: The Economic Survey describes the failure to create the required conditions as potentially producing a 'demographic nightmare'.
27.tq: Apply the condition–consequence relationship to a policy scenario.
xs: It may turn into a **"demographic nightmare"** — option **(3)** is correct.
A **nightmare** = dividend **without health, education, skills and jobs**.
xa: Preconditions from ES **2018-19**.
Lower **dependency ratio** signals a dividend.

27.s: Under the National Youth Policy 2014, the youth population is defined as persons in the age group:
27.x: The National Youth Policy 2014 defines youth as persons aged 15–29 years.
27.tq: Recall the exact age range attached to a named policy.
xs: **Youth** = **15–29** years (National Youth Policy **2014**) — option **(3)** is correct.
The other bands (**10-19**, **15-24**, **20-35**) are not the Policy's definition.
xa: Young-age ratio = **0-14**; old-age ratio = **65+**.
Without skills and jobs, the dividend becomes a **"demographic nightmare"**.

27.s:
Consider the following pairs of States in the context of demographic transition:
a. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
b. Telangana and Uttarakhand
c. Kerala and Tamil Nadu

1. Wide demographic-dividend window
2. Narrowing demographic-dividend window
3. Ageing phase with a falling working-age share

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
27.x: Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have a wide demographic-dividend window. Telangana and Uttarakhand have a narrowing window, while Kerala and Tamil Nadu are ageing and their working-age share is already falling.
27.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes using the demographic-stage comparison.
xs: **a–1, b–2, c–3** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Youthful** (**Bihar, UP**) = wide window; **intermediate** (**Telangana, Uttarakhand**) = narrowing.
**Ageing** (**Kerala, TN**) = working-age share already falling.
xa: Ageing States spend about **30%** of social spending on **pensions**.
**AP** is in **Stage 4**, median age **32.5** (India **28**).

27.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Kerala's projected demographic position by 2036?
o: Its 60+ population is expected to constitute 22.8%, signalling the end of its demographic dividend.
Its 60+ population is expected to constitute 12.8%, thereby widening its demographic-dividend window.
Its 60+ population is expected to remain below 10%, indicating a youthful population structure.
Its 60+ population is expected to constitute 30%, while its working-age share rises sharply.
27.x: Kerala's 60+ population is projected to reach 22.8% by 2036, marking the end of its demographic-dividend phase.
27.tq: Use the exact projected percentage and connect it with the corresponding demographic stage.
xs: Kerala's **60+** share is projected at **22.8%** by **2036**, **ending its dividend** — option **(1)** is correct.
Kerala is an **ageing** State — working-age share **already falling** — so options (2)-(4) are wrong.
xa: Kerala literacy **94%** (female **92.1%**, Census **2011**).
Kerala has the highest 60+ share in SRS **2024**: **15%**.
About **30%** of social spending on pensions in ageing States.

27.s:
With reference to the determinants of birth rate, consider the following statements:
1. Female education influences the birth rate.
2. Higher child survival, reflected in a lower infant mortality rate, can affect fertility decisions.
3. Urbanisation and the cost of raising children influence the birth rate.
4. Access to contraception has no relevance to the birth rate.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Female education, child survival, urbanisation, the cost of raising children and contraception access are determinants of birth rate. Statement 4 is false because contraception access is relevant to fertility decisions.
27.tq: Find the statement that reverses the role of a recognised determinant.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Determinants: **female education + age at marriage**; **child survival (IMR)**; **urbanisation + cost of raising children**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **contraception access** is itself a determinant.
xa: Fall in fertility is why the **dependency ratio** is falling.
TFR **below replacement** for the fifth year (SRS **2024**).
CBR = births per **1,000 mid-year population**; India **18.3**.

27.s: Which of the following correctly describes the projected change in Andhra Pradesh's age composition by 2036?
o: The under-14 population will fall from 25% to 15%, while the 60+ population will rise from 10% to 19%.
The under-14 population will rise from 15% to 25%, while the 60+ population will fall from 19% to 10%.
Both the under-14 and 60+ populations will rise by 10 percentage points.
Both the under-14 and 60+ populations will decline by 10 percentage points.
27.x: By 2036, Andhra Pradesh's under-14 share is projected to decline from 25% to 15%, while its 60+ share is projected to increase from 10% to 19%.
27.tq: Track the direction of change separately for the young and elderly groups.
xs: Option (2) reverses both changes.
xa: AP median age **32.5** vs India **28**.
AP is in **Stage 4** of demographic transition.

27.s:
Assertion (A): States such as Kerala and Tamil Nadu face increasing pressure on pension-related social expenditure.
Reason (R): These States are ageing, and their working-age population share is already falling.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
27.x: Both statements are true, and the ageing of Kerala and Tamil Nadu together with their falling working-age share explains the greater pension-related expenditure pressure.
27.tq: Test whether the demographic trend stated in the Reason directly explains the fiscal consequence in the Assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Kerala and TN** are **ageing** States whose **working-age share is already falling**.
Hence about **30%** of their social spending goes on **pensions**.
xa: **Youthful** States (**Bihar, UP**) have a wide window.
**Intermediate** States (**Telangana, Uttarakhand**): narrowing window.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Andhra Pradesh is placed in Stage 4 of demographic transition.
2. Stage 4 is associated with a low-fertility demographic setting.
3. Andhra Pradesh is described as being in the same wide demographic-dividend phase as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Andhra Pradesh is in Stage 4, reflecting a low-fertility demographic setting. It is not described as being in the same wide-window phase as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, so statement 3 is false.
27.tq: Separate the State's demographic-transition stage from the wider-window classification of other States.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **AP is in Stage 4**.
Statement 2: **Stage 4** = **low** birth and death rates — a low-fertility setting.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Bihar, UP** are **youthful** (wide window); AP is ageing (median age **32.5**).
xa: ⚠ **India** = late Stage 3 into Stage 4.
AP Gram Sabhas (May **2026**) sought feedback on incentives to **reverse falling fertility**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Working-age population
(b) Young dependents
(c) Old dependents
(d) Demographic dividend

List-II
(i) Below 15 years
(ii) Larger working-age share associated with greater potential productive workforce
(iii) 65 years and above
(iv) 15–64 years
27.x: The working-age population is 15–64, young dependents are below 15, old dependents 65 and over, and the demographic dividend is the gain from a larger working-age share. The answer is a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii.
27.tq: Match each group to its age band.
n: The working-age population is aged 15–64 years. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
Young dependents are below 15 years of age. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
Old dependents are aged 65 years and above. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
A larger working-age share leads to a greater potential productive workforce. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]

27.s:
Match the stages in List-I with their birth-rate and death-rate patterns in List-II:
List-I
(a) Stage I
(b) Stage II
(c) Stage III
(d) Stage IV

List-II
(i) Low birth rate, low death rate
(ii) High birth rate, falling death rate
(iii) Falling birth rate, low death rate
(iv) High birth rate, high death rate
27.x: Stage I has high birth and death rates, Stage II a high birth rate and falling death rate, Stage III a falling birth rate and low death rate, and Stage IV low rates for both. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
27.tq: Track birth and death rates stage by stage.
n: In Stage I of demographic transition, the birth rate is high. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage I of demographic transition, the death rate is high. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage II of demographic transition, the birth rate is high. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage II of demographic transition, the death rate is falling. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage III of demographic transition, the birth rate is falling. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage III of demographic transition, the death rate is low. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage IV of demographic transition, the birth rate is low. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]
In Stage IV of demographic transition, the death rate is low. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 102-102]

28.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the evolution of India’s family planning programme.

List-I (Year)
 a. 1952
 b. 1960s
 c. 1976
 d. 1996

List-II (Approach or development)
 i. Target-free approach
 ii. Clinic-based approach
 iii. First National Population Policy
 iv. Extension and target approach with camps

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
28.x: The 1952 programme was clinic-based; the 1960s saw extension and target approaches with camps; 1976 brought the first National Population Policy; and 1996 introduced the target-free approach.
28.tq: Start from the sure year–approach pair and eliminate codes.
xs: **a–ii, b–iv, c–iii, d–i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**1952** programme (1950s) = **clinic-based approach**; **1960s** = **extension-education approach, targets**.
**1976** = **First National Population Policy**; **1996** = **target-free approach**.
xa: **1977**: renamed the **Family Welfare Programme** after the Emergency's forced sterilisations.
**1997**: **Reproductive and Child Health (RCH)**.
**NPP 2000** declared on **15 February 2000**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of India's family planning programme:
1. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment placed population control in the Concurrent List.
2. The first National Population Policy was announced in 1976.
3. The programme was renamed the Family Welfare Programme in 1977.
4. The target-free approach was introduced in 1986.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the 42nd Amendment (1976) put population control in the Concurrent List, the first National Population Policy came in 1976, and the programme was renamed Family Welfare in 1977 after the Emergency's forced sterilisations. Statement 4 is wrong: the target-free approach came in 1996, followed by RCH from 1997. So A misses statement 3, C and D wrongly include statement 4.
28.tq: 1976 = first NPP + 42nd Amendment; 1977 = renamed; 1996 = target-free; 1997 = RCH.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **42nd Amendment** put population control in the **Concurrent List**.
Statements 2 and 3: **first National Population Policy** in **1976**; renamed **Family Welfare Programme** in **1977**.
Statement 4 is wrong: the **target-free approach** came in **1996**, not 1986.
xa: The **1976** policy (**16 April**) raised marriage age to **21/18**.
**1952** = first programme in the world.
**RCH** followed from **1997**.

28.s: India became the first country in the world to launch a national family planning programme in which year?
28.x: India was the first country to launch a national family planning programme, and it was launched in 1952.
28.tq: Use the distinctive first-country and launch-year combination.
xs: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in **1952** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS key).
It began with a **clinic-based approach** in the **1950s** (1st-2nd Plans).
xa: ⚠ **1952** = first programme; **1976** = first policy.
**1977**: renamed **Family Welfare Programme**.
**NPP 2000**: declared **15 February 2000**.

28.s: The National Population Policy, 2000 was declared on:
28.x: The National Population Policy, 2000 was declared on 15 February 2000.
28.tq: Recall the exact policy date from the four national dates.
xs: **NPP 2000** was declared on **15 February 2000** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is **voluntary, informed choice, target-free**.
xa: Medium-term: TFR to **2.1** by **2010**.
Long-term: **stable population by 2045**.
**National Commission on Population** set up in **2000**, chaired by the **Prime Minister**.

28.s:
Which of the following principles formed part of the approach of the National Population Policy, 2000?
1. Target-free implementation
2. Voluntary and informed choice
3. Delivery through government, industry and NGOs
28.x: The policy adopted a target-free, voluntary and informed-choice approach and envisaged delivery through government, industry and NGOs.
28.tq: Check the policy’s approach and implementation channels together.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)**.
NPP 2000 is **target-free**, based on **voluntary, informed choice**.
Delivery through **government + industry + NGOs**.
xa: It promotes the **two-child norm**.
Immediate objective: meet the **unmet need for contraception**.
Long-term: **stable population by 2045**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the shortcomings of India's population policy:
1. It took a narrow, family-planning-centred view with a focus on sterilisation.
2. Emergency-era coercion left a legacy of distrust.
3. The NPP 2000 target of replacement-level TFR (2.1) was achieved by 2010 as planned.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
28.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the policy is criticised as family-planning-centred with a narrow focus on sterilisation, and the 1976-77 coercion left distrust. Statement 3 is wrong: TFR 2.1 was reached only around NFHS-5 (2019-21), not by 2010. So A omits statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
28.tq: Target 2.1 by 2010, actually reached only around NFHS-5 (2019-21).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: a **narrow**, family-planning-centred view with focus on **sterilisation**.
Statement 2: **Emergency-era coercion** left **distrust**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **TFR 2.1** was reached only around **NFHS-5 (2019-21)**, not by **2010**.
xa: ⚠ **TFR 2.1 by 2010** (NPP 2000) vs **2.1 by 2025** (Mission Parivar Vikas).
NFHS-6 (released **29 May 2026**): TFR steady at **2.0**.
Female sterilisation **37.9%** (NFHS-5).

28.s: The National Commission on Population was set up in 2000 under the chairmanship of the:
28.x: The National Commission on Population was established in 2000 under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister.
28.tq: Apply the who-chairs-the-body pattern in institutional questions.
xs: The **National Commission on Population** (**2000**) is **chaired by the Prime Minister** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was set up under **NPP 2000**.
xa: Members include **Chief Ministers** + **Union ministers**.
**State of World Population** report: **UNFPA**.
**NFHS**: MoHFW through **IIPS Mumbai**.

28.s: The State of World Population report is published by:
28.x: The State of World Population report is published by the United Nations Population Fund, or UNFPA.
28.tq: Distinguish among closely related United Nations agencies by their reports.
xs: The **State of World Population** report is published by **UNFPA** — option **(1)** is correct.
**UNFPA** is distinct from the Indian bodies: **NFHS** is run by MoHFW through **IIPS Mumbai**.
xa: **NFHS**: MoHFW through **IIPS Mumbai**.
**National Commission on Population**: chaired by the **Prime Minister**.
NFHS-6 released **29 May 2026**.

28.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the institutional arrangement for the National Family Health Survey?
o: It is conducted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through IIPS, Mumbai.
It is conducted by UNFPA through the National Commission on Population.
It is conducted by the Ministry of Finance through the World Bank.
It is conducted by NITI Aayog through State Election Commissions.
28.x: The NFHS is associated with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and is conducted through the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai.
28.tq: Use the ministry-agency association and reject neighbouring institutional bodies.
xs: NFHS is conducted by the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare** through **IIPS, Mumbai** — option **(1)** is correct.
**UNFPA** publishes the **State of World Population** report, not NFHS.
xa: **NFHS-6** (**2023-24**): CPR **69.1%**; institutional deliveries **90.6%**.
NFHS-6 released **29 May 2026**; TFR steady at **2.0**.
TFR **2.1** was reached around **NFHS-5** (**2019-21**).

28.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the objectives of the National Population Policy, 2000:
List-I (Time frame)
 a. Immediate
 b. Medium-term
 c. Long-term
List-II (Objective)
 i. Achieve a stable population by 2045
 ii. Meet unmet needs for contraception, health infrastructure and personnel
 iii. Bring Total Fertility Rate to replacement level of 2.1 by 2010

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
28.x: The immediate objective concerned unmet needs for contraception and health services; the medium-term objective was TFR 2.1 by 2010; the long-term objective was population stabilisation by 2045.
28.tq: Start from the distinctive long-term target and then match the two service-related objectives.
xs: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Immediate**: meet **unmet need for contraception**, health infrastructure and personnel.
**Medium-term**: TFR to **replacement level (2.1) by 2010**; **long-term**: **stable population by 2045**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes say **2046** — **wrong**; the policy says **2045**.
TFR 2.1 actually reached around **NFHS-5** (**2019-21**).
NPP 2000 promotes the **two-child norm**.

28.s: Janani Suraksha Yojana was launched in 2005 under which programme?
28.x: Janani Suraksha Yojana was launched in 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission.
28.tq: Apply the scheme-parent programme association.
xs: **Janani Suraksha Yojana** (**2005**) was launched under the **National Rural Health Mission (NRHM)** — option **(3)** is correct.
It gives a **cash incentive** for **institutional delivery** (APPSC **2018** key).
xa: Aim: cut **maternal and neonatal mortality**.
**NFHS-6**: institutional deliveries **88.6% → 90.6%**.
**PMMVY 2.0**: maternity benefit for pregnant and lactating women.

28.s: Which of the following States is NOT included among the seven high-fertility States covered by Mission Parivar Vikas?
28.x: The seven States are Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan. Odisha is not included in this list.
28.tq: Find the State that does not belong to the specified programme group.
xs: **Odisha** is not among the seven — option **(3)** is the answer.
The **7** States: **MP, UP, Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan**.
xa: Target: TFR **2.1 by 2025**.
Outreach teams in **146 districts**.
**ASHA** birth-spacing scheme: **2**-year gap after marriage, **3**-year spacing after first child.

28.s: Which scheme provides maternity benefits for pregnant and lactating women?
28.x: PM Matru Vandana Yojana 2.0 is a maternity-benefit scheme for pregnant and lactating women.
28.tq: Match the scheme with its specific target group.
xs: **PM Matru Vandana Yojana 2.0** gives **maternity benefit** to **pregnant and lactating women** — option **(4)** is correct.
**JSY** gives a cash incentive for **institutional delivery**; **Mission Parivar Vikas** targets TFR in **7** States.
xa: NFHS-6 lists PMMVY under **maternal-health drivers**.
**JSY** launched **2005** under **NRHM**.
NFHS-6: institutional deliveries **90.6%**.

28.s: The main objective of the Janani Suraksha Yojana is to:
o: reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional delivery through a cash incentive
provide a pension to elderly women
bring the TFR to 2.1 in seven high-fertility States
give maternity benefit to all lactating women in the organised sector
28.x: JSY (2005, NRHM) gives a cash incentive for institutional delivery to cut maternal and neonatal mortality (APPSC 2018 key). Option C is Mission Parivar Vikas; option D resembles PMMVY; JSY is not a pension scheme.
28.tq: JSY = cash for institutional delivery; MPV = TFR 2.1 in 7 States; PMMVY = maternity benefit.
xs: **JSY** aims to **reduce maternal and neonatal mortality** by a **cash incentive** for **institutional delivery** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC **2018** key).
TFR **2.1** in **7** States is **Mission Parivar Vikas**; maternity benefit for lactating women is **PMMVY**.
xa: JSY launched **2005** under **NRHM**.
NFHS-6: institutional deliveries **88.6% → 90.6%**.
**ASHA** birth-spacing: **2**-year gap after marriage.

28.s: The relatively low impact of family planning programmes in rural areas has been attributed primarily to:
28.x: Social orthodoxy and psychological factors were identified as important causes of the low rural impact of family planning programmes.
28.tq: Match the social outcome with its stated behavioural and cultural causes.
xs: Low rural impact is due to **social orthodoxy and psychological factors** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 **2008** key).
Option (3) is wrong: the barriers are **early marriage** and **low female literacy**, not late marriage.
xa: Other rural factors: **son preference**; children seen as **old-age "insurance"**.
**Early marriage**; **low female literacy**.
Distrust after **1976-77** coercion.

28.s:
Which of the following factors are associated with weak rural acceptance of family planning?
1. Son preference
2. Viewing children as old-age insurance
3. Early marriage
4. Low female literacy
28.x: Son preference, dependence on children as old-age insurance, early marriage and low female literacy are all identified as barriers.
28.tq: Test whether all listed social and demographic barriers belong to the same group.
xs: All four factors — option **(4)**.
**Son preference** and children as **old-age "insurance"** cause low rural impact.
**Early marriage** and **low female literacy** also do.
xa: Primary cause: **social orthodoxy and psychological factors** (APPSC-G2 **2008**).
Reluctance to **sterilisation**, men especially.
Female sterilisation **37.9%** (NFHS-5).

28.s: The Couple Protection Rate refers to the percentage of eligible couples who are:
o: Married before the legal age and protected from early marriage
Eligible for maternity benefits under PMMVY
Effectively protected against childbirth by an approved contraceptive method
28.x: The Couple Protection Rate is the percentage of eligible couples effectively protected against childbirth by an approved contraceptive method.
28.tq: Distinguish a technical demographic indicator from related welfare measures.
xs: **Couple Protection Rate** = % of eligible couples **effectively protected against childbirth** by an **approved contraceptive method** — option **(3)** is correct.
It measures contraceptive protection — not maternity benefits (**PMMVY**) or institutional delivery (**JSY**).
xa: NPP 2000's immediate objective: meet **unmet need for contraception**.
**Contraception access** is a determinant of birth rate.

28.s: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment froze Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats on the basis of the 1971 Census until:
28.x: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 froze the allocation of seats based on the 1971 Census until 2000.
28.tq: Separate the original freeze period from its later extension.
xs: The **42nd Amendment** (**1976**) froze seats on the **1971 Census** until **2000** — option **(2)** is correct.
**2026** relates to the **84th Amendment** extension.
xa: **84th Amendment** (**2001**): freeze **until the first Census after 2026**.
**87th Amendment** (**2003**): boundary readjustment on **2001 Census**.
Seats allotted on population under **Art. 82 and 170**.

28.s: Which amendment extended the freeze on seat allocation until the first Census after 2026?
28.x: The 84th Amendment of 2001 extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026.
28.tq: Distinguish the amendment that created the freeze from the amendment that extended it.
xs: The **84th Amendment** (**2001**) extended the freeze **until the first Census after 2026** — option **(2)** is correct.
**42nd** froze seats until **2000**; **87th** readjusted boundaries on the **2001 Census**.
xa: It was a **motivational measure** under NPP strategy.
It allowed boundary readjustment on the **1991** Census.
Southern States fear losing **8-10 Lok Sabha seats** at delimitation.

28.s: Seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are allotted on the basis of population under which Articles?
28.x: Articles 82 and 170 relate to the allocation and readjustment of seats on the basis of population.
28.tq: Use Article-number discrimination between parliamentary and local-government provisions.
xs: Seats are allotted on population under **Articles 82 and 170** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seat counts themselves were **frozen** — on the **1971 Census** by the **42nd Amendment**, extended by the **84th**.
xa: **42nd Amendment** (**1976**) froze seats on the **1971 Census** until **2000**.
**84th Amendment** (**2001**) extended the freeze until the first Census after **2026**.
**Boundary readjustment** = no change in seat numbers.

28.s: Which Constitutional Amendment allowed readjustment of constituency boundaries on the basis of the 2001 Census, without changing the number of seats?
28.x: The 87th Amendment (2003) allowed boundary readjustment on the 2001 Census. The 84th (2001) extended the seat freeze and had allowed readjustment on the 1991 Census; the 42nd (1976) froze seats on the 1971 Census; the 73rd deals with Panchayats.
28.tq: 42nd freeze till 2000; 84th freeze till after 2026; 87th = 2001 Census boundaries.
xs: The **87th Amendment (2003)** readjusted boundaries on the **2001 Census** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Boundary readjustment** = **no change in seat numbers**.
The **84th** had allowed readjustment on the **1991** Census; the **42nd** froze seats.
xa: **84th Amendment**: **2001**.
**42nd Amendment**: **1976**, freeze till **2000**.
Southern fear: loss of **8-10** Lok Sabha seats.

28.s: According to Census 2011, migration was recorded using which two bases?
o: Place of birth and place of last residence
28.x: The Census recorded migration by place of birth and by place of last residence.
28.tq: Recall the two official migration bases as a paired concept.
xs: Census records migration by **place of birth** and **place of last residence** — option **(1)** is correct.
Female inter-state streams (**2011**) are reported by **last residence**.
xa: **141.2 million** moved during **2001-2011**.
Largest stream overall: **rural→rural**, driven by **marriage**.
Reasons: **marriage** for women; **work** for men.

28.s: Which one of the following was the order of inter-State female migration streams by place of last residence in 2011, from highest to lowest?
28.x: The order was Urban-Urban, Rural-Urban, Rural-Rural and Urban-Rural.
28.tq: Read the ranking carefully instead of applying the general rural-rural migration pattern.
xs: **Urban-Urban > Rural-Urban > Rural-Rural > Urban-Rural** — option **(4)** is correct (JPSC **2023** key).
This is **inter-state female** migration by **last residence** (**2011**).
xa: ⚠ Overall, the largest stream is **rural→rural**, driven by marriage.
**141.2 million** moved during **2001-2011**.
Census bases: **place of birth** + **place of last residence**.

28.s:
Which one of the following correctly matches the main migration reason with the group mentioned?

1. Women — Marriage
2. Men — Work
3. Gulf migration — International migration context
28.x: Marriage is the major stated reason for women’s migration, work for men’s migration, and Gulf migration represents the international migration context.
28.tq: Match reasons and examples with the appropriate migration category.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)**.
**Marriage** for women; **work** for men; **Gulf migration** (UPSC).
xa: Largest stream: **rural→rural**, driven by marriage.
Census bases: **place of birth** + **place of last residence**.
**Todaro**: expected-income rural-urban model.

28.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Push-pull theory and intervening obstacles — Everett Lee
2. Expected-income rural-urban model — Michael Todaro
3. Laws of Migration — E.G. Ravenstein
28.x: Everett Lee is associated with push-pull theory and intervening obstacles, Michael Todaro with the expected-income rural-urban model, and E.G. Ravenstein with the Laws of Migration.
28.tq: Start from the familiar theorist pair and verify all three associations.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4)**.
**Everett Lee**: push-pull / intervening obstacles (**1966**); **Michael Todaro**: expected-income rural-urban model.
**E.G. Ravenstein**: Laws of Migration (**1885**).
xa: Migration reasons: **marriage** for women, **work** for men.
Census bases: **place of birth** + **place of last residence**.
**141.2 million** moved during **2001-2011**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Policy on Older Persons, 1999:
1. It was formulated by the Ministry of Social Justice.
2. It includes health care and nutrition among its areas of intervention.
3. It contains 14 areas of intervention.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: The National Policy on Older Persons, 1999 was associated with the Ministry of Social Justice, covered 14 areas of intervention, and included health care and nutrition.
28.tq: Verify the ministry, scope and numerical composition before selecting the combined option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**National Policy on Older Persons 1999** — **Ministry of Social Justice**.
**14 areas of intervention**, including **health care + nutrition**.
xa: **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007**.
**NPHCE** launched **2010-11**.
**NCOP** = highest advisory body.

28.s: The National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) was launched in
28.x: NPHCE was launched in 2010–11 to provide health care for persons aged 60 years and above.
28.tq: Distinguish the launch year of the health programme from the years of the policy and legislation.
xs: **NPHCE** was launched in **2010–11** — option **(4)** is correct.
It covers **60+** health care.
xa: **1999** = National Policy on Older Persons; **2007** = Maintenance Act.
**NCOP** (National Council for Senior Citizens) = highest advisory body.
Elderly share **9.7%** (SRS **2024**).

28.s: Under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, maintenance of parents and senior citizens is
o: a legal duty of children and relatives
a responsibility of the Union Government alone
a duty imposed exclusively on local bodies
28.x: The Act makes the maintenance of parents and senior citizens a legal duty of children and relatives.
28.tq: Ask who bears the legal responsibility rather than relying on the general welfare objective.
xs: Under the **2007 Act**, maintenance is a **legal duty of children and relatives** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is not merely voluntary — option (3) is wrong.
xa: **National Policy on Older Persons 1999**: **14 areas** of intervention.
AP pillar **Kshema** = elderly care.

28.s: With reference to pension coverage among the elderly, which one of the following is correct?
o: About 40% of both elderly women and men have no formal pension.
Nearly 70% of both elderly women and men have no formal pension.
About 40% of elderly women have no formal pension, compared with nearly 70% of elderly men.
Nearly 70% of elderly women have no formal pension, compared with about 40% of elderly men.
28.x: Nearly 70% of elderly women have no formal pension, whereas the corresponding proportion among elderly men is about 40%.
28.tq: Preserve the direction of the gender comparison while checking both percentages.
xs: Nearly **70%** of elderly **women** lack a formal pension vs about **40%** of elderly **men** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses the two.
xa: Elderly = **9.7%** of population (SRS **2024**).
Elderly projected **230 mn** by **2036**.
IMF: ageing could cut growth by **70 basis points** a year.

28.s: Which change is associated with Andhra Pradesh’s draft population policy of March 2026?
o: Introduction of a three-child norm for local elections
Removal of the two-child norm for local body elections
28.x: The Andhra Pradesh draft policy proposed removing the two-child norm for local body elections.
28.tq: Identify the policy change by spotting the reversal of the existing norm.
xs: AP's March 2026 draft **Population Management Policy** proposes the **removal of the two-child norm for local body elections** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The draft marks a shift **from population control to population management**, so it relaxes, not tightens, family-size rules: no **three-child norm** is introduced.
It offers a **₹25,000** incentive for a **second or third child**.
xa: Its package is called **"Poshana-Shiksha-Suraksha"**.
Five pillars: **Matrutva**, **Shakti**, **Kshema**, **Naipunyam**, **Sanjeevani**.
Health Minister **Satya Kumar Yadav** warned of "**shrinconomics**"; AP's TFR is **1.50**.
**Gram Sabhas** were held in all districts to gather feedback on the draft.

28.s: The draft Population Management Policy of Andhra Pradesh, released in March 2026, marks a shift in emphasis from
28.x: The draft policy shifts the emphasis from population control to population management.
28.tq: Discriminate between the two closely related policy formulations.
xs: AP's draft **Population Management Policy** (**March 2026**) shifts emphasis **from population control to population management** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The pro-natalist shift answers a low **TFR of 1.50**, the opposite of "coercive control".
It proposes a **₹25,000** incentive for a **second or third child** and removes the **two-child norm** for local body elections.
xa: Five pillars: **Matrutva** (maternal health), **Shakti** (women's work), **Kshema** (elderly care), **Naipunyam** (skills), **Sanjeevani** (digital health).
Health Minister **Satya Kumar Yadav** warned of "**shrinconomics**".
⚠ Contrast: **NPP 2000** (national) promoted the **two-child norm**; AP's draft moves away from it.

28.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Pillar)
 a. Matrutva
 b. Shakti
 c. Kshema
 d. Naipunyam

List-II (Focus)
 i. Skills
 ii. Elderly care
 iii. Maternal health
 iv. Women's work participation

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
28.x: Matrutva refers to maternal health, Shakti to women's work participation, Kshema to elderly care and Naipunyam to skills.
28.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with a mismatched pillar.
xs: **Matrutva – maternal health**, **Shakti – women's work participation**, **Kshema – elderly care**, **Naipunyam – skills** — so option **(1)** a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i is correct.
These are four of the **five pillars** of AP's draft **Population Management Policy** (**March 2026**).
xa: The fifth pillar is **Sanjeevani** = **digital health**.
Under **Naipunyam**, the State plans a **skill drive**.
The draft offers **₹25,000** for a **second or third child**.
The policy shifts **from control to management**; it removes the **two-child norm** for local body elections.

28.s: The debate between coercion and choice in India's population policy is especially associated with the contrast between
o: the MWPSC Act 2007 and the Finance Commission
28.x: The coercion-versus-choice debate is framed through the contrast between the 1976–77 approach and the National Population Policy, 2000.
28.tq: Identify the two policy periods forming the stated contrast.
xs: The **coercion vs choice** debate contrasts the **period 1976-77** (Emergency-era coercive sterilisation) with **NPP 2000** (voluntary, informed choice) — so option **(2)** is correct.
NPP 2000 is **target-free**, voluntary and based on **informed choice**.
xa: After the Emergency, the programme was renamed the **Family Welfare Programme** in **1977**.
**1976** saw the **First National Population Policy**; marriage age raised to **21/18**.
The coercion left lasting **distrust** of sterilisation, especially among men.
⚠ **1952** = first programme; **1976** = first policy; **2000** = NPP.

28.s: The pro-natalist turn in southern States is linked to concerns regarding the use of population figures in
o: the National Policy on Older Persons and pension schemes
Gram Sabha elections and skill drives
28.x: The pro-natalist turn is discussed in relation to delimitation and Finance Commission population weights.
28.tq: Link the demographic policy response to the institutional consequences of population weights.
xs: The southern **pro-natalist turn** is debated against **delimitation** and **Finance Commission** population weights in **devolution** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Population weights make up **15-25%** of the devolution criteria; low-fertility States fear losing funds.
Under delimitation, Southern States could lose **8-10 Lok Sabha seats**.
xa: **42nd Amendment (1976)** froze seats on the **1971 Census** until **2000**.
**84th Amendment (2001)** extended the freeze **until the first Census after 2026**.
**Art. 82 and 170**: seats are allotted on population.

29.s: The United Nations defined absolute poverty at the:
o: World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995
29.x: Absolute poverty was defined by the United Nations at the World Summit for Social Development held at Copenhagen in 1995.
29.tq: Match the definition with the correct international summit and year.
xs: The UN defined absolute poverty at the **World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Absolute poverty** = lack of the **minimum resources for survival**, set by a fixed consumption/calorie norm.
xa: Absolute poverty is **India's focus**; **relative** poverty is used in developed economies.
APSES 2024-25 measures absolute poverty by the **World Bank line**.
The first **UN Decade for the Eradication of Poverty** ran **1997-2006**.
**SDG 1**: "End poverty in all its forms everywhere" by **2030**.

29.s: Relative poverty is primarily concerned with:
o: The inability to obtain the minimum resources required for physical survival
An individual's personal feeling about his or her social position
Income being well below the median income of a society
Temporary poverty caused by seasonal employment
29.x: Relative poverty compares a person's income with the income distribution of society, particularly the median. Absolute poverty concerns minimum survival resources, while subjective poverty concerns personal perception.
29.tq: Separate relative poverty from absolute, transient and subjective poverty by its comparison standard.
xs: **Relative poverty** means **income well below the society's median** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Minimum resources for survival = **absolute** poverty; personal feeling about position = **subjective** poverty; temporary seasonal poverty = **transient/cyclical** poverty.
xa: Relative poverty compares **fractile groups** and persists even in the **USA** and **UK**.
⚠ **Absolute** = India's focus; **relative** = developed economies.
**Chronic** poverty lasts over long periods or **generations**.

29.s: Poverty that persists over long periods or across generations is known as:
29.x: Chronic poverty lasts for long periods or is transmitted across generations. Transient or cyclical poverty is temporary and generally arises from shocks, seasons or economic cycles.
29.tq: Use duration as the deciding clue when distinguishing chronic from transient poverty.
xs: Poverty lasting over long periods or across **generations** is **chronic poverty** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Transient** poverty is temporary (shocks, seasons, cycles); **relative** compares income with the **median**; **subjective** rests on a person's own sense of position.
xa: **Culture of poverty** (**Oscar Lewis**): poverty passed on as a **way of life**.
**Absolute** poverty: fixed consumption/**calorie norm** — India's focus.
UN defined absolute poverty at **Copenhagen, 1995**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about poverty measurement and economic development:
1. Absolute poverty is measured by the World Bank poverty line.
2. Relative poverty is widely used in developed economies.
3. Relative poverty is defined exclusively by a fixed calorie norm.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because a fixed consumption or calorie norm is associated with absolute poverty, not relative poverty.
29.tq: Split the fixed-norm concept from the society-comparison concept before selecting the code.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **absolute poverty** is measured by the **World Bank line** (APSES 2024-25).
Statement 2 is correct: **relative poverty** is widely used in **developed economies**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a fixed **calorie norm** defines **absolute**, not relative, poverty — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: Relative poverty = income well below the society's **median**; compares **fractile groups**.
India's calorie norm: **2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban**.
Absolute poverty was defined at the **World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995**.

29.s: The concept of the 'culture of poverty', in which poverty is passed on as a way of life, is associated with:
29.x: Oscar Lewis described the culture of poverty, where poverty is transmitted as a way of life. Amartya Sen is known for the capability approach; Ravenstein and Todaro are migration theorists.
29.tq: Culture of poverty = Oscar Lewis.
xs: The **culture of poverty** — poverty passed on as a way of life — is associated with **Oscar Lewis** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Amartya Sen**, **E.G. Ravenstein** and **Michael Todaro** are not linked to this concept in the notes; Lewis alone describes poverty as a transmitted **way of life**.
xa: **Transient** poverty is temporary — from shocks, seasons or cycles.
**Chronic** poverty persists over long periods or **generations**.
**Subjective** poverty = a person's own sense of relative position.

29.s:
Match List-I (poverty measure) with List-II (what it captures):
List-I
a. Head Count Ratio
b. Poverty Gap Index
c. Squared Poverty Gap
List-II
i. Severity - more weight to the poorest
ii. Incidence - share of population below the line
iii. Depth - average shortfall from the line
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
29.x: Option A is correct: HCR (HC = Nq/N) measures incidence, the PGI measures depth as the average shortfall from the line, and the Squared Poverty Gap measures severity by giving more weight to the poorest. B swaps incidence and depth; C swaps depth and severity; D swaps incidence and severity.
29.tq: Incidence -> Depth -> Severity, in the order HCR -> PGI -> squared gap (the FGT family).
xs: **HCR – incidence**, **PGI – depth**, **Squared Poverty Gap – severity** — so option **(1)** a-ii, b-iii, c-i is correct.
**HC = Nq / N** (share below the line); PGI = average shortfall **(Z − yi)/Z**; squared gap gives **more weight to the poorest**.
xa: All three belong to the **Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT)** family.
⚠ If the poor get poorer, **HCR is unchanged** but **PGI changes**.
Memory aid: **incidence – depth – severity** = **HCR – PGI – squared gap**.

29.s: The Head Count Ratio, Poverty Gap Index and Squared Poverty Gap belong to the:
29.x: HCR, PGI and the squared poverty gap are measures belonging to the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) family.
29.tq: Identify the common methodological family rather than confusing it with related inequality indices.
xs: **HCR**, **PGI** and the **Squared Poverty Gap** belong to the **Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT)** family — so option **(1)** is correct.
They measure **incidence**, **depth** and **severity** of poverty respectively.
xa: HCR formula: **HC = Nq / N**.
PGI: **(1/n) Σ (Z − yi)/Z**; the squared gap squares this shortfall.
**Engel's Law**: as family income rises, the **share spent on food falls**.

29.s: If the poor become poorer while the number of poor people remains unchanged, which one of the following measures will remain unchanged?
29.x: The Head Count Ratio depends only on the number or share of people below the poverty line, so it does not change when existing poor people become poorer. The Poverty Gap Index changes with the depth of poverty.
29.tq: Apply the incidence-depth distinction to a change in the condition of existing poor persons.
xs: The **Head Count Ratio** stays unchanged when the poor get poorer, because it counts only the **share below the line** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Poverty Gap Index** (average shortfall) and **Squared Poverty Gap** (severity) both rise as the poor get poorer.
xa: HCR = **incidence**; PGI = **depth**; squared gap = **severity**.
All three form the **Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT)** family.
HCR formula: **HC = Nq / N**.

29.s: Engel's Law states that, as family income rises:
o: The share of income spent on food rises proportionately
All household expenditure shifts to food
The share of income spent on food falls
The absolute amount spent on food always becomes zero
29.x: Engel's Law states that the proportion of family income spent on food declines as family income rises, although the absolute amount spent may still increase.
29.tq: Distinguish the share of expenditure from its absolute amount when applying Engel's Law.
xs: **Engel's Law**: as family income rises, the **share of income spent on food falls** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Data echo it: HCES food share fell from **₹48 to ₹39 per ₹100 (urban)**, and rural from **₹59**.
xa: **HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24** (MoSPI) were the first full **MPCE** update in over a decade.
India's poverty line is based on **consumption expenditure**, not income.
The **FGT** family: HCR, PGI, squared poverty gap.

29.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the poverty line in India:
1. It is measured on the basis of consumption expenditure.
2. Monthly per capita consumption expenditure is an important basis for measurement.
3. A person is regarded as poor when consumption falls below the poverty line.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements are correct. Indian poverty estimation uses consumption expenditure, including MPCE, and identifies poverty when consumption falls below the specified line.
29.tq: Verify the measurement basis first, then check whether the threshold is consumption or income.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: India's poverty line rests on **consumption expenditure**, not income.
Statement 2 is correct: **MPCE** (from NSS / HCES) is the basis.
Statement 3 is correct: a person is **poor when consumption falls below the line** — so option **(4)** 1, 2 and 3 is correct.
xa: Calorie norm (ICMR, Alagh): **2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban**.
**Poverty Line Basket**: socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs bought in the market.
Tendulkar line (2011-12): **₹816 rural / ₹1,000 urban** per month.

29.s: A Poverty Line Basket (PLB) is best described as:
o: A basket based only on the income tax records of households
A socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs purchased in the market
A basket containing only food grains supplied through the Public Distribution System
A basket consisting exclusively of services provided free by the government
29.x: The Poverty Line Basket is a socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs bought in the market. It is not confined to food grains or government-provided services.
29.tq: Choose the precise official meaning rather than a narrower everyday interpretation.
xs: A **Poverty Line Basket** is a **socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs** bought in the **market** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not limited to **PDS food grains**, tax records or free government services.
xa: Poverty lines differ across **time** and **countries** because basic needs vary (UPPSC 2025 key: A and R true, R explains A).
RBI updated the **Rangarajan line** with HCES 2022-23 using a **PLB-weighted price index**.
Calorie norm: **2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban**.

29.s: According to the Tendulkar Committee estimates for 2011-12, the monthly poverty line was fixed at:
o: ₹816 in rural areas and ₹1,000 in urban areas
₹1,000 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
₹816 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
₹972 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
29.x: For 2011-12, the Tendulkar poverty line was ₹816 per month for rural areas and ₹1,000 per month for urban areas, approximately ₹27 and ₹33 per day respectively.
29.tq: Separate the committee-specific figures from the later revised poverty-line values.
xs: The **Tendulkar** line for **2011-12** was **₹816 rural and ₹1,000 urban** per month — so option **(1)** is correct.
**₹972 rural / ₹1,407 urban** is the **Rangarajan** line; options 2 and 3 mix the two.
That is about **₹27/day rural** and **₹33/day urban**; it was criticised as **too low**.
xa: Tendulkar all-India poverty: **21.9%** (rural **25.7**, urban **13.7**).
⚠ Trap: some notes list ₹816/₹1,000 under "2010-11" — they are **2011-12** figures.

29.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Modified Mixed Reference Period (MMRP):
1. It uses a 7-day recall period for some food items.
2. It records higher consumption and therefore gives a lower poverty estimate.
3. It was first used for poverty estimation by the Tendulkar Committee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: MMRP uses a 7-day recall for some food items, recording about 10-12% higher consumption and so lower poverty. Statement 3 is wrong: MMRP was first used by Rangarajan (Tendulkar moved from URP to MRP). So A omits statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
29.tq: Tendulkar = MRP; Rangarajan = MMRP.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **MMRP** uses a **7-day recall** for some food items.
Statement 2 is correct: it records **10-12% higher consumption**, hence **lower poverty**.
Statement 3 is wrong: MMRP was first used by **Rangarajan**, not Tendulkar — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: Rangarajan (2011-12): **₹972 rural / ₹1,407 urban** per month; poverty **29.5%**.
RBI updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23** using a PLB-weighted price index.

29.s: Under the Rangarajan Expert Group (2011-12), the rural poverty line per person was about:
29.x: Rangarajan's rural line was Rs 972 a month, about Rs 32 a day (APPSC-GS 2025 key). Rs 27 and Rs 33 a day are Tendulkar's rural and urban lines; Rs 47 a day is Rangarajan's urban line.
29.tq: Rangarajan 32/47 a day; Tendulkar 27/33 a day.
xs: **Rangarajan's rural line** (2011-12) was **₹972 a month**, about **Rs 32 a day** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**Rs 27** and **Rs 33** a day are **Tendulkar's** rural and urban lines; **Rs 47** a day is Rangarajan's **urban** line.
xa: Rangarajan all-India poverty: **29.5%**.
**MMRP** (7-day recall) was first used by **Rangarajan**.
⚠ Trap: some notes list **₹972/₹1,407** as Tendulkar's — a mix-up.

29.s: Tendulkar-line poverty was estimated at approximately what percentages in 2022-23 and 2023-24 respectively?
29.x: Tendulkar-line poverty was estimated at 4.7 per cent in 2022-23 and 2.3 per cent in 2023-24.
29.tq: Read the years in sequence and avoid reversing the two reported estimates.
xs: **Tendulkar-line poverty** was **4.7 per cent in 2022-23** and **2.3 per cent in 2023-24** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option 4 reverses the order; **9.20 / 21.92** are AP and India HCRs for **2011-12**; **23.9 / 24.2** are from the UNDP West Asia simulation.
xa: Data from **HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24** (MoSPI).
Critique: subsistence lines **hide vulnerability** just above the threshold.
Share below the World Bank lower-middle-income line fell from over **50%** to about **30%**.

29.s: Why have critics questioned subsistence-based poverty lines?
o: They use a multidimensional index instead of consumption expenditure.
They count every person above the threshold as affluent.
They hide vulnerability among people just above the poverty threshold.
They measure only urban consumption and exclude rural consumption.
29.x: Critics argue that subsistence poverty lines can conceal the vulnerability of people who are just above the officially defined threshold.
29.tq: Apply the criticism to the practical consequence of being marginally above a threshold.
xs: Critics say subsistence lines **hide vulnerability** among people **just above the threshold** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Share below the World Bank lower-middle-income line fell from over **50%** to about **30%** — many remain near poverty.
xa: Lower-middle-income line: **$3.65 to $4.20**; upper-middle-income: **$8.30**.
India under the **$4.20** line: **57.7% → 23.9%** (World Bank Fall 2025 brief).

29.s: The international poverty line of $1.90 per person per day was based on which Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) base year?
29.x: The World Bank revised the international poverty line to $1.90 per person per day in October 2015, using 2011 PPP.
29.tq: Discriminate between closely spaced monetary thresholds and their PPP base years.
xs: The **$1.90** line (October **2015**) was based on **2011 PPP** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
xa: The latest line (June **2025**) is **$3.00** at **2021 PPP**.
⚠ Trap: the **$2.15** line was the **2022** revision; **$3** came in 2025.
Global extreme poverty at $2.15: about **9.2%** (over **700 mn**).

29.s: The latest World Bank international poverty line mentioned for June 2025 is:
29.x: In June 2025, the latest international poverty line was stated as $3.00 per person per day at 2021 PPP.
29.tq: Match the latest figure with its corresponding PPP base year rather than an earlier revision.
xs: The latest World Bank line (June **2025**) is **$3.00 at 2021 PPP** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**$4.20** is the lower-middle-income line; **$1.90** (2011 PPP) and **$2.15** (2017 PPP) are older lines.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes say $3 came "in 2022" — 2022 was the **$2.15** revision.
Upper-middle-income line: **$8.30**.

29.s: Sustainable Development Goal 1 aims to:
o: End hunger only in developing countries by 2025
End poverty in all its forms everywhere by 2030
29.x: SDG 1 is to end poverty in all its forms everywhere by 2030.
29.tq: Identify the exact wording and deadline of the goal instead of accepting an overbroad alternative.
xs: **SDG 1** aims to "**End poverty in all its forms everywhere**" by **2030** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not limited to hunger, employment or income equality.
xa: Third **UN Decade for Eradication of Poverty**: **2018-2027**.
About **9.2%** of the world (over **700 mn**) is in extreme poverty at the $2.15 line.
Latest World Bank line: **$3.00** at **2021 PPP**.

29.s: As per the World Bank estimates referred to in APPSC 2016, which country had the largest number of people living below the international poverty line at that time?
29.x: India had the largest number of people below the Bank's line at that time (APPSC 2016 key); under the old $1.25 line India's poor rose from 421 mn (1981) to 456 mn (2005). China had reduced its poor sharply; Nigeria and Bangladesh had fewer poor than India then.
29.tq: APPSC 2016: India = largest number of poor.
xs: Per the **APPSC 2016 key**, **India** had the largest number of people below the World Bank line at that time — so option **(3)** is correct.
Under the old **$1.25** line, India's poor rose from **421 mn (1981)** to **456 mn (2005)**.
xa: The **$1.25** line was set in **2008** at **2005 PPP**.
India under the **$4.20** line fell **57.7% → 23.9%** (World Bank Fall 2025 brief).
Global extreme poverty at $2.15: about **9.2%** (over **700 mn**).

29.s: Which one of the following best represents the contemporary debate on measuring poverty in India?
o: Income, consumption and multidimensional measures are debated, with a move towards the MPI.
The poverty line has been replaced entirely by the urban HCR.
Only income measures are used, since consumption measures are no longer relevant.
Only calorie intake is accepted as a complete measure of poverty.
29.x: The debate includes income-based, consumption-based and multidimensional approaches. The movement towards the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) is part of this broader shift.
29.tq: Identify the inclusive option that captures the competing approaches and the movement towards a multidimensional measure.
xs: The debate is over **income vs consumption vs multidimensional measures**, with a **move to the MPI** — so option **(1)** is correct.
India still uses **consumption expenditure** (MPCE) and calorie norms; no single income or calorie measure has replaced them.
xa: Critique: subsistence lines **hide vulnerability** just above the threshold.
UNDP simulation: West Asia war could raise poverty **23.9% → 24.2%**.

30.s: Who among the following authored the study titled ‘Poverty in India’ published in 1971?
o: Suresh D. Tendulkar and C. Rangarajan
30.x: The 1971 study ‘Poverty in India’ was authored by V.M. Dandekar and N. Rath.
xs: The **1971** study "**Poverty in India**" was written by **V.M. Dandekar and N. Rath** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was the **FIRST systematic poverty assessment on nutritional norms**, using **1960-61 NSS data** and **2,250 kcal** a day for rural and urban.
**Alagh** chaired the **1979** Task Force; **Lakdawala** (1993), **Tendulkar** (2005) and **Rangarajan** (2012) headed later Expert Groups; **Panagariya** led the 2015 NITI Task Force.
xa: Order to remember: **1971 – 1979 – 1993 – 2005 – 2012** = **Dandekar-Rath – Alagh – Lakdawala – Tendulkar – Rangarajan**.
APPSC-GS 2022 matched **Alagh (1979)** with the nutrition norm and **Dandekar-Rath (1971)** with the first systematic study.
**N.C. Saxena** dealt with the **rural BPL Census**, not poverty estimation.

30.s: The NITI Aayog Task Force on Elimination of Poverty, constituted in 2015, was chaired by:
30.x: The 2015 NITI Aayog Task Force on Elimination of Poverty was chaired by Arvind Panagariya.
xs: The **2015** NITI Aayog **Task Force on Elimination of Poverty** was chaired by **Arvind Panagariya** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**N.C. Saxena** worked on the rural **BPL Census**; **Rangarajan** chaired the **2012** Expert Group; **Alagh** the **1979** Task Force.
xa: Rangarajan's group was set up in **2012** and reported in **2014**.
Tendulkar: set up **Dec 2005**, reported **Dec 2009**.
AP angle: AP's **MPI** fell **0.053 to 0.025**; ranks **9th**.

30.s:
Match List-I (committee or study) with List-II (calorie norm used for the poverty line):
List-I
a. Dandekar-Rath
b. Alagh Task Force
c. Rangarajan Expert Group
List-II
i. 2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban
ii. 2,155 kcal rural / 2,090 kcal urban, plus protein and fat norms
iii. 2,250 kcal for both rural and urban
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Option A is correct: Dandekar-Rath (1971) used 2,250 kcal for both areas, Alagh (1979) used 2,400 kcal rural and 2,100 kcal urban, and Rangarajan used 2,155/2,090 kcal plus protein and fat norms. B swaps Dandekar-Rath and Alagh; C swaps Alagh and Rangarajan; D gives Rangarajan's norm to Dandekar-Rath.
30.tq: One uniform figure = Dandekar-Rath; the round 2,400/2,100 = Alagh; the odd numbers with protein and fat = Rangarajan.
xs: **Dandekar-Rath – 2,250 kcal** both areas; **Alagh – 2,400 rural / 2,100 urban**; **Rangarajan – 2,155 / 2,090 + protein and fat norms** — so option **(1)** a-iii, b-i, c-ii is correct.
Dandekar-Rath used **1960-61 NSS data**; Alagh's Task Force was in **1979**.
xa: Rangarajan treated **food and non-food** needs separately and used **MMRP** data.
⚠ **Tendulkar** moved away from the calorie anchor altogether.
**Lakdawala** kept the calorie basis with **State-specific lines**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Lakdawala methodology:
1. It retained the calorie basis of poverty estimation.
2. It used State-specific poverty lines.
3. It used CPI-AL for rural areas and CPI-IW for urban areas.
4. It continued scaling poverty estimates to National Accounts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the Lakdawala approach stopped scaling poverty estimates to National Accounts.
30.tq: Find the single incorrect methodological feature among closely related statements.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Lakdawala** kept the **calorie basis**.
Statement 2 is correct: it used **State-specific lines**.
Statement 3 is correct: prices updated by **CPI-AL (rural)** and **CPI-IW (urban)**.
Statement 4 is wrong: it **stopped scaling** to **National Accounts** — so option **(1)** 1, 2 and 3 only is correct.
xa: Lakdawala reported in **1993**; accepted in **1997**.
⚠ Tendulkar later used one **urban PLB** for both areas instead of State-wise calorie lines.

30.s: Which of the following was a significant change introduced by the Tendulkar methodology?
o: Replacement of MRP by URP for all items
Use of one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas
Removal of private health expenditure from consumption
30.x: The Tendulkar methodology used one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas. It moved away from an exclusive calorie anchor, included private health and education expenditure, and used MRP in place of URP.
30.tq: Identify the methodological reform and reject reversed or extreme alternatives.
xs: **Tendulkar** used **one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It used **MRP in place of URP** (not the reverse), moved **away from the calorie anchor**, and **added** private **health and education** spending.
xa: **MRP** = **365-day recall** for five low-frequency items.
Tendulkar Expert Group: set up **Dec 2005**, report **Dec 2009**.
Tendulkar 2011-12 poverty: **21.9%**.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the Rangarajan poverty estimation methodology?
o: Use of calorie, protein and fat norms
Use of a single urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas
Separate treatment of food and non-food requirements
30.x: The single urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas was associated with Tendulkar. Rangarajan used separate food and non-food requirements, nutritional norms and MMRP data.
30.tq: Identify the method belonging to the neighbouring committee.
xs: A **single urban poverty line basket** for rural and urban areas was **Tendulkar's** feature, not Rangarajan's — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rangarajan** treated **food and non-food** needs separately, used calories **2,155 rural / 2,090 urban** plus **protein and fat** norms, and used **MMRP** data.
xa: Rangarajan group: set up **2012**, report **2014**; poverty **29.5%** (2011-12).
**RBI (2025)** updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23** using PLB food + non-food weights.
Updated line: rural poverty highest in **Chhattisgarh (25.1%)**, lowest in **HP (0.4%)**.

30.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes URP from MRP?
o: URP uses a 30-day recall period for all items, whereas MRP uses 365 days for selected low-frequency items.
URP uses a 365-day recall period for every item, whereas MRP uses 30 days for every item.
MRP is used only for urban poverty estimation.
Both URP and MRP use only annual income data.
30.x: URP uses a 30-day recall period for all items. MRP uses a 365-day recall period for five low-frequency items such as clothing, footwear, durables, education and institutional medical care.
30.tq: Split the two recall-period concepts by comparing their time spans and coverage.
xs: **URP** = **30-day recall for all items**; **MRP** = **365-day recall for five low-frequency items** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The five MRP items: **clothing, footwear, durables, education, institutional medical care**.
Both measure **consumption**, not income, and both apply to rural and urban estimates.
xa: URP was used **up to 1993-94**.
Both URP and MRP measure the **incidence of poverty** (APPSC 2018 key).
**Tendulkar** moved from URP to **MRP**; **Rangarajan** used **MMRP**.

30.s: The Uniform Reference Period (URP) and the Mixed Reference Period (MRP) are both used to measure the:
30.x: URP and MRP are recall methods for consumption data, and both are used to measure the incidence of poverty (APPSC 2018 key). They are not measures of inflation, unemployment or inequality.
30.tq: URP/MRP = consumption recall periods -> poverty incidence.
xs: **URP** and **MRP** are recall methods that both measure the **incidence of poverty** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
They gather **consumption** data; they do not measure inflation, unemployment or inequality.
xa: **URP**: **30-day** recall for all items; used up to **1993-94**.
**MRP**: **365-day** recall for clothing, footwear, durables, education, institutional medical care.
**Tendulkar** replaced URP with **MRP**.

30.s: N.C. Saxena’s report of August 2009 was primarily concerned with:
o: Preparing the rural BPL Census methodology
30.x: N.C. Saxena’s report, prepared for the Ministry of Rural Development, dealt with the method for the rural BPL Census rather than poverty estimation itself.
30.tq: Separate BPL identification from poverty-line estimation.
xs: **N.C. Saxena's** report (Ministry of Rural Development, **Aug 2009**) gave the method for the **rural BPL Census** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was **not** about poverty estimation; the **urban BPL** method came from **S.R. Hashim**.
xa: Automatic **exclusion**: e.g. **income-tax payers**.
Automatic **inclusion**: **PVTGs**, single-woman-headed, destitute + homeless households, **bonded labourers**.
⚠ **Saxena** = rural BPL; **Hashim** = urban BPL.

30.s: Which of the following was proposed as an example of automatic inclusion in the rural BPL identification approach associated with N.C. Saxena?
30.x: The proposed automatic-inclusion categories included PVTGs, single-woman-headed households, destitute and homeless households, and bonded labourers. Income-tax payers were examples of automatic exclusion.
30.tq: Distinguish automatic inclusion from automatic exclusion categories.
xs: **PVTGs** were an **automatic inclusion** category in **N.C. Saxena's** rural BPL approach — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Income-tax payers** were an example of **automatic exclusion**.
xa: Other automatic-inclusion groups: **single-woman-headed**, **destitute + homeless** households, **bonded labourers**.
Saxena's report: Ministry of Rural Development, **Aug 2009**.
⚠ **Hashim** = urban BPL identification.

30.s: The Planning Commission working group associated with the identification of urban BPL families was chaired by:
30.x: S.R. Hashim headed the Planning Commission working group concerned with identifying urban BPL families.
30.tq: Match the expert with the specific BPL-identification task.
xs: The Planning Commission working group to **identify urban BPL** families was chaired by **S.R. Hashim** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**N.C. Saxena** handled the **rural BPL Census**; **Alagh** and **Lakdawala** worked on poverty estimation, not BPL identification.
xa: ⚠ **Saxena** = rural BPL; **Hashim** = urban BPL.
Saxena's report came in **Aug 2009** for the Ministry of Rural Development.
Saxena's automatic inclusion: **PVTGs**, bonded labourers, destitute households.

30.s: According to the poverty ratio estimates for 1993–94, which of the following combinations is correct?
o: 45.3% under the Lakdawala Committee and 36.0% under the Tendulkar Committee
29.8% under the Lakdawala Committee and 21.9% under the Tendulkar Committee
36.0% under the Lakdawala Committee and 45.3% under the Tendulkar Committee
27.5% under the Lakdawala Committee and 37.2% under the Tendulkar Committee
30.x: For 1993–94, the poverty ratio was estimated at 36.0% using the Lakdawala methodology and 45.3% using the Tendulkar methodology.
30.tq: Match the year with the correct pair of estimates before comparing the committees.
xs: For **1993-94**: **36.0%** under **Lakdawala** and **45.3%** under **Tendulkar** — so option **(3)** is correct.
xa: Source: **Annexure 9.1** (2024-25).

30.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the poverty ratio estimates for 2011–12?
30.x: For 2011–12, the poverty ratio was 21.9% according to the Tendulkar estimate and 29.5% according to the Rangarajan estimate.
30.tq: Discriminate between the two committee estimates for the same round instead of relying on chronology alone.
xs: For **2011-12**: **21.9%** under **Tendulkar** and **29.5%** under **Rangarajan** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 2 swaps them; **29.8%** is Tendulkar 2009-10; **37.2% / 45.3%** are Tendulkar's 2004-05 and 1993-94 figures.
xa: Rangarajan used **MMRP** data, which records higher consumption.
Rangarajan group: set up **2012**, report **2014**.
**RBI (2025)** updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23**.

30.s: Under the Tendulkar methodology, India's poverty ratio for 2004-05 was:
30.x: Tendulkar put 2004-05 poverty at 37.2% (rural 41.8, urban 25.7). 27.5% is the Lakdawala estimate for 2004-05 (and a mistaken Tendulkar urban figure in some tables); 29.8% is Tendulkar for 2009-10; 45.3% is Tendulkar for 1993-94.
xs: **Tendulkar** put **2004-05** poverty at **37.2%** (rural **41.8**, urban **25.7**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**27.5%** is **Lakdawala's** 2004-05 estimate; **29.8%** is Tendulkar 2009-10; **45.3%** is Tendulkar 1993-94.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some tables show Tendulkar urban 2004-05 as **27.5**; correct = **25.7**.
Lakdawala 2004-05: rural **28.3**, urban **25.7**.

30.s: According to the updated Rangarajan poverty line for 2022–23, which of the following correctly identifies the States with the highest poverty ratios?
30.x: Chhattisgarh had the highest rural poverty ratio at 25.1% and also the highest urban poverty ratio at 13.3%.
30.tq: Test whether the same State leads both sectors rather than swapping the highest and lowest entries.
xs: Under the RBI-updated **Rangarajan** line (2022-23), **Chhattisgarh** has the highest poverty both **rural (25.1%)** and **urban (13.3%)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Tamil Nadu** has the **lowest** urban poverty (**1.9%**) and **Himachal Pradesh** the lowest rural (**0.4%**) — not the highest.
xa: The update used **HCES 2022-23** with PLB food + non-food weights.
Rangarajan's own 2011-12 ratio was **29.5%**.
AP's **MPI** fell **0.053 to 0.025**; ranks **9th**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding poverty lines and government policy:
1. A higher poverty line may increase fiscal costs.
2. A lower poverty line may result in exclusion of needy persons.
3. Poverty lines are politically sensitive.
4. Governments may delay action on committee reports because of these considerations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All four statements are correct. Raising the poverty line can increase fiscal costs, while lowering it can exclude needy people, making poverty measurement politically sensitive and sometimes delaying governmental action.
30.tq: Identify the linked cause-and-effect chain rather than treating fiscal and exclusion concerns as mutually exclusive.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: a **higher poverty line** means **higher fiscal costs**.
Statement 2 is correct: a **lower line excludes the needy**.
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: poverty lines are **politically sensitive**, and governments **delay acting on committee reports** — so option **(4)** 1, 2, 3 and 4 is correct.
xa: Lakdawala's report came in **1993** but was accepted only in **1997**.
Tendulkar: set up **2005**, reported **2009**; Rangarajan: set up **2012**, reported **2014**.
**Saxena** (rural BPL) and **Hashim** (urban BPL) dealt with identifying beneficiaries.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The first concept of poverty-line study was associated with Dandekar and Rath in 1971.
II. The Lakdawala Committee was associated with 1989.
III. The Tendulkar Committee was associated with 2005, and its report was published in 2009.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: the Dandekar–Rath poverty-line study came in 1971, the Lakdawala Committee in 1989, and the Tendulkar Committee in 2005, reporting in 2009.
30.tq: Arrange the poverty committees in time order.
n: Dandekar and Rath conducted the first study of the concept of the poverty line in 1971. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Lakdawala Committee was established in 1989. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Tendulkar Committee was established in 2005. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Tendulkar Report was published in 2009. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]

30.s: The Alagh Committee, constituted in which year, was associated with the nutrition/calorie-based poverty line?
30.x: The Alagh Task Force (1979) set the first poverty line based on calorie needs: 2,400 kcal in rural areas and 2,100 in urban areas.
n: The Alagh Committee was established in 1979. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Alagh Committee is associated with a nutrition/calorie-based poverty line. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]

30.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Dandekar and Rath were associated with the poverty-line concept/study in 1971.
Tendulkar Committee was associated with a revised poverty methodology in 2009.
Rangarajan Committee was associated with separate rural/urban consumption baskets in 2009.
Lakdawala Committee was associated with poverty estimation methodology in 1993.
30.x: Option C is incorrect: the Rangarajan Committee, with separate rural and urban consumption baskets, reported in 2014, not 2009. 2009 is the Tendulkar report.
30.tq: Arrange the poverty committees in time order.
n: The Dandekar & Rath study was conducted in 1971. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
Dandekar & Rath are associated with the poverty-line concept/study. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Lakdawala Committee was established in 1993. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Lakdawala Committee is associated with poverty estimation methodology. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Tendulkar Committee was established in 2009. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Tendulkar Committee is associated with a revised poverty methodology. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Rangarajan Committee was established in 2014. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Rangarajan Committee is associated with a separate rural/urban consumption basket. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]

31.s: The World Bank extreme-poverty estimate using the $3-a-day line declined from 27.1 percent in 2011–12 to
31.x: The World Bank extreme-poverty estimate using the $3-a-day line declined to 5.3 percent in 2022–23.
31.tq: Keep the dollar threshold and reference year attached to the correct estimate.
xs: World Bank **$3-a-day** poverty fell from **27.1%** (2011-12) to **5.3 percent in 2022-23** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**11.28%** is the **NITI MPI** (2022-23); **2.3%** is the **Tendulkar** line (2023-24); **6.06%** is AP's MPI headcount (2019-21).
xa: Sources: **ES 2025-26** and **LENS Jun 2025**.

31.s: According to the Tendulkar methodology, the rural poverty ratio in India in 2011-12 was:
31.x: Rural poverty was 25.7% in 2011-12 (APPSC-GS 2018 key). 13.7% was urban poverty, 21.9% the all-India ratio, and 33.8% the rural ratio in 2009-10.
31.tq: 2011-12 Tendulkar: rural 25.7, urban 13.7, total 21.9.
xs: Tendulkar **rural** poverty in **2011-12** was **25.7%** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2018 key).
