31.s: Approximately how many people in India were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2015, as cited in APPSC-GS 2025?
31.x: More than 90 million people were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2015 (APPSC-GS 2025 key). The other figures are either too small or far larger than the cited estimate.
31.tq: 2011-2015: 90 million+ out of poverty.
xs: **More than 90 million** people were lifted out of poverty between **2011 and 2015** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
The MDG target was to halve poverty to **23.9% by 2015**.

31.s: According to NITI Aayog's National MPI, India's multidimensional poverty headcount fell from 55.3% in 2005-06 to:
31.x: The NITI MPI headcount fell from 55.3% (2005-06) to 14.96% (2019-21) and 11.28% (2022-23). Option B mixes Tendulkar-line figures, option C is the World Bank $3/day series, and option D gives Tendulkar estimates.
xs: Option 2 mixes **Tendulkar** figures; option 3 is the **World Bank $3/day** series; option 4 is **Tendulkar** 2009-10 and 2011-12.
xa: AP's MPI headcount (2019-21): **6.06%**, rank **9th**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the regional pattern of poverty in India in 2011-12 (Tendulkar method):
1. Chhattisgarh had the highest poverty ratio among the States.
2. Goa had the lowest poverty ratio among the States.
3. Bihar had the largest number of poor persons.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Chhattisgarh had the highest Tendulkar ratio (39.93%) and Goa the lowest (5.09%). Statement 3 is wrong: Uttar Pradesh, not Bihar, had the largest number of poor (about 5.98 crore). So A omits statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
31.tq: Highest ratio and largest number are different questions: Chhattisgarh for the ratio, UP for the number.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Chhattisgarh** had the highest Tendulkar ratio (**39.93%**).
Statement 2 is correct: **Goa** had the lowest (**5.09%**).
Statement 3 is wrong: the **largest number of poor** was in **Uttar Pradesh** (about **5.98 crore**), not Bihar — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: ⚠ Highest ratio = **Chhattisgarh**; highest MPI = **Bihar**; largest number = **UP**.
National MPI 2023: **Bihar** highest (**0.16**, ranked **28th**), **Kerala** lowest (**0.002**).
Poverty is concentrated in the **BIMARU** belt + East.

31.s: Which one of the following groups correctly represents the BIMARU and eastern belt States identified as having concentrated poverty?
o: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh
Goa, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat and Maharashtra
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Goa, Tamil Nadu and Odisha
Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Goa, Kerala, Sikkim and Gujarat
31.x: The high-poverty belt comprises Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
31.tq: Match the complete regional grouping rather than selecting a few familiar States.
xs: The **BIMARU** belt + East with concentrated poverty = **Bihar, UP, MP, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh** — so option **(1)** is correct.
These sit at the **bottom of the MPI table** (UP **0.103**, Jharkhand **0.131**).
**Kerala, Goa, Tamil Nadu** are the **lowest**-MPI States, not the high-poverty belt.
xa: **Convergence**: high-poverty States fell fastest.
MPI exits: **UP 5.94 crore**, Bihar **3.77**, MP **2.30**, Rajasthan **1.87**.
Rural Odisha fell **47.8% to 8.6%**; urban Bihar **50.8% to 9.1%** (2011-12 to 2022-23).

31.s: According to the National MPI 2023 (NFHS-5, 2019-21), the States with the highest and lowest multidimensional poverty were respectively:
31.x: Bihar had the highest MPI (0.16, ranked 28th) and Kerala the lowest (0.002), followed by Goa and TN. UP and Jharkhand are also near the bottom but below Bihar; Chhattisgarh was highest under the Tendulkar 2011-12 ratio, not the MPI.
31.tq: MPI: Bihar worst, Kerala best. Tendulkar 2011-12: Chhattisgarh worst, Goa best.
xs: National MPI 2023 (2019-21): **Bihar** highest (MPI **0.16**, ranked **28th**) and **Kerala** lowest (**0.002**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**UP (0.103)** and **Jharkhand (0.131)** are near the bottom but below Bihar; **Chhattisgarh** topped the **Tendulkar 2011-12** ratio, not the MPI.
xa: After Kerala, the lowest MPI States are **Goa** and **TN**.
⚠ Highest ratio = **Chhattisgarh** (Tendulkar); highest MPI = **Bihar**; largest number = **UP**.
India's MPI score: **0.066**; AP's **0.025**.

31.s: Which social group has the highest poverty ratio in India according to the Tendulkar estimates for 2011-12?
31.x: Scheduled Tribes had the highest poverty ratio among social groups; rural ST poverty was about 45%, followed by Scheduled Castes.
31.tq: Use the social-group ranking rather than the overall rural or urban ranking.
xs: **Scheduled Tribes** have the highest poverty (Tendulkar 2011-12: **rural ST about 45%**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Scheduled Castes** come **next**.
xa: In AP, districts with **large tribal populations** have higher poverty.
Education gap: **35.1%** of those with no formal education are poor vs **14.9%** with post-secondary education.
North Coastal Andhra's poverty is linked to **tribal/ITDA agency tracts**.

31.s: Which one of the following best explains the regional contrast in agricultural poverty within Andhra Pradesh?
o: Greater dependence on irrigated agriculture in Rayalaseema and lower productivity in delta districts
Uniform irrigation coverage and similar agricultural productivity across all districts
Higher agricultural productivity in delta districts and greater dependence on rain-fed agriculture in Rayalaseema
Predominance of plantation agriculture in both delta districts and Rayalaseema
31.x: Delta districts generally benefit from better irrigation and higher agricultural productivity, whereas rain-fed Rayalaseema faces greater agricultural vulnerability and poverty.
31.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap by distinguishing irrigated delta areas from rain-fed Rayalaseema.
xs: **Delta districts** have higher **agricultural productivity and irrigation**, while **Rayalaseema** is **rain-fed** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 1 reverses the two regions; irrigation is not uniform across districts.
xa: Rayalaseema's **Kurnool** (**12.84%**) is AP's poorest district by MPI.
**West Godavari** (delta) is the least poor (**2.42%**).
Other causes: **seasonal unemployment**, **climate vulnerability**, rural-urban divide.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of regional poverty differences in Andhra Pradesh:
1. A skill mismatch arises as the economy shifts towards technology.
2. Remoteness of tribal areas contributes to poverty.
3. Delta districts are poorer than Rayalaseema because they depend on rain-fed agriculture.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: skill mismatch as the economy shifts to technology, and tribal remoteness, are listed under infrastructure and human capital. Statement 3 is wrong: Rayalaseema is the rain-fed and poorer region, while the irrigated delta districts are the least poor. So A omits statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
31.tq: Delta = irrigated and least poor; Rayalaseema = rain-fed and poorer.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **skill mismatch** arises as the economy shifts to **technology**.
Statement 2 is correct: **tribal remoteness** adds to poverty (infrastructure and human capital).
Statement 3 is wrong: **Rayalaseema** is rain-fed and poorer; **delta districts** are least poor — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: Least poor: **West Godavari** (**2.42%**); poorest: **Kurnool** (**12.84%**).
**Social transfers** (PMGKAY, MGNREGA, PMAY-G) helped cut poverty.

31.s: Which of the following correctly compares Andhra Pradesh and India under the Tendulkar method for 2011-12?
o: AP rural 5.81%, urban 10.96%, total 9.20%; India rural 13.70%, urban 25.70%, total 21.92%
AP rural 25.70%, urban 13.70%, total 21.92%; India rural 10.96%, urban 5.81%, total 9.20%
AP rural 10.96%, urban 5.81%, total 9.20%; India rural 25.70%, urban 13.70%, total 21.92%
AP rural 9.20%, urban 10.96%, total 5.81%; India rural 21.92%, urban 25.70%, total 13.70%
31.x: The correct comparison is AP: 10.96% rural, 5.81% urban and 9.20% total; India: 25.70%, 13.70% and 21.92% respectively.
31.tq: Keep the order rural–urban–total unchanged while comparing the two jurisdictions.
xs: Tendulkar 2011-12: **AP rural 10.96%, urban 5.81%, total 9.20%**; **India rural 25.70%, urban 13.70%, total 21.92%** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 1 swaps AP's rural and urban; option 2 swaps AP and India; option 4 jumbles the figures.
xa: AP MPI headcount (2019-21): **6.06%** vs India **14.96%**.
AP MPI score **0.025** vs India **0.066**.

31.s: The multidimensional poverty ratio in Andhra Pradesh declined from 41.6% in 2005-06 to approximately what level according to the cited 2023 estimate?
31.x: The cited APPSC-GS 2023 figure records a decline in AP’s multidimensional poverty from 41.6% to 21%.
31.tq: Distinguish this estimate from the later 2019-21 MPI figure of 6.06%.
xs: AP's **multidimensional poverty** fell from **41.6% (2005-06)** to **21%** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2023 key).
**6.06%** is AP's 2019-21 MPI headcount; **9.20%** is AP's Tendulkar 2011-12 ratio; **14.96%** is India's MPI headcount.
xa: Focus areas: years of schooling, drinking water, sanitation, bank accounts, child-adolescent mortality, nutrition.

31.s: Which district had the highest MPI poverty headcount ratio among the districts listed for Andhra Pradesh?
31.x: Kurnool had the highest listed MPI poverty headcount ratio at 12.84%, with an MPI of 0.054.
31.tq: Identify the maximum value while separating it from other high-poverty districts.
xs: **Kurnool** had the highest MPI headcount among AP districts — **12.84%** (MPI **0.054**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Vizianagaram (8.66%)**, **Visakhapatnam (7.60%)** and **Anantapur (6.74%)** follow.
xa: ⚠ **West Godavari** = least poor (**2.42%**); **Kurnool** = poorest.
Also higher-poverty: **Prakasam (6.28%)**, **East Godavari (6.13%)**.
Poorer belts: **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal Andhra**.

31.s: Which regional pattern of poverty is correctly associated with Andhra Pradesh?
o: Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra are poorer, while delta districts are generally least poor.
Delta districts and Coastal Andhra are poorer, while Rayalaseema is least poor.
Only urban districts of Rayalaseema show higher poverty.
All districts of Coastal Andhra have uniformly high poverty, irrespective of geography.
31.x: Poverty is higher in Rayalaseema districts such as Kurnool and Anantapur and in North Coastal Andhra, while delta districts are generally least poor.
31.tq: Use the regional contrast rather than judging districts by coastal or inland labels alone.
xs: **Rayalaseema** (Kurnool, Anantapur) and **North Coastal Andhra** (Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam) are **poorer**, while **delta districts** are least poor — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option 2 reverses the pattern; poverty is not uniform across Coastal Andhra.
xa: North Coastal poverty is tied to **tribal/ITDA agency tracts**.
Delta districts gain from **irrigation**; Rayalaseema is **rain-fed**.
Least poor: **West Godavari 2.42%**, **YSR Kadapa 3.34%**, **Guntur 4.36%**, **Krishna 4.38%**.

31.s: Which district of Andhra Pradesh had the lowest MPI poverty headcount ratio among the districts listed?
31.x: West Godavari had the lowest headcount ratio (2.42%, MPI 0.010). YSR Kadapa (3.34%), Guntur (4.36%) and Krishna (4.38%) followed it.
31.tq: Lowest = West Godavari; highest = Kurnool.
xs: **West Godavari** had the lowest MPI headcount — **2.42%** (MPI **0.010**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**YSR Kadapa (3.34%)**, **Guntur (4.36%)** and **Krishna (4.38%)** follow.
xa: ⚠ **West Godavari** = least poor; **Kurnool** = poorest (**12.84%**).
Least poor are **delta districts**.
Poorer belts: **Rayalaseema** + **North Coastal Andhra**.

31.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: IKP — Mission for Elimination of Poverty in Municipal Areas
Velugu — District Poverty Initiatives Project, World Bank aided, run by SERP
MEPMA — Rural women’s SHGs established in 2000
SERP — Urban SHGs in municipal areas established in 2007
31.x: Velugu was the World Bank-aided District Poverty Initiatives Project implemented through SERP. MEPMA concerns urban SHGs, SERP rural mobilisation, and IKP was the renamed Velugu programme.
31.tq: Identify the correctly matched institution by separating rural, urban and renamed programmes.
xs: **Velugu** = **District Poverty Initiatives Project**, **World Bank aided**, **run by SERP** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**IKP** is Velugu renamed (**Indira Kranthi Patham**); **SERP** works with the **rural** poor in women's SHGs, not urban areas.
xa: **SERP** = **Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty** (**2000**).
⚠ **Velugu** → renamed **IKP** in **2004-05**.
**APMSS** = **Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha** (APPSC 2018 key).

31.s: In Andhra Pradesh, SERP stands for, and is primarily concerned with:
o: Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty: mobilising the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods
State Employment and Relief Programme: wage employment in urban areas
Scheme for Elimination of Rural Poverty: cash transfers to farmers
Society for Economic Reforms and Planning: drafting the State budget
31.x: SERP is the Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (2000), which mobilises the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods (APPSC 2021 key). The other expansions are invented and describe roles SERP does not play.
31.tq: SERP = rural SHGs; MEPMA = urban; Velugu -> IKP.
xs: **SERP** = **Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty**: **mobilising the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2021 key).
It is not a wage-employment, cash-transfer or budget body.
xa: SERP was set up in **2000** and ran **Velugu**.
**MoUs**: SERP + MEPMA with **ISB, XLRI, IIM-Visakhapatnam**.

31.s: APMSS, an Andhra Pradesh poverty-alleviation body for rural and urban poor households, stands for:
o: Andhra Pradesh Mission for Social Security
31.x: APMSS is the Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha, working on poverty alleviation for rural and urban poor households (APPSC 2018 key). The other expansions are made up.
31.tq: APMSS = Mahila Sadhikara Samstha.
xs: **APMSS** = **Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha**, for **rural and urban poor** households — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
Its role is **poverty alleviation**; the other expansions do not appear among AP's poverty bodies.
xa: **SERP** = Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (**2000**).
**IKP** = **Indira Kranthi Patham**, Velugu renamed (**2004-05**).
SHG loans **Mar 2026**: **₹10,100 crore** under SERP, MEPMA, Stree Nidhi, PMEGP.

31.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the poverty-reduction or livelihood model associated with it?
1. Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana — Bihar
2. Poverty-eradication model — Kerala
3. Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana — Centre under DAY-NRLM
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
31.x: Bihar’s Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana, Kerala’s poverty-eradication model and the Centre’s Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana under DAY-NRLM are all cited as models based on the graduation approach.
31.tq: Start from the sure institutional pair and verify all three state or Centre associations.
xs: All three pairs are correct **graduation-approach** models: Bihar's **Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana**, **Kerala's** poverty-eradication model, and the Centre's **Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana** under **DAY-NRLM** — so option **(4)** 1, 2 and 3 is correct.
They are cited as current relevance for **2025-26**.
xa: **VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025**: rural job guarantee raised to **125 days**.
Social protection coverage: **22% (2016) to 64.3% (2025)**.
Kerala has the **lowest MPI** (**0.002**).

31.s: The VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025, passed by Parliament on 18 December 2025, raised the rural job guarantee to how many days?
31.x: The VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025, passed on 18 December 2025, increased the rural job guarantee to 125 days.
31.tq: Distinguish the revised numerical entitlement from the familiar earlier figure.
xs: The **VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025** (passed **18 Dec 2025**) raised the **rural job guarantee** to **125 days** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of India's **social protection** expansion.
xa: Social protection coverage: **22% (2016) to 64.3% (2025)**.
**MGNREGA** is listed among transfers that helped cut poverty.
Graduation-approach model: Centre's **Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana** under **DAY-NRLM**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Lorenz curve:
1. The X-axis shows the cumulative percentage of population (poorest first) and the Y-axis the cumulative percentage of income.
2. The farther the curve bows away from the 45-degree line, the lower the inequality.
3. It shows inequality visually but gives no single number; the Gini coefficient provides that.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the axes are cumulative population (X) and cumulative income (Y), and the Lorenz curve is only a visual tool, with the Gini giving the single number. Statement 2 is wrong: the 45-degree diagonal is perfect equality, so bowing farther away means greater inequality. So A omits statement 3, and C and D wrongly include statement 2.
32.tq: Diagonal = perfect equality; the bigger the bow, the bigger the inequality (and the bigger the Gini).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **X-axis** = cumulative % of **population** (poorest first); **Y-axis** = cumulative % of **income**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **45° diagonal** is perfect equality, so bowing further away means **greater** inequality.
Statement 3 is correct: the curve gives **no single number**; the **Gini** does — so option **(2)** 1 and 3 only is correct.
xa: Lorenz curve: **Max Lorenz**, **1906**.
Gini = area between curve and equality line ÷ whole area under that line.
Gini range: **0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything)**.

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Curve)
a. Lorenz curve
b. Phillips curve
c. Laffer curve
 d. Marshall curve
List-II (Relationship shown)
i. Tax rate and tax revenue
 ii. Demand, price and quantity demanded
 iii. Distribution of income or wealth
 iv. Inflation and unemployment

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Lorenz, Phillips, Laffer and Marshall curves respectively represent distribution, inflation–unemployment, tax rate–revenue and demand relationships.
32.tq: Start from the sure pair for the Lorenz curve and eliminate codes containing wrong pairings.
xs: **Lorenz – distribution of income or wealth**; **Phillips – inflation and unemployment**; **Laffer – tax rate and tax revenue**; **Marshall – demand (price vs quantity)** — so option **(1)** a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii is correct.
The **Phillips** curve shows an **inverse** link between inflation and unemployment.
xa: **Kuznets curve**: inequality vs per capita income (**inverted U**, **1955**).
**Gini coefficient**: **Corrado Gini**, **1912**.
⚠ **1906 – 1912 – 1955** = Lorenz – Gini – Kuznets.

32.s: Who proposed the Gini coefficient in 1912 in the work titled “Variability and Mutability”?
32.x: Corrado Gini proposed the coefficient in 1912 in “Variability and Mutability”.
32.tq: Use the author–year–work combination to distinguish the Gini coefficient from the Lorenz curve.
xs: The **Gini coefficient** was proposed by **Corrado Gini** in **1912** in "**Variability and Mutability**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Max Lorenz** gave the **Lorenz curve (1906)**; **Simon Kuznets** the inverted-U **Kuznets curve (1955)**; **Amartya Sen** wrote **Inequality Reexamined**.
xa: Gini range: **0 to 1**; **Gini index** = value × **100**.
**Higher value means more inequality** (JPSC 2023 key).
The Gini is derived from the **Lorenz curve**.

32.s: The Gini coefficient is derived from the Lorenz curve as:
o: The difference between urban and rural MPCE divided by urban MPCE
The ratio of tax revenue to per capita income
The area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line divided by the whole area under the equality line
The area under the Lorenz curve divided by total population
32.x: The Gini coefficient is the area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line divided by the whole area under that equality line.
32.tq: Translate the geometric definition into the precise area ratio.
xs: The **Gini coefficient** = **area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line ÷ whole area under the equality line** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is not an MPCE ratio or a tax ratio.
xa: Range: **0 (perfect equality)** to **1 (one person has everything)**.
The **equality line** is the **45° diagonal**.
Gini index = coefficient × **100**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Gini coefficient:
1. Its value ranges from 0 to 1.
2. A value of 0 indicates that one person holds all the income.
3. A higher value indicates greater inequality.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the Gini runs from 0 to 1 and a higher value means more inequality (JPSC 2023 key). Statement 2 is wrong: 0 is perfect equality, while 1 means one person has everything. So options A, C and D wrongly include statement 2.
32.tq: Gini 0 = perfect equality; 1 = total inequality.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the Gini ranges from **0 to 1**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **0 = perfect equality**; **1** = one person has everything.
Statement 3 is correct: a **higher value means more inequality** — so option **(2)** 1 and 3 only is correct (JPSC 2023 key).
xa: **Gini index** = coefficient × **100**.
The Gini is derived from the **Lorenz curve**.
**Corrado Gini** proposed it in **1912**.

32.s: With reference to the Environmental Kuznets Curve, which one of the following is correct?
o: Per-capita income is on the Y-axis and environmental degradation is on the X-axis; the curve is U-shaped.
Tax rate is on the X-axis and revenue is on the Y-axis; the curve is inverted-U shaped.
Per-capita income is on the X-axis and environmental degradation or pollution is on the Y-axis; the curve is inverted-U shaped.
Inflation is on the X-axis and unemployment is on the Y-axis; the curve is downward sloping.
32.x: The Environmental Kuznets Curve places per-capita income on the X-axis and environmental degradation or pollution on the Y-axis. Degradation initially rises, reaches a peak and then falls, producing an inverted-U shape.
32.tq: Check both axes before identifying the curve’s shape.
xs: The **Environmental Kuznets Curve** has **per capita income** on the **X-axis**, **environmental degradation/pollution** on the **Y-axis**, and is **inverted-U** shaped — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 1 swaps the axes and the shape; tax rate–revenue is the **Laffer** curve; inflation–unemployment is the **Phillips** curve.
xa: Degradation **rises** in early growth, **peaks**, then **falls** as income rises.
Message: "**the solution to pollution is economic growth**".
It is borrowed from the **Kuznets Curve** (inequality vs income).

32.s: Which one of the following best describes the Kuznets hypothesis for a developing economy?
o: Inequality first rises and then falls as the economy grows
Inequality continuously falls as per capita income rises
Inequality remains unchanged at all levels of development
Inequality first falls and then rises as per capita income increases
32.x: The Kuznets hypothesis describes an inverted-U relationship: inequality rises during the initial phase of development and falls at higher income levels.
32.tq: Identify the direction of change on the two sides of the inverted-U relationship.
xs: Kuznets hypothesis: as a developing economy grows, **inequality first rises and then falls** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This gives an **inverted-U** between inequality and **per capita income**; option 4 describes a U, the reverse.
xa: **Simon Kuznets** proposed it in **1955**.
The **Environmental Kuznets curve** borrows the same inverted-U shape for pollution.
⚠ **1906 – 1912 – 1955** = Lorenz – Gini – Kuznets.

32.s: The indicator used in NSSO/NSO household surveys for measuring household inequality is generally:
32.x: Household inequality in these surveys is assessed through consumption expenditure, particularly monthly per capita consumption expenditure (MPCE), rather than income or wealth.
32.tq: Distinguish the survey indicator from the two commonly confused concepts of income and wealth.
xs: **NSSO/NSO** surveys measure inequality through **consumption expenditure (MPCE)**, not income or wealth — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
India has **no official income survey**; **wealth** is measured by the **All India Debt and Investment Survey**.
xa: **HCES** (MoSPI) gives rural + urban MPCE every **five** years.
Consumption data make inequality **look lower** than other measures.
Critique: consumption data **understate top-end incomes**.

32.s:
Match List-I (type of inequality) with List-II (main data source in India):
List-I
a. Consumption inequality
b. Income inequality
c. Wealth inequality
List-II
i. All India Debt and Investment Survey (NSS), plus WID/Oxfam estimates
ii. NSS/HCES of MoSPI
iii. PLFS wages, tax data and the World Inequality Database (no official income survey)
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: Option A is correct: consumption inequality rests on NSS/HCES (MoSPI); income inequality, with no official income survey, is estimated from PLFS wages, tax data and the WID; wealth inequality uses the All India Debt and Investment Survey plus WID/Oxfam. B swaps consumption and income; C swaps income and wealth; D swaps consumption and wealth.
32.tq: Official data exist only for consumption (HCES); income is estimated; wealth = AIDIS.
xs: **Consumption – NSS/HCES (MoSPI)**; **income – PLFS wages, tax data, WID** (no official income survey); **wealth – All India Debt and Investment Survey + WID/Oxfam** — so option **(1)** a-ii, b-iii, c-i is correct.
Official inequality estimates rest on **consumption** data.
xa: WID: income inequality **rising**; top 10% median earnings = **13 times** bottom 10% (**2023-24**).
Top 10% hold about **77%** of national wealth (older Oxfam figure).
Land: about **46%** of rural households are **landless**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding land inequality in rural India:
1. About 46 percent of rural households are landless.
2. Inequality is higher in former zamindari areas than in former princely States.
3. These findings are associated with the World Inequality Lab’s cited analysis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: About 46 percent of rural households are reported to be landless, and land inequality is higher in former zamindari areas than in former princely States; the cited analysis is associated with the World Inequality Lab.
32.tq: Combine the numerical fact, regional comparison and institutional attribution.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: about **46%** of rural households are **landless**.
Statement 2 is correct: land inequality is higher in former **zamindari** areas than in former **princely States**.
Statement 3 is correct: these come from the **World Inequality Lab** (**Apr 2026**) — so option **(4)** 1, 2 and 3 is correct.
xa: **Ceiling on land holdings** is a **direct** measure to cut inequality (APPSC-G2 2008 key).
World Inequality Lab is based at the **Paris School of Economics**.
Top 10% hold about **77%** of national wealth.

32.s: According to the NSS 2011–12 figures, the rural and urban MPCE were respectively:
32.x: The NSS 2011–12 figures were ₹1,430 for rural MPCE and ₹2,630 for urban MPCE.
32.tq: Compare the survey-year labels before matching the numerical pair.
xs: **NSS 2011-12**: rural MPCE **₹1,430**, urban **₹2,630** — so option **(3)** is correct (gap about **₹1,200**, APPSC-GS 2018 key).
xa: Urban MPCE was about **84%** above rural in **2011-12**.
HCES (MoSPI) is the official consumption source.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding nominal HCES 2023–24 MPCE is correct?
o: Rural MPCE was ₹1,430 and urban MPCE was ₹2,630
Rural MPCE was ₹4,122 and urban MPCE was ₹6,996
Rural MPCE was ₹2,079 and urban MPCE was ₹3,632
Rural MPCE was ₹3,773 and urban MPCE was ₹6,459
32.x: Nominal HCES 2023–24 MPCE was ₹4,122 in rural areas and ₹6,996 in urban areas, with the urban figure about 70 percent higher.
32.tq: Distinguish nominal HCES data from the separately reported LENS series.
xs: Nominal **HCES 2023-24** MPCE: **rural ₹4,122** and **urban ₹6,996** (about **70%** gap) — so option **(2)** is correct.
xa: The 2022-23 urban-rural gap was about **71%**; 2011-12 about **84%**.
HCES is run by **MoSPI**.
Debate: consumption data **understate top-end incomes**.

32.s: With reference to intra-State disparities in Andhra Pradesh, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Only the Coastal districts are identified as lagging regions.
The State has no significant district-level variation in MPI headcount.
West Godavari and Kurnool have identical MPI headcounts.
Rayalaseema and North Coastal districts are identified as lagging regions.
32.x: Rayalaseema and North Coastal districts lag in the context of intra-State disparities. Andhra Pradesh also shows variation in district MPI headcount, ranging from 2.42% to 12.84%.
32.tq: Identify the precise regional comparison instead of accepting an absolute or reversed statement.
xs: **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal** districts are the **lagging regions** in AP — so option **(4)** is correct.
District MPI headcount varies widely: **West Godavari 2.42%** to **Kurnool 12.84%** — not identical, not uniform.
xa: District-level **MPI** gaps are AP's inequality measure in **APSES**.
Inter-State MPI range: **Kerala 0.002** to **Bihar 0.16**.

32.s: Which of the following is a DIRECT measure for reducing inequality?
32.x: A ceiling on land holdings directly redistributes assets. Taxes such as wealth tax, capital gains tax and progressive income tax are indirect measures.
32.tq: Classify asset redistribution as direct and taxation-based intervention as indirect.
xs: A **ceiling on land holdings** is a **direct** measure that **redistributes assets** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2008 key).
**Capital gains tax**, **progressive income tax** and **wealth tax** are **indirect** measures (through taxes and policy).
xa: Other direct measures: **land reforms**, **tenancy laws**.
Other indirect measures: **estate duty** (introduced **1953**, abolished **1985**).
**Art. 39(c)**: prevents concentration of wealth.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding taxes on wealth in India:
1. The Wealth-tax Act of 1957 was revised in 1992 on the advice of the Raja Chelliah Committee.
2. Wealth tax was abolished from 1 April 2016 because of low yield and high compliance cost.
3. Estate duty was introduced in 1953 and abolished in 1992.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 1957 Wealth-tax Act was revised in 1992 on the Raja Chelliah Committee's advice and abolished from 1 April 2016 (low yield, high compliance cost), with the rich now taxed through income-tax surcharges. Statement 3 is wrong: estate duty was abolished in 1985, not 1992. So A omits statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
32.tq: Estate duty 1953-1985; wealth tax 1957-2016 (1992 = Chelliah revision).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Wealth-tax Act 1957** was revised in **1992** on the **Raja Chelliah** Committee's advice.
Statement 2 is correct: it was **abolished from 1 April 2016** for **low yield + high compliance cost**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **estate duty** (introduced **1953**) was abolished in **1985**, not 1992 — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: The rich are now taxed through **income-tax surcharges**.
Wealth tax, estate duty, capital gains tax are **indirect** measures against inequality.
⚠ **Art. 38(2)** = income inequalities; **Art. 39(c)** = concentration of wealth.

32.s: Which Articles of the Constitution respectively direct the State to minimise inequalities in income and prevent concentration of wealth?
32.x: Article 38(2) concerns minimising inequalities in income, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth.
32.tq: Match each constitutional provision with its specific directive rather than relying on the general theme.
xs: **Articles 38(2)** and **39(c)**: Art. 38(2) directs the State to **minimise inequalities in income**; Art. 39(c) to **prevent concentration of wealth** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are cited as UPSC facts on reducing inequality.
xa: ⚠ Do not swap them: **38(2)** = income; **39(c)** = wealth.
Direct measure: **ceiling on land holdings** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).
**Wealth tax** abolished from **1 April 2016**.

32.s: Which organisation is associated with inequality reports released in contexts such as Davos?
32.x: Oxfam International is associated with inequality reports released in contexts such as Davos.
32.tq: Use the report theme and organisation pairing rather than confusing it with wealth databases.
xs: Inequality reports released at **Davos** are by **Oxfam International** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Credit Suisse** published the **Global Wealth Report**; the **World Inequality Lab** (Paris School of Economics) publishes the **World Inequality Report**.
xa: Oxfam's older figure: top 10% hold about **77%** of India's wealth.
**Credit Suisse** is now **UBS**.
**Joseph Stiglitz** — **The Price of Inequality (2012)**.

32.s:
Match the following works with their authors:
List-I (Work)
a. The Price of Inequality
b. Inequality Reexamined
c. Capital in the Twenty-First Century
 d. World Inequality Report
List-II (Author or publisher)
i. Thomas Piketty
 ii. Amartya Sen
 iii. Joseph Stiglitz
 iv. World Inequality Lab

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Price of Inequality is by Joseph Stiglitz; Inequality Reexamined is by Amartya Sen; Capital in the Twenty-First Century is by Thomas Piketty; and the World Inequality Report is associated with the World Inequality Lab.
32.tq: Start with the well-known author–title pairs and use the remaining publisher association to complete the code.
xs: **The Price of Inequality – Joseph Stiglitz**; **Inequality Reexamined – Amartya Sen**; **Capital in the Twenty-First Century – Thomas Piketty**; **World Inequality Report – World Inequality Lab** — so option **(1)** a–iii, b–ii, c–i, d–iv is correct.
Stiglitz's book appeared in **2012**.
xa: World Inequality Lab is part of the **Paris School of Economics**; it also runs the **World Inequality Database**.
**Oxfam International** releases inequality reports at **Davos**.
**Credit Suisse** (now UBS) — **Global Wealth Report**.

32.s: The district-level Multidimensional Poverty Index gaps are used in Andhra Pradesh primarily as a measure of:
32.x: In Andhra Pradesh, district-level MPI gaps serve as a measure of inequality within the State. They capture disparities among districts rather than merely measuring urbanisation or agricultural productivity.
32.tq: Apply the indicator to the level of analysis at which it is used.
xs: In AP, district-level **MPI** gaps serve as the State's measure of **intra-State inequality** in **APSES** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They compare districts, not urbanisation, inter-State income or farm productivity alone.
xa: Range: **West Godavari 2.42%** to **Kurnool 12.84%** (Table **9.4**).
Lagging: **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal** districts.
Inter-State MPI: **Kerala 0.002** to **Bihar 0.16**.

32.s: Which one of the following is identified as a limitation of consumption-based inequality estimates?
o: They may understate the incomes of the highest-income groups.
They measure only inter-State per capita income gaps.
They necessarily show that inequality is falling.
They exclude all information about poverty.
32.x: Consumption data may understate the incomes of the top end, thereby affecting the assessment of inequality. Such data do not necessarily measure only inter-State gaps or prove that inequality is declining.
32.tq: Find the specific limitation and reject absolute claims about what the data necessarily show.
xs: Consumption-based estimates may **understate the incomes of the top end** (highest-income groups) — so option **(1)** is correct.
They do not necessarily show falling inequality; they are household data, not inter-State income gaps.
xa: Official estimates rest on **consumption** (NSS/HCES), so inequality **looks lower** than on other measures.
India has **no official income survey**; estimates use **PLFS** wages, tax data and **WID**.
Debate: **poverty falls while inequality rises**.

32.s: Who authored the book *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*?
32.x: J.M. Keynes wrote 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936), which founded Keynesian economics. Adam Smith wrote 'The Wealth of Nations'.
32.tq: Match each book to its author.
n: The author of The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money is J.M. Keynes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
J.M. Keynes is associated with General Theory. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Book)
a. The Wealth of Nations
b. On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
c. The Economic History of India
d. The Price of Inequality

List-II (Author)
i. R.C. Dutt
ii. Joseph E. Stiglitz
iii. Adam Smith
iv. David Ricardo
32.x: Adam Smith wrote 'The Wealth of Nations', Ricardo the 'Principles of Political Economy and Taxation', R.C. Dutt 'The Economic History of India', and Stiglitz 'The Price of Inequality'. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
32.tq: Match each book to its author.
n: The author of The Wealth of Nations is Adam Smith. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation is David Ricardo. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of The Economic History of India is R.C. Dutt. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of The Price of Inequality is Joseph E. Stiglitz. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
David Ricardo is associated with Principles of Political Economy & Taxation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]

32.s: Arthashastra is associated with which thinker?
32.x: The Arthashastra, ancient India's treatise on statecraft and economics, is by Kautilya (Chanakya).
32.tq: Recall the author of the Arthashastra.
n: Kautilya is also known as Chanakya. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Kautilya is associated with the Arthashastra. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]

33.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of unemployment)
A. Seasonal
B. Technological
C. Cyclical
D. Structural

List-II (Predominant area or condition)
1. Manufacturing and routine services
2. Industry and services during recession
3. Whole economy over the long run
4. Agriculture, tourism and agro-industries

Select the correct code:
33.x: Seasonal unemployment is associated with agriculture, tourism and agro-industries; technological unemployment with manufacturing and routine services; cyclical unemployment with recession-hit industry and services; and structural unemployment with the whole economy over the long run.
33.tq: Start from the sure pairs and eliminate codes with a misplaced sector.
xs: **Seasonal – agriculture, tourism, agro-industries**; **Technological – manufacturing, routine services**; **Cyclical – industry and services in recession**; **Structural – whole economy, long run** — so option **(1)** A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3 is correct.
Cyclical stems from a **fall in aggregate demand**; structural from a **skills–jobs mismatch**.
xa: **Technological** unemployment is a **sub-type of structural** unemployment.
**Disguised** unemployment is also predominant in **agriculture** (family farms).
**Educated** unemployment is mainly **urban**.

33.s: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes rural and urban unemployment in India?
o: Educated unemployment is mainly rural, whereas disguised unemployment is mainly urban.
Seasonal and disguised unemployment are associated mainly with rural areas, whereas educated unemployment is mainly urban.
Structural unemployment is confined to agriculture, whereas technological unemployment is confined to tourism.
Cyclical unemployment occurs only in rural areas, whereas seasonal unemployment occurs only in cities.
33.x: NCERT identifies seasonal and disguised unemployment as major rural forms, while educated unemployment is predominantly urban.
33.tq: Compare the rural and urban pairs directly instead of matching one type with one area only.
xs: NCERT rule: **seasonal and disguised** unemployment are mainly **rural**; **educated** unemployment is mainly **urban** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option 1 reverses the areas; structural is economy-wide, technological hits **manufacturing and routine services**, and cyclical hits industry and services in **recession**.
xa: Under **PLFS**, open unemployment is higher in **urban** areas.
Seasonal rural unemployment is higher than urban (APP notes).

33.s: Which type of unemployment is predominantly found in Indian agriculture, where more family members work on a farm than are actually needed?
33.x: Disguised unemployment is predominant in agriculture (family farms): output stays unchanged if some workers are withdrawn. Educated unemployment is mainly urban, cyclical arises in industry and services during recession, and technological unemployment occurs in manufacturing and routine services.
33.tq: Agriculture: disguised first; seasonal if disguised is not an option.
xs: More family members on a farm than needed = **disguised unemployment**, predominant in **agriculture** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Educated** is mainly **urban**; **cyclical** arises in industry and services during **recession**; **technological** in **manufacturing and routine services**.
xa: Test: withdrawing some workers leaves **total output unchanged** (**MPL = 0**).
⚠ APPSC 2025 asked "predominant in agriculture" twice: **Disguised** in GS, **Seasonal** in G2 (when disguised was not an option).
It is **hidden**, not open, unemployment.

33.s: Which one of the following is the defining test for identifying disguised unemployment?
o: Withdrawal of some workers leaves total output unchanged.
Workers remain unemployed throughout the business cycle.
Workers change jobs frequently in search of higher wages.
Withdrawal of some workers causes output to double.
33.x: Disguised unemployment is identified when removing some workers does not reduce total output, implying zero marginal productivity of those workers.
33.tq: Apply the marginal-productivity test to the employment situation.
xs: Disguised unemployment is identified when **withdrawing some workers leaves total output unchanged** — so option **(1)** is correct.
That means the **marginal productivity of labour is zero** (or negative).
xa: It is common among **family members in agriculture**.
It is **hidden** unemployment; **PLFS** headline rates do not capture it.
Rural areas = **seasonal + disguised** unemployment (NCERT).

33.s: Which one of the following is a distinguishing feature of disguised unemployment in relation to PLFS headline unemployment rates?
o: It is fully captured because all workers report themselves as unemployed.
It is captured only during the contraction phase of the business cycle.
It is generally not captured because the persons appear to be employed.
It is measured exclusively through urban establishment surveys.
33.x: Persons in disguised unemployment appear employed, so this hidden form is not captured by headline unemployment rates in the same way as open unemployment.
33.tq: Distinguish apparent employment from measured open unemployment.
xs: Disguised workers **appear employed**, so **PLFS** headline rates **generally do not capture** it — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is **hidden** unemployment, unlike **open** unemployment, which surveys do record.
xa: The surplus workers add no productive value: **MPL = 0** or negative.
It is common on **family farms** in agriculture.
Criticism: a falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**.

33.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes frictional unemployment from structural unemployment?
o: Frictional unemployment requires structural reform, whereas structural unemployment ends with a short job search.
Frictional unemployment exists only during depression, whereas structural unemployment disappears during recession.
Frictional unemployment is short-term job-search unemployment, whereas structural unemployment is long-term skill-job mismatch.
Frictional unemployment is caused by technology, whereas structural unemployment is caused by seasonal agriculture.
33.x: Frictional unemployment results from the temporary time lag involved in changing or searching for jobs, while structural unemployment is long-term and arises from a mismatch between skills and available jobs.
33.tq: Separate the two types using cause and duration together.
xs: **Frictional** = **short-term job-search** unemployment; **structural** = **long-run skills–jobs mismatch** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 1 reverses them; depression causes **cyclical** unemployment; technology causes **technological** (structural) unemployment, and seasons cause **seasonal** unemployment.
xa: Frictional exists **even at full employment**; it is normal.
Structural is **deep-rooted** and needs **reskilling/structural reform**.
**Natural rate of unemployment** = frictional + structural.

33.s: Which situation best illustrates structural unemployment?
o: A firm laying off workers during a recession
A worker changing jobs after voluntarily quitting
A farm worker remaining idle during the agricultural off-season
A labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production
33.x: A shift from labour-intensive to capital-intensive production changes the demand for labour and creates a long-term structural mismatch.
33.tq: Match the example to long-term structural change rather than a temporary interruption.
xs: A **labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production** illustrates **structural** unemployment — so option **(4)** is correct.
Recession layoffs = **cyclical**; voluntary job change = **frictional**; idle in the off-season = **seasonal**.
xa: Structural unemployment is **long-run** and needs **reskilling**.
**Technological** unemployment is a sub-type of structural.
**Indian unemployment is basically structural** — labour demand < supply.

33.s: Technological unemployment is best understood as:
o: Job loss caused exclusively by a fall in aggregate demand
Unemployment caused by a worker voluntarily rejecting the prevailing wage
Temporary unemployment during the agricultural off-season
Job loss caused by changes in technology and treated as a subtype of structural unemployment
33.x: Technological unemployment results from technological change and is a subtype of structural unemployment.
33.tq: Use the cause-and-classification link to distinguish technological from cyclical unemployment.
xs: **Technological unemployment** = job loss from **changes in technology**, a **sub-type of structural** unemployment — so option **(4)** is correct.
A fall in aggregate demand causes **cyclical**; rejecting the wage is **voluntary**; off-season idleness is **seasonal**.
xa: Drivers: **automation in manufacturing** and **AI in services**.
It hits **low-skilled, routine** jobs.
Predominant in **manufacturing** and **routine services**.

33.s: Cyclical unemployment arises primarily from
o: The seasonal closure of agricultural activities
A fall in aggregate demand for goods and services
The time taken to search for a new job
A mismatch between acquired skills and available jobs
33.x: Cyclical unemployment results from deficient aggregate demand during recession or depression, leading firms to reduce employment.
33.tq: Match the unemployment type with its immediate macroeconomic cause.
xs: **Cyclical** unemployment comes from a **fall in aggregate demand** for goods and services during **recession/depression** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Agricultural closure = **seasonal**; job-search time = **frictional**; skills mismatch = **structural**.
xa: Firms **lay off workers to cut costs** in the downturn.
⚠ "Unemployment caused by depression" = **Cyclical** (APPSC 2019).
**Keynes**: unemployment in developed economies = **deficiency in effective demand**.

33.s: According to Keynes, unemployment in developed economies primarily results from
o: A mismatch caused only by technological change
33.x: Keynes explained unemployment in developed economies mainly through deficiency in effective demand, which is associated with demand-deficient or cyclical unemployment.
33.tq: Associate the economist with the precise explanation rather than a related unemployment type.
xs: **Keynes**: unemployment in developed economies stems from a **deficiency in effective demand** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is **cyclical/demand-deficient** unemployment; a farm-labour surplus describes India's **disguised** unemployment instead.
xa: India differs: its unemployment is basically **structural**, plus **disguised** and seasonal.
**Milton Friedman** — **natural rate of unemployment**.
**A.W. Phillips (1958)** — inverse unemployment–inflation link.

33.s: Educated unemployment in India is predominantly associated with urban areas mainly because
o: Education automatically causes workers to leave the labour force.
Agricultural work is unavailable in every rural month.
Urban workers are excluded from all formal employment.
Educated persons are unable to find jobs matching their qualifications and industry requirements.
33.x: Educated unemployment is an urban phenomenon in which qualified persons fail to find employment matching their education and the needs of industry.
33.tq: Connect the location of educated unemployment with the qualification-job mismatch.
xs: **Educated** unemployment is **urban** because educated persons **cannot find jobs matching their qualifications** and **industry** needs — so option **(4)** is correct.
Its cause is a **curriculum mismatch** with industry needs.
xa: Only **46%** of graduates employable (**India Skills Report 2024**).
PLFS 2025: **secondary schooling and above = 6.5%** (more than double the national rate).
**40.1%** of tertiary-educated youth are **NEET**.

33.s: An MBA graduate working full-time as a driver at a very low income is an example of
33.x: Invisible underemployment exists when a person works full-time but earns very little or works below their ability, as in the example of an MBA working as a driver.
33.tq: Look beyond the number of hours and identify underutilisation of skills or income.
xs: An **MBA** working full-time as a driver at low income is **invisible underemployment** — full-time work **below one's ability** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Visible** underemployment means fewer than normal hours; **seasonal** and **frictional** involve no job at all for a time.
xa: **Educated** unemployment: qualified persons unable to find matching jobs (**urban**).
Only **46%** of graduates employable.
Criticism: falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**.

33.s: According to PLFS 2025, the unemployment rate among youth aged 18-29 was about 14.8%. What was it for tertiary-educated youth in that age group?
33.x: Tertiary-educated youth recorded an unemployment rate of 29.4%, about double the overall youth rate of 14.8%. 6.5% is the rate for persons with secondary schooling and above, 11.9% is the Gen Z (15-26) rate, and 40.1% is the share of tertiary-educated youth who are NEET.
33.tq: Youth 14.8% doubles to 29.4% for graduates.
xs: PLFS 2025: youth (18-29) UR **14.8%**, rising to **29.4%** for **tertiary-educated** youth — so option **(3)** is correct.
**6.5%** = secondary and above; **11.9%** = **Gen Z** (15-26); **40.1%** = share of tertiary-educated youth who are **NEET**.
xa: Female Gen Z graduates UR **36.9%**; male **29%** (**22 Jul 2026**).
AP youth (15-29) UR **17.5%**; urban female youth **29.1%**.
Cause: **curriculum mismatch** with industry needs.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding voluntary and involuntary unemployment:
1. Voluntary unemployment occurs when a person is unwilling to work at the prevailing wage.
2. Involuntary unemployment occurs when a person is willing to work at the prevailing wage but cannot find a job.
3. The labour force counts only voluntary unemployment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: voluntary unemployment means unwillingness to work at the prevailing wage, involuntary means willing at the going wage but finding no job. Statement 3 is false: the labour force counts only involuntary unemployment, not voluntary.
33.tq: Find the statement that reverses the voluntary–involuntary distinction.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **voluntary** = **unwilling at the prevailing wage**.
Statement 2 is correct: **involuntary** = **willing at the going wage but no job**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the labour force counts only **involuntary** unemployment — so option **(1)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: Causes of voluntary unemployment: **high benefits**, **high marginal tax**, **waiting for a better job**.
Involuntary unemployment comes from **market structure/aggregate demand**.
**Unemployment trap**: benefits discourage work.

33.s:
With reference to full employment, consider the following statements:
1. Every person willing to work at the prevailing wage finds work.
2. Full employment implies that frictional unemployment cannot exist.
3. Structural unemployment may still exist at full employment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Full employment means that everyone willing to work at the prevailing wage finds work, but frictional and structural unemployment may still exist.
33.tq: Reject the absolute claim that full employment eliminates every form of unemployment.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: at **full employment**, everyone **willing at the prevailing wage finds work**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **frictional** unemployment still exists.
Statement 3 is correct: **structural** unemployment may also exist — so option **(2)** 1 and 3 only is correct.
xa: **Natural rate of unemployment** = frictional + structural at full employment.
**Milton Friedman** is linked to the natural rate.
Friedman-Phelps: long-run **Phillips curve vertical** at the natural rate.

33.s: The natural rate of unemployment is composed of:
33.x: The natural rate is the combination of frictional and structural unemployment existing at full employment.
33.tq: Recall the exact components of a standard composite concept.
xs: The **natural rate of unemployment** = **frictional + structural** at full employment — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Cyclical** and **seasonal**, **open** and **disguised**, and **voluntary/involuntary** are other classifications.
xa: Associated with **Milton Friedman**.
Friedman-Phelps: long-run Phillips curve **vertical** at the natural rate.
**Okun's law**: unemployment above the natural rate cuts output.

33.s: The concept of the natural rate of unemployment is particularly associated with:
33.x: The concept of the natural rate of unemployment is associated with Milton Friedman.
33.tq: Link the named economist with the specific concept rather than a related curve or law.
xs: The **natural rate of unemployment** is associated with **Milton Friedman** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**A.W. Phillips** gave the **Phillips curve (1958)**; **Keynes** linked unemployment to **deficient effective demand**; **Arthur Okun** gave **Okun's law**.
xa: **Friedman-Phelps**: long-run Phillips curve is **vertical** at the natural rate.
Natural rate = **frictional + structural**.
⚠ **Phillips** = unemployment vs inflation; **Okun** = unemployment vs output.

33.s: Which combination best explains the structural nature of unemployment in India?
o: Only seasonal rainfall variations and tourism cycles
High labour mobility, labour-intensive production and low population growth
Rapid population growth, labour immobility and a shift towards capital-intensive production
Short job-search periods and temporary workplace transfers
33.x: Rapid population growth, labour immobility and the shift towards capital-intensive production contribute to a long-run shortfall of labour demand relative to supply.
33.tq: Select the option containing the structural causes rather than temporary causes.
xs: India's unemployment is basically **structural** due to **rapid population growth**, **labour immobility** and a **shift to capital-intensive production** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Labour **demand < supply** in the **long run**; option 2 lists the opposites.
xa: Also high **seasonal** + **disguised** unemployment and underemployment.
It differs from the **Keynesian** demand-deficient unemployment of developed countries.
**Jobless growth**: growth driven by **IT, finance**.

33.s: Which one of the following is NOT a structural cause of unemployment in India identified in the context of the secondary sector?
o: Jobless growth and inadequate focus on MSMEs
Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing generating abundant jobs
Slow infrastructure and delays in official paperwork
Neglected structural transformation of the secondary sector
33.x: Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing generating abundant jobs would reduce, rather than cause, structural unemployment. The other factors are identified structural impediments.
33.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of a stated structural cause.
xs: **Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing** creating jobs is NOT a cause — it would cut unemployment — so option **(2)** is correct.
Real structural causes: **neglected structural transformation** of the secondary sector, **jobless growth**, less focus on **MSMEs**, **slow infrastructure** and paperwork delays.
xa: Also: **stringent labour laws** and an **import-oriented** rather than export-led economy.
Exam angle: odd-one-out questions slip in "**high growth of labour-intensive manufacturing**" as a non-cause.
Other causes: skill-curriculum mismatch, ~**90%** informal workforce, low female **LFPR**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements regarding unemployment in India:
1. A large agricultural workforce contributes to seasonal and disguised unemployment.
2. Indian unemployment differs from the demand-deficient unemployment emphasised by Keynes for developed economies.
3. Underemployment is also a feature of the Indian labour market.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: All three statements are correct. India has substantial seasonal, disguised and underemployment, while its basic unemployment problem is structural rather than solely Keynesian demand deficiency.
33.tq: Combine the sectoral, theoretical and labour-market dimensions before choosing the code.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: a large **agricultural workforce** brings **seasonal + disguised** unemployment.
Statement 2 is correct: India's unemployment differs from the **Keynesian** demand-deficient kind of developed countries.
Statement 3 is correct: **underemployment** is also a feature — so option **(4)** 1, 2 and 3 is correct.
xa: Core nature: Indian unemployment is basically **structural**.
Causes: **rapid population growth**, **labour immobility**, shift to **capital-intensive** production.
~**90%** of the workforce is informal.

33.s: Jobless growth is more likely when economic growth is driven mainly by:
o: Labour-intensive manufacturing rather than capital-intensive activities
Capital-intensive sectors such as information technology and finance rather than labour-intensive manufacturing
33.x: Growth led by capital-intensive sectors such as IT and finance, instead of labour-intensive manufacturing, can produce jobless growth.
33.tq: Focus on the reversed capital-intensive versus labour-intensive comparison.
xs: **Jobless growth** occurs when growth is driven by **capital-intensive sectors such as IT and finance**, not **labour-intensive manufacturing** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Option 3 reverses it; agriculture and casual work are not growth drivers here.
xa: Jobless growth is listed among India's **structural** causes of unemployment.
Others: less focus on **MSMEs**, **import-oriented** economy.
Indian unemployment is basically **structural**.

33.s: The traditional trade-off between inflation and unemployment breaks down in a situation of:
o: Stable prices with potential output growth
Stagflation, characterised by high inflation and high unemployment
33.x: Stagflation combines high inflation with high unemployment and therefore breaks down the traditional Phillips-curve trade-off.
33.tq: Identify the unusual combination that contradicts the traditional inverse relationship.
xs: The Phillips trade-off **breaks down** in **stagflation** — **high inflation and high unemployment** together — so option **(3)** is correct.
The curve normally pairs **lower unemployment** with **higher inflation**.
xa: Friedman-Phelps: long-run curve **vertical** at the natural rate.
**Milton Friedman** — natural rate of unemployment.

33.s: According to Okun's law, a one percentage point rise in unemployment above the natural rate is associated approximately with:
o: A 2% rise in output above potential GDP
A 1% rise in output above potential GDP
A 2% fall in output below potential GDP
A 5% fall in output below potential GDP
33.x: Okun's law states that a one percentage point increase in unemployment above the natural rate is associated with roughly a 2% reduction in output below potential GDP.
33.tq: Track both parts of the quantitative relationship: the unemployment point and the output percentage.
xs: **Okun's law**: a **1 percentage point** rise in unemployment above the natural rate → roughly a **2% fall in output below potential GDP** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Output **falls**, not rises; the figure is about **2%**, not 1% or 5%.
xa: Implication: an **inverse link between growth and unemployment**.
⚠ **Okun** = unemployment vs output; **Phillips** = unemployment vs inflation.
Given by **Arthur Okun**.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the Phillips curve:
1. It shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation.
2. In the long run it is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, as argued by Friedman and Phelps.
3. It was put forward by Arthur Okun.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
33.x: Statement 1 is correct: lower unemployment goes with higher inflation. Statement 2 is correct: Friedman-Phelps argued the long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate. Statement 3 is wrong: the curve is named after A.W. Phillips (1958); Arthur Okun gave Okun's law linking unemployment and output.
33.tq: Phillips = inflation vs unemployment; Okun = output vs unemployment.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Phillips curve** shows an **inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation**.
Statement 2 is correct: **Friedman-Phelps** held the long-run curve **vertical at the natural rate**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is named after **A.W. Phillips (1958)**; **Arthur Okun** gave **Okun's law** — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only is correct.
xa: The curve breaks down in **stagflation**.
Okun's law: **1 percentage point** rise in unemployment → about **2%** output fall.
**Keynes**: unemployment from **deficiency in effective demand**.

33.s: A decline in the measured unemployment rate may fail to indicate genuine job creation when it results from:
o: A rise in potential GDP caused by technology
A permanent reduction in the labour force due to higher wages
33.x: A falling unemployment rate may reflect people entering low-productivity work under distress rather than the creation of good or adequate jobs.
33.tq: Distinguish an apparently favourable indicator from its possible underlying labour-market condition.
xs: A falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**, not real job creation — so option **(1)** is correct.
Expansion of high-productivity jobs would be genuine job creation.
xa: **Disguised** unemployment is hidden and not captured by **PLFS** headline rates.
**Invisible underemployment**: full-time work at very low income (e.g. **MBA** as driver).
~**90%** of the workforce is informal.

33.s: Which of the following comparisons between India and developed countries is correct?
o: India mainly faces cyclical unemployment, whereas developed countries mainly face disguised unemployment.
Developed countries mainly face seasonal unemployment, whereas India mainly faces classical unemployment.
India mainly faces structural and disguised unemployment, whereas developed countries mainly face cyclical, demand-deficient unemployment.
Both India and developed countries mainly face only frictional unemployment.
33.x: India's unemployment is characterised as structural and disguised, while developed countries are described as facing mainly cyclical or demand-deficient unemployment.
33.tq: Keep both sides of the comparative classification aligned with the stated economic context.
xs: **India** = **structural + disguised** unemployment; **developed countries** = mainly **cyclical, demand-deficient** (**Keynes**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
Options 1 and 2 swap or misassign the types; frictional is not the main type in either.
xa: India also has high **seasonal** unemployment and **underemployment**.
Keynes: **deficiency in effective demand**.
India's structural causes: **population growth**, **labour immobility**, **capital-intensive** production.

33.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Frictional unemployment is associated with transition between jobs.
Underemployment refers to surplus labour with zero marginal output.
Institutional unemployment can arise from regulatory and policy barriers.
Structural unemployment involves a mismatch of skills or geography.
33.x: Option B is incorrect: surplus labour adding nothing to output is disguised unemployment. Underemployment means workers are not using their full skills or hours.
33.tq: Discriminate disguised unemployment from underemployment.
n: Frictional unemployment is caused by transitions between jobs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Structural unemployment is caused by a mismatch of skills or geography. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Disguised unemployment is caused by surplus labour with zero marginal productivity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Underemployment is caused by the underutilization of worker capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Institutional unemployment is caused by regulatory and policy barriers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Underemployment involves working below one’s skill level or being forced into involuntary part-time work. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Institutional unemployment arises from labour laws, high minimum wages, or union rules. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]

33.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Frictional unemployment
(b) Structural unemployment
(c) Cyclical unemployment
(d) Vulnerable unemployment

List-II
(i) Lack of formal contracts and social security
(ii) Deficiency in aggregate demand
(iii) Transition between jobs
(iv) Mismatch of skills or geography
33.x: Frictional unemployment is the gap between jobs, structural is a mismatch of skills or place, cyclical comes from weak demand, and vulnerable means no contract or social security. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
33.tq: Match each type of unemployment to its cause.
n: Frictional unemployment is caused by transitions between jobs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Structural unemployment is caused by a mismatch of skills or geography. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Cyclical unemployment is caused by a deficiency in aggregate demand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Vulnerable unemployment is caused by a lack of formal contracts and social security. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Frictional unemployment is voluntary, short-term, and a normal part of labour churn. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Vulnerable unemployment involves high job insecurity and is common in informal sectors. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]

33.s:
Assertion (A): A recent graduate searching for a first job is an example of frictional unemployment.
Reason (R): Frictional unemployment arises during the transition between jobs.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
33.x: Both are true: a graduate looking for a first job is frictionally unemployed because frictional unemployment covers the time spent moving into a job. R explains A.
33.tq: Ask whether the definition explains the example.
n: A recent graduate searching for a first job is an example of frictional unemployment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]

33.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Agricultural labourers or resort staff unemployed during the off-season
(b) Five family members working on a farm plot that needs only two workers
(c) Employers halting hiring because of rigid layoff regulations
(d) Daily-wage construction labour or unorganized street vending

List-II
i. Seasonal unemployment
ii. Disguised unemployment
iii. Institutional unemployment
iv. Vulnerable unemployment
33.x: Off-season joblessness is seasonal, five people on a two-person plot is disguised, rigid layoff laws cause institutional unemployment, and daily-wage work is vulnerable. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
33.tq: Match each example to its type.
n: Agricultural labourers or resort staff unemployed during the off-season are examples of seasonal unemployment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Five family members working on a farm plot that needs only two workers are an example of disguised unemployment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Employers halting hiring because of rigid layoff regulations is an example of institutional unemployment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Vulnerable unemployment is associated with daily-wage work. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Construction labour or unorganized street vending is an example of vulnerable unemployment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]

34.s: What was the principal recommendation of the Dantwala Committee regarding unemployment estimation?
o: To replace NSS surveys with CMIE surveys
To provide separate estimates by status and by category
To use one single national number for all forms of unemployment
34.x: The Dantwala Committee rejected a single-number estimate and recommended separate estimates by usual, weekly and daily status, as well as by category.
34.tq: Identify the committee recommendation that rejects an over-simplified single measure.
xs: The **Dantwala Committee** recommended **separate estimates by status and by category** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It **rejected a single-number estimate**, so option 3 is the opposite; it did not drop daily status or bring in CMIE.
xa: Status = **usual, weekly, daily** — the basis of UPS, CWS and CDS.
Dantwala Committee: **1970**.
**Bhagwati Committee (1973)** reviewed estimates + **employment-oriented policies**.

34.s: Which committee reviewed unemployment estimates and employment-oriented policies in 1973?
o: Standing Committee on Labour Force Statistics
34.x: The Bhagwati Committee, constituted in 1973, reviewed unemployment estimates and employment-oriented policies.
34.tq: Match the committee with its year and subject of review.
xs: The **Bhagwati Committee** (Committee on Unemployment, **1973**) reviewed unemployment estimates and **employment-oriented policies** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Dantwala** (**1970**) dealt with estimates by status; the **SCLFS** designed the **PLFS**.
xa: ⚠ **Dantwala 1970** = estimates by status; **Bhagwati 1973** = estimates + policies.
SCLFS was set up on the **National Statistical Commission's** advice.
PLFS launched **April 2017**.

34.s: Under the Usual Principal Status approach, a person is treated as employed when the person has worked for the major part of the reference period. What is the relevant reference period and minimum duration?
o: Each day and 4 hours of work
34.x: UPS uses a reference period of 365 days. A person is considered employed if the major part of the year, generally 183 days or more, was spent working.
34.tq: Match the reference period with the qualifying duration.
xs: **UPS** uses a **365-day** reference period; a person is employed if the **major time (183+ days)** was spent working — so option **(3)** is correct.
**7 days / 1 hour** is **CWS**; **each day / 4 hours** is **CDS**; **30 days** is UPSS subsidiary work.
xa: UPS captures **chronic** (long-term) unemployment.
⚠ **183** days is also the Census **main worker** line — but Census is **not** an NSS approach.
Memory: **365 days – 7 days – half day** = **UPS – CWS – CDS**.

34.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Usual Principal and Subsidiary Status approach?
o: It counts only persons working for 183 days or more in a year.
It counts a person as employed if work was performed for four hours on any day.
It includes principal-status workers and those undertaking subsidiary work for at least 30 days in the year.
It counts a person as employed only if work was performed on each day of the reference week.
34.x: UPSS includes persons employed under principal status as well as those who performed subsidiary work for at least 30 days during the 365-day reference period.
34.tq: Discriminate between principal-status and subsidiary-status conditions.
xs: **UPSS** counts **principal-status** workers plus those doing **subsidiary work for at least 30 days** in the year — so option **(3)** is correct.
**183 days only** is UPS; **4 hours a day** is CDS; the weekly test is CWS.
xa: UPSS gives the **broadest count of workers**.
Reference period: **365 days**.

34.s: In the Current Daily Status approach, the basic time unit used for recording employment is:
34.x: CDS uses a half-day as the unit of measurement. Four or more hours of work are treated as employment for that day.
34.tq: Test the precise quantitative unit used in a statistical approach.
xs: **CDS** records employment in units of **half a day**; **4+ hours** = employed for the day — so option **(4)** is correct.
It covers **each day of the 7 days** of the reference week.
xa: CDS is the **most inclusive**, capturing **daily/intermittent** unemployment.
CDS gives the **highest** rate: NSS 68th CDS **5.6%**.

34.s: Why does the Current Daily Status approach generally produce the highest unemployment rate?
o: It counts days of unemployment even for persons treated as employed under CWS.
It uses a reference period of 365 days.
It includes only persons who are not seeking work.
It excludes all seasonal workers from employment.
34.x: CDS records unemployment separately for each day and therefore captures intermittent unemployment that may not be reflected when a person is counted as employed under CWS.
34.tq: Identify the cause behind a comparison in measured unemployment rates.
xs: **CDS** gives the highest rate because it **counts days of unemployment even for persons "employed" under CWS** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **365-day** period is UPS, not CDS.
xa: CDS unit = **half day**; **4+ hours** = employed for the day.
It captures **daily/intermittent** unemployment.

34.s: Which one of the following is NOT an unemployment measurement approach used in the listed status-based framework?
34.x: Current Monthly Status is not one of the listed NSS status approaches. UPS, CWS and CDS are recognised approaches in this framework.
34.tq: Find the non-method inserted among closely related statistical methods.
xs: **Current Monthly Status** is not an NSS approach — so option **(4)** is correct.
The real approaches: **UPS** (**365 days**), **UPSS**, **CWS** (**7 days**) and **CDS** (**half day**).
xa: Exam angle: odd-one-out lists slip in "**Current Monthly Status**" or "**Rangarajan formula**".
⚠ Census main/marginal worker is also **not** an NSS approach.
Monthly PLFS data use **CWS**, not a "monthly status".

34.s: In Census terminology, which combination is correctly matched?
o: Main worker — worked for less than 183 days in a year
Marginal worker — worked for 183 days or more in a year
Main worker — worked for 183 days or more in a year
Main worker — worked only for one hour during the reference week
34.x: The Census classifies a person who worked for 183 days or more in a year as a main worker. A person working for less than 183 days is a marginal worker.
34.tq: Separate Census worker categories from NSS status approaches.
xs: Census: **main worker** = worked **183+ days** a year — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Marginal worker** = **< 183** days, so options 1 and 2 swap them; **1 hour a week** is the **CWS** test.
xa: ⚠ **183** days is also the **UPS** "major time" line, but Census is **not** an NSS approach.
Census gives main/marginal worker data every **10** years.
UPSS adds subsidiary work of **30 days**.

34.s: Current Weekly Status (CWS) captures short-term or seasonal unemployment because it considers whether a person worked:
o: For at least 30 days in the preceding year
For at least one hour on any day during the preceding seven days
On every day of the preceding month
For at least 183 days in the preceding year
34.x: CWS covers a seven-day reference period and counts a person as employed if the person worked for at least one hour on any day during that period.
34.tq: Link the short reference period and one-hour rule with short-term unemployment.
xs: **CWS** treats a person as employed if they worked **at least one hour on any day** of the preceding **seven days** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**30 days** is UPSS subsidiary work; **183 days** is UPS.
xa: CWS captures **chronic + seasonal** unemployment.
CWS rates exceed **UPSS** rates as the short period catches seasonal unemployment.
Critics: CWS (**1 hour** a week = employed) **masks underemployment**.

34.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Unemployment Rate (UR) from the proportion of unemployed (PU)?
o: UR is unemployed persons as a percentage of labour force; PU is unemployed persons as a percentage of population.
UR is unemployed persons as a percentage of population; PU is unemployed persons as a percentage of labour force.
Both UR and PU are unemployed persons as a percentage of labour force.
Both UR and PU are employed persons as a percentage of population.
34.x: UR is unemployed persons as a percentage of the labour force, whereas PU is unemployed persons as a percentage of the population.
34.tq: Focus on the denominator to distinguish two similar indicators.
xs: **UR** = unemployed ÷ **labour force**; **PU** = unemployed ÷ **population** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option 2 swaps the two denominators.
xa: ⚠ UR divides by **labour force**; PU divides by **population**.
