**CCI** was established on **14 Oct 2003**, with a **Chairperson + 2-6 members**.
It works under the **Ministry of Corporate Affairs**; the Act was amended in **2007**, **2009**, **2023**.
xa: ⚠ Competition Act **2002**; commenced **31 Mar 2003**; CCI **14 Oct 2003**.
If CCI misses a combination deadline, the deal gets **deemed approval** (ES **2025-26**).
CCI fined **Google ₹1,337 crore** (**2022**).

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the Competition Act, 2002:
1. Cartels, bid-rigging and price-fixing are anti-competitive agreements under Section 3.
2. Unfair pricing and denial of market access are dealt with as combinations under Sections 5 and 6.
3. Combinations under Sections 5 and 6 cover mergers and acquisitions above thresholds.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct (Section 3). Statement 2 is wrong: unfair pricing and denial of market access are abuse of dominant position under Section 4. Statement 3 is correct: Sections 5-6 cover M&A above thresholds. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
65.tq: s.3 agreements, s.4 dominance, s.5-6 combinations.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **cartels**, **bid-rigging**, **price-fixing** are anti-competitive agreements (**s.3**).
Statement 2 wrong: **unfair pricing** and **denial of market access** are **abuse of dominant position** (**s.4**).
Statement 3 correct: **combinations** (**s.5-6**) cover mergers/acquisitions above thresholds.
xa: Combinations get **deemed approval** if CCI misses its deadline.
CCI penalised **Meta/WhatsApp ₹213.14 crore** (**2024**).
The Act was recommended by the **S.V.S. Raghavan Committee** (**2000**).

65.s: What is the consequence when the CCI does not decide a combination within the prescribed deadline?
o: The parties are required to seek approval from the Finance Commission.
The combination is automatically prohibited forever.
The combination is deemed to be approved.
The matter is transferred to BIFR.
65.x: A combination is deemed to have been approved if the CCI misses the prescribed decision deadline.
65.tq: Apply the statutory time-limit consequence to a transaction scenario.
xs: If CCI misses its deadline, the combination is **deemed to be approved** — option **(3)** is correct (ES **2025-26**).
**BIFR** was dissolved in **2016** and never handled mergers.
xa: Combinations (**s.5-6**) = mergers/acquisitions above thresholds.
Abuse of dominant position falls under **s.4**; anti-competitive agreements under **s.3**.
CCI sits under the **Ministry of Corporate Affairs**.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the penalty imposed by the CCI?
65.x: The CCI imposed a ₹213.14 crore penalty on Meta/WhatsApp in 2024. Google was fined ₹1,337 crore in 2022.
65.tq: Pair the entity, year and penalty amount without swapping cases.
xs: **Meta/WhatsApp — ₹213.14 crore in 2024** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Google** was fined **₹1,337 crore** in **2022**; **₹35,294 crore** is the **2022-23** disinvestment realisation.
xa: **NCLAT** (**2025**) upheld the Meta penalty but set aside the **5-year data-sharing ban**.
A **Supreme Court** appeal was pending (Feb **2026**).
NCLAT hears **CCI** appeals from **26 May 2017**.

65.s: With reference to the Meta/WhatsApp case, which statement is correct?
o: NCLAT cancelled the penalty and upheld the five-year data-sharing ban.
NCLAT upheld the penalty but set aside the five-year data-sharing ban; an appeal is pending before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has already finally dismissed all proceedings.
The case concerned only industrial licensing under the IDRA.
65.x: In 2025, NCLAT upheld the penalty but set aside the five-year data-sharing ban; the Supreme Court appeal remains pending.
65.tq: Track the appellate outcome and distinguish penalty from remedial restriction.
xs: **NCLAT upheld the penalty but set aside the five-year data-sharing ban; a Supreme Court appeal is pending** — option **(2)** is correct.
The SC case was still pending in **Feb 2026**, so proceedings are not over; the case is competition law, not IDRA licensing.
xa: CCI's penalty on Meta/WhatsApp: **₹213.14 crore** (**2024**).
NCLAT is set up under **s.410** of the Companies Act and hears **CCI** appeals.
CCI fined **Google ₹1,337 crore** (**2022**).

65.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes disinvestment from privatisation?
o: Disinvestment removes licences and quotas, whereas privatisation integrates the economy with the world economy.
Disinvestment always transfers management control, whereas privatisation may retain government control.
Disinvestment means sale of all government assets, whereas privatisation means sale of only minority shares.
Disinvestment reduces government equity, while privatisation transfers ownership and management control to the private sector.
65.x: Disinvestment is the sale or reduction of government equity, with the government possibly retaining majority ownership and control. Privatisation involves transfer of ownership and management control to the private sector.
65.tq: Separate the two look-alike terms by asking whether ownership and management control are transferred.
xs: **Disinvestment reduces government equity**, while **privatisation transfers ownership and management control** — option **(4)** is correct.
In disinvestment the government **may keep majority and control** (APPSC-GS **2019**).
Removing licences is **liberalisation**; world integration is **globalisation**.
xa: **Strategic sale**: a block of shares (usually **50%+**) plus transfer of management control.
**Complete privatisation**: **100%** sold — the most comprehensive mode.
⚠ **Monetisation** leases assets; disinvestment sells equity permanently.

65.s: Removal of licences, quotas and controls, with the State acting mainly as a facilitator, is known as
65.x: Liberalisation refers to removing licences, quotas and controls and changing the State’s role from controller to facilitator.
65.tq: Identify the LPG term from its defining policy action rather than from ownership changes.
xs: Removing **licences, quotas and controls**, with the State as **facilitator**, is **Liberalisation** — option **(3)** is correct.
Liberalisation involves no sale; disinvestment and privatisation do.
xa: **Globalisation** = integration with the world economy — tariff cuts, **FDI**, **FERA to FEMA**.
**Privatisation** = transfer of ownership and management control.
Post-1991, **APIIC** in AP turned facilitator.

65.s: Integration of the Indian economy with the world economy through tariff cuts, FDI and the transition from FERA to FEMA is termed
65.x: Globalisation denotes integration with the world economy and includes measures such as tariff reduction, FDI and the shift from FERA to FEMA.
65.tq: Use the policy instruments listed in the description to identify the correct LPG concept.
xs: Integration with the world economy through **tariff cuts**, **FDI** and **FERA to FEMA** is **Globalisation** — option **(4)** is correct.
Liberalisation is removing controls; disinvestment and privatisation concern PSU equity.
xa: FERA was **liberalised in 1993**.
**Monetisation** leases brownfield public assets for a fixed period.

65.s: A government retains more than 51 per cent equity and control in a public sector enterprise while selling a part of its holding. This is called
65.x: Under minority disinvestment, the government retains more than 51 per cent ownership and control. Majority disinvestment transfers control while retaining a minority stake.
65.tq: Apply the percentage and control test to distinguish minority and majority disinvestment.
xs: Keeping **more than 51%** and control while selling part is **minority disinvestment** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Majority disinvestment** transfers control but keeps a minority stake; **complete privatisation** sells **100%**.
xa: **Strategic sale** = block of shares (usually **50%+**) + transfer of management control.
The first round (**1991-92**) sold minority stakes in **31 PSUs**.
**Economic Survey 2025-26** proposes letting the stake in listed CPSEs fall to **26%** while keeping "Government company" status.

65.s: A strategic sale generally involves
o: Transfer of all public assets to another government department
Sale of exactly 10 per cent of shares without any change in management
Sale of a block of shares, usually 50 per cent or more, along with transfer of management control
Removal of industrial licences without any sale of equity
65.x: A strategic sale normally involves a block of shares, usually 50 per cent or more, together with transfer of management control to a strategic partner.
65.tq: Test the defining combination of a substantial share block and management control.
xs: A **strategic sale** = **a block of shares, usually 50% or more, with transfer of management control** — option **(3)** is correct.
Removing licences without selling is **liberalisation**, not a sale.
xa: The **Disinvestment Commission (1996)** recommended strategic sales.
First strategic sales came in **1999-2004**.
Since **2016**, in-principle approval for strategic sale of **36 CPSEs**; **13 completed**.

65.s: The term ‘disinvestment’ was introduced in the Indian policy framework through which of the following?
65.x: The term ‘disinvestment’ was introduced in the Interim Budget presented in July 1991.
65.tq: Use the exact year and policy document rather than associating the term with a later committee.
xs: The term **disinvestment** was introduced in the **Interim Budget, July 1991** — option **(2)** is correct.
It means **reducing government share** in the public sector, the government possibly keeping majority and control.
xa: First round: **1991-92**, minority stakes in **31 PSUs** (**20%** announced).
First-year target: **Rs 2,500 crore**.
**C. Rangarajan Committee** (**1993**) recommended the disinvestment policy.

65.s:
With reference to the first round of disinvestment in India, consider the following statements:
1. It was undertaken during 1991–92.
2. Minority stakes in 31 public sector undertakings were offered.
3. A disinvestment limit of 20 per cent was announced.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: The first round of disinvestment took place in 1991–92, involved minority stakes in 31 PSUs and announced a 20 per cent disinvestment limit.
65.tq: Combine the date, number of enterprises and percentage in one statement set.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
First round in **1991-92**; minority stakes in **31 PSUs**; a **20%** limit announced.
xa: The term itself came in the **Interim Budget, July 1991**.
**1991-98** minority sales raised **₹17,557 cr**.
The **1991-92** target was **Rs 2,500 crore**.

65.s: The Rangarajan Committee, constituted in 1993, recommended which of the following regarding disinvestment?
o: Retention of at least 74 per cent government ownership in every PSU
Complete privatisation of all public sector undertakings
A ban on strategic sales of public enterprises
Disinvestment up to 49 per cent in PSUs reserved for the public sector
65.x: The Rangarajan Committee recommended disinvestment up to 49 per cent in PSUs reserved for the public sector. It also suggested up to 74 per cent disinvestment in other enterprises.
65.tq: Test the committee’s recommendation through the specific percentage associated with it.
xs: The **Rangarajan Committee** (**1993**) recommended disinvestment **up to 49% in PSUs reserved for the public sector** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS **2025** key).
For other PSUs it suggested up to **74%** — so retention of 74% everywhere is wrong.
xa: ⚠ **Rangarajan** = **49%** / 74%; **Arjun Sengupta** = MoU, not disinvestment.
The **Disinvestment Commission** (**1996**, first chair **G.V. Ramakrishna**) recommended strategic sales.
The **V. Krishnamurthy Committee** (**1991**) set out an early approach.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: V. Krishnamurthy Committee — 1991 — Early disinvestment approach
Disinvestment Commission — 1993 — Faster disinvestment and governance reforms
Vijay Kelkar Committee — 1984 — PSU autonomy and MoUs
65.x: The V. Krishnamurthy Committee (1991) set out an early disinvestment approach, so A is correct. The Rangarajan Committee was 1993 (49% in reserved PSUs), the Disinvestment Commission was 1996 (case-by-case sale advice, strategic sales), and PSU autonomy/MoUs in 1984 belong to Arjun Sengupta, not Vijay Kelkar.
65.tq: Match each committee with its year and distinctive policy contribution.
xs: **V. Krishnamurthy Committee — 1991 — early disinvestment approach** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Rangarajan** was **1993** (49% limit); **case-by-case sale advice** was the **Disinvestment Commission** (**1996**).
**PSU autonomy and MoUs** in **1984** belong to **Arjun Sengupta**.
xa: **Department of Disinvestment** set up **1999**; renamed **DIPAM** in **2016**.
The Disinvestment Commission's first chair was **G.V. Ramakrishna**.
The term "disinvestment" came in the **Interim Budget, July 1991**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the Disinvestment Commission:
1. It was set up in 1996 with G.V. Ramakrishna as its first chair.
2. It gave case-by-case advice on the sale of public enterprises and recommended strategic sales.
3. It recommended disinvestment of up to 49% in PSUs reserved for the public sector.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Commission (1996) was first chaired by G.V. Ramakrishna and gave case-by-case sale advice, recommending strategic sales. Statement 3 is wrong: the 49% limit was the Rangarajan Committee (1993) recommendation. Hence '1 only', '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' are wrong.
65.tq: Rangarajan 1993 = 49%; Commission 1996 = G.V. Ramakrishna, case-by-case.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: set up in **1996**, first chair **G.V. Ramakrishna**.
Statement 2: it gave **case-by-case sale advice** and recommended **strategic sales**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **49%** limit was the **Rangarajan Committee** (**1993**).
xa: First strategic sales followed in **1999-2004**.
**Department of Disinvestment**: **1999**; **DIPAM**: **2016**.
**Arjun Sengupta** (**1984**) dealt with PSU autonomy and MoUs.

65.s: The Department of Disinvestment was later renamed as DIPAM in
65.x: The Department of Disinvestment was renamed the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) in 2016.
65.tq: Use the renaming year to separate the department’s creation from its later institutional transformation.
xs: The Department of Disinvestment was renamed **DIPAM** in **2016** — option **(4)** is correct.
It was set up in **1999** (Dec 1999; some notes say **2000**) and later became a Ministry.
xa: DIPAM = **Department of Investment and Public Asset Management**, under the **Ministry of Finance**.
DIPAM's modes: **strategic sale**, **OFS**, **IPO/FPO**, **CPSE ETF**.
**1991** is when the term disinvestment was introduced.

65.s: Which one of the following was associated with PSU autonomy and Memoranda of Understanding rather than with the disinvestment policy recommendations?
65.x: Arjun Sengupta’s 1984 work was associated with PSU autonomy and Memoranda of Understanding, not with the later disinvestment recommendations.
65.tq: Separate a nearby but distinct reform theme from the committees directly concerned with disinvestment.
xs: **Arjun Sengupta** (**1984**) is linked to **PSU autonomy and MoUs**, not disinvestment — option **(2)** is correct.
**Rangarajan** (**1993**) and **G.V. Ramakrishna** (Disinvestment Commission, **1996**) were about disinvestment.
xa: Rangarajan recommended up to **49%** in reserved PSUs, **74%** in others.
Post-1991, PSUs also got greater autonomy through **MoUs**.
The Disinvestment Commission recommended **strategic sales**.

65.s: Which of the following is NOT a method or instrument managed in the context of Central Government disinvestment by DIPAM?
65.x: Strategic sale, Offer for Sale, IPO/FPO and CPSE ETF are disinvestment-related instruments. Statutory liquidity ratio is a monetary and banking instrument, not a disinvestment method.
65.tq: Find the one item belonging to monetary policy rather than public-asset management.
xs: **Statutory liquidity ratio** is not a disinvestment method — option **(3)** is the answer.
DIPAM's modes: **strategic sale**, **OFS**, **IPO/FPO**, **CPSE ETF**.
xa: DIPAM manages **Central Government equity + disinvestment** under the **Ministry of Finance**.
**Bharat Bond ETF (2019)** raised **₹32,400 crore**.
**LIC IPO** (**17 May 2022**) was the biggest IPO then, with about **73 lakh** applications.

65.s:
Arrange the following phases of disinvestment in chronological order:
A. First strategic sales
B. Minority sales
C. Period in which about 70 per cent of cumulative proceeds since 1991 were realised
65.x: Minority sales characterised 1991–98, first strategic sales occurred during 1999–2004, and the period from 2014 onwards accounted for about 70 per cent of cumulative proceeds since 1991.
65.tq: Anchor the sequence with the earliest phase and then place the later strategic-sale phase.
xs: The order is **B, A, C** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Minority sales** (**1991-98**) → **first strategic sales** (**1999-2004**) → **2014 onwards** (~**70%** of proceeds since 1991).
xa: 1991-98 minority sales raised **₹17,557 cr**.
Disinvestment receipts have been **falling since 2022-23**, while dividends rise.
Since **FY24**, no separate disinvestment head; merged into **Miscellaneous Capital Receipts**.

65.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated rationale for disinvestment?
o: Facilitating market listing of public-sector enterprises
Ensuring that all public-sector enterprises remain outside the capital market
Improving the efficiency of public-sector enterprises
65.x: Disinvestment is justified by poor returns from many PSUs, fiscal pressures, efficiency considerations and market listing. Keeping PSUs permanently outside the capital market is not a rationale for disinvestment.
65.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated rationale of the policy.
xs: **Keeping all PSEs outside the capital market** is not a rationale — option **(2)** is the answer; **market listing** is itself a rationale.
Stated rationale: **poor returns** of many PSUs, **fiscal deficit**, **efficiency**, **market listing**.
xa: Critics call it "**selling the family silver**".
Other concerns: **undervaluation**, loss of **dividend income**, **national-security** risks.
Singapore's **Temasek model**: government as **passive shareholder**.

65.s: Which of the following correctly describes DIPAM?
o: It manages government equity and disinvestment under the Ministry of Finance.
It conducts trade negotiations under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
It manages only surplus land under the Department of Public Enterprises.
It regulates monetary policy under the Reserve Bank of India.
65.x: DIPAM, the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management, manages government equity and disinvestment under the Ministry of Finance.
65.tq: Apply the ‘who performs this function?’ method to distinguish government departments.
xs: **DIPAM** **manages government equity and disinvestment under the Ministry of Finance** — option **(1)** is correct.
Surplus land of CPSEs is handled by **NLMC** under **DPE**, not DIPAM.
xa: DIPAM was renamed from the **Department of Disinvestment** in **2016**.
**NLMC**: **100%** GoI, incorporated **3 June 2022**, monetises surplus land/buildings of CPSEs.
Modes: **strategic sale**, **OFS**, **IPO/FPO**, **CPSE ETF**.

65.s: The National Investment Fund (NIF) was set up on which date?
65.x: The National Investment Fund was set up on 3 November 2005.
65.tq: Use the precise date to distinguish the fund from later disinvestment institutions.
xs: The **National Investment Fund** was set up on **3 November 2005** — option **(3)** is correct.
**28 May 2016** = IBC enacted; **31 March 2003** = Competition Act commenced.
xa: Disinvestment proceeds were credited to NIF; **only its income** was used.
Since **FY24**, no separate disinvestment head — **Miscellaneous Capital Receipts**.
**2026-27** disinvestment target: **Rs 80,000 crore**.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the use of proceeds credited to the National Investment Fund?
o: Only the income generated from the fund is used.
The entire principal is distributed annually to CPSE employees.
The proceeds are transferred exclusively to State governments.
The fund is used only for purchasing foreign exchange.
65.x: The proceeds are credited to the National Investment Fund, but only the income generated from it is used.
65.tq: Test the distinction between principal proceeds and income generated from a fund.
xs: Proceeds are credited to the **National Investment Fund**, and **only its income** is used — option **(1)** is correct.
The principal is not distributed to employees or States.
xa: NIF was set up on **3 November 2005**.
Criticism: proceeds used to **bridge the fiscal deficit** — "**selling the family silver**".
**2022-23** realisation: **Rs 35,294 crore** (ONGC, LIC, GAIL, IRCTC stakes).

65.s:
With reference to disinvestment targets, consider the following statements:
1. The target for 2020–21 from PSBs and financial institutions was ₹90,000 crore.
2. The target for 2025–26 was ₹47,000 crore.
3. The target for 2026–27 was ₹80,000 crore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: All three statements are correct: the respective targets were ₹90,000 crore, ₹47,000 crore and ₹80,000 crore.
65.tq: Compare closely placed budget years and figures.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
xa: **2019-20** target: **Rs 1,05,000 crore** (incl. Air India).
**2021-22**: target **Rs 1.75 lakh crore**, realised only about **Rs 13,534 crore**.
**2017-18**: **HPCL** sold to **ONGC** for **Rs 36,915 crore**.

65.s: Since which financial year has there been no separate disinvestment head in the Budget, with disinvestment receipts merged into Miscellaneous Capital Receipts?
65.x: Since FY24, there has been no separate disinvestment head; it has been merged into Miscellaneous Capital Receipts.
65.tq: Use the time marker to identify the change in budget classification.
xs: Since **FY24** (FY 2024), there is **no separate disinvestment head**; receipts are in **Miscellaneous Capital Receipts** — option **(3)** is correct.
This reflects falling disinvestment receipts, with **no separate disinvestment heading** in the Budget.
xa: Policy has shifted from **selling PSUs → earning dividends**.
Disinvestment receipts have fallen since **2022-23**.
**NMP 2.0** was launched on **1 Mar 2026**.

65.s: The disinvestment target set for 2019-20, which included the proposed sale of Air India, was:
65.x: The 2019-20 target was Rs 1,05,000 crore. Rs 47,000 crore was the 2025-26 target, Rs 80,000 crore is the 2026-27 target, and Rs 1.75 lakh crore was the 2021-22 target (of which only about Rs 13,534 crore was realised).
xs: The **2019-20** target, including **Air India**, was **Rs 1,05,000 crore** — option **(3)** is correct.
xa: 2021-22 realised only about **Rs 13,534 crore**.
**Air India** went to the **Tata Group** in **2021-22**.
2020-21 PSB/FI target: **Rs 90,000 crore** (UPPSC **2021**).

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding strategic disinvestment:
1. In-principle approval has been given since 2016 for strategic disinvestment of 36 CPSEs.
2. Of these, 13 strategic disinvestments had been completed.
3. Strategic disinvestment refers only to sale of minority shares through an exchange offer.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Strategic disinvestment is not limited to sale of minority shares through an exchange offer.
65.tq: Find the false definition hidden among numerical statements.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Since **2016**, in-principle approval for strategic disinvestment of **36 CPSEs**; **13 completed**.
Statement 3 wrong: a strategic sale transfers **management control** with usually **50%+** shares, not minority shares.
xa: **Stalled**: **Pawan Hans** and **Central Electronics**.
**Pipeline**: **IDBI Bank** strategic sale; OFS in Coal India, LIC, IRFC.
**BPCL** (**52.8%** stake) sale was called off in mid-**2022**.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
65.x: Modern Food Industries was sold to Hindustan Lever. BALCO was sold to Sterlite, VSNL to the Tata group and Air India to Tata Group.
65.tq: Start from the sure buyer-company pair and eliminate swapped buyers.
xs: **Modern Food Industries — Hindustan Lever** is correctly matched — option **(1)** (sold in **2000**).
**BALCO** went to **Sterlite (Vedanta)**; **VSNL** to the **Tata group**; **Air India** to the **Tata Group**.
xa: ⚠ **BALCO** = Sterlite; **VSNL**, **Air India** = Tata; **REC** = PFC; **BPCL** = called off.
BALCO was sold in **2001**, VSNL in **2002**.
**NINL** went to the **Tata Steel group**, with no proceeds to the exchequer.

65.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the disinvestment outcome stated?
o: LIC IPO — conducted in 2019 with about 32 lakh applications
NINL — sale proceeds credited to the exchequer from government equity
REC — acquired by PFC for ₹14,500 crore
BPCL — strategic sale completed in mid-2022
65.x: REC was acquired by PFC for ₹14,500 crore in 2018–19. NINL yielded no proceeds to the exchequer because the government held no equity; the BPCL sale was called off and the LIC IPO was in 2022 with about 73 lakh applications.
65.tq: Check the company, transaction and outcome together rather than recognising only the company name.
xs: **REC — acquired by PFC for ₹14,500 crore** is correctly matched — option **(3)** (**2018-19**).
**LIC IPO** was on **17 May 2022** with about **73 lakh** applications; **₹32,400 crore** in **2019** is the Bharat Bond ETF.
**NINL** gave **no proceeds** (government held no equity); **BPCL** sale was **called off** in mid-2022.
xa: NINL went to the **Tata Steel group**.
BPCL stake on offer was **52.8%**; bidders withdrew.
**HPCL** was sold to **ONGC** for **Rs 36,915 crore** (**2017-18**).

65.s: The strategic sale of Air India, completed in 2021-22, was made to:
65.x: Air India was sold to the Tata Group. Sterlite (Vedanta) bought BALCO, Hindustan Lever bought Modern Food Industries, and PFC acquired REC.
65.tq: Air India, VSNL and NINL all went to Tata companies.
xs: **Air India** was sold to the **Tata Group** (**2021-22**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Sterlite (Vedanta)** bought **BALCO**; **Hindustan Lever** bought **Modern Food Industries**; **PFC** acquired **REC**.
xa: **VSNL** also went to the **Tata group** (**2002**).
The **2019-20** target of **Rs 1,05,000 crore** had included Air India.
**IDBI Bank** strategic sale is in the pipeline.

65.s: The expression “selling the family silver” is used in criticism of disinvestment because:
o: all public assets are sold below their book value in every transaction
the proceeds are used to bridge the fiscal deficit instead of building assets
disinvestment necessarily increases dividend income for the government
the proceeds are exclusively invested in new public enterprises
65.x: The expression criticises the use of disinvestment proceeds to bridge the fiscal deficit rather than to create or build assets.
65.tq: Interpret an idiomatic expression through the policy criticism it represents.
xs: "**Selling the family silver**" criticises using **proceeds to bridge the fiscal deficit instead of building assets** — option **(2)** is correct.
Disinvestment actually means **loss of dividend income**, not more.
xa: Other concerns: **undervaluation** of PSU assets; **national-security** concerns in oil, defence, transport.
Debates also note **union resistance** and the **risk of private monopolies**.
NIF rule: proceeds credited, **only income** used.

65.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or concern relating to disinvestment?
o: Automatic improvement in public ownership of strategic assets
National-security concerns in oil, defence and transport
65.x: The identified concerns include undervaluation, loss of dividend income and national-security risks in sectors such as oil, defence and transport. Automatic improvement in public ownership is not a criticism of disinvestment.
65.tq: Find the option that is inconsistent with the stated criticism of the policy.
xs: **Automatic improvement in public ownership** is not a concern — option **(2)** is the answer; disinvestment reduces public ownership.
Listed concerns: **undervaluation**, **loss of dividend income**, **national-security** concerns in **oil, defence, transport**.
xa: Main criticism: "**selling the family silver**" to fill the **fiscal deficit**.
**Risk of private monopolies** and **union resistance** are also debated.
**New PSE Policy 2021** keeps a "**bare minimum**" **1-4** CPSEs in **4** strategic sectors.

65.s: The National Renewal Fund, established in 1992, was intended primarily to provide:
o: A safety net and voluntary retirement support for workers affected by restructuring
Foreign exchange support to export-oriented industries
Direct loans to State electricity regulators
65.x: The National Renewal Fund provided a safety net, including VRS support, for workers affected by industrial restructuring.
65.tq: Match the fund with its beneficiary and policy purpose.
xs: The **National Renewal Fund (1992)** was a **safety net with VRS support for workers affected by restructuring** — option **(1)** is correct.
It was a worker-protection fund, not an export, acquisition or electricity-loan fund.
xa: **BIFR** (under **SICA 1985**) was dissolved on **1 Dec 2016**; cases → **NCLT/NCLAT**.
**IBC 2016** was enacted on **28 May 2016**; **IBBI** is the regulator.
**NCLT** was set up on **1 June 2016** under **s.408** of the Companies Act 2013.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about BIFR:
1. It was created under SICA, 1985.
2. It was dissolved on 1 December 2016.
3. After its dissolution, its cases were transferred to CCI and SEBI.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: BIFR was created under SICA 1985 and dissolved on 1 Dec 2016. Statement 3 is wrong: its cases went to NCLT/NCLAT under the IBC, not CCI and SEBI. So only option '1 and 2 only' fits.
65.tq: BIFR cases -> NCLT/NCLAT (IBC), not regulators.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **BIFR** was created under **SICA 1985**.
Statement 2: it was **dissolved on 1 Dec 2016**.
Statement 3 wrong: its cases went to **NCLT/NCLAT** under the **IBC**, not CCI and SEBI.
xa: **IBC 2016** came from the **T.K. Viswanathan BLRC 2015**; it is **creditor-in-control**.
NCLT was set up on the **Eradi Committee**'s advice.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
o: It provides a time-bound, creditor-in-control resolution process.
It restores the earlier debtor-in-control SICA process.
It regulates only foreign exchange transactions.
It abolished the NCLT appellate structure.
65.x: The IBC provides a time-bound resolution process based on creditor control. Its regulator is the IBBI.
65.tq: Identify the core operational features of the law rather than its year alone.
xs: The **IBC 2016** provides a **time-bound, creditor-in-control resolution** process — option **(1)** is correct.
It replaced the **SICA** regime, where the debtor stayed in possession.
It works through the **NCLT** and appellate **NCLAT** — it did not abolish them; forex is **FEMA**'s domain.
xa: IBC was enacted on **28 May 2016**, from the **T.K. Viswanathan BLRC 2015**.
**IBBI** is the regulator.
**BIFR** was dissolved on **1 Dec 2016**; its cases went to NCLT/NCLAT.

65.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was enacted on 28 May 2016 following the recommendations of which body?
o: T.K. Viswanathan-led Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee
65.x: The IBC followed the recommendations of the T.K. Viswanathan-led Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee, which reported in 2015.
65.tq: Discriminate between committees associated with insolvency, company law and competition policy.
xs: The IBC (**28 May 2016**) followed the **T.K. Viswanathan-led Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee** (**2015**) — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Eradi Committee** led to the **NCLT**; **S.V.S. Raghavan** to the **Competition Act**; the **Disinvestment Commission** advised on PSU sales.
xa: IBC = **time-bound**, **creditor-in-control** resolution; **IBBI** = regulator.
IBC replaced the **SICA 1985** regime.

65.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The NCLT was set up under Section 408 of the Companies Act, 2013 on 1 June 2016.
2. The NCLAT also hears appeals against CCI orders since 26 May 2017.
3. The NCLT was set up on the recommendation of the T.K. Viswanathan Committee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct (s.408, 1 June 2016). Statement 2 is correct (NCLAT, s.410, hears CCI appeals from 26 May 2017). Statement 3 is wrong: the NCLT followed the Eradi Committee; T.K. Viswanathan's BLRC led to the IBC. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
65.tq: NCLT = s.408 + Eradi; NCLAT = s.410; IBC = Viswanathan BLRC.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **NCLT** under **s.408** of the Companies Act 2013, set up **1 June 2016**.
Statement 2: **NCLAT** (**s.410**) hears **CCI** appeals from **26 May 2017**.
Statement 3 wrong: NCLT came from the **Eradi Committee**; **T.K. Viswanathan** led to the IBC.
xa: NCLT is the **adjudicating authority** under IBC.
IBC was enacted on **28 May 2016**.
BIFR cases went to **NCLT/NCLAT** after **1 Dec 2016**.

65.s: Under the New PSE Policy, 2021, which of the following is classified as a strategic sector?
65.x: Atomic energy, space and defence constitute one of the four strategic-sector groupings under the New PSE Policy, 2021.
65.tq: Recognise the official strategic-sector grouping rather than a general public-sector activity.
xs: **Atomic energy, space and defence** is a strategic sector under the **New PSE Policy 2021** — option **(1)** is correct.
The other strategic groups are **transport & telecom**; **power, petroleum, coal, minerals**; **banking, insurance, financial services**.
xa: The policy is part of **Atmanirbhar Bharat**.
Only a "**bare minimum**" of **1-4** CPSEs stays in each strategic sector.
Non-strategic CPSEs are to be **privatised, merged or closed**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the New PSE Policy, 2021:
1. Banking, insurance and financial services is classified as a non-strategic sector.
2. Only a bare minimum of 1 to 4 CPSEs is to be retained in each strategic sector.
3. CPSEs in non-strategic sectors are to be privatised, merged or closed.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is wrong: banking, insurance and financial services is one of the four strategic sectors. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: a bare minimum of 1-4 CPSEs per strategic sector, and non-strategic CPSEs are privatised, merged or closed. Hence '2 and 3 only'.
65.tq: Four strategic sectors include banking/insurance/financial services.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: **banking, insurance and financial services** is one of the **4 strategic sectors**.
Statement 2 correct: a "**bare minimum**" of **1-4** CPSEs per strategic sector.
Statement 3 correct: non-strategic CPSEs are **privatised, merged or closed**.
xa: Strategic sectors: atomic energy/space/defence; transport & telecom; power/petroleum/coal/minerals; banking/insurance/financial services.
**16th FC**: close **308** inactive State PSUs; privatise **DISCOMs**.
**ES 2025-26**: let stake in listed CPSEs fall to **26%**.

65.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: 16th Finance Commission — closure of 308 inactive State PSUs and privatisation of DISCOMs
IBBI — hearing appeals against CCI orders
BIFR — monetisation of surplus CPSE land
65.x: The 16th Finance Commission proposed closing 308 inactive State PSUs and privatising DISCOMs, so A is correct. NLMC monetises surplus CPSE land and buildings (combinations are regulated by CCI), CCI appeals are heard by NCLAT (IBBI is the IBC regulator), and BIFR dealt with sick companies under SICA.
65.tq: Use institutional-function matching and reject authority swaps.
xs: **16th Finance Commission — closure of 308 inactive State PSUs and privatisation of DISCOMs** is correct — option **(1)**.
**NLMC** monetises surplus CPSE land; combinations are regulated by **CCI**.
**CCI** appeals go to **NCLAT** (IBBI is the IBC regulator); **BIFR** dealt with sick companies under **SICA**.
xa: **NLMC**: **100%** GoI, incorporated **3 June 2022** under **DPE**.
NCLAT hears CCI appeals from **26 May 2017**.
ES **2025-26** proposes a **26%** floor for government stake in listed CPSEs.

65.s: The Economic Survey 2025–26 proposal regarding listed CPSEs seeks to permit government shareholding to fall to:
o: 49%, while converting them into private companies
65.x: The proposal allows government stake in listed CPSEs to fall to 26% while retaining their Government company status.
65.tq: Test the percentage threshold together with its qualifying condition.
xs: **Economic Survey 2025-26** proposes letting government stake in listed CPSEs fall to **26%**, **retaining Government company status** — option **(1)** is correct.
It keeps "Government company" status, so it does not convert them into private companies.
xa: **Minority disinvestment** = government keeps **more than 51%** and control.
**New PSE Policy 2021** keeps **1-4** CPSEs per strategic sector.
**2026-27** disinvestment target: **Rs 80,000 crore**.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes asset monetisation from disinvestment?
o: Asset monetisation applies only to surplus land, whereas disinvestment applies only to roads and power lines.
Asset monetisation leases brownfield public assets for a fixed period while ownership remains with the government, whereas disinvestment permanently sells equity.
Asset monetisation permanently sells government equity, whereas disinvestment leases public assets temporarily.
Both asset monetisation and disinvestment transfer ownership of public assets permanently to private operators.
65.x: Asset monetisation involves leasing existing public assets to private operators for a fixed period, after which the assets return to the government. Disinvestment involves the permanent sale of government equity.
65.tq: Discriminate between two closely related policy instruments by comparing ownership and duration.
xs: **Asset monetisation leases brownfield public assets for a fixed period, ownership staying with the government**; **disinvestment permanently sells equity** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses the two; in monetisation the assets **return** to the government.
xa: Monetised assets include **roads**, **railways**, **power lines**, **pipelines** — all **de-risked** brownfield assets.
**Strategic sale** transfers management control.
**NMP 2.0** was launched on **1 Mar 2026**.

65.s: The principal objective of asset monetisation is to:
o: use new financial structures to unlock value from existing public assets
transfer ownership of all public assets to private companies
raise funds only through the sale of government equity
replace all public-sector enterprises with private monopolies
65.x: Asset monetisation enables public asset owners to use new financial structures to unlock value from existing assets without permanently transferring ownership.
65.tq: Identify the precise objective rather than confusing monetisation with outright sale.
xs: Asset monetisation lets public asset owners **use new financial structures to unlock value from existing assets** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G1 **2024** key).
Ownership stays with the government, so it is not a transfer of ownership or an equity sale.
xa: Assets are leased to private operators for a **fixed period** and then return.
⚠ Monetisation leases assets vs disinvestment sells equity permanently.
**NLMC** (**3 June 2022**) monetises surplus CPSE land and buildings.

65.s:
With reference to the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP), consider the following statements:
1. It was launched in August 2021.
2. It envisaged monetisation of assets worth Rs 6 lakh crore over FY 2022–25.
3. It primarily concerns brownfield public assets such as roads, railways, power lines and pipelines.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: The NMP was launched in August 2021 and envisaged Rs 6 lakh crore of monetisation during FY 2022–25. Its focus is on existing brownfield public assets, including roads, railways, power lines and pipelines.
65.tq: Combine date, quantitative and scope details in a coded statement question.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **National Monetisation Pipeline** was launched in **Aug 2021**, with **Rs 6 lakh crore** over **FY22-25**.
It covers **brownfield** public assets — **roads, railways, power lines, pipelines**.
xa: **NMP 2.0** was launched on **1 Mar 2026**.
Ownership **stays with government**; assets return after the lease.
**NLMC** handles surplus land and buildings of CPSEs.

65.s: The National Land Monetisation Corporation (NLMC) is associated with the monetisation of:
o: foreign exchange reserves held by the Government of India
surplus land and buildings of Central Public Sector Enterprises, including loss-making enterprises
only privately owned industrial land acquired by the government
only the shares of listed Central Public Sector Enterprises
65.x: NLMC monetises surplus land and buildings belonging to Central Public Sector Enterprises, including those that are loss-making.
65.tq: Match the specialised institution with its precise asset and beneficiary group.
xs: **NLMC** monetises **surplus land and buildings of CPSEs, including loss-making ones** — option **(2)** is correct.
It does not sell CPSE shares — that is **DIPAM**'s work.
xa: NLMC is **100% GoI**, incorporated **3 June 2022** under **DPE**.
DIPAM modes: **strategic sale**, **OFS**, **IPO/FPO**, **CPSE ETF**.
Monetisation objective: **new financial structures** to unlock value.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
65.x: The Competition Act was enacted in 2002 and commenced on 31 March 2003. The other pairs are correctly matched.
65.tq: Find the wrong year among a set of familiar regulatory enactments.
xs: **Competition Act — 2016** is wrongly matched; the Act is of **2002** — option **(4)** is the answer.
Correct pairs: **FEMA 1999**, **MRTP 1969**, **FERA 1973**.
xa: The Competition Act commenced on **31 Mar 2003**; **CCI** was established **14 Oct 2003**.
**2016** is the year of the **IBC**.
⚠ Replacements: **FERA → FEMA**; **MRTP → Competition Act**; **SICA → IBC**.

65.s: Which Act was replaced by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 in relation to the earlier sick-industrial-company regime?
65.x: The IBC, 2016 replaced the SICA regime, which had been associated with the functioning of BIFR.
65.tq: Identify the predecessor regime rather than the more widely known foreign-exchange replacement.
xs: The **IBC 2016** replaced the **SICA, 1985** regime — option **(3)** is correct.
**MRTP** was replaced by the **Competition Act**; **FERA** by **FEMA**.
xa: SICA created **BIFR** (functioning **1987**).
BIFR → **NCLT**; its appeals forum → **NCLAT**.
**IDRA 1951** was the licensing law.

65.s: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the enactment of FEMA, the Competition Act and the IBC?
65.x: FEMA was enacted in 1999, the Competition Act in 2002 and the IBC in 2016.
65.tq: Arrange the Acts by their enactment years, not their commencement dates.
xs: The order is **FEMA, Competition Act, IBC** — option **(2)** is correct.
**FEMA 1999** → **Competition Act 2002** → **IBC 2016**.
xa: FERA was **liberalised in 1993** before FEMA replaced it.
The Competition Act commenced on **31 Mar 2003**.

65.s:
Which combination represents the major concerns associated with disinvestment debates?
1. Union resistance
2. Risk of private monopolies
3. Use of proceeds to fill the fiscal deficit
4. Guaranteed preservation of public control in all sectors
65.x: Union resistance, the risk of private monopolies and the use of proceeds to fill the fiscal deficit are recognised concerns. Disinvestment does not guarantee preservation of public control in every sector.
65.tq: Separate genuine criticisms from an absolute and unsupported guarantee.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are concerns — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Debates cite **union resistance**, **risk of private monopolies**, and proceeds used to **fill the fiscal deficit** ("selling family silver").
Statement 4 wrong: disinvestment reduces, not guarantees, public control.
xa: Other concerns: **undervaluation**, **loss of dividend income**, **national-security** concerns in oil, defence, transport.
Rationale: **poor returns**, fiscal deficit, **efficiency**, **market listing**.
The **Temasek model** treats government as a passive shareholder.

65.s: Which of the following best describes the recent shift in the Centre’s approach to public-sector enterprises?
o: From disinvestment to complete nationalisation of private firms
From earning dividends to selling all public assets
From selling PSUs towards earning from them through dividends and asset monetisation
From public ownership to abolition of all ETFs
65.x: The policy emphasis has shifted from selling PSUs towards earning from them, particularly through dividends and asset monetisation, while disinvestment receipts have declined.
65.tq: Identify the direction of policy change rather than a single isolated measure.
xs: Policy has moved **from selling PSUs towards earning from them through dividends and asset monetisation** — option **(3)** is correct.
Disinvestment receipts have been **falling since 2022-23**, while **dividends are rising**.
xa: No separate disinvestment heading in the Budget since **FY24**.
**NMP 2.0** launched on **1 Mar 2026**.
**2014 onwards** had produced ~**70%** of all proceeds since 1991.

65.s: The Temasek model of Singapore is generally characterised by the government acting as a:
o: mandatory manager of every investee enterprise
65.x: Singapore’s Temasek model is cited as one in which the government functions as a passive shareholder.
65.tq: Use the institutional role—shareholder versus manager—to identify the comparative model.
xs: Singapore's **Temasek model** has the government as a **passive shareholder** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a comparative model for managing state-owned holdings.
xa: Disinvestment **sells equity**; monetisation **leases assets**; a strategic sale **transfers control**.
ES **2025-26** proposes letting stake in listed CPSEs fall to **26%**.
DIPAM manages **Central Government equity**.

65.s: After 1991, the Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (APIIC) came to function primarily as a:
65.x: After 1991, APIIC’s role in Andhra Pradesh shifted towards that of a facilitator for industrial development.
65.tq: Identify the changed institutional role from the post-reform context.
xs: After **1991**, **APIIC** turned **facilitator** — option **(2)** is correct.
This mirrors the national shift where the State acts as **facilitator** under liberalisation.
xa: AP's PPP ports: **Krishnapatnam** and **Gangavaram**.
**Liberalisation** = removal of licences, quotas and controls.
After 1991, licensing was cut to **18** industries, now **5**.

65.s: Which of the following pairs of ports is associated with public-private partnership in Andhra Pradesh?
65.x: Krishnapatnam and Gangavaram ports are identified as examples of PPP ports in Andhra Pradesh.
65.tq: Recall the exact pair instead of selecting a nearby port combination.
xs: **Krishnapatnam and Gangavaram** are AP's **PPP ports** — option **(2)** is correct.
They illustrate the post-1991 public-private partnership approach in AP.
xa: Post-1991, **APIIC** turned **facilitator**.
**Monetisation** leases brownfield assets to private operators for a fixed period.
**Privatisation** transfers ownership and management control.

65.s: Which of the following statements regarding the National Investment Fund is incorrect?
o: Its objective is to generate returns by depleting the corpus.
Its corpus is intended to be permanent.
It is classified under the Public Account.
65.x: Option B is incorrect: the National Investment Fund (2005) aims to earn returns without using up its permanent corpus. It sits in the Public Account.
65.tq: Watch for a reversed objective.
n: The National Investment Fund was established in November 2005. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The corpus of the National Investment Fund is intended to be permanent. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The government objective for the National Investment Fund is to generate returns without depleting its corpus. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The National Investment Fund is classified under the Public Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Investment Fund:
I. It is professionally managed.
II. It is classified under the Public Account.
III. It was created in 1995–96.
IV. It channels proceeds from disinvestment of CPSEs.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: I, II and IV are correct: the NIF is professionally managed, sits in the Public Account and receives CPSE disinvestment proceeds. III is false because it was set up in 2005; 1995–96 is RIDF.
65.tq: Discriminate the NIF from RIDF.
n: The purpose of the National Investment Fund is to channelise proceeds from the disinvestment of Central Public Sector Enterprises. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The National Investment Fund is professionally managed. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The National Investment Fund is classified under the Public Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund was created in 1995–96. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]

66.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011:
1. It aimed to raise the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25% within a decade.
2. It targeted the creation of 100 million jobs.
3. Its proposals were sector-specific and technology-specific, favouring selected industries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct: the NMP 2011 targeted a 25% manufacturing share of GDP within a decade. Statement 2 is correct: it aimed at 100 million jobs. Statement 3 is wrong: the policy was sector-neutral, location-neutral and technology-neutral, with only green technology getting incentives. Hence 1 and 2 only.
66.tq: NMP 2011 = 25%, 100 million jobs, neutral on sector, location and technology; 143 million jobs = National Manufacturing Mission.

66.s: In Andhra Pradesh, NIMZs have been proposed in which districts?
66.x: NIMZs have received in-principle approval in Chittoor and Prakasam districts of Andhra Pradesh.
66.tq: Apply the location trap by matching the initiative with the correct districts.
xs: AP's NIMZs are proposed in **Chittoor and Prakasam** — option **(3)** is correct.
They have **in-principle approval**, and a **TEFS** report was submitted (**2025-26**).
xa: **NIMZs** are large integrated industrial townships with **zoned land use**, **clean technology** and **social infrastructure**.
NIMZs differ from SEZs in **size**, **infrastructure planning**, **governance**, **exit policy** and **fiscal incentives**.
AP's **Rayalaseema manufacturing hub** includes JSW steel **Kadapa**, **Kia** and Royal Enfield **Tirupati**.

66.s: Which of the following best describes a National Investment and Manufacturing Zone (NIMZ)?
o: A rural credit institution for financing manufacturing units
A large integrated industrial township with zoned land use, clean technology and social infrastructure
A tax-free trading port governed exclusively by the customs authority
A small export-only industrial estate without social infrastructure
66.x: NIMZs are conceived as large integrated industrial townships with zoned land use, clean technology and social infrastructure.
66.tq: Match the official institutional term with its defining features.
xs: An **NIMZ** is a **large integrated industrial township** with **zoned land use, clean technology and social infrastructure** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is not a small export-only estate, a port or a credit institution.
xa: NIMZs differ from **SEZs** in size, infrastructure planning, governance, exit policy and fiscal incentives.
AP NIMZs: **Chittoor** and **Prakasam** (in-principle approval).
An **SEZ** is an export-oriented enclave treated as **foreign territory** for trade and duties.

66.s: With reference to the National Manufacturing Policy, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It specifically included skilling of rural youth as a measure.
It replaced all industrial training with fiscal incentives.
It restricted skill development to metropolitan areas.
It discouraged skilling initiatives for rural youth.
66.x: Skilling of rural youth was specifically included among the policy measures.
66.tq: Identify the positive policy objective instead of a reversed negative formulation.
xs: The National Manufacturing Policy **specifically included skilling of rural youth** — option **(1)** is correct.
It did not limit skilling to metros or replace training with incentives.
xa: Infrastructure was on a **PPP** basis.
Design: **sector-, location- and technology-neutral**.
Notified **November 2011**.

66.s: Under the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011, infrastructure development was envisaged primarily on which basis?
66.x: The National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 provided for infrastructure on a PPP basis. It did not restrict funding to the public sector, foreign grants or cooperatives.
66.tq: NMP 2011 infra = PPP.
xs: NMP 2011 envisaged infrastructure on a **public-private partnership (PPP)** basis — option **(1)** is correct.
It did not restrict funding to the State, foreign aid or cooperatives.
xa: It also focused on skilling **rural youth**.
Targets: **25%** of GDP, **100 million** jobs.
It was **technology-neutral**, except for incentives to **green technology**.

66.s: The National Manufacturing Mission announced in Budget 2025-26 aims by 2035 to achieve which combination?
o: Manufacturing share of 20 percent and 100 million jobs
Manufacturing share of 25 percent and 75 million jobs
Manufacturing share of 25 percent and 143 million jobs
Manufacturing share of 30 percent and 100 million jobs
66.x: The National Manufacturing Mission targets a 25 percent manufacturing share and 143 million jobs by 2035.
66.tq: Distinguish the latest mission's target from the earlier policy targets.
xs: The **National Manufacturing Mission** targets a **25 percent** share and **143 million jobs** by **2035** — option **(3)** is correct.
**100 million** jobs was the NMP 2011 / Make in India target.
xa: The Mission was announced in **Budget 2025-26**.
ES **2025-26** credits **PLI** and the Mission with driving investment.
Industry GVA grew **7.0%** in **H1 FY26**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about Make in India:
1. It was launched on 25 September 2014.
2. Its logo is a tiger made of cogwheels.
3. DPIIT is the nodal department for manufacturing and the Department of Commerce for services.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct (25 Sept 2014). Statement 2 is wrong: the logo is a lion made of cogwheels. Statement 3 is correct: under the Ministry of Commerce & Industry, DPIIT handles manufacturing and the Department of Commerce services. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
66.tq: Lion of cogs; DPIIT = manufacturing.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: Make in India launched on **25 September 2014**.
Statement 2 wrong: the logo is a **lion made of cogwheels**, not a tiger.
Statement 3 correct: **DPIIT** handles manufacturing, the **Department of Commerce** services.
xa: Nodal ministry: **Ministry of Commerce & Industry**.
Linked slogans: '**Vocal for Local**', "Make in India for the World".
Original coverage: **25** sectors.

66.s: Which one of the following was NOT an original quantitative target of Make in India?
o: Raising the manufacturing share of GDP to 50 per cent by 2030
Manufacturing growth of 12–14 per cent annually
Increasing the manufacturing share of GDP from 16 per cent to 25 per cent
66.x: The stated targets were 12–14 per cent annual manufacturing growth, a rise in the manufacturing share from 16 to 25 per cent, and 100 million additional jobs. A 50 per cent share by 2030 was not an original target.
66.tq: Find the quantitative statement that does not belong to the stated target set.
xs: **50 per cent of GDP by 2030** was not a Make in India target — option **(1)** is the answer.
Original targets: manufacturing growth **12-14%** a year; share **16% → 25%**; **100 million** additional jobs.
xa: The share target date was **2022**, later **2025**.
Manufacturing remains only **~16.3-17.5%** of GVA/GDP.
Strategy has shifted to **global value chains** and design capability.

66.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Pillar)
a. New Processes
b. New Infrastructure
c. New Sectors
d. New Mindset

List-II (Feature)
i. Government as facilitator rather than regulator
ii. Corridors and smart cities
iii. Single window and e-Biz
iv. FDI in defence, insurance and medical devices

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
66.x: New Processes involve single window and e-Biz; New Infrastructure includes corridors and smart cities; New Sectors include selected FDI areas; and New Mindset views government as a facilitator.
66.tq: Start from the sure pair between a pillar and its defining feature.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**New Processes** = single window/**e-Biz**; **New Infrastructure** = **corridors**, **smart cities**.
**New Sectors** = **FDI** in defence, insurance, medical devices; **New Mindset** = government as **facilitator**, not regulator.
xa: New Processes also covers **ease of doing business** and land.
New Sectors also includes **construction** and **railway infrastructure**.
Some notes add **FDI liberalisation** as a fifth point.

66.s: Make in India 2.0 covers how many priority or champion sectors, and how are they distributed between manufacturing and services?
o: 27 sectors: 12 manufacturing under DPIIT and 15 services under the Department of Commerce
27 sectors: 15 manufacturing under DPIIT and 12 services under the Department of Commerce
66.x: Make in India 2.0 covers 27 sectors, comprising 15 manufacturing sectors under DPIIT and 12 services sectors under the Department of Commerce.
66.tq: Separate the total from its two departmental components.
xs: **Make in India 2.0** (**2021**) has **27** sectors: **15 manufacturing under DPIIT** and **12 services under the Department of Commerce** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) swaps the two counts; **25** was the original sector count.
xa: The **Action Plan for Champion Services Sectors** covers **12** sectors.
⚠ Trap: the APPSC **2018** key gave "**10**" for this count.
Original Make in India covered **25** sectors.

66.s: Which of the following best describes the present status and strategic shift of Make in India?
o: Manufacturing remains about 16.3–17.5 per cent of GVA, and the strategy has shifted towards global-scale manufacturing, design capability and global value-chain integration.
The programme has shifted exclusively from manufacturing to agriculture.
Manufacturing has already reached 25 per cent of GVA, so the original target has been fully achieved.
Manufacturing has fallen below 5 per cent of GVA, leading to a complete withdrawal of the initiative.
66.x: Manufacturing remains around 16.3–17.5 per cent of GVA, below the 25 per cent target, prompting a strategic emphasis on scale, design and global value chains.
66.tq: Use the comparison between the target share and the reported present share.
xs: Manufacturing is still **~16.3-17.5%** of GVA, and strategy has shifted to **global-scale manufacturing, design capability and global value-chain integration** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **25%-by-2025** target was **missed**, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: The shift was noted in **Jun 2026**.
Criticism: "**Assemble in India**" vs value addition; PLI gains concentrated in **electronics** and **semiconductors**.
Medium- and high-tech manufacturing = **46.3%** of total (ES **2025-26**).

66.s: Which strategy most directly reflects the central approach of Make in India?
o: Replacing digital services with traditional services
Restricting manufacturing to wholly state-owned enterprises
Attracting foreign direct investment and global firms to manufacture in India
Promoting only domestic consumption without export orientation
66.x: Attracting FDI and global firms to establish manufacturing in India is the strategy most typical of Make in India.
66.tq: Match the initiative with its characteristic strategy rather than its general developmental effects.
xs: The most typical Make in India strategy is **attracting FDI and global firms to manufacture in India** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not about state-only manufacturing or domestic-only consumption.
xa: Slogan: "**Make in India for the World**".
**New Sectors** pillar opened **FDI** in defence, insurance, medical devices.
EoDB and PLI aim to join global value chains (**"China+1"**).

66.s: The original Make in India initiative launched in September 2014 covered how many sectors?
66.x: The original Make in India covered 25 sectors across manufacturing, infrastructure and services. 27 is the count of priority/champion sectors under Make in India 2.0 (2021); 14 is the number of PLI sectors; 12 is the number of champion services sectors.
xs: Original Make in India covered **25** sectors — option **(1)** is correct.
**27** = Make in India 2.0 (**2021**); **14** = PLI sectors; **12** = champion services sectors.
xa: The 25 spanned **manufacturing**, **infrastructure** and **services**.
Make in India 2.0 = **15** manufacturing (DPIIT) + **12** services (Commerce).
Launched **25 September 2014**.

66.s: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme was designed primarily to provide incentives on which basis?
o: Incremental sales of goods manufactured in India
66.x: PLI provides incentives linked to incremental sales of goods made in India; in electronics, the incentive is stated as 4–6 per cent.
66.tq: Apply the scheme’s name to identify the production-and-sales trigger.
xs: PLI gives incentives on **incremental sales of goods manufactured in India** — option **(3)** is correct.
In electronics the incentive is **4-6%**.
xa: PLI supports **sunrise industries**.
⚠ PLI **4-6%** on incremental sales vs MPMS **2.25-5%** on eligible sales.
**PLI-Auto** (**Rs 25,938 crore**) needs at least **50%** domestic value addition.

66.s: Which one of the following is NOT a sector included in the PLI scheme as listed?
66.x: White goods, solar PV modules and specialty steel are included sectors. Coal mining equipment is not included in the listed PLI sectors.
66.tq: Use the complete sector list to eliminate the outside item.
xs: **Coal mining equipment** is not a PLI sector — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Specialty steel**, **solar PV modules** and **white goods** are PLI sectors.
xa: Other PLI sectors: mobiles/electronics, IT hardware, telecom, bulk drugs, pharma, medical devices, food products.
Also: auto & components, **ACC battery**, textiles (**MMF** & technical), **drones**.
PLI covers **14 sectors** with **Rs 1.97 lakh crore**.

66.s:
Which of the following statements about the PLI scheme is correct?
1. It supports sunrise industries.
2. In the electronics sector, incentives are stated at 4–6 per cent of incremental sales.
3. PLI-Auto has an outlay of ₹25,938 crore.
4. PLI-Auto requires at least 50 per cent domestic value addition.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
66.x: All four statements are correct: PLI supports sunrise industries, electronics incentives are 4–6 per cent, PLI-Auto has an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, and it requires at least 50 per cent domestic value addition.
66.tq: Combine design features, sector-specific figures and an eligibility condition.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
PLI supports **sunrise industries**; electronics incentives are **4-6%** of incremental sales.
**PLI-Auto** has **Rs 25,938 crore** and needs at least **50% domestic value addition**.
xa: PLI covers **14 sectors**, **Rs 1.97 lakh crore** (announced **2020**).
Results to **Sep 2025**: **12.60 lakh** jobs.
PLI-LSEM ended on **31 March 2026**, replaced by **MPMS**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about PM E-DRIVE:
1. It was launched by the Ministry of Heavy Industries on 29 September 2024.
2. Its outlay is Rs 11,500 crore.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: PM E-DRIVE's outlay is Rs 10,900 crore; Rs 11,500 crore was FAME-II (2019-24), which it succeeded. Hence '1 only'; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
66.tq: 10,900 = PM E-DRIVE; 11,500 = FAME-II.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **PM E-DRIVE** launched by the **Ministry of Heavy Industries** on **29 Sept 2024**.
Statement 2 wrong: its outlay is **₹10,900 crore**; **₹11,500 crore** was **FAME-II** (**2019-24**).
xa: It **succeeded FAME-II** and **subsumed EMPS-2024**.
First-ever support for **e-trucks** and **e-ambulances**.
e-2W/3W support till **31 Mar 2026**; others till **31 Mar 2028**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme approved for FY2026-27 to FY2030-31:
1. It replaces PLI-LSEM and gives an incentive of 2.25-5% on eligible sales.
2. It gives up to 1.5% extra incentive for domestic sourcing.
3. It gives 3% extra incentive for design and R&D by foreign brands.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the 3% extra is for design and R&D by Indian brands. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
66.tq: Extra 3% rewards Indian brands' design/R&D.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: MPMS **replaces PLI-LSEM** with **2.25-5%** incentive on eligible sales.
Statement 2: up to **1.5%** extra for **domestic sourcing**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **3%** extra is for design and R&D by **Indian brands**, not foreign ones.
xa: MPMS outlay: **Rs 62,500 crore** for **FY2026-27** to **FY2030-31**.
PLI-LSEM ended on **31 March 2026**.
⚠ PLI **4-6%** on incremental sales vs MPMS **2.25-5%** on eligible sales.

66.s: India’s position in mobile phone manufacturing is best described as follows:
o: The second-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The fifth-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The third-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
66.x: India is identified as the second-largest mobile phone manufacturer.
66.tq: Use the precise rank rather than assuming that the largest domestic market is the largest manufacturer.
xs: India is the world's **second-largest mobile phone manufacturer** — option **(1)** is correct.
Some **2026** notes say "**among the top 3** in volume".
xa: Mobile output rose from **₹18,900 crore (2014-15)** to **₹5.45 lakh crore (2024-25)**, CAGR ~**40%**.
**99.2%** of phones used in India are made domestically.
Smartphones were the **largest export category in 2025**.

66.s:
With reference to the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), consider the following statements:
1. Twelve projects have been approved under the Mission.
2. The approved projects involve commitments of about ₹1.64 lakh crore.
3. Capital assistance under the Mission may extend up to 50 per cent.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: ISM approved 12 projects involving about ₹1.64 lakh crore of commitments, and capital assistance may extend up to 50%.
66.tq: Combine the project count, financial commitment and assistance ceiling only after verifying each statement.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**ISM 1.0** approved **12 projects** worth about **₹1.64 lakh crore**, most from **Tata Electronics**.
Capital assistance goes up to **50%**.
xa: ISM 1.0 outlay: **Rs 76,000 crore**.
Project locations: Gujarat **6**, Odisha **2**, Assam, UP, Punjab, **AP 1 each**.
**ISM 2.0** aims at **70-75%** self-sufficiency by **2029**.

66.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the institutional position and scope of the India Semiconductor Mission?
o: It functions under the Department of Commerce and supports only semiconductor imports.
It functions under the Digital India Corporation and supports fabs, OSAT/ATMP units and chip design.
It functions under the Reserve Bank of India and supports only mobile-phone assembly.
It functions under NITI Aayog and supports only electronics exports.
66.x: ISM operates under the Digital India Corporation of MeitY and supports fabs, OSAT/ATMP and chip design.
66.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to identify the correct institutional role.
xs: **ISM** works under the **Digital India Corporation** and supports **fabs, OSAT/ATMP units and chip design** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is under **MeitY**, not the Department of Commerce, RBI or NITI Aayog.
xa: Capital assistance up to **50%**.
ISM 1.0: **12 projects**, ~**Rs 1.64 lakh crore**.
ATMP unit at **Sanand**: **₹22,516 crore**.

66.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Semicon India or ISM programme is correct?
o: It is a DBT programme approved in 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,000 crore.
It is an MoES programme approved in 2021 with an outlay of ₹4,077 crore.
It is a MeitY programme approved in 2021 with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore.
It is a DST programme approved in 2023 with an outlay of ₹6,003.65 crore.
66.x: Semicon India or ISM is under MeitY, was approved in 2021 and has an outlay of ₹76,000 crore.
66.tq: Use the ministry–year–outlay combination to avoid mission substitution.
xs: **Semicon India / ISM** is a **MeitY** programme approved in **2021** with **₹76,000 crore** — option **(3)** is correct.
It sits under the **Digital India Corporation** of MeitY.
xa: ISM was set up in **Dec 2021**.
ISM 2.0 (**₹1,27,500 crore**) approved by Cabinet (**16 Jul 2026** report).
ISM supports **fabs**, **OSAT/ATMP** and **chip design**.

66.s: Which one of the following semiconductor units is NOT correctly matched with its location?
o: Tata Electronics–PSMC wafer fab — Dholera, Gujarat
Tata OSAT (Tata Semiconductor Assembly & Test) — Morigaon (Jagiroad), Assam
66.x: Kaynes Semicon's OSAT is at Sanand, Gujarat, not Dholera. The Tata–PSMC wafer fab (India's first semiconductor-fab SEZ) is at Dholera, Tata OSAT at Jagiroad in Morigaon, Assam, and Micron's ATMP at Sanand.
66.tq: Fab = Dholera; OSAT/ATMP cluster = Sanand; Assam = Morigaon.
xs: **Kaynes Semicon OSAT — Dholera** is wrongly matched; it is at **Sanand**, Gujarat — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Tata Electronics–PSMC** wafer fab — **Dholera**; **Tata OSAT** — **Morigaon (Jagiroad)**, Assam; **Micron** ATMP — **Sanand**.
xa: The Dholera fab is India's **first semiconductor-fab SEZ**.
**CG Power** (Renesas, Stars) OSAT at Sanand is in **commercial production**.
Dholera also hosts the first **GaN micro-LED display fab**.

66.s: Which one of the following is NOT a pillar of Atmanirbhar Bharat?
66.x: The five pillars are Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography and Demand. Privatisation is not listed as one of these pillars.
66.tq: Find the odd policy term that does not belong to the stated five-pillar framework.
xs: **Privatisation** is not a pillar of Atmanirbhar Bharat — option **(2)** is the answer.
The five pillars: **Economy**, **Infrastructure**, **System**, **Vibrant Demography**, **Demand**.
xa: The **May 2020** package was ~**Rs 20 lakh crore** (~**10%** of GDP).
**Vocal for Local** is linked with Make in India.
Make in India links with '**Vocal for Local**' and "Make in India for the World".

66.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The National Logistics Policy was launched in September 2022.
2. PM GatiShakti was launched in September 2022.
3. Logistics costs in India have historically been about 13-14% of GDP.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: PM GatiShakti came in October 2021. Statement 3 is correct: both initiatives target logistics costs of about 13-14% of GDP. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
66.tq: GatiShakti Oct 2021 came before NLP Sept 2022.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **National Logistics Policy** — **September 2022**.
Statement 2 wrong: **PM GatiShakti** came in **October 2021**.
Statement 3 correct: logistics costs were historically **13-14% of GDP**.
xa: Make in India's **New Infrastructure** pillar covers **corridors** and **smart cities**.
**ISM** also dates from **Dec 2021**.
**NSWS** gives access to **686** central and **7,498** state approvals.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about Special Economic Zones:
1. Only the Central Government can set up an SEZ.
2. The SEZ Act, 2005, with the SEZ Rules, came into force on 10 February 2006.
3. An SEZ is an export-oriented enclave treated as foreign territory for trade and duties.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Central Government, a State Government or any person (private, joint or foreign developer) can set up an SEZ. Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Hence '2 and 3 only'.
66.tq: SEZ developers: Centre, State or any person.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the **Central Government, a State Government or any person** (private, joint, foreign developer) can set up an SEZ.
Statement 2 correct: **SEZ Act 2005** + Rules in force **10 February 2006**.
Statement 3 correct: an SEZ is an export enclave treated as **foreign territory** for trade and duties.
xa: **Sec 10AA**: **100%** export income tax exemption for **5 years**, then **50%** for 5 years.
Sunset: only units operational by **30 June 2020** get 10AA benefits.
Proposed **DESH** framework (**Jun 2026**) would drop compulsory **positive NFE**.

66.s: Under Section 10AA, the income-tax exemption on export income of an eligible SEZ unit is structured as:
o: 100 per cent for five years, 50 per cent for the next five years and 50 per cent of ploughed-back profit for a further five years
50 per cent for five years, 100 per cent for the next five years and nil thereafter
50 per cent for the entire fifteen-year period
100 per cent for ten years followed by 25 per cent for five years
66.x: Section 10AA provides 100 per cent exemption for the first five years, 50 per cent for the next five years and 50 per cent of ploughed-back profit for another five years.
66.tq: Track the exemption sequence and distinguish the successive time periods.
xs: **Sec 10AA**: **100%** for **five years**, **50%** for the next five, and **50% of ploughed-back profit** for a further five — option **(1)** is correct.
The exemption is on **export income** of an eligible SEZ unit.
xa: Only units operational by **30 June 2020** get this (extended from **31 March 2020**).
The **SEZ Act, 2005** came into force on **10 February 2006**.
SEZs are **single-window**, export-oriented enclaves.

66.s:
Which of the following is proposed under the DESH framework for Development of Enterprise & Service Hubs?
1. Dropping the compulsory positive NFE requirement
2. Allowing sales to the Domestic Tariff Area
3. Making the framework WTO-compliant
4. Prohibiting all domestic sales by SEZ units
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
66.x: The proposed DESH framework would drop compulsory positive NFE, permit sales to the Domestic Tariff Area and be WTO-compliant. It would not prohibit all domestic sales.
66.tq: Find the false reversal in the statement on domestic sales.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are proposed — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**DESH** (**Jun 2026**) would **drop compulsory positive NFE**, allow **sales to the Domestic Tariff Area**, and be **WTO-compliant**.
Statement 4 wrong: it allows, not bans, domestic sales.
xa: DESH = **Development of Enterprise & Service Hubs**, a proposed reform of the **SEZ Act, 2005**.
SEZ **Sec 10AA** benefits end for units not operational by **30 June 2020**.
SEZs are treated as **foreign territory** for trade and duties.

66.s: The World Bank Doing Business framework was conceptualised by the:
66.x: The Doing Business framework was conceptualised by the International Finance Corporation.
66.tq: Identify the correct international institution rather than a neighbouring financial body.
xs: The **Doing Business** framework was conceptualised by the **International Finance Corporation (IFC)** — option **(2)** is correct.
IFC is the **World Bank Group**'s private-sector arm; the report was published by the World Bank Group.
xa: Rankings mainly guided **foreign investors** (APPSC-GS **2019**).
It was **discontinued in 2021** over data irregularities and ethics concerns.
Its replacement is **B-READY**, with **3** pillars.

66.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. India’s Doing Business rank in 2014 — 142nd
2. India’s Doing Business rank in DB 2020 — 63rd
3. Doing Business report — discontinued in 2021 over data irregularities

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
66.x: India moved from 142nd in 2014 to 63rd in the Doing Business 2020 report, and the report was discontinued in 2021 because of data irregularities.
66.tq: Link the rank sequence with the subsequent discontinuation of the report.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
India ranked **142** in **DB 2015** (2014) and **63** in **DB 2020**, the last edition.
The report was **discontinued in 2021** over **data irregularities** and ethics concerns.
xa: Doing Business was conceptualised by the **IFC** and published by the **World Bank Group**.
Its replacement is **B-READY**.

66.s: Which of the following correctly represents the three pillars of the World Bank's B-READY framework?
o: Regulatory framework, public services and operational efficiency
66.x: The three B-READY pillars are regulatory framework, public services and operational efficiency.
66.tq: Recall the exact three-part framework and avoid substituting broad economic objectives.
xs: B-READY's three pillars are **regulatory framework, public services and operational efficiency** — option **(2)** is correct.
Taxation, exports or investment-employment triads are not its pillars.
xa: ⚠ Doing Business = **10** parameters; B-READY = **3** pillars; NITI Investment Friendliness Index = **8** pillars.
B-READY replaced **Doing Business**, discontinued in **2021**.
India joins the **third** B-READY report.

66.s: The World Bank's Doing Business rankings were meant mainly to guide which of the following?
66.x: Per the APPSC-GS 2019 key, the Doing Business rankings mainly guide foreign investors on the ease of doing business in a country. They are not meant for consumers, election bodies or monetary policy.
