3. Privatisation involved nationalisation of private companies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
71.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: disinvestment was first used to bridge the fiscal deficit (later for efficiency), and autonomy came through Navratna/Maharatna status. Statement 3 is wrong: nationalisation is the odd one out, not part of the 1991 NEP. So '1 and 2 only'.
71.tq: Privatisation = disinvestment + autonomy; nationalisation is never part of the NEP.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **disinvestment** was first used to **bridge the fiscal deficit**, later for efficiency.
Statement 2 correct: autonomy through **Navratna/Maharatna** status.
Statement 3 wrong: **nationalisation** was the odd one out — **not** part of the 1991 NEP (**APPSC 2018**).
xa: **Dereservation** (1991) opened public-sector-reserved industries to private players.
**New PSE Policy (2021)** for **Atmanirbhar Bharat**.

71.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy?
71.x: Nationalisation was not a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy. The policy instead promoted delicensing, disinvestment and greater foreign investment.
71.tq: Find the measure that reverses the reform direction.
xs: **Nationalisation** was NOT a 1991 NEP feature — option **(2)**.
It was the **odd one out** in **APPSC 2018**.
**Disinvestment**, **FDI liberalisation** and **delicensing** were NEP features.
xa: Also NOT NEP: strengthening the **License Raj/MRTP**, import substitution, more SSI reservation.
The economy was opened to foreign and private investment in **1991** (APPSC 2018).
FDI up to **100%** via automatic route in high-priority industries.

71.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the 1991 New Economic Policy is correct?
1. Full capital-account convertibility was not adopted.
2. Demonetisation formed part of the 1991 reform package.
3. Foreign direct investment was liberalised through an automatic route in high-priority industries.
4. Devaluation, tariff cuts and removal of import quotas were included among the external-sector measures.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
71.x: Statement 2 is false: demonetisation was not part of the 1991 package (India's demonetisations were in 1978 and 2016). Statement 1 is true because full capital-account convertibility was never adopted. Statements 3 and 4 (automatic-route FDI in high-priority industries; devaluation, tariff cuts and removal of import quotas) were 1991 measures, so the answer is 1, 3 and 4.
71.tq: Reject the famous-word traps and retain the measures that match the 1991 reform direction.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **full capital account convertibility** is still not adopted.
Statement 2 wrong: **demonetisation** was not part of 1991 (India's were in **1978** and **2016**).
Statements 3 and 4 correct: **automatic-route FDI** in high-priority industries; **devaluation, tariff cuts, import-quota removal**.
xa: ⚠ **FDI in retail and defence** opened only much later.
**100% FDI in insurance** is now in place (May 2026).
**Nationalisation** was the odd one out (APPSC 2018).

71.s:
Consider the following statements about the impact of globalisation on India:
1. Trade in goods and services expanded.
2. Access to foreign technology increased.
3. Imports grew faster than exports.
4. Exports grew faster than imports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Globalisation expanded trade and access to foreign technology, but imports grew faster than exports. Therefore, statement 4 is false.
71.tq: Catch the reversed comparison between export and import growth.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: rapid growth of **exports and imports**, more FDI, **access to foreign technology**.
Statement 3 correct: **imports grew faster than exports**.
Statement 4 wrong: "exports rose more than imports" is **not true** (**PYQ 2025; APPSC 2025**).
xa: India's world trade share had fallen from **1.78%** (1950) to **0.6%** (1995).
IT/outsourcing boom **cushioned the CAD**.
CAD peaked at **4.8%** of GDP (**FY13**).

71.s: The expansion of India's information-technology and outsourcing sector helped to
o: widen the current account deficit without any offsetting effect
71.x: The IT and outsourcing boom generated services exports and helped cushion India's current account deficit.
71.tq: Link the service-export boom with its balance of payments effect.
xs: The IT/outsourcing boom helped **cushion the current account deficit** — option **(3)**.
**Outsourcing** is a major feature of globalisation.
xa: **1,800+ Global Capability Centres** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in **July 2026**.
CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peak **4.8%** (FY13).
**ES 2025-26**: persistent CAD = structural cause of India's **high cost of capital**.

71.s: Which adverse outcome was associated with the pattern of growth after economic reforms?
o: Growth became entirely dependent on public-sector employment.
Agriculture received all investment and labour-intensive sectors disappeared.
Capital-intensive sectors generated more jobs than the available labour force.
Agriculture was neglected and capital-intensive growth generated too few jobs.
71.x: The pattern of growth was criticised for neglecting agriculture and concentrating growth in capital-intensive sectors, which created too few employment opportunities.
71.tq: Identify the stated distributional and employment consequence rather than the aggregate growth benefit.
xs: **Agriculture was neglected** and **capital-intensive** growth created **too few jobs** — option **(4)**.
This is the **Beyond GDP essay** criticism.
xa: **Jobless growth**: output rose faster than jobs; many graduates end in **gig work**.
**Agrarian neglect**: public investment in agriculture lagged.
**Crony capitalism**: gains concentrated among large, politically connected firms.

71.s:
Arrange the following GDP growth outcomes in chronological order:
A. Growth of 6.3 percent
B. Growth of less than 1 percent
C. Growth of 5 percent

1. 1991–92
2. 1992–94
3. 1994–95

Select the correct sequence.
71.x: GDP growth was below 1 percent in 1991–92, around 5 percent during 1992–94, and 6.3 percent in 1994–95.
71.tq: Fix the earliest year first and then place the later growth figures in sequence.
xs: Growth recovered steadily after the 1991 stabilisation.
xa: Average growth: **5.18%** in the 1980s vs **6.8%** from **1993-94**.
GDP growth had been **1.1%** in **1990-91**.

71.s: Foreign-exchange reserves increased from approximately $975 million in 1991 to about
71.x: Foreign-exchange reserves rose from about $975 million in 1991 to approximately $701.4 billion, providing around 11 months of import cover as stated.
71.tq: Handle changes in units carefully when comparing a million figure with a billion figure.
xs: Reserves rose from **$975 million** (1991) to about **$701.4 billion** — option **(3)**.
That gives about **11 months** of import cover.
xa: ⚠ Forex cover: **2 weeks (1991)** vs **over 11 months** now.
In **1991** **67 tonnes of gold** had to be pledged abroad.
PM's **May 2026** appeal to save forex was not made even in 1991.

71.s: Which of the following developments correctly reflects the post-1991 reform direction?
o: FDI and FPI were invited, while IT and services exports provided an important cushion
FDI was prohibited and services exports were discouraged
Tariffs were raised uniformly to protect all domestic producers
Export promotion was replaced by a complete ban on imports
71.x: The post-reform approach lowered tariffs, invited foreign direct and portfolio investment, and benefited from IT and services exports as a cushion.
71.tq: Choose the option that combines the complementary openness measures without an absolute claim.
xs: **FDI and FPI were invited**, and **IT/services exports** became a **cushion** — option **(1)**.
Tariffs were **lowered**, not raised.
xa: Direction: **import substitution → export promotion**.
Economy moved to **enhanced global integration** (**PYQ 2025**).
**1,800+ GCCs** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in July 2026.

71.s: Which one of the following sectors remained largely a state monopoly after the reforms?
71.x: Railways remained a state monopoly, although modernisation continued to be pursued. The other sectors experienced greater private-sector participation or competition.
71.tq: Find the sector that was comparatively untouched among reform-exposed industries.
xs: **Railways** remained a **state monopoly** — option **(2)**.
Modernisation is still in progress (**LENS, May 2026**).
**Civil aviation**, **consumer electronics** and **telecom** saw private entry.
xa: Other slow sectors: **power distribution** (DISCOM privatisation debated), **agriculture**, **ports**.
**Civil aviation** saw **private airlines** enter.
Telecom: falling prices after private and foreign entry.

71.s:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding sectors affected by post-1991 reforms?
1. Civil aviation saw the entry of private airlines.
2. Automobiles and consumer electronics were reshaped by reforms.
3. Power distribution underwent complete and uncontested privatisation.
4. Major ports were only recently undergoing corporatisation.
Select the correct answer.
71.x: Private airlines entered civil aviation, and automobiles and consumer electronics were reshaped by reforms. Power-distribution privatisation remained debated, while corporatisation of major ports was only recently progressing.
71.tq: Reject the absolute claim of complete privatisation while retaining the sectoral comparisons.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **civil aviation** — private airlines.
Statement 2 correct: **automobiles and consumer electronics** were reshaped.
Statement 3 wrong: **DISCOM privatisation** is **still debated**; statement 4 correct: major ports' corporatisation only now.
xa: **Telecom** and **banking** were also reshaped.
**Railways** remained a state monopoly.
Source of the slow-sector notes: **LENS, May 2026**.

71.s: Which of the following best illustrates the criticism of crony capitalism?
o: Agricultural investment increases uniformly across regions
Small firms exclusively control public-sector disinvestment
All firms receive equal access to public resources
Gains are concentrated among large, politically connected firms
71.x: Crony capitalism is criticised because economic gains become concentrated among large firms with political connections.
71.tq: Recognise the concept through its distributional consequence.
xs: Crony capitalism = **gains concentrated among large, politically connected firms** — option **(4)**.
It is one of three main criticisms of the reforms.
xa: **Jobless growth**: output rose faster than jobs.
**Agrarian neglect**: public investment in agriculture lagged.
**Washington Consensus** is now seen as obsolete (14 Mar 2026).

71.s:
Which one of the following combinations correctly represents elements of the Washington Consensus?
1. Privatisation
2. Deregulation
3. Property rights
4. Expansion of import quotas
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
71.x: Privatisation, deregulation and protection of property rights were among the ten rules associated with the Washington Consensus. Expansion of import quotas was not included.
71.tq: Use the policy-list approach and identify the item that reverses liberalisation.
xs: **1, 2 and 3** — privatisation, deregulation, property rights — option **(2)**.
The **Washington Consensus** (**10 rules**): fiscal discipline, tax reform, trade and FDI liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, property rights.
Expanding **import quotas** is the opposite of trade liberalisation.
xa: It is blamed for the **1997** and **2008** crises.
It is now seen as **obsolete** (14 Mar 2026).
SAP conditions also included **currency devaluation** and **austerity**.

71.s: The criticism of 'jobless growth' made against India's post-1991 growth refers to a situation in which:
o: Unemployment was eliminated but output stagnated
71.x: Jobless growth means output grew much faster than jobs, so many people, including graduates, ended up in gig work. Employment rising faster than output is the reverse. A fall in both is a recession, and stagnant output with no unemployment does not describe the criticism.
71.tq: Jobless growth = GDP up, jobs lag.
xs: Jobless growth = **output rose faster than employment** — option **(1)**.
Many **graduates** end up in **gig work**.
Option (2) is the reverse of the criticism.
xa: Growth was concentrated in **capital-intensive** sectors.
Other criticisms: **agrarian neglect** and **crony capitalism**.
Some formalisation, but the **informal sector** stays dominant.

71.s: Which sequence correctly represents the broad stages described as Reforms 1.0, Reforms 2.0 and the Reforms 3.0 debate?
o: DPI in 1991 → LPG from 2014 → Reforms 3.0 before 1991
LPG in 1991 → DPI from 2014 onwards → debate on Reforms 3.0
LPG in 2014 → DPI in 1991 → Reforms 3.0 in 2021
Strategic disinvestment in 1991 → LPG in 2014 → DPI before 1991
71.x: Reforms 1.0 refers to liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation in 1991; Reforms 2.0 refers to digital public infrastructure from 2014 onwards; Reforms 3.0 remains a debate.
71.tq: Arrange reform phases by their stated years and distinguishing themes.
xs: **Reforms 1.0 = LPG (1991)** → **Reforms 2.0 = DPI from 2014** → **Reforms 3.0** debate — option **(2)**.
Reforms 2.0 = digital public infrastructure: **DPI, UPI, Jan Dhan, DBT**.
xa: The "Reforms 3.0" debate is current (**Jul 2026**).
Post-reform the economy moved to **enhanced global integration** + larger private sector (APPSC 2025).
LPG = **liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation**.

71.s: Which two global financial crises have been blamed, in the stated criticism, on the Washington Consensus?
71.x: The Washington Consensus has been criticised in connection with the 1997 and 2008 financial crises.
71.tq: Associate the criticised policy framework with the specified crisis years.
xs: The Washington Consensus is blamed for the **1997** and **2008** crises — option **(1)**.
It is now **widely questioned** (**14 Mar 2026**).
xa: It had **10 rules**: fiscal discipline, tax reform, trade/FDI liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, property rights.
SAP outcomes: growth fell from **3.2% to 0.7%** a year in the Global South.
SAPs raised **poverty and inequality** in the Global South.

71.s: Persistent current account deficit has been identified as the structural cause of India’s
71.x: Persistent CAD has been identified as a structural cause of India’s high cost of capital.
71.tq: Connect the macroeconomic indicator with its stated structural consequence.
xs: Persistent **CAD** is the structural cause of India's **high cost of capital** — option **(3)**.
This is from the **ES 2025-26** (Economic Survey).
xa: CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peaked at **4.8%** (FY13).
In 1991 the CAD was **3.1-3.2%** of GDP.
IT/services exports help **cushion the CAD**.

71.s: Which one of the following correctly states the broader significance attributed to the post-reform Indian economy?
o: It replaced all private investment with foreign aid
It moved towards enhanced global integration and a larger private sector
It restored universal industrial licensing and public-sector monopoly
It moved towards complete economic isolation and a smaller private sector
71.x: The post-reform economy is characterised by greater global integration and an expanded role for the private sector.
71.tq: Select the balanced long-term outcome rather than an absolute reversal.
xs: Post-reform the economy moved to **enhanced global integration** and a **larger private sector** — option **(2)**.
This was the **APPSC 2025** key.
Restoring licensing or isolation is the opposite of reform.
xa: Reforms 1.0 = **LPG (1991)**; Reforms 2.0 = **DPI (2014 onwards)**.
FDI inflows **rose sharply**; reserves rose to **$701.4 bn**.
Services became the **largest sector**.

71.s: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced primarily to address which of the following?
o: Dominance of the public and joint sectors
Decline in agriculture's share of GDP
71.x: The 1991 New Economic Policy was a response to a severe balance-of-payments crisis, when foreign reserves covered only about two weeks of imports.
71.tq: Recall the trigger for the 1991 reforms.
n: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced to address the severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

71.s: Which of the following statements about post-1991 trends is incorrect?
o: The share of agriculture in GDP increased enormously.
India's share in global exports grew.
71.x: Option B is incorrect: after 1991, agriculture's share of GDP fell, as services grew. Forex reserves, FDI and India's share of world exports all rose.
71.tq: Watch for a reversed trend.
n: Foreign Direct Investment inflows increased after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
India's foreign-exchange reserves expanded after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
India's share in global exports grew after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Agriculture's share in GDP did not increase enormously after the 1991 reforms. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Agriculture's share in GDP declined after the 1991 reforms. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

71.s:
Consider the following statements about globalisation under the 1991 reforms:

I. It involved integration of the domestic economy with the world economy.
II. It facilitated greater participation of Multinational Corporations.
III. It was facilitated through trade, capital including FDI, and cross-border technology.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
71.x: All three are correct: globalisation linked India to the world economy through trade, FDI and technology flows, and drew in more multinational companies.
71.tq: Recall the elements of globalisation.
n: Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded participation of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through foreign direct investment capital. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through cross-border technology. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates technology flows. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation promotes greater global integration. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded entry of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

71.s:
Assertion (A): Liberalisation removes or reduces domestic controls.
Reason (R): Liberalisation focuses on removing state controls through industrial de-licensing, import deregulation and private-sector expansion.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true: liberalisation reduces domestic controls, and it does this through de-licensing, freer imports and more room for the private sector. R explains A.
71.tq: Ask whether the tools explain the aim.
n: Liberalisation removes or reduces domestic controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation focuses on removing state controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import deregulation is an instrument of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Private-sector expansion is an aspect of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) De-licensing
(b) Import liberalisation
(c) Disinvestment
(d) Globalisation

List-II
(i) Abolition of industrial licensing for most industries
(ii) Reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions
(iii) Sale of government equity in public sector enterprises
(iv) Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy
71.x: De-licensing abolished industrial licensing for most industries, import liberalisation cut tariffs and quantitative curbs, disinvestment sold government equity in PSEs, and globalisation integrated India with the world economy, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
71.tq: Define each 1991 reform tool by what it actually changed.
n: De-licensing is associated with international trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Deregulation is associated with foreign investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import liberalisation is associated with multinational corporation participation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation promotes greater market orientation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

71.s:
Assertion (A): The New Industrial Policy was associated with LPG.
Reason (R): LPG stands for liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true: the New Industrial Policy is linked to LPG, and LPG stands for liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. Expanding the short name does not explain the link, so R does not explain A.
71.tq: Ask whether an expansion explains a link.
n: The New Industrial Policy was associated with LPG. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
LPG stands for liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Stabilisation is short-term in nature.
II. Stabilisation is demand-side in nature.
III. Structural adjustment is long-term in nature.
IV. Structural adjustment is supply-side in nature.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: All four are correct: stabilisation is short-term and works on demand, while structural adjustment is long-term and works on supply.
71.tq: Discriminate stabilisation from structural adjustment.
n: Stabilisation is short-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Stabilisation is demand-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is long-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is supply-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]

71.s: Which of the following best describes free trade?
o: Reduction or removal of trade barriers
Provision of an internationally competitive environment
Creation of a level playing field for exports
71.x: Free trade means reducing or removing trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas. The other options are SEZ objectives.
71.tq: Discriminate free trade from SEZ aims.
n: Free trade involves the reduction or removal of trade barriers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]

71.s: LPG reforms were associated with which of the following?
71.x: The LPG reforms opened the door to multinational corporations. Licensing, the joint sector and public-sector dominance belong to the pre-1991 policies.
71.tq: Discriminate pre- and post-1991 features.
n: LPG reforms were associated with multinational corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]

72.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Reform measure)
a. Tariff cuts and removal of import licensing
b. Factor-market reforms
c. Making Panchayati Raj Institutions fully functional
d. Industrial delicensing
List-II (Generation)
i. First generation
 ii. Second generation
 iii. Third generation

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
72.x: Tariff cuts and industrial delicensing are first-generation reforms; factor-market reforms are second-generation reforms; and fully functional Panchayati Raj Institutions represent third-generation reforms.
72.tq: Start with the distinctive third-generation pair and then classify the remaining measures.
xs: **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**First generation (1991-2000)**: **tariff cuts**, removal of import licensing, **industrial delicensing**.
**Second generation**: **factor markets** (land, labour, capital); **third generation**: fully functional **Panchayati Raj Institutions**.
xa: Second-generation areas also include **public sector**, **oil sector**, government institutions, **fiscal** reform.
First generation also had **FDI up to 51%** and **MRTP reform**.
Regulators and the **CCI** were strengthened in the second generation.

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's first-generation economic reforms:
1. They are associated with the period 1991-2000.
2. Industrial licensing was retained for only six industries.
3. FDI was permitted up to 74 per cent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: Statement 1 is correct: first-generation reforms ran 1991-2000. Statement 2 is correct: after delicensing only 6 industries need a licence. Statement 3 is wrong: the 1991 reforms allowed FDI up to 51 per cent, not 74. Hence only 1 and 2 (B); A misses statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
72.tq: 1991 package numbers: 6 licensed industries, 51% FDI.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: first-generation reforms = **1991-2000**.
Statement 2 correct: licensing now applies to only **6 industries**.
Statement 3 wrong: 1991 allowed FDI up to **51%**, not 74%.
xa: Other first-generation steps: **MRTP reform**, **interest-rate deregulation**, FDI **automatic route**.
Second generation (2000s onward) targets **factor markets**.
Third generation: **Panchayati Raj Institutions** made fully functional.

72.s: Which one of the following was treated as NOT belonging to the Government's second-generation reform list in the relevant classification?
o: Reform of government and public institutions
72.x: In the cited classification, Legal System Reforms was treated as not belonging to the Government's second-generation list, although broader reform discussions also refer to IPC, CrPC, labour and company-law reforms.
72.tq: Use the stated classification key and distinguish it from broader descriptions of reform areas.
xs: **Legal System Reforms** was treated as NOT on the Government's second-generation list — option **(1)**.
This was the **UPPSC 2009** key: **oil sector**, **public sector**, **government/public institutions** were on the list.
⚠ UPSC notes do mention **IPC/CrPC** and labour/company-law reforms — but follow the key.
xa: Second-generation areas: **factor markets** (land, labour, capital) and **fiscal** reform.
Sectors: **oil, power, telecom**; **CCI** strengthened (UPSC notes **p.51**).
Third generation: **Panchayati Raj** institutions.

72.s:
The four-factor-market reform framework identifies which of the following combination of reforms?
1. Land reforms involving digitisation of land records
2. Labour reforms through four Labour Codes
3. Capital reforms involving IBC and capital-market reform

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
72.x: The framework covers land, labour and capital: land-record digitisation, four Labour Codes, and IBC and capital-market reforms.
72.tq: Test the three pillars of factor-market reform together.
xs: All three — **land, labour, capital** — option **(4)**.
**Land**: **DILRMP, ULPIN, NGDRS** digitise land records.
**Labour**: **Four Codes**; **Capital**: **IBC** and capital-market reform.
xa: Corporates are **moving to non-bank funding** (ES 2025-26).
"Next Generation Reforms" pillars start with **land** (easier acquisition) + **labour** (simpler laws).
**29** central labour laws were merged into **4** Codes.

72.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of initiatives for digitising land records?
72.x: DILRMP, ULPIN and NGDRS are associated with digitising land records.
72.tq: Identify the complete set belonging to one factor market.
xs: **DILRMP, ULPIN and NGDRS** digitise land records — option **(2)**.
**IBBI** relates to insolvency (capital market), not land.
xa: Land-record digitisation was noted on **9 Jun 2026**.
Capital-market reform: **IBC**.
Next-generation reform pillars begin with **land** and **labour**.

72.s: The pillars of the next-generation reforms begin with which two factor markets?
72.x: The stated pillars begin with land, including easier acquisition, and labour, including simpler laws.
72.tq: Recall the opening pillars rather than the broader reform list.
xs: Next-generation reform pillars begin with **land** (easier acquisition) and **labour** (simpler laws) — option **(4)**.
Capital, energy and services are not named as the starting pillars.
xa: Land: **DILRMP, ULPIN, NGDRS**.
Labour: **29** laws → **4 Codes**.
Capital: **IBC**, capital-market reform.

72.s: Which of the following is the correct number of Central laws merged into the four Labour Codes?
72.x: The four Labour Codes merged 29 Central labour laws.
72.tq: Distinguish the total number of laws from the individual code-wise counts.
xs: The four Codes merged **29** central labour laws — option **(3)**.
⚠ Trap: some notes say the **Code on Wages** merges 29 — it merges only **4**; 29 is all four Codes together.
xa: Split: **4 – 3 – 9 – 13** = Wages – IR – Social Security – OSH.
Sections cut from **1,232 to 480**; rules from **1,436 to 401**.
Codes operational from **21 November 2025**.

72.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: OSH and Working Conditions Code — 13 laws
72.x: The Industrial Relations Code subsumed three laws, not four. The Code on Social Security, OSH Code and Code on Wages subsumed 9, 13 and 4 laws respectively.
72.tq: Compare the code-wise counts and identify the deliberately altered figure.
xs: **Industrial Relations Code — 4 laws** is NOT correctly matched — option **(2)**.
The **IR Code** subsumes **3** laws: **Trade Unions Act 1926**, **Standing Orders Act 1946**, **Industrial Disputes Act 1947**.
Wages **4**, Social Security **9**, OSH **13** are correct.
xa: ⚠ **4 – 3 – 9 – 13** laws = **Wages – IR – Social Security – OSH**.
Only the Code on Wages is from **2019**; the rest are **2020**.
Industrial Disputes Act year **1947** was asked in **APPSC 2019**.

72.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Labour Code)
 a. Code on Wages
 b. Industrial Relations Code
 c. Code on Social Security
 d. Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code

List-II (Year)
 i. 2019
 ii. 2020
 iii. 2020
 iv. 2020

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
72.x: The Code on Wages was enacted in 2019. The Industrial Relations Code, Code on Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code were enacted in 2020.
72.tq: Start with the unique year pair and then match the three codes carrying the same year.
xs: **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
Only the **Code on Wages** is **2019**; the **IR**, **Social Security** and **OSH** Codes are **2020**.
xa: Codes operationalised from **21 November 2025**.
Central Rules for all four notified **May 2026**.
Draft central rules came in **Dec 2025**.

72.s: Labour is placed in which List of the Constitution of India?
72.x: Labour is included in the Concurrent List, allowing both the Union and the States to legislate on the subject.
72.tq: Use the subject classification to discriminate between Union, State and Concurrent powers.
xs: Labour is on the **Concurrent List** — option **(1)**.
So both the Centre and States frame rules under the Codes.
xa: **29** central laws → **4** Codes.
Central Rules for all four were notified in **May 2026**, nearly six years after enactment.
Sections were cut from **1,232 to 480**; rules from **1,436 to 401**.

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the four Labour Codes:
1. The Codes were operationalised from 21 November 2025.
2. The Central Rules for all four Codes were notified in May 2026.
3. The Economic Survey 2025-26 expects a GDP gain of 1.25% by 2029-30 from the Codes.
4. Draft central rules for the Codes were released in December 2024.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
72.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the Codes came into force on 21 November 2025, Central Rules for all four were notified in May 2026, and ES 2025-26 projects a 1.25% GDP gain by 2029-30. Statement 4 is wrong: draft central rules came in December 2025, not 2024. So A leaves out a true statement, C and D include the false one.
72.tq: Anchor the sequence: in force Nov 2025, draft rules Dec 2025, final rules May 2026.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: Codes operationalised from **21 November 2025**.
Statement 2 correct: Central Rules for all four notified **May 2026**.
Statement 3 correct: ES 2025-26 expects **1.25%** GDP gain by **2029-30**; statement 4 wrong — drafts came in **Dec 2025**.
xa: Formalisation expected to rise from **60.4% to 75.5%**.
Trade unions call the Codes **anti-worker**; the 2026 rules did not soften them.
Sections cut from **1,232 to 480**.

72.s: Which one of the following laws is NOT merged into the Code on Wages, 2019?
72.x: The Code on Wages subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Wages Act, Payment of Bonus Act and Equal Remuneration Act. The Contract Labour Act is merged into the OSH and Working Conditions Code, not the Code on Wages.
72.tq: Find the wrongly placed law by distinguishing neighbouring Codes.
xs: The **Contract Labour Act 1970** is NOT in the Code on Wages — option **(3)**.
It is part of the **OSH Code** (**UPPSC 2021** PYQ).
Code on Wages merges **Payment of Wages 1936**, **Minimum Wages 1948**, **Payment of Bonus 1965**, **Equal Remuneration 1976**.
xa: OSH Code (**13** laws) also has the **Factories Act 1948**, **Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979**, **BOCW Act 1996**.
The Code on Wages is the only **2019** Code.
⚠ The Code on Wages merges **4** laws, not 29.

72.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Labour Code)
a. Code on Wages, 2019
b. Industrial Relations Code, 2020
c. Code on Social Security, 2020
 d. OSH and Working Conditions Code, 2020
List-II (Principal law)
i. Factories Act, 1948

72.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Labour Code concerned?
o: Crèche at 50 or more employees — OSH Code
Women working night shifts with consent — Code on Wages
Safety committees at 500 or more workers — Industrial Relations Code
26-week maternity leave — Code on Social Security
72.x: The Code on Social Security provides for 26 weeks of maternity leave. The OSH Code contains provisions concerning women working night shifts with consent and safety committees at 500 or more workers, while the crèche threshold is associated with the Code on Social Security.
72.tq: Use subject-area matching to detect provisions assigned to the wrong Code.
xs: **26-week maternity leave — Code on Social Security** — option **(4)**.
**Crèche at 50+** is also in the **Social Security Code**, not OSH.
**Night shifts** with consent and **safety committees at 500+** are in the **OSH Code**.
xa: ⚠ **300** = IR Code threshold; **50+** = crèche; **500+** = OSH safety committee.
Code on Wages: **8-hour day, 48-hour week** (2026 Rules).
IR Code: gratuity for fixed-term workers after **1 year**.

72.s:
Which of the following statements about the Code on Wages, 2019 is correct?
1. It provides for a universal minimum wage.
2. The Centre fixes a national floor wage.
3. It prohibits gender discrimination, including discrimination against transgender persons.
4. Its 2026 Rules provide for an eight-hour day and a 48-hour week.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
72.x: All four statements correctly describe provisions or rules associated with the Code on Wages.
72.tq: Use the all-inclusive option only after verifying each provision separately.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Code on Wages: **universal minimum wage**; Centre fixes a **national floor wage**.
**No gender discrimination**, including against **transgender** persons.
**2026 Rules**: **8-hour day, 48-hour week**.
xa: **50% rule** on allowances for PF/gratuity/bonus.
It merges **4** laws and is the only **2019** Code.

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding fixed-term employment under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018:
1. It was extended to all sectors.
2. It made it easier for firms to end employment.
3. No notice of termination is needed for a temporary workman.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
72.x: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 extended fixed-term employment to all sectors. They made it easier for firms to end employment and removed the need for a termination notice for a temporary workman. All three statements are correct, as in the UPSC 2019 key.
72.tq: Check each consequence of fixed-term employment instead of assuming ordinary permanent-worker protections.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
The **2018 Standing Orders rules** extended **fixed-term employment** to **all sectors**.
They made it **easier to lay off/end employment**; **no termination notice** for a temporary workman.
xa: ⚠ Trap: both statements correct in the **UPSC 2019** PYQ.
IR Code 2020: fixed-term workers get **parity + gratuity after 1 year**.
Unions call the IR Code **hire-and-fire** (12 Jun 2026).

72.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Industrial Relations Code, 2020?
o: Prior permission threshold for lay-off, retrenchment and closure was raised from 100 to 300 workers
Fixed-term workers are excluded from parity with permanent workers
Fixed-term workers receive gratuity only after five years
Standing orders apply to establishments with 100 or more workers
72.x: The threshold for prior permission was raised from 100 to 300 workers. Fixed-term workers receive parity and gratuity after one year, while standing-order requirements apply to establishments with 300 or more workers.
72.tq: Use threshold and entitlement comparisons to reject reversed or exaggerated statements.
xs: Prior permission threshold for lay-off/retrenchment/closure raised **from 100 to 300 workers** — option **(1)**.
Fixed-term workers get **parity** and gratuity after **1 year**, not five.
Standing orders apply only to **300+** workers, not 100.
xa: Unions call this **hire-and-fire** (12 Jun 2026).
⚠ **300** = IR Code; **500+** = OSH safety committee.
IR Code subsumes **3** laws.

72.s: The Goods and Services Tax came into force in India on:
72.x: GST came into force on 1 July 2017.
72.tq: Distinguish the constitutional amendment date from the implementation date.
xs: GST came into force on **1 July 2017** — option **(2)**.
**8 Sep 2016** was the assent to the **101st Amendment**.
xa: **Art. 246A** = power to levy GST; **Art. 279A** = GST Council; **Art. 269A** = IGST.
First State to ratify: **Assam**.
ES 2025-26 calls **GST 2.0** the most radical overhaul since **2017**.

72.s: Article 246A, which provides the constitutional basis for GST legislation by Parliament and the States, was inserted by the:
72.x: The 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016 inserted Article 246A.
72.tq: Match the constitutional article with the correct amendment number.
xs: **Art. 246A** was inserted by the **101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016** — option **(1)**.
Assent: **8 Sep 2016**.
xa: ⚠ **246A** = power to levy GST; **269A** = IGST; **279A** = GST Council.
GST in force from **1 July 2017**.
Origin: **Vijay Kelkar Committee**; **Canadian model**.

72.s:
Which of the following taxes was subsumed under GST as a Central tax?
1. Central excise duty
2. Service tax
3. Central Sales Tax
4. State VAT

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
72.x: Central excise, service tax and CST were among the Central taxes subsumed under GST; State VAT was a State tax.
72.tq: Separate Central and State taxes in a coded statement question.
xs: **1, 2 and 3** — **central excise, service tax, CST** — option **(1)**.
**State VAT** is a **State** tax, not a Central one.
xa: GST ended **cascading** through input tax credit.
**IGST** (Art. **269A**) applies to inter-state supply and imports.
GST in force from **1 July 2017**.

72.s:
Consider the following statements about the origins of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India:
1. The GST reform is associated with the Vijay Kelkar Committee.
2. India's dual GST is modelled on the Canadian model.
3. Gujarat was the first State to ratify the Constitution Amendment relating to GST.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: GST traces to the Vijay Kelkar Committee and follows the Canadian (dual) model. Statement 3 is wrong: Assam, not Gujarat, was the first State to ratify the GST amendment. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses statement 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
72.tq: Kelkar + Canada + Assam first: the trap is the State that ratified first.

72.s:
Consider the following statements about Next-Generation GST (GST 2.0):
1. It was announced on the 79th Independence Day in August 2025.
2. It introduced a 40% slab for sin and luxury goods.
3. It abolished input tax credit to simplify returns.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: GST 2.0 was announced on the 79th Independence Day (Aug 2025) with rate rationalisation and a 40% slab for sin and luxury goods. Statement 3 is wrong: input tax credit is the core of GST and stops cascading, so it was not abolished. '1 only' misses the 40% slab, and the options with 3 are wrong.
72.tq: GST 2.0 = Aug 2025, 40% sin slab, 90% export refund in 7 days.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **GST 2.0** announced on the **79th Independence Day (Aug 2025)**.
Statement 2 correct: **40% slab** for **sin/luxury** goods.
Statement 3 wrong: **input tax credit** is the core of GST that ends cascading — not abolished.
xa: GST 2.0 also gave **90%** provisional export refunds in **7 days** (Sep 2025).
ES 2025-26: most radical overhaul since **2017**.
Rate rationalisation was the main plank.

72.s: NITI Aayog was established in 2015 primarily to replace the Planning Commission and promote:
72.x: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission and promotes cooperative and competitive federalism.
72.tq: Match an institutional reform with its stated objective.
xs: **NITI Aayog** (**2015**) replaced the Planning Commission to promote **cooperative and competitive federalism** — option **(2)**.
Centralised licensing and exclusive public ownership run against the post-1991 reform direction.
xa: **DBT** began on **1 Jan 2013** (**JAM** trinity).
Corporate tax cut: **Sept 2019**.
**Jan Vishwas** Act 2023 decriminalised minor offences.

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the corporate tax cut:
1. The base rate for existing companies was cut to 22 per cent.
2. New manufacturing units were given a rate of 15 per cent.
3. The cut was announced in September 2020.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: 22 per cent for existing firms and 15 per cent for new manufacturing units. Statement 3 is wrong: the cut came in September 2019, not 2020. So B; A omits the true statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
72.tq: Corporate tax cut = Sept 2019, 22/15.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: base rate **22%** for existing firms.
Statement 2 correct: **15%** for new manufacturing units.
Statement 3 wrong: the cut came in **Sept 2019**, not 2020.
xa: **PLI** came in **2020** (Atmanirbhar **₹20 lakh crore** package).
Three **farm Acts** came in **Sept 2020** and were repealed in **2021**.
S&P upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB** (ES 2025-26).

72.s: Which of the following correctly states the principal purpose of the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023?
o: Ranking of States on business competitiveness
72.x: The Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 decriminalised minor offences to facilitate compliance and reduce the burden of criminal provisions.
72.tq: Match the Act with its core reform objective rather than its administrative platform.
xs: **Jan Vishwas Act 2023** = **decriminalisation of minor offences** — option **(1)**.
**Bill 2025** covers **16 Acts**, **355 provisions** (**288** decriminalised) (IYB 2026).
xa: Compliance burden: **48,000+** compliances reduced; **3,400+** provisions decriminalised.
**Over 350** reforms incl. fewer **Quality Control Orders** (Budget 2026-27).
Critics want "**ease of living**" above "ease of doing business".

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP):
1. It was announced in August 2021.
2. It envisaged about ₹6 lakh crore over FY2022-25.
3. It covers core assets of State governments and municipalities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: NMP was announced in August 2021 with a ₹6 lakh crore target over FY2022-25. Statement 3 is wrong: it covers core assets of central ministries and CPSEs, not State or municipal assets. So B; A omits statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
72.tq: NMP = Centre's brownfield assets: Aug 2021, ₹6 lakh crore, FY22-25.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: NMP announced **Aug 2021**.
Statement 2 correct: **₹6 lakh crore** over **FY2022-25**.
Statement 3 wrong: it covers core assets of **central ministries and CPSEs**, not States/municipalities.
xa: Model: **brownfield**, de-risked assets leased (**OMT**, **InvITs**).
**Ownership stays with government**; assets handed back; **no land sale**.
⚠ Largest share = **Roads**, then railways, then power.

72.s: Which of the following correctly describes the asset monetisation model under the National Monetisation Pipeline?
o: Brownfield, de-risked assets are leased through mechanisms such as OMT and InvITs, while ownership remains with the government
Only shares of private companies are transferred to the government
Government land is sold without any contractual transfer
Greenfield assets are sold permanently to private parties
72.x: NMP uses brownfield, de-risked assets and mechanisms such as OMTs and InvITs; ownership remains with the government and assets are handed back after the lease period.
72.tq: Distinguish monetisation through leasing from outright sale.
xs: **Brownfield, de-risked assets** leased via **OMT and InvITs**, **ownership stays with government** — option **(1)**.
Assets are **handed back**; there is **no land sale** — options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: NMP: **₹6 lakh crore** over **FY2022-25** (announced **Aug 2021**).
Shares: **Roads ~27%**, **railways ~25%**, **power ~15%**.
IYB 2026 lists an **SPV for Land Monetisation** (surplus CPSE land).

72.s: Which of the following correctly represents the approximate NMP sectoral shares?
72.x: The approximate shares are roads 27 per cent, railways 25 per cent and power 15 per cent.
72.tq: Preserve the order of sectors and their percentages in a comparison table.
xs: **Roads 27%, railways 25%, power 15%** — option **(4)**.
⚠ Largest share = **Roads**, then **railways**, then **power**.
xa: NMP covers core assets of **central ministries and CPSEs**.
Model: brownfield assets leased via **OMT** and **InvITs**.
Value: **₹6 lakh crore** over **FY2022-25**.

72.s: According to the World Bank's Doing Business ranking, India's rank improved from 142 in 2014 to:
72.x: India's World Bank Doing Business rank improved from 142 in 2014 to 63 in 2019.
72.tq: Pair the institution, years and ranks without mixing them with IMD figures.
xs: India's Doing Business rank rose from **142 (2014)** to **63 in 2019** — option **(1)**.
The ranking was conceived by the **IFC** (World Bank).
xa: **AP** has been **ranked No. 1 since BRAP 2016**.
Compliance: **48,000+** compliances reduced; **3,400+** provisions decriminalised.
AP angle: **District Industries Centres** run the **single window** and implement the **MSMED Act**.

72.s: Andhra Pradesh has ranked first since which edition of the Business Reforms Action Plan?
72.x: Andhra Pradesh has ranked number one since BRAP 2016.
72.tq: Distinguish the first release year from the edition associated with Andhra Pradesh's ranking.
xs: AP has been **ranked No. 1 since BRAP 2016** — option **(1)**.
BRAP = **Business Reforms Action Plan**, the States' ease-of-doing-business ranking.
xa: AP's **Single Desk Portal** is linked to the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor** EoDB loan.
**District Industries Centres** run the **single window** and implement the **MSMED Act**.
India's World Bank Doing Business rank: **142 (2014) → 63 (2019)**.

72.s: According to the Budget 2026–27 reference, the number of reforms counted was:
72.x: The Budget 2026–27 counts more than 350 reforms.
72.tq: Read the threshold carefully; “350+” means more than 350, not an exact figure.
xs: Budget 2026-27 counts **more than 350** reforms — option **(2)**.
They include **GST simplification**, **Labour Codes** and rationalised **Quality Control Orders**.
xa: ES 2025-26 "slew of reforms": GST overhaul, insurance **100% FDI**, nuclear power opened to private sector.
S&P upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB**.
Labour Codes operational since **Nov 2025**.

72.s: The Single Desk Portal in Andhra Pradesh is linked to the:
o: Andhra Pradesh Power Distribution Recapitalisation Fund
72.x: The Single Desk Portal is linked to the Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor ease-of-doing-business loan.
72.tq: Use the distinctive institutional and corridor pairing to avoid confusing related State initiatives.
xs: AP's **Single Desk Portal** is linked to the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor EoDB loan** — option **(3)**.
Source: **APSES Ch. 6**.
xa: **District Industries Centres** run the **single window** + implement the **MSMED Act**.
AP **ranked No. 1 since BRAP 2016**.
World Bank Doing Business was conceived by the **IFC**.

72.s:
The improvement in India’s Market Distortions Performance Index position was credited to which of the following?
1. GST
2. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
3. Trade facilitation
4. Restoration of import quotas
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
72.x: GST, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and trade facilitation were credited with the improvement. Restoration of import quotas was not cited.
72.tq: Select the reforms that support market efficiency and reject the protectionist distractor.
xs: **1, 2 and 3** — **GST**, **IBC** and **trade facilitation** — option **(3)**.
**Restoring import quotas** would be a distortion, not a reform, and was not cited.
xa: The index rank moved from **82nd (2010)** to **57th (2023)** (Competere Foundation).
**IBC** is a **capital**-market factor reform.
GST came into force on **1 July 2017**; **GST 2.0** announced **Aug 2025**.

72.s:
Consider the following statements regarding GST-related constitutional provisions:
I. Article 246A empowers Parliament and State Legislatures to levy GST.
II. Article 269A deals with the levy and collection of IGST on inter-State supplies.
III. Article 279A provides for the GST Council.
IV. Article 366(12A) gives the constitutional definition of GST.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
72.x: All four are correct: Article 246A gives the power to levy GST, 269A covers IGST, 279A the GST Council, and 366(12A) defines GST.
72.tq: Match each Article to its GST role.
n: Article 246A empowers Parliament and State Legislatures to levy GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Article 269A relates to the levy and collection of IGST on inter-State supplies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Article 279A relates to the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Article 366(12A) provides the constitutional definition of GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Parliament and State Legislatures have GST legislative powers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

72.s: Which Article provides restrictions relating to taxation of supplies outside a State and import-export?
72.x: Article 286 limits States from taxing supplies outside the State or in the course of import and export. Article 269A covers IGST on inter-State supply.
72.tq: Match each Article to its GST role.
n: Article 286 provides restrictions relating to taxation of supplies outside a State and import-export. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

73.s: The net terms of trade (NTT) is calculated as:
o: Import price index divided by export price index multiplied by 100
Export quantity index divided by import quantity index multiplied by 100
Export price index divided by import price index multiplied by 100
Import quantity index divided by export quantity index multiplied by 100
73.x: Net terms of trade equals the export price index divided by the import price index, multiplied by 100.
73.tq: Keep price indices separate from quantity indices in formula-based questions.
xs: The net terms of trade = **export price index ÷ import price index × 100** — so option **(3)** is correct.
With the revised base of **Mar 2026**, **NTT = export price index / import price index**.
Option (4), **import quantity ÷ export quantity**, is the **gross terms of trade (GTT)**, not NTT.
xa: **Income terms of trade (ITT)** = **NTT × export quantity index**.
⚠ NTT uses **price** indices; GTT uses **quantities** — the usual pairing trap.
**Devaluation/depreciation** makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**, which moves the terms of trade.

73.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Gross terms of trade — export price index/import price index
Income terms of trade — import quantity/export quantity
Gross terms of trade — import quantity index/export quantity index
Net terms of trade — import quantity index/export quantity index
73.x: Gross terms of trade is defined as the import quantity index divided by the export quantity index. NTT uses price indices, while ITT is NTT multiplied by the export quantity index.
73.tq: Start with the sure distinction between price-based NTT and quantity-based GTT.
xs: **Gross terms of trade = import quantity index / export quantity index** — so option **(3)** is correctly matched.
**Export price index / import price index** is the **net terms of trade (NTT)**, so option (1) is wrong.
**Income terms of trade (ITT)** = **NTT × export quantity index**, so option (2) is wrong.
NTT uses **price** indices, not quantity indices, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: The NTT base was revised in **Mar 2026**.
⚠ Trap: GTT and ITT both involve **quantity**; only GTT is a pure quantity ratio.
**Volume** in trade statistics means the **money value** of exports and imports.

73.s: A country has an absolute advantage in producing a commodity when it:
o: Produces it at a lower absolute cost than other countries
Produces it at a lower opportunity cost than every other commodity
Exports it below its home-market price
Restricts imports through a quantitative ceiling
73.x: According to Adam Smith's concept, absolute advantage means producing a good at a lower absolute cost than others.
73.tq: Discriminate between absolute cost and opportunity cost.
xs: **Absolute advantage** (**Adam Smith**) = producing a good at a **lower absolute cost than other countries** — option **(1)**.
Option (2), lower **opportunity cost**, is **comparative advantage** (**Ricardo**).
Option (3) describes **dumping**; option (4) describes an **import quota**.
xa: ⚠ **Adam Smith** = absolute advantage; **Ricardo** = comparative advantage.
**Dumping** (exporting below home-market price or cost) is met with an **anti-dumping duty**.
India's **services surplus** vs structural merchandise deficit reflects a **Ricardian comparative advantage** in services.

73.s: Comparative advantage requires a country to specialise in producing the good with the:
73.x: Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage focuses on specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost.
73.tq: Use the defining keyword opportunity cost to identify comparative advantage.
xs: Under **comparative advantage** (**Ricardo**), a country specialises in the good with the **lowest opportunity cost** — option **(3)**.
Producing at lower **absolute** cost is Adam Smith's **absolute advantage**, a different idea.
An **import quota** is a quantitative restriction on imports, not a basis of specialisation.
xa: ⚠ **Adam Smith** = absolute advantage; **Ricardo** = comparative advantage.
India's **services surplus** alongside a structural **merchandise deficit** is read as Ricardian comparative advantage in services.
**Intra-industry trade** = a country imports and exports the **same product** (PYQ 2025).

73.s: Export promotion and import substitution are respectively described as:
73.x: Import substitution is an inward-looking strategy, whereas export promotion is an outward-looking strategy.
73.tq: Test the paired terms by reversing them mentally and checking their policy orientation.
xs: **Export promotion** is **outward-looking**; **import substitution** is **inward-looking** — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses the pair.
The **1991 New Trade Policy** moved India away from **import substitution** and **QRs** to a price-based regime.
xa: The 1991 shift came with a two-step **rupee devaluation (July 1991)**.
**FTP 2023** targets **$2 trillion** exports by **2030** — an export-promotion goal.
An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction (QR)** on imports.

73.s: Dumping occurs when a firm:
o: Imports goods only under a tariff quota
Exports a product at a price below its home-market price or cost
Receives a domestic subsidy for exports
73.x: Dumping means exporting a product at a price below its home-market price or below its cost. It may attract anti-dumping duties.
73.tq: Distinguish the pricing practice of dumping from subsidies and re-exporting.
xs: **Dumping** = exporting a product at a price **below its home-market price or cost** — option **(2)**.
It is met with an **anti-dumping duty**.
Re-exporting imports (option 4) is **entrepot trade**; offsetting subsidies is the job of a **countervailing duty**.
xa: **Countervailing duty** offsets foreign subsidies — e.g. US preliminary CVD of **125.87%** on an Indian product (**Mar 2026**).
**Import quota** = a **quantitative restriction** on the amount of imports.
**Rules of origin** decide which goods qualify for **FTA** concessions.

73.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Rules of origin — fix the international price of exports
Anti-dumping duty — offsets foreign government subsidies
Countervailing duty — responds to dumped imports below home-market price
Countervailing duty — offsets the effect of foreign subsidies
73.x: Countervailing duty offsets the effect of foreign subsidies. Anti-dumping duty addresses imports sold below home-market price or cost, while rules of origin determine the national source of goods.
73.tq: Separate the remedies for dumping and foreign subsidies before eliminating the mismatched pairs.
xs: **Countervailing duty** offsets the effect of **foreign subsidies** — option **(4)**.
**Anti-dumping duty** answers **dumping** (exports below home-market price or cost), not subsidies — options (2) and (3) swap the two.
**Rules of origin** decide which goods qualify for **FTA concessions**; they do not fix prices.
xa: Example: US preliminary **CVD of 125.87%** on an Indian product (**Mar 2026**).
India has **14 FTAs and 6 PTAs** (**Apr 2026**), but exports to FTA partners fell **7%**.
**Entrepot trade** = re-export of imports.

73.s: When a country both imports and exports the same product, for example cars, the trade is called:
73.x: Intra-industry trade is the import and export of the same product by a country. Entrepot trade is re-exporting imported goods. Inter-industry trade is exchanging different products, as comparative advantage predicts. Dumping is exporting below the home-market price or cost.
73.tq: Same product both ways = intra-industry trade.
xs: A country importing and exporting the **same product** carries on **intra-industry trade** — option **(2)** (PYQ 2025).
**Entrepot trade** is the **re-export of imports**.
**Dumping** is exporting below home-market price or cost.
xa: **Comparative advantage** (**Ricardo**): specialise in the good with lower opportunity cost.
**Composition** = items traded; **direction** = country-wise/region-wise pattern.
**Volume** = money value of exports and imports.

73.s: An import quota is best described as:
o: A tax levied as a percentage of the value of imports
A quantitative restriction on the amount of a good that can be imported
A duty imposed to offset subsidies given by the exporting country
A rule deciding which goods qualify for FTA concessions
73.x: An import quota is a quantitative restriction (QR) that caps the amount of a good that can be imported. A percentage tax on import value is an ad valorem tariff. A duty that offsets foreign subsidies is a countervailing duty, and rules of origin decide which goods qualify for FTA concessions.
73.tq: Quota = quantity limit (QR); tariff = price-based.
xs: An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction** on the amount of a good that can be imported — option **(2)**.
A duty offsetting foreign subsidies is a **countervailing duty** (option 3).
**Rules of origin** decide which goods qualify for **FTA concessions** (option 4).
xa: The **1991 New Trade Policy** moved from **QRs** to a **price-based regime**.
**Dumping** is met with an **anti-dumping duty**.
⚠ Quota = quantity ceiling; duty = price-based measure.

73.s: In the context of India’s foreign trade, the term ‘volume’ refers to the
o: money value of exports and imports
73.x: In foreign-trade statistics, volume denotes the money value of exports and imports. It is distinct from the physical quantity of goods traded.
73.tq: Use the precise meaning of the technical term rather than its everyday usage.
xs: In foreign-trade terms, **volume** is the **money value of exports and imports** — option **(2)**.
It is not the physical quantity traded or the number of partners.
xa: **Composition** = the **items traded**.
**Direction** = the **country-wise/region-wise pattern** of trade.
Total trade in **2024-25** was **$1,745.16 bn**.

73.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes composition from direction of India’s foreign trade?
o: Composition refers to items traded, while direction refers to the country-wise or region-wise pattern of trade.
Composition refers to trade volume, while direction refers to trade value.
Composition refers to country-wise trade, while direction refers to items traded.
Composition refers only to exports, while direction refers only to imports.
73.x: Composition means the items traded, whereas direction means the country-wise or region-wise pattern of exports and imports.
73.tq: Separate two closely related trade concepts by identifying what each one classifies.
xs: **Composition** = **items traded**; **direction** = the **country-wise or region-wise pattern** — option **(1)**.
Option (3) swaps the two; **volume** is the money value of trade, not composition.
xa: Composition example: **petroleum products** were the largest export (**14.48%**) in 2024-25.
Direction example: **USA** was the top export destination (**19.77%**); **China** the top import source (**15.73%**).
**Volume** = money value of exports and imports.

73.s: Which of the following was the largest export item of India in 2024-25 by share?
73.x: Petroleum products constituted the largest listed export item in 2024-25, with a share of 14.48 percent.
73.tq: Identify the leading item from a ranked composition list.
xs: **Petroleum products** were India's largest export in **2024-25**, with a **14.48%** share — option **(1)**.
**Telecom instruments** came second (**5.96%**), **drug formulations, biologicals** third (**5.52%**).
**Electric machinery and equipment** had only **3.29%**.
xa: ⚠ **Petroleum products** = largest export; **crude petroleum** = largest import (**19.84%**).
**Electronics** exports rose **32.46%** to **$38.56 bn** in 2024-25; **smartphones = 62.5%** of them.
**Non-petroleum exports**: **$374.32 bn** (**+6.07%**).

73.s:
Arrange the following export items of India in descending order of their shares in 2024-25:
A. Electric machinery and equipment
B. Drug formulations and biologicals
C. Petroleum products
D. Pearls, precious and semi-precious stones
73.x: The shares are petroleum products (14.48%), drug formulations and biologicals (5.52%), pearls and precious stones (3.56%), and electric machinery and equipment (3.29%).
73.tq: Rank the items by their numerical shares, starting with the largest.
xs: Order: **petroleum products (14.48%)** > **drug formulations (5.52%)** > **pearls and precious stones (3.56%)** > **electric machinery (3.29%)** — **C, B, D, A**, option **(1)**.
These are **2024-25** shares (IYB 2026).
xa: **Telecom instruments** (**5.96%**) stood second overall, between petroleum products and drugs.
Top imports: **crude petroleum 19.84%**, **gold 8.04%**, petroleum products **5.92%**.
**Smartphones** formed **62.5%** of electronics exports.

73.s: Which one of the following was the largest import item of India in 2024-25 by share?
73.x: Crude petroleum was the largest listed import item in 2024-25, accounting for 19.84 percent of imports.
73.tq: Select the highest value from a ranked import-composition table.
xs: **Crude petroleum** was India's largest import in **2024-25**, at **19.84%** — option **(2)**.
**Gold** came second (**8.04%**), **petroleum products** third (**5.92%**), **electronic components** **5.1%**.
xa: ⚠ **Petroleum products** = largest export; **crude petroleum** = largest import.
**POL / crude** has been the largest import through most of the post-reform period (PYQ 2018).
**Crude, gold and petroleum products** together are about **one-third** of imports.
Gold imports jumped **82%** in **April 2026**.

73.s: Which of the following groups accounted for approximately one-third of India’s imports in 2024-25?
o: Crude petroleum, gold and petroleum products
73.x: Crude petroleum, gold and petroleum products together accounted for approximately one-third of India’s imports.
73.tq: Combine the leading categories rather than selecting only the single largest item.
xs: **Crude, gold and petroleum products** make up about **one-third** of India's imports (ES 2025-26) — option **(3)**.
Their **2024-25** shares: crude **19.84%**, gold **8.04%**, petroleum products **5.92%**.
xa: **Coal, coke, briquettes** had **4.31%**; **electronic components** **5.1%**.
**Oil and gold** are named among the factors widening the trade deficit since 1991.
The FY26 Q4 deficit alone was **$83.4 bn**, driven by oil and gold.

73.s: Which one of the following is classified as a non-bulk import?
73.x: Capital goods are included among non-bulk imports. Crude and petroleum products, cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertiliser, metals and ores are listed as bulk imports.
73.tq: Discriminate between two classifications by recalling the category membership.
xs: **Capital goods** are a **non-bulk import** — option **(2)**.
**Edible oils**, **pulses** and **fertiliser** are all **bulk imports**.
xa: Bulk imports: crude and products, cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertiliser, **metals and ores**.
Non-bulk imports: **capital goods**, **precious products**, **chemicals**.
Import liberalisation of capital goods, APIs and electronic components is a deficit factor since **1991**.

73.s: The stagnation in India’s merchandise exports referred to in the Economic Survey was associated mainly with
73.x: The Economic Survey 2025-26 traced the stagnation in merchandise exports to petroleum and gems-and-jewellery exports; non-petroleum, non-gems-and-jewellery goods, which make up 78.7% of merchandise exports, were not the source of the stagnation.
73.tq: Link the stated trend with its identified commodity sources.
xs: The **Economic Survey 2025-26** traced the export stagnation to **petroleum and gems-and-jewellery** — option **(1)**.
**Non-petroleum, non-gems-and-jewellery goods** (**78.7%** of merchandise exports) were not the source.
**Electronics** in fact grew **32.46%** in 2024-25.
xa: **Non-petroleum exports**: **$374.32 bn** (**+6.07%**).
**Pearls, precious and semi-precious stones**: **3.56%** of exports.
**May 2026** goods exports hit a record **$45.2 bn**.

73.s: Which one of the following gives the correct order of India's major imports from first to fifth?
o: Crude petroleum, coal, gold, machinery and electronic goods
Gold, crude petroleum, coal, machinery and electronic goods
Electronic goods, crude petroleum, gold, coal and machinery
Crude petroleum, gold, coal, electronic goods and machinery
73.x: The order is crude petroleum first, followed by gold, coal, electronic goods and machinery.
73.tq: Test sequence within a ranked import basket.
xs: Major imports in order: **crude petroleum, gold, coal, electronic goods and machinery** — option **(4)** (PYQ 2018).
**POL / crude petroleum** stayed the largest import through most of the post-reform period, followed by **gold**.
xa: 2024-25 shares: crude **19.84%**, gold **8.04%**, coal, coke, briquettes **4.31%**.
⚠ Crude = largest import; **petroleum products** = largest export.
Gold imports jumped **82%** in **April 2026**.

73.s: Which country was India’s largest export destination in 2024-25?
73.x: The United States was India’s largest export destination in 2024-25, receiving 19.77 percent of India’s exports.
73.tq: Identify the leader in the destination ranking before considering later partner changes.
xs: The **United States of America (USA)** was India's largest export destination in **2024-25**, with **19.77%** — option **(1)**.
**UAE** was second (**8.37%**), **Netherlands** third (**5.2%**), **China** only **3.26%**.
xa: India runs a **surplus with the USA** and the Netherlands.
⚠ **USA** = top export destination; **China** = top import source and largest partner in **FY 2025-26**.
US **50% tariffs** cut exports to the US by **20.4%** in **Sep 2025**.

73.s: Which one of the following was India’s largest source of imports in 2024-25?
73.x: China was India’s largest import source in 2024-25, accounting for 15.73 percent of imports.
73.tq: Distinguish the largest import source from the largest export destination.
xs: **China** was India's largest import source in **2024-25**, at **15.73%** — option **(2)**.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**, overtaking the USA.
Imports from China: **APIs**, **solar PV cells**, semiconductor chips, telecom machinery.
**H1 2026** imports from China: a record **$79.41 bn**.

73.s: On the basis of the 2024-25 direction-of-trade data, India ran a trade surplus with which of the following groups?
73.x: India ran a surplus with the United States and the Netherlands. It ran deficits with China, Russia, the UAE and Saudi Arabia because imports exceeded exports with those partners.
73.tq: Infer surplus or deficit by comparing the relative export and import positions.
xs: India runs a **surplus with the United States and Netherlands** — option **(2)**.
It runs **deficits** with **China, Russia, UAE and Saudi Arabia**, where oil and goods imports exceed exports.
xa: USA took **19.77%** of exports; Netherlands **5.2%**.
Saudi Arabia supplied **4.18%** of imports.
With China, the goods deficit was **over $100 bn** (Jun 2026).

73.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects recent changes in the direction of India’s trade?
o: India concentrated its crude imports in a single source and shifted labour-intensive exports to China alone.
India’s labour-intensive exports and crude-import sources remained unchanged.
Labour-intensive exports shifted from the United States towards the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia, while crude-import sources became more diversified.
Labour-intensive exports shifted from the Middle East and Africa towards only the United States.
73.x: Labour-intensive exports shifted from the United States towards the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia. At the same time, India diversified its sources of crude imports.
73.tq: Select the option that correctly captures both directions of the stated structural change.
xs: Per **ES 2025-26**, **labour-intensive exports** moved from the **US** to the **Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia**, and **crude import sources diversified** — option **(3)**.
So sources were not concentrated (option 1) nor unchanged (option 2).
xa: US **50% tariffs** cut exports to the US (**-20.4%** in **Sep 2025**), pushing the **Oct 2025** deficit to **$21.8 bn**.
India is **3rd** in the **Global South** for trade-partner diversity (**UNCTAD TDR 2025**).
**Russia** supplied **8.85%** of imports in 2024-25.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about India's imports from China:
1. China supplies about 16% of India's imports.
2. China supplies APIs and solar cells to India.
3. India exports iron ore, cotton and marine products to China.
4. India imports iron ore from China as a major import item.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false: India does not import iron ore; it exports iron ore, including to China.
73.tq: Use the import-export direction reversal as the key trap.
xs: Statement 1 correct: China supplied **15.73%** (about 16%) of India's imports in 2024-25.
Statement 2 correct: imports from China include **APIs**, **solar PV cells**, chips, telecom machinery.
Statement 3 correct: India **exports iron ore, cotton, chemicals, marine products** to China.
Statement 4 wrong: **iron ore** is an export to China, not an import — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**; trade **$151.1 bn**.
**Calendar 2025** (Chinese data): trade **$155.62 bn**, deficit **$116.12 bn**.
China dependence for APIs, solar cells, chips → responses: **QCOs**, **NTBs**, **PLI**.

73.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes India’s trade-partner position in FY 2025–26?
o: China was the largest export market and the United States ceased to be a major partner.
The United States remained the largest export market although China became the largest overall trading partner.
The United States remained the largest overall trading partner and China was only a minor partner.
Saudi Arabia became both the largest trading partner and the largest export market.
73.x: China became the largest overall trading partner, while the United States remained India’s largest export market.
73.tq: Separate total trade ranking from export-market ranking.
xs: In **FY 2025-26**, **China became the largest overall trading partner**, while the **United States remained the largest export market** — option **(2)**.
China was not the largest export market: it took only **3.26%** of exports in 2024-25.
xa: ⚠ **USA** = top export destination (surplus); **China** = top import source and largest partner (deficit).
India–China trade: **$151.1 bn**; goods deficit **over $100 bn** (Jun 2026).
USA's export share in 2024-25: **19.77%**.

73.s: India’s trade deficit with China in FY 2025–26 was:
o: Between US$10 billion and US$25 billion
73.x: India’s trade deficit with China was reported to be over US$100 billion. It is distinct from India’s total merchandise trade deficit of US$337.3 billion.
73.tq: Avoid confusing a bilateral deficit with the total merchandise deficit.
xs: India's goods deficit with China was **over US$100 billion** (Jun 2026) — option **(3)**.
**$337.3 bn** is India's **total** merchandise deficit for **FY26**, not the China deficit.
xa: India–China trade: **$151.1 bn** in FY 2025-26.
**Calendar 2025** (Chinese data): deficit **$116.12 bn** on trade of **$155.62 bn**.
**H1 2026** imports from China: a record **$79.41 bn**.

73.s: With reference to India’s trade with BRICS in FY26, which one of the following is correct?
o: Trade was $131.6 billion and imports from China were $417.5 billion.
Trade was $226.1 billion and the deficit was $417.5 billion.
Trade was $417.5 billion with a surplus of $226.1 billion.
Trade was $417.5 billion and the deficit was $226.1 billion.
73.x: India’s BRICS trade in FY26 was $417.5 billion, while the trade deficit was $226.1 billion. Imports from China amounted to $131.6 billion.
73.tq: Separate total trade, deficit and imports from one country.
xs: India's BRICS trade was **$417.5 bn** in **FY26**, with a **deficit of $226.1 bn** — option **(4)**.
**$131.6 bn** is imports from **China**, not total trade; it was a deficit, not a surplus.
xa: BRICS trade grew from **$203.1 bn (FY21)**; deficit from **$74.5 bn**.
**UAE** is the largest BRICS export market (**$37.4 bn**).
China is India's largest overall partner in **FY 2025-26**.

73.s: Which of the following correctly states India’s merchandise trade figures for 2024-25?
o: Exports were 825.25 billion US dollars and imports were 919.92 billion US dollars.
Exports were 919.92 billion US dollars and imports were 825.25 billion US dollars.
Exports were 437.70 billion US dollars and imports were 721.20 billion US dollars.
Exports were 721.20 billion US dollars and imports were 437.70 billion US dollars.
73.x: In 2024-25, merchandise exports were 437.70 billion US dollars and merchandise imports were 721.20 billion US dollars. The higher figures include goods and services together.
73.tq: Separate merchandise figures from total goods-and-services figures.
xs: **Merchandise** exports were **$437.70 bn** and imports **$721.20 bn** in **2024-25** — option **(3)**.
**$825.25 bn** and **$919.92 bn** are the **goods + services** totals, so option (1) is wrong.
xa: **Services** exports: **$387.54 bn**; services imports **$198.72 bn**.
FY25 merchandise deficit: **$283.5 bn** (ES 2025-26).

73.s: The merchandise trade deficit of India in FY25, according to the Economic Survey 2025–26, was:
73.x: The merchandise trade deficit in FY25 was $283.5 billion, representing an increase of 17.6%. RBI balance-of-payments data placed it at $286.9 billion.
73.tq: Distinguish the Economic Survey estimate from the separate RBI balance-of-payments estimate.
xs: The **ES 2025-26** puts the FY25 merchandise deficit at **$283.5 billion** (**+17.6%**) — option **(2)**.
**$337.3 bn** is **FY26**; **$198.72 bn** is services imports; **$437.70 bn** is merchandise exports.
xa: ⚠ The **RBI BoP basis** puts FY25 at **$286.9 bn** — quote the source.
FY26 Q4 alone: **$83.4 bn** (oil, gold).
The **services surplus** hit a record **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.

73.s: Which one of the following was the merchandise trade deficit figure for FY26 mentioned in the current economic data?
73.x: The merchandise trade deficit for FY26 was reported at $337.3 billion, with the fourth quarter alone accounting for $83.4 billion.
73.tq: Match the year with the closest numerical figure and avoid confusing FY25 with FY26.
xs: The FY26 merchandise deficit was **$337.3 billion** (**RBI BoP basis**) — option **(3)**.
**$283.5 bn** and **$286.9 bn** are **FY25** figures; **$387.54 bn** is services exports.
xa: **Q4** of FY26 alone: **$83.4 bn**, on oil and gold.
**Aug 2026**: total deficit down to **$9.4 bn**; goods exports **+26.1%** to **$43.8 bn**.
⚠ India has had a trade surplus only in **1972-73 and 1976-77**.
