73.s: Which of the following factors has NOT contributed to the widening of India's trade deficit since 1991?
o: Non-tariff barriers imposed by trading partners
Import liberalisation of capital goods and electronic components
73.x: Services performed well and generated a surplus; therefore, lacklustre services performance was not a cause of the widening trade deficit. Oil, gold, import liberalisation and external competition were among the contributing factors.
73.tq: Find the exception by separating causes of the goods deficit from the performance of services.
xs: **Lacklustre services** is **NOT** a factor — services did well (PYQ 2017) — option **(1)**.
**Non-tariff barriers** of partners, **competition from China** and **import liberalisation** are all listed factors since 1991.
xa: Other factors: the **South-East Asian crisis 1997-98**, **oil and gold**.
**Services surplus**: record **$188.8 bn** in FY25.
**Twin deficit hypothesis**: rising fiscal deficit goes with rising trade deficit.

73.s: India recorded a trade surplus after independence only in which of the following years?
73.x: Since independence India has run a trade surplus in only two years, 1972-73 and 1976-77; in every other year imports exceeded exports.
73.tq: Use the paired-year recall method for an exceptional historical record.
xs: India recorded a trade surplus only in **1972-73 and 1976-77** since independence — option **(1)**.
In every other year imports exceeded exports.
xa: FY26 merchandise deficit: **$337.3 bn**.
**Aug 2026**: first time merchandise exports grew more than imports in absolute value.
Deficit causes since 1991 include the **South-East Asian crisis 1997-98**.

73.s: The twin deficit hypothesis states that:
o: A services surplus always causes a merchandise surplus
A current account surplus necessarily causes a fiscal deficit
A rising trade surplus is associated with a rising fiscal surplus
A rising fiscal deficit is associated with a rising trade deficit
73.x: The twin deficit hypothesis links a rising fiscal deficit with a rising trade deficit.
73.tq: Translate the economic hypothesis into its direct cause-and-association relationship.
xs: **Twin deficit hypothesis**: a **rising fiscal deficit** goes with a **rising trade deficit** — option **(4)**.
It links two deficits, not surpluses, so options (1)–(3) are wrong.
xa: Current deficit drivers: **oil and gold**, electronics components, rising imports from China/FTA partners.
A **services surplus** offsets the goods deficit.
**Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation helps only if elasticities sum to **greater than 1**.

73.s: Which of the following correctly describes the major external trade measures introduced in the early 1990s?
o: The 1991 policy strengthened import substitution and abolished rupee devaluation
The 1991 policy shifted from import substitution and quantitative restrictions to a price-based regime, followed by two-step rupee devaluation
The 1991 policy introduced full capital-account convertibility immediately
The 1991 policy prohibited imports of capital goods and electronic components
73.x: The 1991 New Trade Policy shifted from import substitution and quantitative restrictions to a price-based regime, accompanied by a two-step rupee devaluation in July 1991.
73.tq: Identify the policy transition and reject options that exaggerate or reverse the reform.
xs: The **1991 New Trade Policy** moved from **import substitution and QRs** to a **price-based regime**, with a two-step **rupee devaluation (July 1991)** — option **(2)**.
It liberalised imports of capital goods and electronic components rather than banning them.
xa: **Import substitution** = inward-looking; **export promotion** = outward-looking.
**Devaluation** makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.
**J-curve**: after depreciation the trade balance first **worsens**, then improves.

73.s: According to the WTO (April 2025), According to the WTO (April 2025), India ranked what among world commercial services exporters in 2024?
73.x: India was the eighth-largest exporter of commercial services in the world in 2024.
73.tq: Distinguish India's services-export rank from its merchandise-export and services-import ranks.
xs: **WTO (April 2025)**: India was **8th** in world commercial services exports in **2024** (**4.3%**) — option **(1)**.
**18th** is India's **merchandise** exporter rank; **9th** its services importer rank.
xa: ⚠ The **Economic Survey** calls India the **7th-largest** services exporter — quote the source with the rank.
Services importer: **9th** (**3.4%**).
Services exports grew **13.63%** in **2024-25**.

73.s: India's share in world services exports increased from approximately 2% in 2005 to:
73.x: India's share in world services exports rose from 2% in 2005 to 4.3% in 2024.
73.tq: Use the beginning and end values in the trend rather than the separate policy target.
xs: India's share of world services exports rose from **2% (2005)** to **4.3% (2024)** — option **(1)**.
**4.2% by 2022** was the **FTP target**, not the outcome.
xa: Rank (WTO): **8th** services exporter in 2024.
Services are about **49%** of total exports, up from **39%** in **2014**.

73.s: The Foreign Trade Policy target for India's share in world services exports by 2022 was:
73.x: The Foreign Trade Policy had set a target of 4.2% for India's share in world services exports by 2022.
73.tq: Distinguish a policy target from the later achieved share.
xs: The **FTP** target was a **4.2%** share in world services exports **by 2022** (PYQ 2019) — option **(3)**.
**4.3%** is the actual **2024** share; **2%** the **2005** share.
xa: **FTP 2023** targets **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
**WTO**: India **8th** services exporter (2024); ES says **7th**.
Record **services surplus**: **$188.8 bn** in FY25.

73.s: Which of the following best explains how India's services sector cushions the merchandise trade deficit?
o: Remittances are recorded as merchandise exports
Services imports exceed services exports and increase the deficit
The services surplus, particularly from IT and IT-enabled services, along with remittances, offsets the merchandise deficit
The services sector eliminates the need for merchandise imports
73.x: The services surplus, especially from IT and IT-enabled services, together with remittances, offsets a substantial part of the merchandise deficit.
73.tq: Link the surplus-generating sector with the deficit it helps to offset.
xs: The **services surplus** (**IT/ITeS**) plus **remittances** offsets the merchandise deficit — option **(3)**.
Services exports exceed services imports (**$387.54 bn** vs **$198.72 bn** in 2024-25), so option (2) is wrong.
xa: Record services surplus: **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.
**Services surplus** vs structural **merchandise deficit** → Ricardian comparative advantage in services.
Services share of total exports: about **49%**.

73.s: The share of services in India's total exports rose from 39% in 2014 to approximately what level in 2026?
73.x: Services accounted for about 49% of India's total exports, compared with 39% in 2014.
73.tq: Compare the two endpoints of the structural shift in export composition.
xs: Services make up about **49%** of India's total exports, up from **39%** in **2014** (18 May 2026) — option **(3)**.
The rise reflects strong **services exports** and a record **services surplus**.
xa: Services exports grew **13.63%** in **2024-25**.
Share of world services exports: **2% (2005) → 4.3% (2024)**.
The services surplus cushions the merchandise deficit.

73.s: India's share in world merchandise exports increased from 1% in 2005 to what percentage in 2024?
73.x: India's share in world merchandise exports rose from 1% in 2005 to 1.8% in 2024.
73.tq: Distinguish the export share of 1.8% from the import share of 2.8%.
xs: India's share in world merchandise exports rose from **1% (2005)** to **1.8% (2024)** — option **(2)**.
**2.8%** is India's share of world **imports**.
xa: **WTO 2024**: **18th** merchandise exporter, **9th** importer.
⚠ Merchandise exporter rank **18th** vs services exporter rank **8th**.
Services share: **2% → 4.3%** over the same period.

73.s: The services surplus in FY25 reached approximately:
73.x: India's services surplus reached a record $188.8 billion in FY25.
73.tq: Separate the services surplus from the merchandise deficit and quarterly deficit figures.
xs: India's services surplus hit a record **$188.8 billion** in **FY25** — option **(2)**.
**$83.4 bn** is the FY26 Q4 goods deficit; **$283.5 bn** and **$337.3 bn** are merchandise deficits.
xa: Services exports **$387.54 bn**, imports **$198.72 bn** (2024-25).
The surplus (**IT/ITeS**) plus remittances offsets the merchandise deficit.
Services exports grew **13.63%** in **2024-25**.

73.s: India was the world's ____ largest importer in 2024, with a share of ____ in global imports.
73.x: India ranked ninth among importers in 2024 and accounted for 2.8% of global imports.
73.tq: Pair the correct global rank with its corresponding share.
xs: India was the world's **9th** largest importer in **2024**, with a **2.8%** share — option **(4)** (WTO).
**18th; 1.8%** is India's **merchandise export** rank and share.
xa: Services: **8th** exporter (**4.3%**), **9th** importer (**3.4%**).
⚠ Economic Survey calls India the **7th-largest** services exporter.

73.s: After a currency depreciation, the J-curve effect implies that the trade balance generally:
o: Worsens only when exports become cheaper abroad
Remains unchanged because prices do not change
Improves immediately and then worsens permanently
First worsens and improves only after export and import volumes adjust
73.x: Under the J-curve effect, import bills rise immediately after depreciation, so the trade balance initially worsens; it improves later as quantities adjust.
73.tq: Apply the time sequence—initial price effect followed by volume adjustment—to the trade balance.
xs: **J-curve**: after depreciation the trade balance **first worsens** (import bills rise at once) and **improves only as volumes adjust** — option **(4)**.
It does not improve immediately, so option (3) is the reverse of the J-curve.
xa: **Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation improves the balance only if export + import demand elasticities sum to **greater than 1**.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.
The weak rupee was credited in part for the **Aug 2026** export surge.

73.s: Which of the following correctly describes the immediate effects of devaluation or depreciation?
o: Exports become cheaper abroad and imports become dearer at home
Exports become dearer abroad and imports become cheaper at home
Both exports and imports become cheaper at home
Neither export nor import prices are affected
73.x: Devaluation or depreciation makes domestic exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports more expensive in the domestic market.
73.tq: Track the direction of price changes separately in foreign and domestic markets.
xs: **Devaluation/depreciation** makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the effect.
xa: The Commerce Secretary credited the **weak rupee** in part for the **Aug 2026** export surge.
**J-curve**: trade balance first worsens, improves later.
**1991**: two-step rupee devaluation in **July 1991**.

73.s: According to the Marshall–Lerner condition, devaluation improves the trade balance when:
o: Only export demand is perfectly inelastic
The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is greater than one
The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is equal to zero
The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is less than one
73.x: The Marshall–Lerner condition is satisfied when the sum of the absolute values of export and import demand price elasticities exceeds one.
73.tq: Recall the threshold condition and distinguish greater than one from less than one.
xs: **Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation improves the trade balance only if export + import demand price elasticities sum to **greater than 1** — option **(2)**.
A sum less than one or zero fails the condition.
xa: **J-curve**: the trade balance first worsens after depreciation.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.
**Terms of trade** (NTT) = export price index / import price index × **100**.

73.s:
With reference to Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023, consider the following statements:
1. It came into effect from 1 April 2023.
2. It has a fixed end date of 31 March 2028.
3. It is reviewed as needed.
4. It targets exports of 2 trillion US dollars by 2030.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: FTP 2023 came into effect on 1 April 2023, has no fixed end date, is reviewed as needed and targets 2 trillion US dollars in exports by 2030. Statement 2 is false.
73.tq: Spot the false fixed-end-date statement in a policy described as dynamic.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **FTP 2023** runs from **1 April 2023**.
Statement 2 wrong: it has **no end date**.
Statement 3 correct: it is **reviewed as needed**.
Statement 4 correct: target **$2 trillion** exports by **2030** — so **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Framed and monitored by the **Department of Commerce**.
Pillars: duty-free input schemes, **Districts as Export Hubs**, logistics, better FTA use.
**RoDTEP** replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20**.
**RBI** rupee trade settlement uses **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts**.

73.s: Which department frames and monitors India's Foreign Trade Policy?
73.x: The Department of Commerce frames and monitors India's Foreign Trade Policy.
73.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish neighbouring government departments.
xs: The **Foreign Trade Policy** is framed and monitored by the **Department of Commerce** — option **(1)**.
**FTP 2023** came into force from **1 April 2023**, with no end date, reviewed as needed.
xa: FTP 2023 targets **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
**APEDA**, the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones, also works under the **Department of Commerce**.
Pillars: duty-free input schemes, **Districts as Export Hubs**, logistics, better FTA use.

73.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated pillar of FTP 2023?
73.x: The stated pillars include duty-free input schemes, Districts as Export Hubs, logistics and better utilisation of FTAs. Compulsory nationalisation of export firms is not a pillar.
73.tq: Identify the invented policy instrument among genuine FTP pillars.
xs: **Compulsory nationalisation of export firms** is not a pillar of **FTP 2023** — option **(4)**.
The pillars are **duty-free input schemes**, **Districts as Export Hubs**, **logistics** and better **FTA use**.
xa: FTP 2023 runs from **1 April 2023** with **no end date**.
Target: **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
**RoDTEP** replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20**.

73.s: RoDTEP stands for:
o: Reduction of Duties on Trade and Export Programmes
Rebate of Duties for External Trade and Production
Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products
Refund of Domestic Export Trade Expenses and Production
73.x: RoDTEP means Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products.
73.tq: Discriminate between similar-looking expansions of an official acronym.
xs: **RoDTEP** = **Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products** — option **(3)**.
It replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20**.
xa: **FTP 2023** is framed and monitored by the **Department of Commerce**.
⚠ "Remission", not "Reduction" or "Refund" — the usual expansion trap.
FTP 2023 pillars include **duty-free input schemes**.

73.s: RoDTEP replaced which WTO-challenged scheme of FTP 2015–20?
73.x: RoDTEP replaced the WTO-challenged Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of FTP 2015–20.
73.tq: Match the successor scheme with the scheme it replaced.
xs: **RoDTEP** replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20** — option **(4)**.
RoDTEP = **Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products**.
xa: **FTP 2023**: from **1 April 2023**, target **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
A **countervailing duty** offsets foreign subsidies — the risk export incentives face abroad.
e.g. US preliminary **CVD of 125.87%** on an Indian product (**Mar 2026**).

73.s: The principal purpose of India's rupee trade settlement framework is to:
o: Replace the WTO dispute settlement system
Encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade
73.x: The framework is intended to encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade; it does not prohibit all foreign-currency transactions.
73.tq: Apply the stated purpose of a financial mechanism to a practical trade situation.
xs: The **RBI rupee trade settlement framework** aims to **encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
It works through **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts**; it does not ban foreign-currency transactions.
xa: FTP 2023 is framed by the **Department of Commerce**.
**EXIM Bank** gives **Lines of Credit** to foreign governments and buyer's/seller's credit.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Special Economic Zones (SEZs):
1. The SEZ concept was proposed in the EXIM Policy 1997–2002.
2. The SEZ policy was announced in April 2000.
3. The SEZ Act was enacted in 2005.
4. The SEZ Rules were notified in 2006.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All four statements are correct: the concept was proposed in EXIM Policy 1997–2002, the policy was announced in April 2000, the Act was enacted in 2005 and the Rules were notified in 2006.
73.tq: Check the full sequence of policy concept, policy announcement, Act and Rules.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the **SEZ concept** was proposed in the **EXIM Policy 1997-2002**.
Statement 2 correct: the **SEZ policy** was announced in **April 2000**.
Statements 3 and 4 correct: **SEZ Act 2005**, **SEZ Rules 2006** — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
xa: ⚠ The PYQ key gives **EXIM Policy 2000-01** for the SEZ concept.
**SEZs** are duty-free enclaves treated as **foreign territory** for trade and tariff purposes.
India's first **EPZ**: **Kandla, 1965**.

73.s: The nodal agency for Agri Export Zones in India is:
73.x: The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones.
73.tq: Identify the institution assigned the specific export-promotion function.
xs: **APEDA** is the nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones** — option **(1)** (PYQ key).
APEDA works under the **Department of Commerce**; **EXIM Bank** is a finance body, not the nodal agency.
xa: ⚠ **APEDA** = agri exports; **MPEDA** = marine products.
**Agriculture Export Policy 2018** aimed to double agri exports.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.

73.s: Which of the following is NOT a function of EXIM Bank mentioned in relation to export finance?
o: Providing lines of credit to foreign governments
73.x: EXIM Bank provides lines of credit, buyer's and seller's credit, project-export finance and SME export windows. Framing and monitoring foreign trade policy is not its function.
73.tq: Find the institution-function mismatch among closely related trade bodies.
xs: **Determining India's foreign trade policy** is not an **EXIM Bank** function — option **(2)**; FTP is framed by the **Department of Commerce**.
EXIM Bank gives **Lines of Credit** to foreign governments, **buyer's/seller's credit** and **project-export finance**.
xa: EXIM Bank also runs **SME export windows**.
**APEDA** = agri exports; **MPEDA** = marine products.
**FTP 2023** target: **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding agricultural export promotion:
1. APEDA works under the Department of Commerce.
2. The Agriculture Export Policy, 2018 aimed to double agricultural exports.
3. MPEDA handles marine products.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. APEDA functions under the Department of Commerce, the Agriculture Export Policy 2018 sought to double agricultural exports, and MPEDA handles marine products.
73.tq: Combine institutional responsibility with policy objectives and sector-specific roles.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **APEDA** works under the **Department of Commerce**.
Statement 2 correct: the **Agriculture Export Policy 2018** aimed to **double** agri exports.
Statement 3 correct: **MPEDA** handles **marine products** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: APEDA is the nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones**.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.
**Marine products** are among India's exports to **China**.

73.s: Which of the following correctly describes the treatment of a duty-free enclave in an SEZ?
o: It is treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes.
It can import goods only after payment of the basic customs duty.
It is treated as domestic territory for all customs purposes.
It is exempt only from State taxes and not customs duties.
73.x: A duty-free enclave is treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes, although it remains within India territorially.
73.tq: Apply the special customs-status rule to distinguish legal treatment from geographical location.
xs: An **SEZ** is a duty-free enclave **treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes** — option **(1)**.
So it is neither domestic territory for customs nor liable to basic customs duty on imports.
xa: SEZ policy announced **April 2000**; **SEZ Act 2005**; **SEZ Rules 2006**.
The SEZ concept was proposed in the **EXIM Policy 1997-2002**.
First **EPZ**: **Kandla, 1965**.

73.s: India's first Export Processing Zone was set up in 1965 at:
73.x: Kandla (Gujarat) got India's first EPZ in 1965. Santacruz (Mumbai), Falta (West Bengal) and Visakhapatnam got EPZs later, and these were converted into SEZs after the 2000 SEZ policy.
73.tq: First EPZ = Kandla 1965 (also Asia's first).
xs: India's first **Export Processing Zone** came up at **Kandla** in **1965** — option **(2)**.
Kandla's EPZ came decades before the **SEZ** framework of **April 2000**.
xa: The **SEZ** policy followed in **April 2000**; the **SEZ Act** in **2005**.
SEZs are treated as **foreign territory** for trade and tariff purposes.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.

73.s: India's first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre was set up in May 2021 at:
73.x: The first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre was set up at Pune in May 2021. Nashik, Hyderabad and Guntur are agri-export hubs, but none of them had the first such centre.
73.tq: First AEFC = Pune, May 2021.
xs: India's first **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre** was set up at **Pune** in **May 2021** — option **(3)** (PYQ key).
Nashik, Hyderabad and Guntur did not get the first centre.
xa: **APEDA** is the nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones**.
**Agriculture Export Policy 2018** aimed to double agri exports.
First EPZ: **Kandla, 1965**.

73.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the recent tariff-related trade developments stated for India?
o: US tariffs increased India's exports to the US by 20.4% in September 2025 and eliminated the October deficit.
US tariffs affected only India's services exports and not merchandise trade.
India's exports to the US fell by 7% in October 2025 and the deficit was $2.18 billion.
US tariffs reduced India's exports to the US by 20.4% in September 2025 and the October 2025 deficit reached $21.8 billion.
73.x: The stated figures are a 20.4% fall in exports to the US in September 2025 and an October 2025 trade deficit of $21.8 billion.
73.tq: Match the correct percentage, month and deficit figure without shifting units or periods.
xs: US **50% tariffs** **reduced** India's exports to the US by **20.4%** in **September 2025**, and the **October 2025 deficit reached $21.8 billion** — option **(4)**.
The **7%** fall is for exports to **FTA partners**, not the US, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: India has **14 FTAs and 6 PTAs** (**Apr 2026**).
**Aug 2026**: goods exports **+26.1%** narrowed the trade deficit.
USA stays the top export destination (**19.77%** in 2024-25).

73.s: India was ranked third among Global South countries for:
73.x: India ranked third in the Global South for trade-partner diversity according to the stated UNCTAD assessment.
73.tq: Identify the exact indicator associated with the international ranking.
xs: India ranked **3rd** in the **Global South** for **trade-partner diversity** (**UNCTAD TDR 2025**) — option **(2)**.
The ranking is about the spread of **trade partners**, not reserves or deficits.
xa: Labour-intensive exports shifted from the US to the **Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia** (ES 2025-26).
**Crude import sources** were diversified.
India has **14 FTAs and 6 PTAs** (Apr 2026).

73.s: Which of the following is NOT listed as a response to India's dependence on China for APIs, solar cells and chips?
73.x: The listed responses are QCOs, NTBs and PLI. Abolition of all import regulations is not listed as a response.
73.tq: Find the policy measure that contradicts the stated strategic response.
xs: **Abolition of all import regulations** is not a listed response — option **(3)**.
Responses to China dependence for **APIs**, **solar cells**, **chips** are **QCOs**, **NTBs** and **PLI**.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**; goods deficit **over $100 bn**.
**H1 2026** imports from China: a record **$79.41 bn**.
China was the top import source in 2024-25 (**15.73%**).

73.s: The statement that services may show a surplus while merchandise trade remains structurally in deficit is associated with India's:
o: Absolute advantage in all manufactured goods
73.x: The comparison is explained through India's Ricardian comparative advantage in services, alongside a structural merchandise trade deficit.
73.tq: Connect the observed trade pattern with the specified comparative-advantage explanation.
xs: A **services surplus** with a structural **merchandise deficit** reflects India's **Ricardian comparative advantage in services** — option **(1)**.
**Absolute advantage** is Adam Smith's idea and does not fit "all manufactured goods" with a goods deficit.
xa: Record services surplus: **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.
**Comparative advantage** = specialise in the good with lower opportunity cost.
Services are about **49%** of total exports.

73.s: Which one of the following statements correctly captures the debate regarding India's FTAs?
o: FTAs have achieved complete utilisation by Indian exporters.
FTAs are criticised only because they prohibit services exports.
FTAs have been criticised for widening deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea and for weak utilisation.
FTAs have eliminated India's merchandise deficit with all Asian partners.
73.x: The stated criticism is that FTAs have widened deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea and have suffered from weak utilisation.
73.tq: Select the balanced statement containing both the trade-deficit and utilisation concerns.
xs: FTAs are criticised for **widening deficits** with **ASEAN, Japan and Korea** and for **weak utilisation** — option **(3)**.
Exports to FTA partners actually **fell 7%**, so options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: India has **14 FTAs and 6 PTAs** (**Apr 2026**).
**Rules of origin** decide which goods qualify for FTA concessions.
FTP 2023 pillars include **better FTA use**.

73.s:
Assertion (A): Positive net exports result in a trade surplus.
Reason (R): Negative net exports result in a trade deficit.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true: positive net exports mean a trade surplus, and negative net exports a trade deficit. They are two sides of one rule, so R does not explain A.
73.tq: Ask whether the opposite case explains the first.
n: Positive net exports result in a trade surplus. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Negative net exports result in a trade deficit. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

73.s: A closed economy is one which has:
73.x: A closed economy has no foreign trade, neither exports nor imports. An open economy has both.
73.tq: Recall the definition of a closed economy.
n: A closed economy has neither exports nor imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]

73.s:
Assertion (A): SEZs promote exports, investment, employment, infrastructure and additional economic activity.
Reason (R): SEZs provide simplified procedures and a business-friendly environment.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true: SEZs boost exports, investment, jobs and infrastructure because they offer simple procedures and an easy business environment. R explains A.
73.tq: Ask whether the features explain the outcomes.
n: A Special Economic Zone is a designated area created to promote exports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone is a designated area created to promote investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone is a designated area created to promote employment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone is a designated area created to promote infrastructure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone is a designated area created to promote additional economic activity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone has simplified procedures. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]
A Special Economic Zone provides a business-friendly environment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]

73.s: SEZ is an abbreviation for which of the following?
73.x: SEZ stands for Special Economic Zone. The traps replace 'Economic' with 'Export' or 'Strategic'.
73.tq: Expand the short name.
n: SEZ stands for Special Economic Zone. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 26-27]

73.s:
Assertion (A): SEZs are a major export-promotion instrument.
Reason (R): The objective of SEZs includes export, investment, employment and infrastructure.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true: SEZs are a major tool for promoting exports because exports, along with investment, jobs and infrastructure, are their aims. R explains A.
73.tq: Ask whether the aim explains the role.
n: SEZ is a major export-promotion instrument. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
The objectives of SEZs include exports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
The objectives of SEZs include investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
The objectives of SEZs include employment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
The objectives of SEZs include infrastructure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]

73.s: Which of the following best describes Anti-dumping measures?
o: Determination of country of origin for trade-policy purposes
Protection against goods exported below normal value
73.x: Anti-dumping duties protect against imports sold below their normal value. A quota limits quantity, and licensing is an administrative control.
73.tq: Match each trade tool to its meaning.
n: Anti-dumping measures protect against goods exported below normal value. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: An FTA is a Free Trade Agreement.
CECA stands for Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
A Customs Union involves a common external tariff and free internal trade.
CEPA stands for Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
73.x: Option B is incorrect: CECA is the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement. CEPA is the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
73.tq: Discriminate CECA from CEPA.
n: FTA means Free Trade Agreement. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
CEPA means Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
CECA means Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A customs union has a common external tariff. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A customs union has free internal trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s:
Assertion (A): An import quota is a quantity restriction on imports.
Reason (R): A tariff is a tax on imports.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true: a quota limits the quantity of imports, and a tariff taxes them. They are different tools, so R does not explain A.
73.tq: Ask whether two tools explain each other.
n: A tariff is a tax on imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
An import quota is a quantity restriction on imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Rules of Origin determine the country of origin for trade-policy purposes.
Statement B: Entrepot trade involves importing, storing or trading, and then re-exporting goods.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: rules of origin decide where goods come from, and entrepot trade means importing goods, storing them and re-exporting them.
73.tq: Recall the trade terms.
n: Rules of origin determine the country of origin for trade-policy purposes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
Entrepot trade involves importing goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
Entrepot trade involves storing or trading imported goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
Entrepot trade involves re-exporting goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Free trade has little or no tariff.
Statement B: Free trade has little or no quantitative restriction.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: free trade has little or no tariff and little or no quantity limit on imports.
73.tq: Recall the definition of free trade.
n: Free trade has little or no tariff. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
Free trade has little or no quantitative restriction. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s: Which of the following is an administrative restriction on imports?
73.x: Import licensing is an administrative restriction. A tariff is a tax, a quota a quantity limit, and anti-dumping a defence against cheap imports.
73.tq: Match each trade tool to its type.
n: Import licensing is an administrative restriction on imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

73.s: Which of the following statements about India's import basket is incorrect?
o: Crude oil and petroleum products (POL) are India's largest import item by value.
Gold is among India's major import items.
Electronic goods are among India's major import items.
Pulses are India's largest import item by value.
73.x: Option D is incorrect: pulses are a small import; crude oil and petroleum products are India's largest import by value, followed by items such as electronic goods and gold.
73.tq: Recall which item dominates India's import bill.
n: The major-import hierarchy is Fuel > Petroleum, Oil & Lubricants > Capital Goods > Chemicals > Gold/Silver. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The SEZ Policy was announced on 1 April 2000 under the Globalisation framework.
Statement B: The primary objectives of the SEZ Policy included boosting export competitiveness and attracting FDI.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: the SEZ Policy was announced on 1 April 2000, under globalisation, to make exports competitive and attract FDI.
73.tq: Recall the SEZ Policy date.
n: The Special Economic Zone Policy was announced on 1 April 2000. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy was announced under the Globalisation framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The primary objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy was to boost export competitiveness. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy aimed to attract foreign direct investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy aimed to create an internationally competitive trade environment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

73.s: What was the objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy in relation to the business environment?
o: To establish a mixed economic model
To provide an internationally competitive environment
To create a long-term fiscal policy
73.x: One SEZ objective was an internationally competitive business environment. Licensing and the mixed economy belong to older policies.
73.tq: Recall the SEZ objectives.
n: The objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy was to provide an internationally competitive environment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]

74.s: Which of the following best describes import substitution?
o: Increasing dependence on imported capital goods
Promoting only agricultural exports through export subsidies
Reducing import dependence by producing import substitutes at home
74.x: Import substitution is an inward-looking strategy aimed at producing goods domestically in order to reduce import dependency.
74.tq: Apply the inward-looking versus outward-looking distinction to a policy description.
xs: **Import substitution** means **reducing import dependence by producing import substitutes at home** — option **(4)** (PYQ).
It is an **inward-looking** strategy; **export promotion** is the outward-looking one.
xa: Import substitution ran in India for about **four decades**.
The **1991 Trade Policy** moved from **QRs** to a **price-based** regime.
An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction** on imports (PYQ 2019).

74.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Introduction of Foreign Trade Policy
B. Introduction of EXIM Policy
C. Partial current-account convertibility
D. 1991 Trade Policy shift to a price-based regime
74.x: EXIM Policy began in 1985-88, the 1991 Trade Policy brought the shift to a price-based regime, partial current-account convertibility followed in 1992, and Foreign Trade Policy replaced EXIM Policy from 2004.
74.tq: Anchor the sequence with the earliest EXIM Policy and the latest 2004 Foreign Trade Policy.
xs: **B** EXIM Policy (**1985-88**) → **D** 1991 Trade Policy (**1991**) → **C** partial convertibility (**1992**) → **A** Foreign Trade Policy (**2004**) — option **(1)**.
The 1991 policy moved from **QRs** to a **price-based** regime.
xa: In **1992**, **60%** of forex moved at the market rate and **40%** at the official rate.
Raw materials and capital goods were placed under **OGL** in 1992.
The current **FTP 2023** came into force on **1 April 2023**.

74.s: The Foreign Trade Policy is administered through the Directorate General of Foreign Trade under the:
o: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
74.x: The Foreign Trade Policy is administered by the Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, through the DGFT.
74.tq: Use the ‘which ministry’ trap to separate the Department of Commerce from neighbouring ministries.
xs: FTP is administered by the **Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, through **DGFT** — option **(3)**.
Finance, MSME or External Affairs ministries do not administer the FTP.
xa: **DGFT** is an attached office of the Dept of Commerce, HQ **Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi**.
DGFT issues FTP authorisations and runs **Districts as Export Hubs** and the **Export Promotion Mission**.
EXIM policies gave way to the **Foreign Trade Policy from 2004**.

74.s: Under the partial current-account convertibility introduced in 1992, foreign exchange transactions were divided as follows:
o: 60% at the official rate and 40% at the market rate
50% at the official rate and 50% at the market rate
20% at the official rate and 80% at the market rate
40% at the official rate and 60% at the market rate
74.x: In 1992, partial current-account convertibility provided for 40% of foreign exchange at the official rate and 60% at the market rate.
74.tq: Watch for the reversal of the two percentages in quantitative reform questions.
xs: Under **1992** partial current-account convertibility, **40%** of forex went at the **official rate** and **60%** at the **market rate** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the split.
xa: Raw materials and capital goods were placed under **OGL**.
It followed the **1991 Trade Policy** shift from **QRs** to a price-based regime.
**FTP** replaced EXIM policies from **2004**.

74.s: Which one of the following trade policy instruments is a quantitative restriction?
74.x: An import quota sets a ceiling on the quantity of a good that may be imported, so it is a quantitative restriction. An ad valorem tariff is a tax on the value of imports. Countervailing and anti-dumping duties are also price-based duties, not quantity limits.
74.tq: Quota limits quantity; duties and tariffs act on price.
xs: An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction** on the amount of imports — option **(2)** (PYQ 2019).
A **tariff** is a **tax on imported goods**, a price measure, not a quantity limit.
xa: The **1991 Trade Policy** moved from **QRs** to a **price-based** regime.
**Import substitution** aimed at **reducing import dependency**.
**Rules of origin** fix a product's **national source**.

74.s:
Consider the following statements about the Foreign Trade Policy 2023:
1. It came into force on 1 April 2023.
2. It has a fixed statutory end date.
3. It aims at exports of 2 trillion US dollars by 2030.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: The policy came into force on 1 April 2023 and set an export target of 2 trillion US dollars by 2030. It has no end date, so statement 2 is false.
74.tq: Spot the false fixed-end-date assertion against a policy described as having no end date.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **FTP 2023** came into force on **1 April 2023**.
Statement 2 wrong: it has **no end date**.
Statement 3 correct: target **$2 trillion by 2030** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ FTP target **$2 trillion** vs **Piyush Goyal's $1 trillion** exports goal (Board of Trade, **Jul 2026**).
Approach: shift from **incentives to remission** and entitlement-based support.
**Districts as Export Hubs** brings a district-level export focus.

74.s: Which one of the following is a feature of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
o: A shift from remission and entitlement support to only quantitative restrictions
A shift from incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support
A complete withdrawal of electronic initiatives
74.x: FTP 2023 shifts the emphasis from conventional incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support, while also promoting e-initiatives and merchanting trade.
74.tq: Reject the options that reverse the direction of policy change.
xs: **FTP 2023** shifts **from incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support** — option **(3)**.
It also promotes **e-initiatives** and **merchanting trade**, so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: One-time **amnesty scheme** for **EPCG/Advance Authorisation** export-obligation defaults.
New **Towns of Export Excellence** added.
**EPCG green list** widened to **BEVs**, vertical farming, green hydrogen.

74.s:
Which of the following combinations is associated with the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
1. Rupee trade settlement
2. New Towns of Export Excellence
3. One-time amnesty for certain export-obligation defaults
4. Promotion of merchanting trade
74.x: FTP 2023 includes rupee trade settlement, new Towns of Export Excellence, a one-time amnesty for EPCG and Advance Authorisation export-obligation defaults, and promotion of merchanting trade.
74.tq: Recognise the cluster of distinctive policy features rather than an isolated incentive.
xs: All four are **FTP 2023** features: **rupee trade settlement** (trade in **INR**), new **Towns of Export Excellence**, one-time **amnesty**, and **merchanting trade** — option **(4)**.
The amnesty covers **EPCG/Advance Authorisation** export-obligation defaults.
xa: **EPCG green list** widened to **BEVs**, vertical farming, wastewater recycling, rainwater harvesting, green hydrogen.
**Districts as Export Hubs**: district-level export focus.
Export target: **$2 trillion by 2030**.

74.s: Under the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-20, MEIS and SEIS respectively related to:
74.x: MEIS provided support for exports of goods, while SEIS related to exports of services under FTP 2015-20.
74.tq: Separate the two similar-sounding schemes by their covered sectors.
xs: Under **FTP 2015-20**, **MEIS** covered **goods exports** and **SEIS** **services exports** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the pair.
xa: **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS**; **SEIS** was discontinued.
⚠ **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL** (apparel and made-ups).
**EPCG** = capital goods; **Advance Authorisation** = inputs.

74.s: RoDTEP replaced which scheme and seeks to refund which category of burden?
o: SEIS; only income tax paid by exporters
MEIS; unrebated central, state and local taxes
RoSL; only customs duties on imported inputs
74.x: RoDTEP replaced MEIS and refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes, including electricity duty and VAT on transport fuel.
74.tq: Separate the replaced scheme from the similar RoSCTL and RoSL schemes.
xs: **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS** and refunds **unrebated central, state and local taxes** — option **(3)**.
Examples: **electricity duty**, **VAT on transport fuel**.
**RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL**; **SEIS** was a services scheme — so options (1), (2), (4) mismatch.
xa: RoDTEP is run online by **CBIC** (IYB 2026).
**Duty drawback** refunds **customs duty** on imported inputs used in exports.
⚠ RoDTEP = replaced MEIS; RoSCTL = replaced RoSL.

74.s: RoSCTL replaced RoSL and provides a rebate mainly for:
74.x: RoSCTL replaced RoSL and provides a rebate for apparel and made-ups.
74.tq: Match the scheme with its specific product category.
xs: **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL** and gives a rebate for **apparel and made-ups** — option **(3)**.
Services exports were covered by **SEIS**; capital goods imports by **EPCG**.
xa: ⚠ **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS**; **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL**.
**Budget 2026-27** extended the Advance Authorisation export period for leather/textile garments and footwear from **6 months to 1 year**.
**SEIS** was the services exports reward under **FTP 2015-20**.

74.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Advance Authorisation — Duty-free import of inputs for export production
SEIS — Reward for services exports under FTP 2015-20
EPCG — Zero-duty import of capital goods against export obligation
Duty drawback — Refund of income tax on export profits
74.x: Duty drawback refunds customs duty on imported inputs used in exports; it does not refund income tax on export profits.
74.tq: Reject the option that changes a customs-duty refund into an income-tax refund.
xs: **Duty drawback — refund of income tax on export profits** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
Duty drawback refunds **customs duty on imported inputs** used in exports.
The other pairs are right: **Advance Authorisation** = duty-free inputs; **SEIS** = services reward; **EPCG** = zero-duty capital goods.
xa: ⚠ **EPCG** = capital goods; **Advance Authorisation** = inputs.
One-time **amnesty** in FTP 2023 for **EPCG/Advance Authorisation** obligation defaults.
**RoDTEP** refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes.

74.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Export Promotion Mission is correct?
o: It is run by ECGC and targets only large exporters.
It is run by DGFT, merges Interest Equalisation and Market Access Initiative, and targets MSMEs and first-time exporters.
It is run by CBIC and concerns only customs assessment.
It is run by EXIM Bank and replaces the Foreign Trade Policy.
74.x: The Export Promotion Mission is run by DGFT, merges the Interest Equalisation and Market Access Initiative, and focuses on MSMEs and first-time exporters.
74.tq: Identify the implementing body, merger and target beneficiaries together.
xs: The **Export Promotion Mission** is run by **DGFT**, merges **Interest Equalisation** + **Market Access Initiative**, and targets **MSMEs and first-time exporters** — option **(2)**.
**ECGC** implements the **RELIEF** scheme under it, not the Mission itself.
xa: Niryat Disha tools: **TRACE**, **FLOW**, **LIFT**, **INSIGHT**.
**RELIEF Scheme 2026**: **₹497 crore** under EPM via ECGC.

74.s: The RELIEF Scheme 2026, implemented through ECGC, provides support mainly for:
o: Interest subsidy on domestic housing loans
War-risk and logistics costs in West Asia
74.x: RELIEF Scheme 2026 provides support for war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia through ECGC under the Export Promotion Mission.
74.tq: Link the risk described in the scenario with the specialised insurance-support scheme.
xs: **RELIEF Scheme 2026** covers **war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia** — option **(4)**.
It provides **₹497 crore** under the **EPM**, via **ECGC**.
xa: **Egypt and Jordan** were added in **April 2026**.
The **West Asia** conflict also led to procedural flexibility in export authorisations (TH, **3 Mar 2026**).
**ECGC** = export credit insurance.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Special Economic Zones (SEZs):
1. They are governed by the SEZ Act, 2005.
2. They are duty-free enclaves treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes.
3. FDI in SEZ manufacturing is capped at 49 per cent under the automatic route.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
74.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the SEZ law is the SEZ Act 2005, and SEZs are duty-free enclaves treated as foreign territory. Statement 3 is wrong: 100 per cent FDI is allowed under the automatic route for most manufacturing. So B; A omits statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
74.tq: SEZ: Act 2005, foreign territory, 100% automatic FDI.
xs: Statement 1 correct: SEZs are governed by the **SEZ Act 2005**.
Statement 2 correct: they are duty-free enclaves treated as **foreign territory** for trade and tariffs.
Statement 3 wrong: **100% FDI** is automatic for most manufacturing, not 49% — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Budget 2026-27**: measures to use **idle SEZ manufacturing capacity** hit by global trade.
⚠ SEZ = enclave (foreign territory); **EOU/EHTP/STP** = can be located anywhere.
EOU/EHTP/STP export all output and get **duty-free inputs**.

74.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: SEZ — units that must be located anywhere outside a designated enclave
74.x: B is correct: EHTP units deal in electronics hardware and get duty-free inputs. EOUs cover goods generally (not only software), STPs cover software (not agricultural machinery), and an SEZ is itself a designated duty-free enclave, whereas it is EOU/EHTP/STP units that can be located anywhere.
74.tq: Start from the sure sector-to-incentive pair and eliminate swapped associations.
xs: **EHTP** covers **electronics hardware** with duty-free inputs — option **(2)**.
**EOU** covers **goods**, **STP** covers **software** — so options (1) and (3) are wrong.
An **SEZ** is itself an enclave; it is **EOU/EHTP/STP** units that can be located anywhere.
xa: EOU/EHTP/STP units **export all output**.
SEZs allow **100% FDI** automatic for most manufacturing.
SEZ law = **SEZ Act 2005**.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding EOUs, EHTPs and STPs:
1. These units export all their output.
2. They can be located anywhere.
3. They receive duty-free inputs appropriate to their activity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: EOUs, EHTPs and STPs export all their output, may be located anywhere, and receive duty-free inputs suited to their respective activities.
74.tq: Test the distinction between location-based SEZs and activity-based export units.
xs: All three are correct: **EOU/EHTP/STP** units **export all output**, **can be located anywhere**, and get **duty-free inputs** — option **(4)**.
EOU = **goods**; EHTP = **electronics hardware**; STP = **software**.
xa: ⚠ SEZ = enclave treated as **foreign territory**; EOU/EHTP/STP = located anywhere.
SEZs: **100% FDI** automatic for most manufacturing.
SEZ law = **SEZ Act 2005**.

74.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: DGFT — Headquarters at Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi
EXIM Bank — Headquarters at Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi
ECGC — Issues Foreign Trade Policy authorisations
EPCs — Provides buyers’ and sellers’ credit
74.x: DGFT is headquartered at Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi. DGFT issues FTP authorisations; EXIM Bank provides lines of credit and buyers’ and sellers’ credit, while ECGC provides export credit insurance.
74.tq: Match each body with its institutional role and location.
xs: **DGFT** has its HQ at **Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi** — option **(1)**.
**EXIM Bank** is in **Mumbai**; FTP authorisations are issued by **DGFT**, not ECGC.
**EXIM Bank**, not EPCs, gives **buyer's/seller's credit**.
xa: DGFT is an attached office of the **Department of Commerce**.
DGFT runs **Districts as Export Hubs** and the **Export Promotion Mission**.
**ECGC** = export credit insurance; implements **RELIEF 2026**.

74.s:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade performs which of the following functions?
1. Issuing Foreign Trade Policy authorisations
2. Running Districts as Export Hubs
3. Running Export Promotion Mission
4. Providing export credit insurance
74.x: DGFT issues FTP authorisations and runs Districts as Export Hubs and the Export Promotion Mission. Export credit insurance is provided by ECGC, so statement 4 is false.
74.tq: Separate the functions of DGFT from the insurance role of ECGC.
xs: **DGFT** issues **FTP authorisations** and runs **Districts as Export Hubs** and the **Export Promotion Mission** — statements **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **export credit insurance** is **ECGC**'s role.
xa: DGFT HQ: **Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi**.
FTP is administered by the **Department of Commerce** through DGFT.
**NIRVIK (2019)**: bigger ECGC insurance cover for export credit.

74.s:
Consider the following statements regarding EXIM Bank and ECGC:
1. EXIM Bank was set up on 1 January 1982 under the EXIM Bank Act, 1981.
2. EXIM Bank provides lines of credit, buyer's/seller's credit and project-export finance.
3. Export credit insurance is the principal role of EXIM Bank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
74.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: EXIM Bank (Mumbai) was set up on 1 Jan 1982 under the 1981 Act and gives lines of credit, buyer's/seller's credit and project-export finance. Statement 3 is wrong: export credit insurance is ECGC's role. So B; A omits statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
74.tq: EXIM Bank lends; ECGC insures.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **EXIM Bank** set up **1 Jan 1982** under the **EXIM Bank Act 1981**.
Statement 2 correct: it gives **lines of credit**, **buyer's/seller's credit**, **project exports** finance.
Statement 3 wrong: **export credit insurance** is **ECGC**'s role — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ EXIM Bank Act **1981** → bank set up **1 Jan 1982**.
EXIM Bank is headquartered in **Mumbai**.
**ECGC** implements **RELIEF 2026**.

74.s:
Match List-I (Export-import document) with List-II (Purpose):
List-I
a. Indent
b. Shipping bill
c. Mate's receipt
d. Letter of credit
List-II
i. Ship's mate acknowledges goods loaded on board
ii. Importer's bank guarantees payment to the exporter
iii. Importer's order to buy goods
iv. Customs document for clearing export goods
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
74.x: Indent = importer's order to buy goods (iii); shipping bill = customs document for clearing export goods (iv); mate's receipt = ship's mate acknowledges goods loaded on board (i); letter of credit = importer's bank guarantees payment (ii). Option B swaps indent and shipping bill; option C swaps mate's receipt and letter of credit; option D is wrong throughout.
74.tq: Order (indent) -> customs (shipping bill) -> loading (mate's receipt); payment guarantee is the letter of credit.

74.s: A bill of lading serves as:
o: A shipping company’s receipt and a document of title to the goods
An exporter’s application for a duty drawback
A customs order fixing the tariff rate
74.x: A bill of lading is the shipping company’s receipt and also functions as a document of title to the goods.
74.tq: Select the option that contains both parts of the document’s legal function.
xs: A **bill of lading** is the **shipping company's receipt** and a **document of title to the goods** — option **(1)**.
It is not a quota certificate, drawback claim or tariff order.
xa: ⚠ Bill of lading = document of title; **mate's receipt** = goods loaded on board.
**Shipping bill**: customs document for clearing export goods.
**Indent**: importer's order to buy goods.

74.s: The principal purpose of rules of origin is to determine:
o: The international price of a product
The amount of countervailing duty payable
The national source of a product
74.x: Rules of origin establish the national source of a product and help determine eligibility for free-trade agreement concessions.
74.tq: Identify the administrative question answered by the rule rather than its possible trade consequence.
xs: **Rules of origin** are criteria that fix a product's **national source** — option **(4)**.
They tell customs **which duties and rules apply** (BPSC 2023 PYQ — all statements correct).
xa: Quantity limits are **import quotas**, a **quantitative restriction**.
**Bill of lading** is a **document of title** to goods.
**Letter of credit**: importer's bank guarantees payment.

74.s: ICEGATE is best described as which of the following?
o: A postal export network of India Post
A logistics ranking index of NITI Aayog
A single-window system for foreign investment approvals
A customs e-filing portal of CBIC
74.x: ICEGATE is the customs e-filing portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).
74.tq: Identify the responsible authority behind the digital trade platform.
xs: **ICEGATE** is **CBIC**'s **customs e-filing portal** — option **(4)**.
**SWIFT** is the single window for import clearance; **LEADS** ranks States on logistics.
xa: **CBIC** also runs **RoDTEP** online.
**PM Gati Shakti** (**2021**) and **National Logistics Policy** (**2022**) aim to cut export logistics costs.
**Shipping bill**: customs document for clearing exports.

74.s: The SWIFT system in the context of trade facilitation is associated with which function?
74.x: SWIFT functions as a single window for import clearance.
74.tq: Separate a clearance mechanism from portals, rankings and export-support institutions.
xs: **SWIFT** is the **single window for import clearance** — option **(1)**.
Export credit insurance is **ECGC**'s job; **LEADS** ranks States on logistics.
xa: **ICEGATE** = **CBIC**'s customs e-filing portal.
**PM Gati Shakti** + **National Logistics Policy** aim to cut export logistics costs.
**DGFT** runs **Districts as Export Hubs**.

74.s: Which recent development was identified as having disrupted cargo movement and prompted procedural flexibility in export authorisations?
o: The merger of ODOP with DEH
A global shortage of software exports
The introduction of the LEADS index
74.x: The West Asia conflict disrupted cargo movement, following which the Government allowed procedural flexibility in export authorisations.
74.tq: Connect the external event with its direct trade-policy consequence.
xs: The **West Asia conflict** disrupted cargo, so the Govt allowed **procedural flexibility in export authorisations** (TH, **3 Mar 2026**) — option **(3)**.
**LEADS** is a logistics ranking, not a disruption.
xa: **RELIEF Scheme 2026** (**₹497 crore**, via **ECGC**) covers war-risk + logistics costs in West Asia.
**Egypt and Jordan** were added to RELIEF in **April 2026**.
**DGFT** issues FTP authorisations.

74.s:
Which of the following were among the export-related matters raised by Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu?
1. Regulation of fish-meal exports
2. Export incentives for aquaculture
3. Export incentives for tobacco
Which of the statements given above are correct?
74.x: The matters raised included regulation of fish-meal exports and export incentives for both aquaculture and tobacco.
74.tq: Check whether all three sector-specific demands belong to the same policy intervention.
xs: AP CM **Chandrababu Naidu** sought **regulation of fish-meal exports** and export incentives for **aquaculture** and **tobacco** — all three, option **(4)** (TH, **21 Jul 2026**).
So all three statements are correct — the **AP angle** of export policy.
xa: **MPEDA** handles marine products.
**RoDTEP** refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes on exports.
**Districts as Export Hubs** gives a district-level export focus.

74.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (ECGC)
(b) Minerals and Metals Trading Corporation of India Limited (MMTC)
(c) State Trading Corporation of India Limited (STC)
(d) NIRVIK

List-II
(i) Canalising agency for bulk commodities, set up in 1956
(ii) Government-owned export credit insurance company
(iii) ECGC scheme enhancing insurance cover on export credit
(iv) Trading in minerals, metals and precious metals
74.x: ECGC is the government's export credit insurer, MMTC trades in minerals and metals, STC (1956) is a canalising agency for bulk commodities, and NIRVIK is ECGC's scheme widening cover on export credit, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
74.tq: Recall each body's main line of business.
n: ECGC is the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
ECGC provides export credit-risk insurance. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
MMTC is the Minerals and Metals Trading Corporation of India Limited. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
MMTC is a foreign trade and trading organisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
STC is the State Trading Corporation of India Limited. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
STC is engaged in foreign trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
NIRVIK stands for Niryat Rin Vikas Yojana. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
NIRVIK provides export credit insurance. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]
NIRVIK provides enhanced insurance cover. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 79-80]

74.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Customs Union
(b) Common Market
(c) Economic Union
(d) Free Trade Agreement

List-II
(i) Common market plus coordinated economic policies
(ii) Tariffs removed among members, each keeping its own external tariff
(iii) Customs union plus free movement of factors
(iv) Common external tariff plus free internal trade
74.x: An FTA removes tariffs among members, who keep their own external tariffs; a customs union adds a common external tariff; a common market adds free movement of factors; and an economic union adds coordinated policies. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
74.tq: Rank the stages of economic integration from loosest to closest.
n: FTA means Free Trade Agreement. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A customs union has a common external tariff. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A customs union has free internal trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A common market is a customs union with free movement of factors. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
An economic union is a common market with coordinated economic policies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
A common market has free movement of factors. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
An economic union has coordinated economic policies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]

75.s: Under the Balance of Payments framework, which of the following best distinguishes the presentation followed by the IMF from that generally followed by the Reserve Bank of India?
o: The IMF uses only current and capital accounts, whereas the RBI uses current, capital and financial accounts separately.
The IMF uses only trade and services accounts, whereas the RBI uses current and financial accounts.
The IMF uses current, capital and financial accounts, whereas the RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts.
Both the IMF and the RBI invariably present the Balance of Payments through exactly three separate accounts.
75.x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts. The RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts under the heading ‘capital account’.
75.tq: Separate the IMF classification from the RBI presentation instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: The **IMF (BPM6)** uses **three accounts — current, capital, financial**, while the **RBI combines** the last two as **"Capital Account"** — option **(3)**.
So the RBI does not keep them separate (option 1), and the two do not invariably use three accounts (option 4).
xa: **BoP** = systematic record of all transactions of residents with the rest of the world, on **double-entry** bookkeeping.
BoP has a **current account and a capital account** (PYQ 2025; APPSC-G2 2025 key).
Identity: Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = **0**.

75.s: A capital-account transaction involving the purchase of foreign assets by residents is recorded as:
o: A current-account credit because assets are goods
A debit because foreign exchange flows out for acquiring the assets
A credit because foreign exchange enters the country
75.x: Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit. Conversely, sale of Indian assets to foreigners is recorded as a credit.
75.tq: Follow the direction of the financial flow to distinguish a debit from a credit.
xs: **Purchase of foreign assets** by residents is a capital-account **debit** — foreign exchange flows out — option **(3)**.
**Sale of Indian assets to foreigners** is a **credit**.
xa: BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping, so it always balances in accounting terms.
Capital account items: **FDI**, **FPI/FII**, ADRs/GDRs, **ECB**, NRI deposits.
Surplus in one account = **deficit** in another.

75.s:
With reference to invisibles in the balance of payments, consider the following statements:
1. Invisibles include services, primary income and transfers.
2. Non-factor services include shipping, banking, tourism and software.
3. Factor income is distinct from non-factor services.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Invisibles comprise services, primary income and transfers. Services include non-factor activities such as shipping, banking, tourism and software, while factor income is separately identified.
75.tq: Group the components of invisibles and distinguish factor from non-factor services.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **invisibles = services + primary income + transfers**.
Statement 2 correct: **non-factor** services = **shipping, banking, tourism, software**.
Statement 3 correct: services = non-factor + **factor income**, two separate parts — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Primary income = **interest, dividends, profits, wages**.
Secondary income = **remittances**, gifts, grants.
**Software services** are the largest part of the services surplus.

75.s: The balance of the current account is represented by which of the following expressions?
o: Exports minus imports of goods and services plus net primary and net secondary income
Capital inflows minus capital outflows plus errors and omissions
Exports and imports of goods only plus changes in foreign exchange reserves
Foreign direct investment plus portfolio investment minus external debt
75.x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
75.tq: Reconstruct the identity by adding goods, services, primary income and secondary income.
xs: **Current account balance** = (exports − imports of **goods and services**) + **net primary income** + **net secondary income** — option **(1)**.
Capital flows and reserve changes (options 2, 3) belong to the capital account.
xa: APPSC-GS 2019 key: exports minus imports of goods **and services** + net unilateral transfers.
⚠ **BoT** = goods only; current account balance = goods **and services** + transfers.
A **CAD** must be financed by a capital account surplus or by drawing down reserves.

75.s: Which of the following correctly represents the Balance of Payments identity?
o: Current balance + capital balance + financial balance + errors and omissions = zero
Current balance + merchandise exports = financial balance
Current balance − capital balance = trade balance
75.x: The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.
75.tq: Recall the complete identity rather than restricting the BoP to the trade balance.
xs: BoP identity: **Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = 0** — option **(2)**.
BoP always **balances in accounting terms**; a surplus in one account = a deficit in another.
xa: BoP uses **double-entry** bookkeeping.
IMF **BPM6** has three accounts; RBI merges capital and financial into **"Capital Account"**.
**Overall BoP** positive → adds to reserves; negative → draws them down.

75.s:
Consider the following statements about transactions in the balance of payments:
1. Autonomous transactions take place for their own sake.
2. Accommodating transactions are undertaken to fill the gap arising from other transactions.
3. Reserve changes and official borrowing are examples of accommodating transactions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Autonomous transactions are motivated by their own economic purpose. Accommodating transactions, including reserve changes and official borrowing, help finance or fill the resulting gap.
75.tq: Distinguish transactions by their purpose rather than by the account in which they appear.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **autonomous** transactions happen **for their own sake**.
Statement 2 correct: **accommodating** transactions **fill the gap**.
Statement 3 correct: examples are **reserve changes** and **official borrowing** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: The **monetary authority** is the ultimate financier of any BoP deficit.
**Overall BoP** negative → draws down reserves.
The **IMF** is the **last resort** when reserves cannot cover the deficit.

75.s: What is the usual effect of the overall balance of payments position on foreign exchange reserves?
o: The overall balance has no relationship with reserve movements.
A positive overall balance reduces reserves, while a negative balance increases them.
A positive overall balance adds to reserves, while a negative balance draws them down.
Both positive and negative balances increase reserves because the BoP always balances in accounting terms.
75.x: A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down. If reserves become insufficient, a balance of payments crisis may result.
75.tq: Use the direction of reserve movement to identify the correct surplus-deficit relationship.
xs: A **positive overall BoP adds to reserves**; a **negative** one **draws them down** — option **(3)**.
If reserves run short → **BoP crisis**.
xa: **July 2026**: overall BoP **$20.8 bn surplus**; capital account **$27.7 bn surplus**.
Forex reserves **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
Reserve components: **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs**, **Reserve Tranche Position**.

75.s: For how many consecutive years did India record a current account surplus during the period 2001-02 to 2003-04?
75.x: India recorded a current account surplus for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.
75.tq: Match the duration directly with the specified financial-year range.
xs: India ran a current account **surplus three years running** in **2001-02 to 2003-04** — option **(4)**, **three years**.
Such a run is **rare** in India's record.
xa: **Q4 2023-24** also saw a **surplus**, due to a **surge in services exports**.
CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13** (taper tantrum).

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India’s current account position:
1. The current account recorded a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2023-24.
2. The surplus was driven by a surge in services exports.
3. The surplus was primarily caused by a sharp rise in gold imports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the surplus was associated with a surge in services exports, not a rise in gold imports.
75.tq: Separate the stated cause of a surplus from a plausible but opposite trade-pressure factor.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the current account was in **surplus in Q4 2023-24**.
Statement 2 correct: it came from a **surge in services exports** (PYQ 2025).
Statement 3 wrong: **gold imports** widen the CAD — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **FY24 recovery**: moderation in merchandise exports + **sharp fall in imports**.

75.s: The external-sector recovery in FY24 was mainly associated with:
o: A decline in remittances and a rise in primary-income outgo
A complete elimination of the merchandise deficit
Moderation in merchandise exports along with a sharp fall in imports
A sharp rise in merchandise imports and a fall in services exports
75.x: The FY24 external-sector recovery came from moderation in merchandise exports accompanied by a sharp fall in imports.
75.tq: Select the precise cause-effect combination and reject reversed trade trends.
xs: The **FY24 recovery** came from **moderation in merchandise exports** plus a **sharp fall in imports** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2024 key).
The merchandise deficit was not eliminated; the **Q4 2023-24 surplus** came from services exports.
xa: Record **services surplus**: **$188.8 bn in FY25**.

75.s:
Which of the following are structural causes of India’s current account deficit?
1. Dependence on imported oil and gold
2. Low export competitiveness
3. Savings-investment gap
4. Temporary global slowdown alone
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
75.x: Imported oil and gold, low export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural causes. A temporary global slowdown is a cyclical cause, not a structural cause.
75.tq: Classify permanent structural pressures separately from temporary cyclical shocks.
xs: **Structural** causes: **oil (>80% imported) and gold**, **low export competitiveness**, **savings-investment gap** — statements **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
A **global slowdown** is a **cyclical** cause, not structural.
xa: Cyclical causes: **commodity shocks**, global slowdown, **rupee volatility**.
**May 2026**: PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the Iran conflict raised prices.
**FY26** merchandise deficit: **$337.3 bn**.

75.s: India's current account deficit reached its peak of about 4.8% of GDP in:
o: 1990-91, during the balance of payments crisis
FY24, after the fall in imports
H1 FY26, after the US tariffs
75.x: The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period. In the 1990-91 crisis it was about 3.1-3.2% of GDP. FY24 saw a recovery, with a surplus in Q4, and H1 FY26 had a CAD of only 0.8% of GDP.
75.tq: CAD peak = 4.8% FY13; crisis year 1990-91 = ~3.1%.
xs: India's CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13**, around the **taper tantrum** — option **(2)**.
The **1990-91** crisis CAD was **3.1-3.2%**; **FY24** saw a recovery; **H1 FY26** CAD was only **0.8%**.
xa: In the **2013** taper tantrum **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
**Rangarajan Committee**: sustainable CAD about **1.6% of GDP**.

75.s: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed approximately what proportion of the merchandise deficit?
75.x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about two-thirds of the merchandise deficit. Remittances also acted as a cushion.
75.tq: Identify the comparative proportion rather than treating the services surplus as full financing of the merchandise deficit.
xs: The record **services surplus** of **$188.8 bn** in **FY25** financed about **two-thirds** of the merchandise deficit — option **(4)**.
**Remittances** were the other **cushion**.
xa: **Software services** = largest part of the services surplus.
Net services in **Q1 FY27**: **$51.6 bn**.
Net **primary income** is an outflow — **$10.5 bn** in Q1 FY27.

75.s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
75.x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
75.tq: Use the paired numerical figures and distinguish the annual estimate from other remittance measures.
xs: India, the **world's largest recipient**, got **$135.4 billion** (**3.5%** of GDP) in **FY25** — option **(1)**.
**$188.8 bn** is the **services surplus**; **$110.47 bn** and **$87.55 bn** are **workers' remittances** for FY26 and the year before.
xa: ⚠ **$135.4 bn** (FY25 total) vs **$110.47 bn** (FY26, workers' remittances — narrower measure).
Remittances exceed gross **FDI** inflows.

75.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of remittances in India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
75.x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.
75.tq: Apply the contrast between stable transfer inflows and debt-creating capital flows.
xs: Remittances are **counter-cyclical** and create **no debt burden / no repayment obligation** — option **(1)**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, they need no repayment; they are not FDI (they in fact **exceed gross FDI** inflows).
xa: Remittances = **$135.4 bn (3.5% of GDP)** in **FY25**.
Workers' remittances: **$110.47 bn** in **FY26**.
Critics warn of dependence on remittances + one-time deposit schemes instead of stable **FDI**.

75.s: The post-1991 pattern in which capital surplus covered the current account deficit was disrupted because:
