Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
76.x: Both are true: inflation and a fiscal deficit can both weaken a currency's exchange value.
76.tq: Recall what moves the exchange rate.
n: Inflation can affect the exchange value. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
A fiscal deficit can affect the exchange value. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]

76.s:
Assertion (A): Devaluation necessarily improves the trade balance.
Reason (R): Devaluation makes exports relatively cheaper.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
76.x: A is false and R is true: devaluation makes exports cheaper, but it does not always improve the trade balance, since import costs rise too. 'Necessarily' makes A false.
76.tq: Watch for 'necessarily'.
n: Devaluation does not necessarily improve the trade balance. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]

76.s: Which of the following statements regarding the IMF is incorrect?
o: India joined the IMF on 27 December 1945.
The IMF was conceived at the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944.
The IMF was formally established on 27 December 1944.
The IMF was formally established on 27 December 1945.
76.x: Option C is incorrect: the IMF was formally set up on 27 December 1945, after being planned at Bretton Woods in 1944. India was a founding member.
76.tq: Discriminate the year planned from the year set up.
n: The IMF was conceived at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 41-43]
The IMF was formally established on 27 December 1945. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 41-43]
India joined the IMF on 27 December 1945. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 41-43]
The IMF is a Bretton Woods institution. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 41-43]

76.s:
Arrange the following developments relating to exchange-rate reform in India in chronological order:
A. Unified exchange rate introduced
B. LERMS introduced
C. Full current account convertibility accepted through Article VIII of the IMF
D. Second Tarapore Committee set up
76.x: LERMS was introduced in 1992-93, the unified rate was introduced on 1 March 1993, full current account convertibility followed in August 1994, and the second Tarapore Committee was set up in 2006.
76.tq: Fix the sequence using the dated milestones before placing the later committee.
xs: **B** LERMS (**1992-93 Budget**) → **A** unified rate (**1 March 1993**) → **C** Article VIII acceptance (**August 1994**) → **D** second Tarapore Committee — option **(1)**.
**LERMS** came first, and the unified rate preceded full **current account convertibility**.
xa: LERMS split: **40%** official / **60%** market.
Rupee delinked from **sterling** in **September 1975**.
**FEMA** enacted **1999**, in force **1 June 2000**.

77.s: The Uruguay Round of multilateral trade negotiations is correctly described as the:
o: Sixth round, held from 1973 to 1979 with 23 contracting parties
Seventh round, held from 1980 to 1985 with 92 contracting parties
Eighth round, launched at Punta del Este in September 1986 and concluded in 1993 with 123 contracting parties
Ninth round, launched at Marrakesh in 1994 with 166 contracting parties
77.x: The Uruguay Round was the eighth GATT round, launched at Punta del Este in September 1986 and concluded in 1993, with 123 contracting parties.
77.tq: Verify round number, dates, venue and participation together.
xs: The **Uruguay Round** was the **eighth round**, launched at **Punta del Este** in **September 1986** and concluded in **1993** with **123 contracting parties** — option **(3)**.
**Marrakesh** (**April 1994**) is where the agreement creating the WTO was signed, not the launch of a "ninth round".
**166** is the WTO's membership in **Apr 2026**, not the Uruguay Round's participants.
xa: Uruguay Round aims: cut **farm subsidies**, open **services**, cover **investment** and **IPR**.
The **Dunkel Draft** (**December 1991**) carried **Arthur Dunkel**'s proposals for the Uruguay Round agreements.
⚠ **123** is also the number India got when it deposited its **AFS** Instrument of Acceptance (**July 2026**).
GATT itself was signed in **1947** with **23 countries** and held **8 rounds** in all.

77.s: The Dunkel Draft consisted principally of:
o: A schedule of tariff concessions adopted at Nairobi in 2015
Proposals by Arthur Dunkel for the Uruguay Round multilateral trade agreements
A declaration on fisheries subsidies adopted at Geneva in 2022
A treaty establishing the International Monetary Fund
77.x: The Dunkel Draft contained proposals made by Arthur Dunkel, the GATT Director-General and Chair of the Trade Negotiations Committee, for the Uruguay Round agreements.
77.tq: Link a named document with its author and negotiation context.
xs: The **Dunkel Draft** was a set of **proposals by Arthur Dunkel** for the **Uruguay Round multilateral trade agreements** — option **(2)**.
**Arthur Dunkel** was the **GATT Director-General** and chair of the **Trade Negotiations Committee**.
The fisheries subsidies agreement was adopted at **MC12 Geneva (2022)**, and **Nairobi 2015 (MC10)** ended farm export subsidies — neither is the Dunkel Draft.
xa: The draft was tabled in **December 1991** (some notes say **20 October 1991**).
The Uruguay Round ran **1986-1993** with **123** contracting parties.
It led to the **Marrakesh Agreement** (**April 1994**) and the **WTO** (**1 January 1995**).
The WTO is called the **third pillar** of the world economy, with the **IMF** and the **World Bank**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about the WTO:
1. Its headquarters is in Geneva and its Director-General is Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala.
2. It is called the third pillar of the world economy along with the IMF and the World Bank.
3. India was a founding member of GATT but not of the WTO.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: India is a founding member of both GATT and the WTO. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
77.tq: India = founding member of both GATT (1947) and WTO (1995).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: WTO HQ is **Geneva** and the DG is **Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**.
Statement 2 is correct: the WTO is the **third pillar** of the world economy with the **IMF** and **World Bank**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **India** is a founding member of **both GATT and the WTO** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: The WTO was established on **1 Jan 1995** and had **166 members** in **Apr 2026**.
India ranked **18th** in merchandise exports with a **1.8%** share (**WTO Global Trade Outlook, April 2025**).
Only two new WTO agreements in **30 years**: **TFA** and **AFS**.
The **AFS** is the WTO's first agreement with an **environmental-sustainability objective**.

77.s: A country grants an advantage in customs treatment to one WTO trading partner. Under the Most-Favoured-Nation principle, it must generally:
o: Apply the advantage only to domestic producers
Extend the same advantage to other WTO trading partners
Extend the advantage only to countries with which it has a customs union
Withdraw the advantage from all trading partners
77.x: MFN requires non-discrimination among trading partners, so an advantage granted to one partner should generally be extended to other WTO trading partners, subject to permitted exceptions.
77.tq: Apply the non-discrimination principle to a trade-policy situation.
xs: **MFN** means **no discrimination among trading partners**, so an advantage given to one must be **extended to other WTO trading partners** — option **(2)**.
Treating imports like domestic goods once inside is a different principle — **national treatment**.
xa: ⚠ **US unilateral tariffs** (**2025-26**) violate **MFN** and bound-rate obligations.
**National treatment**: imports are treated like domestic goods **once inside** the market.
The **Singapore issues** (**MC1, 1996**): investment, competition, procurement transparency, trade facilitation.
Plurilaterals such as the **E-Commerce Agreement** (**66 members**) and **IFD** are debated against WTO **consensus**.

77.s: Which situation best illustrates the national-treatment principle under WTO rules?
o: A country gives an export subsidy to domestic firms.
A country grants the same tariff concession to every foreign trading partner.
An imported product, after entering the domestic market, is treated like a similar domestic product for internal taxation and regulation.
A country imposes a quantitative restriction on all imports.
77.x: National treatment requires imported goods to be treated like domestic goods once they have entered the market, particularly in internal taxation and regulation. Equal treatment among foreign trading partners is the MFN principle.
77.tq: Separate national treatment from MFN by focusing on the point after importation.
xs: **National treatment** means an **imported product**, once **inside** the domestic market, is **treated like a similar domestic product** — option **(3)**.
Giving the same tariff concession to every foreign partner is **MFN** (no discrimination among trading partners), not national treatment.
xa: **MFN** = no discrimination **among** trading partners; national treatment = no discrimination between **imports and domestic goods**.
⚠ **US unilateral tariffs** (**2025-26**) violate **MFN** and bound-rate obligations.
**TRIMS** deals with investment measures affecting trade, e.g. **local-content rules**.
India lost the **solar cells** case (**US, DS456**) over **domestic content** in the **National Solar Mission**.

77.s: As of April 2026, the World Trade Organization had how many members?
77.x: The WTO had 166 members as of April 2026. 123 was the number of contracting parties in the Uruguay Round (and India was the 123rd member to accept the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement); 164 and 150 are older or wrong membership figures.
77.tq: WTO 2026: 166 members, HQ Geneva.
xs: The WTO had **166 members** in **April 2026** — option **(4)**.
**123** is the number of **Uruguay Round contracting parties** (and India's number as an **AFS** acceptor), not WTO membership.
xa: ⚠ "**110** countries" is a later GATT-era membership, and **23** was GATT's founding number.
**MC14** at **Yaounde** (**Mar 2026**) was attended by all **166** members.
The **IFD** plurilateral was backed by **129 of 166** members, but **India blocked** it at MC14.
WTO: established **1 Jan 1995**; HQ **Geneva**; DG **Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**.

77.s: The highest decision-making body of the World Trade Organization is required to meet:
o: Only when requested by the Director-General
At least once every two years
77.x: The WTO Ministerial Conference is the highest decision-making body and meets at least once every two years under the Marrakesh Agreement.
77.tq: Recall the institutional hierarchy and minimum meeting frequency.
xs: The **Ministerial Conference**, the WTO's highest decision-making body, meets **at least once every two years** under the **Marrakesh Agreement** — option **(2)**.
It is not tied to a DG's request, and the rule is not yearly or five-yearly — the text says **at least once every two years**.
xa: **MC1** was at **Singapore (1996)**; **MC14** at **Yaounde, Cameroon (26-29 Mar 2026)**.
**MC14** ended with **no ministerial declaration** — only a draft "**Yaounde package**".
⚠ **MC11 Buenos Aires (2017)** also produced **no ministerial declaration**.
Earlier breakdowns: **Seattle 1999** and **Cancún 2003**.

77.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding WTO Ministerial Conferences:

List-I (Conference)
a. First Ministerial Conference
b. Second Ministerial Conference
c. Third Ministerial Conference
d. Fourth Ministerial Conference

List-II (Venue and year)
i. Seattle, 1999
ii. Singapore, 1996
iii. Doha, 2001
iv. Geneva, 1998

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
77.x: MC1 was held at Singapore in 1996, MC2 at Geneva in 1998, MC3 at Seattle in 1999 and MC4 at Doha in 2001.
77.tq: Start from the sure venue-year pair and eliminate codes.
xs: **MC1 Singapore 1996**, **MC2 Geneva 1998**, **MC3 Seattle 1999**, **MC4 Doha 2001** — so **a–ii, b–iv, c–i, d–iii**, option **(1)**.
**Singapore** gave the "**Singapore issues**" and ITA; **Geneva 1998** began the **e-commerce moratorium**.
**Seattle** collapsed amid protests; **Doha** launched the **Doha Development Agenda**.
xa: **MC5 Cancun (2003)** collapsed over agriculture/Singapore issues; the **G-33** was formed.
**MC6 Hong Kong (2005)**: farm export subsidies to end; **duty-free quota-free** for LDCs.

77.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the outcome of the Fourth WTO Ministerial Conference held at Doha in 2001?
o: The Bali Package and interim Peace Clause were adopted.
The e-commerce moratorium was begun and the Singapore issues were introduced.
The Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies was adopted.
The Doha Development Agenda was launched and a TRIPS-public health declaration was adopted.
77.x: The Doha Conference launched the Doha Development Agenda and adopted the declaration concerning TRIPS and public health.
77.tq: Use the conference’s signature agenda and declaration to identify the correct option.
xs: **MC4 Doha (2001)** launched the **Doha Development Agenda** and adopted a **TRIPS-public health declaration** — option **(4)**.
The Bali Package and Peace Clause were **MC9 (2013)**; the moratorium was **MC2 (1998)**; the **AFS** was **MC12 (2022)**.
xa: The **Doha Round** is the "**development round**" (agriculture, **NAMA**, services) — still **unfinished**.
The **G-33** was formed in **2003** during the Doha process.
**NAMA-11**: developing countries (incl. India) on non-agricultural market access.
**G-90** = **African Group** + **ACP** + **LDCs**.

77.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: MC9 — Bali — Trade Facilitation Agreement and interim Peace Clause on food stockholding
MC11 — Buenos Aires — Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies
MC12 — Geneva — Elimination of agricultural export subsidies
77.x: The Bali Ministerial Conference of 2013 produced the Bali Package, including the Trade Facilitation Agreement and an interim Peace Clause on food stockholding.
77.tq: Match the conference with its characteristic package while rejecting swapped outcomes.
xs: **MC9 Bali (2013)** adopted the **Bali package** — **Trade Facilitation Agreement** and interim **Peace Clause** on food stockholding — option **(1)**.
**MC10 Nairobi** eliminated **agricultural export subsidies** (the Doha agenda began in **2001**).
**MC11 Buenos Aires** had only a **fisheries work programme**; **MC12 Geneva** adopted the **AFS**.
xa: India **ratified the TFA in 2016**; the TFA simplifies **customs procedures**.
The **Peace Clause** shields developing-country **public stockholding** from disputes until a permanent solution.
India first invoked the Peace Clause for **rice** in **2020**.
Only two new agreements in **30 years**: **TFA** and **AFS**.

77.s: The elimination of agricultural export subsidies was associated with the WTO Ministerial Conference held at:
77.x: The Nairobi Ministerial Conference of 2015 adopted the outcome concerning elimination of agricultural export subsidies.
77.tq: Use the distinctive agricultural outcome to identify the correct conference.
xs: The **elimination of agricultural export subsidies** came at **MC10, Nairobi, 2015** — option **(4)**.
**Bali 2013** = TFA + Peace Clause; **Buenos Aires 2017** = no declaration; **Geneva 2022** = AFS.
xa: **MC6 Hong Kong (2005)** first agreed that farm export subsidies would end.
**Export competition** is one of the three **AoA** pillars, with domestic support and market access.
**SCM Agreement** classes subsidies as **prohibited**, **actionable** and **non-actionable**.
⚠ India lost the **export subsidies** case (**US, DS541**) over **MEIS, SEZ, EOU** schemes in **2019**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about the Twelfth WTO Ministerial Conference held at Geneva in June 2022:
1. The Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies was adopted.
2. A COVID-related TRIPS waiver was adopted.
3. The e-commerce customs-duty moratorium was permanently abolished.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: MC12 adopted the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies and a COVID-related TRIPS waiver. The e-commerce moratorium was extended, not permanently abolished, so statement 3 is false.
77.tq: Find the false later-development statement by separating extension from abolition.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **MC12 Geneva (June 2022)** adopted the **Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies** (Phase 1).
Statement 2 is correct: it adopted a **COVID TRIPS waiver**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the e-commerce moratorium was **extended**, not abolished — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: The **AFS** entered into force in **September 2025**.
**India** became the **123rd** member to deposit its Instrument of Acceptance (**July 2026**).
The moratorium **lapsed on 31 Mar 2026** for the first time (**MC14**).
AFS is the WTO's **first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Fourteenth WTO Ministerial Conference at Yaounde in March 2026:
1. It produced only a draft ‘Yaounde package’ and no ministerial declaration.
2. The e-commerce moratorium lapsed on 31 March 2026.
3. Sixty-six members signed a separate E-Commerce Agreement barring duties on digital trade.
4. A permanent solution on public stockholding was achieved.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: MC14 produced no ministerial declaration, the e-commerce moratorium lapsed, and 66 members signed a separate agreement barring duties on digital trade. The permanent public-stockholding solution remained deadlocked, so statement 4 is false.
77.tq: Check each conference outcome separately and reject the over-claim of a settlement.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **MC14** gave only a draft "**Yaounde package**", **no ministerial declaration**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **e-commerce moratorium lapsed on 31 Mar 2026** for the first time.
Statement 3 is correct: **66 members** signed a separate **E-Commerce Agreement** barring duties on digital trade.
Statement 4 is wrong: no **permanent solution on PSH** — still deadlocked; so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: The **TRIPS non-violation moratorium** also lapsed at MC14.
**India blocked** adding the **IFD** plurilateral to **Annex 4** (backed by **129 of 166**).
Fisheries **Phase 2** was deferred to the **General Council, Geneva**.
MC14 is widely seen as a **failure**.

77.s: Which one of the following developments was associated with the WTO Ministerial Conference at Yaounde in 2026?
o: India blocked the addition of the Investment Facilitation for Development plurilateral agreement to Annex 4.
India proposed making the e-commerce moratorium permanent without opposition.
The Doha Development Agenda was launched.
The fisheries Phase 2 negotiations were concluded.
77.x: At MC14, India blocked addition of the IFD plurilateral agreement to Annex 4, although it had the backing of 129 of 166 members. Fisheries Phase 2 was deferred.
77.tq: Identify the relevant negotiating position while rejecting outcomes belonging to earlier conferences.
xs: At **MC14 Yaounde (2026)**, **India blocked** adding the **Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD)** plurilateral to **Annex 4** — option **(1)**.
The IFD was backed by **129 of 166** members.
The Doha agenda was launched in **2001**; fisheries **Phase 2** was **deferred** to the General Council; the moratorium **lapsed**.
xa: Debate: **plurilaterals** (**IFD**, **E-Commerce Agreement**) vs **consensus**; India fears **fragmentation**.
The **TRIPS non-violation moratorium** lapsed at MC14.
No **permanent solution on PSH** at MC14.
MC14 was held on **26-29 Mar 2026** at **Yaounde, Cameroon**.

77.s: Which one of the following correctly states the status and principal areas of the Doha Round?
o: It began in 1995 and was completed on agriculture alone.
It began in 2001, covers agriculture, NAMA and services, and remains unfinished.
It began in 2013 and covers only trade facilitation.
It began in 2022 and covers only fisheries subsidies.
77.x: The Doha Round began in 2001, is concerned with agriculture, non-agricultural market access and services, and remains unfinished.
77.tq: Check the year, scope and completion status together to reject partially correct alternatives.
xs: The **Doha Round** began in **2001**, covers **agriculture, NAMA and services**, and **remains unfinished** — option **(2)**.
**1995** is when the WTO began; **2013** (Bali) gave the **TFA**; **2022** gave the **AFS** — none started the Doha Round.
xa: It is called the "**Development round**"; launched at **MC4 Doha** with a **TRIPS-public health declaration**.
**NAMA-11**: developing countries (incl. India) negotiating **non-agricultural market access**.
**G-33** formed in **2003** during the Doha talks at **Cancun**.
⚠ "Doha Round concluded" is a trap — it **never concluded**.

77.s: The G-33 was formed in 2003 during the Doha process primarily to address:
o: Food security, special safeguard mechanisms and special products
77.x: The G-33 is a group of more than 40 developing countries, including India, focusing on food security, the Special Safeguard Mechanism and special products.
77.tq: Identify the negotiating group's agenda rather than its membership alone.
xs: The **G-33** (formed **2003**) focuses on **food security**, the **Special Safeguard Mechanism** and **special products** — option **(4)**.
It is a group of **40+** developing countries including **India**.
xa: It was formed at **MC5 Cancun (2003)**, which collapsed over agriculture and Singapore issues.
**NAMA-11**: developing countries on **non-agricultural market access**.
**G-90** = **African Group** + **ACP** + **LDCs**.
The fisheries issue is handled by the **AFS**, not the G-33.

77.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Doha Round — Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies only
G-33 — African Group, ACP and LDCs
G-90 — Food security and special products only
NAMA-11 — Developing countries negotiating on non-agricultural market access
77.x: NAMA-11 is a group of developing countries, including India, concerned with non-agricultural market access. The G-90 consists of the African Group, ACP countries and LDCs.
77.tq: Use group-purpose matching and reject the swapped descriptions of G-33, G-90 and NAMA-11.
xs: **NAMA-11** is a group of **developing countries** (incl. India) on **non-agricultural market access** — option **(4)**.
**G-33** focuses on food security and special products, while **G-90** = **African Group + ACP + LDCs** — options (2) and (3) swap them.
The **Doha Round** covers agriculture, **NAMA** and services, not fisheries only.
xa: **G-33**: formed **2003**; **40+** developing countries; **Special Safeguard Mechanism**.
The **Doha Round (2001)** is the "**Development round**" — still unfinished.
⚠ The fisheries agreement (**AFS**) came separately at **MC12 (2022)**.

77.s: The Fourteenth WTO Ministerial Conference (MC14), held in March 2026, took place at which of the following places?
77.x: WTO MC14 was held at Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 26 to 29 March 2026.
77.tq: Use the venue-based direct-recall method for international conferences.
xs: **MC14** was held at **Yaoundé, Cameroon**, on **26-29 Mar 2026** — option **(3)**.
xa: MC14 ended with **no ministerial declaration** — only a draft "**Yaounde package**".
The **e-commerce moratorium** and **TRIPS non-violation moratorium** lapsed.
**India blocked** adding the **IFD** to **Annex 4**.
⚠ MC9 Bali = TFA + Peace Clause; MC12 Geneva = AFS; MC14 Yaounde = no declaration.

77.s:
Arrange the following WTO events in chronological order:
A. MC12 adopted Phase 1 of the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement.
B. MC9 adopted the Peace Clause for food-security stockholding.
C. MC14 was held at Yaoundé.
D. MC13 was held at Abu Dhabi.
77.x: The correct order is MC9 in 2013, MC12 in 2022, MC13 in 2024 and MC14 in 2026.
77.tq: Fix the earliest and latest conferences first, then place the middle events by year.
xs: **MC9 Bali 2013** (Peace Clause) → **MC12 Geneva 2022** (AFS Phase 1) → **MC13 Abu Dhabi 2024** → **MC14 Yaoundé 2026**: **B, A, D, C**, option **(1)**.
Years: **2013**, **2022**, **2024**, **2026** — the Peace Clause (B) comes first, Yaoundé (C) last.
xa: **MC10 Nairobi (2015)** and **MC11 Buenos Aires (2017)** fall between Bali and MC12.
**MC13** extended the moratorium to **31 Mar 2026**; it lapsed after **MC14**.
The **AFS** entered into force in **September 2025**.
India first invoked the **Peace Clause** for **rice** in **2020**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about the subsidy boxes under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture:
1. Green Box support, such as agricultural research and disease control, is not trade-distorting and has no limits.
2. Blue Box support consists of direct payments under production-limiting programmes and is subject to reduction commitments.
3. Amber Box support includes price- or quantity-linked support such as MSP and input subsidies, measured as AMS.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
77.x: Statement 1 is correct: Green Box covers research, disease control, infrastructure etc., is not trade-distorting and has no limits. Statement 2 is wrong: Blue Box payments limit production and are trade-distorting but EXEMPT from cuts. Statement 3 is correct: Amber Box covers MSP, power, fertiliser, seed and irrigation subsidies, measured as AMS and subject to reduction. So '1 and 3 only'.
77.tq: Green = free, Blue = production-limiting but exempt, Amber = trade-distorting and cut.

77.s: The de minimis limit for agricultural domestic support is what percentage of production value for developed and developing countries, respectively?
77.x: The de minimis limit is 5% of production value for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.
77.tq: Read the paired percentages in the correct developed-country/developing-country order.
xs: **De minimis** Amber support allowed without penalty is **5%** of agricultural output value for **developed** and **10%** for **developing** countries — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses the two figures.
xa: **Tariffication**: developed cut **36%** over **6 years**; developing **24%** over **10 years**.
**Amber Box** support (**MSP**, power, fertiliser, seed, irrigation) is measured as **AMS**.
India's **NFSA** procurement counts in the Amber box on an **outdated reference price**.
The **Peace Clause** shields food-security procurement even if it breaches **AoA** limits.

77.s: The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) rests on which of the following three pillars?
o: Domestic support, market access and export competition
Market access, investment protection and government procurement
Export competition, services and industrial subsidies
Domestic support, intellectual property and trade facilitation
77.x: The AoA has three pillars: domestic support, market access and export competition.
77.tq: Identify the standard three-part structure of the agreement.
xs: The **AoA (1995)** rests on **domestic support, market access and export competition** — option **(1)**.
Investment, IPR and trade facilitation belong to **TRIMS**, **TRIPS** and the **TFA**, not the AoA pillars.
xa: Domestic support is sorted into **Green**, **Blue** and **Amber** boxes.
Market access: **tariffication** of non-tariff barriers.
Export competition: **MC10 Nairobi (2015)** eliminated agricultural export subsidies.
The **Uruguay Round** aimed to cut **farm subsidies**.

77.s: Which one of the following is NOT an official subsidy box under the Agreement on Agriculture?
77.x: Green, Blue and Amber are the subsidy boxes under the AoA. Red, Orange and Yellow are not AoA boxes; a prohibited-subsidy category described as a red-light category belongs to the SCM context.
77.tq: Find the odd term in a closely related list of official categories.
xs: **Red Box** is not an AoA box — option **(3)**.
The AoA boxes are **Green**, **Blue** and **Amber**.
xa: ⚠ "**Red box**", "**Orange box**" and "**Yellow box**" are all distractors.
A "**red light**" category exists only for **prohibited subsidies** under the **SCM Agreement**.
**Green** = not trade-distorting; **Blue** = production-limiting; **Amber** = trade-distorting.
SCM classes: **prohibited**, **actionable** (countervailing duty), **non-actionable**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about market access under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture:
1. Conversion of non-tariff barriers into tariffs is called tariffication.
2. Developed countries were to cut tariffs by 36% over 6 years.
3. Developing countries were to cut tariffs by 24% over 6 years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: developing countries had to cut 24% over 10 years, not 6. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
77.tq: 36% / 6 years for developed vs 24% / 10 years for developing.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: converting non-tariff barriers to tariffs is **tariffication**.
Statement 2 is correct: **developed** countries cut **36%** over **6 years**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **developing** countries cut **24%** over **10 years**, not 6 — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Market access** is one of the three AoA pillars with **domestic support** and **export competition**.
**De minimis**: **5%** (developed) vs **10%** (developing) of agricultural output value.
The **AoA** dates from **1995**.

77.s: Under the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (SCM), subsidies for research and development, regional development and environmental purposes have been classed as:
77.x: The SCM Agreement groups subsidies as prohibited (the 'red light' category), actionable (open to countervailing duty) and non-actionable (R&D, regional and environmental). Amber Box is an Agreement on Agriculture category for trade-distorting farm support, not an SCM class.
77.tq: SCM traffic lights: prohibited (red), actionable, non-actionable (R&D, regional, green).
xs: Subsidies for **R&D, regional and environmental** purposes are **non-actionable** under the **SCM Agreement** — option **(3)**.
**Prohibited** subsidies form the "**red light**" category; **actionable** ones attract **countervailing duty**.
**Amber Box** is an **AoA** category, not an SCM class.
xa: ⚠ "Red box" is not an AoA box — "red light" belongs only to the **SCM** prohibited category.
**Amber Box** = trade-distorting farm support measured as **AMS**.
India lost the **export subsidies** case (**US, DS541**) over **MEIS, SEZ, EOU** schemes.

77.s: The Peace Clause adopted at Bali in 2013 provides protection to developing countries from disputes concerning:
o: Trade in banking and insurance services
77.x: The Bali Peace Clause shields developing-country public stockholding programmes from disputes until a permanent solution is found.
77.tq: Link the clause to its conference, year and specific agricultural issue.
xs: The **Peace Clause (Bali MC9, 2013)** shields developing countries' **public stockholding for food security** from disputes — option **(2)**.
It is **interim** protection until a **permanent solution** — no legal challenge even if procurement breaches **AoA** limits.
xa: India first invoked the Peace Clause for **rice** in **2020**.
**MC14 (2026)** still produced no **permanent solution on PSH**.
The **Bali package** also included the **Trade Facilitation Agreement**.
India's **GI** protection works through **TRIPS** (not the **Lisbon Agreement**) — a separate issue.

77.s: Which country first invoked the WTO Peace Clause for rice in 2020?
77.x: India was the first country to invoke the Peace Clause for rice in 2020.
77.tq: Distinguish the invoking country from countries associated with India’s sugar dispute.
xs: **India** first invoked the **Peace Clause** for **rice** in **2020** — option **(3)**.
**Brazil**, **Australia** and **Guatemala** were complainants against India in the **sugar** dispute, not Peace Clause users.
xa: The Peace Clause comes from **Bali MC9 (2013)**, shielding **public stockholding**.
India's demand: a **permanent solution** — **MSP** procurement for **NFSA** counts in the **Amber box**.
**India** + **African Group** want a permanent shield for programmes like the **NFSA**.
The **sugar** panel went against India in **2021**; India appealed.

77.s:
Consider the following statements regarding public stockholding at MC14 in 2026:
1. No permanent solution was reached on public stockholding.
2. India and the African Group sought a permanent shield for programmes such as the NFSA.
3. The issue was declared permanently settled at MC14.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. MC14 did not produce a permanent solution; India and the African Group continued to seek a permanent shield for programmes such as the NFSA.
77.tq: Reject the extreme finality of “permanently settled” when the issue remains unresolved.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **MC14 (2026)** reached **no permanent solution on PSH** — still deadlocked.
Statement 2 is correct: **India** and the **African Group** sought a permanent shield for programmes like the **NFSA**.
Statement 3 is wrong — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **MC13 Abu Dhabi (2024)** also produced **no PSH solution**.
The interim **Peace Clause** dates from **Bali MC9 (2013)**.
India first invoked the Peace Clause for **rice** in **2020**.
MSP procurement counts in the **Amber box** on an **outdated reference price**.

77.s: Why does India's public stockholding issue under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture involve an outdated reference price?
o: Because the reference price is fixed by the World Bank every five years
Because MSP procurement for the National Food Security Act is calculated using a historical reference price
Because the reference price excludes all procurement by government agencies
Because the reference price is based on the international price of food imports in 2013
77.x: India argues that MSP procurement for the National Food Security Act is treated as an Amber Box subsidy using an outdated historical reference price.
77.tq: Test the precise technical detail behind a current policy controversy rather than its general description.
xs: **MSP procurement for the NFSA** is counted in the **Amber box** on an **outdated (historical) reference price** — option **(2)**.
So India's support looks larger against **AoA** limits; India demands a **permanent solution**.
xa: **De minimis** limit for developing countries: **10%** of the value of agricultural output.
The **Peace Clause (Bali, 2013)** gives interim protection from disputes.
India first invoked it for **rice** in **2020**.
**MC14 (2026)**: no permanent PSH solution.

77.s: Which one of the following is NOT prohibited under the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies?
o: Subsidies for fishing on unregulated high seas
Subsidies for illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing
Subsidies for fishing in overfished stocks, unless rebuilding conditions apply
77.x: The Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies covers marine wild capture fishing and at-sea support. Aquaculture and inland fishing are exempt.
77.tq: Find the excluded activity rather than selecting one of the prohibited forms of fishing support.
xs: Subsidies for **inland fishing** are **not banned** — **aquaculture and inland fishing are exempt** from the AFS — option **(2)**.
The AFS covers **marine wild capture** and **at-sea support**.
It bans subsidies to **IUU fishing**, **unregulated high seas** and **overfished stocks** (unless rebuilding) — options (1), (3), (4).
xa: Developing countries/LDCs get a **2-year** EEZ exemption; a **Fish Fund** helps poorer members.
Adopted at **MC12 (2022)**; **in force September 2025**.
**Phase 2** (overcapacity, overfishing) was deferred at **MC14** to the **General Council**.
AP angle: AFS rules matter for **AP's marine fisher folk**; fisher bodies sought a "**fisher-centric**" approach.

77.s: Which one of the following correctly states the recent status of the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies?
o: It was adopted in 2022 and entered into force in September 2025.
It was adopted in 2025 and entered into force in September 2026.
It was adopted in 2013 and entered into force in 2016.
It was adopted in 2020 but has not yet entered into force.
77.x: The agreement was adopted at MC12 in 2022 and entered into force in September 2025.
77.tq: Check both the adoption year and the later entry-into-force date.
xs: The **AFS** was **adopted in 2022** (**MC12 Geneva**) and **entered into force in September 2025** — option **(1)**.
**2013** and **2016** belong to the **TFA** (Bali adoption, India's ratification).
xa: AFS is the WTO's **first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective**.
Only two new WTO agreements in **30 years**: **TFA** and **AFS**.
**India** joined as the **123rd** member to deposit acceptance in **July 2026**.
⚠ **123** is also the number of **Uruguay Round** contracting parties.

77.s: The Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies is significant in WTO history because it is the first WTO agreement with which of the following objectives?
77.x: The Fisheries Subsidies Agreement is the WTO's first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective.
77.tq: Identify the distinctive historical first associated with an agreement.
xs: The **AFS** is the WTO's **first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective** — option **(4)**.
It bans subsidies to **IUU fishing**, fishing on **unregulated high seas** and **overfished stocks** (unless rebuilding).
xa: Only two new WTO agreements in **30 years**: the **TFA** and the **AFS**.
Adopted at **MC12 Geneva (2022)**; **in force September 2025**.
**India** became the **123rd** member to deposit its Instrument of Acceptance (**July 2026**).
**Aquaculture and inland fishing** are exempt; a **Fish Fund** helps poorer members.

77.s: India became the 123rd WTO member to deposit its Instrument of Acceptance for the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies in:
77.x: India deposited its Instrument of Acceptance in July 2026, becoming the 123rd WTO member to do so.
77.tq: Combine a membership number with the exact month and year of a treaty action.
xs: India deposited its **AFS Instrument of Acceptance** as the **123rd member** in **July 2026** — option **(4)**.
**September 2025** is when the AFS **entered into force**; **March 2026** was **MC14** at Yaounde.
xa: ⚠ **123** is also the number of **Uruguay Round** contracting parties.
The AFS was adopted at **MC12 (2022)** — the WTO's first agreement with an **environmental** objective.
Developing countries/LDCs get a **2-year** EEZ exemption.
AP angle: the rules matter for **AP's marine fisher folk**; fisher bodies sought a "**fisher-centric**" approach.

77.s: Which pair of WTO agreements is identified as the only two new agreements concluded in the last 30 years?
o: TFA and Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies
77.x: The Trade Facilitation Agreement and the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies are identified as the only two new WTO agreements concluded in the last 30 years.
77.tq: Start from the distinctive pair and eliminate agreements belonging to the original WTO package.
xs: The only two new WTO agreements in **30 years** are the **TFA** and the **Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies** — option **(2)**.
**TRIPS**, **GATS**, **TRIMS**, **SPS/TBT** date from the WTO's start (**TRIPS 1995**); the **ITA** dates from **1996**.
xa: **TFA**: **Bali MC9 (2013)**; simplifies **customs procedures**; India ratified in **2016**.
**AFS**: adopted **MC12 (2022)**; in force **September 2025**.
AFS = WTO's **first agreement with an environmental-sustainability objective**.
**India blocked** adding the **IFD** plurilateral to **Annex 4** at **MC14**.

77.s: With reference to the WTO e-commerce customs-duty moratorium, which one of the following is correct?
o: It was replaced by the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement in 2025.
It was introduced in 2022 and made permanent in 2026.
It applies only to agricultural exports and was renewed at MC14.
It has prohibited customs duties on electronic transmissions since 1998 and lapsed on 31 March 2026.
77.x: The moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions had existed since 1998 and lapsed for the first time on 31 March 2026.
77.tq: Separate the exact subject, duration and outcome instead of relying on a familiar WTO term.
xs: The moratorium has barred **customs duties on electronic transmissions since 1998** and **lapsed on 31 March 2026** — option **(4)**.
It began at **MC2 Geneva (1998)**, not 2022, and was never made permanent.
It concerns **electronic transmissions**, not agricultural exports, and has nothing to do with the **AFS**.
xa: **MC12 (2022)** extended it; **MC13 (2024)** extended it to **31 Mar 2026**.
It lapsed **for the first time** at **MC14** (**Yaounde**).
Developing countries **lose tariff revenue** on digital imports.
**66 members** separately signed an **E-Commerce Agreement**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about Phase 2 of the WTO fisheries subsidies negotiations:
1. It deals with subsidies contributing to overcapacity and overfishing.
2. It was concluded and adopted at MC14 in Yaounde.
3. It was deferred to the General Council in Geneva.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statement 1 is correct: Phase 2 covers overcapacity and overfishing. Statement 2 is wrong: it was not concluded at MC14. Statement 3 is correct: it was sent to the General Council, Geneva. So '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
77.tq: Phase 1 adopted MC12 (2022); Phase 2 (overcapacity/overfishing) deferred at MC14.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Phase 2** deals with **overcapacity and overfishing**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it was **deferred at MC14**, not concluded.
Statement 3 is correct: it was sent to the **General Council, Geneva** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: **Phase 1** (the **AFS**) was adopted at **MC12 (2022)** and entered into force in **September 2025**.
AFS bans subsidies to **IUU fishing**, unregulated high seas and overfished stocks.
MC14 also left **PSH** deadlocked and saw the **moratorium** lapse.

77.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Agreement)
a. TRIPS
b. TRIMS
c. GATS
d. SPS/TBT
List-II (Subject)
i. Trade in services
ii. Minimum intellectual-property standards
iii. Investment measures affecting trade
iv. Food safety, plant and animal health, and technical standards
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
77.x: TRIPS concerns minimum IPR standards, TRIMS concerns trade-related investment measures, GATS concerns services, and SPS/TBT concern health and technical standards.
77.tq: Start from the sure pair TRIPS–IPR and complete the agreement-subject mapping.
xs: **TRIPS** = minimum IPR standards, **TRIMS** = investment measures affecting trade, **GATS** = services, **SPS/TBT** = food safety and technical standards: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv**, option **(1)**.
Option (3) wrongly gives TRIMS to services; option (2) swaps TRIPS and TRIMS.
xa: TRIPS compliance: **Patents Act** amended **2005** (product patents); **GI of Goods Act, 1999**.
TRIMS example: **local-content rules** — India phased out local-content conditions.
SPS/TBT compliance: **Food Safety and Standards Act 2006**.
**TFA (Bali 2013)** simplifies customs; **ITA (1996)** gives zero duty on IT products.

77.s: Which Indian law was enacted in 2005 to comply with the TRIPS requirement relating to product patents?
o: The Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001
77.x: India amended its Patents Act in 2005 to introduce product patents in accordance with TRIPS requirements.
77.tq: Match the legal enactment with the specific TRIPS-related compliance measure.
xs: India **amended the Patents Act in 2005** to bring in **product patents** under **TRIPS** — option **(1)**.
The **GI of Goods Act, 1999** and **PPV&FR Act 2001** are other TRIPS-linked laws but not about product patents; the **Food Safety and Standards Act 2006** is SPS/TBT compliance.
xa: **TRIPS (1995)** sets **minimum IPR standards**.
India is not in the **Lisbon Agreement**; it prefers **TRIPS** for **GI** protection.
The **Doha (2001)** conference adopted a **TRIPS-public health declaration**.
**MC12 (2022)** adopted a **COVID TRIPS waiver**.

77.s: Which statement best describes India's position regarding the Lisbon Agreement on appellations?
o: India is a founding member but has suspended its membership.
India is a member and prefers it to TRIPS for GI protection.
India applies the Lisbon Agreement only to agricultural exports.
India is not a member and prefers TRIPS for GI protection.
77.x: India is not a member of the Lisbon Agreement on appellations and prefers to use TRIPS for geographical-indication protection.
77.tq: Discriminate between two international frameworks dealing with geographical indications.
xs: India is **not in the Lisbon Agreement** on appellations and **prefers TRIPS for GI protection** — option **(4)**.
So India was never a founding or suspended member, and does not apply Lisbon to any exports.
xa: India's GI law: the **GI of Goods Act, 1999**.
**TRIPS (1995)** sets **minimum IPR standards**.
Other TRIPS-linked laws: **Patents Act** amended **2005**; **PPV&FR Act 2001**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA):
1. It was concluded as part of the Bali package at MC9 in 2013.
2. It aims to simplify customs procedures.
3. India ratified it in 2016.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: All three are correct: the TFA came out of the Bali package (MC9, 2013), it simplifies customs procedures, and India ratified it in 2016. So each option that leaves out a statement is wrong.
77.tq: TFA: Bali 2013, customs simplification, India ratified 2016.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **TFA** was part of the **Bali package** (**MC9, 2013**).
Statement 2 is correct: it **simplifies customs procedures**.
Statement 3 is correct: **India ratified it in 2016** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Bali also gave the interim **Peace Clause** on food stockholding.
TFA and **AFS** are the only two new agreements in **30 years**.
**Trade facilitation** was one of the "**Singapore issues**" from **MC1 (1996)**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about the WTO Appellate Body crisis:
1. The Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019 because the US has blocked appointments.
2. The MPIA is an EU-led stop-gap appeal arrangement set up in 2020.
3. India has joined the MPIA.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: India has not joined the MPIA. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
77.tq: US blocks appointments (Dec 2019); MPIA = EU-led 2020 stop-gap; India stays out.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **US blocked appointments**, so the **Appellate Body** is non-functional since **Dec 2019**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **MPIA** is an **EU-led** stop-gap from **2020**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **India has not joined** the MPIA — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: MPIA = **Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement**.
India's **DS541** loss (**2019**) was "**appealed into the void**".
**BRICS New Delhi Declaration (Sep 2026)** sought restoration of the **two-tier WTO dispute settlement**.

77.s:
Consider the following WTO disputes involving India and their outcomes:
1. Solar cells (DS456, US) - India lost in 2016.
2. Export subsidies under MEIS, SEZ and EOU (DS541, US) - panel ruled in India's favour in 2019.
3. ICT tariffs (EU, Japan, Taiwan) - panel ruled against India in 2023.
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
77.x: Pair 1 is correct: India lost DS456 in 2016. Pair 2 is wrong: the DS541 panel ruled against India in 2019 and India appealed into the void. Pair 3 is correct: the ICT panel ruled against India in 2023. So '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
77.tq: India lost all four: solar 2016, DS541 2019, sugar 2021, ICT 2023.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: India **lost** the **solar cells** case (**DS456**) in **2016**.
Pair 2 is wrong: the **DS541** panel went **against** India in **2019**; India **appealed into the void**.
Pair 3 is correct: the **ICT tariffs** panel ruled against India in **2023** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: **Sugar** case (**Brazil, Australia, Guatemala**): panel against India **2021**; appealed.
Appeals go "into the void" because the **Appellate Body** is non-functional since **Dec 2019**.
India has **not joined** the stop-gap **MPIA**.

77.s: The WTO dispute brought by Brazil, Australia and Guatemala against India related to:
o: Steel safeguards imposed by the United Kingdom
Tariffs on ICT products under the ITA
77.x: The sugar dispute involved India's cane pricing and export subsidies. The panel ruled against India in 2021, after which the matter was appealed.
77.tq: Match the complainant countries with the commodity and policy issue in dispute.
xs: **Brazil, Australia and Guatemala** challenged India's **cane price and export subsidies** (sugar) — option **(4)**.
The panel ruled **against India in 2021**; India **appealed**.
**Solar cells** was a **US** case; **ICT tariffs** under the ITA was brought by the **EU, Japan, Taiwan**.
xa: ⚠ Appeals are stuck: the **Appellate Body** has been non-functional since **Dec 2019**.
**DS541** (**US**): MEIS, SEZ, EOU — panel against India **2019**.
The **MPIA** (**EU**-led, **2020**) is a stop-gap; India has not joined.

77.s: The BRICS New Delhi Declaration of September 2026 called for which of the following reforms?
o: A permanent ban on all WTO dispute settlement proceedings
Abolition of the IMF and World Bank
IMF and World Bank quota and voting reform and restoration of the WTO Appellate Body
Replacement of the WTO by a BRICS-only trade organisation
77.x: The declaration sought reform of IMF and World Bank quotas and voting, along with restoration of the two-tier WTO dispute-settlement system.
77.tq: Link a declaration with its specific institutional demands.
xs: The **BRICS New Delhi Declaration (Sep 2026)** asked for **IMF/World Bank quota and voting reform** and restoration of the **two-tier WTO dispute settlement** (Appellate Body) — option **(3)**.
It sought **reform**, not abolition of the IMF/World Bank or of WTO dispute settlement.
xa: The **Appellate Body** is paralysed since **Dec 2019** — the **US** blocked appointments.
The **MPIA** (**EU**-led, **2020**) is a stop-gap; India has not joined.
The WTO is the **third pillar** of the world economy with the **IMF** and **World Bank**.

77.s: Which one of the following best describes India's concern regarding plurilateral initiatives such as the Investment Facilitation for Development and the E-Commerce Agreement?
o: They apply exclusively to agricultural subsidies and food security.
They may fragment the WTO system by moving away from consensus-based negotiations.
They would make the Appellate Body fully functional without appointments.
They would automatically abolish all WTO agreements.
77.x: India fears that plurilateral initiatives such as the IFD and E-Commerce Agreement may fragment the WTO by weakening the consensus-based multilateral approach.
77.tq: Apply the institutional principle of consensus to a contemporary negotiating debate.
xs: India fears **plurilaterals** may **fragment** the WTO by moving away from **consensus** — option **(2)**.
At **MC14**, **India blocked** adding the **IFD** to **Annex 4** though it had **129 of 166** members' backing.
xa: The **E-Commerce Agreement** was signed separately by **66 members**, barring duties on digital trade.
The WTO's **Ministerial Conference** is the highest decision-making body.
MC14 (**Yaounde**, **Mar 2026**) failed to issue a declaration.

77.s: Why are the WTO fisheries-subsidy rules of particular relevance to Andhra Pradesh?
o: They affect the interests of Andhra Pradesh's marine fisher folk, who have sought a fisher-centric approach.
They prohibit all fishing activity along the Andhra Pradesh coast.
They concern only software exports from Visakhapatnam.
They directly regulate only inland irrigation projects in Andhra Pradesh.
77.x: The rules are relevant to Andhra Pradesh's marine fisher folk, and Indian fisher bodies have sought a fisher-centric approach to their implementation.
77.tq: Connect an international policy issue with its concrete regional stakeholder impact.
xs: The **AFS** rules matter for **AP's marine fisher folk**; Indian fisher bodies sought a "**fisher-centric**" approach — option **(1)**.
The AFS does not ban fishing — it targets **subsidies**, and **inland fishing** and **aquaculture** are exempt.
xa: The AFS covers **marine wild capture** + at-sea support.
Developing countries get a **2-year** EEZ exemption and a **Fish Fund**.
India joined the AFS in **July 2026** as the **123rd** member.

77.s: Which of the following statements regarding the WTO is incorrect?
o: It was established through the Marrakesh Agreement, 1994.
Its headquarters is in Geneva, Switzerland.
77.x: Option C is incorrect: the WTO began on 1 January 1995, under the Marrakesh Agreement signed in 1994. Its head office is in Geneva.
77.tq: Discriminate the year signed from the year it began.
n: WTO was established on 1 January 1995. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
The agreement associated with WTO is the Marrakesh Agreement of 1994. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
The headquarters of WTO is in Geneva, Switzerland. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
WTO was established in 1995. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]

77.s:
Assertion (A): The WTO has a broader multilateral trade framework than the GATT.
Reason (R): The WTO covers goods, services, intellectual property rights and investment measures, whereas the GATT mainly dealt with goods.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
77.x: Both are true: the WTO is wider than GATT because it covers goods, services, intellectual property and investment, while GATT dealt mainly with goods. R explains A.
77.tq: Ask whether the coverage explains the breadth.
n: GATT mainly covered goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
WTO covered goods, services, intellectual property rights, and investment measures. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
WTO provided a broader multilateral trade framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT provided a framework for trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]

77.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) GATT signing date
(b) GATT came into effect
(c) GATT signing place
(d) GATT founding contracting parties

List-II
(i) Geneva
(ii) 1948
(iii) 30 October 1947
(iv) 23
77.x: GATT was signed on 30 October 1947 in Geneva by 23 founding parties and came into force in 1948. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
77.tq: Match each GATT fact to its value.
n: GATT was signed on 30 October 1947. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT had 23 founding contracting parties. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT was signed at Geneva. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT came into effect in 1948. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]

77.s: Consider the following statements: I. The WTO originated from the Uruguay Round of GATT. II. The main focus of the GATT was the reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions. III. The WTO came into effect in 1948. IV. The GATT was established on 1 January 1995. Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: I and II are correct: the WTO grew out of GATT's Uruguay Round, and GATT focused on cutting tariffs and quotas. III and IV are false because they swap the dates: GATT dates from 1948 and the WTO from 1995.
77.tq: Watch for swapped dates.
n: WTO originated from the Uruguay Round of GATT. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT came into effect in 1948. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
The main focus of GATT was the reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
GATT was established in 1947. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
WTO was established in 1995. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]

77.s:
Assertion (A): The WTO replaced the GATT.
Reason (R): The WTO is an international trade organization.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
77.x: Both are true: the WTO replaced GATT, and it is an international trade organisation. Being an organisation does not explain why it replaced GATT, so R does not explain A.
77.tq: Ask whether a nature explains a replacement.
n: WTO replaced GATT. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]
WTO is an international trade organization. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 15-16]

77.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Expansion of the trade framework beyond goods
(b) GATS
(c) TRIPS
(d) TRIMS

List-II
(i) Trade in Services
(ii) Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights
(iii) Trade-Related Investment Measures
(iv) Uruguay Round expansion beyond goods
77.x: The Uruguay Round extended trade rules beyond goods, through GATS (services), TRIPS (intellectual property) and TRIMS (investment measures). The answer is a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
77.tq: Expand each agreement's name.
n: The Uruguay Round expanded the trade framework beyond goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
The Uruguay Round expanded the trade framework to include GATS. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
The Uruguay Round expanded the trade framework to include TRIPS. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
The Uruguay Round expanded the trade framework to include TRIMS. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]

78.s: For a listed company, foreign investment is generally classified as FDI when the investor’s equity holding is:
78.x: Under the threshold associated with the Arvind Mayaram Committee classification, an equity holding of 10% or more in a listed company is treated as FDI. Holdings below 10% are classified as portfolio investment.
78.tq: Separate the threshold from the maximum sectoral cap.
xs: A holding of **10% or more** (**>=10%**) of equity in a **listed** company is **FDI** — option **(3)**.
Below **10%** (**<10%**) in a listed company is **FPI**, so "less than 10%" and "less than 5%" describe portfolio holdings.
xa: In an **unlisted** company, **any stake** counts as FDI.
The 10% line comes from the **Arvind Mayaram Committee** (under **FEMA**).
FDI = long-term, **management control**, technology; FPI = short-term, liquid "**hot money**".
⚠ The **March 2026** PN3 amendment also uses a **10%** line — for Chinese/HK beneficial ownership.

78.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes FDI from FPI?
o: FDI is restricted to unlisted companies, whereas FPI is restricted to government securities
FDI is always debt, whereas FPI is always equity
FDI is regulated only by SEBI, whereas FPI is regulated only by the RBI
FDI is generally long-term and may involve management control, whereas FPI is generally liquid and short-term
78.x: FDI is generally long-term and may bring management control and technology. FPI is portfolio investment, usually more liquid and potentially short-term or ‘hot money’.
78.tq: Compare investments across nature, control and liquidity rather than ownership alone.
xs: **FDI** is **long-term** with **management control** and technology; **FPI** is **short-term, liquid** "hot money" — option **(4)**.
Both FDI and FPI are **non-debt** capital, so "FDI is always debt" is wrong.
FDI involves **DPIIT + RBI**, FPI **SEBI + RBI** — neither has a single regulator.
xa: Threshold: **>=10%** in a listed company = FDI; **<10%** = FPI.
FPI opened in India in **1992**; **FII and FPI** are essentially the same.
FPI flows are driven by the **US Fed**/interest rates and global risk appetite — "**flight to safety**" outflows.

78.s:
Consider the following statements about FDI and FPI:
1. FDI may enter through the automatic or government route and is associated with DPIIT and RBI oversight.
2. FPI investors must be registered with SEBI and are subject to SEBI and RBI oversight.
3. FII and FPI are essentially different categories with no substantive relationship.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. FII and FPI are essentially the same category in the classification described, so statement 3 is false.
78.tq: Use the confusable-pair trap involving FII and FPI.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: FDI comes via the **Automatic/Government route**, with **DPIIT + RBI**.
Statement 2 is correct: FPIs are **SEBI-registered**, under **SEBI + RBI**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **FII and FPI are essentially the same** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Law for FPIs: **SEBI (FPI) Regulations 2019**.
FPI opened in India in **1992**.
**DPIIT** is under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**.

78.s:
Foreign capital in India includes which of the following?
1. Foreign direct investment
2. Trade credit
3. Non-resident Indian deposits
4. External commercial borrowings
Select the correct answer using the code below.
78.x: Foreign capital includes FDI, trade credit, NRI deposits and external commercial borrowings. All four categories are included.
78.tq: Check the full enumeration rather than treating foreign capital as equity alone.
xs: Foreign capital includes **FDI, trade credit, NRI deposits and ECBs** — **all four**, option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2019** key).
So any option leaving out one of them — e.g. **trade credit** or **ECBs** (both debt) — is incomplete.
xa: **FDI** and **FPI** are **non-debt**; **ECB, trade credit, FCCB** are **debt**.
**NRI deposits** (**FCNR(B), NRE**) are **banking capital** (debt).
**ADR/GDR** equity raised abroad is counted as **portfolio investment** in BoP data.

78.s: Which one of the following is correctly classified as debt capital?
78.x: External commercial borrowing is debt capital. FDI and FPI are non-debt forms, while ADRs represent equity raised abroad through depository receipts.
78.tq: Separate debt instruments from non-debt equity instruments.
xs: An **External Commercial Borrowing (ECB)** is **debt** — option **(3)**.
**FDI** and **FPI** are **non-debt**; **ADR** equity is counted as **portfolio investment**.
xa: Other debt forms: **trade credit** and **FCCB**.
**ECBs are regulated by RBI** under **FEMA, 1999**.
**NRI deposits** (**FCNR(B), NRE**) count as banking capital (debt).

78.s: Participatory notes issued by registered FPIs are best described as:
o: Debt instruments issued by the RBI to domestic investors
Offshore derivative instruments issued to overseas investors not registered with SEBI
Government securities issued under the external commercial borrowing route
Shares issued only by unlisted Indian companies
78.x: Participatory notes are offshore derivative instruments issued by registered FPIs to overseas investors who are not registered with SEBI. They provide a portfolio investment channel.
78.tq: Identify the issuer, recipient and registration status in the instrument’s definition.
xs: **Participatory notes** are **offshore derivative instruments** issued by registered FPIs to **overseas investors not registered with SEBI** — option **(2)**.
They are a **portfolio channel** — not RBI debt, G-secs or unlisted shares.
xa: **ADR/GDR** = equity raised abroad via depository receipts, counted as **portfolio investment**.
FPI = **<10%** of a listed company; regulated by **SEBI + RBI**.
**FII and FPI** are essentially the same.

78.s: In balance of payments data, ADRs and GDRs are counted as:
78.x: ADRs and GDRs represent equity raised abroad through depository receipts and are counted as portfolio investment in balance of payments data.
78.tq: Distinguish the form of fund-raising from its classification in BoP data.
xs: **ADRs/GDRs** — equity raised abroad through depository receipts — are counted as **portfolio investment** in **BoP** data — option **(4)**.
**NRI deposits** are banking capital; **ECBs** and **trade credit** are debt.
xa: **Participatory notes** are also a **portfolio channel**.
**FPI** is **non-debt**, portfolio (**<10%**) and liquid.
**FCCBs** are **debt**.

78.s: Foreign currency convertible bonds are classified as:
78.x: FCCBs are debt instruments and are classified under external commercial borrowings, even though they may carry a conversion feature.
78.tq: Do not confuse convertibility into equity with the instrument’s initial debt classification.
xs: **FCCBs** are classified as **debt**, along with **ECB** and **trade credit** — option **(2)**.
They are not portfolio equity, FDI or NRI deposits.
xa: **ECBs** are regulated by the **RBI** under **FEMA, 1999**.
**FDI** and **FPI** are **non-debt** forms of foreign capital.
**NRI deposits** (**FCNR(B), NRE**) are banking capital (debt).

78.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Foreign Portfolio Investment in India is correct?
o: FPI was opened to India in 2000 and is regulated exclusively by the Ministry of Finance
FPI was opened to India in 1991 and is regulated exclusively by the RBI under FEMA
FPI was opened to India in 1992 and is regulated by SEBI under the FPI Regulations, 2019, along with the RBI
FPI was opened to India in 2019 and is regulated exclusively by SEBI without any role for the RBI
78.x: Foreign Portfolio Investment was opened to India in 1992. It is regulated by SEBI under the FPI Regulations, 2019, with the RBI also having a regulatory role.
78.tq: Combine the opening year with the two relevant regulators rather than selecting an exclusive regulator.
xs: **FPI** opened in India in **1992** and is regulated by **SEBI (FPI Regulations, 2019) + RBI** — option **(3)**.
No single regulator (Finance Ministry, RBI or SEBI alone) controls FPI — it is a **joint SEBI-RBI** role.
xa: **FII and FPI** are essentially the same.
FPI debt limits (General Route): **6%** of Central G-secs, **2%** of State securities.
**VRR** and **FAR** steadied debt flows.
India's inclusion in the **JP Morgan EM bond index** draws passive bond inflows.

78.s: The 10% equity threshold that separates FDI from foreign portfolio investment in a listed Indian company is associated with which committee?
78.x: The Arvind Mayaram Committee gave the 10% threshold: 10% or more in a listed company counts as FDI, below 10% as FPI. The Tarapore Committees dealt with capital account convertibility, the Narasimham Committees with banking reform, and the Rangarajan Committee with the balance of payments, among other areas.
78.tq: FDI vs FPI 10% line = Mayaram.
xs: The **10%** FDI/FPI threshold comes from the **Arvind Mayaram Committee** — option **(2)**.
It draws the line under **FEMA**: **>=10%** of a listed company is FDI, below that FPI.
xa: **>=10%** in a listed company = **FDI**; **<10%** = **FPI**.
In an **unlisted** company, **any stake** is FDI.
The threshold applies under **FEMA, 1999**, which replaced **FERA, 1973**.

78.s: With reference to the automatic route for foreign direct investment in India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Approval of SEBI is required before the investment is made
Only approval of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board is required
Prior approval of the concerned Ministry is mandatory before investment
No prior approval of the RBI or the Government is required, but post-facto reporting to the RBI is necessary
78.x: Under the automatic route, no prior approval of the RBI or the Government is required. The investment is subject to post-facto reporting to the RBI.
78.tq: Distinguish the approval stage from the reporting stage.
xs: Under the **automatic route**, **no prior RBI/Government approval** is needed — only **post-facto reporting to RBI** — option **(4)**.
Prior Ministry approval is the **Government route**; the **FIPB** was **abolished in June 2017**.
xa: Government-route applications go via the **FIF Portal** (**FIFP**), part of **NSWS** since **Aug 2022**.
**Negative list**: more than **90% of sectors** are automatic.
Government route examples: defence beyond **74%**, multi-brand retail, broadcasting, print media.

78.s:
Which of the following statements regarding India’s FDI policy is correct?
1. The Foreign Investment Promotion Board was abolished in June 2017.
2. DPIIT is the nodal department for FDI policy.
3. India follows a positive-list approach under which FDI is permitted only in specifically named sectors.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
78.x: The FIPB was abolished in June 2017 and DPIIT is the nodal department. India follows a negative-list approach, not a positive-list approach.
78.tq: Identify the reversed policy concept in statement 3.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **FIPB** was **abolished in June 2017**.
Statement 2 is correct: **DPIIT** is the **nodal department** for FDI policy.
Statement 3 is wrong: India follows a **negative list**, not a positive list — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Under the negative list, FDI is up to **100% automatic in most sectors**.
DPIIT issued the **Consolidated FDI Policy 2020**.
Applications now go to **concerned ministries/departments** via the **FIF Portal**.

78.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the nature of an FDI project?
o: Greenfield investment — establishment of a new facility, such as Hyundai at Sriperumbudur
Greenfield investment — acquisition of an existing company
Brownfield investment — establishment of a new facility
Brownfield investment — construction of a facility without acquiring an existing business
78.x: A greenfield investment creates a new facility; Hyundai’s facility at Sriperumbudur is an example. A brownfield investment involves acquisition of an existing business, as in Vodafone’s acquisition of Hutchison Essar.
78.tq: Discriminate between the two similar project classifications by asking whether an existing facility is acquired.
xs: **Greenfield** FDI = a **new facility**, e.g. **Hyundai, Sriperumbudur** — option **(1)**.
**Brownfield** FDI = an **acquisition**, e.g. **Vodafone-Hutchison Essar** — so options (2), (3), (4) swap the two.
xa: ⚠ Pharma: **greenfield 100% automatic**; **brownfield 74% automatic**, beyond needs approval.
FDI brings **technology and jobs** and finances the **CAD** with stable capital.

78.s: After the abolition of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), where are Government-route FDI applications submitted?
o: Only to the Reserve Bank of India through the ECB Portal
To the concerned ministries or departments through the FIF Portal run by DPIIT
Directly to the Ministry of Finance without any online portal
To the abolished FIPB through the Foreign Investment Facilitation Committee
78.x: FIPB was abolished in June 2017. Government-route applications are submitted to the concerned ministries or departments through the FIF Portal operated by DPIIT.
78.tq: Use the successor institution and the correct application channel rather than the abolished body.
xs: After the **FIPB** was abolished (**June 2017**), applications go to the **concerned ministries/departments** via the **FIF Portal run by DPIIT** — option **(2)**.
The FIPB no longer exists, and the **RBI** handles ECBs, not Government-route FDI.
xa: The **FIF Portal** has been part of the **National Single Window System** since **August 2022**.
**DPIIT** is under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**.
Government route covers defence beyond **74%**, **multi-brand retail**, broadcasting and print media.

78.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT):
1. It is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
2. It is the nodal department for FDI policy and FDI data.
3. Since August 2022, its FIF Portal has formed part of the National Single Window System.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: All three statements are correct. DPIIT is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, handles the nodal role for FDI policy and data, and its FIF Portal has been part of the National Single Window System since August 2022.
78.tq: Verify the department, its nodal responsibility and the portal integration date separately.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **DPIIT** is under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is **nodal for FDI policy and FDI data**.
Statement 3 is correct: the **FIF Portal** is part of **NSWS** since **August 2022** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: DPIIT issued the **Consolidated FDI Policy 2020**.
It replaced the role of the **FIPB** (abolished **June 2017**).
**July 2026**: DPIIT allowed FDI in **inventory e-commerce** for **exports** of domestically made goods.

78.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship among FEMA, FERA and External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs)?
o: FERA, 1973 replaced FEMA, 1999, and ECBs are regulated by SEBI under FERA
FEMA, 1999 regulates only domestic currency transactions, while ECBs are outside its scope
ECBs are regulated by the Ministry of Commerce under the Consolidated FDI Policy and not under FEMA
FEMA, 1999 replaced FERA, 1973, and ECBs are regulated by the RBI under FEMA
78.x: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973. External Commercial Borrowings are regulated by the RBI under FEMA.
78.tq: Keep the replacement sequence and the regulator’s role distinct from the earlier law.
xs: **FEMA, 1999** **replaced FERA, 1973**, and **ECBs are regulated by the RBI under FEMA** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the Acts; ECBs are with the **RBI**, not SEBI or the Commerce Ministry.
xa: FEMA governs **foreign exchange transactions**.
The **10%** FDI/FPI line (**Arvind Mayaram Committee**) operates under FEMA.
Insurance **100%** FDI was enabled by amending the **FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019**.

78.s: The foreign investment ceiling in private-sector banks was raised to 74% in:
78.x: The foreign investment ceiling in private-sector banks was raised to 74% in 2004.
78.tq: Test the year associated with a specific policy change rather than the present sectoral cap.
xs: The foreign investment cap in **private-sector banks** was raised to **74%** in **2004** — option **(3)**.
Of that **74%**, **49%** is via the **automatic route**, the rest via the **Government route**.
xa: Private banks: **74%** — **49% automatic**, beyond via **Government route**.
**Public sector banks**: **20%**, Government route.
Private banks are the example of "**automatic up to a cap, approval beyond**".

78.s: Which of the following statements about FDI in e-commerce is correct?
o: The marketplace model permits 100% FDI through the automatic route, while the inventory model is generally barred.
The inventory model permits 100% FDI through the automatic route, while the marketplace model is barred.
Both models permit only 51% FDI through the Government route.
Neither model permits foreign investment in India.
78.x: The marketplace model permits 100% FDI through the automatic route. FDI in the inventory model is generally not allowed, subject to the later export-related relaxation.
78.tq: Discriminate between marketplace and inventory models instead of applying one cap to both.
xs: E-commerce **marketplace model**: **100% FDI automatic**; **inventory model**: FDI **not allowed** — option **(1)**.
The inventory ban protects **small traders** and keeps the **multi-brand retail** curbs.
xa: **Jul 2026**: inventory FDI allowed where inventory is used to **export domestically made goods**.
It is the first big relaxation in nearly a decade.
India's e-commerce exports are only **~$5 bn** vs **China**'s **$300 bn**.
**Multi-brand retail**: **51%**, Government route.

78.s: In July 2026, FDI in inventory-based e-commerce was allowed in a specific situation when:
o: The inventory is used for exporting domestically manufactured goods.
The platform operates only as a marketplace.
The inventory is owned entirely by foreign companies for domestic resale.
The inventory is used to sell imported goods in the domestic market.
78.x: The July 2026 relaxation allowed inventory-based e-commerce FDI where the inventory is used to export domestically manufactured goods.
78.tq: Identify the precise condition attached to a policy relaxation rather than its broader sector label.
xs: **DPIIT** (**July 2026**) allowed inventory-based e-commerce FDI when **the inventory is used for exports of domestically manufactured goods** — option **(1)**.
Selling imported or foreign-owned inventory in the domestic market stays **barred**; marketplace was already **100% automatic**.
xa: First big relaxation in nearly a **decade**.
India's e-commerce exports: **~$5 bn** vs **China**'s **$300 bn**.
Inventory model was barred to **protect small traders**.

78.s: Which one of the following statements regarding FDI policy is NOT correct?
o: Caps were raised after 2014 in sectors including defence, insurance and pension.
The marketplace model in e-commerce permits 100% FDI through the automatic route.
All sectors are exclusively on the automatic route.
More than 90% of sectors are on the automatic route.
78.x: The statement that all sectors are exclusively on the automatic route is incorrect. Although more than 90% of sectors are on the automatic route, some sectors retain Government-route requirements.
78.tq: Find the absolute statement that goes beyond the stated proportion.
xs: "**All sectors are exclusively on the automatic route**" is wrong — option **(3)**.
More than **90% of sectors** are automatic, but the **Government route** remains (multi-brand retail, broadcasting, print media, defence beyond **74%**).
Options (1), (2) and (4) are correct: post-**2014** caps rose in defence, insurance, pension; marketplace e-commerce is **100% automatic**.
xa: India follows a **negative list** approach.
Some sectors are fully **prohibited** — e.g. **lottery**, **chit funds**, **atomic energy**.
Government-route applications use the **FIF Portal** (**NSWS**).

78.s: Which of the following pairs relating to pharmaceuticals and medical devices is correctly matched?
o: Greenfield pharma — 100% automatic; brownfield pharma — 74% automatic, beyond which approval is required
Greenfield pharma — 74% automatic; brownfield pharma — 100% automatic
Greenfield pharma — 20% Government route; brownfield pharma — 49% automatic
78.x: Greenfield pharmaceutical projects permit 100% FDI automatically. Brownfield projects permit 74% automatically, with approval required beyond that; medical devices permit 100% automatically.
78.tq: Match the project classification with its distinct cap and route.
xs: Pharma: **greenfield 100% automatic**; **brownfield 74% automatic**, beyond needs approval — option **(1)**.
**Medical devices** are **100% automatic**, not 51% Government route.
xa: **Greenfield** = new facility; **brownfield** = acquisition.
Also **100% automatic**: **NBFCs**, construction and real-estate broking.
⚠ **20%** Government route is the **public sector bank** limit, not pharma.

78.s: Which of the following is NOT a sector prohibited for FDI in India?
