FDI involves capital along with technology and management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FII is primarily associated with securities markets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FII is portfolio investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]

78.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified FIIs under the FPI framework.
The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified QFIs under the FPI framework.
The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 excluded FIIs from the FPI framework.
The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified sub-accounts under the FPI framework.
78.x: Option C is incorrect: SEBI's FPI Regulations, 2019, brought FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs together under the FPI framework.
78.tq: Recall the FPI merger.
n: The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified FIIs under the FPI framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified sub-accounts under the FPI framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
The SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 unified QFIs under the FPI framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
The SEBI FPI Regulations were issued in 2019. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]

78.s:
Assertion (A): A P-Note enables an overseas investor to gain exposure to Indian stocks without directly registering with SEBI.
Reason (R): A P-Note is issued by a registered FII/FPI to an overseas investor.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
78.x: Both are true: a P-Note gives an overseas investor exposure to Indian shares without SEBI registration, because a registered FII/FPI issues it to them. R explains A.
78.tq: Ask whether the issuer explains the access.
n: A P-Note is an instrument issued by a registered FII or FPI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
A P-Note is issued to an overseas investor. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
A P-Note enables an overseas investor to obtain exposure to Indian stocks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
An overseas investor using a P-Note does not directly register with SEBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]

78.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) FII
(b) FDI
(c) SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019
(d) Participatory Note

List-II
(i) Capital plus technology/management
(ii) Unified FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs into one category
(iii) Primarily financial capital and more volatile
(iv) Lets unregistered overseas investors gain exposure to Indian stocks
78.x: FII is mainly volatile financial capital, FDI brings capital with technology and management, the SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019 merged FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs, and a P-Note gives unregistered overseas investors exposure to Indian stocks. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
78.tq: Link each term to its distinguishing feature.
n: FII primarily involves financial capital. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FDI involves capital along with technology and management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FII is more volatile. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FDI is less volatile than FII, according to the source. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]
FII is portfolio investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]

78.s: FII stands for:
78.x: FII stands for Foreign Institutional Investor, now covered under the FPI framework.
78.tq: Expand the short name.
n: FII stands for Foreign Institutional Investor. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 29-30]

79.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of instruments or markets associated with the organised financial system?
o: Artisans, farmers, small traders and nidhis
Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit
Indigenous bankers, chit funds, nidhis and moneylenders
Unregulated loan companies, repo, nidhis and moneylenders
79.x: Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit are components of the organised financial system. The other sets include unorganised institutions or users.
79.tq: Classify each item before selecting the all-organised set.
xs: **Call money, T-bills, commercial bills and CDs** are all instruments of the **organised** (RBI-regulated) money market — option **(2)**.
**Indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated loan companies are **unorganised**; farmers, artisans and small traders are users, not instruments.
xa: Other organised instruments: **CPs**, **repo**, **MMMFs**.
Organised institutions: commercial banks, cooperative banks, foreign banks, **DFHI**, provident funds, **STCI**, mutual funds.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key: **finance companies** are **not** part of the organised money market.

79.s: An indigenous banker is best described as one who:
o: Accepts deposits and lends, while also combining banking with trade or commission business
Provides only long-term loans to infrastructure companies
Operates exclusively under the supervision of the RBI
Only lends in kind and does not accept deposits
79.x: An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, while combining banking activities with trade or commission business. Shroffs and Mahajans are examples.
79.tq: Use the functional definition and reject the extreme ‘only’ statement.
xs: An **indigenous banker** **accepts deposits and lends**, combining banking with **trade/commission business** — option **(1)**.
⚠ One who "**lends only in kind**" is **not** an indigenous banker; they are part of the **unorganised** sector, not RBI-supervised.
xa: They deal in **hundis**.
Examples: **Shroffs, seths, Mahajans, Multanis, Chettiars**.
**Moneylenders** are a separate group under **state money-lending laws**.

79.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of indigenous bankers?
o: Chit funds, loan companies, moneylenders and RRBs
79.x: Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.
79.tq: Identify the complete membership of a traditional financial-intermediary group.
xs: **Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars** are indigenous bankers — option **(3)**.
**RRBs**, **DCCBs**, **StCBs**, **NABARD**, banks and **NBFCs** are all organised/regulated institutions.
xa: **Mahajans** are also indigenous bankers.
Indigenous bankers deal in **hundis** and combine banking with trade/commission business.
⚠ "Lends only in kind" does **not** describe an indigenous banker.

79.s: Which one of the following statements regarding unregulated non-bank intermediaries is correct?
o: Loan companies are treated as scheduled commercial banks.
All chit funds are regulated exclusively by the RBI.
Professional and agricultural moneylenders fall under state money-lending laws.
Indigenous bankers are prohibited from dealing in hundis.
79.x: Professional and agricultural moneylenders are governed by state money-lending laws. Chit funds are associated with state government regulation under the Chit Funds Act, 1982.
79.tq: Match the intermediary with the authority or law governing it.
xs: **Moneylenders** — **professional or agricultural** — fall under **state money-lending laws** — option **(3)**.
**Chit funds** are regulated by the **State Government** (**Chit Funds Act 1982**), not the RBI; indigenous bankers do deal in **hundis**.
**Loan companies** are **unregulated** non-bank intermediaries, not scheduled banks.
xa: Unregulated non-bank intermediaries: **indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **loan companies**, **chit funds**.
**Nidhis** are also part of the unorganised market.

79.s: Shadow banking refers to:
o: only illegal lending by unlicensed moneylenders
credit intermediation outside full bank regulation, including activity by NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds
the issue of currency by the central bank
79.x: Shadow banking is bank-like credit intermediation outside full banking regulation; NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds are examples.
79.tq: Apply the definition to distinguish broad shadow banking from illegal lending alone.
xs: **Shadow banking** is **bank-like credit intermediation** (**NBFCs**, **money-market/liquid funds**) **outside full bank regulation** — option **(2)**.
It is not just illegal moneylending, nor cooperative deposit-taking.
xa: **Liquid debt mutual funds** are NBFCs' main **short-term funding** source.
Criticism: **regulatory arbitrage** (shadow banking).
RBI's response to NBFC stress: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.
**IL&FS (Sep 2018)** defaults triggered a liquidity crisis.

79.s: Which of the following belongs to the unorganised money market?
o: Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper
79.x: Indigenous bankers and moneylenders form part of the unorganised money market. T-Bills, commercial bills, CDs, CPs and repos belong to the organised segment.
79.tq: Classify the lender or instrument by the organised–unorganised divide.
xs: **Indigenous bankers and moneylenders** belong to the **unorganised** money market — option **(3)**.
**CDs, CPs, repos, call money, T-bills, commercial bills** are **organised** market instruments.
xa: Unorganised: also **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated finance/loan companies.
The unorganised market serves **farmers, artisans, small traders**.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key placed **finance companies** outside the organised market.

79.s: As per the APPSC Group 2 (2017) answer key, which one of the following is NOT a part of the organised money market in India?
o: Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI)
79.x: The APPSC-G2 2017 key treated finance companies as outside the organised money market. Commercial banks, DFHI and cooperative banks are RBI-regulated constituents of the organised money market.
79.tq: APPSC 2017 key: finance companies = not organised money market.
xs: The APPSC-G2 **2017** key treats **finance companies** as **not** part of the organised money market — option **(3)**.
**Commercial banks**, **DFHI** and **cooperative banks** are listed as **RBI-regulated** organised players.
xa: ⚠ The notes' general table does list finance companies under organised — follow the **key** for the PYQ.
Unregulated **finance/loan companies** sit in the **unorganised** column.
Organised also includes **STCI**, provident funds, mutual funds.

79.s: Which one of the following regulator–entity pairs is correctly matched?
79.x: Chit fund companies are regulated by the State Government. Merchant bankers are regulated by SEBI, insurance companies by IRDAI and NBFCs by RBI.
79.tq: Start with the sure regulator–entity pair and eliminate swapped authorities.
xs: **Chit fund companies** are regulated by the **State Government** — option **(3)**.
**Merchant bankers** come under **SEBI**, **insurance companies** under **IRDAI**, and **NBFCs** under the **RBI**.
xa: Chit funds: **Chit Funds Act 1982**.
**PFRDA** regulates pension/**NPS** under the **PFRDA Act, 2013**.
**IFSCA** (**April 2020**) is the unified regulator of **IFSCs** (GIFT City).

79.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. IRDA Act — 1999
2. PFRDA Act — 2013
3. IFSCA Act — 2019
4. SEBI statutory status — 1992
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: The IRDA Act dates to 1999, the PFRDA Act to 2013, the IFSCA Act to 2019, and SEBI became statutory in 1992.
79.tq: Test a group of statutory dates using an all-inclusive option.
xs: **IRDA Act 1999**, **PFRDA Act 2013**, **IFSCA Act 2019**, SEBI statutory **1992** — all four correct: **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(3)**.
**IFSCA** itself began functioning in **April 2020** under the 2019 Act.
xa: **PFRDA** regulates pension/**NPS**.
**HFC** regulation moved from **NHB** to **RBI** in **2019**.
**Chit fund companies** are regulated by the **State Government**.

79.s: The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) began functioning in April 2020 primarily as the regulator of:
o: all insurance companies and pension funds
International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City
79.x: IFSCA is the unified regulator for International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City, and began functioning in April 2020.
79.tq: Distinguish the unified IFSC regulator from sector-specific regulators.
xs: **IFSCA** (**April 2020**) is the **unified regulator of IFSCs**, including **GIFT City** — option **(4)**.
FPIs come under **SEBI**, insurance under **IRDAI**, pensions under **PFRDA**; cooperative banks under **RBI/NABARD**.
xa: It was set up under the **IFSCA Act 2019**.
**PFRDA** is statutory under the **PFRDA Act, 2013**.
First meeting of RBI's **Payments Regulatory Board**: **Jan 2026**.

79.s: Which of the following institutions performs a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies?
79.x: NHB plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.
79.tq: Match the quasi-regulator with the financial institution category it relates to.
xs: **NHB** is the **quasi-regulator** for **HFCs** — option **(1)**.
**NABARD** plays this role for **RRBs/cooperatives** and **SIDBI** for **SFCs**; **SEBI** is a full regulator.
xa: HFC **regulation** moved from NHB to the **RBI** (**Finance Act 2019**); NHB keeps **supervision and refinance**.
**90 HFCs** were registered (**June 2025**).
NHB: statutory, **1988** (**NHB Act 1987**).

79.s: Which one of the following institutions was established on a World Bank initiative and later became a universal bank?
o: Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India
79.x: ICICI was established in 1955 on a World Bank initiative and subsequently became a universal bank.
79.tq: Identify the institution through its founding association and later transformation.
xs: **ICICI** (**1955**) was set up on a **World Bank initiative** and later became a **universal bank** — option **(4)**.
**IFCI** (**1948**) was the first DFI; **IDBI** (**1964**) the apex industrial DFI; **EXIM Bank** (**1982**) finances foreign trade.
xa: ICICI provided **industrial credit**.
Older AIFI class: **IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI, IIBI**.
⚠ **IDBI** later became a **commercial bank**, reclassified **private** after **LIC** control (**2019**).

79.s: The establishment of NABARD was based on the recommendations of which committee?
79.x: NABARD was established on the basis of the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations relating to CRAFICARD.
79.tq: Use the committee–institution association rather than the sector alone.
xs: **NABARD** was based on the **B. Sivaraman Committee / CRAFICARD** — option **(1)**.
The **C. Rangarajan** high-level group is linked to **NHB**, not NABARD.
xa: NABARD: **12 July 1982**, **NABARD Act 1981**; HQ **Mumbai**.
It refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs** and runs **RIDF** (funded by banks' **PSL** shortfalls).
It inspects **RRBs** and **cooperative banks**.

79.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the present classification of IDBI Bank after LIC acquired majority control in 2019?
o: It became a refinance institution under RBI.
It was reclassified as a cooperative bank.
It was reclassified as a private sector bank.
It was converted into a foreign bank.
79.x: After LIC acquired majority control in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a private sector bank.
79.tq: Apply the ownership change to the resulting regulatory classification.
xs: After **LIC** took majority control (**2019**), **IDBI** was reclassified as a **private** sector bank — option **(3)**.
It is now a **commercial bank**, not a refinance institution, cooperative or foreign bank.
xa: IDBI: **1964** under RBI; autonomous **1976**; reverse-merged **2004-05**.
Govt + LIC are offloading a combined **60.72%** stake (bidding under way).
**LIC** was set up in **1956**.

79.s: For regulatory purposes, which of the following are classified by the Reserve Bank of India as refinance institutions?
79.x: RBI classifies NABARD, NHB and SIDBI as refinance institutions. EXIM Bank is classified as a term-lending institution.
79.tq: Separate refinance institutions from term-lending institutions.
xs: RBI classes **NABARD, NHB and SIDBI** as **refinance institutions** — option **(4)**.
**EXIM Bank** is a **term-lending institution**; IFCI, IDBI, LIC and NaBFID are not refinance institutions.
xa: APPSC GS **2024** picked **NHB** against **IFCI, TFCI and EXIM**.
The **5** RBI-regulated AIFIs: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, NaBFID**.
NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs**; NHB refinances **HFCs and banks**.

79.s: Which of the following institutions are regulated and supervised by the Reserve Bank of India as All-India Financial Institutions?
o: IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, IIBI and LIC
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
NABARD, LIC, GIC, UTI and SIDCs
NHB, SIDBI, IFCI, TFCI and SFCs
79.x: The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.
79.tq: Start with the sure institutional names and eliminate older classifications.
xs: The **5** RBI-regulated and supervised **AIFIs** are **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI** and (since **2022**) **NaBFID** — option **(2)**.
**LIC, GIC, UTI** are investment institutions; **SFCs, SIDCs** are state-level FIs; **IFCI** is now an NBFC.
xa: Older notes list only the first **four**.
⚠ APPSC GS **2024** ("out of **17** AIFIs") keyed **9** — the notes do not explain that count.
**NaBFID** (**2021**) is the newest DFI.

79.s: Which of the following institutions was NOT included among the institutions helped to be set up by the Reserve Bank of India?
79.x: The RBI helped set up IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB. SEBI is not included in this list.
79.tq: Find the institution outside the RBI-promoted development-finance group.
xs: **SEBI** was not set up by the RBI — option **(1)**.
The **RBI-promoted** institutions: **IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB**.
xa: Their ownership has since **moved to the Government**.
**NHB** was wholly RBI-owned until **2019**.
SEBI regulates securities markets and became **statutory** in **1992**.

79.s: Which development finance institution was the first DFI in India and was established for long-term industrial finance?
79.x: IFCI, established in 1948, was the first development finance institution and provided long-term industrial finance.
79.tq: Link the institutional first and its distinctive purpose.
xs: **IFCI** (**July 1948**, special Act) was **India's first DFI**, for long-term industrial credit — option **(1)**.
**IDBI** came in **1964**, **EXIM Bank** in **1982**, **SIDBI** in **1990**.
xa: Exam angle: IFCI's setting up **began the era of development financing** (APPSC GS **2018**).
It gave long-term project loans (**25 years+**).
Today IFCI is a **public sector NBFC-ND-SI** that manages **PLI** projects.
FIRST/LAST: IFCI first (**1948**); **NaBFID** newest (**2021**).

79.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Institution)
a. ICICI
b. IDBI
c. Exim Bank
d. SIDBI
List-II (Primary purpose)
i. MSME finance
ii. Export-import finance
iii. Private-sector industrial credit
iv. Apex industrial development banking
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: ICICI provided private-sector industrial credit, IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank financed export-import activity, and SIDBI focused on MSME finance.
79.tq: Start from the distinctive export-import and MSME purposes to fix the code.
xs: **ICICI** = industrial credit, **IDBI** = apex industrial DFI, **EXIM Bank** = export-import finance, **SIDBI** = MSME finance: **a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i**, option **(1)**.
The other codes misassign each institution's role.
xa: Years: **ICICI 1955**, **IDBI 1964**, **EXIM Bank January 1982**, **SIDBI 1990**.
ICICI was set up on a **World Bank** initiative.
SIDBI began as an **IDBI subsidiary**.

79.s:
With reference to NABARD, consider the following statements:
1. It was established under an Act of 1981.
2. It supervises Regional Rural Banks and cooperative institutions.
3. It took over the RBI’s agricultural-credit functions and the refinance portfolio of ARDC.
4. It was established primarily for housing finance refinance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
79.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Housing finance refinance is the purpose of NHB, not NABARD; therefore statement 4 is false.
79.tq: Identify the institution-swapped purpose in the fourth statement.
xs: Statements 1-3 are correct: **NABARD Act 1981**; it **supervises RRBs and cooperative banks**; it took over **RBI's agricultural-credit functions** and **ARDC's refinance portfolio**.
Statement 4 is wrong: housing refinance is **NHB**'s role — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: NABARD runs the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** (pilot **1992**).
It manages **RIDF** plus funds like **LTIF**, **MIF**.
Quasi-regulator for **RRBs/cooperatives**.

79.s:
With reference to housing finance companies, consider the following statements:
1. Regulation of HFCs moved from NHB to RBI under the Finance Act, 2019.
2. NHB continues to exercise supervision and provide refinance.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
79.x: Both statements are correct. RBI assumed regulation of HFCs under the Finance Act, 2019, while NHB retained supervision and refinance functions.
79.tq: Separate regulation from supervision and refinance functions.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **HFC regulation moved from NHB to RBI** (**Finance Act 2019**).
Statement 2 is correct: **NHB** keeps **supervision and refinance** — so **both 1 and 2**, option **(3)**.
xa: ⚠ Older notes still list NHB as the regulator.
**90 HFCs** registered (**June 2025**).
HFC minimum **NOF**: **₹20 crore**.

79.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the RMBS Development Company Limited (RDCL):
1. The Reserve Bank of India granted it a Certificate of Registration in January 2025.
2. NHB contributed equity to it.
3. It is intended to develop the residential mortgage-backed securities market.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
79.x: All three statements are correct. RDCL received RBI registration in January 2025, had equity participation from NHB and was created to deepen the residential mortgage-backed securities market.
79.tq: Treat the date, institutional participation and objective as separate checks.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: RBI gave **RDCL** its **Certificate of Registration** in **Jan 2025**.
Statement 2 is correct: **NHB contributed equity**.
Statement 3 is correct: it aims to deepen the **residential mortgage-backed securities** market — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: RMBS **PTCs** are listed on **NSE**.
APPSC GS **2024** PYQ: **both** statements on RDCL **correct**.
NHB launched **RESIDEX (2007)**.

79.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the National Housing Bank is correct?
o: It was wholly owned by SEBI until 2019.
It was wholly owned by the RBI until the Centre took it over in 2019.
It was established in 1982 to take over agricultural credit functions.
It has always been owned exclusively by private banks.
79.x: NHB was established in 1988 and remained wholly RBI-owned until ownership was taken over by the Central Government in 2019.
79.tq: Combine ownership history with the correct institutional timeline.
xs: **NHB** was **wholly RBI-owned** until the **Centre took it over in 2019** — option **(2)**.
NHB was set up in **1988** for housing — **1982** + agricultural credit is **NABARD**.
xa: NHB Act **1987**; apex housing finance body; **C. Rangarajan** high-level group.
HFC **regulation** also moved to **RBI** in **2019**.
NHB launched **RESIDEX** in **2007**.

79.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding institutions and their years of establishment:

List-I (Institution)
a. LIC
b. UTI
c. GIC
 d. CRISIL

List-II (Year)
i. 1956
ii. 1964
iii. 1972
iv. 1987

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: LIC was established in 1956, UTI in 1964, GIC in 1972 and CRISIL in 1987.
79.tq: Start from the sure year-institution pairs and eliminate the remaining codes.
xs: ⚠ UPSC notes give GIC as **1971** — the year the Government took over management of general insurers.
xa: **ICRA 1991**; **CARE Ratings 1993**.
LIC, UTI, GIC = public sector **investment institutions**.

79.s: LIC, UTI and GIC were collectively regarded as the:
79.x: LIC, UTI and GIC were the public-sector investment institutions.
79.tq: Identify the common classification shared by three institutions.
xs: **LIC, UTI and GIC** were the **public sector investment institutions** — option **(2)**.
Refinance institutions are **NABARD, NHB, SIDBI**; regulators include **SEBI, IRDAI**; credit-rating bodies are **CRISIL, ICRA, CARE**.
xa: Older classes: **specialised FIs** (**RCTC**, **TFCI**), **state-level FIs** (**SFCs**, **SIDCs**).

79.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly describes the principal business test for registration as an NBFC?
o: Financial assets exceed 50% of total assets and financial income exceeds 50% of gross income
Financial assets exceed 50% of total assets and financial income exceeds 25% of gross income
Financial assets and financial income must each exceed 75%
Financial assets exceed 25% of total assets and financial income exceeds 50% of gross income
79.x: An NBFC satisfies the 50-50 test when financial assets constitute more than 50% of total assets and financial income constitutes more than 50% of gross income.
79.tq: Apply the exact numerical threshold rather than confusing the two parts of the 50-50 test.
xs: **Principal business (50-50) test**: **financial assets >50%** of total assets **and** **financial income >50%** of gross income — option **(1)**.
**75%** belongs to the **NBFC-MFI** rule (microfinance loans' share of assets), not this test.
xa: NBFCs are registered under the **Companies Act**.
**NBFC-MFI**: non-deposit-taking; at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans.
Microfinance loan (RBI, **March 2022**): household income up to **₹3 lakh**/yr; repayment **≤50%** of income.

79.s: NBFCs in India are registered under which of the following laws?
79.x: An NBFC is registered under the Companies Act, although it is regulated by the Reserve Bank for the activities covered by the applicable regulatory framework.
79.tq: Distinguish the statute of incorporation from the regulator exercising financial supervision.
xs: NBFCs are **registered under the Companies Act** — option **(3)**.
Cooperatives register under **State Cooperative Societies Acts** + the **BR Act 1949** — not NBFCs.
xa: NBFCs are regulated by the **RBI**.
Categories: AFC, Loan Co., Investment Co., IFC, **NBFC-MFI**, **CIC**, **HFC**, IDF.
**100% FDI** in NBFCs via the automatic route.

79.s:
Consider the following statements regarding NBFCs:
1. NBFCs can accept demand deposits.
2. An NBFC cannot issue cheques drawn on itself.
3. Deposits with NBFCs carry deposit-insurance cover.
4. NBFCs have no access to the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
79.x: Statement 1 is wrong: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits. Statement 2 is correct: an NBFC cannot issue cheques drawn on itself. Statement 3 is wrong: NBFC deposits carry no deposit-insurance cover. Statement 4 is correct: NBFCs have no access to the RBI's LAF. So only 2 and 4 are correct; options A, C and D each include at least one false statement.
79.tq: NBFC = no demand deposits, no cheques, no payment system, no DICGC cover, no LAF - any statement giving an NBFC a bank privilege is false.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: NBFCs take **no demand deposits**.
Statement 2 is correct: an NBFC **cannot issue cheques on itself**.
Statement 3 is wrong: NBFC deposits have **no DICGC deposit-insurance cover**.
Statement 4 is correct: NBFCs have **no access to RBI's LAF** (repo) — so **2 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: NBFCs are **not part of the payment and settlement system** (LENSD, **Aug 2026**).
NBFCs keep **no CRR**; deposit-taking NBFCs keep **liquid assets** instead.
NBFCs are registered under the **Companies Act**.

79.s: Which one of the following is NOT an NBFC category listed in the regulatory classification?
79.x: AFC, Loan Company, Investment Company, IFC, NBFC-MFI, CIC, HFC and IDF are listed NBFC categories. ‘Regional Rural Banking Company’ is not one of them.
79.tq: Find the invented-looking category that does not belong to the recognised list.
xs: "**Regional Rural Banking Company**" is not an NBFC category — option **(2)**.
Listed categories: AFC, Loan Co., Investment Co., **IFC**, **NBFC-MFI**, **CIC**, **HFC**, IDF — so **CIC**, **IFC** and **HFC** are valid.
xa: **RRBs** are banks under the **RRB Act 1976**, not NBFCs.
Minimum NOF: **NBFC-MFI ₹10 crore**; **HFC ₹20 crore**.
Under SBR, **HFCs, IFCs, CICs** sit in the **Middle Layer**.

79.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to minimum net owned fund?
1. NBFC-MFI — ₹10 crore
2. NBFC-ICC — ₹10 crore
3. HFC — ₹20 crore
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: The minimum net owned funds are ₹10 crore for NBFC-MFI, ₹10 crore for general NBFC-ICC and ₹20 crore for HFCs.
79.tq: Compare category-specific thresholds and select the complete set of correctly matched figures.
xs: **NBFC-MFI ₹10 crore**, **NBFC-ICC ₹10 crore**, **HFC ₹20 crore** — all three correct: **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
The NBFC-MFI figure follows the APPSC GS **2023** key (as on **March 2022**).
xa: NBFC-ICC NOF was raised from **₹2 crore** under **SBR**, with a glide path to **Mar 2027**.
**NBFC-MFI**: at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans.
HFC regulation moved from **NHB** to **RBI** in **2019**.

79.s: Which statement correctly describes reserve requirements for banks and NBFCs?
o: Banks must maintain both CRR and SLR; NBFCs do not maintain CRR, while deposit-taking NBFCs maintain liquid assets instead.
Banks maintain neither CRR nor SLR; NBFCs maintain both.
Banks maintain only CRR; all NBFCs maintain both CRR and SLR.
Both banks and NBFCs are exempt from reserve and liquid-asset requirements.
79.x: Banks must maintain CRR and SLR. NBFCs do not maintain CRR, while deposit-taking NBFCs maintain liquid assets instead.
79.tq: Separate the mandatory reserve requirement from the alternative liquid-asset requirement.
xs: **Banks** must keep **both CRR and SLR**; **NBFCs** keep **no CRR**, and **deposit-taking NBFCs** keep **liquid assets** instead — option **(1)**.
So neither "banks exempt" nor "NBFCs keep both" is right.
xa: NBFCs have **no RBI LAF (repo)** access.
NBFCs are **not covered** by deposit insurance (**DICGC**).
All deposit-taking NBFCs fall in the SBR **Middle Layer**.

79.s: Under the Scale-Based Regulation framework, which is the correct order of the four NBFC layers from lower to higher regulatory intensity?
79.x: The four layers are Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and Top Layer, with regulation increasing across the framework.
79.tq: Arrange the regulatory layers in their stated progression from base to top.
xs: SBR layers in rising regulation: **Base (BL) → Middle (ML) → Upper (UL) → Top (TL)** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) gives the reverse order; options (1) and (2) mix up Middle and Upper.
xa: **Base**: small non-deposit NBFCs; **Middle**: all deposit-taking NBFCs, HFCs, IFCs, CICs.
**Upper**: identified by RBI; bank-like norms for at least **5 years**; **listing within 3 years**.
**Top**: kept empty — only for a sharp rise in **systemic risk**.

79.s: The Top Layer under Scale-Based Regulation is intended to be used when:
o: there is a sharp rise in systemic risk
79.x: The Top Layer is kept empty in normal circumstances and is intended for a sharp rise in systemic risk.
79.tq: Apply the exceptional-use condition to identify when the otherwise empty layer becomes relevant.
xs: The **Top Layer** is kept **empty** — used only for a **sharp rise in systemic risk** — option **(1)**.
It has nothing to do with HFC supervision, the **50-50 test** or deposits.
xa: Layers: **Base → Middle → Upper → Top**.
**Upper Layer**: bank-like norms for at least **5 years**; listing within **3 years**.
NBFC-UL list **2026-27**: **17 companies**, incl. **Tata Sons**.

79.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Upper Layer is correct?
o: It is reserved exclusively for cooperative banks.
It is identified by the RBI, follows bank-like norms for at least five years and requires listing within three years.
It consists only of small non-deposit NBFCs and has no listing requirement.
It is automatically assigned to every NBFC with foreign investment.
79.x: The RBI identifies entities in the Upper Layer. They are subject to bank-like norms for at least five years and must list within three years.
79.tq: Combine the authority, duration and listing requirements without swapping the regulatory layer.
xs: The **Upper Layer** is **identified by RBI**, follows **bank-like norms** for at least **five (5) years** and requires **listing within three (3) years** — option **(2)**.
Small non-deposit NBFCs form the **Base** layer; cooperative banks are not in SBR.
xa: NBFC-UL list **2026-27**: **17 companies** (earlier **15** as of **Apr 2026**), incl. **Tata Sons**.
Proposed: a single **₹1 lakh crore** asset test for UL instead of the **parametric scoring model**.
RBI rejected **Tata Sons**' bid to surrender its licence and asked it to **list**.

79.s: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was subsequently merged into:
79.x: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was merged into the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021.
79.tq: Arrange the institutional schemes by identifying the later integrated framework.
xs: The **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** merged into the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021** — option **(4)**.
**RB-IOS** is an RBI scheme, not a SEBI or other scheme.
xa: RB-IOS now also covers **state and central cooperative banks**.
**RBI** regulates **NBFCs** and **HFCs**.

79.s: In September 2018, the default of which entity set off a liquidity crisis in India?
o: National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development
79.x: Defaults by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited (IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.
79.tq: Use the date-event association to distinguish the two major NBFC stress episodes.
xs: **IL&FS** (**Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services**) defaults in **Sep 2018** set off a **liquidity crisis** — option **(3)**.
**DHFL** was a **2019** episode; **Tata Sons** and **NaBFID** had no such default.
xa: IL&FS was an **infrastructure NBFC**.
Govt **superseded the board** (**NCLT** order); the new board handled asset sales.
Response: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.

79.s: With reference to the IL&FS episode, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: The RBI acquired IL&FS under the special FSP rules of the IBC.
The company was resolved through the Malegam Committee.
The Government superseded its board through an NCLT order.
79.x: Following the IL&FS defaults, the Government superseded its board through an order of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
79.tq: Apply the wrong-authority and wrong-event trap to separate IL&FS from DHFL.
xs: After the IL&FS defaults, the **Government superseded its board** through an **NCLT order** — option **(4)**.
The **special FSP rules** and **Piramal (2021)** belong to **DHFL**; the **Malegam Committee** dealt with microfinance.
xa: IL&FS defaults (**Sep 2018**) caused a liquidity crisis.
The new board handled **asset sales**.
⚠ **DHFL (2019)** was the **first financial services company resolved under IBC**.

79.s: Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) is significant in the history of financial-sector resolution because it was:
o: The first NBFC-UL required to list on a stock exchange
The first DFI established in India
The first financial services company resolved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
The first NBFC to be regulated under the SBR framework
79.x: DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, using the special FSP rules made under Section 227; Piramal acquired it in 2021. The first DFI was IFCI (1948), and listing within 3 years is a later Upper Layer rule under SBR.
79.tq: Test the distinctive first associated with DHFL rather than its acquirer or year of acquisition.
xs: **DHFL (2019)** was the **first financial services company resolved under the IBC** — option **(3)**.
The first DFI was **IFCI (1948)**; listing within **3 years** is an SBR **Upper Layer** rule.
xa: It used **special FSP rules** under **Sec 227**.
It was acquired by **Piramal (2021)**.
Response to such stress: the **SBR framework**.

79.s: Which one of the following companies was specifically included in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27?
79.x: Tata Sons was included among the 17 companies named in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27.
79.tq: Identify the company from the list while separating it from regulators and development institutions.
xs: **Tata Sons** is on the **NBFC-UL list 2026-27** (**17 companies**) — option **(1)**.
**NHB** and **NABARD** are AIFIs; **SEBI** is a regulator.
xa: The list grew from **15** (**Apr 2026**) to **17**.
RBI **rejected** Tata Sons' bid to surrender its NBFC licence and asked it to **list**.
UL entities must list **within 3 years**.

79.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.
List-I (Tier)
 a. State, short-term
 b. District, short-term
 c. Village, short-term
 d. Village, long-term
List-II (Institution)
 i. Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Bank
 ii. State Cooperative Bank
 iii. District Central Cooperative Bank
 iv. Primary Agricultural Credit Society
79.x: The correct matching is State–StCB, District–DCCB, Village short-term–PACS and Village long-term–PCARDB.
79.tq: Start from the state and district institutional pairs, then place the two village-level entities.
xs: State short-term = **StCB**, district = **DCCB**, village short-term = **PACS**, village long-term = **Primary Cooperative ARDB**: **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i**, option **(1)**.
Rural short-term **3-tier**: **PACS** (village) → **DCCB** (district) → **StCB** (state).
xa: Long-term structure at state level: **State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Bank**.
AP: apex **APCOB** (**18** branches), **13 DCCBs** (**436** branches), **2,024 PACS**.
⚠ **2,037** PACS in AP are computerised under the **CSS**.

79.s: Which statement correctly describes the regulatory position of StCBs, DCCBs and PACS?
o: NABARD licenses all three and RBI only audits them.
StCBs and DCCBs are licensed by RBI and inspected by NABARD, whereas PACS are under State Registrars.
PACS are licensed by RBI and StCBs are controlled by State Registrars.
All three are licensed and inspected exclusively by RBI.
79.x: StCBs and DCCBs are licensed by RBI and inspected by NABARD. PACS fall under the jurisdiction of State Registrars.
79.tq: Separate licensing, inspection and state-registration functions among the three institutions.
xs: **StCBs and DCCBs** are **licensed by RBI** and **inspected by NABARD**; **PACS** are under **State Registrars** — option **(2)**.
No single body licenses all three.
xa: **NABARD** is the quasi-regulator for **RRBs/cooperatives**.
**RB-IOS** covers **state and central cooperative banks**.
RBI in-principle nod to NABARD's **Sahakar Sarathi** for rural cooperative banks.

79.s: Urban Cooperative Banks traditionally operated under which form of dual control?
o: State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and RBI
79.x: UCBs traditionally faced dual control by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and the RBI.
79.tq: Identify the two authorities sharing cooperative and banking oversight.
xs: **UCBs** were under **dual control** of the **State RCS** and **RBI** — option **(3)**.
NABARD, IRDAI, SEBI have no such role over UCBs.
xa: **BR (Amendment) Act 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** crisis) put UCBs under RBI supervision like commercial banks.
**NUCFDC** is the UCB umbrella body.

79.s: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 relating to UCBs was enacted after which event mentioned in the framework?
79.x: The amendment strengthening RBI supervision over UCBs followed the PMC Bank crisis.
79.tq: Link the legislative response with the specific banking event rather than a general financial crisis.
xs: The **BR (Amendment) Act 2020** came after the **PMC Bank crisis** — option **(1)**.
**IL&FS** was an NBFC episode (**2018**) and led to the **SBR** framework instead.
xa: It covers **UCBs and multi-state cooperative banks**.
RBI now supervises their **management, capital, audit and resolution**.
**NUCFDC** = UCB umbrella body.

79.s: What change in the licensing policy for Urban Cooperative Banks was indicated by the RBI?
o: Licensing restricted to multi-state cooperative banks only
Resumption of licensing on tap after a pause of more than two decades
Licensing transferred entirely to State Registrars
Permanent prohibition on new UCB licences
79.x: The RBI indicated that it would resume licensing UCBs on tap after a pause of more than two decades.
79.tq: Use the policy-action and time-duration combination to identify the correct statement.
xs: RBI is **resuming licensing UCBs "on tap"** after **more than two decades** (**20+** years) — option **(2)**.
Licensing is not banned or handed to State Registrars.
xa: There are **1,457 UCBs** (**TH, 6 Aug 2026**).
UCB licensing resumed in **Aug 2026**.
UCBs earlier faced **dual control** (State RCS + RBI).

79.s: Which institution was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks?
79.x: NUCFDC was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks.
79.tq: Match the institutional acronym with its sector rather than with rural cooperative banking.
xs: **NUCFDC** is the **umbrella body** for **UCBs** — option **(1)**.
**NHB** is a housing DFI; **APCOB** is AP's apex cooperative bank.
xa: **Sahakar Sarathi** (NABARD) is a shared-services entity for **rural** cooperative banks.
RBI is resuming UCB licensing **on tap**.

79.s: Which of the following activities is NOT permitted to Payments Banks?
o: Accepting deposits within the permitted framework
79.x: Payments Banks cannot lend. Their role includes deposits and payment services, but not credit provision.
79.tq: Find the prohibited activity among functions of a specialised bank.
xs: **Payments banks cannot lend** — option **(4)**.
The notes list lending as their only bar, so the other activities are not ruled out.
xa: Other rural players: **11 Small Finance Banks**; **28 RRBs**.
SCB rural branches: **56,193** (**July 2025**).
First meeting of RBI's **Payments Regulatory Board**: **Jan 2026**.

79.s: The group-lending idea associated with the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme is derived from the model of:
o: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh founded by Muhammad Yunus
79.x: The group-lending idea is associated with Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
79.tq: Identify the source institution and associated personality.
xs: The group-lending idea came from **Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank** (**Bangladesh**) — option **(2)**.
**Malegam**, **RIDF** and the **AP MFI Ordinance** came later and deal with regulation/funding, not the idea.
xa: **SHG-Bank Linkage**: NABARD pilot, **1992**.
**JLGs** (NABARD, **2006**): **4-10** members giving a mutual loan guarantee.
Microfinance borrowers: **95% women**, **80% rural**.

79.s: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by which law?
79.x: RRBs were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976. The BR Act 1949 is the general banking law, the NABARD Act 1981 created NABARD (which supervises RRBs), and the 1912 Act concerns cooperatives.
79.tq: RRBs: 1975-76, RRB Act 1976.
xs: **Regional Rural Banks** (set up **1975-76**) are governed by the **RRB Act 1976** — option **(3)**.
The **NABARD Act 1981** created **NABARD**, which **supervises** RRBs — it is not the RRBs' own law.
xa: Now **28 RRBs**, **22,000+** branches in **700** districts.
NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs**.
AP's four RRBs merged into **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank**.

79.s: The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, described as the world's largest microfinance movement, was launched as a pilot by NABARD in:
79.x: NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme as a pilot in 1992. 1982 is NABARD's own establishment, 2006 is the JLG scheme, and 2010 is the AP microfinance crisis.
79.tq: SHG-BLP pilot: NABARD, 1992.
xs: **NABARD** launched the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** as a pilot in **1992** — option **(2)**.
**1982** is NABARD's founding; **2006** the **JLG** scheme; **2010** the **AP microfinance crisis**.
xa: It is the **world's largest microfinance movement**.
Banks lend directly to **SHGs** of mostly women members.
Idea from **Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank**.

79.s: Which institution manages the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), funded by banks' priority-sector lending shortfalls, and refinances StCBs, RRBs and land development banks?
79.x: NABARD manages RIDF (funded by banks' PSL shortfalls), refinances StCBs, RRBs and land development banks and supervises RRBs and cooperative banks. SIDBI serves MSMEs, NHB housing finance, and RBI is the central bank, not the RIDF manager.
79.tq: RIDF = NABARD.
xs: **NABARD** manages **RIDF** (funded by banks' **PSL** shortfalls) and refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs** — option **(2)**.
**SIDBI** serves **MSMEs**, **NHB** housing; the **RBI**'s agricultural-credit functions passed to NABARD.
xa: Refinance disbursed **2024-25**: **₹3,25,497.81 crore**.
NABARD also runs **LTIF** and **MIF**.

79.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the RBI microfinance framework (March 2022) and NBFC-MFIs:
1. At least 75% of an NBFC-MFI's assets must be in microfinance loans.
2. A microfinance loan is given to a household with annual income up to ₹3 lakh.
3. Loan repayment obligations are capped at 50% of household income.
4. Microfinance loans must be backed by collateral.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
79.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: NBFC-MFIs keep at least 75% of assets in microfinance loans, the household income cap is ₹3 lakh a year and repayment is capped at 50% of income. Statement 4 is wrong: microfinance loans are collateral-free. So A omits a true statement, while C and D include the false statement 4.
79.tq: Remember 75-3-50 and 'collateral-free' - any mention of collateral in a microfinance statement is the trap.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **NBFC-MFIs** keep at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: household income up to **₹3 lakh**/yr; repayment **≤50%** of income.
Statement 4 is wrong: microfinance loans are **collateral-free** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: NBFC-MFIs are **non-deposit-taking**.
NBFC-MFI minimum NOF: **₹10 crore**.
The separate **NBFC-MFI** category came from the **Malegam Committee**.

79.s: Which of the following was NOT a major feature of the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis of 2010?
o: A rapid expansion of the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh
79.x: The crisis involved multiple lending, over-indebtedness, coercive recovery and borrower suicides; the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh collapsed rather than rapidly expanding.
79.tq: Identify the reversed trend among consequences of a financial crisis.
xs: A **rapid expansion** of AP's MFI loan book was **not** a feature — the loan book **collapsed** — option **(2)**.
The crisis did feature **multiple lending**, **over-indebtedness**, **coercive recovery** and **borrower suicides**.
xa: It led to the **AP MFI Ordinance (Oct 2010)**, later an **Act (2011)**.
RBI set up the **Malegam Committee** (**2010-11**).
This chain → today's **NBFC-MFI** regulation.

79.s:
Which of the following was provided by the Andhra Pradesh MFI Ordinance, 2010?
1. Registration of MFIs with district authorities
2. Restrictions on doorstep recovery
3. A cap on interest
4. Complete exemption of MFIs from state regulation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: The Ordinance required district registration, restricted doorstep recovery and capped interest. It did not exempt MFIs from state regulation.
79.tq: Find the false institutional consequence among otherwise correct regulatory measures.
xs: The Ordinance required **registration with district authorities**, **restricted doorstep recovery** and **capped interest** — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 4 is wrong: it tightened state regulation, not exempted MFIs.
xa: Issued **Oct 2010**; later an **Act, 2011**.
Cause: **multiple lending**, **over-indebtedness**, **coercive recovery** → borrower suicides.
**Malegam Committee**: no more than **2 MFIs per borrower**.

79.s: The Malegam Committee was constituted by the RBI primarily after the:
o: formation of the first RRB in 1975
launch of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1992
79.x: The RBI constituted the Malegam Committee in 2010–11 after the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis.
79.tq: Link a committee to the event that triggered its constitution.
xs: The **Malegam Committee** (RBI, **2010-11**) was set up after the **AP microfinance crisis (2010)** — option **(3)**.
**MFIN (2009)**, the **SHG-Bank Linkage pilot (1992)** and RRBs (**1975**) came earlier and did not prompt it.
xa: It proposed a separate **NBFC-MFI** category.
Margin and interest caps; loan-size and borrower-income limits.
No more than **2 MFIs per borrower**.

79.s: Which of the following was NOT among the proposals associated with the Malegam Committee?
o: Unlimited lending by MFIs to every borrower
Limits on loan size and borrower income
79.x: The committee proposed limits on lending, including no more than two MFIs per borrower; it did not support unlimited lending.
79.tq: Reject an extreme statement that reverses a prudential recommendation.
xs: **Unlimited lending** was **not** proposed — Malegam capped it at **2 MFIs per borrower** — option **(1)**.
It did propose **margin and interest caps**, **loan-size and borrower-income limits** and a **separate NBFC-MFI category**.
xa: Set up by RBI in **2010-11** after the **AP crisis**.
**MFIN** (set up **2009**) and **Sa-Dhan** were recognised as **SROs** by RBI in **2014**.
NBFC-MFI: at least **75%** assets in microfinance loans.

79.s: In March 2025, the largest share of the microfinance loan portfolio was held by:
79.x: In March 2025, NBFC-MFIs accounted for the largest share at 39%, followed by banks at 32%, SFBs at 16% and other NBFCs at 12%.
79.tq: Compare the listed sector shares and select the largest category.
xs: In **Mar 2025**, **NBFC-MFIs** held the largest share — **39%** — option **(2)**.
**Banks 32%**, **SFBs 16%**, other **NBFCs 12%**.
xa: Loans outstanding **fell 14%** in **FY25**.
Industry portfolio down **22%** YoY (**Dec 2025**).
Banks' MFI portfolio fell **40%** YoY to **₹65,687 crore** in **Q3 FY26** (Equifax-SIDBI).

79.s: The Microfinance Industry Network (MFIN), the association of NBFC-MFIs that was later recognised by the RBI as a self-regulatory organisation, was set up in:
79.x: MFIN was set up in 2009 (APPSC GS 2024). 2014 is when RBI recognised MFIN and Sa-Dhan as SROs, 1992 is the SHG-Bank Linkage pilot, and 2006 is NABARD's JLG scheme.
79.tq: MFIN 2009; SRO status 2014.
xs: **MFIN** was set up in **2009** (APPSC GS **2024**) — option **(3)**.
**2014** is its recognition as an **SRO**; **1992** the **SHG-Bank Linkage** pilot; **2006** NABARD's **JLG** scheme.
xa: MFIN is the association of **NBFC-MFIs**.
**Sa-Dhan** was recognised as an SRO alongside MFIN.
**NBFC-MFIs** held **39%** of microfinance loans in **Mar 2025**.

79.s: Which pair of Andhra Pradesh laws is correctly matched with its year?
o: AP Cooperative Societies Act — 1964; AP MACS Act — 1995
AP Cooperative Societies Act — 1956; AP MACS Act — 1985
AP Cooperative Societies Act — 1972; AP MACS Act — 2005
AP Cooperative Societies Act — 1964; AP MACS Act — 2000
79.x: The relevant laws are the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964 and the AP Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies Act, 1995.
79.tq: Match each law with its exact year and avoid swapping the two enactments.
xs: **AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964** and **AP MACS Act, 1995** — option **(1)**.
MACS = **Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies**.
xa: The **AP Cooperative Tribunal** (**Sec. 75**, 1964 Act) is **appellate** under the 1964 Act.
It has **original jurisdiction** under the **MACS Act**.
Cooperative societies are registered under **State Cooperative Societies Acts** + the **BR Act 1949**.

79.s: Which statement correctly describes the jurisdiction of the AP Cooperative Tribunal?
o: It has only advisory jurisdiction under both Acts.
It has original jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and appellate jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It has appellate jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It exercises jurisdiction only over Urban Cooperative Banks.
79.x: Under Section 75 of the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964, the Tribunal is appellate under that Act and has original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
79.tq: Compare the two Acts carefully because the Tribunal’s jurisdiction is reversed between them.
xs: The **AP Cooperative Tribunal** is **appellate** under the **1964 Act** and has **original jurisdiction** under the **MACS Act** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses the two roles.
xa: It is set up under **Sec. 75** of the **AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964**.
MACS Act year: **1995**.
**UCBs** are under **RBI** supervision after the **BR (Amendment) Act 2020**.

79.s:
Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank was formed through the merger of which of the following banks?
1. Andhra Pragathi Grameena Bank
2. Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas Bank
3. Chaitanya Godavari Grameena Bank
4. Saptagiri Grameena Bank
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
79.x: Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank resulted from the merger of all four listed RRBs.
79.tq: Test complete membership of a merger through an inclusive option.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank** merged all four: **Andhra Pragathi**, **AP Grameena Vikas**, **Chaitanya Godavari** and **Saptagiri** Grameena Banks — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(2)**.
So any option leaving one out is incomplete.
xa: First-year (**2025-26**) business: **₹1,36,337 crore**.
Nationally, amalgamation left **28 RRBs** with **22,000+** branches.
RRBs date from **1975-76** (**RRB Act 1976**).

79.s: Why are development financial institutions (DFIs) important in the financial system?
o: They fill the long-term finance gap that banks cannot adequately meet because of asset-liability mismatch.
They provide only short-term working capital to retail borrowers.
They replace all NBFCs in providing microfinance.
79.x: DFIs fill the long-term finance gap because banks face an asset-liability mismatch in supplying long-term finance.
79.tq: Apply the asset-liability mismatch concept to identify the role of DFIs.
xs: **DFIs** fill the **long-term finance gap** that banks cannot meet due to **asset-liability mismatch** — option **(1)**.
They do not give only short-term retail credit, replace NBFCs in microfinance, or regulate stock exchanges (that is **SEBI**).
xa: **IFCI** (**1948**) was the **first DFI**; **NaBFID** (**2021**) the newest.
IFCI gave long-term project loans (**25 years+**).
NaBFID focuses on **infrastructure** with initial capital **₹20,000 crore**.

79.s: The term ‘regulatory arbitrage’ in the context of shadow banking refers to:
o: The transfer of cooperative banks to the stock market
The allocation of all public debt to development finance institutions
The compulsory conversion of every NBFC into a bank
Using differences in regulatory treatment to conduct financial activities outside the stricter banking framework
79.x: Regulatory arbitrage describes the use of differences in regulatory treatment to conduct activities through less strictly regulated financial entities, a criticism associated with shadow banking.
79.tq: Translate the paired concept ‘shadow banking–regulatory arbitrage’ into its practical implication.
xs: **Regulatory arbitrage** = using differences in regulation to run bank-like activity **outside the stricter banking framework** — option **(4)**.
It is the main criticism of **shadow banking** (NBFCs, money-market/liquid funds).
xa: Shadow banking: **bank-like credit intermediation** outside full bank regulation.
NBFCs keep **no CRR**, have **no DICGC** cover and **no LAF** access.
RBI response: **SBR** — bank-like norms for **Upper Layer** NBFCs.

79.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Establishment of IFCI
B. Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis
C. IL&FS defaults and liquidity crisis
D. DHFL resolution under the IBC
79.x: IFCI was set up in 1948, the AP microfinance crisis came in 2010, IL&FS defaulted in September 2018, and DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, with Piramal acquiring it in 2021. So the order is A, B, C, D.
79.tq: Fix the earliest institutional milestone first and then place the two later NBFC stress episodes.
xs: **IFCI 1948** → **AP microfinance crisis 2010** → **IL&FS defaults Sep 2018** → **DHFL resolution under IBC (2019)**: **A, B, C, D**, option **(1)**.
DHFL was resolved under special FSP rules and acquired by **Piramal (2021)**.
xa: IL&FS: Govt **superseded the board** (**NCLT** order).
The AP crisis → **Ordinance (Oct 2010)** → **Malegam Committee**.
Response to NBFC stress: **SBR framework**.

79.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
79.x: DHFL was acquired by Piramal in 2021, not 2019. The other pairs correctly associate IFCI, NaBFID and IL&FS with their stated milestones.
79.tq: Check the year attached to the event rather than accepting a broadly familiar association.
xs: **DHFL — Acquired by Piramal — 2019** is wrong: **Piramal** acquired DHFL in **2021** — option **(4)**.
**2019** is DHFL's own episode — the **first financial services company resolved under IBC**.
The others are right: **IL&FS 2018**, **NaBFID 2021** (newest DFI), **IFCI 1948** (first DFI).
xa: DHFL used special **FSP rules** under **Sec 227**.
IL&FS defaults set off a **liquidity crisis** in **Sep 2018**.
FIRST/LAST: **IFCI** first DFI; **NaBFID** newest.

80.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. RBI was nationalised
B. Hilton Young Commission was appointed
C. RBI Act was passed
D. RBI started functioning

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
80.x: The correct sequence is Hilton Young Commission in 1926, RBI Act in 1934, commencement of RBI operations in 1935 and nationalisation in 1949.
80.tq: Fix the first and last events, then place the Act and commencement between them.
xs: **Hilton Young Commission** (**1926**) → **RBI Act** (**1934**) → RBI starts functioning (**1 April 1935**) → **nationalised** (**1 January 1949**): **B, C, D, A**, option **(1)**.
⚠ Nationalisation came under the Act of **1948**, effective **1949** — still the last event.
xa: **Ambedkar**'s evidence to the Commission (**1925**) shaped the RBI concept.
RBI began as a **private shareholders' bank** with Central Office at **Calcutta**; moved to **Bombay** in **1937**.
**RBI@90**: **1 April 2024**; 85th Foundation Day: **1 April 2020**.

80.s: The Central Office of the Reserve Bank of India was shifted from Calcutta to Bombay in
80.x: The RBI’s Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in 1937.
80.tq: Use a close-date chronology trap involving commencement, relocation and nationalisation.
xs: RBI's Central Office moved from **Calcutta to Bombay** in **1937** — option **(2)**.
**1935** is when RBI began (at Calcutta); **1949** is nationalisation.
xa: HQ today: **Mumbai** ("**Mint Street**"), with offices in **31** locations.
**1937** also ended **Sir Osborne Smith**'s term (**1935-37**).
Nationalised under the **RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.

80.s: The Reserve Bank of India was nationalised under the
80.x: The RBI was nationalised under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948, with effect from 1 January 1949.
80.tq: Separate the name of the enabling Act from the effective date of nationalisation.
xs: RBI was nationalised under the **RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**, effective **1 January 1949** — option **(2)**.
The **Banking Regulation Act** is a **1949** law for **banks** (licensing, SLR, audit), not RBI's nationalisation.
xa: ⚠ Act **1934** → functioning **1935** → nationalised **1949** (Act of **1948**).
**C. D. Deshmukh** (**1943-49**), the first Indian Governor, was in office at nationalisation.
RBI had started as a **private shareholders' bank**.

80.s: The seal of the Reserve Bank of India depicts
o: an elephant and a banyan tree
a lion and a palm tree
a tiger and a palm tree
80.x: The RBI seal contains a tiger and a palm tree. The tiger replaced the lion in the East India Company double-mohur design.
80.tq: Use a visual-symbol distinction involving the replaced animal.
xs: RBI's seal shows a **tiger and a palm tree** — option **(4)**.
It was based on the **East India Company double mohur** (**lion and palm tree**); the **lion** was replaced by the **tiger**.
xa: RBI started functioning on **1 April 1935**.
RBI's accounting year is **April-March** since **2020-21** (earlier July-June).
HQ nickname: "**Mint Street**".

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the governance of the Reserve Bank of India:
1. The Governor and Deputy Governors are appointed by the Government of India, with the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet approving.
2. The Governor and Deputy Governors hold office for not more than 5 years.
3. The Central Board has 21 members, and its directors hold office for 5 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
80.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Government of India appoints them, with ACC approval. Statement 2 is correct: tenure is up to 5 years. Statement 3 is wrong: the Central Board has 21 members but directors hold office for 4 years, not 5. Hence 1 and 2 only.
80.tq: 5 years is the cap for Governor/DGs; Board directors get 4.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Government of India** appoints the Governor and Deputy Governors, with **ACC** approval.
Statement 2 is correct: tenure is **not more than 5 years**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the board has **21 members**, but directors hold office for **4 years** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Government can **supersede the Board** (**Sec 30**).
**Sec 7**: Centre may give RBI directions after consulting the Governor.
Current Governor: **Sanjay Malhotra** (since **Dec 2024**).

80.s:
Which of the following combinations correctly describes the usual composition of the four Deputy Governors of the Reserve Bank of India?

1. Two from the RBI ranks
2. One commercial banker
3. One economist associated with monetary policy
4. Two representatives of State Governments
80.x: The four Deputy Governors comprise two from within the RBI, one commercial banker and one economist who heads monetary policy. State Government representatives are not part of this stated composition.
80.tq: Reject the swapped membership inserted into an otherwise familiar composition.
xs: The **four Deputy Governors**: **two from within RBI**, **one commercial banker**, **one economist** (heads monetary policy) — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
**State Government** representatives are not part of this composition.
xa: **Rohit Jain** joined in **May 2026** for **3** years, replacing **T. Rabi Sankar**.
Other DGs: **Swaminathan J**, **Poonam Gupta**, **S. C. Murmu**.
Tenure: **not more than 5 years**.

80.s: C. D. Deshmukh is associated with which of the following distinctions?
o: First Indian Governor of the RBI
First Deputy Governor from the commercial banking sector
80.x: C. D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India and served from 1943 to 1949.
80.tq: Distinguish ‘first Governor’ from ‘first Indian Governor’.
xs: **C. D. Deshmukh** (**1943-49**) was the **first Indian Governor** of the RBI — option **(2)**.
The **first Governor** was **Sir Osborne Smith** (**1935-37**).
xa: Osborne Smith **signed no Indian note** (King **Edward VIII** had abdicated).
RBI was nationalised on **1 January 1949**, during Deshmukh's term.
Current Governor: **Sanjay Malhotra** (since **Dec 2024**).

80.s: Which of the following statements regarding Sir Osborne Smith is correct?
o: He was the first Governor of the RBI and signed no Indian note
He introduced the Minimum Reserve System in 1956
He was the first Indian Governor of the RBI and signed the first Indian banknote
He was the Governor during the 2016 demonetisation
80.x: Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor of the RBI from 1935 to 1937 and signed no Indian note because King Edward VIII had abdicated.
80.tq: Combine the office-holder fact with the specific exception about note signing.
xs: **Sir Osborne Smith** (**1935-37**) was the **first Governor** and **signed no Indian note** — option **(1)**.
He signed none because **King Edward VIII** had abdicated.
The **first Indian Governor** was **C. D. Deshmukh**; the **Minimum Reserve System** came in **1956**.
xa: RBI began functioning on **1 April 1935** at **Calcutta**.
**Shaktikanta Das** (**2018-2024**) gave the "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" speech (**2020**).
The **2016** demonetisation withdrew **₹500** and **₹1,000** notes.

80.s: Who is the current Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, in office since December 2024, who also chairs the Monetary Policy Committee and the Payments Regulatory Board?
80.x: Sanjay Malhotra has been RBI Governor since December 2024 and chairs the MPC and the Payments Regulatory Board. Shaktikanta Das was Governor 2018-2024; T. Rabi Sankar was a Deputy Governor, replaced by Rohit Jain in May 2026.
80.tq: Governor since Dec 2024: Sanjay Malhotra.
xs: **Sanjay Malhotra** is Governor since **Dec 2024** and **chairs the MPC** and the **Payments Regulatory Board** — option **(2)**.
**Shaktikanta Das** was Governor **2018-2024**; **T. Rabi Sankar** and **Rohit Jain** are Deputy Governors.
xa: The **PRB** (**Oct 2025**) has **six members**, incl. **3** Government nominees; first meeting **Jan 2026**.
The **MPC** is a **six-member** statutory body that sets the **repo rate**.
Repo **5.25%** unchanged (**Aug 2026**).

80.s: Which one of the following is NOT an autonomous institute associated with the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research
Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology
80.x: NIBM, IGIDR and IDRBT are autonomous institutes. The Reserve Bank Staff College is a training college, not an autonomous institute in this classification.
80.tq: Find the item belonging to the neighbouring institutional category.
xs: The **Reserve Bank Staff College** (**Chennai**) is a **training college**, not an autonomous institute — option **(3)**.
**IGIDR**, **NIBM** and **IDRBT** are RBI's **autonomous institutes**.
xa: Other training college: **College of Agricultural Banking, Pune**.
RBI-owned presses (**BRBNMPL**): **Mysuru** and **Salboni**.

80.s: Which RBI committee deals specifically with cyber security?
80.x: The RBI's Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee deals with cyber security matters.
80.tq: Associate the specialised function with the exact committee name.
xs: The **Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee** deals with **cyber security** (APPSC **2019** PYQ) — option **(2)**.
**BFS** (**1994**) does integrated supervision; the **Bimal Jalan Committee** is the **Economic Capital Framework**; the **MPC** sets the repo rate.
xa: **Tarapore** (**2006**): roadmap to **capital account convertibility**.
**Payments Regulatory Board** replaced the **BPSS** under the **PSS Act, 2007**.
RBI issued **data-governance guidance** for banks (**Jul 2026**).

80.s: Which of the following best describes the primary objective of monetary policy formulated by the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Financing the fiscal deficit without limitation
Maintaining a fixed exchange rate under all circumstances
Maintaining price stability, while keeping growth as a secondary consideration
80.x: The RBI’s monetary policy framework gives primary importance to price stability, while also keeping growth in consideration.
80.tq: Identify the precise primary and secondary objectives instead of choosing an extreme fiscal objective.
xs: RBI's monetary policy aims at **price stability** as the **primary** goal, with **growth secondary** — option **(3)**.
RBI does not set taxes or guarantee unlimited deficit financing; **fiscal policy** is the **Finance Ministry**'s.
xa: The six-member statutory **MPC** sets the **repo rate**.
**Inflation-targeting law (2016)** gives operational independence on rates.
The Finance Ministry **sets the target with RBI**.

80.s:
With reference to the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of India, consider the following statements:
1. It is a statutory body under the RBI Act.
2. It is a six-member body.
3. It determines the repo rate as an instrument of monetary policy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: The MPC is a six-member statutory body under the RBI Act and sets the policy repo rate as part of the monetary policy framework.
80.tq: Combine legal basis, composition and function in a coded statement question.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **MPC** is **statutory** (RBI Act).
Statement 2 is correct: it has **six members**.
Statement 3 is correct: it **sets the repo rate** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: It is chaired by the Governor, **Sanjay Malhotra**.
Repo **5.25%** unchanged (**Aug 2026**).
⚠ The **Payments Regulatory Board** also has **six members**.

80.s: Under which provision of the Reserve Bank of India Act does the RBI have the sole right to issue banknotes, subject to the exception of the one-rupee note?
80.x: Section 22 of the RBI Act confers the sole right to issue banknotes on the RBI, except for the one-rupee note.
80.tq: Use the exact statutory provision to distinguish the bank-of-issue function.
xs: **Section 22** of the RBI Act gives RBI the **sole right to issue notes** except the **Re 1 (₹1) note** — option **(4)**.
**Sec 20** covers RBI's business with the **Centre**; **Sec 21/21A** with **State Governments**.
xa: The **Re 1 note** is issued by the **Government of India**, signed by the **Finance Secretary**.
**Sec. 24**: highest denomination **₹10,000**.
**Sec. 26(2)**: demonetisation power.

80.s: Which one of the following is NOT included in the currency authority function of the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Issuing banknotes except the one-rupee note
80.x: The RBI issues and manages banknotes, but coins are minted by the Government of India. The RBI does not mint coins.
80.tq: Find the activity that belongs to the Government rather than the RBI.
xs: RBI does **not mint coins** — the **Government of India** does — option **(2)**.
RBI does **issue notes** (except Re 1) and **exchanges and destroys unfit notes**.
xa: RBI only **distributes coins** as the Government's agent.
Coins can be issued up to **₹1,000** (**Coinage Act**).
**SPMCIL** mints: **Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata, Hyderabad**.

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the RBI’s role as banker, agent and adviser to governments:
1. Section 20 relates to the RBI’s business with the Central Government.
2. Sections 21 and 21A relate to State Governments.
3. The RBI manages public debt through its Public Debt Office.
4. Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts are connected with this function.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: The RBI’s government-banking function is based on Section 20 for the Centre and Sections 21 and 21A for States, and includes receipts, payments, public debt management, Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts.
80.tq: Test several provisions and functions together while avoiding a single-fact recall question.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Sec 20** — business with the **Centre**.
Statement 2 is correct: **Sec. 21/21A** — **State Governments** (by agreement).
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: **Public Debt Office**; **Ways and Means Advances**, overdrafts — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
xa: The function also covers **payments, receipts** and **G-sec operations**.
A **Public Debt Management Cell** eases the debt-vs-monetary-policy **conflict of interest**.
RBI is the **banker, agent and adviser** to Government.

80.s:
Consider the following statements about the regulatory role of the Reserve Bank of India:
1. RBI regulates payment systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
2. Housing finance companies came under RBI regulation in 2019, moving over from SEBI.
3. RBI regulates banks, NBFCs and All India Financial Institutions, but not the securities market.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
80.x: Statement 1 is correct: payment systems are regulated under the PSS Act, 2007. Statement 2 is wrong: HFCs moved to RBI in 2019 from the NHB, not SEBI. Statement 3 is correct: RBI regulates banks, NBFCs and AIFIs, while SEBI regulates the securities market. Hence 1 and 3 only; options with 2 are wrong.
80.tq: HFCs came from NHB (2019); SEBI never regulated them.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: payment systems under the **PSS Act, 2007**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **HFCs** moved to RBI in **2019** from the **NHB**, not SEBI.
Statement 3 is correct: RBI regulates **banks, NBFCs, AIFIs**; **SEBI** handles the securities market — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: NBFCs come under **Chapter IIIB** of the RBI Act.
The **Payments Regulatory Board** draws its powers from the **PSS Act**.
No bank or NBFC may open **without an RBI licence**.

80.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the roles of the RBI and the Finance Ministry in the monetary-policy framework?
o: The RBI sets all tax rates, while the Finance Ministry fixes the repo rate.
The Finance Ministry frames monetary policy, while the RBI only implements fiscal policy.
The RBI frames and implements monetary policy, while the Finance Ministry handles fiscal policy and sets the inflation target in consultation with the RBI.
Both institutions independently fix the repo rate.
80.x: The RBI frames and implements monetary policy, and the MPC fixes the repo rate. The Finance Ministry handles fiscal policy and sets the inflation target in consultation with the RBI.
80.tq: Ask which authority would perform the monetary task and which would perform the fiscal task.
xs: **RBI** frames and implements **monetary policy**; the **Finance Ministry** handles **fiscal policy** and **sets the inflation target with RBI** — option **(3)**.
The **MPC** (RBI) fixes the **repo rate** — not the Finance Ministry, and not both.
xa: Operational independence comes from the **MPC + inflation-targeting law (2016)**.
⚠ **Sec 7** lets the Centre give RBI directions after consulting the Governor — consultations in **2018** sparked the autonomy debate.
The Government can **supersede the Board** (**Sec 30**).

80.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the legal status of currency issued by the Reserve Bank of India and coins issued by the Government of India?
o: RBI notes are limited legal tender, whereas coins are unlimited legal tender
RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, whereas coins are limited legal tender
Both RBI notes and coins are limited legal tender
Neither RBI notes nor coins are legal tender unless specifically notified
80.x: Every RBI note is unlimited legal tender. Coins are limited legal tender.
80.tq: Test the distinction between two closely related legal-tender categories.
xs: Every **RBI note** is **unlimited legal tender**; **coins** are **limited legal tender** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses the two.
xa: Coins and the **Re 1 note** are issued by the **Government of India**.
Coins can be issued up to **₹1,000** (**Coinage Act**).
⚠ The **₹2,000 note** was withdrawn in **May 2023** but **remains legal tender**.

80.s:
With reference to currency and coin issuance in India, consider the following statements:
1. RBI notes are signed by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.
2. The one-rupee note is signed by the Finance Secretary.
3. The Reserve Bank of India distributes coins as an agent of the Government of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: The Governor signs RBI notes, the one-rupee note is signed by the Finance Secretary, and the RBI distributes coins on behalf of the Government of India.
80.tq: Split the options by identifying the issuer, signatory and distributing agency.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: RBI notes are **signed by the Governor**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **Re 1 note** is signed by the **Finance Secretary**.
Statement 3 is correct: RBI **distributes coins** as the **Government's agent** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Coins are **minted** by the **Government of India**.
Notes carry **17 languages**: Hindi and English on the front, a **15**-language panel on the back.
**MANI** app (RBI, **2020**) helps visually impaired users identify notes.

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Minimum Reserve System:
1. It replaced the proportional reserve system after 1956.
2. It requires a minimum reserve of ₹200 crore.
3. The gold component of the minimum reserve is ₹115 crore.
4. Once the minimum reserve is maintained, the RBI can issue currency without a statutory quantitative limit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: All four statements correctly describe the Minimum Reserve System and its reserve composition of ₹200 crore, including ₹115 crore in gold.
80.tq: Check each numerical component and the consequence of maintaining the minimum reserve.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Minimum Reserve System** replaced the **Proportional Reserve System** in **1956**.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: at least **₹200 crore** of gold and forex, of which **₹115 crore** gold.
Statement 4 is correct: beyond that floor, RBI can **issue currency without limit** — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
xa: ⚠ The system came in **1956**; the **₹200 crore** floor applied from **1957**.
Old rule: **2/5** in gold or sterling, with gold at least **₹40 crore**.

80.s: The highest denomination of currency note permitted under Section 24 of the Reserve Bank of India Act is:
80.x: Section 24 of the RBI Act permits a highest denomination of ₹10,000.
80.tq: Distinguish the statutory maximum from denominations currently in circulation.
xs: **Sec. 24** of the RBI Act allows a highest denomination of **₹10,000** — option **(4)**.
**₹1,000** is the limit for **coins** (Coinage Act).
xa: ₹10,000 note: introduced **1938** → demonetised **1946** → reintroduced **1954** → demonetised **1978**.
**Sec. 26(2)** is the demonetisation power.

80.s: The power to demonetise bank notes under the Reserve Bank of India Act is exercised under:
80.x: Section 26(2) of the RBI Act provides the power relating to demonetisation of bank notes.
80.tq: Test the precise statutory provision instead of the broader subject of currency issue.
xs: Demonetisation power lies in **Section 26(2)** of the RBI Act — option **(1)**.
**Sec. 24** sets the highest denomination; **Sec. 22(1)** of the **BR Act** licenses payments banks.
xa: ⚠ **Sec 7** = directions from Centre; **Sec 47** = surplus to Centre.

80.s: Which of the following correctly represents the denominations withdrawn from circulation during the 2016 demonetisation?
80.x: On 8 November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were demonetised.
80.tq: Discriminate between denominations associated with different demonetisation episodes.
xs: **8 Nov 2016** demonetisation withdrew **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes — option **(3)**.
**₹10,000** was demonetised in **1978**; **₹2,000** was withdrawn in **May 2023**, not demonetised.
