80.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the ₹2,000 note is correct?
o: It was never declared legal tender by the Reserve Bank of India
It was withdrawn from circulation in November 2016 and remains legal tender only for banks
It was demonetised in May 2023 and ceased to be legal tender immediately
It was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 but continues to be legal tender
80.x: The ₹2,000 note was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 but continues to have legal-tender status.
80.tq: Separate withdrawal from circulation from cancellation of legal-tender status.
xs: The **₹2,000** note was **withdrawn from circulation in May 2023** but **remains legal tender** — option **(4)**.
It was not demonetised — the **2016** move covered only **₹500** and **₹1,000**.
xa: Every RBI note is **unlimited legal tender**.
The SC upheld the 2016 demonetisation **4:1** in **2023**.

80.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to currency-note printing presses in India?

1. Currency Note Press — Nashik
2. Bank Note Press — Dewas
3. RBI-owned press — Mysuru

xs: **Currency Note Press, Nashik** and **Bank Note Press, Dewas** (SPMCIL); **Mysuru** and **Salboni** (RBI-owned **BRBNMPL**) — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India’s mints:
1. They are operated by SPMCIL.
2. They are located at Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata and Hyderabad.
3. They are owned by the Reserve Bank of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: SPMCIL operates the Government of India’s mints at Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata and Hyderabad. They are not owned by the RBI.
80.tq: Catch the ownership swap between Government mints and RBI-owned presses.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the mints are run by **SPMCIL**.

80.s: Indian currency notes carry how many languages in total?
80.x: Indian currency notes carry 17 languages in total: Hindi and English on the front and 15 scheduled languages in the language panel on the back.

Highest denomination allowed by the RBI Act is **₹10,000** (**Sec. 24**).
⚠ **15** is only the back-panel count, not the total — a common trap.

80.s: Payments banks are licensed under which provision of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949?
80.x: Payments banks are licensed under Section 22(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
80.tq: Recall the specific licensing provision and reject provisions belonging to other regulatory subjects.
xs: Payments banks are licensed under **Section 22(1)** of the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** — option **(4)**.
Example: **India Post Payments Bank (IPPB)**, licensed in **2018**.
**Section 26A** of the BR Act is the **DEA Fund** provision (unclaimed deposits), not licensing.
xa: The BR Act also governs branch opening, amalgamation, **SLR**, audit and inspection of banks.
Payments banks may open branches **without prior approval** if **25%** of new branches are in unbanked rural areas (Aug 2026).
No bank or NBFC may open without an **RBI licence**.

80.s: Non-Banking Financial Companies are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India under which chapter of the RBI Act?
80.x: NBFCs are regulated under Chapter IIIB of the Reserve Bank of India Act.
80.tq: Test the exact chapter number, a common statutory-provision trap.
xs: **NBFCs** are regulated by the RBI under **Chapter IIIB** of the **RBI Act** — option **(1)**.
Banks themselves are regulated mainly under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.
xa: No bank or **NBFC** may open without an **RBI licence**.
RBI also regulates **AIFIs**, and **HFCs** since **2019** (moved over from **NHB**).
⚠ RBI does not regulate the securities market (**SEBI**), insurance (**IRDAI**) or pensions (**PFRDA**).

80.s: The Reserve Bank Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) 2026, effective from 1 July 2026, is based on which principle?
80.x: RB-IOS 2026 follows the principle of “One Nation, One Ombudsman” and covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and payment operators.
80.tq: Identify the official slogan and distinguish it from neighbouring regulatory formulations.
xs: **RB-IOS 2026** is based on **"One Nation, One Ombudsman"** — option **(1)**.
It takes effect from **1 July 2026**.
It covers **banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs** and non-bank **payment operators**, with **no cap on dispute amount**.
xa: **MANI** (2020) is RBI's note-identification app for the visually impaired — not part of the ombudsman scheme.
RBI regulates **payment systems** under the **PSS Act, 2007**.
The **Payments Regulatory Board** (Oct 2025) is chaired by the **RBI Governor**.

80.s: Which statement correctly describes the treatment of unclaimed deposits under the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund?
o: Only deposits of exactly ten years are transferred and no claim is thereafter possible
The Fund applies exclusively to foreign-currency deposits
Deposits unclaimed for ten or more years are transferred, but the depositor’s right survives
Deposits unclaimed for less than one year are transferred and the depositor’s right ends
80.x: Under Section 26A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, unclaimed deposits of ten or more years are transferred to the DEA Fund, but the depositor’s right to claim survives.
80.tq: Separate transfer to the Fund from extinguishment of the depositor’s claim.
xs: Deposits **unclaimed for ten or more years are transferred, but the depositor's right survives** — option **(3)**.
The **DEA Fund** was set up in **2014** under **Sec. 26A** of the **Banking Regulation Act**.
Options (1) and (4) are wrong because the depositor's **right is not extinguished**; option (2) is wrong since the Fund is not limited to foreign-currency deposits.
xa: The **BR Act, 1949** also covers licensing, branch opening, amalgamation, **SLR**, audit and inspection.
Payments banks are licensed under **Sec. 22(1)** of the BR Act.
⚠ **Sec 26A BR Act** = DEA Fund; **Sec 26(2) RBI Act** = demonetisation power.

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding branch expansion by banks and certain banking institutions:
1. Banks, small finance banks and payments banks may open branches without prior approval subject to specified conditions.
2. At least 25% of new branches are required to be opened in unbanked rural areas.
3. Regional Rural Banks are excluded from this facility.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: Banks, SFBs, payments banks, LABs and RRBs may open branches without prior approval provided 25% of new branches are in unbanked rural areas. Thus, statement 3 is false.
80.tq: Locate the exclusion trap in an otherwise correct regulatory list.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **banks, SFBs, payments banks**, LABs and RRBs may open branches **without prior approval** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is correct: the condition is that **25%** of new branches be in **unbanked rural areas** (Aug 2026).
Statement 3 is wrong: **RRBs** are included in the facility, not excluded.
xa: No bank or NBFC may open without an **RBI licence**.
RBI to resume **'on tap'** licensing of **UCBs** after more than **20 years**; India has **1,457** UCBs.
Branch opening is one of the areas governed by the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

80.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Approval of bank amalgamations — Reserve Bank of India
Winding up of every bank without legal process — Reserve Bank of India
Licensing of all insurance companies — Reserve Bank of India
Conduct of monetary policy by commercial banks — Reserve Bank of India
80.x: The RBI approves amalgamations of banks and can seek the winding up of a bank. The other functions are either overstated or belong to other institutions.
80.tq: Use the authority-function pairing and reject absolute powers.
xs: **Approval of bank amalgamations — Reserve Bank of India** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
RBI can **seek** the winding up of a bank, not wind up every bank on its own — option (2) overstates it.
**Insurance** is regulated by **IRDAI**, not RBI — option (3) is wrong.
Monetary policy is run by the **RBI** through the **MPC**, not by commercial banks — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Amalgamation of banks is covered by the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.
RBI does not regulate the securities market (**SEBI**) or pensions (**PFRDA**).
The six-member statutory **MPC** sets the **repo rate**.

80.s:
Consider the following statements about the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS):
1. It was set up in 1994 under the Reserve Bank of India.
2. It provides integrated supervision of banks, financial institutions and NBFCs.
3. It derives its powers from the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
80.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: BFS was set up in 1994 under RBI for integrated supervision of banks, FIs and NBFCs. Statement 3 is wrong: it is the Payments Regulatory Board that draws powers from the PSS Act, 2007. Hence 1 and 2 only.
80.tq: BFS = 1994, integrated supervision; PSS Act 2007 belongs to the payments board.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **BFS** was set up in **1994** under the RBI — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)**.
Statement 2 is correct: it provides **integrated supervision** of **banks, FIs and NBFCs**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is the **Payments Regulatory Board** that draws its powers from the **PSS Act, 2007**.
xa: The **PRB** (Oct 2025) has **six members**, is chaired by the **RBI Governor**, and replaced the **BPSS**.
**Tarapore** committee: roadmap to **capital account convertibility** (**2006**).
An **Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee** deals with **cyber security** (APPSC **2019**).

80.s:
Consider the following statements about the Payments Regulatory Board (PRB):
1. It has six members, including three Government nominees.
2. It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
3. It replaced the BPSS and draws its powers from the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
80.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PRB has six members including 3 Government nominees. Statement 2 is wrong: it is chaired by the RBI Governor. Statement 3 is correct: it replaced the BPSS and gets its powers from the PSS Act, 2007. Hence 1 and 3 only.
80.tq: Government nominees sit on the board, but the RBI Governor chairs it.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **PRB** has **six members** including **3 Government nominees** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it is chaired by the **RBI Governor**, not the Finance Minister.
Statement 3 is correct: it replaced the **BPSS** and draws powers from the **PSS Act, 2007**.
xa: The PRB was set up in **Oct 2025**; its first meeting was in **Jan 2026**.
Current Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** chairs both the **MPC** and the PRB.
⚠ **BFS** (**1994**) = supervision of banks, FIs, NBFCs; **PRB** = payment systems.

80.s: Which of the following is NOT a source of income of the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Interest on domestic and foreign securities
Income tax collected from individual taxpayers
80.x: RBI income includes interest on securities and loans, foreign exchange gains and fees. Collection of income tax from individual taxpayers is not an RBI income source.
80.tq: Find the option belonging to a different public authority.
xs: **Income tax collected from individual taxpayers** is not RBI income — option **(4)**.
RBI earns **interest on domestic and foreign securities** and on loans to Governments and banks.
It also earns **forex gains** and **fees** — so options (1), (2) and (3) are genuine sources.
xa: Under **Section 47** of the RBI Act, net profit after provisions is paid to the **Centre**.
Surplus for **FY 2025-26**: record **₹2.86 lakh crore**, **6.7%** above FY25.
The surplus was driven by **high global interest rates** and **forex gains**.

80.s: Under which provision is the net profit of the Reserve Bank of India, after making provisions, transferred to the Central Government?
80.x: Section 47 of the RBI Act provides for transferring the net profit remaining after provisions to the Central Government.
80.tq: Match the statutory provision with the specific power or financial arrangement.
xs: Net profit after provisions goes to the Centre under **Section 47 of the RBI Act** — option **(3)**.
**Section 7** lets the Centre give RBI **directions** after consulting the Governor.
**Section 30** lets the Government **supersede the Board**.
xa: ⚠ **Sec 7** = directions; **Sec 47** = surplus; **Sec 26(2)** = demonetisation.
Record surplus for **FY 2025-26**: **₹2.86 lakh crore**, highest ever.
Earlier record: **₹2.6+ lakh crore** for **2024-25**.

80.s: The Reserve Bank of India recorded a surplus of approximately what amount for the financial year 2025–26?
80.x: The RBI recorded a surplus of ₹2.86 lakh crore for 2025–26, described as its highest-ever surplus.
80.tq: Distinguish closely spaced numerical options using the exact reported figure.
xs: RBI's surplus for **FY 2025-26** was a record **₹2.86 lakh crore** — option **(2)**.
It was **6.7%** above FY25 and the **highest ever**.
It was driven by **high global interest rates** and **forex gains**.
xa: The surplus is transferred under **Section 47** of the RBI Act.
The earlier record was **₹2.6+ lakh crore** for **2024-25**.
RBI income: interest on securities and loans, forex gains, and fees.
The **Bimal Jalan Committee** framework sets how much is kept back as the **Contingent Risk Buffer**.

80.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Contingent Risk Buffer under the revised Economic Capital Framework of the Reserve Bank of India?
o: It is maintained within a band of 7.5% to 10.5% of the balance sheet.
It is maintained within a band of 5.5% to 6.5% of the balance sheet.
It is maintained within a band of 4.5% to 7.5% of the balance sheet.
It is maintained as a fixed 4.5% of the balance sheet.
80.x: The CRB band was revised in 2025 to 4.5%–7.5% of the balance sheet. The earlier band was 5.5%–6.5%.
80.tq: Separate the revised range from the earlier range.
xs: The revised **Contingent Risk Buffer** band is **4.5% to 7.5%** of the balance sheet — option **(3)**.
The band was widened in **2025**.
The original band was **5.5-6.5%** — option (2) is the old figure.
xa: The CRB comes from the **Bimal Jalan Committee**'s **Economic Capital Framework** (**2018**).
The framework separates **realised equity** from **revaluation balances**.
Remaining net profit goes to the Centre under **Section 47**.

80.s: The Bimal Jalan Committee's Economic Capital Framework primarily sought to distinguish between which of the following?
80.x: The framework distinguished realised equity from revaluation balances and provided for a Contingent Risk Buffer.
80.tq: Identify the precise accounting distinction associated with the committee.
xs: The **Bimal Jalan Committee** framework separated **realised equity and revaluation balances** — option **(1)**.
It is the **Economic Capital Framework** (**2018**).
It also required a **Contingent Risk Buffer (CRB)**.
xa: CRB band: first **5.5-6.5%** of the balance sheet, widened to **4.5-7.5%** in **2025**.
**Tarapore** committee: roadmap to **capital account convertibility**.
Surplus left after provisions goes to the Centre under **Section 47**.

80.s: Under Section 7 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, the Central Government may give directions to the RBI in the public interest after consulting which authority?
80.x: Section 7 permits the Central Government to issue directions in the public interest after consultation with the RBI Governor.
80.tq: Identify the authority that must be consulted before the statutory direction is issued.
xs: Under **Section 7**, the Centre may direct RBI in the public interest **after consulting the RBI Governor** — option **(3)**.
Consultations under Sec 7 in **2018** set off the **autonomy debate**.
xa: **Sec 30**: the Government can **supersede** the Central Board.
The Governor and Deputy Governors are appointed by the **Government of India** (the **ACC** approves), for up to **5 years**.
⚠ **Sec 7** = directions; **Sec 47** = surplus; **Sec 26(2)** = demonetisation.

80.s: Which development gave the Reserve Bank of India operational independence in determining policy rates while retaining the statutory monetary policy framework?
o: The 2016 Monetary Policy Committee and inflation-targeting law
The 2007 Payment and Settlement Systems Act
The 2019 transfer of ownership of NHB
80.x: The MPC framework and inflation-targeting law introduced in 2016 gave the RBI operational independence on policy rates.
80.tq: Link the institutional reform to the specific year and policy arrangement.
xs: Operational independence on rates came from the **2016** **Monetary Policy Committee** and **inflation-targeting law** — option **(1)**.
The **MPC** is a six-member statutory body that sets the **repo rate**.
The **PSS Act, 2007** governs payment systems, not rate-setting; the NHB shift in **2019** was about **HFC** regulation.
xa: The **Finance Ministry** handles fiscal policy and **sets the inflation target with RBI**.
RBI's primary objective is **price stability**; growth is secondary.
The MPC is chaired by the Governor, currently **Sanjay Malhotra**.

80.s: Under which section of the RBI Act can the Central Government supersede the RBI's Central Board?
80.x: Section 30 lets the Government supersede the Central Board. Section 7 allows directions after consulting the Governor, Section 22 gives the sole right of note issue, and Section 47 covers transfer of surplus profit.
80.tq: Sec 7 directions; Sec 30 supersession.
xs: The Government can **supersede** RBI's Central Board under **Section 30** — option **(3)**.
**Section 7**: directions from the Centre after consulting the Governor.
**Section 22**: RBI's **sole right to issue notes**; **Section 47**: surplus to the Centre.
xa: The **Central Board** has **21 members**; directors hold office for **4 years**.
The Government appoints the Governor, Deputy Governors and the Board.
Demonetisation power lies in **Sec. 26(2)** of the RBI Act.

80.s: Which of the following best expresses the significance of the RBI's independence and surplus transfers?
o: They are central to fiscal-monetary coordination.
They eliminate the need for a Union Budget.
They transfer monetary policy entirely to State Governments.
80.x: RBI independence and the transfer of its surplus are important elements of fiscal-monetary coordination. They do not eliminate the Budget or public borrowing.
80.tq: Choose the balanced institutional implication and reject extreme consequences.
xs: RBI's independence and surplus transfers are **central to fiscal-monetary coordination** — option **(2)**.
They do not make the **Union Budget** or public borrowing unnecessary.
Monetary policy stays with the **RBI** (through the **MPC**), not State Governments.
xa: Surplus is paid to the Centre under **Section 47**; record **₹2.86 lakh crore** for **FY 2025-26**.
RBI manages **public debt** through the **Public Debt Office**.
A **Public Debt Management Cell** was created to ease the debt-vs-monetary-policy **conflict of interest**.

80.s: The Reserve Bank of India was established on which date?
80.x: The RBI began work on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934. It was nationalised in 1949.
80.tq: Discriminate the Act year, start date and nationalisation year.
n: The RBI Act is from 1934. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India was nationalised in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Reserve Bank of India is incorrect?
o: It became fully owned by the Government of India after nationalisation.
Its permanent headquarters is in Mumbai.
It was originally headquartered in Kolkata.
80.x: Option A is incorrect: the RBI was nationalised in 1949, not 1937. Its head office moved from Kolkata to Mumbai in 1937.
80.tq: Discriminate the year the office moved from the year of nationalisation.
n: The Reserve Bank of India was nationalised in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The original headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India was in Kolkata. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The permanent headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India are in Mumbai. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India is fully owned by the Government of India after nationalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The permanent headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India have been in Mumbai since 1937. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s:
Assertion (A): The RBI acts as the Lender of Last Resort for banks.
Reason (R): The RBI provides emergency liquidity to banks when required.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
80.x: Both are true: the RBI is the lender of last resort because it gives banks emergency liquidity when no one else will. R explains A.
80.tq: Ask whether the act explains the role.
n: The Reserve Bank of India acts as the Lender of Last Resort. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India provides emergency liquidity to banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India lends to banks when required. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Banker to Government
(b) Controller of credit
(c) Forex management
(d) Payment systems

List-II
(i) Manages foreign exchange reserves
(ii) Oversight of payment and settlement systems
(iii) Controls money and credit through monetary policy
(iv) Banking transactions and public debt management
80.x: As banker to government it handles transactions and public debt; as controller of credit it runs monetary policy. It also manages forex reserves and oversees payment systems. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
80.tq: Match each RBI role to its task.
n: The Reserve Bank of India is the banker to the Government of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India conducts banking transactions for the government. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India manages public debt. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India controls credit. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India controls money and credit through monetary policy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India manages foreign exchange reserves. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India oversees payment and settlement systems. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India is responsible for conducting monetary policy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India through the Ministry of Finance.
Statement B: Coins are issued by the Reserve Bank of India.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
80.x: A is true and B is false: the Government of India (Ministry of Finance) issues both the ₹1 note and coins. The RBI issues all other notes.
80.tq: Discriminate what the government issues from what the RBI issues.
n: The Government of India, through the Ministry of Finance, issues the ₹1 note. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Government of India issues coins. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes except the ₹1 note. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s:
Assertion (A): The Reserve Bank of India acts as the banker to banks.
Reason (R): Commercial banks keep deposits and reserves with the Reserve Bank of India.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
80.x: Both are true: the RBI is the bankers' bank because commercial banks keep their deposits and reserves with it. R explains A.
80.tq: Ask whether the practice explains the role.
n: The Reserve Bank of India is the banker to banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]
Commercial banks keep deposits and reserves with the Reserve Bank of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

80.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Reserve Bank of India issues other currency notes.
The Government of India issues coins.
The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India through the Ministry of Finance.
The Reserve Bank of India issues the ₹1 note.
80.x: Option D is incorrect: the ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India (Ministry of Finance), not the RBI. The government also issues coins.
80.tq: Discriminate what the government issues from what the RBI issues.
n: The Reserve Bank of India issues other currency notes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 10-12]

81.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the class of function of money?
1. Medium of exchange — Primary
2. Store of value — Secondary
3. Basis of credit — Contingent
4. Production of goods — Primary
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: Medium of exchange is a primary function, store of value is a secondary function and basis of credit is a contingent function. Production of goods is not a function of money.
81.tq: Classify each function and identify the deliberately inserted non-function.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3 only** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Medium of exchange** is a **primary** function; **store of value** is **secondary**; **basis of credit** is **contingent**.
Pair 4 is wrong: **production of goods is NOT a function of money** at all (APPSC **2025**).
xa: Primary functions: **medium of exchange** and **measure of value** (unit of account).
Secondary: store of value, **standard of deferred payments**, **transfer of value**.
Contingent: basis of credit, **distribution of national income**, gives **liquidity**.

81.s: Which one of the following is classified as a contingent function of money?
81.x: The contingent functions include acting as a basis of credit, distribution of national income and giving liquidity.
81.tq: Recall the less commonly tested contingent-function group.
xs: **Giving liquidity** is a **contingent** function of money — option **(2)**.
Other contingent functions: **basis of credit** and **distribution of national income**.
**Unit of account** and **medium of exchange** are **primary**; **standard of deferred payments** is **secondary**.
xa: Secondary functions: **store of value**, standard of deferred payments, **transfer of value**.
⚠ **Production of goods** is NOT a function of money — asked in APPSC **2025**.

81.s: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, placed India on which monetary standard?
81.x: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, put India on the gold standard.
81.tq: Match the enactment with the monetary standard it established.
xs: The **Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899** (**Curzon**) put India on the **gold standard** — option **(3)**.
It was passed in **1899**, after the **Paper Currency Act, 1861** had given the Government the note-issue monopoly.
xa: Note issue passed to the **RBI** in **1935**.
**Decimal coinage** came from **1 April 1957** under the **Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955**.

81.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Establishment of the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar
B. Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act
C. Introduction of decimal coinage
D. Transfer of note issue to the RBI
81.x: The correct sequence is 1773, 1899, 1935 and 1957: General Bank of Bengal and Bihar, the 1899 Act, transfer to RBI and decimal coinage.
81.tq: Fix the earliest and latest dates first, then place the two intermediate developments.
xs: The order is **A, B, D, C** — option **(1)**.
A: **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar** — **1773**; B: **Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act** — **1899**.
D: note issue to **RBI** — **1935**; C: **decimal coinage** — **1957**.
xa: **Bank of Hindostan** (**1770-1832**) was even earlier than the General Bank.
**Paper Currency Act, 1861** sits between A and B: monopoly of note issue to the Government.
Under decimal coinage, **₹1 = 100 naye paise**; "naya" was dropped in **1964**.

81.s: The monopoly of note issue was given to the Government by which enactment?
o: Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899
81.x: The Paper Currency Act, 1861, gave the Government the monopoly of note issue, replacing the earlier private and presidency-bank pattern of issuance.
81.tq: Distinguish the enactment granting note-issue monopoly from later coinage and RBI legislation.
xs: The **Paper Currency Act, 1861** gave the Government the **monopoly of note issue** — option **(2)**.
The **1899** Act put India on the **gold standard**; the **1955** amendment brought **decimal coinage**.
The **RBI Act, 1934** later led to note issue being handed to RBI in **1935**.
xa: Earlier issuers: **Bank of Hindostan** (**1770**) and **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar** (**1773**).
Before 1861, the **Presidency Banks** and currency circles issued paper currency.

81.s:
Consider the following statements about decimal coinage in India:
1. It was introduced from 1 April 1957 under the Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955.
2. Under it, one rupee was divided into 100 naye paise.
3. The word 'naya' was dropped in 1957 itself.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: decimal coinage began on 1 April 1957 under the 1955 amendment Act, with ₹1 = 100 naye paise. Statement 3 is wrong: 'naya' was dropped in 1964, not 1957. Hence 1 and 2 only.
81.tq: 1955 Act, 1957 start, 1964 'naya' dropped.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: decimal coinage began **1 April 1957** under the **Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is correct: **₹1 = 100 naye paise**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **"naya" was dropped in 1964**, not 1957.
xa: The **1899** Act (Curzon) put India on the **gold standard**.
A rupee coin is a **token coin**: its face value is above its metal value.
Coins are only **limited legal tender**.

81.s: A ₹500 note costs approximately ₹4 to produce. The difference between its face value and production cost is known as:
81.x: Seigniorage is the difference between the face value of currency and its cost of production. It represents the issuer's profit and is a source of RBI surplus.
81.tq: Apply the definition to a numerical currency-production example.
xs: The gap between face value and production cost is **seigniorage** — option **(3)**.
A **₹500** note costs about **₹4** to print; the difference is the issuer's profit.
Seigniorage is a **source of RBI surplus** (profit to central bank/government).
xa: **Token coin**: face value above metal value — not the same as seigniorage.
**Fiat money**: notes and coins with **no intrinsic value**, money by government order.
**Legal tender**: money a creditor **is legally bound to accept** (UPSC **2018**).

81.s: Which one of the following is an example of near money?
o: Currency notes held by the public
81.x: Time deposits are highly liquid assets but cannot directly be used to pay for goods and services, making them near money. Other examples include Treasury bills, bills of exchange and savings certificates.
81.tq: Distinguish directly spendable money from highly liquid but non-payment assets.
xs: **Time deposits with banks** are **near money** — option **(3)**.
Near money = **highly liquid assets** that **cannot directly pay** for things.
Currency notes, the **Digital Rupee** and rupee coins are legal tender, i.e. money itself, not near money.
xa: Other near money: **T-bills**, **bills of exchange**, bonds near redemption, **savings certificates**.
**M3** = M1 + **time deposits** with the banking system (**broad money**).
**Plastic money** (debit/credit cards) is **not legal tender**.

81.s: A rupee coin is called a token coin because:
o: Its metal value is higher than its face value.
It can be used only for token payments.
Its face value is higher than the value of the metal contained in it.
It is not issued under government authority.
81.x: A rupee coin is a token coin because its face value exceeds the value of the metal contained in it.
81.tq: Use the direction of the value comparison to distinguish token coin from intrinsic-value coin.
xs: A rupee coin is a **token coin** because its **face value is higher than the value of the metal** in it — option **(3)**.
Option (1) reverses the relation.
Coins are issued by the **Government**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Coins are **limited legal tender**; RBI notes are **unlimited**.
**Seigniorage** = face value − cost of production (e.g. **₹500** note costs about **₹4**).
The **Government** creates **coins and the ₹1 note**; RBI creates reserve money (notes).

81.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes hard money from soft money?
o: Hard money is paper backed by government bonds, whereas soft money is backed by gold.
Hard money is backed by gold or credible assets, whereas soft money is paper backed by government bonds.
Both are backed exclusively by gold reserves.
Neither is connected with the backing of currency.
81.x: Hard money is backed by gold or credible assets. Soft money refers to paper money backed by government bonds.
81.tq: Test a paired distinction by checking whether the backing has been reversed.
xs: **Hard money is backed by gold or credible assets**; **soft money is paper backed by government bonds** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) swaps the two definitions.
xa: **Bank money vs cash**: bank money = **secondary money**; cash = **high-powered money**.
**Fiat money** has **no intrinsic value**; it is money by government order.
**Digital Rupee** is legal tender under the RBI Act, amended by the **Finance Act 2022**.

81.s: Which one of the following statements about legal tender is NOT correct?
o: Every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender.
RBI notes are unlimited legal tender anywhere in India.
A creditor is legally bound to accept legal tender in settlement of a claim.
81.x: Not every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender; near money such as time deposits and Treasury bills cannot directly settle ordinary payments. RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, while coins are limited legal tender.
81.tq: Reject the sweeping statement that treats liquidity as equivalent to legal-tender status.
xs: **"Every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender"** is NOT correct — option **(2)**.
**Near money** (time deposits, T-bills) is highly liquid but **cannot directly pay** for things.
Options (1), (3) and (4) are correct: coins are **limited** legal tender; **RBI notes** are **unlimited** legal tender anywhere in India.
A creditor **is legally bound to accept** legal tender (UPSC **2018**).
xa: **Digital Rupee** = legal tender (RBI Act, amended by **Finance Act 2022**).
**Plastic money** (debit/credit cards) = **not legal tender**.

81.s: Which one of the following is NOT legal tender in India?
o: Currency notes issued by the RBI
81.x: Plastic money (debit/credit cards) is not legal tender. RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, coins are limited legal tender, and the Digital Rupee is legal tender under the RBI Act as amended by the Finance Act 2022.
81.tq: e₹ = legal tender; cards ≠ legal tender.
xs: **Debit and credit cards (plastic money)** are **not legal tender** — option **(4)**.
**RBI notes** are **unlimited legal tender** anywhere in India; **coins** are **limited legal tender**.
The **Digital Rupee (e₹)** is legal tender under the RBI Act (amended by **Finance Act 2022**).
xa: e-Rupee is a **direct liability of RBI**; UPI/wallet money is a **commercial-bank liability**.
e-Rupee pilots: **wholesale Nov 2022**, **retail Dec 2022**.
Legal tender = money a creditor **is legally bound to accept** (UPSC **2018**).

81.s: Currency in circulation includes which one of the following combinations?
o: Notes, foreign exchange assets and bankers' deposits
Notes, demand deposits and time deposits
Rupee coins, government securities and small coins
Notes, rupee coins and small coins
81.x: Currency in circulation comprises notes, rupee coins and small coins. It is held partly by the public and partly as cash in hand with banks.
81.tq: Split the aggregate into its physical currency components.
xs: Currency in circulation = **notes, rupee coins and small coins** — option **(4)**.
It equals **currency with the public + cash in hand with banks**.
Demand/time deposits and bankers' deposits are not currency; they belong to **M1/M3** or **M0** separately.
xa: **M0** = currency in circulation + **bankers' deposits with RBI** + **'other' deposits with RBI**.
Notes in circulation (May **2026**): **174 billion** notes worth over **₹42.12 lakh crore**.
That is up **~137%** from **₹17.74 lakh crore** (Nov **2016**).

81.s:
With reference to high-powered money in India, consider the following statements:
1. It is also known as reserve money and central bank money.
2. It forms the basis of credit creation.
3. Bank money is regarded as high-powered money, whereas cash is secondary money.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: High-powered money is also called reserve money, monetary base and central bank money, and it provides the basis for credit creation. Cash is high-powered money, while bank money is secondary money; therefore statement 3 is false.
81.tq: Find the reversed meaning in the statement contrasting cash and bank money.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: high-powered money is also called **reserve money**, monetary base and **central bank money** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is the **basis of credit creation**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **cash is high-powered money**; **bank money is secondary money**.
xa: M0 is the **most important money indicator for RBI**.
Formula (PYQ): **H = currency held by the public + cash reserves of banks + other deposits with RBI** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0**.

81.s:
In the uses or components approach, high-powered money comprises which of the following?
1. Currency held by the public
2. Cash in hand with banks
3. Deposits of banks with RBI
4. Other deposits with RBI
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: The uses-side composition of high-powered money includes currency held by the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with RBI and other deposits with RBI.
81.tq: Test a complete component list by checking whether any item has been omitted.
xs: All four are components — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Uses side**: **currency held by the public** + **cash reserves of banks** + **other deposits with RBI**.
Banks' cash reserves = **cash in hand** + **deposits with RBI** (statements 2 and 3).
xa: This formula was the APPSC-G2 **2025** answer.
High-powered money is also called **reserve money, base money, monetary base, central bank money**.
It is the **basis of credit creation**.

81.s:
With reference to monetary aggregates in India, consider the following statements:
1. M2 is obtained by adding post office savings bank deposits to M1.
2. M3 is obtained by adding time deposits with the banking system to M1.
3. M4 excludes National Savings Certificates from all post office deposits.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: All three statements are correct. M2 equals M1 plus post office savings bank deposits; M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with the banking system; and M4 includes all post office deposits except NSCs.
81.tq: Check each aggregate definition separately and identify the repeated exclusion of NSCs.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **M2 = M1 + post office savings bank deposits**.
Statement 2: **M3 = M1 + time deposits** with the banking system.
Statement 3: **M4 = M3 + all post office deposits** excluding **NSCs**.
xa: ⚠ M3 is built on **M1**, not on M2.
**M1** = **narrow money**, most liquid; **M3** = **broad money**, the main aggregate RBI tracks.
The M1-M4 scheme comes from the **Second Working Group on Money Supply (1977)**.

81.s:
Arrange the following monetary aggregates in descending order of liquidity:
A. M3
B. M1
C. M4
D. M2
81.x: Liquidity declines in the order M1, M2, M3 and M4. Therefore, the descending order is M1, M2, M3, M4.
81.tq: Use the stated liquidity sequence and place the most liquid aggregate first.
xs: Descending liquidity is **M1 > M2 > M3 > M4**, i.e. **B, D, A, C** — option **(1)**.
**M1** is the **most liquid** (narrow money); **M4** is the **least liquid** (broad).
xa: M1 = currency with the public + **demand deposits** + other deposits with RBI.
M3 = M1 + **time deposits** — called **aggregate monetary resources**.
Exam angle: "which is the **broadest**/**most liquid**" aggregate.

81.s: In Indian monetary statistics, M3 is also known as:
81.x: M3 is broad money and is described as aggregate monetary resources. It comprises M1 and time deposits with the banking system.
81.tq: Test the official descriptive label associated with the principal broad-money aggregate.
xs: **M3** is called **aggregate monetary resources** — option **(4)**.
It is **broad money**: **M1 + time deposits** with the banking system.
**Reserve money** is **M0**, not M3.
xa: M3 is the **main aggregate RBI tracks**.
M3 grew **12.1%** while M0 grew only **2.9%** (data to **31 Dec 2025**).
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0** = **6.21** (31 Dec 2025).

81.s: Which one of the following correctly describes M0 or reserve money?
o: M3 + all post office deposits excluding NSCs
Currency in circulation + bankers’ deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
M1 + post office savings bank deposits
Currency with the public + demand deposits + time deposits
81.x: M0, or reserve money, consists of currency in circulation, bankers’ deposits with the RBI and other deposits with the RBI. It is the monetary base.
81.tq: Distinguish the monetary base M0 from the deposit-based aggregates M1 to M4.
xs: **M0 (reserve money)** = **currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) is **M4**; option (3) is **M2**.
Option (4) ignores M0's bankers' deposits and mixes in time deposits (the M3 idea).
xa: M0 is also called **monetary base**, **base money** and **high-powered money**.
It is the **basis of credit creation** and RBI's most important money indicator.
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0**.

81.s: The present framework of monetary aggregates M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the:
o: Second Working Group on Money Supply
81.x: The monetary aggregate framework from M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the Second Working Group on Money Supply in 1977.
81.tq: Link the institutional recommendation with the year and monetary classification.
xs: M1-M4 came from the **Second Working Group on Money Supply** (**1977**) — option **(2)**.
The later **1998** group (the third) gave **NM0-NM3** and **L1-L3**.
xa: The **1998** group was chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**.
⚠ M2 = **M1** + PO savings; M3 = **M1** (not M2) + time deposits.
M4 = M3 + all post office deposits except **NSCs**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements about the RBI Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (1998):
1. It was the Second Working Group on Money Supply.
2. It was chaired by Y. V. Reddy.
3. It proposed the residency-based new monetary aggregates NM0 to NM3.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the 1998 group was the third working group; the Second Working Group (1977) gave M1-M4. Statement 2 is correct: it was chaired by Y. V. Reddy. Statement 3 is correct: it proposed NM0-NM3 (residency-based) along with L1-L3. Hence 2 and 3 only.
81.tq: Second WG 1977 = M1-M4; third WG 1998 (Reddy) = NM0-NM3.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: the **1998** group was the **third** working group; the Second (**1977**) gave **M1-M4** — so **2 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
Statement 2 is correct: it was chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**.
Statement 3 is correct: it proposed residency-based **NM0-NM3**.
xa: It also proposed liquidity aggregates **L1, L2, L3**.
NM aggregates **separate short-term from long-term deposits**.
L1-L3 add **post office deposits**, **term money/CDs** of FIs, and **public deposits of NBFCs**.

81.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the new monetary aggregates from the liquidity aggregates proposed by the RBI working group?
o: NM0–NM3 are residency-based, while L1–L3 add specified broader liquidity components.
NM0–NM3 measure fiscal deficits, while L1–L3 measure public expenditure.
NM0–NM3 are confined to equity shares, while L1–L3 cover government securities.
NM0–NM3 consist only of foreign-exchange reserves, while L1–L3 consist only of coins.
81.x: NM0–NM3 are residency-based aggregates that distinguish short-term from long-term deposits. L1–L3 broaden the coverage by adding specified post-office, financial-institution and NBFC liabilities.
81.tq: Separate the two families by their coverage and basis of compilation.
xs: **NM0-NM3 are residency-based**, while **L1-L3 add broader liquidity components** — option **(1)**.
NM aggregates **separate short-term from long-term deposits**.
L1-L3 add **post office deposits**, **term money/CDs of FIs** and **public deposits of NBFCs**.
xa: Both came from the **1998** RBI Working Group chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**.
The earlier **M1-M4** came from the **Second Working Group (1977)**.

81.s:
Which of the following are added in the broader liquidity aggregates L1–L3?
1. Post-office deposits
2. Term money and certificates of deposit of financial institutions
3. Public deposits of NBFCs
4. Gold reserves held by the RBI
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: L1–L3 add post-office deposits, term money and certificates of deposit of financial institutions, and public deposits of NBFCs. RBI gold reserves are not one of these additions.
81.tq: Find the one item outside the stated liquidity-aggregate coverage.
xs: L1-L3 add items **1, 2 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
They add **post office deposits**, **term money and CDs of FIs**, and **public deposits of NBFCs**.
**Gold reserves held by RBI** are not among these additions.
xa: They were proposed by the **1998** Working Group (**Y. V. Reddy**).
The same group gave the residency-based **NM0-NM3**.
⚠ **M4** = M3 + post office deposits except **NSCs** — different series from L1-L3.

81.s:
An increase in which of the following is likely to lower the money multiplier, other things remaining unchanged?
1. Cash reserve ratio
2. Statutory liquidity ratio
3. Currency-deposit ratio
4. Banking habit
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: A higher CRR, SLR or currency-deposit ratio lowers the money multiplier. A stronger banking habit raises the multiplier, so statement 4 is false.
81.tq: Separate variables that reduce deposit multiplication from the one that strengthens it.
xs: **1, 2 and 3 only** lower the multiplier — option **(1)**.
Higher **CRR**, higher **SLR** and higher **currency-deposit ratio (cdr)** all **lower the multiplier**.
A stronger **banking habit raises** the multiplier (UPSC **2019**), so item 4 is wrong.
xa: Formula: **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)**; rdr is driven by **CRR and SLR**.
**Cash withdrawal** raises cdr and cuts bank reserves → money supply contracts.
**Weak banking habits** (high cash preference) limit India's credit multiplier.

81.s: With a reserve requirement of 10 per cent and no leakages assumed, ₹100 of reserve money can support deposits of approximately:
81.x: With a 10 per cent reserve requirement, the simple deposit multiplier is 1/0.10, or 10. Thus, ₹100 of base money can support deposits approaching ₹1,000.
81.tq: Convert the reserve ratio into its reciprocal before selecting the expansion value.
xs: With **10%** reserves, **₹100** of base can expand deposits towards **₹1,000** — option **(3)**.
Banks keep the required reserve and lend the rest; **each loan creates a new deposit**.
xa: The fuller formula is **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)** — leakages into cash lower it.
Actual Indian multiplier: **6.21** (**31 Dec 2025**).
Higher **CRR/SLR** = lower multiplier.

81.s: The Cash Reserve Ratio was reduced by 100 basis points to what level of Net Demand and Time Liabilities, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore?
81.x: The CRR was reduced by 100 basis points to 3.0 per cent of NDTL, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore by December 2025.
81.tq: Combine the basis-point change, final ratio and liquidity-release figure without confusing percentage points.
xs: The **CRR** was cut **100 bps to 3.0 per cent** of **NDTL** — option **(2)**.
It released about **₹2.5 lakh crore** by **Dec 2025**.
xa: A lower CRR lowers rdr and so **raises the multiplier** (to **6.21**).
Recent **OMO purchases**: **₹2 lakh crore** (Dec 2025-Jan 2026).
March **2026**: ₹50,000 crore and **₹1 lakh crore** amid the **West Asia war**.

81.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the institutions responsible for the creation of the indicated forms of money?
o: Commercial banks issue currency notes; RBI creates only coins
Government creates reserve money; RBI creates all deposit money directly
RBI creates reserve money; commercial banks create deposit money through lending beyond required reserves
RBI creates coins; commercial banks issue the ₹1 note
81.x: The RBI creates reserve money through the issue of notes, while commercial banks create deposit money by lending beyond the reserves they are required to hold under CRR and SLR rules.
81.tq: Match the monetary function with the correct institutional authority.
xs: **RBI creates reserve money**; **commercial banks create deposit money through lending beyond required reserves** — option **(3)**.
The **Government** creates **coins and the ₹1 note** — so options (1) and (4) are wrong.
Option (2) is wrong: reserve money comes from **RBI** (notes), and deposit money from banks.
xa: Banks hold **CRR and SLR** and lend the rest; each loan creates a **new deposit**.
⚠ **Cash** = high-powered money; **bank money** = secondary money.

81.s: Which of the following is a likely consequence of a high preference for cash in the economy?
o: An unlimited rise in the credit multiplier
A conversion of M3 into M0
A limitation on India’s credit multiplier
81.x: Weak banking habits and a high preference for cash raise the currency-deposit ratio, limiting the credit multiplier and the expansion of deposits.
81.tq: Connect the behavioural variable—cash preference—with the banking-system outcome.
xs: High cash preference results in **a limitation on India's credit multiplier** — option **(4)**.
It reflects **weak banking habits** and raises the **cdr**, which **lowers the multiplier**.
xa: A stronger **banking habit** raises the multiplier (UPSC **2019**).
**Cash withdrawal** raises cdr + reduces reserves → money supply contracts.
Higher **CRR/SLR** also lowers the multiplier.

81.s: Which one of the following policy actions directly injects reserve money into the banking system?
o: RBI sells government securities in the open market
The public withdraws deposits as cash
RBI purchases government securities in the open market
81.x: An RBI purchase of government securities credits reserves to the banking system and injects reserve money, supporting an expansion of money supply.
81.tq: Ask whether the transaction adds or drains banking-system reserves.
xs: **RBI purchasing government securities** (**OMO purchase**) **injects reserve money** — option **(4)**.
**RBI selling G-secs** **reduces money supply** (UPSC **2012**) — option (1) is the opposite.
A higher reserve-deposit ratio and **cash withdrawal** both **lower the multiplier**.
xa: **Government borrowing from RBI** (monetisation) also injects reserve money.
OMO purchases: **₹2 lakh crore** (Dec 2025-Jan 2026); **₹1 lakh crore** (March 2026).

81.s: If cdr is the currency-deposit ratio and rdr the reserve-deposit ratio, the money multiplier (m) is given by:
81.x: The money multiplier is m = (1 + cdr)/(cdr + rdr), so a higher cdr or rdr (CRR, SLR) lowers it. The second option is its reciprocal, and the other two are not the standard formula.
81.tq: m = (1+cdr)/(cdr+rdr); with cdr = 0 it becomes 1/rdr.
xs: **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)** — option **(1)**.
**cdr** = currency-deposit ratio (preference for cash); **rdr** = reserve-deposit ratio (**CRR, SLR**-driven).
Option (2) is the reciprocal of the correct formula.
xa: In aggregate terms, the multiplier = **M3/M0**.
Higher **cdr** or **rdr** → **lower multiplier**.

81.s:
According to the Keynesian theory of liquidity preference, the demand for money arises from which of the following motives?
1. Transactions motive
2. Precautionary motive
3. Speculative motive
4. Production motive
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: Keynes identified transactions, precautionary and speculative motives for holding money. Production is not one of the three liquidity-preference motives.
81.tq: Identify the standard triad and reject the unrelated fourth item.
xs: Keynes' **liquidity preference** motives are **transactions, precautionary and speculative** — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
There is no "production motive" in Keynes' theory.
xa: **Speculative demand** varies **inversely with the interest rate**.
Some notes name only the **transaction** and **speculative** motives.
⚠ **MV = PT** = **Fisher**; **M = kPY** = Cambridge (**Marshall, Pigou**).
Inventory-theoretic demand: **Baumol** (**1952**), **Tobin** (**1956**).

81.s: If the supply of money remains fixed and the demand for money rises, what is the most likely immediate effect?
o: The price of gold becomes fixed.
The demand for money becomes zero.
81.x: With a fixed money supply, an increase in money demand raises the interest rate; a fall in money demand lowers it.
81.tq: Use the fixed-supply adjustment mechanism to determine the direction of the interest-rate change.
xs: With a **fixed money supply**, a rise in money demand **raises the interest rate** — option **(4)**.
Conversely, a **fall** in money demand **lowers** it — option (3) is that reverse case.
xa: The **value of transactions** sets money demand.
At **higher interest rates, money demanded falls**.
Fisher: **MV = PT**; Cambridge: **M = kPY** (k = **1/V**).

81.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Theory)
(a) Quantity theory
(b) Cash-balance approach
(c) Liquidity preference theory
(d) Modern quantity theory

List-II (Economist)
(i) J. M. Keynes
(ii) Irving Fisher
(iii) Milton Friedman
(iv) Marshall and Pigou

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: Irving Fisher is associated with the quantity theory, Marshall and Pigou with the Cambridge cash-balance approach, Keynes with liquidity preference, and Friedman with the modern quantity theory.
81.tq: Start from the sure economist-theory pairs and eliminate the codes that break them.
xs: The correct match is **a–ii, b–iv, c–i, d–iii** — option **(1)**.
Quantity theory (**MV = PT**) — **Irving Fisher**; cash-balance approach — **Marshall and Pigou** (Cambridge).
**Liquidity preference** — **J. M. Keynes**; **modern quantity theory** — **Milton Friedman**.
xa: Cambridge equation: **M = kPY**, where k = **1/V**.
Keynes' motives: **transactions, precautionary, speculative**.
Inventory-theoretic transactions demand: **Baumol** (**1952**), **Tobin** (**1956**).

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Irving Fisher expressed the quantity theory of money as MV = PT.
2. The Cambridge cash-balance approach may be expressed as M = kPY.
3. In the Cambridge equation, k is the reciprocal of velocity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: All three statements are correct. Fisher used MV = PT, while the Cambridge form is M = kPY, with k equal to 1/V.
81.tq: Check the equations and then verify the meaning of the coefficient k.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Irving Fisher** — **MV = PT**.
Statement 2: Cambridge cash-balance — **M = kPY** (**Marshall, Pigou**).
Statement 3: **k = 1/V**, the reciprocal of velocity.
xa: ⚠ **MV = PT** = Fisher; **M = kPY** = Cambridge — a frequent matching trap.
**Velocity** = average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a period.
**Milton Friedman** gave the **modern quantity theory**.

81.s: Velocity of money refers to
o: the average number of times a unit of currency changes hands during a period
the total quantity of currency printed by the central bank in a year
the percentage of bank deposits kept as reserves
the rate at which coins are minted by the government
81.x: Velocity is the average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a given period. A ₹10 note used twice generates ₹20 of transactions.
81.tq: Choose the precise definition instead of related monetary terms.
xs: **Velocity** is **the average number of times a unit of currency changes hands during a period** — option **(1)**.
Example: a **₹10** note used twice = **₹20** of transactions.
xa: Velocity is **higher among low-income spenders** and **in booms**.
In Fisher's **MV = PT**, V is velocity; in Cambridge **M = kPY**, k = **1/V**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements about the e-Rupee (CBDC):
1. Its wholesale pilot began in November 2022 and its retail pilot in December 2022.
2. It is a direct liability of the RBI.
3. UPI and wallet money are also direct liabilities of the RBI.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statement 1 is correct: wholesale pilot Nov 2022, retail pilot Dec 2022. Statement 2 is correct: the e-Rupee is a direct liability of the RBI. Statement 3 is wrong: UPI and wallet money are commercial-bank liabilities. Hence 1 and 2 only.
81.tq: Only the e-Rupee is RBI's liability; UPI/wallet money sits with banks.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **wholesale pilot Nov 2022**, **retail pilot Dec 2022** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is correct: the e-Rupee is a **direct liability of RBI**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **UPI/wallet money** are **commercial-bank liabilities**.
xa: e-Rupee had **7 million** retail users (Jan **2026**).
Features: offline payments, **programmable money for DBT**, cross-border pilot with **UAE**.
**Digital Rupee** is legal tender under the RBI Act, amended by the **Finance Act 2022**.

81.s:
Which of the following are identified as possible features or uses of the e-Rupee?
1. Offline payments
2. Programmable money for direct benefit transfer
3. Cross-border pilot with the UAE
4. Mandatory replacement of all bank deposits
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
81.x: Offline payments, programmability for DBT and a cross-border pilot with the UAE are identified features or uses. Complete mandatory replacement of bank deposits is not stated.
81.tq: Accept the three supported applications and reject the absolute replacement claim.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3 only** are e-Rupee features — option **(2)**.
**Offline payments**, **programmable money for DBT** and a **cross-border pilot with UAE** are listed.
**Mandatory replacement of all bank deposits** is not a feature.
xa: **Digital Food Currency** pilot in **Puducherry** (**2026**): usable only for nutritional food.
Pilots: **wholesale Nov 2022**; **retail Dec 2022**.
e-Rupee = **direct liability of RBI**.

81.s: Which one of the following correctly states the denominations covered by the 1978 demonetisation?
81.x: The High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978, under Morarji Desai, demonetised the ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes to curb black money. Option B (₹500, ₹1,000, ₹10,000) is how one source lists it, and option D is the 1946 episode.
81.tq: Use denomination discrimination to distinguish 1978 from 1946 and 2016.
xs: The **1978** demonetisation covered **₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000** — option **(1)**.
It was done under the **High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act**, under **Morarji Desai**, to curb **black money**.
Option (4) is the **1946** episode.
xa: ⚠ One source (APP) lists **₹500, ₹1,000, ₹10,000** for 1978 — option (2) reflects that variant.
**2016**: **₹500, ₹1,000** withdrawn; legal basis **Section 26(2)** of the RBI Act.

81.s: The demonetisation announced on 8 November 2016 primarily withdrew which notes from circulation?
81.x: The 2016 announcement withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, effective from midnight. New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were subsequently issued.
81.tq: Distinguish the withdrawn denominations from the newly issued denominations.
xs: The **8 November 2016** move withdrew **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes — option **(3)**.
New **₹500** and **₹2,000** notes were then issued.
It was effective from midnight, so some keys say **9 Nov 2016**.
xa: Objectives: **black money**, **counterfeit currency (FICN)**, corruption, **terror financing**.
**₹2,000** was withdrawn from circulation in **May 2023** but stays legal tender.
SC upheld the move **4:1** (**2023**).

81.s: The legal basis cited for the 2016 demonetisation was:
o: Section 26(2) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 10 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
81.x: The legal basis was Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, on the recommendation of the RBI’s Central Board.
81.tq: Apply the article-or-section trap by matching the power with the correct statute.
xs: The legal basis was **Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934** — option **(3)**.
It acted on the **recommendation of RBI's Central Board**.
Option (1) names the wrong Act — Sec 26(2) is in the **RBI Act**, not the BR Act.
xa: SC upheld the **2016** move by **4:1** in **2023**.
**1978** used a special law: the **High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act**.

81.s: Which one of the following statements best reflects the reported debate regarding demonetisation and black money?
o: Demonetisation eliminated all counterfeit currency within one year.
The black-money gains of demonetisation have been conclusively established and cash disappeared.
The persistence of cash proves that no notes were ever withdrawn.
The black-money gains remain unproven, while cash and fake notes continue to persist.
81.x: The reported criticism is that demonetisation's black-money gains remain unproven, while cash use and fake notes continue to persist.
81.tq: Reject absolute claims and select the balanced statement containing both reported observations.
xs: The debate: **black-money gains remain unproven**, while **cash and fake notes persist** — option **(4)**.
Notes in circulation rose **~137%** from Nov **2016** to **₹42.12 lakh crore** (May **2026**).
Fake currency is still seized ten years later (**NCRB 2024**) — so option (1) is false.
xa: **FICN** seized: **₹54.61 crore** (NCRB Crime in India **2024**).
Objectives of **2016**: black money, **FICN**, corruption, terror financing.

81.s:
Assertion (A): An increase in SLR reduces the investible loan funds of commercial banks.
Reason (R): A higher SLR locks a greater percentage of bank funds in liquid assets.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
81.x: Both are true: a higher SLR leaves banks less to lend because more of their funds are locked in liquid assets. R explains A.
81.tq: Follow higher SLR to less lending.
n: Increasing the SLR causes banks to lock a higher percentage of funds in liquid assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
Increasing the SLR reduces banks’ investible loan funds. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]

81.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) SLR maintenance
(b) CRR maintenance
(c) SLR increase
(d) SLR decrease

List-II
(i) Reserve maintained with the RBI
(ii) Frees capital for loans
(iii) Liquid assets maintained by the bank itself
(iv) Reduces investible loan funds
81.x: SLR is held by the bank itself and CRR with the RBI; raising SLR cuts loanable funds and lowering it frees them. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
81.tq: Discriminate CRR from SLR.
n: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) consists of liquid assets maintained by the bank itself. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) consists of cash reserves maintained with the RBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
SLR assets are the bank’s own holdings. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
CRR is an RBI-held reserve. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
CRR is deposited with the RBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
Increasing the SLR reduces banks’ investible loan funds. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
An SLR decrease frees up capital for loans. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
Decreasing the SLR causes banks to hold fewer funds in mandatory liquid assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]
An SLR decrease expands banks’ lending capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 61-62]

81.s: Which of the following is the most commonly used measure of broad aggregate money supply?
81.x: M3 (broad money) is the most used measure of money supply. M1 is narrow money, and M0 is reserve money.
81.tq: Discriminate M0, M1 and M3.
n: M3 is broad money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M3 is the most commonly used measure of broad aggregate money supply. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: M1 includes currency with the public.
Other deposits with RBI are included in both M1 and M3.
Time deposits with banks are included in M1 but excluded from M3.
M3 includes time deposits with banks.
81.x: Option C is incorrect: time deposits are not part of M1 but are part of M3. M1 is currency, demand deposits and other RBI deposits.
81.tq: Use M3 = M1 + time deposits.
n: Currency with the public is included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are not included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M1 consists of currency with the public. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M1 consists of other deposits with the RBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits are excluded from M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Currency with the public
(b) Demand deposits with banks
(c) Time deposits with banks
(d) Other deposits with RBI

List-II
i. Locked for a fixed period; least liquid
ii. Instant withdrawal on demand from a bank account
iii. Immediate cash in hand
iv. Balances of foreign central banks and international bodies held with the RBI
81.x: Currency is cash in hand, demand deposits can be withdrawn at once, time deposits are locked for a fixed term and least liquid, and other deposits with the RBI are balances of foreign central banks and international bodies. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
81.tq: Rank each item by liquidity.
n: Currency with the public is immediate cash in hand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Demand deposits with banks can be withdrawn instantly on demand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are locked for a fixed period. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are the least liquid deposits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are highly liquid balances. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
The liquidity order is currency, savings deposits, demand deposits, and time deposits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Cash is the most liquid form of money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Fixed or time deposits are the least liquid form of money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The money multiplier is the ratio of total money supply to base money.
II. The money multiplier is represented as M3 divided by M0.
III. An increase in CRR increases credit creation.
IV. An increase in banking habits increases the money multiplier.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: I, II and IV are correct: the money multiplier is M3 divided by M0, and more banking habit raises it. III is false because a higher CRR reduces credit creation.
81.tq: Follow how CRR affects credit.
n: The money multiplier equals total money supply divided by base money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
The money multiplier is expressed as M3 divided by M0. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
An increase in banking habits increases the money multiplier. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
An increase in the cash reserve ratio decreases credit creation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with banks.
Statement B: M3 minus M1 equals time deposits with banks.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
81.x: Both are true: M3 is M1 plus time deposits with banks, so M3 minus M1 is time deposits.
81.tq: Use M3 = M1 + time deposits.
n: M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M3 minus M1 equals time deposits with banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s:
Assertion (A): A cash withdrawal does not change the aggregate money supply.
Reason (R): On withdrawing ₹1 lakh from demand deposits, demand deposits fall by ₹1 lakh while currency with the public rises by ₹1 lakh.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
81.x: Both are true: withdrawing ₹1 lakh cuts demand deposits and raises currency with the public by the same amount, so total money supply stays the same. R explains A.
81.tq: Check that both parts are inside M1.
n: A cash withdrawal does not change the aggregate money supply. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Withdrawing ₹1 lakh from demand deposits reduces demand deposits by ₹1 lakh. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Withdrawing ₹1 lakh from demand deposits increases currency with the public by ₹1 lakh. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]

81.s:
Assertion (A): J.M. Keynes is associated with effective demand.
Reason (R): Keynesian economics is linked with the explanation of economic fluctuations.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
81.x: Both are true: Keynes is known for effective demand, and Keynesian economics explains economic ups and downs. The school's broad scope does not explain the specific idea, so R does not explain A.
81.tq: Ask whether a broad theme explains a specific idea.
n: J.M. Keynes is associated with Effective Demand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
J.M. Keynes is associated with the Keynesian explanation of economic fluctuations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Friedrich Hayek is associated with liberal or market-oriented economics.
Statement B: Milton Friedman is associated with monetarism and money supply.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
81.x: Both are true: Hayek stood for liberal, market-based economics, and Friedman for monetarism and the role of money supply.
81.tq: Match each economist to their school.
n: Friedrich Hayek is associated with Liberal economics. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Friedrich Hayek is associated with market-oriented economics. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Milton Friedman is associated with Monetarism. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Milton Friedman is associated with Money supply. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. R.G. Hawtrey is associated with the Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle.
II. J.M. Keynes is associated with the Keynesian explanation of economic fluctuations.
III. F.A. Hayek is associated with the Austrian/business-cycle approach.
IV. J.R. Hicks is associated with the IS-LM model.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: All four are correct: Hawtrey gave the monetary trade-cycle theory, Keynes explained fluctuations through demand, Hayek gave the Austrian cycle theory, and Hicks the IS-LM model.
81.tq: Match each economist to their idea.
n: R.G. Hawtrey is associated with the Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
J.M. Keynes is associated with the Keynesian explanation of economic fluctuations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Friedrich Hayek is associated with the Austrian business-cycle approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
J.R. Hicks is associated with the IS-LM model. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]

82.s:
Consider the following statements about monetary policy in India:
1. It is formulated and implemented by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934.
2. Economic growth is its paramount objective.
3. Financial stability and external balance are among its objectives.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is correct: the RBI formulates and implements monetary policy under the RBI Act, 1934. Statement 2 is wrong: price stability, not growth, is the paramount objective. Statement 3 is correct: growth, financial stability, external balance and development goals are also pursued. So '1 and 3 only' is right; '1 only' misses statement 3, and options with 2 include a false statement.
82.tq: Paramount = price stability; growth is pursued but is not paramount.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **RBI** formulates and implements monetary policy under the **RBI Act, 1934** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **price stability** (not growth) is the **paramount** objective.
Statement 3 is correct: **financial stability** and **external balance** are among its objectives, with growth and development goals.
xa: The RBI-as-authority point was asked in APPSC-GS **2023**.
Since **2016** India follows **flexible inflation targeting**.
The **MPC** sets the **policy repo rate** to hit the inflation target.

82.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the monetary policy framework followed in India during 1985–1998?
82.x: During 1985–1998, India followed monetary targeting with feedback, with M3 as the principal monetary aggregate.
82.tq: Directly identify the framework associated with the given period.
xs: During **1985-1998** India followed **monetary targeting with feedback** (using **M3**) — option **(3)**.
The **multiple indicator approach** came in **1998-2016**; **flexible inflation targeting** from **2016**.
xa: Landmarks of that phase: **Chakravarty Committee 1985**, **Vaghul Committee 1987** (money market).
Multiple-indicator landmarks: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **Base Rate 2010**, **MSF 2011**, **MCLR 2016**.
**Shaktikanta Das** traced these phases in "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" (**24 Jan 2020**).

82.s:
Arrange the following developments in the evolution of India's monetary policy in chronological order:
A. Introduction of the Marginal Standing Facility
B. Introduction of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility
C. Introduction of the Market Stabilisation Scheme
D. Introduction of the Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate
82.x: LAF was introduced in 2000, MSS in 2004, MSF in 2011 and MCLR in 2016.
82.tq: Use the known years to fix the first and last developments before ordering the middle items.
xs: The order is **B, C, A, D** — option **(1)**.
xa: **Base Rate** came in **2010**, between MSS and MSF.
**SDF** began in **April 2022**, under the FIT phase.
All four belong to the **1998-2016** multiple indicator era (MCLR at its end).

82.s: The flexible inflation-targeting framework in India is associated with which of the following sequence of developments?
o: Kelkar Committee, Fiscal Responsibility Agreement, and introduction of MSF
Urjit Patel Committee, Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, and amendment of the RBI Act
Chakravarty Committee, Vaghul Committee, and introduction of MSS
Narasimham Committee, FRBM Act, and introduction of LAF
82.x: The Urjit Patel Committee reported in 2014, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement was signed in 2015, and the RBI Act was amended in 2016.
82.tq: Link a framework to the committee, agreement and legislative milestones that established it.
xs: FIT followed the **Urjit Patel Committee** (**2014**), the **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement** (**2015**) and the **RBI Act amendment** (**2016**) — option **(2)**.
**Chakravarty** and **Vaghul** belong to the 1985-1998 monetary-targeting phase.
xa: **SDF** (**2022**) is a later landmark of the FIT phase.
Under FIT, the **repo rate** is the **single operating policy rate**.
**Price stability** is the paramount objective.

82.s: Who traced the phases of India's monetary-policy evolution in the lecture titled “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy”?
82.x: Governor Shaktikanta Das traced these phases in “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy” on 24 January 2020 at St. Stephen's College.
82.tq: Test the speaker, title and date as a linked current-affairs fact.
xs: **Shaktikanta Das** gave "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" — option **(2)**.
It was delivered on **24 Jan 2020** at **St. Stephen's College** (APPSC-GS **2024** statement).
xa: Phases: **1985-1998** monetary targeting; **1998-2016** multiple indicators; **2016** onwards FIT.
FIT came via **Urjit Patel Committee 2014**, **MPFA 2015**, RBI Act amended **2016**.

82.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of India's monetary policy:
1. The multiple indicator approach was followed during 1998–2016.
2. The flexible inflation-targeting framework began in 2016.
3. The multiple indicator approach gave primary importance only to the money supply and ignored exchange rates.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: The multiple indicator approach operated from 1998 to 2016 and considered growth, inflation, exchange rates and credit. Statement 3 is false because the framework used several indicators rather than only money supply.
82.tq: Reject the statement that incorrectly narrows a broad multi-indicator framework to a single variable.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **multiple indicator approach** ran **1998-2016** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is correct: **flexible inflation targeting** began in **2016**.
