xs: Statement 1 is correct: **accommodative** = ready to **cut rates or add liquidity** to support growth — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **withdrawal of accommodation** is a **tightening bias**, **draining excess liquidity**.
xa: **Neutral**: can move rates either way depending on the data.
The stance went neutral → **accommodative** in **April 2025**, then back to **neutral**.

83.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the recent change in the monetary-policy stance?
o: It changed from accommodative to neutral in April 2025 after a repo-rate increase.
It changed from neutral to accommodative in April 2025 after the repo rate was cut to 6 per cent, and was neutral in 2026 after the rate was held at 5.25 per cent.
It changed from tightening to withdrawal of accommodation in June 2025 after the CRR cut.
It remained accommodative throughout 2025 and 2026 despite all rate decisions.
83.x: The stance moved from neutral towards accommodative in April 2025 when the repo rate was cut to 6 per cent. It was neutral in February, June and August 2026 when the repo rate was held at 5.25 per cent.
83.tq: Track the stance change together with the relevant rate movement and later status.
xs: The stance moved **neutral to accommodative in April 2025** (repo cut to **6%**), and was **neutral in 2026** at **5.25%** — option **(2)**.
It returned to **neutral** in **Jun 2025** (ES **2025-26**).
xa: The **Apr 2025** cut of **25 bps** was the **2nd cut of 2025**.
Governor **Malhotra**: hardening inflation "may suggest a **recalibration**".

83.s:
Which of the following are recognised spillover channels through which global monetary tightening may affect India?
1. Capital outflows
2. Pressure on the rupee
3. Imported inflation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
83.x: Global monetary tightening can encourage capital outflows from India, put pressure on the rupee and raise imported inflation through exchange-rate and import-cost channels.
83.tq: Treat each transmission channel as an independent statement before choosing the combination.
xs: All three are spillover channels — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**Capital outflows**, **rupee pressure** and **imported inflation**.
xa: In **June 2026** major central banks were **gearing up to tighten**.
RBI's special **FCNR(B)** and forex measures drew about **$32 bn** after the June policy.

83.s: The failure clause under the flexible inflation targeting framework was first invoked in which year, and March 2026 represented what development in relation to the original target?
o: First invoked in 2023; second revision of the original target
First invoked in 2022; first revision of the original target
First invoked in 2022; second retention of the original target
First invoked in 2021; first retention of the original target
83.x: The failure clause was first invoked in 2022. March 2026 marked the second retention of the original inflation target.
83.tq: Use the paired year-and-sequence distinction to avoid confusing invocation, retention and revision.
xs: **First invoked in 2022**; March 2026 = **second retention of the original target** — option **(3)**.
The **25 March 2026** notification kept **4% +/- 2%** for **2026-2031**.
xa: First retention: **March 2021** (April 2021 to March 2026).
The original target was notified in **August 2016**.

83.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the debate on flexible inflation targeting:
1. After a decade of flexible inflation targeting, evidence on its effect on output and jobs remains mixed.
2. Critics argue that headline inflation should be replaced by core inflation as the target.
3. Food and supply shocks are entirely within the control of the Monetary Policy Committee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because food and supply shocks are outside the MPC's direct control; this is one reason for the criticism of headline targeting.
83.tq: Find the false statement by testing the absolute claim about the MPC's control over supply shocks.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: after a **decade of FIT**, evidence is **mixed** on output and jobs — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is correct: critics want **core inflation** instead of the **headline** target.
Statement 3 is wrong: **food and supply shocks sit outside the MPC's control**.
xa: Target **4% +/- 2%** retained to **March 2031**.
The failure clause was first invoked in **2022**.

83.s: Which one of the following correctly compares Andhra Pradesh’s retail inflation with the national rate mentioned for May 2026?
83.x: Andhra Pradesh’s CPI inflation was 4.9%, above the national rate of 3.9% mentioned for the comparison.
83.tq: Check the direction of the State-versus-national comparison before the figures.
xs: Option (1) swaps the two.
xa: AP has been **above the national rate for five months in a row**.
AP was placed on the State's "**Needs Attention**" watchlist (Jul **2026**).

84.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the first bank in India?
84.x: Bank of Hindustan is regarded as the first bank in India. The Presidency Bank of Bengal was the first bank of the East India Company.
84.tq: Use the direct first-in-the-list recall approach.
xs: The first bank in India was the **Bank of Hindustan** (**1770**) — option **(4)**.
**1770** is the standard date (one APP note says **1779**).

The **Presidency Bank of Bengal** (**1806**) was the first bank of the **East India Company**; **Oudh (Awadh) Commercial Bank** (**1881**) the first run by Indians; **PNB** the first with wholly Indian capital.
xa: First credit card: **Central Bank of India** (**1980**).
First ATM: **HSBC**, Mumbai, **1987**.

84.s: The first Presidency bank in India was established as the:
84.x: The first Presidency bank was set up in 1806 as the Bank of Calcutta (also called the Presidency Bank of Bengal) and was later renamed the Bank of Bengal. The Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843) came later.
84.tq: Distinguish the original name from the later renamed institution.
xs: The first Presidency bank was the **Bank of Calcutta** (**1806**) — option **(4)**.
It was also called the **Presidency Bank of Bengal** and renamed **Bank of Bengal**.
**Bank of Bombay** (**1840**) and **Bank of Madras** (**1843**) came later.
xa: The three Presidency banks merged into the **Imperial Bank of India** (**1921**).
Imperial Bank became **SBI** under the SBI Act, **1955**.

84.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
84.x: Awadh Commercial Bank was established at Faizabad in 1881. Andhra Bank was founded at Machilipatnam, Punjab National Bank at Lahore and Equitas Small Finance Bank has its head office at Chennai.
84.tq: Use the location filter to separate similar banking institutions.
xs: **Awadh Commercial Bank — Faizabad** is correct — option **(1)**; it was founded in **1881**.
**Andhra Bank** was founded at **Machilipatnam**, not Lahore; **PNB** at **Lahore**.
**Equitas SFB** has its head office in **Chennai**; **Jalandhar** is **Capital SFB**.
xa: Oudh Commercial Bank: **limited liability**, **all-Indian board** — first bank established by Indians.
⚠ **Allahabad Bank (1865)** is the oldest **joint-stock** bank — sometimes wrongly called the first Indian bank.

84.s: Which one of the following statements about banking in nineteenth-century Andhra is correct?
o: Several Presidency banks were established in Andhra during the nineteenth century.
The first bank in Andhra was established at Machilipatnam in 1804.
Andhra had a banking network before Madras received its first banks.
There were no banks in nineteenth-century Andhra, although banking later reached towns such as Machilipatnam.
84.x: There were no banks in nineteenth-century Andhra. Banking later reached towns such as Machilipatnam; the listed early banks in Madras included Karnataka Bank, Madras Bank and Asiatic Bank.
84.tq: Reject the absolute historical claims and identify the carefully worded regional statement.
xs: **There were no banks in nineteenth-century Andhra**; banking later reached towns such as **Machilipatnam** — option **(4)**.
Early regional banks were in **Madras**: **Karnataka Bank (1788)**, **Madras Bank (1795)**, **Asiatic Bank (1804)**.
So option (2) is wrong: **1804** is the **Asiatic Bank**, in Madras.
xa: **Andhra Bank** was founded at **Machilipatnam** on **20 Nov 1923**.
Its head office was "**Pattabhi Bhavan**".

84.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Capital Small Finance Bank — Jalandhar
2. Equitas Small Finance Bank — Chennai
3. SBI’s first overseas banking unit — Mumbai
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
84.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Capital Small Finance Bank was established at Jalandhar, Equitas Small Finance Bank has its head office at Chennai and SBI’s first overseas banking unit was located in Mumbai.
84.tq: Verify each institution-location pair independently before selecting the code.
xs: All three pairs are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**Capital SFB** — **Jalandhar** (**2016**), the first small finance bank.
**Equitas SFB** — head office **Chennai** (APPSC-GS **2024**); SBI's first **OBU** — **Mumbai** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
xa: SFBs: **11** operational (Jul **2026**).
SFB licences have been **on tap since 2019**.

84.s: The first bank with wholly Indian capital and management was:
84.x: Punjab National Bank is described as the first bank with wholly Indian capital and management. Awadh Commercial Bank was the first bank run by Indians with limited liability and an all-Indian board.
84.tq: Distinguish the broader ownership-and-management distinction from the first Indian-run bank.
xs: **Punjab National Bank** (Lahore, **1894**/95) was the first bank with **wholly Indian capital and management** — option **(1)**.
**Oudh (Awadh) Commercial Bank** (**1881**) was the first run by Indians; PNB was the **second** bank established by Indians.
⚠ **Allahabad Bank (1865)** = oldest joint-stock bank, not the standard answer.
xa: **Lala Lajpat Rai** was among PNB's founders; HQ now **New Delhi**.
**United Bank of India** and **Oriental Bank of Commerce** are now part of **PNB**.

84.s: Which one of the following was the first private bank established after the 1994 liberalisation of banking in India?
o: UTI Bank, now known as Axis Bank
84.x: UTI Bank was the first private bank established after the 1994 liberalisation of banking. It is now known as Axis Bank.
84.tq: Match the historical first with its former and present identity.
xs: **UTI Bank** (now **Axis Bank**) was the first private bank after the **1994** liberalisation — option **(3)**.
**Capital SFB** and **Equitas** are small finance banks; **Andhra Bank** dates from **1923**.
xa: First SFB: **Capital Small Finance Bank**, Jalandhar (**2016**).
Commercial banks are now licensed "**on tap**".

84.s: Which of the following institutions was NOT founded by Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya?
84.x: Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Insurance Company, Bharat Lakshmi Bank and the Krishna District Co-operative Bank. Punjab National Bank was established separately in 1894.
84.tq: Find the one institution outside the founder’s associated group.
xs: **Punjab National Bank** was NOT founded by Pattabhi Sitaramayya — option **(2)**; PNB was founded at Lahore (**1894**/95), with **Lala Lajpat Rai** among its founders.
Pattabhi founded **Andhra Insurance Co. (1925)**, **Bharat Lakshmi Bank** and **Krishna District Co-operative Bank**.
xa: He founded **Andhra Bank** (**20 Nov 1923**, **Machilipatnam**).
He was **INC President (1948-49)**.

84.s: Dr. Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was also the President of the Indian National Congress during:
84.x: Dr. Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was also INC President in 1948–49.
84.tq: Use the precise year range rather than the bank’s year of establishment.
xs: Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was **INC President** in **1948-49** — option **(2)**.
**1923** is the year he founded **Andhra Bank**, not his Congress presidency.
xa: His ventures: **Andhra Insurance Co. (1925)**, **Bharat Lakshmi Bank**, **Krishna District Co-operative Bank**.
Andhra Bank merged into **Union Bank of India** in **2020**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Allahabad Bank was established in 1865.
2. Allahabad Bank was merged into Indian Bank.
3. Canara Bank was founded by Ammembal Subba Rao Pai.
4. Canara Bank took over Syndicate Bank.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All four statements are correct. Allahabad Bank dates from 1865 and merged into Indian Bank, while Canara Bank was founded by Ammembal Subba Rao Pai and took over Syndicate Bank.
84.tq: Verify each bank’s year, merger, founder and takeover separately.
xs: All four statements are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Allahabad Bank** — **1865**, merged into **Indian Bank**.
**Canara Bank** — founded by **Ammembal Subba Rao Pai** (**1906**, Mangaluru), took over **Syndicate Bank**.
xa: Allahabad Bank is the **oldest joint-stock bank**.
Both Allahabad and Syndicate were among the **14 banks** nationalised in **1969**.

84.s: The Imperial Bank of India was formed through the merger of:
o: Punjab National Bank, Allahabad Bank and Canara Bank
The three Presidency banks and the State Bank of India
The Imperial Bank and three Regional Rural Banks
84.x: The Imperial Bank of India was formed by merging the three Presidency banks.
84.tq: Identify the constituent institutions rather than the later successor.
xs: The **Imperial Bank of India** (**1921**) was formed by merging **the three Presidency banks** — option **(1)**.
The three were the Banks of **Bengal**, **Bombay** and **Madras**.
**SBI** came later — Imperial Bank became SBI in **1955** — so option (3) is wrong.
xa: Under the **SBI Act, 1955**, RBI bought **92%** of its shares.
SBI was the **first public sector bank**.

84.s: Andhra Bank, set up at Machilipatnam in 1923, was founded by whom, and into which bank was it merged in 2020?
o: Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya; Union Bank of India
Lala Lajpat Rai; Punjab National Bank
Ammembal Subba Rao Pai; Canara Bank
84.x: Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Bank (20 Nov 1923, Machilipatnam), and it merged into Union Bank of India in 2020. Indian Bank absorbed Allahabad Bank, not Andhra Bank. Lala Lajpat Rai is linked with PNB (Lahore), and Ammembal Subba Rao Pai founded Canara Bank (Mangaluru).
84.tq: Andhra Bank: Pattabhi, Machilipatnam 1923 -> Union Bank 2020.
xs: **Andhra Bank** was founded by **Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya** and merged into **Union Bank of India** (**2020**) — option **(1)**.
**Indian Bank** absorbed **Allahabad Bank**, not Andhra Bank.
**Lala Lajpat Rai** is linked with **PNB**; **Ammembal Subba Rao Pai** founded **Canara Bank**.
xa: **Corporation Bank** (also 1980 batch) merged into **Union Bank** too.
In AP, **Union Bank of India** is the **lead bank / SLBC convener**.

84.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Nationalisation of the Reserve Bank of India
B. Conversion of the Imperial Bank into the State Bank of India
C. Nationalisation of 14 major commercial banks
D. Nationalisation of six commercial banks
84.x: The correct sequence is RBI nationalisation in 1949, SBI formation in 1955, nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969 and nationalisation of six banks in 1980.
84.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the 1955 and 1969 milestones between them.
xs: The order is **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**RBI** nationalised **1 Jan 1949**; Imperial Bank → **SBI** in **1955**.
**14 banks** nationalised **19 July 1969**; **6 banks** on **15 April 1980**.
xa: **SBI subsidiaries** came in **1959**.
The **Lead Bank Scheme** also began in **1969**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about bank nationalisation in India:
1. On 19 July 1969, 14 banks with deposits of over ₹50 crore were nationalised.
2. On 15 April 1980, 6 banks with deposits of over ₹100 crore were nationalised.
3. Both rounds took place under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the 1980 round covered banks with deposits of over ₹200 crore, not ₹100 crore. So '1 and 3 only'; the other options include statement 2 or leave out a true one.
84.tq: 1969: 14 banks, ₹50 crore; 1980: 6 banks, ₹200 crore.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **19 July 1969** — **14 banks** with deposits **over ₹50 crore** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **1980** round covered banks with deposits **over ₹200 crore**.
Statement 3 is correct: both rounds were under **Indira Gandhi**.
xa: The 1969 banks held about **85%** of deposits.
The **50th anniversary** fell on **19 July 2019**.

84.s:
Consider the following pairs relating to banks nationalised in 1969:
1. Syndicate Bank — Canara Bank
2. Allahabad Bank — Indian Bank
3. United Bank of India — Punjab National Bank
4. Dena Bank — Bank of India
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
84.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Dena Bank was merged with Bank of Baroda, not Bank of India, making pair 4 incorrect.
84.tq: Start from the sure merger pairs and identify the swapped successor in the remaining pair.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Syndicate** → **Canara**; **Allahabad** → **Indian Bank**; **United Bank of India** → **PNB**.
Pair 4 is wrong: **Dena Bank** is now part of **Bank of Baroda**, not Bank of India.
xa: Other 1969 banks: **BoB, BoI, BoM, Central, IOB, UCO, Union**.
The 1969 nationalisation took **14** banks holding about **85%** of deposits.

84.s:
Which of the following was a major motive behind bank nationalisation in India?
1. To bring credit under greater social control.
2. To shift credit towards agriculture and small industries.
3. To ensure that industrial houses retained exclusive control over bank credit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Nationalisation sought to reduce the control of industrial houses and remedy the neglect of agriculture and small units; it did not aim to preserve exclusive control by them.
84.tq: Detect the reversed objective in the third statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Motives: **social control of credit** and a **shift of credit to agriculture and small industry**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the reason was that **industrial houses controlled banks** — nationalisation aimed to end this.
xa: Results: **branch expansion** + **priority-sector lending**.
Intent: Indira Gandhi's note "**Stray Thoughts on Bank Nationalisation**".

84.s: Which of the following was a significant result associated with bank nationalisation?
o: Exclusive lending to large industrial houses
Expansion of bank branches and growth of priority-sector lending
Withdrawal of institutional credit from agriculture
Reduction in branch expansion and contraction of rural banking
84.x: Bank nationalisation was associated with expansion of branches and increased lending to priority sectors, including agriculture and small units.
84.tq: Choose the outcome consistent with the stated social-control objective.
xs: Nationalisation brought **expansion of bank branches** and **priority-sector lending** — option **(2)**.
Before it, **agriculture and small units were neglected** while industrial houses controlled banks.
xa: Motive: **social control of credit**.
The **Lead Bank Scheme** (**1969**) assigned each district a lead bank for credit planning.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about scheduled banks:
1. They are listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934.
2. They must have paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 crore.
3. They may borrow from the RBI at the bank rate, repo or MSF.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the requirement is paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakh, not ₹5 crore. So '1 and 3 only'; the other options include statement 2 or leave out a true one.
84.tq: Scheduled bank: Second Schedule, ₹5 lakh, access to RBI windows.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: scheduled banks are in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the requirement is **₹5 lakh** of paid-up capital and reserves, not ₹5 crore.
Statement 3 is correct: they may **borrow from RBI** at bank rate/repo/MSF.
xa: Five ownership groups: **SBI, nationalised banks, RRBs, foreign banks, private banks**.
Also **SFBs**, **payments banks** and **local area banks**.

84.s: Which principle is associated with the governance of co-operative banks?
84.x: Co-operative banks follow the principle of one member, one vote.
84.tq: Distinguish the co-operative voting principle from share-based corporate voting.
xs: Co-operative banks follow **one member, one vote** — option **(4)**.
They are registered under **State Co-operative Societies Acts** and regulated by RBI (**BR Act**).
xa: India has **1,457** urban co-op banks (Aug **2026**).
RBI is resuming **on-tap UCB licences** (Aug **2026**).
AP rural co-op credit: **APCOB** (**18** branches), **13 DCCBs**, **2,024 PACS**.

84.s: The associate banks of the State Bank of India and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI on
84.x: The associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI with effect from 1 April 2017.
84.tq: Use the year-specific merger date to distinguish closely spaced alternatives.
xs: SBI's **associate banks** and **Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged into SBI on **1 April 2017** — option **(2)**.
The merger took effect at the start of the financial year **2017** — not **2015**, **2016** or **2018**.
xa: SBI was created from the **Imperial Bank** in **1955**.
**SBI subsidiaries** were formed in **1959**.
SBI's first **overseas banking unit** is in **Mumbai** (APPSC-GS **2025**).

84.s: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation was formed in 1978 by merging which two institutions?
84.x: DICGC was formed in 1978 through the merger of the Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India.
84.tq: Match the institution with its constituent predecessor organisations.
xs: **DICGC** was formed in **1978** by merging the **DIC** and **CGCI** — option **(2)**.
The DIC dated from **1962**.
xa: **NBFC** deposits are **not DICGC-insured**.
**NABARD** and **Exim** are **DFIs** in the organised sector.

84.s:
Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Small Finance Bank from a Payments Bank?
1. A Small Finance Bank can undertake lending, whereas a Payments Bank cannot undertake lending.
2. A Payments Bank can accept only demand deposits, subject to the prescribed limit per customer.
3. A Small Finance Bank is required to direct 75% of its Adjusted Net Bank Credit to the priority sector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All three statements are correct. Small Finance Banks can lend and must allocate 75% of ANBC to PSL, while Payments Banks accept only demand deposits and cannot lend.
84.tq: Split the options by comparing the core activities and regulatory obligations of the two differentiated banks.
xs: All three are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**SFBs lend**; **payments banks** have **no lending, no credit cards**.
Payments banks take **demand deposits only**, max **₹2 lakh** per customer; SFBs give **75%** of **ANBC** to **PSL**.
xa: SFB purpose: credit to **small units**, **small/marginal farmers**, unorganised sector.
Payments bank purpose: **payments and remittances** for migrants, low-income households.

84.s: The maximum deposit that a Payments Bank may accept from an individual customer is presently
84.x: The present maximum deposit limit for a customer of a Payments Bank is ₹2 lakh; the earlier limit was ₹1 lakh.
84.tq: Use the updated figure and distinguish it from the earlier regulatory limit.
xs: A payments bank may take up to **₹2 lakh** per customer — option **(2)**.
The **earlier** limit was **₹1 lakh** — option (1) is outdated.
xa: Payments banks take **demand deposits only** and **cannot lend**.
**75%** of demand deposits must be in **SLR G-secs/T-bills** of up to **1** year; CRAR **15%**.
RBI **cancelled Paytm Payments Bank's licence**.

84.s: The minimum capital requirement specified for both Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks in the stated regulatory framework is
84.x: The minimum capital specified for Small Finance Banks is ₹100 crore, while Payments Banks require ₹100 crore of paid-up voting equity capital.
84.tq: Compare the common capital threshold rather than the different activity profiles.
xs: The minimum capital is **₹100 crore** for both — option **(3)**.
SFBs: **₹100 crore** (2014 guidelines); payments banks: **₹100 crore paid-up voting equity**.
xa: Both came from the **Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)**.
Payments banks are public limited companies under the **Companies Act, 2013**.

84.s:
Which of the following statements regarding differentiated banking licences is correct?
1. The Nachiket Mor Committee submitted its recommendations in 2013.
2. Both Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks emerged from differentiated or niche banking licences.
3. Commercial banks are now licensed on an on-tap basis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All three statements are correct. The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted in 2013, and both categories arose from niche licences; commercial banks are now licensed on tap.
84.tq: Combine the committee reference with the distinction between niche and on-tap licensing.
xs: All three are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
**Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)** gave rise to **SFBs and payments banks**.
Both came from **differentiated (niche) licences**; commercial banks are now licensed **"on tap"**.
xa: Licence types: **universal** and **differentiated** (niche).
SFB licences **on tap since 2019**.

84.s: Payments banks in India are licensed under which provision?
o: Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
84.x: Payments banks are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and are public limited companies under the Companies Act, 2013. Section 42 of the RBI Act governs CRR, Section 45ZB constitutes the MPC, and Section 24 of the BR Act governs SLR.
84.tq: Bank licence = Sec 22 BR Act; Sec 24 = SLR; Sec 42 RBI Act = CRR.
xs: Payments banks are licensed under **Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** — option **(1)**.
They are public limited companies under the **Companies Act, 2013** ("2019" in some notes is a slip).
xa: Payments banks: **no lending, no credit cards**; deposits up to **₹2 lakh**.
Paid-up voting equity of at least **₹100 crore**.

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the origin of Regional Rural Banks?
o: They were recommended by the Narasimham Working Group, and Prathama Grameen Bank was the first RRB.
They were recommended by the Khusro Committee, and Prathama Grameen Bank was established in 1982.
They were recommended by the Vyas Committee, and five RRBs were established in 1998.
They were recommended by the Sivaraman Committee, and the first RRB was established in 1992.
84.x: The Narasimham Working Group recommended RRBs in 1975. Prathama Grameen Bank was the first RRB, and five RRBs were established in 1975.
84.tq: Use the recommendation–institution pair and reject swapped committee names and years.
xs: RRBs were recommended by the **Narasimham Working Group** (**1975**), and **Prathama Grameen Bank** was the first — option **(1)**.
Prathama Grameen Bank opened on **2 Oct 1975**; **five** RRBs were set up in **1975**.
xa: RRBs were created by **ordinance**, then the **RRB Act, 1976**.
Ownership: **Centre 50% : sponsor bank 35% : State 15%**.

84.s: The shareholding pattern of a Regional Rural Bank is:
o: Centre 50 per cent, State Government 15 per cent and sponsor bank 35 per cent
Centre 40 per cent, State Government 30 per cent and sponsor bank 30 per cent
Centre 15 per cent, State Government 35 per cent and sponsor bank 50 per cent
Centre 35 per cent, State Government 50 per cent and sponsor bank 15 per cent
84.x: An RRB has a 50:15:35 shareholding pattern among the Central Government, State Government and sponsor bank, respectively.
84.tq: Read the three-way ownership ratio in the stated order.
xs: RRB shares: **Centre 50 per cent**, **State 15 per cent**, **sponsor bank 35 per cent** — option **(1)**.
The **sponsor PSB** gives **capital, technology and management**.
xa: RRBs are **regulated by RBI**, **supervised by NABARD**.
RRB **PSL** target: **75%**.

84.s: The Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance before being placed under which legislation?
84.x: Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance and were subsequently governed by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976.
84.tq: Test the legislative sequence rather than recalling only the year of establishment.
xs: RRBs were created by **ordinance**, then placed under the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976** — option **(3)**.
They followed the **Narasimham Working Group** (**1975**).
xa: First RRB: **Prathama Grameen Bank** (**2 Oct 1975**).
RRBs were allowed **commercial interest rates** from the late 1990s.

84.s: Which one of the following pairs correctly represents the regulatory and supervisory arrangement for Regional Rural Banks?
84.x: RRBs are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India and supervised by NABARD.
84.tq: Start with the sure institutional pair and eliminate options that interchange regulatory roles.
xs: RRBs: **RBI — regulation**; **NABARD — supervision** — option **(1)** (UPSC).
Option (2) swaps the two roles.
xa: **One State-One RRB**: **15** RRBs amalgamated from **1 May 2025** → **28** today.
AP: **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank** merged the four AP RRBs (May **2026**).

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Service Area Approach introduced in 1989?
o: Each bank branch is restricted to financing only one crop.
Each State is assigned one commercial bank for all credit operations.
Each rural branch prepares credit plans for a designated group of villages.
Each district is assigned a separate RBI banking circle.
84.x: Under the Service Area Approach, each rural bank branch plans credit for a specified set of villages.
84.tq: Match the approach with its operational unit and area of responsibility.
xs: Under the **Service Area Approach (1989)**, **each rural branch prepares credit plans for a designated group of villages** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It refined the **Lead Bank Scheme**, which assigned each district a lead bank for credit planning.
Assigning one bank per State or RBI circles per district is not what the approach does.
xa: The **Lead Bank Scheme** began in **1969**, the same year **14 banks** were nationalised.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district-level forum; the **SLBC** works at State level.
RBI issued a **draft revision of the Lead Bank Scheme** in **Feb 2026** to strengthen SLBCs and LDM offices.
⚠ **1969** = Lead Bank Scheme; **1989** = Service Area Approach.

84.s: Which bank acts as the Lead Bank and SLBC convener in Andhra Pradesh?
84.x: Union Bank of India acts as the Lead Bank and the convener of the State Level Bankers’ Committee in Andhra Pradesh.
84.tq: Test the specific State-level institutional assignment rather than the general Lead Bank concept.
xs: **Union Bank of India** is the lead bank and **SLBC convener** in Andhra Pradesh — so option **(1)** is correct.
**NABARD** supervises RRBs; **AP Grameena Bank** is AP's merged RRB — neither convenes the SLBC.
xa: The **236th SLBC** met on **16 Sep 2026**: CM **Naidu** asked banks to lend more to MSMEs, tenant farmers and **PM Surya Ghar**.
**Andhra Bank (1923)** was absorbed into **Union Bank** in **2020**.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district-level forum under the **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)**.

84.s: The Lead Bank Scheme, under which each district is assigned a lead bank to coordinate credit planning, began in:
84.x: The Lead Bank Scheme began in 1969, the same year 14 banks were nationalised. 1975 is the year the first RRB was set up, 1980 is the second round of nationalisation, and 1989 is when the Service Area Approach was introduced.
84.tq: Lead Bank 1969 (same year as nationalisation); Service Area Approach 1989.
xs: The **Lead Bank Scheme** began in **1969** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1969** was also the year **14 banks** were nationalised (**19 July 1969**).
**1975** = first RRB, **1980** = second nationalisation round (**6 banks**), **1989** = **Service Area Approach**.
xa: Each district is assigned a lead bank to coordinate credit planning, with branch expansion district by district.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district forum; the **SLBC** is the State-level forum.
RBI issued a **draft revision** of the scheme in **Feb 2026**.

84.s: Which of the following activities is an example of para-banking?
o: Distributing mutual funds and providing insurance services
84.x: Para-banking refers to services beyond the traditional acceptance of deposits and provision of loans, including credit cards, insurance, factoring and mutual fund distribution. Credit to paramilitary personnel is not para-banking merely because of the category of borrower.
84.tq: Apply the definition by separating ancillary financial services from ordinary banking or lending.
xs: **Distributing mutual funds and providing insurance** is para-banking — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Para-banking** = services beyond deposits and loans: **credit cards, insurance, factoring**, mutual fund distribution.
**Credit to paramilitary personnel** is not para-banking — a known trap; plain deposits or term loans are core banking.
xa: The **APPSC-G1 2022** key on para-banking was **I, II and IV**, excluding the paramilitary option.
**SFBs** can distribute **MFs and insurance**; **payments banks** cannot lend or issue credit cards.
**Cheque validity** is **3 months** from date of issue (since **1 April 2012**).

84.s: Which one of the following is a liability of a commercial bank?
84.x: Customer deposits are liabilities because the bank owes these amounts to depositors. Loans, investments and cash reserves are assets of the bank.
84.tq: Apply the ownership-and-obligation test to distinguish assets from liabilities.
xs: **Deposits accepted from customers** are a **liability** of a bank — so option **(4)** is correct.
The bank owes deposits back to depositors.
**Cash in hand**, **SLR investments** and **loans and advances** are **assets**.
xa: Liabilities: **capital and reserves**, **deposits** (current, savings, term), **borrowings**.
Assets: cash in hand, **balances with RBI (CRR)**, investments, loans and advances, fixed assets.
⚠ Deposits = liabilities vs loans = assets — the commonest balance-sheet trap.

84.s: Which of the following statements regarding collateral-free credit is correct?
o: Only loans to large industries up to ₹25 lakh are collateral-free.
MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and all PMEGP units must be collateral-free, with banks permitted to raise the limit to ₹25 lakh.
Collateral-free lending is available only to agricultural borrowers.
All MSE loans above ₹20 lakh must compulsorily be secured by collateral.
84.x: MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and all PMEGP units must be provided without collateral. Banks may raise the collateral-free limit to ₹25 lakh under the applicable RBI directions.
84.tq: Read the threshold and the exception together instead of treating the limit as universal.
xs: **MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and all PMEGP units** must be collateral-free, and banks may raise the limit to **₹25 lakh** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This comes from **RBI directions, Feb 2026**.
Collateral-free credit is for **MSEs**, not large industries or only farmers.
xa: **Para-banking**: credit cards, insurance, factoring, mutual fund distribution.
**SFBs**: **50%** of loans must be **≤ ₹25 lakh**; **75%** of ANBC to PSL.
ATM cash-out penalty: **₹10,000** per ATM empty more than **10 hours in a month** (from **1 Oct 2021**).

84.s: Since 1 April 2012, a cheque in India is valid for how long from its date of issue?
84.x: Since 1 April 2012, cheques have been valid for 3 months from the date of issue. The earlier validity was 6 months. 1 month and 12 months were never the general rule.
84.tq: Cheque validity: 3 months since April 2012 (was 6).
xs: Since **1 April 2012**, a cheque is valid for **3 months** from its date of issue — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other durations are not the rule given in the notes.
xa: **Aadhaar** can be used for KYC verification **with the customer's consent** (APPSC-GS 2019).
ATM penalty from **1 Oct 2021**: **₹10,000** per ATM out of cash beyond **10 hours in a month**.
**Para-banking** covers **credit cards, insurance, factoring** and MF distribution.

84.s: Which one of the following statements about the use of Aadhaar by banks is correct?
o: Aadhaar can be used for KYC verification with the customer's consent
Aadhaar must be used for KYC for every account, whether or not the customer consents
Aadhaar cannot be used for KYC verification by banks
Only payments banks may use Aadhaar for KYC verification
84.x: Banks can use Aadhaar for KYC verification with the customer's consent (APPSC-GS 2019). It is neither mandatory regardless of consent nor barred, and it is not limited to payments banks.
84.tq: Aadhaar KYC: allowed, but voluntary (needs consent).
xs: **Aadhaar can be used for KYC verification with the customer's consent** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This was the **APPSC-GS 2019** key: Aadhaar is neither compulsory without consent, nor barred, nor limited to payments banks.
xa: **Cheque validity**: **3 months** from issue since **1 April 2012**.
**Para-banking**: services beyond deposits and loans — credit cards, insurance, factoring, MF distribution.
Collateral-free MSE loans up to **₹20 lakh** and all **PMEGP** units.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh's credit-deposit ratio:
1. It was 162% in December 2024.
2. It declined to 157.40% in December 2025.
3. The December 2025 ratio was above the RBI norm of 60%.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All three statements are correct. The ratio declined from 162% to 157.40%, but remained substantially above the RBI norm of 60%.
84.tq: Track both the time trend and the comparison with the regulatory benchmark.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1: AP's CD ratio was **162%** in **Dec 2024** (APSES 2024-25) — correct.
Statement 2: it fell to **157.40%** in **Dec 2025** — correct.
Statement 3: the **RBI norm** is **60%**, so 157.40% is far above it — correct.
xa: AP Dec 2025: deposits **₹6,08,834 crore**, credit **₹9,58,277 crore**, **8,555** branches.
District CD ratios (Dec 2024): **Konaseema 213%**, **Nandyal 202%**; lowest **Tirupati 85%**.
AP's CD ratio (**157%**) is among the highest in India.

84.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding district-level credit-deposit ratios in Andhra Pradesh in December 2024?
84.x: Konaseema recorded a credit-deposit ratio of 213%. Nandyal recorded 202%, while Tirupati had the lowest ratio at 85%.
84.tq: Match each district with its distinctive ratio and reject the swapped values.
xs: **Konaseema — 213%** is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Nandyal** was **202%** (not 85%); **Tirupati** was the lowest at **85%** (not 202%).
**162%** was the State-wide CD ratio, not Konaseema's.
xa: Several AP districts had CD ratios above **200%** (Annexure **7.24**).
The State CD ratio fell to **157.40%** in Dec 2025.
The RBI norm for the CD ratio is **60%**.

84.s: Which of the following correctly represents the banking-sector indicators mentioned for 2025–26?
o: PSB 4R strategy and GNPA at 2.2% in September 2026
PSB 5R strategy and GNPA at 2.2% in September 2025
PSB 3R strategy and GNPA at 5.2% in September 2025
PSB 4R strategy and GNPA at 2.2% in September 2025
84.x: The banking-sector significance highlighted is the 4R strategy for public sector banks and GNPA of 2.2% in September 2025, a multi-decadal low.
84.tq: Check both the strategy label and the date-linked percentage before selecting the pair.
xs: The indicators are the **4R strategy** for PSBs and **GNPA at 2.2% in September 2025** — so option **(4)** is correct.
2.2% GNPA is a **multi-decadal low**; option (1) has the wrong year and options (2)/(3) the wrong strategy.
xa: The **UFBU** PSB strike on **12 Sep 2026** sought a **5-day week**.
AP's CD ratio (**157%**) is among the highest.
First RRB = **Prathama Grameen Bank**; first SFB = **Capital SFB**.

84.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The first RRB was Prathama Grameen Bank.
The first RRB was established on 2 October 1974.
SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank of India.
84.x: Option C is incorrect: the first RRB, Prathama Grameen Bank, opened on 2 October 1975, not 1974. SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank on 1 July 1955.
84.tq: Recall the first RRB year, 1975.
n: The SBI was established on 1 July 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
Prathama Grameen Bank was the first Regional Rural Bank. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The first Regional Rural Bank was established on 2 October 1975. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]

84.s:
Assertion (A): C.D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor of the RBI.
Reason (R): C.D. Deshmukh served as Finance Minister from 1950 to 1956.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
84.x: Both are true: C.D. Deshmukh was the first Indian RBI Governor, and he was Finance Minister in 1950–56. His later ministry does not explain his earlier post, so R does not explain A.
84.tq: Ask whether a later role explains an earlier one.
n: C.D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor of the RBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
C.D. Deshmukh served as Finance Minister from 1950 to 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]

84.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Location of the first Regional Rural Bank
(b) First phase of bank nationalisation
(c) Second phase of bank nationalisation

List-II
(i) Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh
(ii) 1969
(iii) 1980
(iv) 1975
84.x: The first RRB was at Moradabad (UP), the first bank nationalisation was in 1969 and the second in 1980. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii.

n: The first Regional Rural Bank was located in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The first phase of bank nationalisation took place in 1969. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The second phase of bank nationalisation took place in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]

84.s: RBI was nationalised on which date under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948?
84.x: The RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. 1 July 1955 is SBI, and 19 July 1969 the bank nationalisation.
84.tq: Match each date to its event.
n: RBI was nationalised on January 1, 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
RBI was nationalised through the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
RBI was nationalised in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]

84.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The nationalisation of LIC involved merging over 240 private insurers and societies.
LIC was nationalised through the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956.
84.x: Option C is incorrect: LIC was formed on 1 September 1956 under the LIC Act, 1956, by merging over 240 insurers and societies. 19 July 1969 is the date 14 commercial banks were nationalised.
84.tq: Separate the 1956 LIC date from the 1969 bank nationalisation date.
n: LIC was nationalised on September 1, 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC was nationalised through the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC nationalisation merged over 240 private insurers and societies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]

84.s:
Arrange the following milestones in chronological order:
A. SBI was established.
B. LIC was nationalised.
C. The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act was passed.

84.tq: Arrange the milestones in time order.
n: SBI was established in 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC was nationalised in 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act was passed in 1959. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
