84.s: In which year was the Banking Regulation Act enacted?
84.x: The Banking Regulation Act was passed in 1949, the same year the RBI was nationalised.
84.tq: Recall the 1949 banking events.
n: The Banking Regulation Act was enacted in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]

84.s:
How many of the following banks were among the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980?
1. Andhra Bank
2. Corporation Bank
3. New Bank of India
4. Oriental Bank of Commerce
5. Punjab & Sind Bank
6. Vijaya Bank
84.x: All six were nationalised in 1980: Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank and Vijaya Bank.
84.tq: Recall the six banks of 1980.
n: Andhra Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Corporation Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
New Bank of India was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Oriental Bank of Commerce was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Punjab & Sind Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Vijaya Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]

84.s: The 14 major commercial banks were nationalised under which legislation in 1969?
o: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969
84.x: The 14 banks were nationalised under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969.
84.tq: Match each event to its Act.
n: The 14 major commercial banks were nationalised under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]

85.s:
Consider the following statements about post-1991 financial-sector reforms:
1. The SLR stood at 28.5 per cent in 1991-92 before it was cut.
2. Prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning were introduced, with CRAR from 1992.
3. FDI up to 74 per cent was allowed in private banks in 2004.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the SLR was 38.5 per cent in 1991-92. Statement 2 is correct: prudential norms (income recognition, asset classification, provisioning) came with CRAR in 1992. Statement 3 is correct: FDI up to 74 per cent in private banks was allowed in 2004. Hence 2 and 3 only; every option containing 1 is wrong.
85.tq: Remember 38.5% SLR (1991-92), CRAR 1992, 74% FDI in private banks 2004.

85.s:
Consider the following statements regarding post-1991 financial-sector reforms:
1. SEBI was made a statutory body in 1992.
2. The Banking Ombudsman was introduced in 1995.
3. Asset Reconstruction Companies and Debt Recovery Tribunals were associated with recovery of stressed assets.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: SEBI received statutory status in 1992, the Banking Ombudsman was introduced in 1995, and ARCs and DRTs were associated with recovery mechanisms.
85.tq: Test dates and institutional functions together in a coded statement question.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1: **SEBI** was made statutory in **1992** — correct.
Statement 2: the **Banking Ombudsman** came in **1995** — correct.
Statement 3: **ARCs** and **DRTs** were created for **recovery** — correct.
xa: Market-determined exchange rate: **1993**.
**FERA** replaced by **FEMA** in **1999**; insurance opened by the **IRDA Act 1999**.
⚠ **Bank nationalisation (1969/1980)** and **FRBM Act 2003** do not belong to the 1991 financial-sector reforms.

85.s: A major change in the regulatory structure after financial-sector reforms was that:
o: SEBI assumed direct control over all public sector banks
The Finance Ministry’s Banking Division became the sole regulator of banks
The Banks Board Bureau replaced the RBI as the monetary authority
The RBI became the primary regulator and dual control with the Finance Ministry’s Banking Division ended
85.x: The RBI became the primary regulator, ending dual control with the Finance Ministry’s Banking Division. The reforms also promoted greater autonomy for public sector banks.
85.tq: Identify the correct authority and reject swapped institutional powers.
xs: **RBI became the primary regulator**, ending **dual control** with the Finance Ministry's **Banking Division** — so option **(4)** is correct.
RBI also moved from regulator towards **facilitator**; PSBs got more **autonomy**.
The **Banks Board Bureau** (from **2016**) selects PSB heads; it never became a monetary authority.
xa: Ending dual control was a **Narasimham-I** recommendation (APPSC-G1 2022 key).
**SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.
The **Banking Ombudsman** was introduced in **1995**.

85.s: Which of the following does NOT belong to the financial-sector reforms initiated after 1991?
85.x: The FRBM Act, 2003 was a fiscal reform, not a financial-sector reform. The other three were components of post-1991 financial-sector reforms.
85.tq: Separate financial-sector reforms from a fiscal-policy measure.
xs: The **FRBM Act, 2003** does NOT belong — it is a **fiscal** reform — so option **(4)** is correct.
**SLR/CRR cuts**, **private bank entry** and **prudential norms** were all core post-1991 financial-sector reforms.
xa: ⚠ **Bank nationalisation (1969/1980)** is also pre-reform and does not belong.
SLR was **38.5%** in **1991-92** before the cuts.
**HDFC** and **ICICI** entered by **1995**; **FDI up to 74%** in private banks (**2004**).

85.s: Which one of the following pairs of post-1991 reforms and years is correctly matched?
o: Insurance opened by the IRDA Act - 2003
85.x: The exchange rate became market-determined in 1993. FEMA replaced FERA in 1999, not 1991. The IRDA Act was passed in 1999; 2003 is the FRBM Act, which is a fiscal reform. SEBI became statutory in 1992.
85.tq: SEBI 1992 -> market exchange rate 1993 -> FEMA and IRDA 1999.
xs: **Market-determined exchange rate — 1993** is correctly matched — so option **(1)** is correct.
**FEMA** replaced **FERA** in **1999**, not 1991.
The **IRDA Act** was **1999**; **2003** is the **FRBM Act**; **SEBI** became statutory in **1992**, not 1999.
xa: **Banking Ombudsman**: **1995**.
**CRAR** introduced in **1992**.
The **Malhotra Committee (1993)** led to the **IRDA Act 1999**.

85.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Narasimham-I and Narasimham-II Committees:
1. Narasimham-I recommended reduction of SLR and CRR.
2. Narasimham-II recommended a three-tier banking structure.
3. Narasimham-II proposed that weak and unviable banks should be closed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: All three statements are correct. Narasimham-I focused on foundational banking reforms, while Narasimham-II emphasised consolidation, a three-tier structure and resolution of weak banks.
85.tq: Test the different recommendations of two similarly named committees through statement combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1: **Narasimham-I** recommended lower **SLR/CRR** — correct.
Statement 2: **Narasimham-II** proposed a **3-tier structure** — correct.
Statement 3: Narasimham-II wanted **weak/unviable banks closed** — correct.
xa: Narasimham-I = **Committee on the Financial System (1991)**; Narasimham-II = **Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (1998)**.
Narasimham-II also recommended **CRAR 10%** and **universal banking**.
The merger idea ("fewer, stronger banks") fed the **2020** "ten into four" PSB merger.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about the Narasimham-II Committee:
1. It was set up in December 1997 and submitted its report in April 1998.
2. Its official title was the Committee on the Financial System.
3. It recommended raising CRAR to 10 per cent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: set up Dec 1997, report April 1998. Statement 2 is wrong: 'Committee on the Financial System' is Narasimham-I (1991); Narasimham-II was the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms. Statement 3 is correct: it raised CRAR to 10%. Hence 1 and 3 only; options containing 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
85.tq: N-I (1991) = Committee on the Financial System; N-II (1997-98) = Committee on Banking Sector Reforms.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: set up **Dec 1997**, report **April 1998** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Committee on the Financial System** was **Narasimham-I (1991)**; Narasimham-II was the **Committee on Banking Sector Reforms**.
Statement 3: it recommended **CRAR 10%** — correct.
xa: ⚠ APPSC GS 2019 key called the 1991 body "Committee on Banking Sector Reforms" — the official title is **Committee on the Financial System**.
Narasimham-II's **3-tier structure**: 2-3 international, 8-10 national, many local banks.

85.s: Which of the following correctly represents the three-tier banking structure suggested by the Narasimham-II Committee?
o: Two to three national banks, eight to ten international banks and no local banks
Two to three international banks, eight to ten national banks and many local banks
One international bank, five national banks and several regional banks
Only regional rural banks, cooperative banks and payment banks
85.x: The proposed structure consisted of two or three international banks, eight to ten national banks and many local banks.
85.tq: Match the committee’s structural proposal with its precise numerical tiers.
xs: Narasimham-II's 3-tier structure: **two to three international banks, eight to ten national banks and many local banks** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the international and national tiers and drops local banks.
xa: Narasimham-II also recommended merging strong banks and DFIs and closing weak ones.
It raised the **CRAR** target to **10%** and backed **universal banking**.
PSB count fell from **27 (2017) to 12 (2020)** through mergers.

85.s: How many parameters were used for identifying weak banks by the M.S. Verma Committee?
85.x: The M.S. Verma Committee identified weak banks using seven parameters.
85.tq: Recall the exact count attached to a committee’s diagnostic framework.
xs: The **M.S. Verma Committee (1999)** used **7 parameters** to identify weak banks — so option **(2)** is correct.
It dealt with **Restructuring Weak PSBs**.
xa: **P.J. Nayak (2014)** studied governance of PSB boards → **Banks Board Bureau**.
**Narasimham-II** wanted weak/unviable banks closed.
⚠ Do not confuse with **Indradhanush's 7-point plan (A-G)** of **2015**.

85.s: The Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms is associated with the report titled:
85.x: The Raghuram Rajan Committee’s report was titled “A Hundred Small Steps.”
85.tq: Identify a committee through its distinctive report title.
xs: The **Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008)** wrote "**A Hundred Small Steps**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
"**7 parameters** for weak banks" belongs to the **M.S. Verma** Committee.
xa: Some notes date the Rajan report **2009**.
**Nachiket Mor (2013)** = SFBs and payments banks.
**Bimal Jalan (2019)** = RBI's Economic Capital Framework.

85.s: The S.H. Khan Working Group of 1998 was concerned with:
o: Determining the contingent risk buffer of the RBI
Restructuring weak public sector banks through seven parameters
Setting up the Banks Board Bureau
Harmonising the roles of banks and Development Finance Institutions
85.x: The S.H. Khan Working Group examined how the roles of banks and Development Finance Institutions could be harmonised, leading towards universal banking.
85.tq: Separate the universal-banking recommendation from committee work on weak banks and RBI reserves.
xs: The **S.H. Khan Working Group (1998)** dealt with **harmonising the roles of banks and DFIs** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This led to **universal banking**.
The **contingent risk buffer** is **Bimal Jalan**; **7 parameters** is **M.S. Verma**; **BBB** is **P.J. Nayak**.
xa: **Narasimham-II (1998)** also backed universal banking and merging strong banks and DFIs.
**Rangarajan (2006)** dealt with financial inclusion.

85.s: The Economic Capital Framework of the RBI, associated with Bimal Jalan, dealt particularly with:
o: Merging strong banks and closing weak banks
Transfer of reserves and surplus to the Government
85.x: Bimal Jalan chaired the committee on the RBI’s Economic Capital Framework, including the issue of reserves and surplus transfer to the Government.
85.tq: Distinguish RBI balance-sheet and surplus issues from banking-structure reforms.
xs: The **Bimal Jalan** Economic Capital Framework dealt with **RBI reserves and surplus transfer to the Government** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Merging strong / closing weak banks = **Narasimham-II**; customer service = **Goiporia**; payments banks = **Nachiket Mor**.
xa: It set a **Contingent Risk Buffer** of **5.5-6.5%**.
Jalan's committee sat **2018-19** (report **2019**).

85.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Committee)
a. Goiporia
b. Malhotra
c. C. Rangarajan
d. P.J. Nayak

List-II (Subject)
i. Insurance reform
ii. Governance of bank boards
iii. Customer service in banks
iv. Financial inclusion

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
85.x: Goiporia dealt with customer service, Malhotra with insurance reform, C. Rangarajan with financial inclusion, and P.J. Nayak with bank-board governance.
85.tq: Start from the sure committee-subject pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.
xs: Correct matching: **a–iii, b–i, c–iv, d–ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Goiporia** = customer service in banks; **Malhotra** = insurance reform (**IRDA**).
**C. Rangarajan (2006)** = financial inclusion; **P.J. Nayak (2014)** = governance of bank boards.
xa: ⚠ Two **Rangarajan** committees: **1993** = disinvestment, **2006** = financial inclusion.
Nayak led to the **Banks Board Bureau** (**2016**), replaced by **FSIB** in **2022**.

85.s: The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted in 2013 and is associated with recommendations concerning:
o: Small finance banks and payments banks
85.x: The Nachiket Mor Committee, constituted in 2013, examined differentiated banks, including small finance banks and payments banks.
85.tq: Use the year and distinctive institutional reform as confirmation clues.
xs: The **Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)** led to **small finance banks and payments banks** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Surplus transfer to Govt was the **Bimal Jalan** committee.
xa: It dealt with **differentiated banking / financial inclusion** and universal bank accounts.
It laid the groundwork for **PMJDY**.
⚠ **Rangarajan (2006)** was the earlier financial-inclusion committee.

85.s: The Basel Accords are framed by which of the following bodies?
o: International Organization of Securities Commissions under the BIS
Financial Stability Board under the International Monetary Fund
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision under the Bank for International Settlements
International Monetary Fund under the World Bank
85.x: The Basel Accords are formulated by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), which functions under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
85.tq: Identify the correct international body and distinguish it from neighbouring financial institutions.
xs: The Basel Accords are framed by the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** under the **Bank for International Settlements (BIS)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They cover **capital risk, market risk and operational risk**.
xa: BIS was set up in **1930**, the world's oldest international financial organisation.
Basel I **1988**, Basel II **2004**, Basel III post-2008 crisis (India from **1 Jan 2013**).
⚠ The **Basel Convention (1989)** is a UNEP treaty on **hazardous wastes**, not banking.

85.s: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) was established in which year?
85.x: The BIS was established in 1930 and is described as the world's oldest international financial organisation.
85.tq: Use the year-based elimination method with closely spaced numerical options.
xs: The **BIS** was established in **1930** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is the **world's oldest international financial organisation**.
xa: The **BCBS** under the BIS frames the **Basel Accords**.
Basel I (**1988**) covered credit risk only, with a minimum of **8%** of risk-weighted assets.
Basel II (**2004**) rests on three pillars.

85.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the principal focus of Basel I?
o: Stable funding over a one-year horizon
Liquidity coverage over a 30-day stress period
Market discipline through mandatory public disclosure alone
Credit risk and a minimum capital standard of 8 per cent of risk-weighted assets
85.x: Basel I, introduced in 1988, primarily addressed credit risk and prescribed minimum capital of 8 per cent of risk-weighted assets.
85.tq: Match the accord with its core content rather than with a later liquidity norm.
xs: **Basel I (1988)** covered **credit risk** with a minimum capital of **8% of risk-weighted assets** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Stable funding over **1 year** = **NSFR**; 30-day liquidity = **LCR** — both Basel III.
Market discipline is a **Basel II** pillar.
xa: Basel I used five risk buckets: **0, 10, 20, 50, 100%**.
India set CRAR at **9%** under Basel I (**1999**).

85.s: Which of the following sets correctly represents the three pillars of Basel II?
o: Capital adequacy, monetary stability and deposit insurance
Credit risk, exchange-rate risk and sovereign risk
Liquidity coverage, stable funding and countercyclical lending
Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline
85.x: Basel II rests on three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.
85.tq: Recall the standard three-part framework and reject terms belonging to Basel III liquidity norms.
xs: Basel II's three pillars: **minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Liquidity coverage and stable funding (**LCR**, **NSFR**) came with **Basel III**.
xa: Basel II was issued in **2004**.
Basel III pillars (as notes phrase them): **absorb shocks**; improve risk management and governance; improve transparency and disclosure.
The **leverage ratio** came with Basel III, not Basel II.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about Basel III:
1. It was framed as a response to the global financial crisis of 2007-09.
2. India began implementing it from 1 January 2013.
3. The leverage ratio was first introduced under Basel II.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: Basel III was the reply to the 2007-09 crisis. Statement 2 is correct: India applied it from 1 Jan 2013. Statement 3 is wrong: the leverage ratio came with Basel III, not Basel II. Hence 1 and 2 only; '1 only' misses statement 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
85.tq: Leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR and buffers are all Basel III; Basel II = three pillars.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: Basel III was the reply to the **2007-09 crisis** — correct.
Statement 2: India applied it from **1 Jan 2013** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **leverage ratio** came with **Basel III**, not Basel II.
xa: Basel III features: **CET1**, capital buffers, **leverage ratio**, **LCR**, **NSFR**, counterparty credit risk.
RBI leverage ratio: **4%** for D-SIBs, **3.5%** for others (BCBS **3%**).

85.s: India introduced the Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) in 1992. Under the Basel I framework, India prescribed CRAR at:
85.x: India introduced CRAR in 1992 and prescribed it at 9 per cent under Basel I, one percentage point above the Basel minimum of 8 per cent.
85.tq: Separate the Indian norm from the lower international minimum.
xs: India set CRAR at **9 per cent** under Basel I (**1999**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
That is stricter than the BCBS minimum of **8%**.
**10.5%** is the BCBS CRAR + CCB; **6%** is the BCBS Tier 1 minimum.
xa: RBI introduced CRAR in **1992**, following BIS standards.
**Narasimham-II** recommended **CRAR 10%**.

85.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio or buffer)
a. Common Equity Tier 1
b. Tier 1 capital
c. Capital conservation buffer
d. Countercyclical capital buffer

List-II (BCBS minimum or range)
i. 0–2.5 per cent
ii. 2.5 per cent
iii. 4.5 per cent
iv. 6 per cent

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
85.x: The BCBS minimums are CET1 4.5 per cent, Tier 1 capital 6 per cent, CCB 2.5 per cent and countercyclical buffer 0–2.5 per cent.
85.tq: Start with the distinctive buffer range and then complete the capital-ratio pairs.
xs: Correct matching: **a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
BCBS minimums: **CET1 4.5%**, **Tier 1 6%**, **CCB 2.5%**, **CCyB 0-2.5%**.
xa: RBI norms are stricter: **CET1 5.5%**, **Tier 1 7%**, CRAR **9%**.
⚠ Notes listing "Tier I 4.5%" confuse it with the BCBS **CET1** floor.

85.s: Which of the following correctly defines Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) or CRAR?
o: Total capital divided by risk-weighted assets
Total deposits divided by total advances
Tier 1 capital divided by total non-risk-weighted exposure
Liquid assets divided by short-term liabilities
85.x: CAR or CRAR is calculated as capital divided by risk-weighted assets. The leverage ratio, in contrast, uses total non-risk-weighted exposure.
85.tq: Distinguish risk-weighted capital adequacy from the non-risk-weighted leverage measure.
xs: **CAR/CRAR = capital / risk-weighted assets** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Tier-1 capital / total **non-risk-weighted** exposure is the **leverage ratio**.
xa: RBI CRAR norm **9%** vs BCBS **8%**.
SCB **CRAR** rose to **17.36%**; **PSB CRAR** to **16.10%**.
**HDFC Bank** CAR **19.6%** vs regulatory norm **11.9%** (19 Jul 2026).

85.s: Which of the following statements regarding the components of regulatory capital is correct?
o: Tier 1 capital is composed exclusively of subordinated debt.
Tier 1 capital includes pure equity elements, while Tier 2 may include subordinated debt.
Tier 2 capital consists only of paid-up equity and reserves.
Both Tier 1 and Tier 2 consist entirely of government securities.
85.x: Tier 1 capital includes paid-up capital, reserves and undistributed profits as core equity. Tier 2 has a mixed equity-debt character and may include subordinated debt.
85.tq: Use the core-versus-supplementary capital distinction to identify the accurate composition.
xs: **Tier 1** is pure equity, while **Tier 2** may include **subordinated debt** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Tier 1 = **paid-up capital, reserves, undistributed profits**; Tier 2 = **equity-debt mix**.
xa: **AT-1 bonds** are **perpetual** debt with a call option.
**SBI** raised **₹4,691 crore** in the first Basel III AT-1 bonds of FY27.
RBI Tier 1 norm: **7%**; BCBS **6%**.

85.s: Which of the following correctly presents the RBI norms for CET1, Tier 1 capital and total CRAR?
85.x: The RBI norms listed are CET1 5.5 per cent, Tier 1 capital 7 per cent and total CRAR 9 per cent.
85.tq: Read the three-column ratio comparison without substituting the BCBS minimums.
xs: RBI norms: **CET1 5.5%**, **Tier 1 7%**, **total CRAR 9%** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (4) gives the **BCBS** minimums (4.5%, 6%, 8%); options (1) and (2) mix the two sets.
xa: RBI CRAR + CCB: **11.5%** vs BCBS **10.5%**.
CCB is **2.5%** under both.
RBI's **9%** is stricter than BCBS's **8%**.

85.s: In October 2025, the RBI proposed lower risk weights under Basel III for which of the following sectors?
85.x: In October 2025, the RBI proposed lower Basel III risk weights for MSMEs and real estate.
85.tq: Use the sector-pair association while rejecting plausible but unlisted alternatives.
xs: In **Oct 2025**, RBI proposed (draft) lower **differentiated risk weights** for **MSMEs and real estate** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This would lower minimum capital needs under Basel III.
xa: Risk weights were **raised** on unsecured consumer credit in **Nov 2023** to cool risky lending.
An **ECL** shift may cut Tier-1 ratios by **100-150 bps**.
**LTV caps** limit loans to a share of collateral value (housing, gold).

85.s: Which one of the following statements about the countercyclical capital buffer is correct?
o: It permits 0–2.5 per cent extra capital during credit booms; India introduced it from 2015 but has not activated it.
It requires 2.5 per cent capital in every phase of the credit cycle and is always activated in India.
It limits lending to a share of the collateral value.
It caps total exposure against Tier 1 capital at 3 per cent.
85.x: The CCyB ranges from 0 to 2.5 per cent during credit booms. India has had the framework since 2015, but it has not been activated.
85.tq: Distinguish the purpose and activation status of CCyB from other macroprudential tools.
xs: The **CCyB** allows **0-2.5%** extra capital in credit booms; India has had it since **2015** but **not activated** it — so option **(1)** is correct.
Limiting loans to collateral value is an **LTV cap**; capping exposure against Tier-1 is the **leverage ratio**.
xa: Its main trigger is the **credit-to-GDP gap**.
RBI kept the CCyB inactive in **May 2026**.
CCB is a fixed **2.5%**; ⚠ do not mix CCB with CCyB.

85.s: In India, the countercyclical capital buffer framework was introduced by the RBI in 2015. Its main trigger is the:
85.x: The RBI introduced the countercyclical capital buffer framework in 2015, with the credit-to-GDP gap as its main trigger.
85.tq: Match the macroeconomic indicator with the regulatory buffer it activates.
xs: The CCyB's main trigger is the **credit-to-GDP gap** — so option **(4)** is correct.
RBI introduced the framework in **2015** but has **not activated** it.
xa: CCyB range: **0-2.5%** of extra capital.
CCB is a separate fixed **2.5%** buffer.
Other macroprudential tools: **LTV caps**, risk weights, liquidity ratios (**LCR**, **NSFR**).

85.s:
Consider the following statements about Basel III ratios:
1. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires a stock of high-quality liquid assets enough to survive a 30-day stress.
2. The Net Stable Funding Ratio concerns stable funding over a one-year horizon.
3. The leverage ratio is Tier-1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: LCR = HQLA for a 30-day stress. Statement 2 is correct: NSFR = stable funding over 1 year. Statement 3 is wrong: the leverage ratio is Tier-1 capital over total (non-risk-weighted) exposure; capital over risk-weighted assets is CRAR. Hence 1 and 2 only.
85.tq: LCR = 30 days, NSFR = 1 year; leverage ratio ignores risk weights.

85.s:
Which of the following are classified as Level 1 high-quality liquid assets for the purpose of LCR?
1. Cash
2. Government securities
3. Central-bank reserves
4. Highly rated corporate bonds
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
85.x: Cash, government securities and central-bank reserves are Level 1 HQLA. Highly rated corporate bonds are classified as Level 2 HQLA.
85.tq: Separate the core Level 1 assets from the corporate-bond example belonging to Level 2.
xs: **Cash, G-secs and central-bank reserves** are Level 1 HQLA — so option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
**Highly rated corporate bonds** are **Level 2** HQLA, so item 4 is out.
xa: **LCR** = stock of **HQLA** to survive a **30-day** stress; minimum **100%**.
**NSFR** = stable funding over a **1-year** horizon.
RBI deferred revised LCR norms to **31 Mar 2026**.

85.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Tool)
a. Capital conservation buffer
i. Caps total exposure against Tier 1 capital
b. Leverage ratio
ii. Limits loan to a share of collateral value
c. LTV cap
iii. 2.5 per cent over the minimum under Basel III
d. Risk weights
iv. Raised to cool risky lending such as unsecured consumer credit
Which of the following is the correct answer?
85.x: The capital conservation buffer is 2.5 per cent over the minimum; the leverage ratio caps exposure against Tier 1 capital; LTV caps relate loans to collateral; risk weights can cool risky lending.
85.tq: Start from the sure LTV-collateral pair and complete the regulatory-tool matches.
xs: Correct matching: **a–iii, b–i, c–ii, d–iv** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**CCB** = **2.5%** over the minimum; **leverage ratio** = Tier-1 capital against total exposure.
**LTV cap** = loan limited to a share of collateral value; **risk weights** raised to cool risky lending (unsecured consumer credit, **Nov 2023**).
xa: **CCyB** (**0-2.5%**) checks excess credit growth; trigger = **credit-to-GDP gap**.
RBI leverage ratio: **4%** for D-SIBs, **3.5%** for others; BCBS **3%**.
Liquidity ratios **LCR** and **NSFR** are also macroprudential tools.

85.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the recapitalisation of public sector banks:
1. A package of ₹2.11 lakh crore was announced in October 2017.
2. Recapitalisation bonds formed part of the package.
3. The package was associated with the merger of ten PSBs into four.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the October 2017 package was ₹2.11 lakh crore, of which ₹1.35 lakh crore came through recapitalisation bonds. Statement 3 is wrong: the 'ten into four' PSB merger was a separate consolidation that took effect from 1 April 2020, not part of the recapitalisation package. Hence 1 and 2 only.
85.tq: Separate the package details from the later structural banking reform.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: the **Oct 2017** package was **₹2.11 lakh crore** — correct.
Statement 2: **₹1.35 lakh crore** came via **recapitalisation bonds** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: the "**ten into four**" merger was a separate step, effective **1 April 2020**.
xa: About **₹58,000 crore** was to be raised by banks.
The bonds pushed up **central debt**.
**4R strategy**: Recognition, Resolution, Recapitalisation, Reforms.

85.s: Indradhanush, introduced in August 2015, was primarily associated with which of the following reforms?
o: A seven-point plan for capitalisation and governance reform of public sector banks
A fiscal-deficit reduction programme for the Union Government
A scheme for consolidation of Regional Rural Banks
A framework for regulating private insurance companies
85.x: Indradhanush was a seven-point plan introduced in August 2015 for capital infusion and governance reform in public sector banks.
85.tq: Identify the programme by its distinctive reform objective and date.
xs: **Indradhanush (Aug 2015)** was a **seven-point plan for capitalisation and governance reform of PSBs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is a PSB scheme, not a fiscal, RRB or insurance framework.
xa: **7-point plan (A-G)**: Appointments, **Banks Board Bureau**, Capitalisation, De-stressing, Empowerment, Framework of accountability, Governance.
It provided **₹70,000 crore** of budget capital over **4 years**.
The **BBB** began in **2016** as an Indradhanush idea.

85.s: How do recapitalisation bonds support public sector banks without requiring an equivalent immediate cash outgo from the Union budget?
o: The Government transfers its tax receipts directly to bank depositors
The Government writes off all outstanding bank loans through monetary creation
Banks issue equity directly to the Reserve Bank of India without Government involvement
The Government issues bonds to banks and invests the proceeds back into them as equity
85.x: Under the mechanism, the Government issues bonds to public sector banks and puts the money back into them as equity; therefore, no equivalent fresh cash leaves the budget immediately.
85.tq: Trace the transaction sequence rather than judging the policy only by its name.
xs: The **Government issues bonds to banks and invests the proceeds back into them as equity** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So **no fresh cash leaves the budget** immediately, though it **pushes up central debt**.
xa: The **Oct 2017** package: **₹2.11 lakh crore**, with **₹1.35 lakh crore** via recap bonds.
**4R strategy**: Recognition, Resolution, Recapitalisation, Reforms.
Banks now also raise capital via **AT-1** and **Tier 2** bonds (e.g. **Canara Bank** up to **₹4,500 crore** AT-1).

85.s: The '4R' strategy adopted for cleaning up public sector banks stands for:
85.x: The 4R strategy is Recognition (of NPAs), Resolution, Recapitalisation and Reforms. The other options swap in terms such as Recovery, Restructuring, Regulation, Refinance and Reorganisation, which are not part of the official 4Rs.
85.tq: 4R = Recognise, Resolve, Recapitalise, Reform.
xs: The **4R strategy** = **Recognition, Resolution, Recapitalisation, Reforms** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Recovery, Restructuring, Regulation, Refinance and Reorganisation are not among the 4Rs.
xa: Consolidation + recapitalisation + 4Rs lifted SCB **CRAR to 17.36%** and **PSB CRAR to 16.10%**.
SCB credit grew from **₹67 lakh crore (Mar 2015)** to **₹181 lakh crore (Mar 2025)**.
GNPA fell to a multi-decadal low.

85.s: The Banks Board Bureau was established to perform which of the following functions in relation to public sector banks?
o: Determine the statutory liquidity ratio for all banks
Select chairpersons of public sector banks
Approve the Union Budget on behalf of Parliament
85.x: The Banks Board Bureau selects chairpersons of public sector banks. Its creation followed the recommendations of the P.J. Nayak Committee.
85.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish institutional functions.
xs: The **Banks Board Bureau** selects **PSB chairmen/whole-time directors** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It also advises on governance; it does not fix SLR, regulate securities or approve budgets.
xa: BBB came from **2016** after the **P.J. Nayak Committee (2014)**.
Composition: a chairman + **3** ex-officio members + **5** experts.
Replaced in **2022** by the **Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB)**.

85.s:
Which of the following was proposed by the P.J. Nayak Committee?
1. Creation of a Bank Investment Company
2. Reduction of the Government’s stake below 50 percent
3. Professionalisation of public sector bank boards
85.x: The committee proposed a Bank Investment Company to hold the Government’s stake, reduction of that stake below 50 percent, and professional boards for public sector banks.
85.tq: Recognise the reform package rather than isolating one recommendation.
xs: All three were P.J. Nayak proposals — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
It proposed a **Bank Investment Company** to hold the Govt stake, cutting that stake **below 50%**.
It also called for **professional boards** for PSBs.
xa: The **P.J. Nayak Committee (2014, RBI)** found weak PSB board governance.
It led to the **Banks Board Bureau (2016)**.
Some notes misprint the name as "J. Nayak".

85.s: The Banks Board Bureau was established in 2016 as an idea associated with which initiative?
85.x: The Banks Board Bureau originated from the Indradhanush initiative and began functioning in 2016.
85.tq: Link the institutional reform body with the programme from which it emerged.
xs: The BBB (**2016**) was an **Indradhanush** idea — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Banks Board Bureau** is item "B" of Indradhanush's **7-point plan (A-G)**.
xa: It followed the **P.J. Nayak Committee (2014)**.
It selects **PSB chairmen/whole-time directors**.
Replaced in **2022** by the **FSIB**.

85.s: In 2022, the Banks Board Bureau was replaced by the:
85.x: The Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB) replaced the Banks Board Bureau in 2022.
85.tq: Use the successor institution to resolve a governance-body question.
xs: In **2022**, the BBB was replaced by the **Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Like the BBB, it selects **PSB chairmen/whole-time directors**.
xa: The BBB started in **2016** (an **Indradhanush** idea).
BBB had a chairman + **3** ex-officio members + **5** experts.
The **P.J. Nayak Committee** proposed a **Bank Investment Company** — ⚠ not the same as option (3).

85.s:
Consider the following statements about EASE (Enhanced Access and Service Excellence):
1. It was conceptualised in 2015, launched in 2017 and became the PSB Reforms Agenda from January 2018.
2. It is governed by a board of heads of premier financial institutions.
3. PSBs report quarterly against its benchmarks, overseen by the EASE Steering Committee of the Indian Banks' Association.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: conceptualised 2015, launched 2017, Reforms Agenda from Jan 2018. Statement 2 is wrong (APPSC G1 2024 trap): EASE is run by IBA's EASE Steering Committee, not a board of heads of premier FIs. Statement 3 is correct. Hence 1 and 3 only.
85.tq: EASE = IBA steering committee; 'board of heads of premier FIs' is the trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: conceptualised **2015**, launched **2017**, Reforms Agenda from **Jan 2018** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: "governed by a board of heads of premier FIs" is **false** (APPSC-G1 2024 key).
Statement 3: PSBs report quarterly to the **EASE Steering Committee of the IBA** — correct.
xa: **EASE 5.0-7.0** = **EASENext**, after **PSB Manthan 2.0** (**Apr 2022**).
The **EASE Index** ranks mid-size and large PSBs every quarter.

85.s:
Assertion (A): The EASE Index ranks participating public sector banks on reform performance.
Reason (R): The index benchmarks mid-size and large public sector banks against reform themes every quarter.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
85.x: Both statements are true. Quarterly benchmarking of mid-size and large public sector banks against reform themes provides the basis for ranking them in the EASE Index.
85.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the institutional function stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** of A — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **EASE Index** benchmarks **mid-size and large PSBs** on reform themes **each quarter** and then **ranks** them.
xa: EASE is run by the **IBA's EASE Steering Committee**.
Aims: financial stability, credit growth, **NPA management**, risk mitigation, digital transformation, customer service, inclusion.
**EASE 1.0-4.0**: digitisation, asset quality, governance, HR.

85.s: The four focus areas of EASE 8.0, also called “EASE ₹ise”, for FY2026 are:
o: Risk and Resilience, Innovation, Socio-economic impact, Excellence
85.x: EASE 8.0 or EASE ₹ise focuses on Risk and Resilience, Innovation, Socio-economic impact and Excellence.
85.tq: Match the programme version with its exact four-part theme set.
xs: **EASE 8.0 / "EASE ₹ise"** focuses on **Risk & Resilience, Innovation, Socio-economic impact, Excellence** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The initials spell **R-I-S-E**, matching the name "₹ise".
xa: **EASE 5.0-7.0** = **EASENext**, after **PSB Manthan 2.0** (**Apr 2022**).
EASE was launched in **2017**; PSB Reforms Agenda from **Jan 2018**.

85.s: The merger of 10 public sector banks into 4 came into effect from:
85.x: Ten public sector banks were merged into four with effect from 1 April 2020.
85.tq: Anchor the reform to its exact effective date and distinguish it from the 2017 recapitalisation announcement.
xs: The "**ten into four**" merger took effect from **1 April 2020** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**1 April 2019** was the **Dena + Vijaya → Bank of Baroda** merger.
xa: 2020 mergers: OBC + United → **PNB**; Syndicate → **Canara**; Andhra + Corporation → **Union Bank**; Allahabad → **Indian Bank**.
It followed the **SBI-associates merger of 2017**.
PSB count fell from **27 (2017) to 12 (2020)**.

85.s:
Arrange the following banking-sector amalgamations in chronological order:
A. Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank with Bank of Baroda
B. SBI associates and Bharatiya Mahila Bank with SBI
C. Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank with Union Bank of India
D. Allahabad Bank with Indian Bank
85.x: The mergers took effect in the order: SBI-related merger in 2017, Dena–Vijaya with Bank of Baroda in 2019, and Andhra–Corporation and Allahabad Bank mergers in 2020.
85.tq: Arrange events by their effective dates, giving priority to the distinct 2017 and 2019 milestones.
xs: Order: **SBI associates (2017)** → **Dena + Vijaya (2019)** → **Andhra + Corporation (2020)** → **Allahabad (2020)** — so option **(1) B, A, C, D** is correct.
C and D both took effect on **1 Apr 2020**; B was **1 Apr 2017** and A **1 Apr 2019**.
xa: **Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged into SBI with the associates.
The 2020 step merged **10 PSBs** into **4**.

85.s: Which of the following was NOT an expected gain from the consolidation of public sector banks?
o: Creation of lenders capable of competing globally
Economies of scale and lower costs
Permanent elimination of all non-performing assets
Better capital utilisation and risk management
85.x: The expected gains included scale, lower costs, global-size lenders, better capital use and improved risk management. Permanent elimination of all NPAs was not stated as an expected gain.
85.tq: Reject the extreme outcome that goes beyond the stated objectives of bank consolidation.
xs: **Permanent elimination of all NPAs** was NOT a stated merger gain — so option **(3)** is correct.
Stated gains: **scale**, **global-size lenders**, **lower costs**, **stronger capital**, **better capital use and risk management**.
xa: The idea of fewer, stronger banks came from **Narasimham-II**.
Mergers bring **integration costs** (criticism).
PSB count fell from **27** to **12**.

85.s: The idea of creating fewer and stronger banks through mergers was associated particularly with:
85.x: Narasimham-II recommended consolidation through mergers of strong banks and the creation of fewer, stronger banking institutions.
85.tq: Distinguish the consolidation agenda of Narasimham-II from the foundational reforms of Narasimham-I.
xs: Fewer, stronger banks through mergers was a **Narasimham-II** idea — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Narasimham-I** focused on prudential norms and SLR/CRR cuts; **Goiporia** = customer service; **Malhotra** = insurance.
xa: Narasimham-II: set up **Dec 1997**, report **April 1998**; **3-tier structure**.
It recommended **CRAR 10%** and **universal banking**.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about Regional Rural Banks:
1. Under One State One RRB, RRBs were amalgamated state by state, leaving 28 RRBs.
2. Viability Plan 2.0 was drawn up by NABARD for the period 2023-24 to 2025-26.
3. Viability Plan 2.0 tracks RRBs on 30 parameters such as CRAR, credit-deposit ratio and NPAs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: state-by-state amalgamation left 28 RRBs. Statement 2 is wrong: Viability Plan 2.0 is by DFS and covers 2025-26 to 2027-28. Statement 3 is correct: 30 parameters including CRAR, CD ratio and NPAs. Hence 1 and 3 only.
85.tq: Viability Plan 2.0 = DFS, 2025-26 to 2027-28, 28 RRBs, 30 parameters, 4 pillars.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: **One State-One RRB** left **28 RRBs** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: Viability Plan 2.0 is by **DFS**, for **2025-26 to 2027-28**.
Statement 3: it uses **30 parameters** (CRAR, CD ratio, NPAs) — correct.
xa: **4 pillars**: operational excellence, asset quality, profitability, growth.
**15 RRBs** amalgamated, effective **1 May 2025**.

85.s: How many Regional Rural Banks existed originally, and how many remained after the 2020–21 consolidation?
85.x: There were originally 196 RRBs, and their number came down to 43 after the 2020–21 consolidation.
85.tq: Keep the successive consolidation stages distinct instead of confusing the final figure with the intermediate figure.
xs: RRBs were originally **196**, falling to **43** after the **2020-21** consolidation — so option **(4) 196 and 43 respectively** is correct.
**28** is the count after **One State-One RRB** (May 2026), not after 2020-21.
xa: **15 RRBs** were amalgamated, effective **1 May 2025**.
The Centre keeps its **50%** share.
**Viability Plan 2.0** tracks all **28** RRBs on **30 parameters**.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about the One State-One RRB arrangement:
1. Fifteen RRBs were amalgamated.
2. The arrangement became effective on 1 May 2025.
3. The Centre retains a 50 per cent share in RRBs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: All three statements are correct: 15 RRBs were amalgamated, the arrangement took effect on 1 May 2025, and the Centre retains a 50 per cent share.
85.tq: Combine the consolidation count, effective date and ownership detail.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1: **15 RRBs** were amalgamated — correct.
Statement 2: effective **1 May 2025** — correct.
Statement 3: the Centre keeps its **50%** share — correct.
xa: RRBs now number **28** (May 2026), down from **196** originally and **43** after 2020-21.
**Viability Plan 2.0** (DFS) runs **2025-26 to 2027-28**.

85.s: Which of the following correctly describes the ownership status of DICGC?
o: It is owned by all scheduled commercial banks
It is an autonomous department of the Ministry of Finance
It is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India
It is a jointly owned subsidiary of RBI and SEBI
85.x: DICGC is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India.
85.tq: Apply the ‘who owns or supervises this body?’ test.
xs: **DICGC** is a **wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is not owned by banks, the Finance Ministry or SEBI.
xa: Set up in **1978** by merging the **Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962)** and the **Credit Guarantee Corporation**.
Cover: **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank**.
The premium is **paid by banks**, not depositors.

85.s: The DICGC deposit insurance limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in the Budget for:
85.x: The deposit insurance limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in the 2020–21 Budget, following the PMC Bank crisis.
85.tq: Connect the revised figure with the budget year in which it was introduced.
xs: The limit rose from **₹1 lakh** to **₹5 lakh** in the **2020-21 Budget** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It followed the **PMC Bank** crisis.
xa: DICGC is a wholly owned **RBI subsidiary**, set up in **1978**.
Cover is **per depositor per bank**.
⚠ NBFC deposits are **not** DICGC-insured.

85.s:
Which of the following deposits are NOT covered by DICGC deposit insurance?
1. Inter-bank deposits
2. Deposits accepted by NBFCs
3. Deposits in Indian branches of foreign banks
4. Deposits of State governments
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
85.x: Inter-bank deposits, NBFC deposits and deposits of foreign, Central and State governments are excluded. Deposits in foreign bank branches in India are covered (all commercial banks incl. foreign bank branches). Hence 1, 2 and 4 only; options with 3 are wrong and '1 and 2 only' misses government deposits.
85.tq: Excluded: government deposits, inter-bank, NBFC. Foreign bank branches, RRBs and co-op banks are covered.
xs: Items 1, 2 and 4 are not covered — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only** is correct.
Excluded: **inter-bank deposits**, **NBFC deposits**, deposits of foreign, Central and **State governments**.
Item 3 is covered: DICGC covers all commercial banks **incl. foreign bank branches**.
xa: **RRBs** and **co-operative banks** are also covered.
Cover: **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank**.
Premium is paid by banks.

85.s: With regard to DICGC insurance, who bears the premium burden?
o: The insured bank, and not the depositor
RBI and the depositor in equal shares
85.x: Banks pay the DICGC insurance premium; the depositor does not pay it.
85.tq: Identify the party responsible for payment rather than the beneficiary of insurance.
xs: The DICGC premium is **paid by the insured bank, not the depositor** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Neither the Govt nor the depositor pays it; the bank bears the cost of the insurance.
xa: DICGC: wholly owned **RBI subsidiary**, set up **1978**.
Cover: **₹5 lakh** per depositor per bank (from **₹1 lakh**, in the **2020-21 Budget**).
Excluded: government, inter-bank and **NBFC** deposits.

85.s: LIC acquired a majority stake in IDBI Bank in 2019. What was the consequence of this transaction for the regulatory classification of IDBI Bank?
o: It was reclassified by RBI as a private sector lender
It was classified as a foreign bank subsidiary
It was converted into a cooperative bank
It was classified by RBI as a regional rural bank
85.x: Following LIC’s acquisition of a majority stake in 2019, RBI reclassified IDBI Bank as a private sector lender.
85.tq: Link the transaction to its direct regulatory consequence.
xs: After **LIC** bought a majority stake in **2019**, RBI **reclassified IDBI Bank as a private lender** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was not made a foreign subsidiary, co-operative bank or RRB.
xa: Govt + LIC are selling a combined **60.72%** strategic stake.
Budget **2021-22** announced privatisation of **two PSBs and one general insurance company**.
Minority stake sales were weighed in **UCO**, **BoM**, **Central Bank**, **Punjab & Sind** and **IOB**.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025:
1. The 'substantial interest' threshold was raised from ₹5 lakh to ₹2 crore.
2. The tenure of co-operative bank directors was raised from 8 to 10 years.
3. Unclaimed shares of public sector banks can be transferred to the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the Act. Statement 3 is wrong: unclaimed PSB shares can go to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF), not the Consolidated Fund. Hence 1 and 2 only.
85.tq: Unclaimed shares/dividends always go to IEPF.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: "substantial interest" rose from **₹5 lakh to ₹2 crore** — correct.
Statement 2: co-op bank directors' tenure rose from **8 to 10 years** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: unclaimed PSB shares go to the **IEPF**, not the Consolidated Fund.
xa: The Act came into force on **1 Aug 2025** with **19 amendments**.
**AITUC** called it a "clear call to privatisation" (**2 Feb 2026**).

85.s: The Union Budget 2021–22 announced the privatisation of:
o: Three public sector banks and one general insurance company
Two private banks and one public sector insurer
One public sector bank and two life insurance companies
Two public sector banks and one general insurance company
85.x: The Budget 2021–22 announced the privatisation of two public sector banks and one general insurance company.
85.tq: Keep the numerical composition of the privatisation announcement intact.
xs: Budget **2021-22** announced privatisation of **two PSBs and one general insurance company** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The other options change the number or type of entities named in the Budget.
xa: The debate: **efficiency and governance** vs **social mandate** (rural branches, priority lending).
**IDBI Bank** was reclassified as a private lender after **LIC** bought a majority stake (**2019**).
Govt + LIC are selling a combined **60.72%** IDBI stake.

85.s: Which of the following correctly represents a major argument in the debate over privatisation of public sector banks?
o: Public ownership has no connection with financial inclusion
Privatisation may improve efficiency and governance, while public ownership supports social mandates
Privatisation necessarily eliminates rural branches and priority lending in every case
Privatisation is intended primarily to increase deposit insurance cover
85.x: The debate balances possible gains in efficiency and governance against the social mandate of public sector banks, including rural branches and priority lending.
85.tq: Compare the two sides of the policy debate without treating either as absolute.
xs: The debate is **efficiency and governance (privatisation)** vs the **social mandate** of PSBs — so option **(2)** is correct.
The social mandate means **rural branches** and **priority lending**; option (3) overstates it as "in every case".
xa: Unions say privatisation would weaken **PSL**, rural credit and inclusion (**2 Feb 2026**).
Budget **2021-22**: privatise **two PSBs** and **one general insurer**.
**DICGC** cover is unrelated to privatisation.

85.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under UDAY (November 2015), States took over 75% of DISCOM debt.
2. The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) was launched in 2015 along with UDAY.
3. RDSS provides results-linked DISCOM funding with an AT&C loss target of 12-15%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: UDAY (Nov 2015) shifted 75% of DISCOM debt to States. Statement 2 is wrong: RDSS came in 2021. Statement 3 is correct: results-linked funding, smart meters, AT&C target 12-15%. Hence 1 and 3 only.
85.tq: UDAY 2015 = debt takeover; RDSS 2021 = results-linked funding and smart meters.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: under **UDAY (Nov 2015)**, States took over **75%** of DISCOM debt — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: **RDSS** came in **2021**, not 2015.
Statement 3: RDSS = results-linked DISCOM funding, smart meters, **AT&C target 12-15%** — correct.
xa: **Indradhanush** for PSBs was also launched in **2015** (Aug).
⚠ UDAY = DISCOM debt takeover; RDSS = results-linked funding and smart meters.

85.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Basel Accords — Bank capital, liquidity and risk
2. Basel Convention — Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes
3. Basel Accords — UNEP-administered treaty
4. Basel Convention — BCBS/BIS framework
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
85.x: The Basel Accords concern bank capital, liquidity and risk and are associated with BCBS/BIS. The Basel Convention is a UNEP-administered treaty on hazardous wastes; therefore pairs 3 and 4 are reversed.
85.tq: Separate the similarly named financial framework from the environmental treaty.
xs: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
**Basel Accords** = bank capital, liquidity and risk, framed by **BCBS/BIS**.
**Basel Convention** = transboundary movement of **hazardous wastes**, a **UNEP-administered treaty** — so pairs 3 and 4 swap the bodies.
xa: The Basel Convention was adopted in **1989** and came into force in **1992**.
BIS was set up in **1930**, the world's oldest international financial organisation.
Basel I **1988**, Basel II **2004**, Basel III in India from **1 Jan 2013**.

85.s:
Which of the following was included in the banking-related measures announced in the Union Budget 2026–27?
1. High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat
2. Restructuring of PFC and REC
3. Activation of the countercyclical capital buffer by RBI
85.x: The Budget 2026–27 announced the High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat and restructuring of PFC and REC. RBI had kept the countercyclical capital buffer inactive, so statement 3 is false.
85.tq: Find the one statement that reverses the stated status of a policy instrument.
xs: Items 1 and 2 were Budget **2026-27** measures — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Budget 2026-27 announced the **High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat** and restructuring of **PFC/REC** (**2 Feb 2026**).
Item 3 is wrong: RBI kept the **CCyB un-activated** (May 2026).
xa: The CCyB framework (**0-2.5%**) has existed since **2015**; trigger = **credit-to-GDP gap**.
RBI's **Oct 2025** draft proposed lower risk weights for MSMEs and real estate.
An **ECL** shift may cut Tier-1 ratios by **100-150 bps**.

85.s: Who founded Andhra Bank at Machilipatnam?
85.x: Andhra Bank was founded at Machilipatnam by Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
85.tq: Use the founder–institution association rather than the merger fact.
xs: **Andhra Bank** was founded at **Machilipatnam** (**1923**) by **Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**P.J. Nayak** chaired the **2014** committee on bank board governance.
xa: Andhra Bank lost its identity, merging into **Union Bank of India** on **1 Apr 2020** (APPSC GS 2025 PYQ).
**Corporation Bank** merged into Union Bank at the same time.
Other 2020 mergers: OBC + United → **PNB**; Syndicate → **Canara**; Allahabad → **Indian Bank**.

85.s: Which of the following is cited as a criticism of public sector bank privatisation by trade unions?
o: It would make recapitalisation unnecessary in every case
It would weaken priority sector lending, rural credit and financial inclusion
It would increase the number of rural branches automatically
It would eliminate all integration costs arising from mergers
85.x: Trade unions have argued that privatisation could weaken priority sector lending, rural credit and financial inclusion.
85.tq: Connect the policy proposal with its stated social-sector concern.
xs: Unions argue privatisation would **weaken priority sector lending, rural credit and financial inclusion** — so option **(2)** is correct (**2 Feb 2026**).
The pro-privatisation case is **efficiency and governance**; the counter is the PSB **social mandate**.
xa: **AITUC** called the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act 2025 a "clear call to privatisation".
Budget **2021-22** announced privatisation of **two PSBs and one general insurance company**.
Mergers bring **integration costs** — another criticism.

85.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Tarapore Committee – I
(b) Tarapore Committee – II
(c) Narasimham Committee – I
(d) Narasimham Committee – II

List-II

86.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?

xs: **Sub-standard asset — NPA for 12 months or less** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Doubtful** = NPA for **more than 12 months**, not "standard".
**Standard** = regular account with no overdue beyond **90 days**; **loss** = identified loss not yet written off.
xa: SMA accounts (**1-90 days** overdue) are stressed but still standard.
Sequence: Standard → SMA-0/1/2 → NPA (sub-standard → doubtful → loss).

86.s:

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statement 1 is correct: Net NPA = Gross NPA - provisions. Statement 2 is wrong: PCR is the reverse, provisions held divided by gross NPAs. Statement 3 is correct: stressed assets = NPAs + restructured loans + written-off assets. Hence 1 and 3 only.
86.tq: PCR puts provisions on top; stressed assets is wider than NPAs.

Option (1) reverses the rule.

xa: **PCR** = provisions held / gross NPAs.

86.s:

Statement 2 is wrong: the **2008** crisis and **weak exports hurt** borrowers' cash flows.
xa: **Wilful defaults and fraud**: promoters diverted funds to shell companies.
**Evergreening** kept defaults hidden.
Vicious cycle: lending + shocks → NPAs → provisioning → capital erosion → weak credit.

86.s: Evergreening of loans means:

**Stressed assets** = NPAs + restructured loans + written-off assets.
**Wilful defaulter**: can pay but does not, or diverts funds.

The **2008** crisis and weak exports hurt borrowers' cash flows.
This cycle fed the **twin balance sheet problem**.

Large private banks (June 2026): HDFC **1.17%**, ICICI **1.38%**, Axis **1.28%**.

86.s:
Which of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the banking-sector NPA trend?
1. GNPA has fallen for eight straight years.
2. Agriculture GNPA remains relatively high at about 6.0 per cent.
3. Agriculture GNPA is lower than 1 per cent.
4. September 2025 GNPA was reported at 2.15 per cent.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
86.x: Statement 3 is incorrect because agriculture GNPA was reported at about 6.0 per cent, with another estimate at 5.7 per cent. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct.
86.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the reported sectoral trend.
xs: Only statement 3 is incorrect — so option **(3) 3 only** is correct.
Agriculture GNPA is still high at **6.0%** (some notes say **5.7%**), not below 1%.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct: GNPA fell for **eight straight years**; **Sep 2025** GNPA was **2.15%**.

86.s: Under income-recognition norms, interest on an NPA is booked as income:
o: Only when it is actually received
After the asset is written off
When it is accrued, whether or not received
86.x: Interest on an NPA is not recognised as income until it is actually received. This forms part of the IRACP framework.
86.tq: Apply the recognition rule to distinguish accrual from actual receipt.
xs: Under **income recognition**, interest on an NPA is booked **only when actually received** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Booking on accrual regardless of receipt is what the rule prevents.
xa: It is part of **IRACP**: Income Recognition, Asset Classification, Provisioning.
An asset is an NPA when overdue **more than 90 days**.

86.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the new borrower-level NPA tagging system:
1. The system is to be effective from 1 April 2027.
2. If one loan of a borrower becomes an NPA, all loans of that borrower at the same bank become NPAs.
3. An account can be upgraded even if arrears on one facility remain unpaid.
4. Banks are required to identify NPAs through automated systems.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
86.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. An account is upgraded only after all arrears on every facility have been paid, so statement 3 is false.
86.tq: Find the single reversal in the condition for upgrading an account.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only** is correct.
Statement 1: effective from **1 April 2027** — correct.
Statement 2: **borrower-level tagging** — one NPA loan makes all that borrower's loans NPAs — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: upgrade only after **all arrears on every facility** are paid; statement 4 (**automated systems**) is correct.
xa: The **90-day** overdue test stays.
RBI is moving to a 3-stage **ECL** model.

86.s:
Match the stages of the Expected Credit Loss model with their provisioning treatment.
List-I
 a. Stage 1
 b. Stage 2
 c. Stage 3
 d. EIR method
List-II
 i. Lifetime expected loss
 ii. Effective interest rate method
 iii. 12-month expected loss
 iv. Full lifetime provision for credit-impaired assets
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
86.x: Stage 1 involves 12-month expected loss, Stage 2 lifetime loss, Stage 3 full lifetime provision, and loss allowances use the effective interest rate method.
86.tq: Start with the distinctive EIR pair and then match the three stages by severity.
xs: Correct matching: **a–iii, b–i, c–iv, d–ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Stage 1** = **12-month** expected loss; **Stage 2** = lifetime loss.
**Stage 3** (credit-impaired, over **90 days**) = full lifetime provision; loss allowances use the **EIR** method.
xa: ECL replaces the **incurred-loss** model from **1 April 2027**.
Criticism: ECL **raises capital needs**.

86.s: Under its new provisioning framework, the RBI is moving from which approach to which approach?
o: From a 3-stage ECL model to a 2-stage incurred-loss model
From incurred-loss model to a 3-stage Expected Credit Loss model
From a 90-day overdue test to a 180-day overdue test
86.x: The RBI is shifting from the incurred-loss model to a forward-looking 3-stage Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model; the 90-day overdue test stays.
86.tq: Provide before the loss happens: incurred → expected.
xs: RBI is moving **from the incurred-loss model to a 3-stage ECL model** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses it; the **90-day** test is unchanged.
xa: Stage 1 = **12-month** loss; Stage 2 = lifetime; Stage 3 = full lifetime provision.
Loss allowances use the **effective interest rate (EIR)** method.
ECL may cut Tier-1 ratios — a capital concern.

86.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank in FY26:
1. Its GNPA was reported at 0.91%.
2. Its NNPA was reported as nil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Both statements are correct: Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank reported GNPA of 0.91% and NNPA as nil in FY26.
86.tq: Verify each numerical statement independently before choosing the combined code.
xs: Both statements are correct — so option **(3) Both 1 and 2** is correct.
**Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank** reported GNPA **0.91%** and NNPA **nil** in **FY26**.
xa: National SCB GNPA in March 2026: **1.93%**.
National NNPA: **0.39%** (March 2026).

86.s:
Consider the following statements about the clean-up of bank balance sheets in India:
1. Credit of Scheduled Commercial Banks nearly tripled from about ₹67 lakh crore in 2015 to about ₹181 lakh crore in 2025.
2. The CRAR of Scheduled Commercial Banks stood at about 17.3%.
3. Credit of Scheduled Commercial Banks shrank between 2015 and 2025 as balance sheets were cleaned up.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statement 1 is correct: SCB credit nearly tripled from ₹67 lakh crore (2015) to ₹181 lakh crore (2025). Statement 2 is correct: SCB CRAR was 17.3%. Statement 3 is wrong: credit expanded, it did not shrink. Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' leaves out 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
86.tq: Clean balance sheets → credit tripled (67 → 181 lakh crore), CRAR 17.3%.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: SCB credit nearly tripled, **₹67 lakh crore (2015) → ₹181 lakh crore (2025)** — correct.
Statement 2: SCB **CRAR 17.3%** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: credit **expanded** as balance sheets were cleaned up.
xa: GNPA fell to **1.93%** (March 2026).
GNPA has fallen for **eight straight years**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR):
1. It is calculated as interest payable divided by EBIT.
2. An ICR below 1 means the firm cannot service its interest.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is wrong: ICR = EBIT / interest payable (the ratio is inverted in the statement). Statement 2 is correct: below 1, earnings do not cover interest. So '2 only'.
87.tq: Coverage = what you earn over what you owe: EBIT on top.
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — so option **(2) 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: **ICR = EBIT / interest payable** — the statement inverts it.
Statement 2 is correct: ICR below **1** → the firm **cannot service its interest**.
xa: Lenders use ICR to judge a borrower's **present and emerging risk**.
**PCR** = provisions / gross NPA; higher PCR → more resilient bank.
**Twin Balance Sheet problem**: over-leveraged corporates + capital-starved banks.

87.s: What is meant by ‘evergreening’ of loans?
o: Writing off an old loan after full recovery
Giving a fresh loan to repay an old loan so that the NPA remains hidden
Increasing the maturity of a standard loan without any new borrowing
Converting every NPA into a government-guaranteed bond
87.x: Evergreening occurs when fresh loans are used to repay old loans, thereby concealing the underlying NPA.
87.tq: Discriminate between concealment through fresh lending and genuine recovery.
xs: **Evergreening** = a **fresh loan to repay an old loan**, so the **NPA stays hidden** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **AQR** exposed this practice.
xa: Other causes of NPAs: **loan frauds and diversion of funds**, weak credit appraisal, slow recovery machinery, corporate over-leverage.
The **twin balance sheet problem** stalls private capex and squeezes **MSME** credit.
**ICR** below **1** → the firm cannot service its interest.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR):
1. PCR is provisions divided by gross NPA.
2. A higher PCR indicates a less resilient bank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: PCR = provisions / gross NPA. Statement 2 is wrong: a higher PCR means more of the bad loans are provided for, so the bank is more resilient. So '1 only'.
87.tq: More provisions per rupee of bad loans = more cushion.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
Statement 1: **PCR = provisions / gross NPA** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: a **higher PCR → more resilient** bank.
xa: SCB PCR: **76.3%** (Mar 2025, FSR basis).
Govt data gives **93.14%** for SCBs — a different basis.

87.s: The March 2026 SCB Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was characterised as a:
87.x: The March 2026 Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was described as a decadal low.
87.tq: Match the latest numerical value with its stated trend description.
xs: SCB GNPA of **1.93%** in **Mar 2026** was a **decadal low** — so option **(3)** is correct.
NNPA was **0.39%**.
xa: Up next: **ECL** provisioning and higher risk weights on unsecured consumer credit + NBFC exposures.

87.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the reasons cited for the decline in NPAs?
o: The 4R strategy, higher provisioning, IBC and NARCL
Higher unsecured lending and lower capital adequacy
Evergreening, weaker appraisal and reduced recovery
Lower provisioning, repeal of IBC and closure of NARCL
87.x: The decline in NPAs has been attributed to the 4R strategy, higher provisioning, the IBC and NARCL.
87.tq: Select the option containing the complete set of stated policy drivers.
xs: NPAs fell because of the **4R strategy, higher provisioning, IBC and NARCL** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Options (2)-(4) list causes of stress (or their opposites), not reasons for recovery.
xa: **IBC** delivered **48%** of bank recoveries in FY24.
**NARCL** aggregates stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**.

87.s: Which of the following changes is indicated as the next step in provisioning and credit-risk regulation?
o: Replacing ECL with SMA classification and reducing risk weights on unsecured credit
Using only Gross NPA for provisioning and discontinuing risk weights
Abolishing provisioning for NBFC exposures and all consumer loans
Moving to Expected Credit Loss provisioning and increasing risk weights on unsecured consumer credit and NBFC exposures
87.x: The indicated changes are a move to Expected Credit Loss provisioning and higher risk weights for unsecured consumer credit and NBFC exposures.
87.tq: Identify the forward-looking regulatory changes without reversing their direction.
xs: Next steps: **Expected Credit Loss (ECL) provisioning** and **higher risk weights on unsecured consumer credit and NBFC exposures** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Options (1)-(3) reverse or abolish these measures.
xa: GNPA at a decadal low of **1.93%** (Mar 2026).

87.s: The Debt Recovery Tribunals were established under which enactment?
o: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
87.x: DRTs were established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, and are also used under SARFAESI.
87.tq: Identify the parent enactment while avoiding confusion with the later laws under which DRTs also function.
xs: DRTs were set up under the **Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and FIs Act, 1993 (RDDBFI)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They are **also used under SARFAESI (2002)**, but SARFAESI did not create them.
xa: **39 DRTs** and **5 DRATs**; debts **above ₹20 lakh**.
**e-DRT** launched **1 Oct 2018**; e-filing mandatory from **1 Feb 2023**.
⚠ **1987** = Lok Adalats; **1993** = DRTs; **2002** = SARFAESI.

87.s: The DRT framework described applies to debts above:
87.x: The DRTs and DRATs handle debts above ₹20 lakh under the stated framework.
87.tq: Use ascending monetary thresholds to distinguish DRT jurisdiction from the CIRP default threshold.
xs: DRTs handle debts **above ₹20 lakh** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**₹1 crore** is the minimum default for triggering **CIRP** under the IBC.
xa: DRTs were set up under the **RDDBFI Act, 1993**.
**Lok Adalats** handle **small NPAs** only.
**e-DRT**: launched **1 Oct 2018**.

87.s: Which of the following correctly matches the recovery mechanism with its share of bank recoveries in FY 2024?
87.x: The FY 2024 shares were IBC 48%, SARFAESI 32%, DRTs 17% and Lok Adalats 3%.
87.tq: Match the complete percentage pattern, beginning with the largest recovery channel.
xs: FY24 shares: **IBC 48%**, **SARFAESI 32%**, **DRTs 17%**, **Lok Adalats 3%** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The other options shuffle the same four percentages.
xa: **Lok Adalats** handle small NPAs only.
Comparison: **SARFAESI** (secured lenders, no court) vs **IBC** (collective, NCLT-led) vs **DRT** (tribunal recovery).
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value.

87.s: The Lok Adalats that facilitate settlement of small non-performing assets derive their statutory status from which enactment?
o: The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
87.x: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
87.tq: Identify the statute specifically associated with the forum.
xs: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1993** is the **RDDBFI Act** (DRTs); **2002** is **SARFAESI**; **2016** is the **IBC**.
xa: They offer **quick, fee-free settlement** of small loans by compromise.
**National Lok Adalat (13 Sep 2026)**: **DRT Visakhapatnam bench** settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.
Lok Adalats delivered **3%** of FY24 bank recoveries.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the SARFAESI Act, 2002:
1. Lenders holding 60% of the dues can issue a 60-day notice under Section 13(2).
2. Under Section 13(4), lenders can take possession of the secured asset, take over management or sell it.
3. Under Section 13(8), the borrower can redeem the asset even after the auction notice by paying 25% of the dues.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: lenders with 60% of dues (75% before the 2016 amendment) issue a 60-day notice under Sec 13(2). Statement 2 is correct: Sec 13(4) allows possession, takeover of management or sale. Statement 3 is wrong: under Sec 13(8) the borrower can redeem only by paying the full dues before the auction notice. So '1 and 2 only'.
87.tq: 13(2) notice, 13(4) action, 13(8) redemption - full dues, before the auction notice.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: lenders with **60%** of dues issue a **60-day** notice under **Sec 13(2)** — correct.
Statement 2: **Sec 13(4)** allows possession, takeover of management or sale — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: under **Sec 13(8)** the borrower redeems only by paying **full dues**, and only **until** the auction notice is published.
xa: **Sec 17**: appeal to the **DRT** within **45 days**; **Sec 18** bars civil courts.
The **AP High Court** clarified **Sec 13(8)** redemption and auction rules (May 2026).

87.s: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 was based on the recommendations of the:
87.x: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 was based on the Narasimham Committee.
87.tq: Match a financial reform law with the committee associated with its formulation.
xs: **SARFAESI 2002** was based on the **Narasimham Committee** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Full name: **Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002**.
xa: Core feature: banks enforce security on NPAs **without court intervention**.
⚠ The **IBC** was based on the **T.K. Viswanathan Committee (2015)**, not Narasimham.
**ARCs** under SARFAESI are registered with and regulated by **RBI**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the SARFAESI Act, 2002:
1. Section 13(2) provides for a 30-day demand notice.
2. Under Section 17, an appeal lies to the DRT within 45 days.
3. Section 18 bars civil courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Sec 13(2) demand notice is 60 days. Statement 2 is correct: Sec 17 allows an appeal to the DRT within 45 days. Statement 3 is correct: Sec 18 bars civil courts. So '2 and 3 only'.
87.tq: 60-day notice, 45-day appeal to DRT, civil courts barred.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: the **Sec 13(2)** notice is **60 days**, not 30.
Statement 2: **Sec 17** — appeal to the **DRT** within **45 days** — correct.
Statement 3: **Sec 18** bars civil courts — correct.
xa: ⚠ **60%** of lenders + **60-day** notice; appeal within **45 days**.
**Sec 13(4)**: possession, takeover of management or sale.

87.s: Which of the following correctly describes Asset Reconstruction Companies under the SARFAESI framework?
o: They buy NPAs at a discount and are regulated by the RBI
They issue currency and are regulated by the Ministry of Finance
They buy only performing assets at face value and are regulated by SEBI
They adjudicate appeals from the DRT
87.x: ARCs acquire NPAs, generally at a discount, and are regulated by the RBI.
87.tq: Combine the entity’s activity and regulator to avoid a regulator-swap trap.
xs: **ARCs buy NPAs at a discount** and are **regulated by RBI** — so option **(1)** is correct.
They pay against **security receipts** and are registered with RBI under **SARFAESI**.
Appeals from DRTs go to **DRATs**, not ARCs.
xa: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", pays **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.
SARFAESI is based on the **Narasimham Committee**.

87.s:
Arrange the following earlier debt-resolution mechanisms in chronological order of their introduction:
A. Strategic Debt Restructuring
B. Corporate Debt Restructuring
C. S4A
D. 5/25 scheme
87.x: Corporate Debt Restructuring was introduced in 2001, followed by the 5/25 scheme in 2014, Strategic Debt Restructuring in 2015 and S4A in 2016.
87.tq: Fix the earliest and latest items first, then arrange the intervening years.
xs: CDR is the oldest; S4A, the newest of the four, split debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts.
xa: **Project Sashakt** (Inter-Creditor Agreement) followed in **2018**.
**Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets**: **7 June 2019**.
The **IBC** was enacted in **2016**, the same year as S4A.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about S4A:
1. S4A stands for Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets.
2. It was introduced by the RBI in 2018.
3. It split the debt of a stressed firm into sustainable and unsustainable parts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: S4A = Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets. Statement 2 is wrong: S4A came in 2016; 2018 is Project Sashakt. Statement 3 is correct: it split debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts. Hence '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' leaves out 3, and any option with 2 is wrong.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: **S4A = Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: S4A came in **2016**; **2018** is **Project Sashakt**.
Statement 3: it split debt into **sustainable and unsustainable** parts — correct (UPSC 2017 key).
xa: S4A was an **RBI** scheme to rework the financial structure of stressed firms.
**SDR (2015)** preceded it.

87.s:
