Consider the following statements about Project Sashakt:
1. It was introduced in 2018 on the recommendation of the Sunil Mehta Committee.
2. Its Inter-Creditor Agreement binds all lenders once 51% of lenders approve the resolution plan.
3. Under it, the lead bank drives the resolution plan.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: Project Sashakt (2018) came from the Sunil Mehta Committee. Statement 2 is wrong: the plan binds all once 66% of lenders approve, not 51% (51% is the SDR equity stake). Statement 3 is correct: the lead bank drives the plan. So '1 and 3 only'.
87.tq: Sashakt ICA = 66% of lenders; SDR = 51% equity; SARFAESI = 75% of dues.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: **Project Sashakt (2018)** came from the **Sunil Mehta Committee** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: the plan binds all once **66%** of lenders approve, not 51%.
Statement 3: the **lead bank** drives the plan — correct.
xa: Its **Inter-Creditor Agreement** aimed at **faster resolution of stressed assets** (UPSC 2019 key).
The **Prudential Framework (2019)** made the ICA mandatory.

87.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets?
o: A 30-day review after default, mandatory ICA and resolution within 180 days
A five-day review after default, mandatory auction and resolution within 66 days
A 90-day review after default, no ICA and resolution within 365 days
A 60-day notice, voluntary ICA and resolution within 25 years
87.x: The Prudential Framework requires a 30-day review after default, makes the Inter-Creditor Agreement mandatory and envisages resolution within 180 days.
87.tq: Match the resolution framework with its distinctive review period, ICA rule and deadline.
xs: The Prudential Framework (**7 June 2019**) requires a **30-day review after default, mandatory ICA and resolution within 180 days** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **60-day** notice belongs to **SARFAESI**; **25 years** to the **5/25** scheme; **66%** to **Project Sashakt**.
xa: The **ICA** came from **Project Sashakt (2018)**.
⚠ **180 days** is also the basic **CIRP** period under the IBC.

87.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: ARCs — registered with RBI under SARFAESI
CDR — restructuring outside court for large multi-bank borrowers
Lok Adalats — conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent equity stake
ARCs — purchase bad loans against security receipts
87.x: Conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent or more equity stake is associated with Strategic Debt Restructuring, not Lok Adalats. ARCs, CDR and Lok Adalats have the other stated functions.
87.tq: Find the wrong mechanism-feature pairing by checking who performs the action.
xs: **Lok Adalats — 51% equity conversion** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
Converting debt into a **51%+** equity stake is **SDR (2015)**; Lok Adalats settle small loans by compromise.
The rest are right: **ARCs** are registered with RBI and buy bad loans against **security receipts**; **CDR** restructures large multi-bank loans out of court.
xa: Lok Adalats are statutory under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
ARCs buy NPAs **at a discount**.

87.s: Under which provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 are the NCLT and NCLAT respectively set up?
87.x: NCLT is established under Section 408 and NCLAT under Section 410 of the Companies Act, 2013.
87.tq: Check the order of the statutory provisions instead of treating the two tribunals as interchangeable.
xs: NCLT is set up under **Sections 408** and NCLAT under **410** of the **Companies Act 2013** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses them; **Sec 61** (IBC) is the NCLAT appeal provision; **Secs 202 and 211** relate to IBBI.
xa: Both were constituted on **1 June 2016**.
NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
NCLAT: Principal Bench **New Delhi** + a bench at **Chennai**.

87.s:
The National Company Law Tribunal replaced which of the following bodies?
1. Company Law Board
2. Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction
3. Appellate Authority for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction
4. Securities Appellate Tribunal
87.x: NCLT replaced the Company Law Board, BIFR and AAIFR. It did not replace the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
87.tq: Use the replaced-body list and reject the unrelated appellate tribunal.
xs: NCLT replaced the **Company Law Board, BIFR and AAIFR** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
The **Securities Appellate Tribunal** was not replaced.
xa: **BIFR** was dissolved on **1 Dec 2016**; cases went to NCLT/NCLAT.
The IBC replaced **SICA 1985/BIFR** and scattered Companies Act provisions.
NCLT/NCLAT constituted **1 June 2016**.

87.s: Which authority is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
87.x: The NCLT is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC, 2016. The DRT is the authority for individuals and partnership firms.
87.tq: Ask which body would handle the dispute by distinguishing corporate from individual insolvency.
xs: The **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)** is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency (**companies and LLPs**) — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC GS 2019 key).
The **DRT** handles **individuals and partnership firms**; the **NCLAT** hears appeals.
xa: NCLT also handles **personal guarantors of corporate debtors**.
CIRP is triggered by a default of at least **₹1 crore**.
⚠ NCLT = **companies and LLPs**; DRT = **individuals and partnership firms**.

87.s:
Which of the following bodies are among those from which the NCLAT hears appeals?
1. NCLT
2. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
3. Competition Commission of India
4. National Financial Reporting Authority
87.x: NCLAT hears appeals from all four: NCLT orders (Sec 61 of the IBC), IBBI orders, CCI orders (from 26 May 2017) and NFRA orders (from 7 May 2018). Hence 1, 2, 3 and 4.
87.tq: Test the full appellate-source list rather than only the most familiar source.
xs: NCLAT hears appeals from all four — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
It hears **NCLT** orders (**Sec 61**), **IBBI** and **CCI** orders.
It took on **CCI** appeals from **26 May 2017** and **NFRA** appeals from **7 May 2018**.
xa: Further appeal from NCLAT lies to the **Supreme Court**.
NCLAT sits at **New Delhi** (Principal Bench) and **Chennai**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016:
1. It received assent in May 2016.
2. It was based on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee.
3. It replaced SICA 1985 and the BIFR, which was dissolved on 1 December 2016.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: assent came in May 2016. Statement 2 is wrong: the IBC was based on the T.K. Viswanathan Committee (Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee, 2015); Narasimham is linked to SARFAESI. Statement 3 is correct: it replaced SICA 1985/BIFR, and BIFR was dissolved on 1 Dec 2016. So '1 and 3 only'.
87.tq: IBC = Viswanathan; SARFAESI = Narasimham.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: assent in **May 2016** — correct (enacted **28 May 2016**).
Statement 2 is wrong: the IBC came from the **T.K. Viswanathan Committee** (**Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee, 2015**); Narasimham is linked to **SARFAESI**.
Statement 3: it replaced **SICA 1985/BIFR**; BIFR was dissolved **1 Dec 2016** — correct.
xa: ⚠ PYQ: "September assent" and "13-member IBBI" were both wrong (IBBI has **10** members).
IBC completed **10 years** in May 2026.

87.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes insolvency from bankruptcy?
o: Bankruptcy is the inability to pay debts as they fall due, whereas insolvency is a court-approved resolution plan
Insolvency is a legal declaration, whereas bankruptcy is a financial state
Insolvency is the inability to pay debts as they fall due, whereas bankruptcy is the legal declaration or process that follows
Both insolvency and bankruptcy refer exclusively to liquidation of companies
87.x: Insolvency is the financial state of being unable to pay debts when due. Bankruptcy is the legal declaration or process that follows insolvency.
87.tq: Discriminate between two closely related legal terms by identifying the state and the subsequent legal process.
xs: **Insolvency** = inability to pay debts as they fall due; **bankruptcy** = the legal declaration/process that follows — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps the two — the **BPSC 2023** trap.
xa: Insolvency is a **financial state**; bankruptcy is a **legal** process.
The IBC moved from **debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control**.

87.s: Which change in the control structure of insolvency proceedings was introduced by the IBC?
87.x: The IBC shifted the framework from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control.
87.tq: Test a paired conceptual comparison by identifying the direction of institutional change.
xs: The IBC shifted control **from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the change.
xa: It created a single, **time-bound** process — a structural reform.
The **2026** amendment's **CIIRP** is a hybrid of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
The **Committee of Creditors** (financial creditors) votes on resolution plans.

87.s:
Consider the following statements regarding NCLT and NCLAT:
1. NCLT functions as an adjudicating authority for companies and LLPs.
2. NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT under Section 61 of the IBC.
3. NCLAT is located only in New Delhi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
87.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because NCLAT sits in New Delhi and Chennai.
87.tq: Identify the false location claim after confirming the authority and appellate provisions.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: NCLT adjudicates for **companies and LLPs** — correct.
Statement 2: NCLAT hears appeals under **Sec 61** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: NCLAT has a Principal Bench in **New Delhi** and a bench at **Chennai**.
xa: NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
Further appeal lies to the **Supreme Court**.

87.s: Which of the following functions is performed by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India?
o: It functions as the monetary authority for India
It acts as the appellate tribunal for all NCLT orders
It regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies and information utilities
It directly purchases all non-performing assets from banks
87.x: IBBI regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies and information utilities. It also regulates registered valuers and frames CIRP and liquidation regulations.
87.tq: Use the ‘who does this job?’ method to distinguish the regulator from adjudicatory and monetary bodies.
xs: **IBBI** regulates **insolvency professionals, IP agencies and information utilities** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It also regulates **registered valuers** and frames **CIRP/liquidation regulations**.
Appeals go to the **NCLAT**; buying NPAs is the job of **ARCs/NARCL**.
xa: IBBI (**2016**) is the apex statutory regulator; it has **10** members.
IBBI proposed stronger safeguards for **guarantor insolvency** (**16 Sep 2026**).

87.s: A promoter classified as a wilful defaulter, or a promoter associated with an NPA, is generally barred from bidding under which provision of the IBC?
87.x: Section 29A prevents wilful defaulters and promoters of NPAs from submitting resolution bids, subject to the statutory framework.
87.tq: Direct recall of the relevant statutory provision.
xs: **Section 29A** bars **wilful defaulters**/NPA promoters from bidding for their own firms — so option **(2)** is correct.
They are **barred from bidding under IBC** (May 2026), so they cannot regain the firm cheaply.
xa: The **Committee of Creditors** votes on resolution plans.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: **personal guarantors** stay liable after plan approval.
The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above.

87.s: In the waterfall mechanism under the IBC, which of the following have priority over government dues?
o: Unsecured creditors and equity shareholders only
Only government dues and shareholder claims
Resolution costs, workmen's dues and secured creditors' claims
87.x: Resolution costs, workmen and secured creditors are placed above government dues in the waterfall.
87.tq: Apply the priority sequence rather than choosing a broad but incorrect creditor category.
xs: In the liquidation waterfall, **resolution costs, workmen's dues and secured creditors** rank **above government dues** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The waterfall places these three claims **above** the government's dues (29 May 2026).
xa: The **2026** amendment cut liquidation to **180 + 90 days**.
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
Criticism: **deep haircuts** and guarantor liability.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP):
1. It can be triggered by financial or operational creditors.
2. The minimum default required to trigger it is Rs 1 lakh.
3. The Committee of Creditors, made up of financial creditors, votes on resolution plans.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: financial or operational creditors can trigger CIRP. Statement 2 is wrong: the default must be at least Rs 1 crore. Statement 3 is correct: the CoC of financial creditors votes on resolution plans. So '1 and 3 only'.
87.tq: CIRP threshold = Rs 1 crore; CoC = financial creditors only.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: CIRP can be triggered by **financial or operational creditors** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: the minimum default is **₹1 crore**, not ₹1 lakh.
Statement 3: the **Committee of Creditors** (financial creditors) votes on resolution plans — correct.
xa: CIRP timeline: **180 days** + **90 days**; outer limit **330 days** incl. litigation.
**Sec 29A**: wilful defaulters/NPA promoters cannot bid for their own firms.
NCLT is the adjudicating authority for **companies and LLPs**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements regarding CIRP:
1. Its ordinary deadline is 180 days, subject to extension.
2. The outer limit, including litigation, is 330 days.
3. Cases in practice have always been completed within the statutory outer limit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
87.x: CIRP ordinarily has a 180-day period with an extension and an outer limit of 330 days including litigation. Actual cases have taken longer, so statement 3 is false.
87.tq: Find the incorrect absolute statement while retaining the statutory timelines.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: **180 days**, extendable by **90 days** — correct.
Statement 2: outer limit **330 days** incl. litigation (**2019** amendment) — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: cases average **713 days**; **853 days** for cases closed in **FY25**.
xa: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline (ES 2025-26).
Causes: protracted litigation, NCLT capacity/staff shortages.

87.s: The Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process for MSMEs was introduced in:
87.x: The PPIRP for MSMEs was introduced in 2021 and has a 120-day limit.
87.tq: Combine the launch year and time limit to distinguish the pre-pack process from ordinary CIRP.
xs: **PPIRP** for **MSMEs** came in **2021** with a **120-day** limit — so option **(4)** is correct.
**180 days** is the CIRP period; **330 days** is the CIRP outer limit.
xa: Only **14 admissions in 4 years** under PPIRP (ES 2025-26).
⚠ Timelines: CIRP **180 + 90** (outer **330**); PPIRP **120**; CIIRP **150**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026:
1. The NCLT must admit or reject a CIRP plea within 14 days.
2. The NCLT must rule on resolution plans within 90 days.
3. The new Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (CIIRP) is a 150-day process that needs 51% by value of notified financial creditors.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: admission within 14 days. Statement 2 is wrong: the NCLT must rule on plans within 30 days. Statement 3 is correct: CIIRP runs 150 days and needs 51% by value of notified financial creditors. So '1 and 3 only'.
87.tq: 2026 amendment: 14 days to admit, 30 days to rule, CIIRP 150 days / 51%.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1: NCLT must **admit or reject a CIRP plea within 14 days** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: NCLT must rule on plans within **30 days**, not 90.
Statement 3: **CIIRP** runs **150 days** and needs **51%** by value of notified financial creditors — correct.
xa: CIIRP sits in **Secs 54C-54P**; a hybrid of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
Liquidation cut to **180 + 90 days**.

87.s: The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 changed 'may' to 'shall' in Section 7(5)(a) of the Code. This change overturned the ruling in:
o: Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India
87.x: The change from 'may' to 'shall' in Sec 7(5)(a) makes admission of a financial creditor's CIRP plea mandatory once default is proved, overturning the Vidarbha Industries ruling, which had read 'may' as giving the NCLT discretion. Lalit Kumar Jain (2021) concerns personal guarantors' liability; Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel are other IBC judgments not affected by this change.
87.tq: Sec 7(5)(a) may→shall = Vidarbha overturned.
xs: Changing "may" to "**shall**" in **Sec 7(5)(a)** overturned the **Vidarbha Industries** ruling — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)** is about **personal guarantors** staying liable after plan approval.
xa: Other 2026 changes: NCLT admission within **14 days**, plan ruling within **30 days**.
New **CIIRP**: **150 days**, **51%** of notified financial creditors.
Clean-slate protection + cross-border insolvency framework.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026:
1. The liquidation timeline is cut to 180 days plus a 90-day extension.
2. The Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (CIIRP) is provided in Sections 54C to 54P.
3. CIIRP is a purely debtor-in-possession process with no creditor control.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: liquidation is cut to 180 + 90 days. Statement 2 is correct: CIIRP sits in Secs 54C-54P. Statement 3 is wrong: CIIRP is a hybrid of debtor-in-possession and creditor-in-control. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
87.tq: CIIRP = 150 days, 51% FCs, Secs 54C-54P, hybrid DIP + CIC.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1: liquidation cut to **180 + 90 days** — correct.
Statement 2: **CIIRP** sits in **Secs 54C-54P** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: CIIRP is a **hybrid** of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
xa: CIIRP: **150 days**, needs **51%** by value of notified financial creditors.
Criticism: **limits on who can start CIIRP**.

87.s: NARCL, described as India’s ‘bad bank’, was announced in which Budget?
87.x: The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was announced in Budget 2021–22.
87.tq: Use the announcement-year distinction among closely placed Budgets.
xs: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", was announced in **Budget 2021-22** — so option **(2)** is correct.
NARCL was one of the cited reasons for the fall in NPAs, alongside the **4R strategy** and **IBC**.
xa: It aggregates large stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, targeting about **₹2 lakh crore**.
**IDRCL** resolves the assets, incl. by sale to **AIFs**.
Funding: **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about NARCL:
1. It pays for stressed assets 15% in cash and 85% in Security Receipts.
2. The Government guarantees its Security Receipts up to Rs 30,600 crore for 10 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is correct: 15% cash + 85% Security Receipts. Statement 2 is wrong: the Rs 30,600 crore guarantee runs for 5 years or until settlement, not 10 years. So '1 only'.
87.tq: NARCL: 15:85 cash-SR split; Rs 30,600 crore guarantee for 5 years.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
Statement 1: NARCL pays **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **₹30,600 crore** guarantee runs **5 years** or until settlement, not 10.
xa: NARCL targets about **₹2 lakh crore** of fully or partly provided assets, in phases.
**₹2,410 crore** recovered by **30 Jun 2025**.

87.s: NARCL primarily targets stressed loans above which threshold and an aggregate asset value of approximately what amount?
87.x: NARCL takes over large stressed loans above ₹500 crore, targeting about ₹2 lakh crore of fully or partly provided assets.
87.tq: Combine the eligibility threshold with the aggregate target.
xs: NARCL targets stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, about **₹2 lakh crore** in all — so option **(3)** is correct.
These are **fully or partly provided** assets, taken in phases.
xa: By **30 Jun 2025**: **27 accounts**, **₹1,57,215 crore** exposure.
**IDRCL** resolves them; IDRCL is majority private.

87.s: In the context of banking supervision, PCA stands for:
87.x: PCA stands for Prompt Corrective Action, a framework used by the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in banks with weakening financial health.
87.tq: Test the exact expansion of a frequently confused institutional acronym.
xs: **PCA = Prompt Corrective Action** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2019 key).
RBI uses it to intervene in banks whose financial health is failing.
xa: Introduced by RBI in **2002**.
Current triggers: **capital, asset quality, leverage**.
Curbs: **lending, branch expansion**, risky exposures, **dividends**, management pay.

87.s: The Prompt Corrective Action framework was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in:
87.x: The RBI introduced the Prompt Corrective Action framework in 2002 to monitor and restrict banks whose financial metrics deteriorate.
87.tq: Use the year-based direct-recall method for a regulatory framework.
xs: RBI introduced the **PCA** framework in **2002** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Weak banks are placed under watch and restricted until capital and asset quality recover.
xa: Revised **Nov 2021**, effective **1 Jan 2022**.
The older **profitability (RoA)** trigger was dropped.
⚠ **2002** is also the year of **SARFAESI**.

87.s:
Match List-I with List-II in respect of PCA trigger parameters:
List-I (Trigger parameter)
a. Capital
b. Asset quality
c. Leverage

List-II (Indicator)
i. Net NPA ratio
ii. Tier-1 leverage ratio
iii. CRAR/Common Equity Tier 1

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
87.x: Capital is assessed through CRAR and Common Equity Tier 1, asset quality through the net NPA ratio, and leverage through the Tier-1 leverage ratio.
87.tq: Start from the sure indicator-parameter pair and eliminate codes containing mismatches.
xs: Correct matching: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Capital = **CRAR / CET1**; asset quality = **Net NPA ratio**; leverage = **Tier 1 leverage ratio**.
xa: Revised framework effective **1 Jan 2022**.
2017 framework: Net NPA **6-9%** = threshold 1; **12%** or more = threshold 3.

87.s:
Under the PCA framework, restrictions may relate to:
1. Lending and risky exposures
2. Branch expansion
3. Dividend payments and management pay
4. Capital infusion, change of management or merger ordered by the RBI
Which of the statements given above are correct?
87.x: PCA restrictions can cover lending, risky exposures, branch expansion, dividends and management pay. The RBI may also order capital infusion, a management change or a merger.
87.tq: Recognise that the framework includes both operational restrictions and structural corrective measures.
xs: All four are PCA measures — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
Curbs: **lending, branch expansion**, risky exposures, growth, **dividends**, management pay.
RBI may also order a **capital infusion, change of management, or a merger**.
xa: Curbs last until capital and asset quality improve.
PCA was introduced in **2002**; full form **Prompt Corrective Action**.

87.s:
Consider the following statements regarding personal guarantors in insolvency:
1. Personal guarantors remain liable after approval of a resolution plan.
2. The principle was affirmed by the Supreme Court in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India in 2021.
3. Approval of a resolution plan automatically releases every personal guarantor from liability.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
87.x: Personal guarantors remain liable even after approval of a resolution plan, as affirmed in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India (2021). Statement 3 is false because approval does not automatically release every guarantor.
87.tq: Reject the absolute release claim and retain the judicially affirmed liability rule.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
**Personal guarantors** stay liable after plan approval, per **Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (SC 2021)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: plan approval does not release guarantors.
xa: **IBBI** proposed stronger safeguards for guarantor insolvency (**16 Sep 2026**).
Draft rules for personal-guarantor repayment plans: valuation + bar on related-party voting.
NCLT also handles **personal guarantors of corporate debtors**.

87.s: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 applies to offenders in cases involving amounts of:
87.x: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 covers offenders in cases involving ₹100 crore or more.
87.tq: Recall the statutory monetary threshold without confusing it with NARCL’s loan threshold.
xs: The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above — so option **(1)** is correct.
The ₹500, ₹50 and ₹10 crore figures are not the Act's threshold.
xa: **FIU-IND**: suspicious transaction reports up **45%**.
**Sec 29A** of the IBC bars wilful defaulters from bidding.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: personal guarantors remain liable.

87.s: Which one of the following best explains the deterrent effect attributed to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code?
o: All insolvency cases were completed by NCLT within 330 days.
The Code abolished the liability of personal guarantors.
A large number of cases were settled before admission, encouraging debtors to avoid prolonged default proceedings.
The Code converted every recovery proceeding into a Lok Adalat settlement.
87.x: The settlement of 30,310 cases worth ₹13.78 lakh crore before admission was cited as evidence of the IBC's deterrent effect.
87.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship instead of selecting an absolute claim.
xs: **30,310** cases worth **₹13.78 lakh crore** were **settled before admission** by **Dec 2024** — the IBC's **deterrent effect** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) is wrong: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline; option (2) is wrong: guarantors stay liable.
xa: FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
IBC delivered **48%** of bank recoveries in FY24.

87.s:
With reference to Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. An NCLT bench is located at Amaravati.
2. The DRT Visakhapatnam bench settles cases at Lok Adalats.
3. The DRT Visakhapatnam bench is located at Amaravati.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
87.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The NCLT bench sits at Amaravati, while the DRT Visakhapatnam bench settles cases at Lok Adalats; statement 3 confuses their locations.
87.tq: Separate two Andhra Pradesh institutions by their locations and functions.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
An **NCLT bench** sits at **Amaravati**; the **DRT Visakhapatnam** bench settles cases at **Lok Adalats**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the DRT bench is at **Visakhapatnam**, not Amaravati.
xa: **13 Sep 2026** National Lok Adalat: DRT Visakhapatnam settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.
The **AP High Court** clarified **Sec 13(8)** SARFAESI redemption rules (May 2026).

87.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or debate concerning the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code?
87.x: Protracted litigation, limited NCLT capacity, deep haircuts and guarantor liability are identified concerns. The Code has not eliminated guarantor liability.
87.tq: Find the option that contradicts the listed criticisms through an absolute claim.
xs: **Complete elimination of guarantor liability** is NOT a criticism — so option **(3)** is correct.
The debate is about **guarantor liability** continuing, not ending.
Real criticisms: **deep haircuts**, **protracted litigation**, **NCLT capacity** shortages.
xa: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline.
Limits on who can start **CIIRP** are another debate.

87.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Mechanism)
 a. SARFAESI
 b. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
 c. Debt Recovery Tribunal

List-II (Principal characteristic)
 i. Tribunal-based recovery
 ii. Collective, NCLT-led and time-bound resolution
 iii. Recovery by secured lenders without court intervention

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
87.x: SARFAESI concerns recovery by secured lenders without court intervention; IBC provides collective, NCLT-led and time-bound resolution; DRT is a tribunal-based recovery mechanism.
87.tq: Start from the sure pair and distinguish the three recovery frameworks by their defining features.
xs: Correct matching: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**SARFAESI** = secured lenders, **no court**; **IBC** = **collective, NCLT-led, time-bound**; **DRT** = **tribunal recovery**.
xa: FY24 recovery shares: **IBC 48%**, **SARFAESI 32%**, **DRTs 17%**.

88.s: Who chaired the Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low-Income Households, which provided the basis for PMJDY and payments and small finance banks?
88.x: The Nachiket Mor Committee was constituted in 2013 and recommended comprehensive financial services, including a bank account for every household.
88.tq: Match the committee chairperson with the distinctive subject of the committee.
xs: The **Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)** on comprehensive financial services laid the basis for **PMJDY** — option **(1)**.
It recommended **a bank account for every household** and led to **payments banks** and **small finance banks**.
**Deepak Mohanty (2015)** drew the medium-term path on financial inclusion; **Ratan Watal (2016)** dealt with **digital payments**.
**C. Rangarajan** chaired the committee on **financial inclusion** (**2008**; **2006** in other notes).
xa: Mor also suggested a **universal account**, **basic savings account** and **Aadhaar + mobile banking**.
**Y.H. Malegam (2010)** examined the **microfinance sector** after the AP crisis.
⚠ **Malegam** = microfinance; **Watal** = digital payments; **Naidu** = CMs' committee on digital payments.

88.s:
Match the following committees with their subjects:

a. C. Rangarajan Committee
b. Ratan Watal Committee
c. Deepak Mohanty Committee
d. Y.H. Malegam Committee

i. Digital payments
 ii. Medium-term path on financial inclusion
 iii. Microfinance sector after the Andhra Pradesh crisis
 iv. Financial inclusion

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
88.x: Rangarajan dealt with financial inclusion; Watal with digital payments; Mohanty with the medium-term path on financial inclusion; and Malegam with the microfinance sector after the AP crisis.
88.tq: Start with the distinctive Malegam–microfinance pair and resolve the remaining matches.
xs: Correct code: **a–iv, b–i, c–ii, d–iii** — option **(1)**.
**C. Rangarajan** → **financial inclusion**; **Ratan Watal (2016)** → **digital payments** (MoF).
**Deepak Mohanty (2015)** → **medium-term path on financial inclusion** (RBI).
**Y.H. Malegam (2010)** → **microfinance sector after the AP crisis** (RBI).
xa: **Nachiket Mor (2013)** → comprehensive financial services; basis of **PMJDY**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2016-17)** → **Committee of Chief Ministers on digital payments**.
AP's **2010 microfinance crisis** reshaped national MFI regulation.

88.s: Who chaired the Chief Ministers' Committee on Digital Payments during 2016–17?
88.x: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu chaired the 2016–17 Chief Ministers' Committee on Digital Payments.
88.tq: Match the public office-holder with the specific committee role.
xs: **N. Chandrababu Naidu** chaired the **Committee of Chief Ministers on digital payments** in **2016-17** — option **(4)**.
It worked on **cashless transactions after demonetisation**.
xa: Naidu later hailed **10 years of UPI** (**Aug 2026**).
**Ratan Watal Committee (2016)** of the **Ministry of Finance** also examined **digital payments**.
⚠ **Naidu** = CMs' committee; **Watal** = MoF committee on digital payments.

88.s: The National Mission for Financial Inclusion was announced on which date and formally launched on which date?
88.x: The National Mission for Financial Inclusion was announced on 15 August 2014 and launched on 28 August 2014.
88.tq: Separate announcement and launch dates instead of treating them as identical.
xs: The **National Mission for Financial Inclusion** (PMJDY) was **announced on 15 Aug 2014** and **launched on 28 August 2014** — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses the dates; options (1) and (4) give wrong dates or year.
xa: ⚠ Some notes date the launch itself to **15 Aug**.
**Nodal body:** **DFS, Ministry of Finance**.
**12 years of PMJDY** were marked in **Aug 2026**.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the three tenets associated with financial inclusion under PMJDY?
o: Banking the unbanked, securing the unsecured and funding the unfunded
Saving the surplus, lending to exporters and taxing households
Insuring the insured, taxing the untaxed and funding the funded
Digitising the banks, privatising the banks and regulating the markets
88.x: The three stated tenets are banking the unbanked, securing the unsecured and funding the unfunded.
88.tq: Recall the exact official wording of a three-part formulation.
xs: PMJDY's tenets: **banking the unbanked, securing the unsecured, funding the unfunded** — option **(1)**.
The other options are invented slogans not found among PMJDY's tenets.
xa: "Securing" is delivered via the **RuPay card's ₹2 lakh accident insurance** and **₹30,000** life cover.
"Funding" via the **overdraft up to ₹10,000**.
**JAM** = **Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile**.

88.s:
A basic savings bank deposit account opened under PMJDY generally has which of the following features?
1. Zero minimum balance requirement
2. Interest on the balance
3. RuPay debit card
4. Provision for Direct Benefit Transfer
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
88.x: PMJDY provides zero-balance basic savings accounts with interest, RuPay debit cards and DBT functionality.
88.tq: Use an all-inclusive option when all listed programme features are supported.
xs: All four are PMJDY account features — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
Statement 1 and 2 correct: a **zero-balance BSBD account with interest**.
Statement 3 correct: a **RuPay debit card** with **₹2 lakh accident insurance**.
Statement 4 correct: accounts carry **DBT** and financial literacy.
xa: **Overdraft up to ₹10,000** after **6 months** of good conduct (Phase II **2015-18**).
**Life cover** of **₹30,000** for early enrollees.
Linked to **PMJJBY**, **PMSBY** and **APY**.

88.s:
PMJDY accounts may be linked with which of the following social-security or pension schemes?
1. PMJJBY
2. PMSBY
3. Atal Pension Yojana
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
88.x: PMJDY accounts are linked with the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana and Atal Pension Yojana.
88.tq: Identify the complete set of schemes linked with the account platform.
xs: PMJDY accounts link to **PMJJBY**, **PMSBY** and **Atal Pension Yojana** — option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
The three social security schemes were launched on **9 May 2015**.
xa: **PMJJBY**: **₹2 lakh** life cover, **₹436/yr**, age **18-50**.
**PMSBY**: **₹2 lakh** accidental death/full disability, **₹20/yr**, age **18-70**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY):
1. The RuPay debit card given to account holders carries accident insurance of ₹2 lakh.
2. Account holders can get an overdraft of up to ₹50,000.
3. Jan Dhan accounts form the first layer of the JAM trinity, which made Direct Benefit Transfer possible.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: the RuPay card has ₹2 lakh accident cover. Statement 2 is wrong: the overdraft is up to ₹10,000, not ₹50,000. Statement 3 is correct: Jan Dhan is the first layer of Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile, enabling DBT. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
88.tq: PMJDY: RuPay ₹2 lakh accident, OD ₹10,000, JAM → DBT.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **RuPay debit card** carries **₹2 lakh accident insurance**.
Statement 2 wrong: the overdraft is **up to ₹10,000**, not ₹50,000.
Statement 3 correct: Jan Dhan is the **first layer of the JAM trinity**, enabling **DBT**.
xa: Overdraft started in **Phase II (2015-18)**, after **6 months** of good conduct.
**₹50,000** is the **Shishu** limit under **MUDRA**.
**Life cover** of **₹30,000** for early enrollees.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY):
1. Its annual premium is Rs 20 and it is open to people aged 18-70.
2. It gives Rs 2 lakh life cover for death from any cause.
3. It pays Rs 1 lakh for partial disability.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: Rs 20 a year, age 18-70. Statement 2 is wrong: PMSBY pays Rs 2 lakh only for accidental death or full disability; Rs 2 lakh life cover for any cause is PMJJBY. Statement 3 is correct: Rs 1 lakh for partial disability. So '1 and 3 only'.
88.tq: PMSBY = Suraksha = accident (Rs 20); PMJJBY = Jeevan = life, any cause (Rs 436).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **PMSBY** premium **₹20/yr**, age **18-70**.
Statement 2 wrong: PMSBY gives **₹2 lakh** only for **accidental death/full disability**; life cover for **any cause** is **PMJJBY**.
Statement 3 correct: **₹1 lakh** for **partial disability**.
xa: **PMJJBY**: **₹436/yr**, age **18-50** (premium revised **2022**).
Enrolment: PMSBY **57.92 crore**, PMJJBY **27.33 crore**.
⚠ PMJJBY = **life**; PMSBY = **accident**.

88.s:
Atal Pension Yojana is correctly described by which of the following statements?

1. It replaced Swavalamban.
2. It provides a pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 per month after the age of 60.
3. It is administered under PFRDA.
4. New enrolment of taxpayers has not been permitted from 1 October 2022.

Select the correct answer using the code below.
88.x: APY replaced Swavalamban, provides a monthly pension of ₹1,000–₹5,000 from age 60, is administered by PFRDA, and excludes taxpayers from new enrolment from 1 October 2022.
88.tq: Check the scheme’s predecessor, benefit, regulator and eligibility restriction as separate components.
xs: All four statements describe **APY** — option **(4)**.
APY (**2015**) **replaced Swavalamban**; pension of **₹1,000-5,000**/month from age **60**.
It is administered under **PFRDA**; **no taxpayers** may enrol after **1 Oct 2022**.
xa: Age group: **18-40**; contribution is **age-linked**.
APY enrolment: **8.96 crore**.
Launched with **PMJJBY** and **PMSBY** on **9 May 2015**.

88.s: PMJJBY and PMSBY were launched together on:
88.x: PMJJBY and PMSBY, along with APY, were launched on 9 May 2015.
88.tq: Separate the common launch date from later premium revisions and enrolment dates.
xs: **PMJJBY** and **PMSBY** were launched on **9 May 2015**, along with **APY** — option **(4)**.
**8 April 2015** = launch of **PMMY**; **1 Oct 2022** = APY's taxpayer bar; **30 Jul 2025** = an enrolment date.
xa: Earlier enrolment (**30 Jul 2025**): PMSBY **52.54 crore**, PMJJBY **24.34 crore**.
Latest: PMSBY **57.92 crore**, PMJJBY **27.33 crore**.
Related: **e-Shram** has **31.64 crore** unorganised workers registered.

88.s: Under the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), which of the following is correct?
o: ₹2 lakh life cover for death due to any cause at an annual premium of ₹436
₹2 lakh cover only for accidental death at an annual premium of ₹20
₹1 lakh life cover at an annual premium of ₹330
Pension of ₹1,000-5,000 per month from age 60
88.x: PMJJBY gives ₹2 lakh life cover for death from any cause, at ₹436 a year (revised 2022), for ages 18-50. Accidental-death-only cover at ₹20 is PMSBY. ₹330 was the old pre-2022 premium, and the cover was never ₹1 lakh. A monthly pension of ₹1,000-5,000 is APY.
88.tq: Jeevan Jyoti = life (any cause) ₹436; Suraksha = accident ₹20.
xs: **PMJJBY** gives **₹2 lakh life cover** for death from **any cause** at **₹436/yr** — option **(1)**.
**₹2 lakh accident-only** cover at **₹20** is **PMSBY**.
A pension of **₹1,000-5,000**/month from **60** is **APY**.
xa: PMJJBY age: **18-50**; premium **revised 2022**.
PMJJBY enrolment: **27.33 crore**.
PMSBY pays **₹1 lakh** for partial disability.

88.s: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) was launched on which date?
88.x: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015. MUDRA Ltd was established earlier, on 18 March 2015.
88.tq: Distinguish the scheme launch date from the institutional set-up date.
xs: **PMMY** was launched on **8 April 2015** — option **(3)**.
**18 March 2015** = **MUDRA Ltd** set up; **9 May 2015** = PMJJBY/PMSBY; **24 Oct 2024** = **Tarun Plus**.
xa: ⚠ MUDRA Ltd (**18 March 2015**) came **before** PMMY.
PMMY gives **collateral-free** loans to non-corporate, non-farm micro/small enterprises.
Run by the **Ministry of Finance (DFS)**.

88.s: MUDRA Ltd, which refinances banks, NBFCs and MFIs under PMMY, was established as a subsidiary of which institution?
88.x: MUDRA Ltd was set up as a subsidiary of SIDBI on 18 March 2015 and undertakes refinance functions.
88.tq: Use the institutional-ownership trap by separating SIDBI from other financial regulators and institutions.
xs: **MUDRA Ltd** is a **SIDBI subsidiary** — option **(4)**.
Set up on **18 March 2015**, it **refinances banks, NBFCs and MFIs**.
xa: Guarantees come via **CGFMU**; borrowers get a **MUDRA Card** (RuPay).
**NABARD** is linked with the **SHG-Bank Linkage pilot (1992)**; **PFRDA** with **APY**.
Collateral-free limit: up to **₹20 lakh**.

88.s: Which Union Ministry administers the Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana?
o: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
Ministry of Finance through the Department of Financial Services
88.x: PMMY is run by the Ministry of Finance, specifically through the Department of Financial Services.
88.tq: Apply the ‘which ministry’ trap by distinguishing the implementing ministry from the target sector.
xs: PMMY is run by the **Ministry of Finance** through the **Department of Financial Services** — option **(2)**.
Its refinance arm is **MUDRA Ltd**, a **SIDBI** subsidiary.
xa: Launched **8 April 2015**.
DFS is also the nodal body for **PMJDY**.
Categories: **Shishu**, **Kishore**, **Tarun**, **Tarun Plus**.

88.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the categories of MUDRA loans:

List-I (Category)
a. Shishu
b. Kishore
c. Tarun
d. Tarun Plus

List-II (Loan limit)
i. ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh
ii. Up to ₹50,000
iii. ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh
iv. ₹50,001 to ₹5 lakh

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
88.x: Shishu covers loans up to ₹50,000; Kishore covers ₹50,001–₹5 lakh; Tarun covers ₹5–₹10 lakh; and Tarun Plus covers ₹10–₹20 lakh.
88.tq: Start from the sure pairs and eliminate codes that repeat or shift the category limits.
xs: Correct code: **a–ii, b–iv, c–iii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Tarun** **₹5-10 lakh**; **Tarun Plus** **₹10-20 lakh**.
xa: **Tarun Plus** from **24 Oct 2024** (Budget **2024-25**), for Tarun borrowers who repaid.
By **Oct 2025**: **₹36.18 lakh crore** across **55.45 crore** loans; **67%** to women.

88.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly associated with PMMY?
o: Loans restricted exclusively to large corporate enterprises
88.x: PMMY targets non-corporate, non-farm micro and small enterprises, not large corporate enterprises. Loans are collateral-free up to ₹20 lakh, supported by CGFMU guarantees, and linked with the MUDRA Card.
88.tq: Find the option that reverses the target group of the scheme.
xs: PMMY is **NOT** for **large corporate enterprises** — option **(1)** is the wrong association.
It lends to **non-corporate, non-farm micro/small enterprises**.
Options 2-4 are true: **MUDRA Card** (RuPay), **collateral-free up to ₹20 lakh**, guarantees via **CGFMU**.
xa: Sectors: manufacturing, trading, services, allied agriculture.
Refinance by **MUDRA Ltd** (SIDBI subsidiary) to banks, NBFCs, MFIs.

88.s: The SHG-bank linkage model was pioneered by which organisation during the mid-1980s?
88.x: MYRADA pioneered the SHG-bank linkage approach in the mid-1980s.
88.tq: Separate the pioneer organisation from later banking and government institutions.
xs: **MYRADA** pioneered **SHG-bank linkage** in the **mid-1980s** — option **(1)**.
**MUDRA Ltd** is a **SIDBI** refinance body (**2015**); **SERP** runs AP's SHG model.
xa: **NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage pilot (1992)** → **world's largest microfinance project**.
**DAY-NRLM (MoRD, 2011)**: **90.90 lakh+ SHGs**, repayment **98%+**.
AP precursor: **DWCRA (1982-83)**.

88.s: The NABARD pilot project for linking Self-Help Groups with banks was launched in:
88.x: NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage pilot in 1992. It became the world’s largest microfinance project, with banks lending to SHGs.
88.tq: Distinguish the mid-1980s pioneering phase from the 1992 NABARD pilot.
xs: NABARD's **SHG-Bank Linkage pilot** began in **1992** — option **(3)**.
xa: It became the **world's largest microfinance project**; banks lend to SHGs.
**MYRADA** had pioneered linkage in the **mid-1980s**.
**DAY-NRLM**: **10.05 crore** rural women households.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly describes DAY-NRLM?
o: It is a Ministry of Rural Development programme launched in 2011 for rural livelihoods and SHGs.
It is an RBI programme launched in 1992 for bank recapitalisation.
It is an AP Government programme launched in 1982 for urban women.
It is a Ministry of Finance programme launched in 2015 for urban enterprises.
88.x: DAY-NRLM is associated with the Ministry of Rural Development and was launched in 2011 to promote rural livelihoods through SHGs and related institutions.
88.tq: Use the ministry, year and rural-or-urban distinction together.
xs: **DAY-NRLM** is a **Ministry of Rural Development** programme of **2011** for SHGs — option **(1)**.
**1992** = NABARD's linkage pilot; **1982** = AP's **DWCRA**; **2015** = MUDRA, a Finance Ministry scheme.
xa: DAY-NRLM: **90.90 lakh+ SHGs**, **10.05 crore** rural women households.

88.s: With reference to SHG-bank linkage in Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following is correct?
o: AP ranks first in the country with about 36% of the national share and a recovery rate of about 99.66%
AP ranks first with about 10% of the national share and a recovery rate of about 75%
AP ranks third, behind Tamil Nadu and Kerala, with a recovery rate of about 90%
AP's SHG model is run by NABARD directly, without any State society
88.x: AP ranks 1st in SHG-bank linkage with a 36% national share, 99.66% recovery and about ₹32,190 crore disbursed. The other share, rank and recovery figures are wrong, and the AP model is run by SERP, not directly by NABARD.
88.tq: AP SHG: rank 1, 36% share, 99.66% recovery, run by SERP.
xs: AP ranks **first** with **36% of the national share** and **99.66% recovery** — option **(1)**.
AP is not third; its model is run by **SERP**, not directly by NABARD.
xa: About **₹32,190 crore** disbursed.
SERP: **8.50 lakh SHGs**, **89.21 lakh women**.
AP's **2010 microfinance crisis** reshaped national MFI regulation.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI):
1. It was set up in 2008 by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.
2. It is a Section 8 not-for-profit company under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
3. It is the umbrella organisation for retail payments in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: set up in 2008 by RBI and IBA. Statement 2 is wrong: it is a Section 8 not-for-profit company under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, not the Banking Regulation Act. Statement 3 is correct: it is the umbrella for retail payments. So '1 and 3 only'.
88.tq: NPCI: 2008, RBI + IBA, PSS Act 2007, retail payments.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **NPCI** was set up in **2008** by the **RBI** and the **IBA**.
Statement 2 wrong: it is a **Section 8** company under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007**, not the Banking Regulation Act.
Statement 3 correct: NPCI is the **umbrella for retail payments**.
xa: NPCI products: **UPI**, **RuPay**, **BHIM**, **IMPS**, **AePS**, **NFS**, **NACH**.
UPI abroad goes via **NPCI International Payments Ltd (NIPL)**.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the launch and underlying framework of UPI?
o: Launched in April 2018 with 21 banks on the RTGS framework
Launched in January 2020 with 11 banks on the NACH framework
Launched in April 2016 with 21 banks on the IMPS framework
Launched in December 2016 with 30 banks on the NEFT framework
88.x: UPI was launched in April 2016 with 21 banks and operated on the IMPS framework.
88.tq: Combine the year, participating-bank count and technological framework.
xs: **UPI** was launched in **April 2016** with **21 banks** on the **IMPS** framework — option **(3)**.
**UPI 2.0** came in **2018**; zero MDR began **1 Jan 2020**.
xa: UPI uses a **VPA** (e.g. name@bank) for real-time account-to-account transfers.
**FY 2025-26**: **24,160 crore** transactions worth **₹314 lakh crore**.
UPI turned **10** in **Aug 2026**.

88.s: Which payment system is described as the largest interoperable ATM network in India?
88.x: The National Financial Switch, or NFS, is the largest interoperable ATM network.
88.tq: Use the superlative carefully and distinguish network infrastructure from payment applications.
xs: **NFS (National Financial Switch)** is the **largest interoperable ATM network** — option **(1)**.
**AePS** = Aadhaar micro-ATM banking; **NACH** = bulk payments; **UPI 2.0** = upgraded UPI.
xa: NFS was asked in **APPSC GS 2024**.
**RuPay** is accepted in **Singapore, Bhutan, UAE, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia**.

88.s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. IMPS — 24x7 instant interbank transfer
b. e-RUPI — person- and purpose-specific prepaid digital voucher
c. FASTag — RFID toll payment
d. 123Pay — UPI for feature phones
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
88.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. IMPS provides instant interbank transfers, e-RUPI is a targeted prepaid voucher, FASTag uses RFID for tolls and 123Pay brings UPI to feature phones.
88.tq: Check each product against its distinctive purpose before selecting the complete code.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4)**, **a, b, c and d**.
**IMPS** = 24x7 instant transfer; **e-RUPI** = person- and purpose-specific prepaid voucher.
**FASTag** = RFID toll payment (**NETC**); **123Pay** = UPI for **feature phones**.
xa: e-RUPI is used in **13 govt schemes**.
123Pay works in **20 languages**.
UPI itself runs on the **IMPS** framework.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about RTGS and NEFT:
1. RTGS settles transactions in real time on a gross basis, one by one.
2. NEFT has a minimum transaction amount of Rs 2 lakh.
3. Both RTGS and NEFT are operated by the RBI.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: RTGS is real-time gross settlement. Statement 2 is wrong: the Rs 2 lakh minimum applies to RTGS; NEFT has no minimum and settles in deferred net half-hourly batches. Statement 3 is correct: the RBI operates both. So '1 and 3 only'.
88.tq: The Rs 2 lakh minimum belongs to RTGS, the 'big ticket' system.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **RTGS** settles in **real time, gross** (one by one).
Statement 2 wrong: the **₹2 lakh** minimum is for **RTGS**; **NEFT** has **no minimum**.
Statement 3 correct: **RBI** operates both.
xa: NEFT settles on a **deferred net** basis in **half-hourly batches**.
RBI **removed charges** on NEFT/RTGS.

88.s:
Which of the following is a feature of the newer UPI developments reported for 2026?
1. Credit Line on UPI
2. Hello! UPI
3. UPI LITE X for offline payments
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
88.x: Credit Line on UPI, Hello! UPI and UPI LITE X for offline payments were listed as newer UPI features.
88.tq: Recognise the complete set of current product enhancements without confusing them with older UPI 2.0 features.
xs: All three are newer UPI features — option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
**Credit Line on UPI**, **Hello! UPI** and **UPI LITE X** (offline).
xa: UPI turned **10** in **Aug 2026**, with a **~13,000-fold** volume surge.
**July 2026**: **2,366 crore** transactions (~**7,600** per second).
Monthly transactions first passed **2,000 crore** in **Aug 2025**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on digital payments:
1. Zero MDR has applied to RuPay debit and BHIM-UPI transactions since 1 January 2020.
2. Zero MDR is provided under Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
3. After the recent amendment, UPI is no longer free for consumers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: zero MDR on RuPay debit and BHIM-UPI since 1 Jan 2020. Statement 2 is correct: it rests on Sec 10A of the PSS Act 2007. Statement 3 is wrong: the amendment allows a small MDR only on some high-value transactions, and UPI stays free for consumers. So '1 and 2 only'.
88.tq: Any MDR falls on merchants for high-value payments; consumers still pay nothing.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **zero MDR** on **RuPay debit** and **BHIM-UPI** since **1 Jan 2020**.
Statement 2 correct: it rests on **Sec 10A** of the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007**.
Statement 3 wrong: the amendment allows a small MDR only on some **high-value** transactions; **UPI stays free for consumers**.
xa: **Taxation and other Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026** lets the Centre modify zero-MDR.
Debate: the **cost of zero-MDR** for PSPs.
The incentive scheme is run by **DFS**; nodal agency **NPCI**.

88.s: Promotion of digital payments was shifted from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to the
o: Department of Economic Affairs under the Ministry of Commerce
Department of Telecommunications under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
Department of Financial Services under the Ministry of Finance
Reserve Bank of India under the Ministry of Finance
88.x: Responsibility for promotion of digital payments was shifted from MeitY to the Department of Financial Services under the Ministry of Finance.
88.tq: Apply the 'which department performs this function?' authority test.
xs: Digital payments promotion moved from **MeitY** to the **Department of Financial Services**, **Ministry of Finance** — option **(3)**.
This was the key in **APPSC-G1 2024** (statement I true).
xa: The **RuPay-BHIM UPI incentive scheme** is run by **DFS**.
Incentive: **0.15%** on BHIM-UPI P2M payments up to **₹2,000**.
Nodal agency of the scheme: **NPCI** (**Feb 2026**).

88.s:
Consider the following statements about the RuPay-BHIM UPI incentive scheme:
1. It is run by the Department of Financial Services.
2. It provides an incentive of 0.15% on eligible BHIM-UPI person-to-merchant payments up to ₹2,000.
3. The National Payments Corporation of India is its nodal agency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
88.x: The Department of Financial Services runs the scheme, which provides 0.15% for eligible BHIM-UPI P2M payments up to ₹2,000, with NPCI as nodal agency.
88.tq: Verify the implementing authority, incentive rate and nodal agency as separate elements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **RuPay-BHIM UPI incentive scheme** is run by **DFS**.
Statement 2: it pays **0.15%** on BHIM-UPI **P2M** payments up to **₹2,000** to small merchants.
Statement 3: its nodal agency is **NPCI** (**Feb 2026**).
xa: **Zero MDR** on **RuPay debit** and **BHIM-UPI** since **1 Jan 2020** (**Sec 10A**, PSS Act **2007**).
Digital payments promotion moved from **MeitY** to **DFS (MoF)** (**APPSC-G1 2024**).
RBI removed charges on **NEFT/RTGS**.

88.s: The base year of the Reserve Bank of India's Digital Payments Index (RBI-DPI) is
88.x: The RBI-DPI uses March 2018 as its base, with the index value fixed at 100. January 2021 marks the beginning of its publication, not its base year.
88.tq: Distinguish the index base period from the date of publication.
xs: The **RBI-DPI** base is **March 2018 = 100** — option **(3)**.
**January 2021** is when publication began (**1 Jan 2021**), not the base.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "**2021** as base year" is **false** (**APPSC G1 2024**).
It is published **semi-annually**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the RBI Financial Inclusion Index:
1. It was introduced in 2021.
2. It is released annually in July.
3. It is measured on a scale of 0 to 100.
4. It comprises 97 indicators covering banking, investment, insurance, postal and pension sectors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
88.x: All four statements are correct. The RBI FI-Index was introduced in 2021, is annual and July-based, uses a 0–100 scale and includes 97 indicators across the stated sectors.
88.tq: Test a multi-dimensional index through its year, frequency, scale and coverage.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**, **1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The **FI-Index (RBI)** was introduced in **2021**, is released **annually (July)**, on a **0-100** scale.
It has **97 indicators** across **banking, investment, insurance, postal, pension**.
xa: Sub-indices: **FI-Access (35%)**, **FI-Usage (45%)**, **FI-Quality (20%)**.

88.s: Which of the following correctly represents the weights of the three sub-indices of the RBI Financial Inclusion Index?
88.x: The FI-Index assigns 35% to FI-Access, 45% to FI-Usage and 20% to FI-Quality.
88.tq: Compare the three weights carefully, especially the two close-looking percentages.
xs: FI-Index weights: **Access 35%**, **Usage 45%**, **Quality 20%** — option **(1)**.
**Usage** carries the highest weight; the other options swap the numbers.
xa: The index has **97 indicators** on a **0-100** scale.
Introduced **2021**, released in **July**.
Latest value: **67.0 (2025)**.

88.s: Which country was the first country to adopt UPI services abroad through NPCI International Payments Limited?
88.x: Bhutan was the first country listed for UPI abroad, in 2021.
88.tq: Identify the first country rather than a later participating country.
xs: **Bhutan** was the **first** country to adopt UPI abroad (**2021**) — option **(4)**.
**Singapore** also came in **2021**; **UAE** in **2022**; **France** = **first in Europe**.
xa: UPI abroad goes via **NPCI International Payments Ltd (NIPL)**.
UPI is live in **11 countries** (**25 Aug 2026**).
⚠ **Bhutan** = first country; **France** = first in Europe.

88.s: The UPI-PayNow linkage is associated with:
88.x: Singapore is associated with the UPI-PayNow linkage, which was established in 2023 after the initial 2021 connection.
88.tq: Use the named bilateral linkage to distinguish Singapore from other UPI partner countries.
xs: The **UPI-PayNow** linkage is with **Singapore** — option **(3)**.
Singapore joined in **2021**; the PayNow linkage came in **2023**, for **remittances**.
xa: **Bhutan (2021)** was the first country.
**RuPay** is also accepted in **Singapore**.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly matches countries with the years associated with UPI expansion abroad?
88.x: The stated sequence includes Bhutan in 2021, the UAE in 2022, Nepal in 2024 and Qatar in 2025.
88.tq: Start with the known country-year pairs and eliminate options with reversed chronology.
xs: Correct: **Bhutan 2021**, **UAE 2022**, **Nepal 2024**, **Qatar 2025** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) swaps the years; **Singapore** is **2021**, not paired as in option (3).
xa: **France**: e-commerce, **first in Europe** (**APPSC GS 2025**).
**Cambodia, Greece, Maldives** joined in **2026**.
**Mauritius** and **Sri Lanka** are also live.

88.s: UPI accounted for approximately what share of the world's real-time payments in 2025?
88.x: UPI represented approximately 49% of the world's real-time payments in 2025.
88.tq: Distinguish the global share from India's domestic digital-payment share.
xs: UPI made up **49%** of the world's **real-time payments** in **2025** (IMF) — option **(3)**.
**85%** is UPI's share of **India's digital payment volume** in FY 2025-26, not the world share.
xa: UPI = **~83%** of retail digital payments by volume.
FY 2025-26: **24,160 crore** transactions.
Over **90%** of UPI users still use cash.

88.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched regarding international UPI linkages?
o: Bhutan — first country outside Asia to adopt UPI
Singapore — first country to adopt UPI for domestic cash withdrawals
France — first European country where UPI was enabled for e-commerce
88.x: France became the first European country where UPI was enabled for e-commerce. Singapore is associated with the UPI-PayNow remittance link, while Cambodia joined through NIPL and ACLEDA on the KHQR platform.
88.tq: Use nearby-country associations to detect the swapped international linkage.
xs: **France** is the **first European** country where UPI works (e-commerce) — option **(3)**.
**Bhutan** was the **first country** overall, not outside Asia; **Singapore** = **UPI-PayNow**; **Cambodia** = **KHQR** via **ACLEDA Bank**.
xa: France was asked in **APPSC GS 2025**.
UPI-PayNow linkage: **2023**, for **remittances**.
⚠ **Bhutan** = first; **France** = first in Europe.

88.s: Which statement best explains the continuing hybrid nature of payments in India?
o: More than 90% of UPI users still use cash along with digital payments.
Digital payments are confined mainly to government transactions.
UPI has completely replaced cash for more than 90% of its users.
Cash is used only by persons who do not possess bank accounts.
88.x: Despite widespread UPI use, over 90% of UPI users still use cash, making payment behaviour hybrid rather than exclusively digital.
88.tq: Reject an extreme replacement claim and apply the stated coexistence pattern.
xs: Payments stay **hybrid**: over **90%** of UPI users **still use cash** — option **(1)**.
So UPI has not replaced cash, as option (3) claims.
xa: UPI = **~83%** of retail digital payments by volume.
Criticism: **digital divide** and **skills gaps**.

88.s: The principal objective of the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) is to
o: issue a sovereign digital currency for online purchases
create an open network that reduces the dominance of e-commerce platforms
regulate cryptocurrency exchanges through the RBI
replace Aadhaar with a private digital identity system
88.x: ONDC seeks to create an open digital commerce network and break e-commerce platform monopolies. It is not a currency or cryptocurrency-regulation platform.
88.tq: Match the initiative with its institutional objective and reject unrelated digital-finance functions.
xs: **ONDC** aims to **democratise e-commerce and break platform monopolies** — option **(2)**.
A sovereign digital currency is the **e-rupee (RBI)**; ONDC regulates no crypto and does not replace **Aadhaar**.
xa: ONDC is a **DPIIT** initiative.
It is part of **India Stack** with **Aadhaar**, **UPI**, **DigiLocker**, **Account Aggregator**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements regarding payments banks:
1. They can accept deposits up to the initial limit of ₹1 lakh per customer.
2. They can lend directly to customers and issue credit cards.
3. They can issue ATM or debit cards.
4. They can park funds in Government securities.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
88.x: Payments banks could accept deposits up to the initial ₹1 lakh limit, issue ATM/debit cards and invest in Government securities. They cannot lend or issue credit cards.
88.tq: Split the options by identifying the prohibited lending function.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: deposits up to **₹1 lakh** per customer (initial cap).
Statement 2 wrong: payments banks **cannot lend** or issue **credit cards**.
Statements 3 and 4 correct: they issue **ATM/debit cards** and **park funds in G-secs**.
xa: **SFBs** lend: **50%** of loans up to **₹25 lakh**.
Payments banks came from the **Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)**.

88.s:
With reference to payments banks and small finance banks, consider the following statements:
1. Payments banks cannot lend, whereas small finance banks are intended to provide loans.
2. Small finance banks are required to lend 50% of their loans up to ₹25 lakh.
3. Both types of banks have identical lending mandates.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
88.x: Payments banks cannot lend. Small finance banks lend to underserved segments, with 50% of their loans required to be up to ₹25 lakh. Their mandates are therefore not identical.
88.tq: Use the contrast between a prohibited function and a mandated lending function.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: **payments banks cannot lend**; **SFBs** lend.
Statement 2 correct: SFBs lend **50%** of loans **up to ₹25 lakh**.
Statement 3 wrong: their lending mandates differ.
xa: Payments banks' deposit cap: **₹1 lakh** per customer.
Both stem from the **Nachiket Mor Committee (2013)**.

88.s: An Account Aggregator primarily facilitates:
o: Compulsory transfer of all bank deposits to the RBI
Consent-based sharing of financial data among financial institutions
Direct lending by the Government to first-time borrowers
Issue of physical credit cards by payments banks
88.x: An Account Aggregator facilitates consent-based sharing of financial information, including bank transactions and GST records.
88.tq: Test the exact institutional function rather than the name alone.
xs: An **Account Aggregator** enables **consent-based sharing of financial data** — option **(2)**.
Data shared: **bank transactions**, **GST records**; it speeds up **credit appraisal** for **first-time borrowers**.
xa: AAs are **RBI-regulated NBFC-AAs**.
AA is part of **India Stack**.
**OCEN** links lenders and marketplaces for small-ticket credit.

88.s: OCEN is best described as:
o: A securities settlement system for stock exchanges
A deposit insurance scheme for payments banks
A common protocol linking lenders and marketplaces for small-ticket credit
A tax collection platform for State Governments
88.x: OCEN, or Open Credit Enablement Network, provides common protocols connecting lenders and marketplaces for small-ticket credit.
88.tq: Decode the acronym through its function and participant relationship.
xs: **OCEN (Open Credit Enablement Network)** = **common protocols linking lenders and marketplaces** for **small-ticket credit** — option **(3)**.
It is not a securities, deposit-insurance or tax platform.
xa: **Account Aggregator** feeds such credit by consent-based data sharing.
**UPI-linked credit** grew **without higher defaults**.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly states the regulatory and tax treatment of cryptocurrency in India?
o: Cryptocurrency gains are taxed at 1% with 30% TDS, and private cryptocurrency was banned in 2021.
Cryptocurrency gains are taxed at 30% with 1% TDS; the 2021 bill seeking to ban private cryptocurrency remains pending.
Cryptocurrency is legal tender issued by the RBI and is exempt from tax.
Cryptocurrency gains are taxed at 30% with 1% TDS, and losses may always be freely set off against all income.
88.x: Crypto gains attract a 30% tax and 1% TDS. The 2021 bill proposing a ban on private crypto remains pending; cryptocurrency is not RBI-issued legal tender.
88.tq: Watch for reversed tax rates and the false claim that a pending bill is already law.
xs: Crypto gains are taxed at **30%** with **1% TDS**; the **2021** bill to ban private crypto is **pending** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) swaps the rates and wrongly says crypto was banned; crypto is **not legal tender**.
There is **no loss set-off**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: The **30% / 1% TDS** regime applies since **2022**.
SC (**2020**) struck down RBI's **2018** banking ban.
Crypto: private, decentralised, no central issuer (**Bitcoin 2009**).

88.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the legal framework for the Digital Rupee is correct?
o: The PSS Act, 2007 was amended to make cryptocurrency legal tender.
The RBI Act was amended through the Finance Act, 2022 to cover digital currency.
The Finance Act, 2022 placed UPI under the authority of the RBI as a currency issuer.
The RBI Act was amended in 2018 to prohibit all forms of digital currency.
88.x: The Finance Act, 2022 amended the RBI Act to provide for digital currency. This concerns the Digital Rupee and does not make cryptocurrency legal tender.
88.tq: Identify the correct statute and amendment year instead of swapping neighbouring payment laws.
xs: The **RBI Act** was amended through the **Finance Act 2022** to cover **digital currency** — option **(2)**.
Crypto is **not legal tender**; UPI is a **payment system** under the **PSS Act 2007**, not a currency.
RBI's **2018** step was a **banking ban** on crypto, struck down by the SC in **2020**.
xa: e-rupee = **legal tender** issued by **RBI** in digital form.
Pilots: **e₹-W** from **1 Nov 2022**; **e₹-R** from **1 Dec 2022**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements about India's CBDC (e-rupee):
1. The wholesale pilot (e-rupee-W) began on 1 November 2022.
2. The retail pilot (e-rupee-R) began before the wholesale pilot.
3. The DEA and the RBI are working on interlinking CBDCs for cross-border payments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: the wholesale pilot began on 1 Nov 2022. Statement 2 is wrong: the retail pilot began later, on 1 Dec 2022. Statement 3 is correct: DEA and RBI are working on interlinking CBDCs across borders. So '1 and 3 only'.
88.tq: Wholesale first (Nov 2022), retail a month later (Dec 2022).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: wholesale pilot (**e₹-W**) from **1 Nov 2022**.
Statement 2 wrong: the retail pilot (**e₹-R**) came **later**, on **1 Dec 2022**.
Statement 3 correct: **DEA-RBI** are working on **interlinking CBDCs**.
xa: Benefits: **programmable**, **targeted subsidy delivery**, cheaper remittances.
Bahamas **Sand Dollar** = world's first live retail CBDC (**2020**).

88.s: The Bahamas' Sand Dollar is notable because it was
o: the world's first live retail CBDC, launched in 2020
the first wholesale CBDC pilot in the world
the first CBDC used exclusively for cross-border payments
the first cryptocurrency issued by a central bank
88.x: The Sand Dollar of the Bahamas was the world's first live retail CBDC and was launched in 2020.
88.tq: Distinguish the first live retail CBDC from wholesale pilots and private cryptocurrencies.
xs: The Bahamas **Sand Dollar** is the **world's first live retail CBDC**, launched in **2020** — option **(1)**.
A CBDC is issued by a central bank; it is not a cryptocurrency, which has **no central issuer**.
xa: Other CBDCs: China **e-CNY**, Nigeria **eNaira**, Jamaica **JAM-DEX**.
Sweden **e-Krona**; Eurozone **Digital Euro**.
India's retail pilot **e₹-R** from **1 Dec 2022**.

88.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the e-rupee, UPI and cryptocurrency?
o: The e-rupee is money itself and an RBI liability; UPI moves bank-account money; cryptocurrency is private and has no sovereign backing.
The e-rupee is a private asset; UPI is a cryptocurrency; cryptocurrency is an RBI liability.
UPI is money itself issued by RBI, whereas the e-rupee is only a payment system.
The e-rupee and UPI are both private decentralised currencies, whereas cryptocurrency is issued by NPCI.
88.x: The e-rupee is money itself and a liability of the RBI. UPI is a payment system for moving bank-account money, while cryptocurrency is private, decentralised and lacks sovereign backing.
88.tq: Compare the nature, issuer or liability, and function of all three instruments.
xs: **e-rupee** = money, an **RBI liability**; **UPI** moves bank-account money; **crypto** is private with no sovereign backing — option **(1)**.
The e-rupee is **legal tender**, not a private asset; UPI is not a currency.
xa: Crypto: **no central issuer**, **not legal tender**.
Issuer liability: crypto **none**, e-rupee **RBI**, UPI **bank deposits**.
UPI operates under **NPCI**, **PSS Act 2007**.

88.s: In 2020, the Supreme Court of India, in a case relating to cryptocurrency:
o: Upheld the RBI's 2018 ban on banks dealing in cryptocurrency
Struck down the RBI's 2018 circular barring banks from dealing with cryptocurrency businesses
Declared cryptocurrency to be legal tender
Directed the RBI to launch the Digital Rupee
88.x: In 2020 the SC struck down the RBI's 2018 banking ban on crypto, so it was not upheld. Crypto is still not legal tender, and the 2021 bill to ban private crypto is pending. The Digital Rupee came through an amendment to the RBI Act (Finance Act 2022), not a court order, with pilots in Nov/Dec 2022.
88.tq: RBI ban 2018 → SC struck down 2020 → ban bill 2021 pending → 30% tax 2022.
xs: In **2020** the SC **struck down** the RBI's **2018** banking ban on crypto — option **(2)**.
It did not uphold the ban; crypto is still **not legal tender**.
The **Digital Rupee** came via the **Finance Act 2022** amendment to the RBI Act, not a court order.
xa: The **2021** bill to ban private crypto is **still pending**.
Crypto gains: **30% flat tax**, **1% TDS**.

88.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the proposed changes concerning zero-MDR:
1. The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha.
2. The Bill permits the Centre to modify zero-MDR.
3. UPI is intended to remain free for consumers, while MDR may be imposed on high-value payments.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
88.x: All three statements are correct: the 2026 Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha, permits the Centre to modify zero-MDR, and allows the possibility of MDR on high-value UPI payments while retaining free consumer access.
88.tq: Check whether the legislative change, consumer position and high-value exception all fit together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
The **Taxation and other Laws (Amendment) Bill 2026** passed the **LS** and lets the Centre **modify zero-MDR**.
**UPI stays free for consumers**; **MDR on high-value UPI** payments is possible.
xa: Zero MDR has applied since **1 Jan 2020** under **Sec 10A**, PSS Act **2007**.
Debate: the **cost of zero-MDR** for **PSPs**.

88.s: The microfinance crisis in Andhra Pradesh in 2010 had the wider consequence of:
o: Converting all MFIs into payments banks
Ending the SHG-bank linkage programme across India
Prohibiting all forms of digital payments
Reshaping national regulation of microfinance institutions
88.x: The Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis of 2010 contributed to changes that reshaped national regulation of MFIs.
88.tq: Link a regional event with its national regulatory consequence.
xs: AP's **2010 microfinance crisis** **reshaped national MFI regulation** — option **(4)**.
It did not end SHG-bank linkage; AP still ranks **1st** in it.
xa: **Y.H. Malegam (2010)** committee examined microfinance after the AP crisis (RBI).
AP's SHG model is run by **SERP**.

88.s:
Which of the following is identified as a criticism or challenge associated with the digital financial architecture?
1. Digital divide and skills gaps
2. Cost of the zero-MDR model for payment system providers
3. Dormant Jan Dhan accounts

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
88.x: Digital divide and skills gaps, the cost burden of zero-MDR for payment system providers, and dormant Jan Dhan accounts are all identified concerns.
88.tq: Recognise that a policy can have several simultaneous implementation criticisms.
xs: All three are listed criticisms — option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
**Digital divide + skills gaps**; **cost of the zero-MDR model for PSPs**; **dormant Jan Dhan accounts**.
xa: Over **90%** of UPI users still use cash.
The **2026** Bill lets the Centre modify zero-MDR.

88.s: Which of the following is an objective of financial inclusion?
o: Restricting access to formal financial services
Limiting banking infrastructure to urban areas
88.x: Promoting financial literacy is an aim of financial inclusion, so people know about and use financial services. The other options are the reverse of inclusion.
88.tq: Find the option that widens access.
n: Financial inclusion promotes financial literacy through awareness and informed use. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]
Financial inclusion promotes financial literacy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]

88.s:
Consider the following statements about financial inclusion:
1. It seeks to extend financial services particularly to the poor population.
2. It expands banking infrastructure particularly in metropolitan urban areas.
3. It seeks to provide access to credit especially for weaker sections.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
88.x: Statement 1 is correct: inclusion extends financial services to the poor. Statement 2 is wrong: banking infrastructure is expanded in underserved and rural areas, not metros. Statement 3 is correct: inclusion gives weaker sections access to credit. Hence 1 and 3 only.
88.tq: Inclusion = poor, rural/underserved, weaker sections; any 'urban/elite' focus is the trap.

88.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A bank account is associated with financial inclusion.
Statement B: Credit constraints are associated with financial inclusion.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
88.x: A is true and B is false: having a bank account is a sign of inclusion, while being unable to get credit is a sign of exclusion.
88.tq: Discriminate inclusion from exclusion.
n: Financial inclusion provides access to a bank account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]
Financial exclusion involves credit constraints. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]

88.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Financial inclusion facilitates payments and remittances through the formal financial system.
II. Financial inclusion promotes access to insurance.
III. Financial inclusion seeks to reduce financial security.
