**RCM** shifts liability to the recipient; **anti-profiteering** passes benefits to consumers; **destination principle** assigns revenue to the consuming State.
xa: ITC ends **cascading** (tax on tax); blocked-ITC rules apply.
**Zero-rated** supplies get a **full ITC refund**; nil-rated/exempt get none.
**E-invoicing** helps verify ITC and curb fake invoices.

96.s: Under the Reverse Charge Mechanism in GST, the liability to pay tax is shifted from the:
96.x: Under reverse charge, the recipient, rather than the supplier, pays GST on specified supplies.
96.tq: Distinguish the direction of liability by asking who actually remits the tax.
xs: Under **Reverse Charge (RCM)**, liability shifts from the **supplier to the recipient** — option **(3)**.
The **recipient**, not the supplier, pays GST on **specified supplies**.
xa: **ITC** sets off input tax against output tax.
**Composition scheme**: turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (₹50 lakh services); flat **1%** goods, **6%** services; **no ITC**.
**E-way bill** needed for moving goods worth **> ₹50,000**.

96.s:
Consider the following statements about GST anti-profiteering:
1. Section 171 requires the benefit of rate cuts or ITC to be passed on to consumers.
2. From 1 October 2024, anti-profiteering cases go to the Principal Bench of GSTAT.
3. The National Anti-Profiteering Authority continues to hear these cases after 1 October 2024.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
96.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the National Anti-Profiteering Authority was replaced (functions to CCI in Dec 2022, then the GSTAT Principal Bench from 1 Oct 2024). So 1 and 2 only.
96.tq: NAA -> CCI (2022) -> GSTAT Principal Bench (Oct 2024).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Sec 171** requires rate-cut/ITC benefits to reach **consumers**.
Statement 2 correct: from **1 Oct 2024**, cases go to the **Principal Bench of GSTAT**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **National Anti-Profiteering Authority** was replaced — functions went to **CCI (Dec 2022)**, then GSTAT.
xa: **GSTN** is the IT backbone; it uses **AI tools** for scrutiny.
**GSTIN** is a **15-digit** registration number.

96.s: A registered person opts for the composition scheme. Which one of the following combinations correctly describes the scheme?
o: ₹50 lakh goods turnover, ₹1.5 crore services turnover, 1% goods, 6% services and no ITC
₹1.5 crore goods turnover, ₹50 lakh services turnover, 6% goods, 1% services and full ITC
₹1.5 crore goods turnover, ₹50 lakh services turnover, 1% goods, 6% services and no ITC
₹50 lakh goods turnover, ₹1.5 crore services turnover, 6% goods, 1% services and full ITC
96.x: The composition scheme applies up to ₹1.5 crore for goods and ₹50 lakh for services, with rates of 1% for goods and 6% for services and no input tax credit.
96.tq: Match the turnover limits, rates and ITC consequence as one complete package.
xs: Composition scheme: turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (goods) and **₹50 lakh** (services), flat **1% goods**, **6% services**, **no ITC** — option **(3)**.
Options (1) and (4) swap the turnover limits; options (2) and (4) swap the rates and wrongly allow **full ITC**.
xa: ITC is not available on **exempt or non-taxable** supplies; **nil-rated/exempt** also give no ITC.
Under **RCM**, the **recipient**, not the supplier, pays GST on specified supplies.
**Budget 2026-27**: **automated registration** within **3 working days** for low-risk applicants.

96.s:
Consider the following statements about the electronic way bill:
1. It is an electronic document used for movement of goods.
2. It is required for goods valued above ₹50,000.
3. Its validity is one day for every 200 kilometres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
96.x: An e-way bill is an electronic document for movement of goods valued above ₹50,000, with validity of one day per 200 kilometres.
96.tq: Verify the document, value threshold and validity-period statements together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **e-way bill** is an **electronic document** for moving goods.
Statement 2: it is needed for goods worth **> ₹50,000**.
Statement 3: validity is **1 day per 200 km**.
xa: **E-invoicing**: digital reporting of invoices to curb **fake invoices** and verify **ITC**; uses **HSN/SAC** codes.
**GSTN** is the IT backbone for registration, returns and ITC matching.
**GSTIN** is a **15-digit** registration number.

96.s: The principal purpose of e-invoicing is to:
o: Replace all GST returns with paper invoices
Digitally report invoices, curb fake invoices and verify input-tax credit
Set the GST Council’s voting weights
Determine the annual borrowing limit of States
96.x: E-invoicing digitally reports invoices, helps curb fake invoices and supports verification of input-tax credit.
96.tq: Connect the digital mechanism with its compliance objectives.
xs: **E-invoicing** means **digital reporting of invoices** to **curb fake invoices** and **verify ITC** — option **(2)**.
It works with **HSN/SAC codes**; it does not bring back paper invoices or touch Council voting or State borrowing.
xa: **E-way bill**: electronic document for moving goods worth **> ₹50,000**; valid **1 day per 200 km**.
**GSTN** does **ITC matching** and uses **AI tools**.
**Anti-profiteering (Sec 171)**: ITC benefits must reach consumers.

96.s:
Consider the following statements regarding GST compensation cess:
1. Its levy was extended up to March 2026 to repay loans taken for paying compensation.
2. From 22 September 2025, it was scrapped for all goods without exception.
3. It continued on tobacco after the general withdrawal of the cess.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
96.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The cess was scrapped for all goods except tobacco, so statement 2 is false.
96.tq: Find the exception hidden in an otherwise broad statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the levy was **extended to March 2026** to repay loans taken to pay compensation.
Statement 2 wrong: on **22 Sep 2025** it was scrapped for all goods **except tobacco**.
Statement 3 correct: it continued on **tobacco**.
xa: Compensation cess **ended 31 March 2026**.
From **1 Feb 2026**: higher **excise on tobacco** and **Health Security se National Security Cess** on pan masala.
Compensation itself ended in **June 2022**.

96.s: Which of the following replaced the compensation-cess arrangement for tobacco and pan masala from 1 February 2026?
o: A special State GST on tobacco products
A customs duty collected by the GST Council
Higher excise on tobacco and Health Security se National Security Cess on pan masala units
A surcharge under the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act
96.x: Higher excise was imposed on tobacco under the Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025, while Health Security se National Security Cess was imposed on pan masala units.
96.tq: Match the replacement measures with the correct commodities.
xs: From **1 Feb 2026**: **higher excise on tobacco** and the **Health Security se National Security Cess** on **pan masala units** — option **(3)**.
The tobacco excise comes under the **Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025** — a Central excise, not a State GST, customs duty or IGST surcharge.
xa: The new cess is levied on machine **production capacity**.
It is credited to the **CFI** and **not shared** with States.
Compensation cess **ended 31 March 2026**.

96.s:
Consider the following statements about the Health Security se National Security Cess:
1. It is levied on pan masala units on the basis of machine production capacity.
2. Its proceeds are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India and are not shared with States.
3. It replaced the compensation cess from 1 April 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
96.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the replacement levies apply from 1 February 2026. So 1 and 2 only.
96.tq: New sin-goods levies (Feb 2026) are not shared with States.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: levied on **pan masala units** by **machine production capacity**.
Statement 2 correct: credited to the **CFI**, **not shared** with States.
Statement 3 wrong: the replacement levies apply **from 1 Feb 2026**, not 1 April 2025.
xa: Tobacco faces higher excise under the **Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025**.
Criticism: **cesses** stay **outside the divisible pool**.

96.s:
Which of the following statements regarding compensation cess is correct?
1. It was imposed on specified luxury and sin goods.
2. It was intended to support compensation to States for five years at 14% annual growth over 2015–16.
3. Compensation to States continued indefinitely after June 2022.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
96.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Compensation to States ended in June 2022, although cess collections continued for loan repayment.
96.tq: Reject the indefinite-continuation trap in statement 3.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the cess was on **luxury/sin goods**.
Statement 2 correct: it funded **5-year** compensation at **14%** growth over **2015-16**.
Statement 3 wrong: compensation **ended June 2022**; only the cess continued, to **repay loans**.
xa: Cess scrapped **22 Sep 2025** except tobacco; ended **31 March 2026**.
⚠ Compensation (ended **2022**) vs cess (ended **2026**).

96.s: Goods and Services Tax is regarded as the biggest indirect tax reform in India since Independence primarily because it:
o: replaced the need for all direct taxes
abolished the divisible pool of taxes
created a unified framework for a large number of indirect taxes
transferred all taxation powers to the States
96.x: GST is considered the biggest indirect tax reform since Independence because it established a unified framework for indirect taxation by subsuming several indirect taxes.
96.tq: Identify the precise significance rather than choosing extreme claims about direct taxes or complete transfer of powers.
xs: GST is the **biggest indirect tax reform since Independence** as it **created a unified framework** for many indirect taxes — option **(3)**.
It subsumed **8 Central + 9 State taxes** into a **single destination-based tax** ("one nation, one tax").
It did not replace direct taxes or move all powers to States; States in fact **gave up** indirect-tax powers.
xa: Objective: end **cascading** (tax on tax); **one nation-one market**.
GST applies at **both central and state levels** (APPSC 2023).
Record gross GST: **₹2.43 lakh crore in April 2026**.

96.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the impact of GST on States:
1. States surrendered some of their independent indirect-tax instruments after the introduction of GST.
2. Cesses are outside the divisible pool.
3. Tamil Nadu adopted a resolution relating to fair devolution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
96.x: All three statements are correct. The GST framework led States to give up some independent indirect-tax powers, cesses remain outside the divisible pool, and Tamil Nadu raised the issue of fair devolution through a resolution.
96.tq: Check each statement independently before selecting the comprehensive combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: States **gave up independent indirect-tax powers**.
Statement 2: **cesses are outside the divisible pool**.
Statement 3: **Tamil Nadu** passed a resolution on **fair devolution** (**10 Aug 2026**).
xa: The **Health Security se National Security Cess** is **not shared** with States.
GST Council voting: Centre **1/3**, States **2/3**.
**Mohit Minerals (2022)**: Council recommendations are **persuasive, not binding**.

96.s: For Andhra Pradesh, which is the largest source of the State's own tax revenue (2024-25 RE)?
o: State excise, at about 22% of own tax revenue
Stamp duty and registration, at about 38% of own tax revenue
SGST, at about Rs 36,296 crore or 38% of own tax revenue
Motor vehicle tax, at about 22% of own tax revenue
96.x: SGST/GST is AP's largest own tax source: about Rs 36,296 crore, 38% of own tax revenue in 2024-25 RE. State excise (22%) is second, so A is the runner-up, not the largest. Stamp duty and motor vehicle tax are smaller and the shares given in B and D are wrong.
96.tq: AP own tax revenue: GST 38% first, excise 22% second.
xs: AP's largest own tax source is **SGST**: **₹36,296 crore**, **38%** of own tax revenue (2024-25 RE) — option **(3)**.
Option (2) wrongly gives the **38%** share to **stamp duty**; that share belongs to SGST.
xa: AP HC: Centre and State tax authorities must decide **inter se** who investigates (May **2026**).
Stamp duty and **motor vehicle tax** stay **outside GST** with the States.
**SGST** is levied by the **State** on intra-State supply, in **equal halves** with CGST.

96.s: GST was implemented in India on which date?
96.x: GST came into force on 1 July 2017, after the 101st Constitutional Amendment of 2016.
96.tq: Recall the GST launch date.
n: GST was implemented on 1 July 2017. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

96.s:
Assertion (A): Under GST, revenue ultimately accrues to the jurisdiction where goods or services are consumed.
Reason (R): GST is a destination-based tax rather than a tax based on the place where goods or services are produced.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
96.x: Both are true: GST revenue goes to the State where goods or services are consumed because GST is a destination-based tax. R explains A.
96.tq: Ask whether the principle explains the outcome.
n: GST is a multi-stage, destination-based tax. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
GST revenue ultimately accrues to the jurisdiction where goods or services are consumed. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
GST revenue does not accrue based on where goods or services are produced. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

96.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Creating a common or unified national market is a major objective of GST.
Statement B: Reducing the cascading of taxes is a major objective of GST.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
96.x: Both are true: GST aims to create one national market and to end tax on tax (cascading).
96.tq: Recall the aims of GST.
n: A major objective of GST is to create a common or unified national market. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
A major objective of GST is to reduce cascading of taxes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

96.s: Which of the following statements regarding taxes subsumed under GST is incorrect?
o: Central Excise Duty was subsumed under GST.
State VAT was subsumed under GST.
Various other Central and State direct taxes were subsumed under GST.
Service Tax was subsumed under GST.
96.x: Option C is incorrect: GST replaced indirect taxes such as excise, service tax and State VAT, not direct taxes.
96.tq: Watch for 'direct' replacing 'indirect'.
n: Central Excise Duty was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Service Tax was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
State VAT was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Various other Central and State indirect taxes were subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

96.s: Consider the following statements regarding GST administration: I. The GST Council makes recommendations. II. The Centre administers and collects CGST and IGST. III. States administer SGST. Which of the statements given above are correct?
96.x: All three are correct: the GST Council recommends, the Centre collects CGST and IGST, and the States collect SGST.
96.tq: Recall who collects each GST component.
n: The GST Council makes recommendations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Centre administers and collects CGST and IGST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
States administer SGST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

96.s: Which of the following statements regarding the GST Council is incorrect?
o: The GST Council is provided for under Article 279A.
The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue/Finance is its Chairperson.
The GST Council is a Constitutional Body.
The Union Finance Minister is its Chairperson.
96.x: Option B is incorrect: the Union Finance Minister chairs the GST Council (Article 279A). The Minister of State for Finance is only a member.
96.tq: Discriminate the chair from the members.
n: The GST Council is a constitutional body. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Article 279A provides for the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Union Finance Minister is the chairperson of the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance is a member of the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]

97.s: In which month did monthly gross GST collections first exceed ₹2 lakh crore?
97.x: Monthly gross GST collections crossed ₹2 lakh crore for the first time in April 2024.
97.tq: Test a milestone date using close year alternatives.
xs: Monthly gross GST first exceeded **₹2 lakh crore** in **April 2024** — option **(4)**.
**April 2026** is the later **record** month (**₹2.43 lakh crore**), not the first crossing.
xa: FY 2017-18 average: **₹82,000 cr/month**.
**FY 2024-25**: **₹22.08 lakh crore**, avg **₹1.84 lakh crore**/month.

97.s: Which one of the following correctly represents India’s gross GST collection during FY 2024-25?
o: ₹22.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹1.84 lakh crore per month
₹24.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹2.04 lakh crore per month
₹22.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹2.43 lakh crore per month
₹17.4 lakh crore, with an average of ₹1.82 lakh crore per month
97.x: Gross GST collection in FY 2024-25 was ₹22.08 lakh crore, averaging ₹1.84 lakh crore per month.
97.tq: Separate an annual total from its monthly average using precise numerical matching.
xs: **FY 2024-25** gross GST: **₹22.08 lakh crore**, average **₹1.84 lakh crore** per month — option **(1)**.
**₹2.43 lakh crore** is the **April 2026** record month; **₹17.4 lakh crore** is the **Apr-Dec 2025** total.
xa: Collections **doubled in 4 years**, a **CAGR of 18%**.
FY 2017-18 average was only **₹82,000 cr/month**.

97.s:
Consider the following statements about GST collections in April 2026:
1. Gross GST collection reached a record ₹2.43 lakh crore.
2. Gross collection grew by 8.7%.
3. Net GST collection was ₹2.11 lakh crore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
97.x: All three statements are correct for April 2026: gross collection was ₹2.43 lakh crore, growth was 8.7%, and net collection was ₹2.11 lakh crore.
97.tq: Test whether a complete set of related quantitative statements is internally consistent.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**April 2026**: record gross **₹2.43 lakh crore**, up **8.7%**, net **₹2.11 lakh crore**.
xa: **April 2024** was the first month above **₹2 lakh crore**.
**Apr-Jul 2026**: gross **Rs 8.43 lakh crore** (+10.1%); net **Rs 7.21 lakh crore** (+9.2%).

97.s:
Which of the following correctly describes Andhra Pradesh’s AI-powered GST model?
1. It uses a risk matrix.
2. Its Legal-AI assistant was trained on approximately 22,000 judgments.
3. It has dealt with more than 13,700 cases.
4. It is being studied by several other States.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
97.x: All four statements are correct. The model uses a risk matrix, a Legal-AI assistant trained on about 22,000 judgments, and has covered more than 13,700 cases; other States are studying it.
97.tq: Test a technology initiative through its components, scale and adoption by other States.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
AP's **AI-powered GST model** uses a **risk matrix** and a **Legal-AI assistant** trained on **~22,000 judgments**.
It has handled **13,700+ cases** and is being studied by **TN, Bihar, Rajasthan, Kerala, Assam** and others.
xa: **AI-based enforcement** lifted AP collections despite **GST 2.0** rate cuts.
Up to **Aug 2026**: AP commercial taxes **₹25,449.80 cr** (+18.05%); net GST **₹16,452.62 cr**.
**Dec 2025**: AP net GST **₹2,652 cr** — its highest December ever.

97.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025–26, a cut in GST rates may have what effect on revenue?
o: Volume effects may offset the initial revenue loss
It necessarily eliminates all future GST revenue
It reduces transaction volumes in every sector
It affects only customs revenue and not GST revenue
97.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 observed that increased volume of transactions following a rate cut may offset the associated revenue loss.
97.tq: Recognise the stated dynamic revenue effect instead of assuming a static tax-base response.
xs: **ES 2025-26**: after a rate cut, **volume effects may offset the revenue loss** — option **(1)**.
The Survey does not say a cut wipes out revenue or shrinks volumes.
xa: ES 2025-26 calls **GST 2.0** the **third pillar of tax reform**, with "**no net tax hike**".
**ES 2019-20**: rationalisation shocks raise collections only for **1-3 months**.
GST revenue growth in **H2 2025-26** was only **4.67%**.

97.s: Which of the following is the most direct contribution of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) to inter-State commerce?
o: Replacement of input tax credit by a turnover tax
Creation of a common national market through tax harmonisation
Exemption of all inter-State supplies from taxation
Retention of State border check-posts for all goods
97.x: GST created a common national market by harmonising indirect taxation across States. It also helped reduce the cascading effect through input tax credit.
97.tq: Identify the core objective rather than choosing an extreme or reversed consequence.
xs: GST's key contribution: a **common national market** through **tax harmonisation** — option **(2)**.
**ITC at every stage** was kept, not replaced (ending **cascading**); inter-State supplies are taxed under **IGST**.
Border **check-posts were dismantled**, not retained.
xa: **Digital tools**: e-invoicing, e-way bills, auto-generated returns; reduced human interface.
Taxpayer base: **66.5 lakh (2017) → 1.51 crore (2025)**.

97.s:
Consider the following statements regarding e-way bills under GST:
1. An e-way bill is mandatory for the movement of goods worth over Rs 50,000.
2. An e-way bill is valid for one day for every 100 km.
3. E-way bill volumes grew 21% year-on-year in April-December 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is correct: the threshold is Rs 50,000. Statement 2 is wrong: validity is one day per 200 km. Statement 3 is correct: volumes rose 21% YoY in Apr-Dec 2025. So A; B, C and D include the wrong statement 2.
97.tq: E-way bill: 50,000 rupees, 1 day per 200 km.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: e-way bill is **mandatory** for goods worth over **Rs 50,000**.
Statement 2 wrong: validity is **1 day per 200 km**, not 100 km.
Statement 3 correct: **e-way bill volumes +21%** YoY in **Apr-Dec 2025**.
xa: E-way bills replaced physical checks, so State border **check-posts were dismantled**.
E-way bills with **e-invoicing** and AI scrutiny counter **fake invoicing**.

97.s: The removal of inter-State check-posts after the rollout of e-way bills primarily resulted in:
o: A shift from digital to manual tax reporting
Reduced transit time and logistics costs
The abolition of input tax credit
97.x: The replacement of physical checks and the dismantling of border check-posts reduced truck waiting time, transit time and logistics costs.
97.tq: Link the administrative reform to its practical logistics outcome.
xs: Removing check-posts **cut transit time and logistics costs** — option **(2)**.
It also cut **truck waiting time**, once **entry tax** was subsumed and **e-way bills** replaced physical checks.
It moved reporting **toward digital**, with fewer physical checks — the opposite of options (1) and (3).
xa: E-way bill: needed for goods over **Rs 50,000**; valid **1 day per 200 km**.
E-way bill volumes rose **21%** in Apr-Dec 2025.
**ITC** at every stage ended the **cascading effect**.

97.s: Which of the following best indicates the expansion of formalisation under GST between 2017 and 2025?
o: The taxpayer base remained unchanged at 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 66.5 lakh to 1.51 crore
The taxpayer base declined from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
97.x: The taxpayer base expanded from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to 1.51 crore in 2025, indicating greater formalisation.
97.tq: Compare the direction and magnitude of a two-point trend without reversing the figures.
xs: The GST taxpayer base grew **from 66.5 lakh (2017) to 1.51 crore (2025)** — option **(3)**.
This expansion signals **greater formalisation**.
xa: MSME gains: **credit access/eligibility** and **procurement parity** for small firms.
**Composition scheme**: turnover up to **Rs 1.5 crore** (Rs **50 lakh** for services).
Still a burden: **multiple returns + ITC matching**.

97.s:
Consider the following statements regarding GST compliance for small businesses:
1. The composition scheme and automated registration have eased the compliance burden.
2. Multiple returns and input tax credit matching remain a compliance burden.
3. The reform agenda proposes replacing pre-filled returns with manual filing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is correct: the composition scheme and automated registration eased the burden. Statement 2 is correct: multiple returns and ITC matching remain a burden. Statement 3 is wrong: the reform agenda calls for pre-filled returns, time-bound digital registration and automated exporter refunds. So A; B, C and D include statement 3.
97.tq: Reform direction is always more digital/automated: pre-filled returns, not manual filing.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **composition scheme + automated registration** eased the burden.
Statement 2 correct: **multiple returns + ITC matching** remain a burden.
Statement 3 wrong: the reform agenda wants **pre-filled returns**, not manual filing.
xa: The agenda also seeks **time-bound digital registration** and **automated refunds for exporters** (Aug 2025).
Composition: flat **1%** goods / **6%** services.

97.s:
Consider the following statements about the GST composition scheme:
1. It is available for turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore for goods and Rs 50 lakh for services.
2. It carries a flat rate of 1 per cent for goods and 6 per cent for services.
3. A taxpayer under the scheme can claim input tax credit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is correct: the limit is Rs 1.5 crore (goods) and Rs 50 lakh (services). Statement 2 is correct: flat 1% for goods and 6% for services. Statement 3 is wrong: composition taxpayers cannot claim ITC or collect tax separately. Hence 1 and 2 only.
97.tq: Composition = small turnover, flat low rate, no ITC.

97.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the GST rate structure from 22 September 2025?
o: 0%, 5% as merit rate, 18% as standard rate and 40% as demerit rate
97.x: GST 2.0 rationalised the principal slabs into 0%, 5%, 18% and 40%, with 5% as the merit rate, 18% as the standard rate and 40% as the demerit rate.
97.tq: Compare the post-rationalisation labels and rates as a complete structure.
xs: From **22 Sep 2025** slabs are **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)** — option **(3)**.
**5, 12, 18, 28%** was the pre-2.0 structure; the **12%** slab no longer exists.
xa: Old **12%** slab: ~**99%** of items moved to **5%**.
Approved at the **56th Council** (3-4 Sep 2025).

97.s: The GST rate applicable to rough diamonds and gold, silver and jewellery under the special-rate structure is, respectively:
97.x: Rough diamonds attract a special rate of 0.25%, while gold, silver and jewellery attract 3%.
97.tq: Read paired numerical rates in the order in which the commodities are given.
xs: Special rates: **0.25%** on **rough diamonds**, **3%** on **gold/silver/jewellery** — option **(4)**.
Option (2) reverses the two rates.
xa: Main slabs: **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)**.
**Tractors 12% → 5%**.
**Small cars, bikes ≤350cc, ACs 28% → 18%**.

97.s:
Consider the following statements about GST 2.0 rate rationalisation (from 22 September 2025):
1. About 99% of items in the old 12% slab moved to the 5% slab.
2. About 90% of items in the old 28% slab moved to the 40% slab.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is correct: ~99% of old 12% items moved to 5%. Statement 2 is wrong: ~90% of old 28% items moved to 18%; only the rest went to 40%. So A; B and C include the wrong statement 2, D rejects the correct statement 1.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 correct: ~**99%** of old **12%** items moved to **5%**.
Statement 2 wrong: ~**90%** of old **28%** items moved to **18%**; only the rest went to **40%**.
xa: GST 2.0 is also called the **NextGen GST reforms**; effective **22 Sep 2025**.

97.s: The Economic Survey 2025–26 described GST 2.0 as the:
97.x: GST 2.0 was described as the third pillar of tax reform, after the 2019 corporate tax cut and the 2025 personal income-tax reform.
97.tq: Use the sequence of reforms rather than identifying GST only by its tax rates.
xs: **ES 2025-26** called **GST 2.0** the **third pillar of tax reform** — option **(3)**.
It follows the **2019 corporate tax cut** (first) and the **April 2025 personal income tax reform** (second).
xa: The Survey stressed "**no net tax hike**".
It also said rate-cut **volume effects may offset revenue loss**.
GST 2.0 took effect on **22 Sep 2025**.

97.s: What is identified as the biggest drawback of the multiple-rate structure under GST?
o: Delay in settlement of IGST between the Union and the States
Dependence of States on Finance Commission devolution
Misclassification of goods and services and classification disputes
Complete exclusion of petroleum products from taxation
97.x: The multiple-rate structure creates difficulties in classifying goods and services, resulting in frequent classification disputes.
97.tq: Directly identify the specific weakness associated with a tax structure.
xs: The biggest drawback of multiple rates is **misclassification of goods and services** and **classification disputes** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2017).
Near-identical products land in **different slabs** → disputes and **litigation**.
xa: The **four-slab** structure was meant to be **transitional**.
Pending reform (Aug 2025): "**standardise product classification**".
GST 2.0 cut the main slabs to **5%** and **18%** + **40%**.

97.s: The four-slab structure of GST was originally intended to be:
o: A permanent arrangement for all goods and services
A mechanism for distributing IGST among States
A structure applicable only to petroleum products
97.x: The four-slab GST structure was conceived as a transitional arrangement rather than a permanent structure.
97.tq: Test the intended character of a policy arrangement rather than its numerical details.
xs: The four-slab structure was meant to be **transitional**, ahead of simplification — option **(4)**.
It had slabs **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%** (2017) + exempt goods.
xa: GST 2.0 replaced it with **0, 5, 18, 40%** from **22 Sep 2025**.
Multiple rates caused **misclassification** and **classification disputes**.
Further ask: **GST 3.0** simplification (CII AP, **1 Feb 2026**).

97.s:
Consider the following statements regarding classification disputes under a multi-rate GST structure:
1. Near-identical products may be placed in different tax slabs.
2. Such classification differences can invite litigation.
3. Standardising product classification has been identified as a pending reform.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
97.x: All three statements are correct. Differing classification of similar products creates disputes and litigation, while standardisation of product classification remains a reform issue.
97.tq: Check whether all statements describe linked consequences and reforms.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **near-identical products** sat in **different slabs**.
Statement 2: this caused **disputes + litigation**.
Statement 3: "**standardise product classification**" is a pending reform (Aug 2025).
xa: Misclassification is the **biggest drawback** of multiple rates (APPSC-G1 2017).
Sector pleas: notebook makers hit by the **Sep 2025** rate revision (9 Sep 2026).

97.s: Which of the following correctly represents the original GST rate structure introduced in 2017, apart from exempt goods and compensation cess?
97.x: The original GST structure contained slabs of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, along with exempt goods and compensation cess over 28% for specified goods.
97.tq: Recall the complete original slab sequence.
xs: The **2017** structure had slabs of **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%** + exempt goods — option **(4)**.
A **compensation cess** sat over **28%** on luxury/sin goods.
xa: GST 2.0: **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)**.
Special rates: **0.25%** rough diamonds; **3%** gold/silver/jewellery.

97.s: The GST 2.0 reforms were approved at which GST Council meeting and became effective from which date?
97.x: The GST 2.0 reforms were approved at the 56th GST Council meeting held on 3–4 September 2025 and became effective on 22 September 2025.
97.tq: Pair the reform package with both its approving meeting and effective date.
xs: GST 2.0 was approved at the **56th GST Council meeting** (3-4 Sep 2025), effective **22 September 2025** — option **(4)**.
The **57th** meeting is fixed for **12 Sep 2026**, a year later.
xa: Also called the **NextGen GST reforms**.
Inverted-duty refunds were flagged for the **57th** meeting.
**ES 2025-26**: GST 2.0 = **third pillar of tax reform**.

97.s: Which of the following continue to remain outside the GST framework?
97.x: Petroleum and electricity remain outside the GST framework.
97.tq: Use confusable sector exclusions to distinguish items inside and outside a tax regime.
xs: **Petroleum and electricity** are still **outside GST** — option **(1)**.
Petroleum (**crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas, ATF**) is within GST law but taxed only from a date the **GST Council recommends** (**Art. 279A(5)**).
xa: Other asks: **GST 3.0** simplification (CII AP, **1 Feb 2026**).
Criticism: **vertical fiscal imbalance** and loss of **state tax autonomy**.
Cesses remain **outside the divisible pool**.

97.s: Which practice is characteristic of the ITC fraud involving bogus entities?
o: Paying output tax twice on genuine transactions
Issuing invoices without actual supply of goods or services
Using only government invoices for exports
Claiming refunds on petroleum products outside GST
97.x: Bogus entities issue invoices without any corresponding supply in order to fraudulently claim input tax credit.
97.tq: Identify the fraudulent mechanism from a practical transaction scenario.
xs: In **ITC fraud**, bogus entities **issue invoices without actual supply** — option **(2)**.
An **AP-Telangana-Karnataka** network used **fake registrations + scrap bills** to claim ITC (**3 Jan 2026**).
xa: Countered by **e-invoicing**, **UPI/Aadhaar tracking** and **AI scrutiny**.
AP's **Legal-AI assistant** was trained on ~**22,000 judgments**.
**E-way bills** add to AI-based scrutiny against fake invoicing.

97.s:
Assertion (A): An Inverted Duty Structure can block working capital of businesses.
Reason (R): Input tax credit accumulates when the tax paid on inputs is higher than the tax payable on output.

Choose the correct answer.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
97.x: Both statements are true, and the accumulation of input tax credit caused by higher input taxation directly explains the blockage of working capital.
97.tq: Test the cause-and-effect relationship between the two statements.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
When **input tax > output tax**, ITC **accumulates**, and that **blocks working capital**.
xa: The law allows **refund of unutilised ITC** in such cases.
Domestic refunds rose **72.6%** in **Aug 2026** due to inverted duties.
"IDS definition" is a flagged exam angle for this topic.

97.s:
Consider the following statements about the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT):
1. It was created through the Finance Act, 2024.
2. Its Principal Bench is located in Mumbai.
3. It was formally launched in September 2025 and hearings began in December 2025.
4. Appeals before it are to be filed online within six months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is correct: GSTAT was created via the Finance Act 2024. Statement 2 is wrong: the Principal Bench is at New Delhi. Statement 3 is correct: launched Sep 2025, hearings from Dec 2025. Statement 4 is wrong: appeals are to be filed online within three months. Hence only 1 and 3 (A); B, C and D each include a wrong statement.
97.tq: Remember GSTAT: Finance Act 2024, New Delhi Principal Bench, launch Sep 2025 / hearings Dec 2025, appeal window 3 months.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: GSTAT was created via the **Finance Act 2024**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Principal Bench** is at **New Delhi**.
Statement 3 correct: **formally launched Sep 2025**, **hearings from Dec 2025**; Statement 4 wrong: appeals online **within 3 months**.
xa: GSTAT **Procedure Rules 2025**.
First President = **former Chief Justice of Jharkhand HC**.

97.s: As of mid-2025, which problem was associated with the GST Appellate Tribunal?
o: State benches had exclusive jurisdiction over direct taxes
The tribunal had replaced the Supreme Court as the final court of appeal
Only the New Delhi Principal Bench had been abolished
Functional benches were absent in many States despite notification
97.x: Although GSTAT had been notified, functional benches were absent in many States as of mid-2025, causing appeals to accumulate in High Courts.
97.tq: Distinguish notification or legal creation from actual operationalisation.
xs: Mid-2025: GSTAT was **notified**, but **functional benches were absent in many States** — option **(4)**.
As a result, appeals **piled up in High Courts** (Jul **2025**).
xa: It was **formally launched Sep 2025**, with **hearings from Dec 2025**.
Created via **Finance Act 2024**; **Procedure Rules 2025**.
Appeals are to be filed **online within 3 months**.

97.s: One major fiscal consequence for States of surrendering independent indirect-tax powers under GST has been:
o: Greater dependence on transfers because of weak own revenues
Automatic equalisation of revenues among all States
Complete elimination of State taxation powers
97.x: The surrender of independent indirect-tax powers, combined with weak own revenues, has increased States’ dependence on transfers.
97.tq: Link the loss of fiscal autonomy with the resulting dependence on transfers.
xs: Surrendering indirect-tax powers left States with **weak own revenues** and **greater dependence on transfers** — option **(1)**.
Taxes given up: **VAT, entry tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax, octroi**.
FC devolution was not abolished — **unorganised-sector States depend on FC devolution**.
xa: Only **16 States/UTs** had post-settlement GST growth above the national average.
Compensation: **5 years** at **14%** growth, under the **GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017**.
Criticism: **vertical fiscal imbalance**.

97.s: The destination principle of GST generally favours:
o: States with the highest rates of State excise duty
Producing States because tax is collected at the point of manufacture
Consuming States because taxation follows the place of consumption
97.x: GST follows the destination principle, under which consuming States benefit because revenue is associated with the place of consumption.
97.tq: Distinguish destination-based taxation from origin-based taxation.
xs: The destination principle favours **consuming States**, since taxation follows the **place of consumption** — option **(3)**.
GST revenue goes to the State where goods/services are **consumed, not produced** — so producing States do not gain (option 2).
xa: **IGST** on inter-State supply (**Art. 269A**): levied by the Centre, apportioned; the **destination State** gets the State share.
Manufacturing States (**Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka**) feared loss.
AP, a **consuming State**, benefits via **IGST settlement**.

97.s: Andhra Pradesh, being a consuming State, benefits from GST primarily through:
o: State excise on petroleum under GST
Abolition of its own tax revenue
97.x: As a consuming State, Andhra Pradesh benefits from the destination principle through IGST settlement.
97.tq: Apply the destination principle to the fiscal position of a particular State.
xs: AP, a **consuming State**, benefits mainly through **IGST settlement** — option **(2)**.
Under the destination principle, the **destination State** receives the State share of IGST.
**Petroleum** is still outside GST, so option (3) is impossible.
xa: AP's **Net GST** = **SGST + IGST settlement share**.
GST is AP's largest own-tax source: **38%** = **Rs 36,296 crore** (2024-25 RE).
Up to **Aug 2026**, AP net GST was **₹16,452.62 cr**.

97.s: With respect to an inter-State supply under GST, which of the following is correct?
o: IGST is levied by the Centre and apportioned, with the destination State receiving the State share
CGST and SGST are both collected exclusively by the producing State
IGST is levied by the destination State and transferred to the Centre
SGST is levied and retained entirely by the producing State
97.x: IGST on inter-State supplies is levied by the Centre and apportioned. The destination State receives the State share under the destination-based system.
97.tq: Identify the correct authority and destination for inter-State tax revenue.
xs: On inter-State supply, **IGST** is **levied by the Centre and apportioned**, with the **destination State** receiving the State share — option **(1)**.
IGST is not levied by a State; **CGST/SGST** apply to intra-State supply, and revenue does not stay with the producing State.
xa: IGST rests on **Art. 269A**.
GST is a **destination-based consumption tax**.
The fear of producing States was a key reason for the **5-year compensation guarantee**.

97.s: Which group of States mainly represents manufacturing or producing States that feared revenue loss under the destination-based GST system?
o: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka
97.x: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka were identified as manufacturing States that feared losses because GST revenue follows consumption rather than production. This concern contributed to the five-year compensation guarantee.
97.tq: Match the policy effect with the group of affected producing States.
xs: **Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka** — manufacturing States — feared loss — option **(1)**.
Under the destination principle, revenue goes to the **consuming** State, not the producing one.
xa: This fear was a key reason for the **5-year compensation guarantee**.
Today **manufacturing States gain** from concentrated buoyancy; **unorganised-sector States** depend on FC devolution.
AP, a **consuming State**, benefits via IGST settlement.

97.s: Under the GST compensation arrangement, States were guaranteed compensation for which period and at what annual growth rate over the 2015–16 base?
97.x: States were guaranteed compensation for five years, from July 2017 to June 2022, at an assured annual growth rate of 14% over the 2015–16 base.
97.tq: Link the compensation period with its guaranteed growth rate and base year.
xs: Compensation was guaranteed for **5 years (July 2017 - June 2022)** at **14%** annual growth over the **2015-16** base — option **(4)**.
The law: **GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017**.
xa: The cess continued to **March 2026** to repay **COVID back-to-back loans**.
Cess **scrapped 22 September 2025** except **tobacco products**.
Unused balance: **50%** Centre, **50%** States (by **SGST** revenue).

97.s: The GST compensation cess was continued after the compensation period primarily to:
o: Repay loans taken to pay compensation during the COVID-19 period
97.x: After the compensation period, the cess was continued to repay loans taken for paying GST compensation during the COVID-19 period.
97.tq: Identify the stated purpose behind continuation of a fiscal instrument.
xs: The cess was continued to **repay COVID back-to-back loans** taken to pay compensation — option **(2)**.
It ran to **March 2026** for that purpose, long after compensation ended in **June 2022**.
xa: Scrapped **22 September 2025** except **tobacco products**.
The **tobacco cess** continues until cess-account **loan obligations are discharged**.
Compensation period: **5 years** at **14%** growth.

97.s: With effect from 22 September 2025, the GST compensation cess was scrapped for all goods except:
97.x: The compensation cess was scrapped on 22 September 2025 except for tobacco products, on which it continues until cess-account loan obligations are discharged.
97.tq: Test the exception to a general abolition of the cess.
xs: From **22 September 2025**, the cess was scrapped for all goods except **tobacco products** — option **(3)**.
The tobacco cess continues until **cess-account loan obligations** are discharged.
**Online gaming** and luxury cars now fall in the **40%** demerit slab; aerated drinks lost the cess.
xa: Original cess goods: **luxury cars, aerated drinks, pan masala, tobacco**.
GST 2.0 took effect on the same date, **22 September 2025**.
Unused balance: **50% to Centre**, **50% to States**.

97.s: How is the unused balance of the GST compensation cess to be shared?
o: Entirely to the States in proportion to their population
50% to the Centre and 50% to the States in proportion to their SGST revenue
As per the Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula
97.x: The unused balance goes 50% to the Centre and 50% to the States, with the States' half shared in proportion to their SGST revenue. It does not all go to the Centre (A), it is not shared by population (B), and the Finance Commission formula (D) does not apply because cess is outside the divisible pool.
97.tq: Unused compensation cess: 50:50, States' half by SGST share.
xs: The unused cess balance goes **50% to the Centre** and **50% to the States**, in proportion to **SGST revenue** — option **(3)**.
It is not all to the Centre, not by population, and not by the FC formula — cesses sit **outside the divisible pool**.
xa: Cess **scrapped 22 September 2025** except tobacco.
Compensation: **July 2017 - June 2022** at **14%** growth.
Law: **GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017**.

97.s: For Andhra Pradesh, “Net GST” is defined as:
o: Gross GST collections minus customs revenue
SGST plus the State’s share of IGST settlement
SGST minus the State’s share of IGST settlement
97.x: Andhra Pradesh’s Net GST consists of SGST plus its share received through IGST settlement.
97.tq: Discriminate between a State’s own GST component and its settled IGST share.
xs: AP's **Net GST** = **SGST + the State's share of IGST settlement** — option **(3)**.
IGST settlement is **added**, not subtracted, and **State Excise** is outside GST.
xa: Up to **Aug 2026**: net GST **₹16,452.62 cr**; commercial taxes **₹25,449.80 cr** (+18.05%).
AP benefits as a **consuming State** via IGST settlement.

97.s: According to the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 (RE), which pair correctly gives the two largest contributors to Andhra Pradesh's own tax revenue?
o: GST (38%) first and State Excise (22%) second
State Excise (38%) first and GST (22%) second
GST (48%) first and stamp duty (22%) second
Motor vehicle tax (38%) first and GST (22%) second
97.x: GST is the largest contributor at 38% (Rs 36,296 crore) and State Excise is second at 22% (Rs 21,300 crore). B swaps them, C confuses 48% (own tax revenue as a share of revenue receipts) with GST's share, and D names a minor tax.
97.tq: AP: GST 38% > Excise 22%; own tax = ~48% of revenue receipts.
xs: AP's top two own-tax sources: **GST (38%)** first and **State Excise (22%)** second — option **(1)**.
**GST = Rs 36,296 crore**; **State Excise = Rs 21,300 crore** (APSES 2024-25 RE).
**48%** is own tax revenue's share of revenue receipts, not GST's share (option 3).
xa: AP own tax revenue: **Rs 94,967 crore**, ~**48%** of revenue receipts of **Rs 1,91,142 crore**.
GST's share was **36%** in **2023-24 RE**.
AP **Net GST** = **SGST + IGST settlement share**.

97.s:
Consider the following statements about the Supreme Court judgment in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022):
1. It held that GST Council recommendations are binding on Parliament and State legislatures.
2. It described India as a 'flexible federation' with simultaneous legislative power under Article 246A.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
97.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Court held Council recommendations persuasive, not binding. Statement 2 is correct: India was called a flexible federation with simultaneous power under Art. 246A. So B; A and C include the wrong statement 1, and D rejects the correct statement 2.
97.tq: Mohit Minerals = recommendations persuasive, not binding; Art. 246A simultaneous power.
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — option **(2) 2 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: **Mohit Minerals (2022)** held Council recommendations **persuasive, not binding**.
Statement 2 correct: India is a "**flexible federation**" with **simultaneous legislative power** under **Art. 246A**.
xa: Other landmark rulings: **Safari Retreats**, **VKC Footsteps** (Jul **2025**).
Council voting: Centre **1/3**, States **2/3**; decisions need **3/4**.

97.s: Why does the Centre have an effective veto in the GST Council?
o: Because the Centre’s one-third vote can prevent a three-fourths majority
Because the Centre has two-thirds of the weighted vote
Because State representatives cannot vote on tax matters
Because the Centre alone nominates all State members
97.x: Since three-fourths weighted support is required and the Centre holds one-third of the vote, the Centre can block a proposal without its support.
97.tq: Infer institutional power from the voting weights and decision threshold.
xs: The **Centre's one-third vote** can **prevent a three-fourths majority** — option **(1)**.
With **2/3** weight, the States alone fall short of **3/4**, so no decision passes without the Centre.
The Centre has **1/3**, not 2/3, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: The weights are of **votes present**.
Debate: **loss of state tax autonomy** and **vertical fiscal imbalance**.

97.s: Which of the following groups of petroleum products is covered by the GST law but remains outside GST taxation until a date recommended by the GST Council?
o: Crude oil, petrol, diesel, natural gas and ATF
Natural gas, electricity, alcohol, tobacco and ATF
Coal, electricity, iron ore, cement and steel
Gold, silver, diamonds, petrol and coal
97.x: Crude oil, petrol, high-speed diesel, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel are within the GST law but are taxed outside GST until the Council recommends a date under Article 279A(5).
97.tq: Test the complete list and distinguish legal inclusion from present tax treatment.
xs: **Crude, petrol, diesel (HSD), natural gas, ATF** are within GST law but taxed only from a date the **GST Council recommends** — option **(1)**.
The power is in **Art. 279A(5)**; until then they remain **outside GST**.
**Electricity**, **alcohol**, **coal** and **gold** are not part of this petroleum group.
xa: Coverage gap: **petroleum and electricity** still outside GST.
**Gold/silver/jewellery** are taxed at a special **3%**.

97.s: In May 2026, the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that where Central and State GST investigations overlap, the authorities must:
o: Abandon the investigation if the entity operates in more than one State
Decide inter se which authority will proceed
Transfer every case automatically to the Union Government
Both proceed simultaneously against the same entity
97.x: The Court held that Central and State GST authorities must decide inter se who will proceed against a common entity, thereby preventing dual action.
97.tq: Identify the precise institutional solution to overlapping jurisdiction.
xs: The **AP High Court** (May **2026**) held that Central and State GST authorities must **decide inter se** who proceeds — option **(2)**.
The aim is to **prevent dual action** against one entity — so option (4) is the very thing ruled out.
xa: **Mohit Minerals (2022)**: Council recommendations **persuasive, not binding**.
Fake invoicing is countered by **e-invoicing** + AI-based scrutiny with e-way bills.

97.s: Which of the following is a criticism of cesses in the GST framework?
o: They can be imposed only by State legislatures
They are always included in the divisible pool for distribution to States
They remain outside the divisible pool, contributing to concerns over State fiscal autonomy
97.x: Cesses outside the divisible pool reduce the share available for devolution and are therefore linked with concerns about States’ fiscal autonomy and vertical fiscal imbalance.
97.tq: Connect the fiscal instrument with its federal consequence.
xs: **Cesses remain outside the divisible pool**, feeding concerns over **State fiscal autonomy** — option **(3)**.
They are not in the divisible pool (option 2) and do not remove **vertical fiscal imbalance** (option 4).
xa: Other criticism: **loss of state tax autonomy**; vertical fiscal imbalance.
The unused compensation cess balance is split **50:50** between Centre and States.
States' **weak own revenues** mean **dependence on transfers**.

97.s: GST was introduced in India with effect from 1 July 2017 through which constitutional framework?
o: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 and Articles 246A, 269A and 279A
The 86th Amendment Act and Articles 243G, 243H and 243I
The 73rd Amendment Act and Articles 280, 281 and 282
The 42nd Amendment Act and Articles 301, 302 and 303
97.x: GST came into force on 1 July 2017 under the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, with Articles 246A, 269A and 279A forming its key constitutional basis.
97.tq: Match the reform with its effective date, amendment and constitutional Articles.
xs: GST came in from **1 July 2017** under the **101st Amendment Act, 2016**, with **Arts. 246A, 269A and 279A** — option **(1)**.
**246A** = GST law-making power; **269A** = inter-State supply/IGST; **279A** = GST Council.
xa: GST is the **biggest indirect tax reform since Independence**.
Taxpayer base: **66.5 lakh (2017) → 1.51 crore (2025)**.
FY 2017-18 average: **₹82,000 cr/month**.

98.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 265 — Taxes may be imposed without statutory authority in emergencies
Article 271 — Surcharge on specified Union taxes for the Union
Article 276 — Finance Commission and its recommendations
98.x: Article 271 deals with surcharges on taxes referred to in Articles 269 and 270, and the proceeds are wholly for the Union. Article 265 requires authority of law for taxation, Article 276 concerns professional taxes, and Article 293 concerns State borrowing.
98.tq: Start from the sure article-function pair and eliminate reversals of nearby article numbers.
xs: **Article 271** — **surcharge** on Art. 269/270 taxes, **wholly for the Union** — is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Art. 265** says **no tax except by authority of law** — the opposite of option (1).
**Art. 276** is the **professions tax**; the FC is **Art. 280/281**; **Art. 293** is borrowing **by States**, not the Union.
xa: **Art. 292** = borrowing by the **Union**.
**Art. 269A** = GST on inter-State trade.
⚠ **271** surcharge = wholly Union; surcharges and cesses stay **outside the Art. 270 divisible pool**.

98.s: Which Article is associated with grants in lieu of export duty on jute and jute products to Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha?
98.x: Article 273 provided grants in lieu of export duty on jute and jute products to Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha.
98.tq: Discriminate between the two nearby grant provisions by the specific beneficiary States and purpose.
xs: **Article 273** gives grants **in lieu of jute export duty** to **Assam, Bihar, WB, Odisha** — option **(4)**.
**Art. 275** = statutory FC grants; **Art. 282** = discretionary grants; **Art. 293** = State borrowing.
xa: **Art. 275** grants go to States in need, **ST welfare** and **Scheduled Areas**.
**Art. 276**: tax on professions, trades, callings, ceiling **₹2,500**.
**Art. 280/281**: Finance Commission / its recommendations laid before Parliament.

98.s: The constitutional ceiling on taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments under Article 276 is:
98.x: Article 276 concerns taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments, subject to a ceiling of ₹2,500.
98.tq: Use the exact statutory ceiling and distinguish it from nearby round-value distractors.
xs: The ceiling on taxes on **professions, trades, callings** under **Art. 276** is **₹2,500** — option **(3)**.
The Constitution itself fixes this cap in **Art. 276**; **₹1,000**, **₹2,000** and **₹5,000** are not the ceiling the notes give.
xa: **Art. 265**: no tax except by authority of law.
**Art. 271**: surcharge on Art. 269/270 taxes, wholly for the Union.
**Art. 273**: grants in lieu of **jute export duty**.

98.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 292 and 293?
o: Article 292 concerns grants and Article 293 concerns taxation
Article 292 concerns Union borrowing, whereas Article 293 concerns State borrowing
Article 292 concerns State borrowing, whereas Article 293 concerns Union borrowing
Both Articles concern borrowing by local bodies
98.x: Article 292 deals with borrowing by the Union, while Article 293 deals with borrowing by the States.
98.tq: Discriminate between adjacent article numbers by assigning the Union provision first and the State provision second.
xs: **Art. 292** = **borrowing by the Union**; **Art. 293** = **borrowing by States** — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses them; neither Article deals with grants, taxation or local bodies.
xa: AP raises **SDLs via RBI**.
**Art. 280/281**: Finance Commission and its recommendations.
**Art. 282**: discretionary grants for **any public purpose**.

98.s: What was the principal feature of the 'grand bargain' proposed by the 16th Finance Commission in relation to cesses?
o: All cesses would be transferred directly to local bodies
States would accept a smaller share of a larger pool if most cesses were merged into regular taxes
States would receive a larger share of a smaller pool without any change in cesses
States would impose all Union cesses within their territories
98.x: The proposal envisaged States taking a smaller share of a larger pool if the Centre merged most cesses into regular taxes.
98.tq: Test both linked conditions of a policy proposal rather than only its title.
xs: The **16th FC "grand bargain"** (para **7.67**): **States take a smaller share of a larger pool** if the Centre **merges most cesses into regular taxes** — option **(2)**.
The 16th FC made **no recommendation to curb/cap cesses** directly (**2 Mar 2026**).
xa: Cesses + surcharges per ₹100 of Central tax: **₹13.5** (2021-22, decade high) → **₹11** (2025-26 est.).
Effective devolution is only ~**30-32%** of gross tax revenue.
Centre's defence: it spent **105%** of cess collections on States over six years.

98.s: The amount of cesses and surcharges per ₹100 of Central tax was at a decade high in which year and at what level?
98.x: Cesses and surcharges amounted to ₹13.5 per ₹100 of Central tax in 2021–22, described as a decade high. The estimate for 2025–26 was ₹11.
98.tq: Keep the year-value pair intact and avoid swapping the historical figure with the estimate.
xs: Cesses + surcharges hit a **decade high** of **₹13.5** per ₹100 of Central tax in **2021-22** — option **(3)**.
**₹11** is the **2025-26 estimate**, not the peak.
xa: Effect: effective devolution only ~**30-32%** of gross tax revenue.
States' share in total tax receipts ~**34%** vs **41%** headline.
They are not shared because they sit outside the **Art. 270** divisible pool.

98.s: What was the approximate effective devolution to the States as a percentage of gross tax revenue, despite the headline 41% share of the divisible pool?

xa: States' share in **total tax receipts** is only ~**34%** (2 Feb 2026).

98.s: Which one of the following statements about the debate on cesses is correct?

98.tq: Separate the recommendation actually made from the recommendation attributed to another commission.
xs: The **16th FC** made **no recommendation on capping cesses**, while the **5% cap** is attributed to the **Punchhi Commission** — option **(3)**.

Centre's defence: **105%** of cess collections spent on States.

98.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Article 275 grants from Article 282 grants?

Article 275 grants are recommended by the Finance Commission, whereas Article 282 grants are discretionary grants for any public purpose

98.x: Article 275 provides statutory grants-in-aid recommended by the Finance Commission. Article 282 permits discretionary grants by the Union or State executive for any public purpose.

xs: **Art. 275** grants are **recommended by the Finance Commission**; **Art. 282** grants are **discretionary**, for **any public purpose** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses statutory and discretionary.
Only **Art. 275** grants are **charged on the CFI**; Art. 282 grants are **voted** — so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Art. 275 serves **States in need**, **ST welfare**, **Scheduled Areas**.
Art. 282 grants are used for **CSS** and were once the **larger part** of Central grants.
Criticism: Art. 282 grants are seen as **politically motivated**, **bypassing the FC**.

Discretionary grants once formed the **larger part** of Central grants.

98.s:

xs: All four aggravate vertical fiscal imbalance — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.

xa: Root cause: the **Union holds larger, more buoyant tax bases** (corporate tax, income tax, most of GST).

98.s: The basic cause of vertical fiscal imbalance in India is that:
o: States have larger and more buoyant tax bases than the Union
The Union holds the larger and more buoyant tax bases such as corporation tax, income tax and most of GST
Local bodies collect most of the tax revenue in the country
The Finance Commission fixes the expenditure of States
98.x: Vertical fiscal imbalance arises because the Union controls the larger, more buoyant tax bases (corporation tax, income tax, most of GST) while States carry heavy spending duties. A reverses the position, C is wrong because local bodies collect little, and the Finance Commission does not fix State expenditure (D).
98.tq: VFI = Union has the buoyant taxes, States have the spending duties.
xs: The **Union holds larger, more buoyant tax bases** — **corporate tax, income tax, most of GST** — option **(2)**.
This mismatch between **Union revenue** and **State spending** is vertical fiscal imbalance; option (1) reverses it.
xa: Aggravating factors: **cesses/surcharges**, **loss of indirect taxes to GST**, **CSS conditionalities**, **weak own revenue**.
Effective devolution only ~**30-32%** of gross tax revenue.
States' share in total tax receipts ~**34%**.

100.s: Which Article requires the President to lay the report of the Finance Commission before each House of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken?
100.x: Article 281 requires the President to lay the Finance Commission’s report before each House of Parliament together with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken.
100.tq: Distinguish the Article dealing with presentation of the report from the Article establishing the Commission and its functions.
xs: **Article 281** requires the President to lay the Finance Commission's report before **Parliament** with an action-taken memorandum — option **(3)** is correct.
**Article 280** is the provision under which the President **constitutes** the Commission, not the one on laying its report.
**Article 270** governs the **divisible pool** of shareable Union taxes; **Art. 243I** links the FC to State funds for **Panchayats**.
xa: The Finance Commission is a **quasi-judicial** body constituted **every 5 years** (5th year) or earlier.
Composition: **Chairman + 4 members**; qualifications under the **Finance Commission (Misc. Provisions) Act, 1951**.
Its recommendations are **advisory**, not binding on the government.

100.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Finance Commission:
1. Its recommendations are not binding on the Government.
2. Its recommendations cover cesses and surcharges as part of the divisible pool.
3. It may deal with matters referred to it by the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
100.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool covered by the Finance Commission’s tax-sharing recommendations.
100.tq: Locate the exception in the scope of tax devolution and separate it from the Commission’s advisory character.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: FC recommendations are **advisory** and **not binding** on the government.
Statement 2 is wrong: **cesses and surcharges** are **not covered** — they lie outside the divisible pool.
Statement 3 is correct: under **Art. 280(3)(d)** it handles any matter **referred by the President**.
xa: ⚠ GST revenue sharing is handled by the **GST Council**, not the Finance Commission.
Maintaining **income and expenditure accounts** of Centre and States is not its job (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
Example of a Presidential reference: **disaster-management financing** under the **Disaster Management Act, 2005**.

100.s: The Finance Commission’s function of recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State for supplementing the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities was added through the:
100.x: The relevant function was added by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, 1992, relating respectively to Panchayats and Municipalities.
100.tq: Associate the local-government finance function with the constitutional amendments that strengthened local self-government.
xs: The local-body function was added by the **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, 1992** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is **Art. 280(3)(bb) and (c)**: measures to augment a State's **Consolidated Fund** to support **Panchayats and Municipalities**.
It is linked to **Art. 243I** (Panchayats) and **Art. 243Y** (Municipalities).
xa: **Art. 280(3)(a)**: distribution of **net proceeds of shareable taxes**, vertical and horizontal.
**Art. 280(3)(b)**: principles for **grants-in-aid** (Art. 275) from the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
The **16th FC** gives only **local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) and **disaster** grants.

100.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Finance Commission:
1. It is a quasi-judicial body.
2. It is constituted by the President every fifth year or earlier.
3. Its recommendations are legally binding on the Union Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
100.x: The Finance Commission is quasi-judicial and is constituted every fifth year or earlier. Its recommendations are advisory rather than legally binding.
100.tq: Split the statements by distinguishing constitutional status from the binding nature of recommendations.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the FC is a **quasi-judicial** body under **Art. 280**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **President** constitutes it **every 5 years** (5th year) or earlier.
Statement 3 is wrong: its recommendations are **advisory**, not binding on the government.
xa: Report + action-taken memorandum laid before **Parliament** under **Art. 281**.
Composition: **Chairman + 4 members**; qualifications under the **Finance Commission (Misc. Provisions) Act, 1951**.
"The present Finance Commission" now means the **Sixteenth** (Chairman **Arvind Panagariya**).

100.s: Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Finance Commission under Article 280(3)?
o: Maintaining the income-expenditure accounts of the Union and State Governments
Recommending the distribution of the net proceeds of shareable taxes between the Centre and the States
Recommending principles governing grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India
Recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities
100.x: Maintaining government income-expenditure accounts is not a Finance Commission function. Its duties include tax devolution, grants-in-aid principles and augmentation of State funds for local bodies.
100.tq: Find the administrative accounting function that does not belong to the Finance Commission.
xs: **Maintaining the income-expenditure accounts** of the Union and States is NOT an FC duty — option **(1)** (the **APPSC-G2 2017** key).
Distribution of **net proceeds of shareable taxes** is **Art. 280(3)(a)**.
**Principles for grants-in-aid** from the **Consolidated Fund of India** is **Art. 280(3)(b)**.
Augmenting a State's **Consolidated Fund** for **Panchayats and Municipalities** is **Art. 280(3)(bb), (c)**.
xa: Also outside the FC: **cesses/surcharges**, **GST** revenue sharing (**GST Council**) and plan/discretionary grants.
**Art. 280(3)(d)**: any matter **referred by the President**.
Exam angle: "which is NOT a function" questions are a favourite on this topic.

100.s: Which institution primarily deals with the sharing of GST revenue?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
100.x: GST revenue-sharing recommendations are dealt with through the GST Council, not as a function of the Finance Commission.
100.tq: Use institutional discrimination to separate closely related fiscal bodies.
xs: **GST** revenue sharing is dealt with by the **GST Council** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Finance Commission** does **not** cover GST revenue sharing; it recommends sharing of the **divisible pool** and **grants-in-aid**.
The **CAG** figures only as certifier: the 16th FC recommends annual **CAG-certified** disclosure of net tax proceeds.
xa: The divisible pool includes **CGST** and the **Centre's IGST share** under **Art. 270**.
The FC also does not cover **cesses/surcharges** or plan/discretionary grants.
FC recommendations are **advisory**, not binding.

100.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Article 280(3)?
o: Clause (a) — maintenance of income and expenditure accounts
Clause (b) — principles governing grants-in-aid under Article 275
Clause (d) — conduct of elections to local bodies
100.x: Article 280(3)(b) concerns the principles governing grants-in-aid under Article 275. Clause (d) concerns any other matter referred to the Commission by the President.
100.tq: Use the article-clause-function pairing and reject unrelated constitutional functions.
xs: **Clause (b)** — principles governing **grants-in-aid under Article 275** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Clause (a)** is distribution of **net proceeds of shareable taxes**, not maintaining accounts (which is **not its job**).
**Clause (c)** concerns augmenting State funds for **Panchayats and Municipalities**, not Governors.
**Clause (d)** is any matter **referred by the President**, not local-body elections.
xa: Clauses **(bb), (c)** were added by the **73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992**.
Art. 275 grants are paid from the **Consolidated Fund of India** and are **charged** on it.
Example under clause (d): **disaster-management financing** (**Disaster Management Act, 2005**).

100.s: Which of the following correctly shows the States’ share of central taxes recommended by the 10th to 13th Finance Commissions?

**12th (C. Rangarajan)** 30.5%; **13th (Vijay Kelkar)** 32%.

Consider the following statements about the Tenth Finance Commission's devolution:

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Statement 2 is correct: the 80th Amendment, 2000 gave effect to it. Statement 3 is wrong: the amendment operated from 1 April 1996 and made all central taxes shareable. Hence A (1 only) misses statement 2, C and D wrongly include statement 3; B is correct.

Statement 2 is correct: it was given effect by the **80th Amendment, 2000**.

100.s: The reduction in the States’ share from 42% under the 14th Finance Commission to 41% under the 15th Finance Commission was attributed to:
o: The abolition of the divisible pool
The introduction of the GDP criterion
Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory
100.x: The reduction was attributed to Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory.

xs: The cut from **42% to 41%** was due to **Jammu & Kashmir becoming a Union Territory** — option **(4)** is correct.
